16029-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Number forty-eight of The Great Round World, dated October 7, 1897, opens with peace news from the Near East. After a three-hour conference on September 18, ambassadors and Tewfik Pasha signed a treaty. The Sultan then accepted it. It ended the war between Greece and Turkey on terms set by Lord Salisbury and the Powers. Troops were to leave Thessaly within a month, while the Powers held Greek income until a war indemnity was paid.

The paper retells such diplomacy in short sentences for young readers, who could follow kings, sultans, and treaties without a textbook. Its mix of foreign news and plain explanation made world affairs feel near at hand. The number keeps a child's-eye record of peacemaking in 1897.
23627-messenger-no-48:
James Otis, author of Toby Tyler and The Boy Captain, wrote this eighteen ninety nine boys' book of Messenger Number Forty Eight, printed by Saalfield. Jet, whose full name is Jethro Lewis, opens the tale, answering questions on his name and age with a boy's plain honesty, and running messages through city streets.

Trouble, kidnappers, an engagement, a battle, a bold attempt, an arrest, a detective, a prisoner, close quarters, a snare, a capture, and a stern chase follow. Chapters on the Adirondacks, a small guide, a visit, and a final success also follow. Otis writes for boys who love action and pluck, with a messenger hero who earns his place by speed, sense, and nerve. Young readers will enjoy Jet's run from errand boy to hero.
25066-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
October 1844 brought volume 56, number 348 of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, issued in Edinburgh and London by William Blackwood and Sons. Like other numbers of the long-running Tory monthly, it mixes reviews, fiction, poetry, and topical essays in a single thick issue for general readers.

Its contents open with a memoir of a diplomatist drawn from family papers, followed by a second set of Goethe poems and ballads in translation. Other pieces cover a great drought, a tale called A Tender Conscience, Thierry's history of the Gauls, the closing part of The Witchfinder, a Louisiana courtship story, and Greece under Roman rule.
29187-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-1-j:
George R. Graham and Robert T. Conrad edited this January 1848 number of Graham's American Monthly Magazine of Literature and Art, published in Philadelphia. The magazine boasted leading contributors, from William Cullen Bryant and James Fenimore Cooper to Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Lydia Sigourney, with mezzotint and steel engravings and music.

This number opens with Theodore Fay's Lace and Diamonds, or Take Care What You Do. Other contents range across biography, battle history, and scenery, including a sketch of General William Butler and an account of the Battle of Fort Moultrie. Readers get a month of a leading American literary magazine, rich in names that still anchor the period.
29218-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-2-f:
Graham's Magazine for February 1848, volume 32, number 2, opens with R. Balmann's piece on Stoke Church and Park. Stoke, near Windsor, was the scene of Thomas Gray's Elegy and the residence of the Penns of Pennsylvania. A monument to Gray, erected in 1799, stands among the scenes his poem celebrated.

Balmann describes the manor, its park, and the churchyard where Gray lies, with Slough and Herschel's home nearby and Eton across the Thames. The issue continues the magazine's mix of travel, biography, and literature. Readers get a mid-century magazine number that pairs English scenery with American literary interests, in the illustrated style Graham's readers expected.
29236-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-3-m:
Graham's Magazine for March 1848, volume 32, number 3, opens with Frank Byrne's The Cruise of the Gentile. On the evening of March 25, 1839, the ship Gentile of Boston lies at anchor in the harbor of Valetta, Malta. She is a handsome craft of six or seven hundred tons, high out of the water in ballast trim. Byrne introduces ship and crew in turn, as a yarn about them unfolds.

Other contents include Alfred Street's White Creek and Thomas Buchanan Read's The Alchemist's Daughter, a dramatic sketch set in Ferrara. Readers get a month of Graham's magazine at its mid-century height, mixing sea yarns, poems, and drama for a literate American audience.
29239-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-4-a:
Graham's Magazine for April 1848, volume 32, number 4, opens with T. S. Arthur's Jacob Jones, or The Man Who Couldn't Get Along in the World. Jacob, a clerk earning five hundred dollars a year at twenty-two, saves nothing and owes his tailors fifty to one hundred dollars. His careful employer asks what he has laid by, and Jacob must admit the answer.

Other contents include Blanche Bennairde's The Darling, Henry Hirst's The Poet's Love, Anna Blackwell's Song of the Elves, and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's The Fire of Drift-Wood. Readers get a month of a leading American literary magazine, mixing moral tales, poems, and songs in the illustrated style of the 1840s.
29262-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-5-m:
Graham's Magazine for May 1848, volume 32, number 5, opens with G. G. Foster's Clara Harland, engraved expressly for the magazine. The narrator insists he is no visionary, yet his life has been a struggle between everyday care and shadowy phantoms that haunt him in city, hills, prairie, and sea. Men and women move mechanically around him while he floats along their current.

Other contents include Lyman Long's The Ancient and the Modern Muse, Jane Taylor Worthington's Theresa, or Genius and Womanhood, a tale of domestic life, and John Neal's prediction. Readers get a month of Graham's magazine mixing fiction, poetry, and domestic tales, with the engraved portraiture its readers prized.
29344-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-6-j:
Graham's Magazine for June 1848, volume 32, number 6, opens with Fayette Robinson's life of Captain Samuel Walker, with an engraving. Walker was born in Prince George's County, Maryland, in 1815, to a respectable family without fortune or influence to advance him. Thrown on the world young, dependent on his own exertions, he still attracted more attention than any man of his grade since the Mexican war began.

Other contents include Lamartine to Madame Jorelle, translated from the French, Caroline Butler's Phantoms All, a fantasy, and E. Curtiss Hine's Homeward Bound. Oliver Buckley's Poor Penn, a real reminiscence, and Lydia Jane Peirson's Enchanted Isle complete the number. Readers get a month of Graham's magazine, mixing biography, verse, and tale.
29741-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiii-no-1-:
Graham's American Monthly Magazine of Literature and Art reached Philadelphia readers in July 1848 as volume thirty-three, number one. G. R. Graham, J. R. Chandler, and J. B. Taylor edited it. Its pages were embellished with mezzotint and steel engravings and music, as the title page promises. The list of chief contributors reads like a roll of American letters.

William C. Bryant, J. Fenimore Cooper, Richard H. Dana, Henry W. Longfellow, and N. P. Willis stand beside Lydia H. Sigourney, Catharine M. Sedgwick, Frances S. Osgood, and Emma C. Embury. Tales, poems, and essays fill the volume, from a night on the ice to a legend of Clare. The issue is a rich sample of American magazine writing in 1848.
29959-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiii-no-2-:
Graham's Magazine, volume thirty-three, number two, is dated Philadelphia, August 1848. It opens with The Late Maria Brooks, by Rufus Wilmot Griswold, with a portrait. Griswold calls Brooks one of the first writers of her country, fit to rank with the most celebrated persons of her sex in any nation or age. A handwritten inscription from Maria Brooks fronts the issue.

Maria Gowen, afterward Mrs. Brooks, bore the title Maria del Occidente, conferred originally, Griswold believes, by the poet Southey. She came of a Welsh family settled in Charlestown, near Boston. Griswold sets her among a century of women writers: Agnesi, Dacier, and Chastelet on the continent, More, Burney, Barbauld, and Austen in Britain, and Sedgwick, Child, Beecher, Kirkland, and Fuller at home. Her name, he says, will shine with a clearer, steadier lustre than most.
30076-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiii-no-3-:
Graham's Magazine, volume thirty-three, number three, is dated Philadelphia, September 1848. Its leading tale is Angila Mervale, or Six Months Before Marriage, by F. E. F., author of Aaron's Rod and Telling Secrets. An engraving expressly for the magazine shows J. Addison's Angila Mervale. The tale opens in drawing-room talk between Augusta Lenox and Angila Mervale about a reported engagement.

They say Miss Morton is engaged to Robert Hazlewood, Augusta reports, and Angila asks how she can be. Hazlewood is ugly, Angila says, with a disagreeable red ugliness, not the plain black ugliness she would not mind. They say he is clever, Augusta adds, but Angila doubts it, calling him conceited and disagreeable. He was very attentive to Mary Morton last night, waltzing with her several times, and badly. Mary is too pretty for such an awkward, ugly man, and Angila hopes the report is only an on dit.
30116-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiii-no-4-:
Graham's Magazine, volume thirty-three, number four, is dated Philadelphia, October 1848. Its leading tale is The Unmarried Belle, by Enna Duval, with an engraving made expressly for the magazine. A Longfellow epigraph from Evangeline fronts it: talk not of wasted affection, for affection never was wasted. Till the heart, purified, strengthened, perfected, made godlike, and rendered more worthy of heaven, patience must complete its labor of love.

 Seen at the last concert, where music stirred her and her cheek was delicately flushed, lifting the brilliancy of her eyes, the belle is called perfectly beautiful by her mother. Her lips, just half parted, trembled with feeling. Dressing, for her, is an art and a mystery mastered well, while the other young ladies around her wear brilliant costume at its proudest.
31569-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiii-no-5-:
Graham's Magazine, volume thirty-three, number five, Philadelphia, November 1848, opens with The Bride of Fate, a tale founded upon events in the early history of Venice, by W. Gilmore Simms. Venice was glad that day, Simms writes, as the eve of the feast of the Purification arrived. Maidens whose names were written in the Book of Gold assembled with parents, friends, and lovers. The maidens traveled by gondola to San Pietro de Castella at Olivolo, where the Patriarch resided, on the city's edge.

Simms's Venetian tale gives the issue its center, with a beautiful, isolated church and a crowd of lovers as its stage. Readers of antebellum magazines will find a characteristic number, where American writers borrowed European romance for home readers.
32369-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiii-no-6-:
Graham's Magazine, volume thirty-three, number six, dated Philadelphia, December 1848, opens with Mildred Ward, or The Debut, by Mrs. Caroline H. Butler. Its first chapter introduces Archibald Dundass, a rich Jamaica planter, and his only child Helen, whose English mother died just as Helen entered her thirteenth year. Friends urge Dundass to send Helen to England for a finished education, a plea that pulls against a father's grief.

Helen, with dark blue eyes, golden hair, and her mother's smile and step, stands at the centre of a story about youth, loss, and society. As a magazine issue, the volume also carries the period's usual mix of tales, verse, and engravings, headed by a plate for The Debut. It offers a vivid sample of American periodical fiction in the late 1840s.
32966-revolution-and-counter-revolution-:
Karl Marx's Revolution and Counter-Revolution gathers in book form a set of articles on Germany in 1848 that had waited decades for collection. It was edited by Eleanor Marx Aveling and published in Chicago in 1912. The editor presents them as a companion to Marx's study of Louis Napoleon's coup, both works sharing a gift for grasping great events while they were still unfolding. The focus here is the German uprising and the forces that turned it back.

Marx traces parties, classes, and crowns through revolution and its defeat, arguing that each side's moves followed from its place in society rather than from chance. The prose is dense and polemical, but its argument is clear: a revolution fails not only by bad luck, but by the balance of power around it. Readers gain a first-hand Marxist reading of a turning year in Europe.
39676-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine was a famed Scots monthly of tale and thought. Issue 396 of volume 64 is dated October 1848. Its pages mix tale parts, wealth lore, and verse. The Caxtons, a tale in parts, leads this month's book. Mill's work on wealth laws gets a long look next.

Life in the Far West tells of the wild edge of America. A tale from Antwerp and a talk on novels fill the mid part. Revolt in Europe, Irish revolt, and English want share one grave piece. Byron's speech to the ocean closes the list in verse. Town readers got a rich month from one wrap.
40082-the-thirty-years-war-1618-1648:
The Thirty Years' War, 1618-1648 is a short history by Samuel Rawson Gardiner. It belongs to the Epochs of History series, edited by Edward Morris. Companion volumes treat the Crusades and the Protestant Revolution. Gardiner was the leading English historian of the seventeenth century.

His book tells how a Bohemian revolt grew into a general European war. Armies of the empire, Sweden, France, and Spain fought across Germany for thirty years. The war laid waste whole regions and reshaped the map of Europe. The peace of 1648 closes the story. Gardiner writes with the clearness that made his Epochs volumes school and college standards.
40090-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine number 391, for May 1848, makes up part of the sixty third volume of the famed Scottish monthly. The number opens with part two of The Caxtons, a serial novel then running in its pages. A piece on education in Wales follows, then The Silver Cross and verses named Heigh Ho and The Last Walk.

The eyes of the number are on Europe in upheaval: Republican Paris in March and April 1848, and a survey of the revolutions in Europe, fill its middle. A Scottish kidnapping trial, the case of Peter Williamson, gives the home news its weight. The Spaniard in Sicily and a comic piece on man as a featherless biped round it out.
40128-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwoods Edinburgh Magazine, volume sixty-four, is the August print of that famed sheet for eighteen forty-eight. Its list holds past ten heads. A tale of life in the far west runs in its third part past a famed tale in parts of a house saga. Heads on art, on a far land of the south, and on tours of the day fill the list.

The west tale tells of a hunt band past a stream with black hills past their left hand. Small feeds swell the fork as they seek the sign of the dam beast in vain. The spring hunt has all but wiped the beast from that tract, it seems. Past a next stream they cross a range to a bow stream and find a few lodges. An old hunt man sets his first trap there.
45072-how-we-robbed-mexico-in-1848:
Robert H Howe wrote How We Robbed Mexico in eighteen forty eight, a pamphlet dated nineteen sixteen. One page of our own history is passed over lightly by historians, Howe opens, and America can point to it only with shame. He means the Mexican War. When its causes and results are studied, Mexicans hate of us grows plain, he holds.

Before the war the nation split over chattel slavery, Howe argues. Slavery was abolished north of the Ohio River and the Mason and Dixon line. The South still held the saddle but felt its seat insecure, he says. The nation held twenty eight states, fourteen free and fourteen slave, admitted in pairs to keep the Senate even. Fast growth in the free North threatened slave power supremacy, he notes. Critics get a blunt anti war tract.
57834-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 388, is the February 1848 issue, volume sixty three. William Blackwood and Sons printed it at Edinburgh and London. Eight pieces fill the contents. The lead article reviews a secret history of the Russian court. It calls Russia the most extraordinary country on the globe. History, extent, population, and power all feed that claim. Peter the Great is praised as the moral creator of Russia.

Other pieces include the life of a German headsman told in his own words. Edinburgh after Flodden and a piece on Jerusalem follow. Subjects for pictures, a tale called Now and Then, and the West Indian colonies round out the number. Politics and letters share the issue in the house style.
73422-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine Number 390 for April 1848 is Volume Sixty Three of the long run journal. The issue holds nine main pieces. The lead piece is Fall of the Throne of the Barricades. It treats the fall of Charles the Tenth in France and its long train of woes.

Other pieces treat a route into Canada, the conquest of Naples, and Welsh travel. A life of Lord Hardwicke and a tale of the Tuileries fill more space. Verse holds a German song and two sonnets. The Caxtons, a family tale in parts, closes the issue. The tone is staunch and Tory in its view of France and reform.
75215-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine filled its September 1848 issue with politics, verse, and tales. The number is 395, in Volume 64, printed at Edinburgh by William Blackwood and Sons. A review of the last session of Parliament leads the contents. Verse on a caged skylark and a sonnet to Denmark add light fare.

Life in the Far West runs in its fourth part, and The Caxtons in its sixth. Essays treat George the Second, the Moscow retreat, and unrest in Germany. The lead piece scolds the Whigs for weak rule amid revolt in Ireland and France. Readers gain a sharp Tory view of a year of revolts.
arxiv-2412-00448:
Shuang Ji and Jing Lu settle the fate of waves in a self-attracting quantum gas with an external trap in this 2024 mathematics paper. The model, a focusing Hartree equation with potential, describes condensates whose atoms pull together. Below a set mass-energy line, waves either spread out forever or collapse in finite time, and the boundary case needed proof.

Working in five dimensions with a broad class of potentials, the authors build a combined energy-flow estimate and a test that certifies spreading. Their argument extends earlier work on simpler versions of the equation. The result completes the scattering picture under the threshold for this trapped, nonlocal model, a benchmark for condensate stability theory.
arxiv-2412-00848:
Wojciech Broniowski and Enrique Ruiz Arriola study the pion's inner stresses in a 2024 physics paper. The pion is a light particle made of a quark and an antiquark. Its gravitational form factors describe how energy and pressure are spread inside it, a topic now probed by theory and lattice computing.

The authors work out the sideways density profiles of the energy-momentum tensor. One component is shown to stay positive everywhere, with consequences they trace through several consistency rules. The trace part, tied to a famous anomaly, must change sign across the radius, unlike its positive partners. Pressure inside the pion is positive and sharp at the centre and negative outside, matching stability needs. Results are compared with recent lattice data.
arxiv-2412-00948:
Fourteen researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four presenting a benchmark for language models in African languages. Tests of model knowledge and truthfulness usually cover rich-resource languages, because data in low-resource languages is scarce. Uhura fills that gap for six African languages.

Human translators converted two English test sets: easy multiple-choice science questions, and a truthfulness test spanning health, law, finance, and politics. The authors describe the challenges of translating technical content and how they handled them. Testing showed a wide gap between top commercial models and open ones on these languages.
arxiv-2412-01448:
Jianhui Lin, Xiangdong Zhang, and Moises Bravo-Gaete probe whether a quantum version of a charged black hole keeps a fragile inner edge, in a 2024 paper. Recent work fixed a long-standing clash in quantum gravity in two ways, and one path yields a black hole with an inner horizon like the classic charged one. In the classic case, that inner edge is unstable and blows up under small pushes.

Using a known relation for such horizons, the team finds the same blow-up, which backs a rule that nature hides such edges. Adding a cosmic push term, they find the rule still holds for sound settings. The quantum hole thus fails a test for being fully regular.
arxiv-2412-01548:
The ATLAS Collaboration measured off-shell Higgs boson production in a 2024 paper, using proton collisions recorded at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis covers 140 inverse femtobarns of data at 13 TeV and looks at Higgs bosons decaying into two Z bosons, which then give four leptons. It replaces an earlier result in the same channel.

Instead of standard fitting, the team used a neural method that builds a likelihood ratio for each event with neural networks. The signal strength came out near the expected value, and the evidence for off-shell production grew compared with the older analysis. Combined with a second decay channel, the result also pins down the Higgs boson's total width at about 4.3 MeV.
arxiv-2412-01848:
Patrick Kappl and co-authors extend a classic equation system from pairs of particles to triples, in a 2024 paper. The Bethe-Salpeter equations govern how two interacting particles bind and scatter. Their three-particle vertex, the hub where three lines meet, needs its own ladder equations. The authors generalize the three known pair ladders into ten triple ladders, an exact framework in principle.

Exactness stalls on a missing block: the part of the vertex irreducible in each channel. They approximate it by stitching together pair-level irreducible pieces. Tested against an exact solution for a nonlinear response function, the shortcut fares only qualitatively, and only for weak interactions. The honest verdict maps where cheap three-particle physics can be trusted.
arxiv-2412-02148:
Ashutosh Hathidara, Gaurav Atavale, and Suyash Chaudhary mine tweets about Bitcoin to see whether the chatter tracks, and can even foretell, the coin's price. Their 2024 project starts from the last decade's surge of interest, and the flood of posts that came with it. Millions of users talk the price up and down in public, in near real time.

The team paired the tweet stream with the price record and measured how the two move together. Fresh analysis methods were brought to bear on the text, so mood and themes could be set against daily swings. The same link then served the forecast: models fed on the conversation were asked to call the price ahead. The study weighs how far talk can guide such calls.
arxiv-2412-02648:
Luca Biasco and co-authors proved a long-term balance result in 2024 for a group of nonlinear Schrödinger equations on a circle. The equations carry a smooth contact potential, and the starting waves are taken very regular and small. The central question of KAM theory for such systems is whether most small motions stay orderly forever instead of wandering into turbulence.

The authors construct a set of starting data, asymptotically filling full measure as the height shrinks, whose answers are almost-periodic in time and lie densely on invariant tori. In the region of positive actions these maximal tori form smooth manifolds that slice the phase space into a Cantor-style foliation. As a consequence, for many small starting waves a key regularity norm stays nearly constant for all time. A numeric form of Lyapunov balance and a first KAM result of this strength for such equations.
arxiv-2412-02748:
Benjamin Moy and Eduardo Fradkin entangle two kinds of symmetry in a 2024 physics paper. Their lattice model couples a clock model to a gauge theory through a topological link. The link binds one side's charges to the other side's disorder operators. When those bound pairs condense, new generalized symmetries appear, carrying mixed anomalies.

The resulting phases mix symmetry breaking, topological order, and protected topological order, not as neighbors but as relatives. Boundary states and transitions between the phases get their own theories. A non invertible symmetry extension follows. Modern condensed matter increasingly finds orders that refuse to sit in one box; this model builds that refusal in from the start.
arxiv-2412-02848:
Sylvester Eriksson-Bique and Josh Kline prove that fractional Hardy inequalities improve themselves in rough geometric spaces. Hardy inequalities bound a function's size by its gradient, with a penalty for nearing the boundary. In metric measure spaces, where calculus is scarce, even stating them takes care.

Their key move lifts the problem into a hyperbolic filling, a nicer space built above the rough one, where a classic Hardy inequality lives. Equivalence between the two settings lets a known self-improvement in the filling flow back down. A new theory of well-behaved weights handles improvement in the smoothness exponent. Self-improving estimates are gold in analysis: assume a weak version, receive a stronger one free.
arxiv-2412-02948:
Rama Cont and Fang Rui Lim wrote this 2024 mathematics paper on causal transport between probability laws that live on paths. A path here is a full record of how a random process moves over time. A coupling joins two such laws, and a causal coupling respects time: its choices cannot peek at the future.

The authors first characterize bicausal couplings, causal in both directions, between weak solutions of stochastic differential equations. They then describe all such couplings of Monge type, where each path is sent to one partner path. For Wiener measures, those couplings turn out to come from stochastic integrals with rotation-valued integrands. Last, they give conditions for a bicausal coupling to come from a Monge map at all. Such maps, they show, can approximate any bicausal coupling between laws of well-behaved equations.
arxiv-2412-03048:
Xin Zhong and Naihong Hu rewrite a quantum superalgebra in terms of shuffles of words, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. The algebra is the positive part of the quantum affine superalgebra of type C(2)(2), an object from the theory of quantum groups with both bosonic and fermionic generators.

The algebra is generated by two elements tied by cubic q-Serre relations. Two distinguished bases for it, the Damiani basis and the Beck basis, were known to exist. The authors express both bases in closed form using the q-shuffle superalgebra and Catalan words, a combinatorial encoding. They finish by giving the bosonization of the algebra, a way to realize it inside a more ordinary algebra. Shuffle realizations turn abstract relations into concrete word combinatorics. That makes computations in the superalgebra far more tractable.
arxiv-2412-03148:
Kun Li, Chenwei Dai, Wei Zhou, and Songlin Hu present a 2024 study on how well large language models can copy the way real people act on social media. Strong role play is not the same as true behavior copying. A model needs to read a person's past posts and act as that person would.

The team built a data set from the full posting history of 1,866 users on three platforms. Each act was split into object, type, and content, giving a large set of test questions. They found two main patterns in how the models reason through a copy task. From those patterns they built a fine-tuning method that made the copies better. Tests show their method beat plain approaches. The work gives builders a firmer way to judge fake-user tools.
arxiv-2412-03348:
Ishfaq Ahmad Rather and Grigoris Panotopoulos ask how exotic matter changes neutron stars in a modified theory of gravity. Their 2024 paper works inside regularized four-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity. Neutron stars may host hyperons in their cores, and deeper still, matter may switch to a quark phase.

Two density-based models supply the matter physics, one for the normal phase and one for quarks. Adding hyperons softens the matter's stiffness, and the quark switch softens it further, dropping the sound speed in the heaviest stars. Tuning the gravity coupling shifts the mass-radius curve up or down. Positive values let stars reach the two-solar-mass bar and match telescope measures. The authors fit simple formulas so others can scan the coupling's effect quickly.
arxiv-2412-03548:
Mahtab Bigverdi and colleagues give multimodal language models a scratchpad of perception tokens: internal tokens that carry depth maps and object boxes, so the model can reason over what it sees. Language alone is a clumsy medium for spatial facts. Fine-tuning generalizes poorly, and calling outside vision tools is heavy. Writing in twenty twenty-four, their training method converts intermediate visual representations into token sequences with a vector-quantized autoencoder. Multi-task training then teaches the model to emit and use these tokens mid-reasoning, like a visual chain of thought.

Counting benchmarks improved by roughly ten points across three suites, with better transfer between data sets than fine-tuning achieved. Relative depth judgments improved as well. The authors argue perception should be a native dialect of the model, not a translation it requests from outside.
arxiv-2412-03648:
Cesar Gallegos and co-authors map the phases of a model magnet in a 2024 paper. Their model places tiny spins on a triangular grid, with pulls between nearest and next-nearest neighbors, and a tilt that favors one axis. Such models help physicists sort out which patterns magnetism can take when the pulls fight each other.

Using a heavy computer method plus pen-and-paper insight, the team charted which pattern wins at each setting. A broad spin-liquid region stands out, stretching from the balanced point between two known phases. In a spin liquid, the spins keep moving and never lock into a fixed pattern. The team also studied a phase likened to a supersolid and suggested why it shows no net pull. The map guides the search for real materials with the same habits.
arxiv-2412-04148:
Tomoya Hirobe and Kenta Kasai solve a size question for a family of error-correcting codes built from permutations, in a 2024 paper. A permutation code lists reorderings of symbols so that any two differ enough to survive noise. Their recursive family grows by inserting a new symbol at the front and relabeling the rest, step after step.

Distance here is measured by the Chebyshev rule, the largest single-step gap between two codewords. Each growth step can guard the distance, but later steps can also repair shortfalls, which makes the true maximum size tricky. By tracking disjoint intervals tied to codeword pairs, the pair prove an exact formula for the largest code at each length and distance. Exact maxima close the design question for this family.
arxiv-2412-04348:
Ivan Kostyuk and Benedetta Ciardi ask whether galaxy mergers help light escape young galaxies in a 2024 paper. The light at issue is Lyman continuum radiation, which can ionize gas between galaxies. Drawing on a large cosmic simulation, the team ran an escape model over about six hundred thousand galaxies from the early universe.

Galaxies left alone for seven hundred million years let about three percent of the light out. Right after a merger, the share jumped to as much as fourteen percent, most strongly in small galaxies. Fresh poor gas feeding star birth and shifted gas cover explain the leap. Crowded regions leaked more as well, through faster gas inflow.
arxiv-2412-04448:
Zheng and eight co-authors build a talk film tool with a long past bank in this twenty twenty-four paper. Sound-led face films oft drift in face form cross long runs. Mood match tween voice and face also lags in past tools.

Inside, a past bank holds long tales to steer the film's time flow. That bank keeps face form firm and moves smooth cross the run. A mood read from the voice then tunes face acts in line. Joint sight-sound care swaps the stock cross-care in their build. Tests beat past tools on sync, face keep, and mood match.
arxiv-2412-04948:
Peng Yu, Cheng Deng, Beiya Dai, Xinbing Wang, and Ying Wen align language models with knowledge graphs in a 2024 paper. Models trained to predict the next token write fluently but answer factual queries poorly. Knowledge graphs hold structured facts that could fill the gap, if alignment can avoid dulling generation.

Their method, KaLM, fine tunes a model with two objectives. Explicit alignment shapes the model's knowledge vectors through contrastive learning on two graph views. Implicit alignment teaches fact patterns through triple completion styled as language modeling. Tests on graph completion and question answering showed clear gains. The team presents the joint objective as a way to add facts without losing generative skill.
arxiv-2412-05048:
Turchi, Masciadri, and Fini describe a software suite that runs weather forecasts for telescope sites. Their paper from twenty twenty-four presents FAST. Big ground telescopes need forecasts of air flow and sky blur to plan their nights. Sharp optics gear works best when tuned to the air ahead of time.

FAST runs each forecast step on its own. It fetches start data, runs the air model, and shapes the outputs for staff. Two linked forecast models supply weather and sky-blur values. The suite first served a project for one large telescope, then grew to serve a second site. It now gives forecasts days or hours ahead, by day or night. The authors say the suite is mature and ready for new sites.
arxiv-2412-05648: Richárd Grünwald and Zsolt Páles study forms of two bounds in math, the Hölder and Minkowski bounds, for a broad class of means. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. In place of sums and products, they use a general act, and in place of power means they use a wider family of means that is not symmetric. They bring in the split between a bound that holds near a point and one that holds across the range, and pin down when each holds.
arxiv-2412-05748:
Taehyeun Kim and co-authors design a control scheme that keeps a docking spacecraft within safety limits as it approaches its target. Two craft are involved: a chief that follows a path, and a deputy that must meet it. The scheme works by shifting the deputy's path in time, so it aims at a safe point while the shift shrinks to zero at docking.

Computing the shift fast enough is the hard part. The team trains a neural network, of a kind built for sequences, to predict the shift from states of both craft. The network learns from simulation data before any flight. Tests covered missions in low Earth orbit and on a stretched Molniya orbit. In most cases the scheme computed the shift faster than older methods and still completed the docking. The authors present it as a practical add-on for autonomous rendezvous missions.
arxiv-2412-06148:
Yifang Chen and co-authors prove, in a 2024 paper, hard limits on what a popular alternative to the Transformer can compute. Mamba and its state-space relatives process sequences with a compact memory state, and some hoped they were stronger than Transformers. The authors test that hope using circuit complexity, a framework that sorts problems by the hardware depth needed to solve them. They ask which class these models fall into when their precision and depth are bounded.

The proof shows both model families sit in the same low complexity class as Transformers. That means some problems lie beyond them all, unless a long-standing gap in complexity theory closes. Examples include certain formula and ordering problems. The authors conclude that Mamba's real edge is speed and memory use, not greater computing power.
arxiv-2412-06248:
Six researchers present a pipeline to anonymize people in image data sets in a 2024 paper. Privacy laws demand identity protection, yet crude tools like blur wreck image value, most of all for human scenes. Their method joins 3D rendering with a diffusion image model.

Rendering locks the body's posture while the diffusion step repaints identity traits from a text prompt. That split beats plain diffusion, which loses posture, and older GAN tools, which lack realism and control. The team also built a framework to grade privacy and utility by human judgment. Models trained on their fake data beat real data training on detection tasks in their tests.
arxiv-2412-06348:
Ankit Bhojak, Surjeet Singh Choudhary, Siddhartha Samanta, and Saurabh Shrivastava bound a discrete maximal operator tied to Birch-Magyar averages. Their paper from twenty twenty-four sits in harmonic analysis. The averages run over sparse sequences, thin sets of points with growing gaps. A maximal function takes the largest average over scales at each point. Sparse bounds give a strong grip on such operators.

The team proves a sparse domination rule for the operator. From it, norm bounds follow for all exponents above one. The proof leans on single-scale gains: each fixed-scale average improves norms in a scale-free way. Stacking those gains yields the sparse control. Such bounds feed weighted estimates across analysis. The work extends the sparse program to a number-theoretic family of averages.
arxiv-2412-06648:
Jacob Seeley and Robin Wordsworth simulate rising moist air in hydrogen-rich atmospheres in a 2024 paper. Such light air behaves oddly: a parcel loaded with a heavier vapor can sink even when it is warmer than its surroundings.

Using a three-dimensional model that resolves clouds, the pair varied the background gas and the moisture near the ground. Past a humidity limit first derived in 1995, the clear layer near the ground collapses. A thick cloudy layer takes its place, with temperature falling with height faster than the dry rate. Drier ground air keeps the cloudy layer higher up. Their results predict that worlds crossing that limit should look much cloudier, a pattern telescopes might spot.
arxiv-2412-06748:
Neel Jain, Aditya Shrivastava, Chenyang Zhu, and co-authors tackle a practical safety problem in this 2024 paper. Large language models must refuse some requests, such as instructions for illegal acts or questions past their knowledge. Yet different users want different refusal rates, and training a fresh model for each setting is costly.

The team adds special refusal tokens during training, one for each refusal category or a single shared token. At run time, raising or lowering the chance of that token steers how often the model refuses, category by category. One trained model can thus be tuned on the fly, with no extra fine-tuning. The approach gives builders a cheap dial for matching a model's caution to each user's needs.
arxiv-2412-07448:
Different large language models excel at different tasks, so combining several models can beat any one alone. Jinwu Hu and co-authors propose a dynamic ensemble method that picks which model answers each part of a question. They frame the choice as a decision process and train an agent to route requests between expert models.

A reward function teaches the agent to seek the best answer quality for the least computing cost. A special prompt also helps each later model absorb what earlier ones contributed, so knowledge transfers instead of restarting. In tests, the method used fewer resources than rival ensembles while scoring higher. The authors present dynamic routing as a practical way to make model teams both stronger and cheaper.
arxiv-2412-07748: Calixto, Freitas, and Jorge Pérez prove that gluing formal schemes yields a formal scheme again, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Their algebra route also tells when the glued build keeps a base field trait. One sharp twist follows: the glued scheme is always singular, no matter how smooth the parts may be. The result settles a basic closure point for the formal side of geometry.
arxiv-2412-07848:
Aydemir and Elbistan ask what happens to the expanding universe if a basic symmetry of general relativity is slightly broken. The symmetry, called diffeomorphism invariance, might be absent in a deeper theory from which gravity emerges. The team added the mildest symmetry-breaking terms to the standard equations.

They solved the expansion history for universes filled with radiation, matter, or vacuum energy. The radiation and vacuum cases gave exact solutions, and the matter case was computed numerically. Every solution eased smoothly back to general relativity as the breaking faded. Larger mixed universes showed no instabilities. The authors conclude that small violations of this kind are safe for basic cosmology.
arxiv-2412-07948:
Jan Retkowski, Jakub Stepniak, and Mateusz Modrzejewski introduce a score for judging computer generated symbolic music, in a paper from 2024. Symbolic music is music stored as notes and instructions, rather than as sound. Their score borrows from measures used for images and audio.

The score compares the spread of features in real music with the spread in generated music. That captures abstract musical traits rather than single note errors. Tests across several data sets and models showed the score separates good models from weak ones well. The authors offer it as a shared standard for future work on symbolic music generation.
arxiv-2412-08748:
Kumar and co-authors present an integrated model of material wear at fusion reactor antennas in a 2024 paper. In the WEST tokamak, radio-frequency antennas heat the plasma, but the same fields can knock tungsten atoms off the antenna's guard tiles. That erosion feeds impurities into the plasma. Their framework, called STRIPE, links four simulation tools, each handling a slice of the physics.

Applied to one recorded discharge, the model found a tenfold jump in tungsten erosion when radio-frequency sheath effects were included, compared with heat alone. Highly charged oxygen ions did most of the knocking. A synthetic light signal built from the model matched the measured tungsten glow from the real discharge closely. The team is now extending the framework to other heated devices to guide antenna design.
arxiv-2412-08848:
Zhang and co-authors present a 2024 photonics paper on edge waves that speed themselves up along a material's border. Edge states in topological materials resist scattering off defects, which makes them prized for devices. Their speed usually sits fixed by their momentum. The team shaped valley Hall edge states with an Airy envelope, a wave form known for bending paths.

The shaped states accelerate along the boundary while keeping fixed momentum, and they refuse to spread. Both plain and nonlinear versions were built, with the nonlinear ones reshaping their envelopes strongly. Bent tails let the waves round sharp corners and heal after damage. The authors point to robust light routing as the prize.
arxiv-2412-08948:
Xuehai He and co-authors present Mojito, a video model that takes orders on motion path and strength in two thousand twenty-four. Text-to-video tools now make fine clips, but steering how an object moves, and how hard, stays hard. Training such control in is also costly.

A direction module steers the object's path through cross-attention, with no extra training. A second module reads flow maps from real clips to grade motion strength and guide the output. Tests show the model follows set paths and strength levels closely while staying cheap to run. The motion it makes matches natural movement in real scenes, which suits ads, film drafts, and design work.
arxiv-2412-09348:
Miguel Barroso Varela and Orfeu Bertolami ask whether cosmic data prefer a theory where matter and gravity are directly coupled. Standard cosmology pairs Einstein's gravity with a cosmological constant, but a nonminimal coupling changes how matter shapes curved space. The authors confront that modified theory with several recent sky surveys.

They combine exploding-star distances from two large samples with sound-wave scale measurements from galaxy surveys. Across all dataset combinations, the coupled theory fit the data better than the standard model, with moderate to strong statistical preference. The modified model matched both early-universe and late-universe observations well. One tension remained: the sound-wave measurements pulled against the conclusions drawn from the other data. The paper adds weight to testing gravity theories beyond the standard picture.
arxiv-2412-09448:
Zeyu Wang and co-authors present a 2024 paper on searching data series at scale. Collections of time series keep growing, and indexes must answer likeness searches in milliseconds. Two leading index families trade off build time against search accuracy, and each leaves a weakness.

The team traces the weakness to fanout choices in the index tree and to skewed data spread. Their index, Dumpy, uses a multi-way tree with splits that adapt to the data. A fuzzy variant copies some series to lift accuracy further. The full system, DumpyOS, runs in parallel across cores and fast drives. Pruning search methods keep speed high while the fuzzy search lifts result quality.
arxiv-2412-09748:
Zenon Gniazdowski published a research paper in 2024 on a way to group data attributes of mixed kinds by how alike they are. Numbers cluster easily, but word-like labels, such as colors or job titles, do not fit the same math. His method first recodes labels as numbers in a principled way.

Once all attributes are numeric, a factor method groups them by their likeness to hidden factors. Trials on several sample data sets showed the approach handles numbers alone, labels alone, and both mixed together. That breadth is the point: one tool for the messy tables real analysts face. The paper lays out the recoding and grouping steps in full.
arxiv-2412-10048:
Hanna Muller, Victor Kartsch, Michele Magno, and Luca Benini presented BatDeck in 2024, an ultrasonic sensing deck for nano-drones. Tiny drones suit tight-space rescue and are safe near people, but their small payload limits sensing. Laser and camera sensors fail on clear or shiny surfaces and in the dark.

Taking a cue from bats, the team used low-power ultrasonic sensors facing down and forward to gauge speed and dodge obstacles. The system measured speed with low error and flew for eight minutes in tests, covering a good distance among clear and shiny obstacles. Comparisons with laser and optical methods showed the approaches can back each other up for safer flight.
arxiv-2412-10248:
Jonas Latz, Aretha Teckentrup, and Simon Urbainczyk wrote this 2024 paper on honest uncertainty in image reconstruction. Rebuilding an image from indirect data is guesswork, and knowing how unsure the guess is guides real decisions. The Bayesian approach treats the image as a random function, starts from a prior belief, and updates it with the data.

Plain priors fail here, since real images shift character across scales and places. Deep Gaussian processes fix that with a layered structure that adapts as it goes. The price is hard sampling: the math runs through huge, dense matrices that change with every draw. The paper tackles that sampling problem for deep process priors. The goal is sharper reconstructions that carry trustworthy error bars, not just a single best picture.
arxiv-2412-10348:
Yuan Sun, Zhao Zhang, and Jorge Ortiz present AlignCap, a frame that teaches vision-language models to caption small regions, not just whole images. Their paper from twenty twenty-four names two drags on region skill. Spatial sense is weak, and coarse pre-training blurs the latent match between encoder and decoder. Most setups freeze both ends and tune the middle, so the blur persists.

A latent refinement module sharpens the conditioned features first. A semantic space alignment module then lifts the joint representation quality. Contrastive learning is woven through both in a fresh way. A general object detection pass preps the data, adding region-level spatial cues. Wide tests show clear gains in region captioning across tasks. The authors frame fine latent alignment as the missing step for region talk.
arxiv-2412-10448:
What a neural network remembers of a photo can leak the photo itself. A 2024 paper by Sai Qian Zhang and co-authors improves a method for rebuilding images from those inner features. Such inversion matters most where networks are split across devices, since the shared features may expose private pictures.

The team uses diffusion models, strong image generators, as a prior guide for the rebuild. They also test extra help from text prompts and from links between frames of video. The diffusion-guided rebuilds came out clearly better than those from older methods. The findings show how much visual detail hides in network features, a warning for anyone who shares them.
arxiv-2412-10548:
Giovanni Baccichet, Fabio Palmese, Alessandro Redondi, and Matteo Cesana fingerprint Wi-Fi devices from the probe requests their radios broadcast. Their 2024 paper explains that phones and laptops periodically send these frames while hunting for networks. Tracking them reveals movement patterns useful for city planning and retail analysis, but it also threatens privacy.

Devices randomize their hardware addresses to resist tracking, yet the information fields inside probe frames can still identify them. The team's learning method builds compact binary fingerprints from chosen bit sequences. On public data sets, storage fell by about a hundredfold compared with existing methods. Fingerprinting performance stayed robust despite the compression. Public data sets anchor the evaluation.
arxiv-2412-10648:
Maria Cuellar wrote this 2024 paper examining the statistics beneath shaken baby syndrome diagnoses. The diagnosis, also called abusive head trauma, can decide criminal trials, yet its scientific base is contested. Cuellar argues the data under the diagnosis fail basic statistical tests.

There is no independently verified ground truth for which babies were shaken. Context leaks into judgments, data sets circle back on themselves, and case definitions vary between studies. The famous symptom trio, bleeding under the skull, bleeding in the eyes, and brain swelling, has never had its specificity properly measured. Cuellar recommends that doctors report only what they observe and leave abuse findings to courts. She calls for rich, careful data collection so accuracy can finally be tested.
arxiv-2412-10848:
Hospital records hold a patient's story as a timeline of events. Zeljko Kraljevic and co-authors train Foresight 2, a language model that reads that timeline and forecasts what comes next. Training used the free text of a large intensive care dataset. Concepts were extracted and arranged into patient timelines before fine-tuning. The model suggests diagnoses and forecasts risks, procedures, and medications.

On predicting the next new medical concept it beat the prior best by a wide margin. Disorder prediction improved similarly. On risk forecasting it outperformed GPT-4-turbo and open biomedical models. The authors argue small models fed good hospital data beat giants fed general text.
arxiv-2412-10948:
Justin Le published this overview paper in 2024. Diffusion models are the engines behind image generators like Stable Diffusion and DALL-E, and this paper explains how they work from the ground up. The core idea is two opposing processes. First, data is gradually drowned in noise until nothing remains but static. Then a model learns to run that corruption backward, removing noise step by step until a fresh, plausible sample emerges.

Le gives formal definitions of both the noising and denoising directions. He then lays out the algorithms for training such a model and for generating new samples with it. The presentation suits readers meeting the mathematics for the first time. A final section tests a practical use: generating synthetic examples to balance lopsided datasets, where rare classes starve a classifier. The paper positions diffusion as one member of the modern generative family.
arxiv-2412-11048:
Yu Fu, writing alone in 2024, works on a question in pure math about abelian varieties. These are shapes defined by equations that also carry a group law. In a family of such shapes that shifts with one dial, the typical member may be simple, meaning it does not split into smaller parts.

Fu asks how far that simple trait spreads to other members of the family. Prior work used analytic tools on a narrow set of curve families. Fu widens the result to all families with large symmetry action, using number-based tools instead. The method leans on bounds for covers of the shapes and tunes those covers to get sharp counts.
arxiv-2412-11348:
Shoumi Sarkar and five co-authors model sparse ranked outcomes over time in a 2024 paper. Their test case is tooth stain from too much fluoride, tracked in Iowa youth from age 9 to 23. Stain scores per tooth face are ranked, bunched by child, and mostly zero, a hard mix for stock math.

Their frame splits the ask in two: is there stain, and how deep is it. Two linked score tools share traits across the halves. Joined calls beat split ones in truth and speed. Sparse ranked trails gain a sound gauge.
arxiv-2412-11448:
Gangqiang Hu and co-authors wrote a paper from 2024 on choosing which clients to train with in semi-decentralized federated learning. In this setup, edge servers and their client devices share the work of training one model, passing versions within and between clusters. Clients drift: connections drop, local training wobbles, and data differs by device. Most past work assumed steadier clients than the real world offers.

Their scheduler, named TRAIL, scores each client's state and likely contribution before picking who joins a round. A hidden-state model that adapts over time estimates connection health and usefulness. A greedy rule then pairs clients to servers so as to cut the global training loss, guided by convergence math. On real data sets, the scheduler beat leading rivals with a clear gain in test accuracy. Training loss fell by a wide margin as well.
arxiv-2412-11648:
Arnaud Le Fevre and co-authors measure how much nuclei pass through each other in collisions in a 2024 paper. When heavy nuclei smash head-on, some matter stops and some flies through. That balance, called transparency, tests models of nuclear matter. The team used xenon and tin targets with varied neutron counts.

Collisions ran at a set energy in a large detector in Germany. A new method compared isotope yields at forward and side angles. Cross-bombarding nuclei with different neutron shares sharpened the test. Hydrogen isotopes showed only moderate transparency. Heavier fragments showed high transparency, above half in the measure. Alpha particles showed an oddly large transparency of their own. Possible explanations for that anomaly are discussed. The results constrain how nuclear matter brakes fast fragments. Future models must match the isotope pattern seen.
arxiv-2412-11748:
Simin Yu and nine co-authors build a Brillouin amplifier on suspended lithium niobate nanowaveguides with record gain. Their paper from twenty twenty-four uses thin film lithium niobate, a star platform for chip photonics. Stimulated Brillouin scattering there had been forecast but not won, since light and sound losses must both stay low. The team maps how gain shifts with waveguide angle on the crystal cut.

Anisotropy in the photoelastic response shapes that map. A peak gain value is reported for the best angle. Tone can be tuned by pump frequency or chip heat. With both light and sound modes well confined, the amplifier hits its record mark. The result proves strong guided Brillouin action in this platform. Sensing and signal tasks on chip stand to gain.
arxiv-2412-12048:
Chenxi Liu, Towaki Takikawa, and Alec Jacobson argue in 2024 that style adapters can be read directly, with no sample images needed. Small adapter files called LoRAs fine-tune image models toward set styles, and hundreds of thousands circulate online. Sorting them usually means generating pictures first.

The team shows the adapter weights alone form strong style fingerprints. Those fingerprints stayed steady across training seeds and image picks. Tests on paintings and building photos beat image-based methods at clustering and finding unseen adapters. A check on a larger base model also held up. The route saves computing and prompt work for style search.
arxiv-2412-12248:
João Augusto Sobral, Michael Perle, and Mathias Scheurer blend physics with transformer networks in 2024 to describe quantum states of electrons. Neural networks can sketch complex wave states, but their output depends on the frame chosen and can be hard to read. The team set out to fix both flaws.

Their method first builds a physics-guided frame that holds a rough guess of the true ground state. A transformer then learns just the corrections to that guess, sampling them step by step. Tests on a model with a metal-to-insulator switch showed cleaner results. The network's inner states even lined up with the energy order of the frame's parts.
arxiv-2412-12348:
Tianning Tang and co-authors present a 2024 paper using machine learning to discover, not just fit, the equation that marks where an ocean wave breaks. Standard learning models predict well but explain nothing, leaving physics hidden inside a black box. Knowledge discovery methods instead search for the governing formula itself.

Working from a dataset of computer-simulated waves, the team applied symbolic regression, which assembles candidate equations from mathematical building blocks. The search targeted the boundary condition at breaking, a dramatic event that forecasting still handles crudely. A readable equation, if it holds up, would plug straight into wave models and coastal engineering, with its reasoning open to inspection.
arxiv-2412-12448:
Sheng Cheng and five co-authors teach a network to pick controller settings for each new tracking task in this 2024 paper. Model-based controllers fly well when tuned, but fresh tasks lack tuned parameters. Their Task-Parameter Nexus predicts near-optimal settings at run time.

Training data came from a bank of trajectories spanning speeds and curvatures. For each path, the best parameters were tuned offline and stored as ground truth. The network learned to map task to settings by supervised learning. On a quadrotor, in simulation, it predicted near-optimal parameters across a spectrum of tasks. It also generalized to tasks it had never seen. The authors frame the approach as auto-tuning that travels with the controller.
arxiv-2412-12548:
Blake and a large collaboration team present a mock challenge testing the cosmological analysis pipeline planned for DESI year-one data. The test combines DESI galaxy redshifts with weak lensing data modeled on three imaging surveys. The analysis uses so-called 3x2-point correlation functions, including cosmic shear and galaxy-galaxy lensing.

The team built realistic simulations with halo occupation models, photometric redshift errors, and shear calibration biases. Their analytical covariance, including Gaussian, noise, and super-sample terms, agrees with simulation-based estimates. Bayesian inference recovers the simulation's true cosmological parameters within the expected errors. The study validates the large-scale analysis ahead of the real DESI measurements.
arxiv-2412-13048:
Matteo Fontana, Federico Scali, and Sergio Luigi Cacciatori examine spinning dust clouds whose gravity warps space into a cone at infinity. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. Exact solutions for self-gravitating dust can carry a missing wedge along the rotation axis, like a cosmic string's footprint.

Boundary conditions can erase the wedge on the axis itself. Far away, though, the geometry stays locally flat yet globally conical, never relaxing to ordinary empty space. The trio call such spacetimes asymptotically conically Minkowskian. That distant cone bends light differently than expected. It can also fool an observer into reading the vacuum as full of scalar particles. The effects give far-off watchers a fingerprint of the hidden defect.
arxiv-2412-13248:
Benedikt Placke, Tibor Rakovszky, Nikolas P. Breuckmann, and Vedika Khemani define a new phase of matter that fuses two famous orders. Spin glasses freeze into complex energy landscapes and underpin ideas in machine learning and optimization. Topological order, by contrast, stores quantum information non-locally and powers quantum error correction. The authors ask whether one system can do both.

Their answer is topological quantum spin glass order, which keeps the rugged landscape of a spin glass while holding the long-range entanglement and quantum memory of a topological phase. Using coding theory and a quantum version of Gibbs state decomposition, they build their case. With those tools they show this order is the low-temperature phase of several quantum low-density parity-check codes built on expander graphs, including hypergraph and balanced product codes. They frame the result as a bridge between statistical mechanics and quantum computing.
arxiv-2412-13548:
Jingxiang Guo and co-authors let a far driver see the ghost of their next move ere the true arm makes it, in a study from 2024. Far drive is the well that robot learn drinks from, but hand-to-arm maps baffle new hands and can snap gear. A ghost arm that shows the act first could teach and guard at once.

Their rig, TelePreview, draws that ghost live from the hand's marks, for less than a thousand in kit. The driver can flip twixt ghost view and true run at will. On five tasks it beat past rigs, and new hands learned the maps fast. Ghost first, steel next: the pitch is a school and a shield in one.
arxiv-2412-13948:
Mathias Neufang, Emma Pajak, Damien van de Berg, Ye Seol Lee, and Ehecatl Antonio del Rio Chanona survey surrogate based optimization for process engineering in a 2024 book chapter. Optimization shapes cost, resource use, quality, and sustainability in chemical plants. Their focus is data driven methods that replace an expensive true model with a cheap stand in, needing no derivatives. The chapter teaches theory and practice side by side.

Algorithms covered range from Bayesian optimization and its trust region variant to linear and quadratic approximation methods, tree based tools, and radial basis function strategies. Each gets background, math, and a description. Performance is compared across test functions and two reactor case studies, one high dimensional and stochastic, one small and constrained. The authors aim to equip engineers to choose and use the right surrogate method.
arxiv-2412-14248:
Alessandro Trinca and co-authors ask why many black holes seen in the early universe look too heavy for their galaxies, in a 2024 study. New telescope views show large black holes at high redshift with masses well above the pattern seen nearby. The team uses a model of galaxy growth to trace how such objects could form.

In the model, small and large seeds alike grow through short bursts of very fast feeding, set off by galaxy mergers. Each burst lasts a few million years at most, so most black holes sit quiet most of the time. Growth of hole and galaxy only locks together late. Bright bursts also help explain the glowing centres the telescope finds, while many heavy holes stay dark and inactive.
arxiv-2412-14548:
Araujo-Regado, Höhn, Sartini, and Tomova explore the link between two kinds of boundary modes in gauge theory and gravity. Soft modes live at far away boundaries, and edge modes live at the edge of a finite region. The two have long looked alike. Many assumed the soft ones are just a limiting case of the edge ones, but the authors argue the true link is more interesting.

Working in the simplest gauge theory, electromagnetism, they place a finite region inside the whole spacetime. Edge modes then act as reference frames built from fields inside or outside the region. Only frames built from outside fields yield the extra corner symmetries. With that split, the far-away symmetries and their charges connect to the finite ones without any limit.
arxiv-2412-14948:
Edcarlos Silva and co-authors prove solutions exist for a nonlocal elliptic problem with a set total mass. Their paper from 2024 works with a fractional p-Laplacian operator and a power growth term. Two regimes are covered: one below the critical growth rate and one exactly at it, both under a fixed norm rule.

A wide class of potentials is allowed, from repeating patterns to coercive forms that grow at infinity. In the lower regime, a solution with the set norm is shown for repeating and near repeating potentials. In the critical regime, a solution exists for each small enough positive value of the power term weight. The proofs sit in a fractional Sobolev space frame.
arxiv-2412-15048:
Baptiste Filoche, Stefan Hohenegger, and Taro Kimura studied surface defects in little string theories in a 2024 paper. These theories are built from parallel membranes on a circle, over a twisted background. At low energies they look like a circular chain of gauge groups.

The authors add a defect that breaks each gauge group into smaller parts. They give a counting formula for the exact partition function of this system. That form lets them argue that known hidden symmetries survive with the defect in place. They also study a special limit in detail for one small case, uncover an algebra behind cancelled terms, and extend it to general cases.
arxiv-2412-15248:
Harshvivek Kashid and Pushpak Bhattacharyya tackle error fix for scanned text in low-resource Devanagari languages in a two thousand twenty-four paper. Optical character recognition errors plague digitization, and fix data sets barely exist for these languages.

Their RoundTripOCR technique generates synthetic training data automatically. They release post-OCR fix data sets for Hindi, Marathi, Bodo, Nepali, Konkani, and Sanskrit. The fix model borrows from machine translation: erroneous OCR output is treated as a mistranslation of the true text. Pretrained transformers learn the mapping from corrupted to clean sentence pairs. The approach gives low-resource language digitization projects a useful path to cleaner texts.
arxiv-2412-15348:
Yousseef and co-authors survey the security of self-driving cars, with a focus on threat modeling, in a 2024 paper. Connected, software-heavy vehicles open many doors to attack, from sensors and wireless links to control units and firmware. The survey walks through three standard frameworks for listing threats in a systematic way. Case studies of real hacks on a Jeep Cherokee and a Tesla Model S ground the discussion.

The authors then review defenses on the horizon, including blockchain-secured vehicle messaging, AI-based attack detection, and safe over-the-air updates. Legal and ethical issues, such as privacy, user safety, and regulation, get their own treatment. The paper closes with layered defense advice for makers who must protect cars that drive themselves.
arxiv-2412-15448:
Akash Deep and co-authors test random forest models fed with classic trading indicators at minute speed in this 2024 paper. Market theory casts doubt on whether chart patterns can predict prices. High-frequency data, dominated by market plumbing, is the hardest test. The team used minute-level data on a major market index fund. Thirteen model setups mixed indicators with the learning method. Results split sharply between training and fresh data.

Scores that looked strong in training collapsed to negative in testing. Price-based features dominated the model's attention. The rest added little once those were in. The study is a caution against backtest pride in fast trading. It shows how microstructure noise swamps weak signals. The authors report the gap as the core finding.
arxiv-2412-15548:
Designing a chip that runs neural networks means testing millions of layouts, and full tests are far too slow. Chirag Sakhuja, Charles Hong, and Calvin Lin present a tool pair for that search in a 2024 paper. Their model, Starlight, learns from cheap rough estimates to predict costly detailed results. Transfer learning bridges the gap between the two test levels.

Starlight gives thousands of predictions per second and matches detailed simulation closely. It also trains with far fewer samples than the prior best model. The search tool built on it, Polaris, matched rival designs in a fraction of the time. Given more hours, it found designs with much lower energy-delay scores. The work speeds the hunt for efficient AI hardware.
arxiv-2412-15648: Kaoru Yoneda and Tsuyoshi Yoneda give a sufficient condition for the local limit theorem. Their 2024 paper works in probability theory, where local limit results pin down point probabilities, not just totals. Their construction leans on repeated convolution of probability density functions, applied without end. The note is brief and purely theoretical, addressed to specialists in limit theory, with no data or simulations in view.
arxiv-2412-15848:
Sarah Thomson and co-authors map where search algorithms stall in a 2024 paper. Landscape maps help explain optimizer behavior, but classic local optima networks assume local search steps. Popular methods like CMA-ES never take such steps, so they escape that lens. Trajectory networks are broader but ignore stalls.

The team define attractor networks, a stripped view focused on stall points. They build them for CMA-ES, differential evolution, and random search. Twenty-four standard benchmark problems supply the terrain. Network traits are then compared across algorithms. The maps expose how each method wastes time, guiding fairer comparisons and better tuning of black-box optimizers.
arxiv-2412-16148:
Mingliang Liang and Martha Larson wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2024. It studies how hiding parts of the text during training affects vision-language models, which learn to link images with words.

Training these models is costly, so shrinking the text they see can help. Earlier work compared ways of masking text and crowned a syntax-based method best. Liang and Larson show that what matters is how each method changes the mix of common and rare words left visible. Rare words carry much of the signal. Their method, CLIPF, masks text based on word frequency on purpose. In tests it beat the syntax method, above all when few words were shown. They also found other methods overtake syntax masking given enough training rounds.
arxiv-2412-16348:
Lucas Moriggi and Magno Machado use a new lens to pin down a key number in particle physics. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. When an electron strikes a proton at high energy, the pattern of particles that fly out shows scaling: it looks the same across many settings. A number called the pomeron intercept governs how fast the process grows with energy.

The authors show that a measure based on entropy, drawn from how many particles each event makes, carries the same scaling signal. Entropy is cheaper and cleaner to read from data than the raw cross-section. By fitting both signals together, they pin down the intercept with high precision. The method could sharpen tests at future colliders and deepen our grasp of how dense matter saturates.
arxiv-2412-16448:
Cosmas Kravaris sharpens, in a solo 2024 mathematics paper, a lower bound for a one-size-fits-all tour rule. The traveling salesman task asks for the shortest path through a set of points. A universal rule fixes one master order of the unit square in advance, then visits any point set in that order. Past work showed some sets force such tours to run long.

Kravaris raises that floor. For any master order, he builds point sets of any size whose forced tour runs long by a set factor over the best tour. The factor improves the previous bound from a known 2006 result. His proof splits long walks on a cycle into two kinds. A walk either zigzags between two far points, or it stays inside a set of small diameter for a long time. That split drives the bound.
arxiv-2412-16648:
Maxence Perion, Sara Tucci-Piergiovanni, and Rida Bazzi tackle a weak point in group-based payment systems. Their twenty twenty-four paper notes that small validator groups are easy targets once known. An attacker can bribe, flood, or corrupt a known group.

Their idea, Secret Quorums, keeps group members hidden through the whole check. Members are picked in secret, like a fair lottery, but the proof does not name them. Any group-based protocol can use the layer, from blockchains to split data systems. Readers see how hiding the group can keep a fast design safe from foes who adapt.
arxiv-2412-16748:
Henry Li and Marcus Pereira recast a popular image-repair method as a steering problem. Diffusion models can rebuild a clean image from a blurred, noisy, or partly missing one, a task called an inverse problem. The usual approach samples from a target distribution, which brings tangles: the odds are hard to compute, and early guesses of the clean image are poor. Their 2024 paper takes another road.

The pair treat the image-building process as a chain of control steps and design a controller modeled on an iterative regulator used in robotics. The method accepts any forward model that can be differentiated, from sharpening and filling gaps to highly nonlinear neural classifiers. The older sampling equation falls out as a special case. Tested against rival solvers, the method set a new baseline for reconstruction quality on standard inverse problems.
arxiv-2412-17248:
Yufeng Xin, Sajith Sasidharam, Cong Wang, and Mert Cevik tackled traffic engineering for wide area networks in two thousand twenty-four. Cloud networks carry growing, uneven traffic, and routing must balance quality against compute cost. Existing methods, they argue, ignore how varied demand is and how unevenly links fill up.

They propose new metrics, a critical link set and network criticality, to judge resilient routing more fully. Their tunnel-based algorithm adapts routes as demand changes. Simulations on varied network shapes showed a better balance across goals than prior methods. The authors present the package as a step toward routing that is both resilient and scalable for large cloud backbones.
arxiv-2412-17648:
Tithi Dwary and Krishna wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2024. It describes which networks, or graphs, can be encoded by words, using a standard way of breaking a graph into blocks.

A graph is word-representable when its links can be captured by a pattern of repeated letters in a word. Graphs also split into modules, tight clusters that connect to the rest in a uniform way. The authors characterize the word-representable graphs through this splitting. From the pieces, they derive how many letter repeats a full graph needs, based on its modules and the simpler quotient graph that links them. The work also settles a standing question from Kitaev and Lozin about combining graphs by the lexicographic product.
arxiv-2412-17848:
Diego Mollá and colleagues summarized a 2024 shared task on spotting machine-written sentences inside mixed articles. Modern articles often blend human and AI text paragraph by paragraph, or even sentence by sentence, which defeats simple whole-document detectors. The annual ALTA task asked teams to label each sentence of such hybrid articles as human or automatic.

The overview paper lays out how the task was built, how systems were scored, and how the participating systems performed. Shared tasks like this create a public measuring stick, so later detectors can be compared on the same hybrid material rather than on each team's private examples. The results chart how hard sentence-level detection remains when styles interleave.
arxiv-2412-17948:
Daniel Tan and Neftali Watkinson Medina build a sieve for chess learn sets that keeps calm spots and casts wild ones. Fast net scores now rule top chess tools, but their worth rides on the train set. Wild spots, thick with traps, teach noise; calm spots teach true worth. Their 2024 craft makes and sifts sets of such calm spots by a clear rule chain.

The chain can be run by any team and bent to kin score tools. Tests show real play gains in the tool trained on the sifted set. Set craft, oft kept as lore, is here wrote plain. Calm-set sieves can lift tools in more games than chess.
arxiv-2412-18048:
Weitao Tang, Guanliang Chen, Shuaishuai Zu, and Jiangyi Luo test whether learner models play fair across groups, in this 2024 study. Models that trace what language learners know guide teaching, but their fairness is rarely checked. Using a big app dataset across three course tracks, the team compares a classic machine learning model and a deep one on two fairness fronts: platform and country wealth.

Deep learning won on both accuracy and fairness overall. Both models favored phone users over web users. The classic model also leaned harder against learners from poorer lands. Track by track, deep learning balanced best in two, while the classic model suited the third. The authors press fairness checks as a must for teaching tools.
arxiv-2412-18148:
Zhen Sun and co-authors measure how much of social media text is now written by AI. Machine text can spread false claims and bend public debate, so its scale matters. Their 2024 study gathers about two and a half million posts from three big platforms. They also build a test set from human posts and text made by twelve language models.

With a tuned detector, the team tracked the AI share from early 2022 to late 2024. On two platforms the share soared from about two percent to nearly forty. On the third it crept up only a bit. Machine posts differed from human ones in style, topics, reach, and who posts them. The authors say the trends call for steady watching.
arxiv-2412-18448:
Doimo and co-authors restore chance to a classic ecology model. Metapopulation theory tracks species spread across habitat patches, but its standard form assumes huge local populations, washing out the randomness of births, deaths, and dispersal. Real patches hold finite numbers, and luck can kill a population that averages say should live.

The team derives how survival odds scale with patch capacity near the knife-edge between persistence and extinction. The deterministic capacity, the old model's summary number, still governs the statistics: it sets both survival probability and the moments of extinction time. The formulas give ecologists a way to fold demographic luck into landscape models without abandoning their structure.
arxiv-2412-18548:
A blazar aims its jet almost straight at Earth, and one famous example flares across every band of light. Four astronomers track a decade of its behavior in 2024, asking whether its steady glow comes from the disk feeding its black hole or from the jet itself. They follow a bright hydrogen line and the nearby continuum, using a dominance measure to split disk-led from jet-led spells. The line's width narrows as its brightness rises, in every dataset.

That pattern means the line always comes from the canonical broad-line region, whichever source lights it.
