Jet flares in the continuum arrive with matching flares in the line, placing the jet's base inside that region. From quiet, disk-led spectra the team weighs the black hole at about 285 million suns.
arxiv-2412-18648:
Sourav Bhattacharya and Ashish Yadav study patterns of motion on a three-armed branching shape, called a triod, in a paper from 2024. A pattern records the order in which points of the shape are visited by a map. Each pattern forces a range of rotation speeds. Some patterns, called twists, are known to lock their speed to an end of that range.

The pair prove a condition that forces such locking for any pattern. They then build odd patterns that lock the same way without being twists. Those patterns also lack the block build that twists show. No such examples exist for maps on a circle, so the triod theory parts ways with the circle theory here. They name the new patterns strangely ordered. A construction method yields them at any chosen rotation pair.
arxiv-2412-18848:
Manuel Bolz and co-authors present a 2024 paper on catching crypto pump-and-dump schemes as they form. In these schemes, Telegram groups secretly pick a coin, hype it, and dump on latecomers. Some groups exceed two million members and sell early access, deepening the information gap. The head title frames the work as machine learning-based detection in real time. The team builds a prediction pipeline that reads Telegram traffic with language models. It flags likely target coins before the pump peaks.

From chat history the system identified 2,079 past pump events. In a Poloniex case study it ranked the true target in the top five of fifty coins in over half the events. Market integrity teams get an early-warning design where seconds matter. Detection after the dump only documents the loss. Real-time ranking gives exchanges and investors a chance to freeze, warn, or stay out.
arxiv-2412-19048:
Zhang, Li, Zeng, and Wang shrink top text-embedding models without losing their skill. Embedding models turn text into number lists for search and question answering, but the best ones are huge and slow. Their framework trains a smaller student on several large teachers at once, using three losses, and a matryoshka method trims the student's output size.

The student, Jasper, has two billion parameters and is built on the Stella model. As of late December 2024 it ranks third on the main embedding leaderboard, scoring 71.54 on average across 56 data sets. The team releases the model, the training data, and the code in public.
arxiv-2412-19548:
Petr Stehlík wrote a 2024 paper on waves that stall or reverse in a bistable equation set on trees. The graph is a regular tree that runs on without end in both ways, and the equation blends spread with a reaction that has two stable states. Past work showed such effects for smooth reaction terms but gave no closed forms.

Stehlík uses the piecewise linear McKean form, which lets him write exact pinned waves and check that they hold steady. The pinned zone turns out to have no bound, so waves can reverse even when spread is strong. The results match the smooth case in most ways but break from it on that key point.
arxiv-2412-19648:
Xiaokun Feng and co-authors improve vision-language tracking, the task of following an object in video using both a template image and a written description. Their 2024 paper notes a data imbalance: tracking data sets hold far more images than text, so models learn to align words with pictures only weakly. Text cues that should sharpen tracking go underused.

Their plug-in method, CTVLT, converts each text cue into a visual heatmap showing where the described target likely sits. A second module fuses that heatmap with the search image to steer the tracker. On standard benchmarks, the method reached state-of-the-art results. It works with existing trackers rather than replacing them.
arxiv-2501-00148:
Natig Atakishiyev studies the eigenvectors of a five-dimensional discrete Fourier transform number operator in a paper published in 2024. Operators of this kind sit at the crossroads of signal analysis and quantum-style math.

The approach leans on the symmetry of certain intertwining operators under a reflection. A thinning procedure for those operators makes the structure workable. From it, the author builds a discrete version of a classic formula from the continuous case. The eigenvectors themselves take shape as Newtonian basis polynomials times the lowest eigenvector. The result gives a clean analytic handle on a problem that brute force handles poorly.
arxiv-2501-00648:
David Smith and co-authors build circuit models for resonant antenna elements in a paper from 2024. The catalog lists a later year, but the text head gives 2024, and that year is used here. The elements sit inside waveguides and are built from patterned metal that resonates at set frequencies. Designers need simple models that predict how each element scatters waves as its shape changes.

The team extracts a circuit model from the scattering data of a single element. The model captures electric and magnetic responses with ordinary circuit parts, plus a transformer term unique to resonant designs. It matches full simulations closely. With one or two simulations, designers can then predict many variants, speeding metasurface work.
arxiv-2501-00748: Xi Chen, Shuai Lu, and Ruochong Zhang wrote a paper from 2025 on a hard backwards problem for waves. A wave moves through a medium whose hidden pull no one can see from the outside. All the team can use are the waves that come back out. They ask how well the hidden term can be read from those returns, and how much a small error in the returns can move the answer. Their proof gives bounds that keep the answer steady.
arxiv-2501-00848:
Zhang and five colleagues introduce IllusionBench in twenty twenty-five, a benchmark for visual illusions in vision language models. Such models read images well but struggle with illusions, mainly in real scenes. Older benchmarks focus on classic cognitive illusions that top models have already learned. That leaves gaps in what tests can reveal.

The data set holds more than one thousand images and more than five thousand question answer pairs. It includes classic illusions, real world scene illusions, and gold text descriptions. The team also built trap illusions that look classic but differ in reality. Ten leading models were tested on true false, multiple choice, and open ended tasks. The best model scored well on closed tasks but still lagged humans. Trap illusions exposed hallucinations even in the top model.
arxiv-2501-01048:
Ximing Xie and co-authors published this communications study in 2025. Future wireless networks may mix two kinds of users. Semantic users send meaning rather than raw bits, while conventional users send bits as today. Both can share spectrum through non-orthogonal access, where signals overlap and are separated at the receiver. Making that mix power-efficient is hard, because no formula links a semantic transceiver's quality to the resources it gets.

The team adapts a semantic transceiver so it flexes with changing channel conditions. They fit a data-driven model tying its performance to resource choices. Their network design pairs one semantic and one bit-based user per cluster, easing the interference-removal burden. They formulate a power-minimization problem covering beamforming, bandwidth, and semantic symbol settings. The paper presents the framework as a step toward networks that carry meaning and bits without wasting energy.
arxiv-2501-01248:
Thorben Werner and Lars Schmidt-Thieme teach an active learner to tell two kinds of doubt apart in a paper from 2025. Active learning picks which examples are worth labeling. For regression, doubt is hard to measure, and the field lags classification. Normalizing flows give full predictive distributions, which should help.

Standard heuristics, the authors show, mostly fail on flows. Noise in the world and ignorance in the model get tangled. Their BALSA method adapts a Bayesian classic to separate them. Tests across four datasets and several settings set new best results. Labeling budgets stretch further when each query teaches the most. Regression tasks from prices to sensors stand to gain.
arxiv-2501-01548:
Shuguang Wang and Yuanjing Wang present a neural network that looks at images the way eyes do, in fixations. Their Task-Driven Fixation Network pairs two channels. A low-resolution channel takes in global features of the whole image at once. A high-resolution channel then pulls fine detail from small regions one after another. A hybrid encoding module merges the two streams.

The module holds a fixation point generator that picks where the sharp channel should look next. Fixations form in a task-driven way, so the network skips full high-resolution scans of the whole scene. The design aims to keep task performance high while shrinking network size and compute cost.
arxiv-2501-01948:
Katerina Bolshakova and Sergey Chervon offer in 2025 a new route to key numbers for models of the early universe with more than one field. For a single field, teams know how to work out the strength and tilt of ripples from the inflation era. For many fields, no settled method yet exists.

Their approach starts from an exact solution in a gravity theory with many scalar fields. That solution ties the fields together, which lets the pair compute the ripple measures and compare them with what telescopes observe. The work gives cosmologists a concrete tool for testing whether multi-field models fit the real sky.
arxiv-2501-02048:
Panoptic segmentation labels every pixel of an image by object and instance, and open-vocabulary versions must handle classes they never trained on. Yuanpeng Tu, Xi Chen, Ser-Nam Lim, and Hengshuang Zhao found in 2025 that past gains were mostly on trained classes. Their system, DreamMask, attacks the problem from the data side by making synthetic training images.

An automatic pipeline builds the data with off-the-shelf models, with designs for widening the vocabulary, laying out scenes, and filtering poor samples. A special loss aligns synthetic and real data during training. Added to existing models, DreamMask lifted scores on a standard test set by a clear margin and simplified large-scale data collection.
arxiv-2501-02448:
Hyunwoo Ko, Guijin Son, and Dasol Choi wrote a paper in 2025 on why large language models perform worse at mathematics in some languages than in others. The models excel in high-resource languages such as English. In Korean, a clear performance gap persists. The team built a benchmark of 8,011 English-Korean parallel mathematics problems to investigate the gap.

Their key finding is that the gap stems primarily from difficulty comprehending non-English inputs, rather than from weaker reasoning ability. Their proposed method, called Understand, Solve and Translate, has the model first understand the problem, then solve it using English as an anchor, then translate the answer back. Fine-tuned on synthetic training data, the method improved the benchmark score substantially and cut the multilingual gap almost to zero. The gains also generalized to other Korean domains. The benchmark, training data, and models were all released publicly.
arxiv-2501-02648:
Restrepo and seven co-authors fill gaps in ward lab data with a masked code net in this twenty twenty-five paper. Missed lab reads can bias care calls and the AI tools trained on ward files. Past fill tools miss the time and place links that tie one read to the next.

Inside, their net learns by hiding true reads and then guessing them back from kin reads. Each read is coded with its time stamp, so time gaps shape the guess as well. On a big ward file set, the net beat five known fill tools on all score types. Its grades held even across age, sex, and root groups of patients. The team also weighs the net's carbon cost next to a tree tool.
arxiv-2501-02848:
Chen and co-authors report new decay data for a rare atomic nucleus in this 2025 paper. The nucleus is a heavy form of tantalum with a long-lived, high-spin excited state. Such states test ideas about nuclear shape in a region where shapes are expected to shift.

The team made the excited state by firing a xenon beam at a tungsten target and sorting the products. They directly saw both beta and gamma decay from the state. They also revised its half-life to about 136 seconds. Limits on slow, rule-breaking steps helped pin down the state's spin and parity. Model work links the state to a stretched shape built from five loose particles.
arxiv-2501-02948:
David Bate and Julian Weigt prove a test for when a set in a general space of distances can be counted as rectifiable. That term means it looks like a smooth surface at most points. Their test rests on how the set can be split into curves, a form called an Alberti representation.

If the set's measure has as many free such splits as its dimension, the set must be rectifiable, they show. The result sharpens past work by Bate and Li. The authors note the proof settles many open questions on when sets in such spaces count as well behaved in this sense.
arxiv-2501-03848:
Dung Tran and co-authors introduce Semise, a 2025 method for learning severity aware features from medical images when labeled data is scarce. Medical image sets are often small and unevenly graded, yet downstream tools need features that reflect how severe a case looks, not just which class it falls in.

Semise blends two learning styles. Self supervised learning uses unlabeled and augmented images to teach the encoder broad structure. Supervised learning then steers those features with the labels that do exist. The mix yields richer representations than either style alone. On their tests, classification improved by 12 percent and segmentation by 3 percent over existing methods, the authors report. Better features carry into the downstream tasks clinics care about. The method targets settings where expert labels are the bottleneck, a common reality in medical imaging projects.
arxiv-2501-04048:
Vladimir Rovenski surveys weak metric f-manifolds, a broad class of geometric spaces, in a 2025 paper. A weak f-structure loosens a classic setup from the last century, swapping a rigid complex rule for a skew-symmetric field. That loosening lets old theory be revisited with fresh eyes.

The survey gathers results on special classes of these spaces and their hallmark features. Topics span symmetry flows that preserve shape, leaf-like splits that are fully straight, and soliton and Einstein-type metrics. Links between the topics show how one weak frame can serve many branches of geometry. New uses found along the way round out the tour.
arxiv-2501-04548:
Boris Vexler and Jakob Wagner steer a fluid flow by setting pressure at the edge of its domain, in a 2025 math paper. The control problem rests on the time-moving Navier-Stokes equations, with control fed in through a do-nothing edge term. Such flows can fail to stay well-posed over long times or large data. The authors still gain a sound control problem by picking the right tracking term to chase.

To spell out how smooth the best control, the flow, and the helper state are, they prove fresh smoothness results for a Stokes problem with mixed edge terms.
arxiv-2501-04648:
Gabrielle Littlefair, Niladri Shekhar Dutt, and Niloy Mitra test in 2025 whether language models can design rooms when guided like junior designers. A good layout must fit every needed object, one style, easy movement, and a budget. Raw models cannot yet draw whole rooms, the team found.

Instead, careful prompting draws out object lists and placement rules, the judgment part of design. Those are turned into a layout graph, and a standard solver arranges the room. Benchmarks compare the results with data driven rivals. The split keeps the model's reasoning visible, a point the authors stress.
arxiv-2501-04948:
Hui Luo, Xin Liu, Wei Liu, and Yang Zhang define a new way to compress multi-way data arrays built from reduced biquaternions, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Tensors generalize matrices to many dimensions, and quaternion-style number systems let one entry hold a color pixel's channels together, which suits image data.

Their decomposition arranges the tensor as a ring of small cores, and they detail the matching algorithm, RBTR-SVD. On top of it they build a completion method that fills in missing entries. The completion balances the ring's low-rank structure against total variation regularization, which favors smooth images. Tests on color image and video completion favor their method over alternatives. Keeping color channels coupled inside the number system preserves relationships that splitting channels would lose. The work extends tensor ring tools to a richer number system.
arxiv-2501-05048:
Matthias Kaul, Kelin Luo, Matthias Mnich, and Heiko Röglin study how to split a set of points into clusters at low cost, in this 2025 paper. The cost of each cluster is the weight of its cheapest spanning tree, a stand-in for the effort of visiting every point in the group. Earlier work judged a split only by its most costly cluster.

The authors adapt that earlier algorithm so one split scores near-best under every symmetric monotone norm at once, not just the largest-cost measure. Their method is purely combinatorial, runs in polynomial time, and handled ten thousand points in under a second in tests. They also handle a variant where each cluster must contain one of a given set of depots. Matching hardness results show the clustering problems stay hard to approximate even under a single norm, so the guarantee is close to the best possible.
arxiv-2501-05248:
Laura Puccioni and co-authors show how to carve small coding models out of large language models in a 2025 paper. Big models write code well but demand costly hardware. Trimming a model can shrink it, yet past trimming rarely aimed at one coding language at a time.

Using a trimming method fed with language-matched sample data, the team pulled out sub-models for four languages: Python, Java, C++, and JavaScript. The small models kept good accuracy next to the full models. Tests also showed that each language lights up distinct parts of the big model. Readers get a path to fast, local coding help on home-grade machines.
arxiv-2501-05348:
Nikolay Ulyanov poses an oriented form of the Berge-Fulkerson conjecture in a 2025 paper, the first in a series called Graph Puzzles. The classic claim says each bridgeless cubic graph can be covered by six perfect matchings, with each edge hit just twice, which can be restated as a six-cycle cover claim.

Ulyanov sets out the oriented version of that restated claim as a conjecture. He proves it for one family, the Isaacs flower snarks. From a solution, an orientable surface can be built, and in split cases a second pair as well. Ribbon graphs enter for special cases.
arxiv-2501-05648:
Yingkai Sha, John Schreck, William Chapman and David Gagne wrote a 2025 paper on AI weather forecasts. AI models are strong at medium-range forecasts but can break basic physics rules. Their outputs may fail to conserve mass or energy. The team built add-on schemes to enforce those rules.

The schemes guard dry air mass, water balance and total energy for the whole globe. They are built as modules that fit many model types. Tests used one named AI model set on a coarse grid. Forecasts kept the physics rules better and scored higher, more so at longer lead times. Rain forecasts gained most, with less false drizzle.
arxiv-2501-05748:
Henry Pfister and co-authors give a general frame for bounding when a code fails as a whole block on an erasure channel, based on when single bits fail. Erasure channels drop symbols outright, a clean model for lost data. Their 2025 frame turns on the support weights of small subcodes inside the code.

For each small dimension, they study the least support weight among subcodes of that size. Those numbers link the bit level threshold to the block level one. As a proof of concept, they use the frame to re-derive a famed result: Reed-Muller codes reach channel capacity on the erasure channel for block error. The method may serve other code families too.
arxiv-2501-05848:
Andreas Grendas and co-authors apply a flexible math method to magnet problems in a 2025 paper. The method, called isogeometric analysis, solves physics on the same smooth shapes used in design. Fine detail is needed only in spots, so local refinement that adds detail where it counts saves much computing effort.

Their approach joins layered spline functions with a step that converts patches into standard pieces for fast solving. They apply it to two dimensional magnetostatic problems, where fields stay steady over time. Code built on an open source package lets them compare global and local refinement fairly. The comparison shows where the layered method wins on cost and accuracy.
arxiv-2501-06148:
Berner and co-authors link two ways to train sampling models in a 2025 math and computing paper. The task is to train a diffusion model to draw samples from a known target spread, without having samples from that target. Past training used either full simulation or off policy learning methods borrowed from game play.

The authors prove that, as time steps shrink toward zero, the aims of one family of learning methods match objects from the smooth time view. They then show that a well chosen coarse step size in training can save much work. Tests on standard sampling tasks reached results on par with other methods at lower cost.
arxiv-2501-06248:
Roberto-Rafael Maura-Rivero, Chirag Nagpal, Roma Patel, and Francesco Visin wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reshapes the rewards that train language models, borrowing the shape of utility curves from economics.

Training with mixed human feedback often just averages the reward scores. That flat mean can miss what each score guards, and how they lean on each other. The fix bends each reward so low scores sting more and high scores add less glow. The bend follows the Inada conditions, a classic utility trait. Against plain weighted means, models trained the new way test as more helpful and less harmful. Scores and close reads of the text agree on the gain.
arxiv-2501-06348:
Ruchira Ray and five colleagues present a 2025 study asking which household tasks people actually want robots to take over. Common sense says the most time-consuming chores top the list. Drawing on a large behavior dataset and national time-use surveys, the team compared automation wishes with time spent and with feelings such as happiness, stress, and pain.

Time spent turned out to be a weak guide. Happiness and pain predicted the wish to automate far better. Patterns also split by group: women leaned toward automating stressful tasks, men toward automating ones that made them unhappy, and middle-income respondents targeted chores they found dull or meaningless. The authors urge robot designers to build for feelings, not just minutes saved.
arxiv-2501-06448:
Ziteng Cui and co-authors learn a bespoke color frame for each photo in a 2025 paper. Photo touch up tools map each pixel by grids or curves. Full color grids cost too much memory, while split curves lose cross channel play.

Their IAC method first warps the color space to fit the shot at hand. Curves then work inside that warped frame, jointly learned end to end. The design stays light and runs fast at use time. Tests span retouch, exposure fix, and white balance tasks. Top scores came with the lean design intact. A fitted frame beats one fixed grid for all shots.
arxiv-2501-06648: Dmytro Fedoriaka asks which of the classic one-dimensional cellular automata — simple grids where each cell updates by a fixed rule from its neighbors — can be run on a quantum circuit. There are two hundred fifty-six such rules in the standard counting. Fedoriaka identifies the full list of rules that admit a quantum simulation. The list holds twenty-two rules. For each one, the paper gives an explicit quantum circuit that carries it out, using a number of gates that grows only in step with the grid size.
arxiv-2501-06848:
Raghav Singhal and co-authors present a way to steer diffusion models at run time in 2025. Diffusion models make images, video, and even proteins of high quality. Users still struggle to force traits they want in the output. Retraining for each reward is costly and can narrow variety.

Their steering method runs many sampling paths side by side as particles. At mid steps, paths with better promise are copied and weak ones dropped. Scores come from reward based potentials set by the user. The frame works across data types without new training. It offers control while keeping the model broad output range.
arxiv-2501-07248:
Mathias Lowes and co-authors track heart muscle motion with implicit neural models in a 2025 paper. The left ventricle's wall movement reveals cardiac function. Registering its shape across the heartbeat cycle quantifies that motion. Convolutional approaches demand heavy memory and compute.

Implicit representations evaluate motion at any continuous point cheaply. The team extends them to cardiac CT registration. A distance field of the muscle focuses the registration. Raw scan intensity values ride along as guidance. Tissue information thus steers alignment around the wall. Accuracy proved high in their framework tests. Temporal registration stays robust across the full cycle. Downstream motion analysis builds directly on the output. Strain and function measures become computable per patient. The efficiency suits clinical computing budgets better. Cardiology imaging is the application target.
arxiv-2501-07548:
Some young galaxies leak a special ultraviolet glow, and that leak helped light up the early universe. Keunho Kim and co-authors ask what those galaxies look like in a 2025 study of twenty-three of them, magnified by gravity's lensing so the faintest show up. The galaxies sit at cosmic noon, when star making peaked.

They turned out strikingly small, a few hundred light-years across, packing star birth into a tight space at rates far above typical galaxies. The smaller the galaxy, the stronger the glow relative to its other light. The authors argue the dense packing drives winds that blast escape channels for the glow.
arxiv-2501-07648: Movahedi-Lankarani and Wells revisited bi-Lipschitz embeddings of metric spaces in two thousand twenty-five. An embedding is bi-Lipschitz if it stretches distances by at most a bounded factor in each direction. Their study centers on the distance function that sends each point to its distances from all others. As an application, they give three sufficient conditions for a compact metric-measure space to admit such an embedding into a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
arxiv-2501-07948:
Groups of linked oscillators, from fireflies to power grids, tend to fall into step with each other. Emmanuel Delaleau, Cédric Join, and Michel Fliess show how to force that step on demand in this 2025 paper. Their test case is the Kuramoto model, the standard math model of linked oscillators. Other teams have steered it with neural networks, which can be heavy to run.

The authors use a method called HEOL, which joins two older control ideas: differential flatness and model-free control. They show the oscillator model is flat under a certain kind of control input. Flatness lets them build a control scheme that uses far less computing power. The paper also steps back to discuss what AI tools add to control work, and where leaner math may serve better.
arxiv-2501-08348:
Ashoka Karunarathne and five co-authors listened to ultrasound passing through a carbon sponge as it drank water vapor, to learn where the water goes inside pores too small to see. The material, a carbon xerogel, mixes one-nanometer micropores with eight-nanometer mesopores. As humidity rose in steps, the team weighed the sample and recorded sound speed and fading for waves crossing it, then converted those readings into stiffness measures.

The water in the wider pores behaved almost like ordinary bulk water. In the micropores, its stiffness clearly differed, matching theory for water squeezed at the nanoscale. Sound fading rose while the micropores filled, a sign that water was spread unevenly through the sample rather than coating it uniformly. The authors present ultrasound as a nondestructive probe of adsorption: a way to watch pore filling and judge the state of trapped fluids without cutting the material open.
arxiv-2501-08548:
Xi Zhang and co-authors introduce a survey of star clusters taken with China's LAMOST telescope, in a 2025 paper. Open clusters are families of stars born together, and their chemistry and motion reveal how the Galaxy evolves. The project gathers medium-resolution spectra of cluster member stars, measuring speeds and metal content, to pair with the Gaia mission's precision positions.

So far the team has observed ten cluster fields, collecting over 235,000 spectra of nearly 134,000 stars. For the clusters of special interest, the survey already captures about seventy percent of member stars brighter than a set limit, meeting its design goal. The paper lays out the survey plan and these early results. The authors intend the data to support studies of how open clusters form, change chemically, move, and dissolve over time.
arxiv-2501-09248:
Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space whose source is still debated, and the repeating ones behave much like earthquakes. Wu and co-authors charted the energy patterns of the three most active repeaters in 2025. All three showed the same break in their energy counts at about the same energy. The pattern resembles the bend in earthquake size statistics.

Below the break, weak bursts can start both on the star's surface and deep in its crust. Above it, strong bursts can only start at the surface, because the crust is only so thick. That difference in growing room bends the scaling, the authors argue. With the bursts' earthquake-like timing, they read the break as strong support for starquakes on magnetars as the trigger.
arxiv-2501-09348:
Kyoungsu Heo and K. Hagino visualized quantum interference in nuclear scattering in a 2025 paper. When an alpha particle bounces off a calcium nucleus at modest energy, the scattering pattern wiggles because several wave paths overlap. The authors split the scattering amplitude into four parts: near-side and far-side paths, each divided into waves reflected at the surface barrier and waves that entered the nucleus.

Each part leaves a distinctive mark on the angular pattern. A Fourier transform technique turns those marks into images, where peaks at given angles reveal the position and strength of each interference piece. Structure invisible in raw cross sections becomes readable. The method gives nuclear theorists a clearer diagnostic for optical potential models.
arxiv-2501-10148:
Kenta Hotokezaka, Ryusuke Jinno, and Rin Takada point out a new effect that ripples in the early universe have on how heavy particles drop out of balance, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They call the effect acoustically driven freeze-out. It matters because the standard story of how the universe got more matter than antimatter runs through just such a freeze-out.

When temperature varies from place to place, heavy particles leave the thermal bath at a sharply uneven rate, an effect too strong for simple linear math to catch. The authors work through the case of heavy neutrinos, whose decays can create the matter surplus. They find the ripples always raise the final surplus on average. That loosens the limits on how heavy those neutrinos must be.
arxiv-2501-10548:
Ting-Ruen Wei and Yi Fang survey, in 2025, the fast-growing use of diffusion models in recommendation systems. Diffusion models, which build content by refining noise, reshaped image generation and are now being tried for suggesting items to users. Papers have multiplied, and the field lacked a map organized by the recommendation task itself.

Their taxonomy sorts work along three axes, with the task as the main one, a shift from an earlier survey that sorted by the model's role. Core algorithms and their uses are summarized. Open problems close the survey, and a public repository collects the papers. The aim is to guide the next wave of work.
arxiv-2501-10948:
Two authors study tiny bubble jets inside a tapered chip channel, in a 2025 fluids paper. Gas and liquid flow side by side, and at the narrow zone the gas can fire off a jet of bubbles smaller than a millimeter. Such control matters for lab-on-chip tools.

The pair found self-similar shapes at the taper and built a local model around two new scale measures. Their phase map draws sharp lines between jetting, dripping, and long-bubble regimes. A scaling law ties jet speed to surface pull, inertia, thickness, and the local taper shape. The rules held across flow settings from gentle to brisk. Chip designers gain a shared map for dialing bubble size and speed on demand.
arxiv-2501-11148:
Sanjana Das, writing alone, offers a 2025 math paper on sets of numbers and the gaps between their members. Take a large set where every small subset has many distinct gaps between its numbers. The question is how many distinct gaps the whole set must then have. This is known as the local properties problem for difference sets.

Das studies how the count of gaps grows as the set gets large, for fixed subset size. There is a key threshold where the growth jumps to a square rate. She shows that just below that threshold, the growth stays below the square rate by a fixed margin. The gap in growth rates holds for all even subset sizes.
arxiv-2501-11248:
Luo and a team of physicists report fine-scale evidence on a nickel-based material in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The material, a lanthanum nickel oxide, can superconduct at high pressure. Its transition near eighty kelvin drew wide interest. A density wave order may sit near the superconducting state. Sorting out which kind of wave it is could reveal how the superconductivity arises.

Samples often mix in related phases, which cloud the picture. The team used a resonance method on lanthanum nuclei to single out the phase of interest. Below the transition point, their signals point to both charge and spin density waves. That is a microscopic view, not just a bulk hint. The work sharpens the debate on what drives high-temperature superconductivity in nickel oxides.
arxiv-2501-11448:
Filippo Rambelli and Fabio Sigrist compare fast stand ins for Gaussian process models on spatial data. Their paper from 2025 starts from the cost wall of the true model, which grows with the cube of data size in time and the square in memory. Many shortcuts exist, but their true price in lost accuracy per hour saved was murky.

The team tests the shortcuts on likelihood scoring, parameter fitting, and prediction, with the clock running, across made up and large real data sets. One family, Vecchia approximations, gave the best trade of accuracy for time in most settings. The verdict gives spatial modelers a clear first pick among shortcut types.
arxiv-2501-12048:
Shramana Dey and co-authors present an adaptive class learning framework to screen diabetic eye disorders from fundus images, in a research paper from 2025. Eye disease is rising worldwide, and early finding prevents vision loss. Labeled retinal images are scarce, so a classifier that grows its class set step by step can use limited data well.

The framework first learns healthy versus diabetic retinopathy features. It is then fine-tuned to add glaucoma as a third class. Perturbation methods reveal which image traits drive each call, a check on trust. Overall accuracy reaches near ninety-one percent on public data sets. The staged design suits clinics that must add diseases over time with few new labels.
arxiv-2501-13048:
Raga and co-authors study the Herbig-Haro objects HH 270 and HH 110, where a young star jet seems to bend into a second flow. New JWST views show HH 110 as a chain of distorted working surfaces. Those surfaces look like bent versions of the heads of the incoming HH 270 jet.

Three-dimensional simulations test what kind of shearing surroundings could cause such a bend. A sideways flow speed of about thirty kilometres per second is needed to match the complex shape seen. Such speed could arise where other outflows have strongly stirred the region. The jet and shear layer reading thus fits both the images and the models.
arxiv-2501-13248:
Liangchen Zou studies a hard equation for flow through porous ground in a 2025 math paper. The equation is called the dissipative IPM equation, and it models how a fluid of mixed density moves through soil or rock. Some special solutions of the equation fade over time like heat spreading out.

Zou asks what happens when the starting state sits close to one of these special solutions. The main result proves that the equation then has a smooth solution that lasts for all time, with no blow-up. The proof covers two ranges of how strongly the fluid is damped. Results like this help show when fluid models stay well behaved and can be trusted.
arxiv-2501-13848:
Rezaei and co-authors predict where pedestrians will walk by reading the scene around them, not just their neighbors. Their 2025 paper targets safer self-driving cars, since walkers are the most fragile road users. Past models lean on person-to-person interaction and underuse the setting.

A sparse graph captures how walkers influence each other in space and time. Image enhancement and segmentation pull detailed scene features from the surroundings. A cross-attention step fuses scene and interaction cues, weighting what matters most. A temporal network then rolls the fused signal into future paths. Tests beat prior methods, with average and final errors near a quarter and a third of a meter. The authors credit the scene context for the gain.
arxiv-2501-14048:
Sneh Pandya and four co-authors adapt image classifiers across domains in twenty twenty-five. Neural networks falter under covariate shift, when test data comes from a different distribution. Labels still mean the same thing, but the inputs have changed style. Domain adaptation aims to learn features that ignore that change.

Their algorithm, SIDDA, aligns domains using the Sinkhorn divergence. It is built on equivariant neural networks for image classification. The selling point is minimal hyperparameter tuning and low computational overhead. Earlier adaptation methods often needed extensive tuning, which is costly. Tests ran on multiple simulated and real data sets. Readers in astronomy-adjacent machine learning get an out-of-the-box adaptation method that respects image symmetries.
arxiv-2501-14148:
Shuvendu Roy and Ali Etemad tune vision-language models with few labels in a 2025 paper. Such models link images with words and can sort new classes with little training. But when labels are scarce, the model must label the rest itself, a step called pseudo-labeling. Poorly set confidence makes those self labels noisy, and errors pile up.

Their method, SelfPrompt, groups unlabeled images into clusters to guide cleaner self labels. A confidence-aware module then mixes true-label learning with weak-label learning to use more of the unlabeled pool. A sampling trick picks a small, varied labeled set when the label budget is tight. Across 13 data sets, gains averaged above six percent in the main tests. Single-shot gains were larger still.
arxiv-2501-14348:
Zhengfa Bi and co-authors build seismic wavefields with a diffusion model in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Sparse sensors and sources make imaging the ground below hard, and full physics runs cost too much. Their model makes realistic wavefields with no prior knowledge of the rocks below.

The transformer model works in two stages. First it builds the strength pattern of the field from source and station traits. Then it refines the field by repeated phase fixes. Tests used data from a geothermal field in California. The made-up fields kept smooth spatial flow and matched real ones in strength and phase. The authors see uses in imaging and quake source studies.
arxiv-2501-14448:
Li-Yi Hsu, a solo author, measures how strong the correlations in a mixed quantum-classical network can get, in a 2025 theory paper. In a hybrid network, some sources are classical, some quantum, and some obey only the no-signaling rule of relativity. The maximal correlation strength is the network’s non-classical fingerprint.

Using the stabilizing tools of the matching all-quantum network, Hsu builds custom Bell tests tuned to its shared state. Benchmarks are then set for fully classical, fully quantum, and fully no-signaling versions of the same network. The achievable strength turns on how many of one measurement type and how many non-local sources the network holds. New criteria also mark when a network’s strength cannot be faked by a weaker design.
arxiv-2501-14648:
Leah Ajmani and co-authors argue that research with pushed-aside groups must guard each person's control of knowledge about the self. The work dates to 2025. They call this guard epistemic autonomy. Tech systems keep pushing such groups to the edge, the authors say, despite rich past work on justice.

The paper builds the idea from a trans care rule about self rule. Six short tales from two trans women show how harm looks when the guard is breached. The authors then shape the idea into a full research stance. They give two adapted methods that flow from it, and urge their field to lead the shift.
arxiv-2501-15148:
Muskan, Arindam Dutta, and Subhashish Banerjee study secret key sharing between small satellites and the ground, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The method uses faint light pulses to send keys that no spy can copy without being seen. Two variants are compared, a standard one with decoy pulses and a leaner efficient one.

The link from space is modeled with an oval beam shape, and weather effects are included. Both exact short-block key lengths and long-run rates are worked out. The leaner variant gave better key rates in all weather tested. The team also charts how key rates spread across passes. Readers who plan space links get a clear pick between the variants.
arxiv-2501-15348:
Mingyu Guan, Saumia Singhal, Taesoo Kim, and Anand Padmanabha Iyer present ReInc, a system that speeds up training for graph networks on changing data, in a 2025 paper. Dynamic graph networks serve tasks like traffic forecasting and epidemic modeling, but retraining them on snapshot after snapshot wastes work. ReInc reuses intermediate results and updates aggregations step by step as the graph changes, backed by a two-level cache tuned to the workflow.

A new distributed strategy also removes the chatter of fetching remote features and reshuffling partial results. Across several network designs and real datasets, training ran up to ten times faster than leading frameworks. The gains target large graphs that change over time.
arxiv-2501-15548:
Joep van Sloun examines in 2025 rationalizability in games where players lack full information about opponents. The catalog creator field is blank apart from an acknowledgment note, so the byline in the text governs here. Players hold beliefs about opponents' parameters, drawn from a given set of possible beliefs.

Cases range from one known belief to all possible beliefs, with middle cases allowed. Van Sloun adds an assumption linking choice beliefs and parameter beliefs. Under it, stronger beliefs lead to stronger optimal choices. The extreme rationalizable choices rise with the parameter. An iterative procedure pins down those extremes round by round.
arxiv-2501-15748:
Hiroshi Okada and Yuta Orikasa present a 2025 particle physics paper building a theory that explains neutrino masses and dark matter in one frame. The frame is a modular S3 flavor symmetry in a non-holomorphic form, which dictates how the lightest particles couple. Neutrino masses arise radiatively, generated at one loop rather than directly, the classic seesaw idea executed with loop diagrams.

The authors scan the theory against measured neutrino data with chi-square fits. Then they lay out predictions for four scenarios: normal or inverted mass ordering, with dark matter that is fermionic or bosonic. Lepton flavor violation, rare decays that the theory would permit at some rate, is analyzed alongside. The paper offers testable patterns for experiments hunting both effects.
arxiv-2501-15848:
Amartya Sengupta, Dejan Stojkovic, and De-Chang Dai compute doomsday's warning signs in twenty twenty-five. Measured parameters suggest our universe may sit in a false Higgs vacuum. Its lifetime is very long, but small black holes can catalyze decay. Bubbles of true vacuum might already exist somewhere.

If matter and plasma slow a bubble wall, its signals could arrive before the wall itself. The authors calculate the spectrum of Higgs particles produced as the wall reaches terminal velocity. Friction at that speed adds a large thermal population of Higgs bosons, which keeps growing after the first channel shuts off. The Higgs decays into products that could, in principle, be observed. Readers get a concrete answer to a morbid question: if the vacuum goes, would we see it coming?
arxiv-2501-16448:
Robin Young wrote this 2025 paper on two ways an AI system can fail its users. One failure is deception, where a system hides its true goals behind good-looking behavior. The other is drift, where a system's goals quietly slide away from what people intended.

Young uses information theory to draw a sharp line between the two. Deception, in the model, adds disorder between a system's real goals and what observers can see. Drift adds disorder between the goal people set and the goal the system holds. Because the two faults sit at different points, they call for different fixes. The paper offers this framing as a tool for thinking about safety in large language models.
arxiv-2501-16748:
Garima Chhikara, Abhishek Kumar, and Abhijnan Chakraborty present a 2025 paper testing how well large language models understand India's local cultures, not just its headline traditions. Models often echo dominant narratives and flatten minority practices. The authors probe the Little Traditions, the lived customs around caste, kinship, marriage, and religion that vary by place and community.

Through case studies they check whether models can hold both layers at once, the grand tradition and the local one. They also try prompting in regional languages to see if answers grow more sensitive. The models can voice cultural nuance, the authors find, but unevenly, and the paper maps where the understanding thins.
arxiv-2501-16848:
Ron van Bree, Diego Marcos, and Ioannis Athanasiadis blend physics and learning to predict tree dormancy in a 2025 paper. Fruit trees wake from winter rest when warmth accumulates, and growers plan around the bloom date. Classic heat-sum models exist in many rival forms and need refitting at every site. Pure learning models fit data well but ignore known biology.

Their hybrid grafts a neural network onto the classic models to absorb the gaps between forms. Tested on cherry bloom records from Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland, it beat both parents across years. The network also learned variety-level traits, so the model moved to new orchards without local refitting. Reliable bloom forecasts matter more as winters warm unevenly.
arxiv-2501-16948:
Alfusainey Jallow and Sven Bugiel present a 2025 arXiv paper on whether security research built on Stack Overflow data still holds as the site changes. Code snippets on the platform evolve, and the authors reviewed papers from 2005 to 2023 to find which traits of the data shift over time. Some traits proved non-stationary, which can flip conclusions when studies are rerun.

The team replicated six studies on a newer dataset. Four produced markedly different results, blocking the original conclusions. They advise treating Stack Overflow as a time series source, so that one-shot findings are always read against the moment the data were taken.
arxiv-2501-17148:
Zhengxuan Wu and colleagues benchmarked methods for steering language model behavior in a 2025 paper called AxBench. Fine-grained control matters for safety, and interpretability researchers have proposed steering through internal representations, sparse autoencoders chief among them, as an alternative to prompting and fine-tuning. No shared benchmark compared the contenders until AxBench, which grades both steering success and concept detection across two sizes of an open model family.

Prompting won at steering outright, with fine-tuning second, while simple representation methods like difference-in-means led concept detection. Sparse autoencoders, despite their popularity, were not competitive on either task. A new weakly supervised representation fine-tuning method matched the leaders while keeping interpretability that prompting lacks.
arxiv-2501-17348:
Mert Inan and eight co-authors argue for slow spots in chat AI in a 2025 paper. Most chat design chases smooth, fast talk with no drag. The authors warn that drag-free talk breeds blind trust: users take answers whole, with hidden guesses left unchecked and goals left vague.

Their cure is positive friction, set pauses that make users weigh their aim and the bot's reply. Such pauses, they hold, can sharpen goal fit, the bot's read of the user's mind, and task success. The paper lays out where to place the drag so talk slows just enough.
arxiv-2501-17648:
Igor Furtat, a solo author, studies in 2025 control of systems whose behavior is shaped by a density function that weighs the space they move in. Such a function can mark stable zones, forbidden zones with no solutions, and other regions that steer the system. The work asks how this lens can yield new adaptive control laws with fresh goals, such as holding outputs inside a set band.

Systems with known and unknown settings are treated, both under outside disturbance. New adaptive laws are derived that keep outputs in the chosen set. All results are shown in number simulations. The author offers density thinking as a design tool for control where safe regions matter more than single target points.
arxiv-2501-17748:
Jessy Ayala, Yu-Jye Tung, and Joshua Garcia published this research paper in 2025. It studies how security flaws in open-source software get reported, tracked, and fixed. The authors focus on two kinds of records: GitHub security advisories and bug bounty reports. These records sit between the people who find flaws and the projects that run the affected code.

The team studied 3,798 reviewed GitHub advisories and 4,033 disclosed bug bounty reports. They traced the path a flaw follows, from first report to the global databases and back to projects that need the fix. Missing or delayed CVE numbers often left projects unaware that an update was needed. The paper ends with practical steps and research ideas for making open-source software safer.
arxiv-2501-17848:
Fabrício Olivetti de França and Gabriel Kronberger speed up genetic programming, a method that evolves formulas to fit data. The search breeds and mutates candidate formulas over generations. A hidden waste plagues it: the same formula, or an equal twin in disguise, gets tested again and again.

Their fix keeps every visited formula in an equality graph, a store that holds all known equal forms compactly. Before a breeding step runs, the system checks which building blocks would rebuild something already seen, and filters those out. The adapted method, called eggp, shines for small formulas. On standard benchmark sets and real-world data, it matched strong rival systems while reliably returning short, accurate formulas, and without adding computing cost. Letting evolution keep unused parts in reserve still matters, the authors note, so the filter blocks only exact repeats.
arxiv-2501-17948:
Sean Jordan, Oliver Shorttle, and Paul Rimmer propose a way to map the inner edge of the habitable zone around other stars, in a 2025 paper. That zone marks where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface. Its inner edge has never been tested by observation.

Their idea uses sulfur gases, whose presence can reveal a dry surface more clearly than water can reveal a wet one. Models that couple climate and chemistry show the test depends on the star's ultraviolet light. Most small red stars are dim enough in ultraviolet for the test to work. A population search could define the zone from data.
arxiv-2501-18148:
Yoonha Cha and co-authors explore in 2025 why blind and low vision software workers build their own accessibility tools. Many shop-bought and in-house coding tools shut these workers out, which can hold back their part in projects and their careers. The study draws on interviews with thirty such professionals about the tools they make and use.

The homemade tools served many purposes. Workers said they wanted to keep a professional image and a sense of dignity at work, not just to get tasks done. The tools clearly improved access on the job, yet they stayed mostly private, shared person to person. The authors name the tension the Double Hacker Dilemma. They call for better shared spaces, both peer run and company backed, where such tools and tricks can spread.
arxiv-2501-18348:
Isaac C Radley and a large team of co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on a young multiple star system still forming, observed with three flagship facilities. The system, VLA 1623-2417, holds several protostars in close company. Combining the James Webb Space Telescope, the ALMA array, and the Very Large Array lets the team see it across many wavelengths at sharp detail.

Their study traces where the system's outflows start, how dust grains have grown in its disks, and why one disk looks unsettled. Young multiples are a test bed for how companion stars stir the material that will form planets. The multi-telescope view is the paper's core strength.
arxiv-2501-18648:
Ranjan Sapkota and four co-authors survey work from 2025 on using large multimodal models to grow training data. Such models can make or edit images, text, and speech, giving training sets more range and helping networks avoid overfitting. Older surveys cover classic machine learning methods or one data type at a time, leaving the new multimodal wave unmapped.

The survey sorts the methods by data type and walks through how each one works. It lists the limits of current practice, such as weak checks on made-up content, and gathers fixes proposed in the literature. A public list of the surveyed papers supports follow-up work.
arxiv-2501-18948:
Marios Constantinides and Daniele Quercia ask why AI at work aims so hard at replacing people. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Reward systems prize cost cuts above other gains. Patent records show task replacement dominating the agenda. Human-centered AI, which casts the tech as a partner, stays at the margins. Its principles rarely show up in patents or products.

The authors call this gap the automation trap. They argue the trap costs human agency and fairness. Their field, human-computer interaction, has been oddly absent from the fight. They propose steps to change the incentives inside that field. Support for translational research is one. Cross-disciplinary teamwork is another. The paper is a call to steer AI toward helping workers, not just cutting them.
arxiv-2501-19048:
Rita Pereira and co-authors build slide-read tools that can not cheat on stain hue, in a thesis from 2025. Whole-slide scans are now the gold for cancer calls, but their vast size and thin notes tax learn tools. Bag-style learn, MIL, skips patch notes; graph kin add place. Both can learn false cues, like stain tint shifts twixt labs.

The work sets graph builds, bag tools, and graph-bag blends side by side, then adds a train trick that breaks false cues. Its frame, GMIL-IT, pairs graph bags with that trick. Tests through lab-shift scenes grade which builds hold. True hold, not home-lab shine, is the bar: a call tool needs to read flesh, not dye.
arxiv-2501-19348:
Anne Josiane Kouam, Aline Carneiro Viana, Mariano Beiró, Leo Ferres, and Luca Pappalardo link how people move to how their phones chatter in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Data records from mobile networks give data on acts for services made for each person. Past work put traffic and mobility in sums apart, missing insight at the user level. The team models thirteen features per user spanning traffic and mobility points, in a frame that joins both over time.

User-specific signatures keep the spread of the group while showing dependencies between moving and talking. A Markov model then reads traffic acts from mobility, and mobility from traffic, keeping the dependencies that count and taking up privacy too. Checks used a week of records from over one point three million users in several Chilean provinces. The way proved sound at reading acts and matching mobility-traffic profiles across city settings.
arxiv-2502-00148:
Melo and co-authors study in a 2025 physics article what quantum resource powers the task of telling similar states apart. Some answers in the task may be 'not sure.' The best measurement splits into a sorting step and a final minimum-error step, with a fancier variant that reuses the unsure pile. They measure coherence, a wave-like property, under a broad class of measurements.

In the sorting step, that coherence splits into the helper state's own coherence plus a weaker link between system and helper. The fancy variant needs more coherence than the standard one, since it also reads the unsure pile. Coherence, they argue, is the more basic fuel here.
arxiv-2502-00248:
Li, Swensen, and Hosseinzadeh build nerve-net drives with proof they hold steady. Nets can steer bent sets that stump stock drive plans well. Yet past net drives lack proofs of firm hold or track grade. Wards and craft that need firm vows thus shun net drives. Their plan gives a step frame for bent sets of one class. The class is the bend form where drives add in straight sums.

Proofs show the loop holds firm with the net in place. States drift to a band near the aim point in due time. Band width can be tuned by the plan's free dials. A swung stick sim tests the frame in code runs. A Parrot Bebop 2 drone then tests it in real flight. Both tests back the vows the proofs lay out.
arxiv-2502-00748:
Barabash and co-authors measured, in a 2025 physics paper, a rare double decay of the isotope neodymium-150. In this decay, an atom sheds two electrons at once and lands in an excited state of samarium-150. Rates for such decays test how well nuclear theory handles weak forces.

The team watched a purified neodymium sample of 2.381 kilograms for 5.845 years in an underground lab in Italy. Sensitive germanium detectors caught the gamma rays shed as the samarium settled. The half-life for the path to the first excited level came out near ten to the twentieth power years. A second path to a higher level was also weighed. Both values match past measures and theory based on a standard nuclear model.
arxiv-2502-01448:
Reimann, Leite and their co-authors test whether telling users what a robot can do leads to more natural conversation in 2025. People who meet a robot often have no clear sense of its skills, and robots usually just apologize when talks go wrong.

In a live study, many participants held spoken chats with a social robot in a restaurant setting. Some robots shared their capabilities up front, some only when trouble arose, and some never did. Users preferred the up-front approach and enjoyed those chats more. They also shifted their own style to a more conversational one, the authors found.
arxiv-2502-01748:
Marta Bryan and Eve Lee ask when having a small inner planet predicts a giant outer one, and how the answer depends on the star. Earlier work found the link around metal-rich sun-like stars and its absence around metal-poor ones. The pair now adds eighty-five M-dwarfs hosting super-Earths and resolves the pattern across stellar mass and metal content.

Around M-dwarfs, giants are simply rarer around metal-poor stars, with no true correlation to inner planets either way. The real link switches on at metal-rich K-dwarfs and strengthens toward heavier stars. Giant properties matter too: hot or single giants drive the link for small stars, distant or multiple giants for big ones. The authors explain it through heavier stars' richer planet-building disks.
arxiv-2502-01948:
Kazuki Kamiido and Yutaka Ohira simulate shock waves racing through plasma so hot that relativity rules, in this 2025 study. Such shocks likely occur around the universe's most violent events, but whether they form and accelerate particles in hot plasma was unclear. Cold-plasma shocks were better understood.

Two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations followed an unmagnetized electron-positron plasma. The incoming flow was shredded by the Weibel instability, and a proper relativistic shock formed, much as in the cold case. Once distances were scaled by the temperature-aware inertial length, the shock's density and magnetic shapes barely depended on upstream heat. Pressure anisotropy settles to a finite level because of relativistic beaming. Fast particles emerged with a power-law energy spectrum, again mirroring cold shocks.
arxiv-2502-02048:
Georgios Margaritis, Periklis Petridis, and Dimitris Bertsimas adapt large AI models cheaply for specialized tasks in a 2025 paper. Foundation models that embed images and text are powerful, but fine tuning them needs heavy computing that places like hospitals often lack. Using them frozen, without adaptation, gives weaker results.

Their method keeps the big models frozen and trains only a small nonlinear projection, using contrastive learning to align the embeddings with the task. Across several downstream tasks, this light procedure improved performance significantly while adding minimal computing cost. The authors pitch it as a practical bridge for high standard fields with scarce hardware, such as healthcare, where diagnosis and treatment planning support must run on site.
arxiv-2502-02148:
Christopher Hemmens and Stephan Robert-Nicoud ask whether pure linear algebra can build perfect knockoffs, the fake data columns used to test which variables truly matter. Their 2025 paper works in the Model-X knockoff framework, where each real variable gets a synthetic twin that mimics its ties to the others without copying its link to the outcome. Most work aims at sampling the twins from the right distribution.

Judged by the average absolute correlation between twins and originals, their construction reaches near-perfect quality. The catch is cost: the optimizing routine is very slow. The pair then lay out a series of shortcuts that cut the run time sharply. The note maps a trade between knockoff quality and computing budget that method builders can exploit.
arxiv-2502-02548:
Junha Lee and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a foundation data set and model for labeling 3D scenes in open words. A good 3D learner needs precise region masks, rich text for each region, and scale. Their pipeline borrows top image segmentation and vision-language tools to stamp out mask-text pairs on its own. Run over several scene collections, it yielded over thirty thousand scenes with millions of labeled regions.

On that data they train a model that pairs a 3D encoder with a light mask decoder. It tops rival systems on standard tests for naming and separating objects in scanned rooms. Tests that strip parts of the system away confirm the big auto-made data set is a main source of the gain. The work gives robots and AR tools a broader visual vocabulary.
arxiv-2502-02648:
Adway Kumar Das, Anandamohan Ghosh, and Lea F Santos present a 2025 physics paper on the hidden order in the energy levels of banded random matrices. Such matrices, with entries fading away from the diagonal, model heavy atomic nuclei and disordered quantum systems. Textbook wisdom said their nonergodic phase lacks energy correlations even at short range.

Using three probes that sense short- and long-range patterns, the authors show weak long-range correlations survive there after all. They also derive when correlations switch on and when the key diagnostic curve flattens into its plateau. One surprise: at the longest times the behaviour can defy the standard picture. The results refine how physicists read chaos from spectra.
arxiv-2502-02748:
Jianan Nie and co-authors build a net in a 2025 paper that reads crystals in their echo space. To guess a crystal traits from its form is a core task in stuff science. Crystals repeat without end, so a good read must catch both the near bond and the far wave of the whole.

Past nets read the near well and the far poorly. Their net draws a wave sum from the crystal grid marks and lets learnable filters shape it, then blends that far read with a near graph read. Stuff teams gain a model that hears the whole choir, not just the front row.
arxiv-2502-02948:
Sung-Soo Byun and Eui Yoo study random matrices whose values spread into shapes with different topologies. Their 2025 paper uses elliptic Ginibre ensembles, a standard family of random matrices with complex entries. They fix one value of the matrix in advance, like planting a charge at a chosen point.

As the matrix grows huge, its values fill a droplet shape in the plane. The team shows the droplet takes exactly three forms: one solid piece, one piece with a hole, or two separate pieces. They map which settings of charge, multiplicity, and non-Hermiticity give each form. For two of the forms they give the droplet's exact outline and energy. A result on polynomial moments follows as a bonus.
arxiv-2502-03348:
Mark Lewis and Shannon Tefft study a simple number game played on lists of residues. Their 2025 paper defines a map that replaces each entry with the sum of itself and the next entry, wrapping around at the end and working modulo m. Repeating the map always lands in a cycle. The length of that cycle is the period of the starting list.

The question is which period lengths can actually occur. The authors map out the possible values across different lengths and moduli. They also give conditions on a starting list that force its period to fall short of the maximum. The results add structure to a puzzle that blends basic number theory with repeated maps.
arxiv-2502-03648:
Istvan Balazs and Abel Garab study in 2025 a whole number score for looped systems of delay equations. In such systems, each part feeds the next and the past state shapes the present. Delays can shift with time or with the state itself.

Their score counts sign flips in the parts of a solution path. Under set feedback rules, the score holds the same good traits shown for fixed delay cases. It also holds for the one part case known from past work. The team then applies the score to state based delay cases, which widens its use.
arxiv-2502-03948:
Learning online means hunting through videos, code, documents, and the open web, and Devansh Srivastav and five co-authors build a team of software agents to do the hunting. Their early-stage system gives each kind of resource its own specialist agent: one for video tutorials, one for code repositories, one for documentation, and one for general search.

The agents retrieve material and a generation step stitches it into answers, sparing learners the manual work of gathering and combining sources. A preliminary user study rated the system highly for usability and moderately to highly for usefulness. The authors present the poster work as evidence that dividing retrieval among specialists can make knowledge arrive faster for online learners.
arxiv-2502-04448:
L Harvey and co-authors hunt fast-moving silicon lines in the spectra of exploding white dwarf stars, in a 2025 paper. Type Ia supernovae show a silicon band whose shape splits some events in two: a slow photospheric part and a high-velocity wing. The wing's source is murky, stray matter near the star or clumps in the blast itself, and it could betray how the star died. A fresh data release gave hundreds of early spectra to test.

Fitting each band with a careful statistical sieve, the team found the wing in 85 of 329 spectra. Early on, about three quarters of spectra before the eleventh day carried it, dropping to a third near peak light. Wings far from the photosphere's speed faded first. Twins with and without wings matched on every light and host trait, hinting the wing is near-universal, seen or missed by angle and phase.
arxiv-2502-05248:
Pranav Bhandari and co-authors test personality in language models in a 2025 paper. Psychologists use questionnaires to map human traits such as openness and extraversion. The team asked whether large language models show stable trait patterns when given the same tools.

They used the Big Five Inventory, a standard trait questionnaire, across varied scenarios. Care was taken to guard against the models simply recalling the test from training data. Results showed each model had a distinct profile, with its own dominant traits across the five dimensions. Even models from the same family differed from one another. The authors present the profiles as a window on model behaviour, while noting that machine answers to human questionnaires need careful reading.
arxiv-2502-05448:
Jingyi Wu and Chao Ning propose a robust control method for robots in this 2025 paper. Model predictive control plans moves ahead of time using a model of the system. Gaussian process models are common, but they struggle when disturbances have more than one mode. Real world disturbances often do.

Their method mixes several Gaussian processes, one for each mode found in the data. Each mode gives a mean and spread, which build a data driven set of plausible disturbances. Safety limits are then set to hold across that set. The math is reshaped into a form that solvers can handle fast. Tests on a quadrotor showed lower closed loop cost than prior methods, with proof of stable control.
arxiv-2502-05548:
Mahdi Teimouri published this sports analytics paper in 2025. Judging a soccer goalkeeper on penalty kicks usually rests on simple counts of saves. Those counts miss a real skill: reading the kick early and jumping the right way. Teimouri proposes four new measures built on clustering, a method that groups similar events together. The measures score both the kicks a keeper actually saves and the kicks where he at least chose the correct direction.

He tested the measures on goalkeepers from four important matches. The results lined up with what the measures were designed to capture. The fourth measure is the novel one, since it credits correct direction reading even when the ball still goes in. The paper suggests using these scores alongside the usual save statistics. Together they give coaches a fuller picture of a keeper's penalty performance.
arxiv-2502-05648:
The puzzle game Lights Out asks players to toggle a grid into darkness, each press flipping a light and its neighbors. Gabe Cunningham and Igor Minevich ask what happens when the lights are replaced by elements of an arbitrary group. In their version, a click multiplies a vertex and its neighbors by a chosen group element. The set of reachable configurations then forms a group of its own.

For many graphs, which they call reducible to abelian, the whole problem collapses to integer linear algebra no matter which group is used. The authors build five nested subgroups from commutators and give methods to prove a graph family reducible, including a test using Heisenberg groups that settles the question exactly. Odd-dimensional cubes and certain folded cubes turn out not reducible, marking the boundary of the tidy theory.
arxiv-2502-06048:
Jonas Schmidt, Shaily Verma, and Nadym Mallek open a new front in the hunt for secluded graph structures. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A secluded subgraph is large, well-behaved, and barely connected to the rest. The undirected version has been studied for years. Directed graphs, where edges have arrows, were untouched. Jansen and others had flagged the gap.

Three neighborhood notions arise from the arrows. In-neighbors, out-neighbors, and their union each define a variant. The authors map the parameterized complexity of each. Tractability depends on the property sought and the neighbor budget. Algorithms and hardness results fill the map. Directed network analysis gains a formal notion of quiet corners.
arxiv-2502-06248:
Soot rings drifting between the stars soak up stray carbon, and what happens next shapes the gas around them. Alain Omont and Holger Bettinger work the chemistry in 2025 for one model ring, coronene, standing in for its bigger kin. Their sums map the shapes a caught carbon can take on the ring: new small rings, a spike chain, or a wedge driven into a bond. The charged and plain forms show much the same menu.

Under starlight and hydrogen hits, small dressed rings seem apt to shed a two-carbon scrap again and again. That shed feeds the small carbon goods labs see in bright clouds. Big rings are murkier, the pair grant, and the paths need their energy hills mapped. A side tale may matter too: dressed rings that settle keep a five-sided scar.
arxiv-2502-06448:
Benjamin Burridge and co-authors pin down the distance to a black hole system in a 2025 paper. The system, a black hole feeding from a companion star, lies in our own galaxy, and its distance shapes every other estimate about it.

Radio data from a South African telescope measured how fast neutral hydrogen along the line of sight moves, giving a firm lower bound near 3.6 kiloparsecs. Ultraviolet spectra from a space telescope fixed how much starlight the dust between us and the system dims. Feeding that into simulations, and assuming the companion is an ordinary small star, gave a distance near 5.5 kiloparsecs. That value implies the black hole was born with a strong kick from an uneven explosion.
arxiv-2502-06748:
Qiankun Zhong and co-authors let lab groups rewrite their own game rules in a 2025 paper. Getting groups to adopt cooperative norms is a lasting puzzle. Real people act within rules and also act upon them.

Players here could shift the features of the games they played. Stability, efficiency, and fairness of the setup varied apart. That gave groups second order agency over the rules themselves. The ask was if such dynamism helps or hinders cooperation. Past transfer learning work hints feature play cuts both ways. The lab frame tests if prosocial tweaks steer groups to shared wins.
arxiv-2502-07148:
Jan Bergstra and John Tucker show how two facts for chance, called entropy and cross-entropy, can be writ in a class of fields called common meadows. Such a field adds a rule that makes split by zero give a set base mark. The team adds a base two log for all inputs and aids such as a sign rule.

In these fields, entropy for chance spread on a finite set of picks takes the form of a short term built from field rules. No split by case is need, and no tricks to dodge gaps are need. The text weighs gains of meadow rules next to other ways. The aim is facts for chance that hold for all inputs, writ as one term each.
arxiv-2502-07348:
Michael Lau and Olivier Mathieu study representations of a Lie algebra built from Jordan algebras, and use them to probe free Jordan algebras, in a 2025 math paper. Jordan algebras are a non-associative cousin of matrix algebras. The construction at hand extends the familiar sl2 symmetry using any Jordan algebra, with a universal central extension.

The authors sort the module category for this algebra, defining dominant spaces that play the role of highest weights. They build a family of universal enveloping algebras and prove finiteness results. For augmented Jordan algebras they define smooth modules, whose standard members are finite-dimensional when the algebra is finitely generated. Then comes the twist: deep theorems of Zelmanov about free Jordan algebras block a tempting classification. The smooth category for free algebras on two or more generators, they prove, cannot be a generalized highest weight category.
arxiv-2502-07948:
De Gaetano asks a deceptively simple question: what exactly is a mathematical model, and how does it connect to the real thing it stands for? Modeling is everywhere, from physics to economics to medicine, yet practitioners usually define their models by habit — equations whose parts feel like pieces of reality. No crisp definition of the model itself, or of its link to the phenomenon, had been set down. The paper proposes one.

In the author's framing, a model is an operator on a space of random variables. Running an experiment is then the map between the abstract space where models are built and the working space where statisticians fit them to data. The geometry carries across: the curved surface of possible models matches the prediction surfaces used in estimation. For applied mathematicians, the payoff is a common language for what modeling does.
arxiv-2502-08048:
Shao leads a team of twelve, plus one more author named in its text, on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It fires a fast laser at a long thin metal wire to launch strong terahertz surface waves down its length.

The waves, surface plasmon polaritons, ride both ways from the hit point for a long span. Each pulse is a single cycle with great peak power. The share of laser energy turned into waves sets a record high. The team shows the waves come from coherent transition radiation of electrons the laser knocks free. Particle and field simulations back the read. The gear is a common lab laser, so the route could feed uses that need very strong single-cycle terahertz waves.
arxiv-2502-08148:
Vy Vo and co-authors published this machine learning paper in 2025. It introduces ACCESS, a benchmark for finding and reasoning about cause-and-effect links between everyday events at an abstract level. Existing tests lean on surface word cues and falter on new material. ACCESS instead builds causal graphs over generalized events, such as types of actions rather than one specific story.

The team mined a large dataset of implicit commonsense knowledge to form event abstractions, then extracted about 1,400 causal pairs. Experiments with statistical methods and language models showed that both abstraction finding and causal discovery remain hard. Even so, feeding models the abstract causal knowledge from ACCESS improved their answers on question-answering tasks. The authors offer the benchmark as a harder, more realistic test of causal reasoning in language technology.
arxiv-2502-08348:
Samuel Brookes and three colleagues present a 2025 chemistry study watching carbon dioxide turn into acid exactly at the water's surface. The reaction drives ocean acidification and matters for carbon storage, yet its behavior at the air-water boundary was unclear. Using machine-learned atomic potentials, the team simulated the molecular dance at the interface.

They found an in-and-out mechanism: a carbon dioxide molecule slips into the surface layer, reacts with water to form carbonic acid, and the product is then expelled. The surface layer solvates much like bulk water, so the energy profile nearly matches the deep-water reaction.
