The authors say the interface is an extra, equally viable reaction site, likely speeding overall acidification.
arxiv-2502-08448:
Albert Kjøller Jacobsen and Georgios Arvanitidis present a 2025 paper on finding flat spots in a neural network's loss landscape. Flat minima tend to generalize better to new data. A popular method, sharpness-aware minimization, hunts them by stepping toward a worst-case nearby point. That step uses plain distance, so renaming the parameters can change the answer.

Their variant, Monge SAM, measures distance with a curved metric drawn from the loss surface itself. The method then gives the same result under any reparameterization. It costs about the same to run as the original. Theory places it between the original and plain gradient descent. That middle ground resists bad tuning and avoids saddle traps, the authors show on an alignment task.
arxiv-2502-08548:
Zhe Zhang, Young Kwark, Srinivasan Raghunathan, and Peng Wang ask, in twenty twenty-five, whether splitting advertising from e-commerce platforms would help society. Big platforms now both host third-party sellers and sell top search slots as ads. Regulators worry that this dual role favors the platform and sellers over shoppers, and propose a split. The authors model the split and find the opposite pattern in key ways. Sellers gain from a split, shoppers lose, and total welfare does not necessarily rise.

A key driver is targeting precision. A standalone ad firm lives only on ad revenue. It has less or equal incentive to sharpen targeting than a platform that also earns marketplace commission. Sharper targeting softens price competition, which lifts commission but hurts the contest for ad slots.
arxiv-2502-09048:
Priya Dhawka and Sayamindu Dasgupta interview the people who chart demographic data for a living. Charts of race and gender shape public debate, and scholars increasingly treat every chart as a social product, not a neutral window. Most studies, though, had asked audiences rather than makers. The authors sat down with seventeen practitioners who visualize such data and traced how they think about their own influence.

Designers described a tangle of forces: personal history, values, and views about power, neutrality, and politics all entered their choices. They wrestled with category labels they did not choose and with the risk that a clean chart could harden the very divisions it showed. The authors close with implications for research and practice, urging tools and training that help practitioners make those hidden choices deliberately.
arxiv-2502-09248:
Four authors led by Dana El Hajjar speed up a radar image step that lines up wave phases across a stack of shots. Satellites such as Sentinel-1 now send down huge stacks of radar images of the same ground. Phase linking cleans the stack so ground shift can be read with care. Classic tools for the step cost too much at this scale, and a leaner frame still leans on the full data table at once.

Their fix folds each new block of images into the fit in turn, not the whole stack at once. The math works on a torus shape, since phase values wrap around a full turn. A stepwise shrink method keeps each update sound and fast. New shots can thus join the fit the day they land. Ground watch teams gain a tool that keeps pace with the fleet.
arxiv-2502-09548: Petr Satunin constrains Lorentz violation from a neutrino event in two thousand twenty five. KM3NeT recorded an ultra high energy event, KM3-230213A, and superluminal neutrinos would have split before reaching the detector. Assuming an extragalactic source, the absence of splitting pushes the linear violation scale above ten to the thirtieth GeV and the quadratic scale above ten to the nineteenth GeV.
arxiv-2502-09848:
Deependra Jadoun, Upendra Harbola, Vladimir Chernyak, and Shaul Mukamel model how entangled photon pairs absorb as the pump that makes them grows stronger. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats parametric down-conversion without the usual weak-pump shortcut. A non-perturbative frame handles pumps of any strength. Multi-point field correlations then feed nonlinear spectroscopy signals.

Glauber's correlation function reads the photon statistics. Entanglement time and pump intensity jointly shape those signals. Two-photon absorption grows from linear to strongly nonlinear with pump strength, not the linear-to-quadratic path past work claimed. Wider pump bandwidth stretches the linear zone. The team proposes a lab scheme that keeps only the entangled-photon part of the signal. Filtering out stray photons would let entanglement effects show at high pump power.
arxiv-2502-10148:
Zhiyuan Li, Wenshuai Zhao, and Joni Pajarinen present a 2025 paper on teams of AI agents that plan together using vision and language. Standard multi-agent learning is slow to train, hard to read, and poor at new tasks. Language models plan well, but past uses leaned on text alone and missed the shifting, partly hidden nature of team tasks.

Their system builds and refines plain, readable code strategies, stored in a skill library seeded by expert demos. A structured message chain passes facts about entities between agents, so the team shares one picture. On a hard battle benchmark, the system beat top rivals by a wide margin in one match type.
arxiv-2502-10348:
Adam Górkiewicz and Adam Karczmarz keep shortest paths current in directed graphs that only gain edges. Road and network graphs change over time, and recomputing all routes after each new edge is wasteful. Their data structures maintain near-exact shortest paths between every pair of nodes under insertions, even when an adaptive opponent chooses which edges arrive. Earlier structures against such opponents were much slower.

For sparse graphs, their deterministic version and a randomized version both cut the total update cost by a polynomial factor. The core trick is a near-optimal structure for the special case where every new edge touches the source node. They also give a simple offline version, which settles all updates after seeing them in full. That offline result rules out some hoped-for proofs that online structures cannot be fast.
arxiv-2502-10548:
Inside warm dense matter, atoms sit partly ionized, and how much energy ionization takes shapes everything else the plasma does. Many models predict that energy drop, called ionization potential depression, but they disagree widely. Michael Bonitz and Linda Kordts discuss a newer route in 2025, built on first-principles quantum Monte Carlo simulations and first shown on hydrogen. They give special attention to the Fermi barrier, a threshold an electron must cross when it leaves its atom.

The barrier matters more as the nuclear charge grows, and older models often miss it. The authors present the simulation approach as a firmer base for predicting how dense plasmas behave in stars and in fusion experiments.
arxiv-2502-10748:
Aamir Rashid and Jishnu Aryampilly study how noncommutative geometry reshapes the quantum states of light, in a 2025 paper. Such deformations tweak the rules of position and momentum, and even well-known optical states bend under the change. Coherent states, the most classical light states, are their starting point.

Using the oscillator's raising and lowering tools, the authors build a deformed coherent state tied to the deformation's size. From it they derive deformed squeezed states and then photon-added coherent states. The key question is whether the quantum character survives the change. They probe it through the Mandal parameter, a standard witness of non-classical light. The results show how bent geometry echoes into traits a lab can measure.
arxiv-2502-10848:
Jirka Lhotka and Daniel Probst set out a new way to depict molecules: as continuous vector-valued functions set by neural networks. Molecules have many past forms for compute work. They range from descriptors and strings to graphs, point clouds, and surfaces. Each form opens its own family of machine learning methods.

The team calls their form molecular neural fields. In contrast to surface forms, neural fields catch both the outer traits of a molecule and the hydrophobic core of large molecules such as proteins. In contrast to graphs or points, they are compact. They do not rest on a fixed grid size, and they fit well with blending in space and time. The paper gives a frame and proofs of concept. One rebuilds a protein-ligand complex at superresolution with an auto-decoder.
arxiv-2502-10948:
Steéphane Tchuiaga studies how smooth maps act on currents and forms in a 2025 maths paper. The work looks at compact curved spaces and asks what happens when the maps change with very weak control. It uses tools from shape study, measure, and the study of paths and loops.

Inside, the author proves when pulled-back forms settle to one limit and when pushed currents settle in a weak sense. Pushed currents that can be cut into fine pieces settle in the flat norm, a fact that helps with rough shapes. The results also bear on groups of maps that keep volume or keep key forms fixed.
arxiv-2502-11248:
Zhiyi Chen and co-authors measured how much of the political imagery around the 2024 United States election was made by AI, in a 2025 paper. Using a large dataset from the platform X, they detected AI-generated images in about twelve percent of shared election images. Sharing was lopsided: roughly ten percent of users posted eighty percent of the synthetic images. The heaviest spreaders, who also drew strong engagement, skewed toward premium subscriptions and right-leaning profiles.

Many superspreader profiles were themselves heavy with AI images, and some showed automated behavior. Their AI posts drew more positive and less toxic replies than their ordinary posts. The authors call the study an early map of synthetic media in a live election. They draw lessons for platform governance, from labeling to superspreader monitoring.
arxiv-2502-11548:
Koki Yanagida, a solo author, defines a new topological invariant in a 2025 mathematics paper. Starting from a finite group, he builds an invariant of odd dimensional closed oriented shapes. It is modeled on the Dijkgraaf Witten invariants of physics but formulated through K theory, the branch of topology that tracks vector bundle data.

Yanagida then computes the invariant for a famous family of shapes, the Brieskorn homology spheres. He uses a specific matrix group over a finite field as the input group. He remarks that neither the shapes' fundamental groups nor the chosen group are nilpotent, making the computation notable. The paper adds a K theoretic entry to the catalog of manifold invariants.
arxiv-2502-11948:
A language model can slip one invented name into an otherwise accurate page, and sentence-level detectors miss the forgery. Min-Hsuan Yeh and co-authors build a benchmark that hunts at the level of single entities. Their dataset, HalluEntity, marks which specific names and facts in a text are hallucinated. They then test uncertainty-based detection methods across seventeen modern language models.

Methods that judge single-token probabilities tend to cry wolf, flagging too much. Context-aware methods do better but remain far from reliable. A close qualitative study links hallucination habits to linguistic patterns in the output. The findings point toward detectors that weigh whole contexts, not isolated tokens. For long texts that mix truth and invention, entity-level checking is where the real problem lives.
arxiv-2502-12048:
Shreya Shukla and co-authors survey in 2025 work that turns brain wave recordings into images, text, and sound with generative AI. Note that the head byline lists more authors than the catalog field. Decoding brain activity into readable output is a central aim of brain-computer interfaces. They searched major databases for studies from 2017 to 2025 and extracted methods, data sets, and metrics.

Image models mostly use encoder-decoder designs with adversarial, variational, or diffusion methods. Text decoding leans on transformer language models. Audio methods map signals to spectrograms, then render sound. Small, varied data sets and weak cross-person generalization remain the field's main limits.
arxiv-2502-12348:
Hassan Jafari Ozoumchelooei and Mehdi Hosseinzadeh harden a fore-cast drive law for weak-chip rigs in a 2025 paper on control. The law calls moves by live maths, which taxes small chips in real runs at hand. Short sight spans ease that tax but can shrink the safe pull zone for the rig.

A rest-aware form of the law tracks a set end state with bounds kept at all times. That form adds no fresh tax, yet past takes skip storm hits from the world round it. Their work folds such hits into the law's frame for real use.
arxiv-2502-12748:
Jan Moser, a solo author, reports new equivalent forms of a famous theorem in a 2025 paper. The Fermat-Wiles theorem, once Fermat's Last Theorem, states that a sum of two like powers beyond squares can never equal a third such power. Moser works with objects called Jacob's ladders, built from the Riemann zeta function, a central tool in the study of prime numbers.

The paper obtains fresh sets of statements that stand or fall with the theorem. Alongside, it draws asymptotic links between those statements, families of Dirichlet series, certain partial sums, the zeta function, and the ladders themselves. The abstract is terse and the argument is aimed at analytic number theorists. Readers meet a web of equivalences rather than a new proof of the theorem itself.
arxiv-2502-12848:
Proving a security protocol correct on paper invites human error, so Matteo Busi, Riccardo Focardi, and Flaminia Luccio mechanised a classic proof framework inside a proof assistant. Their system, StrandsRocq, rebuilds strand-space theory faithfully in machine-checked logic, adding modular design and custom tactics that automate the repetitive steps analysts once ground through by hand.

A new notion, the maximal penetrator, lets proofs compose: secure pieces can be assembled into secure wholes. The team verified a family of authentication protocols, including a two-pass standard design and the famous Needham-Schroeder-Lowe protocol. Mechanisation exposed several flaws in the original paper proofs and sharpened a static analysis for a key-management interface. The authors distil the minimal conditions each protocol truly needs.
arxiv-2502-13648:
Youna Kim and co-authors introduce UniKnow in 2025, a framework for testing how language models handle knowledge. A model may rely on what it learned in training, on facts given to it from outside, or on both. Trouble starts when those sources clash, distract, or lack the needed fact, and older tests rarely covered all three cases at once.

UniKnow sets up controlled tests across those knowledge cases and adds new methods built to be aware of which case applies. Tests showed that current methods often fail to carry across cases and lean toward one type of situation. The framework gives researchers a shared base for checking and improving how models use knowledge in a reliable way.
arxiv-2502-13748:
Zhiqiang Wei tackles, in 2025, a geometry problem about placing a curved sphere with two cone-like points into ordinary three-dimensional space without stretching. The sphere's surface has constant positive curvature except at the two singular points. The question of which such surfaces can be realized in space was posed as an open problem by three geometers.

Wei builds a geometric correspondence between these singular metrics and surface placements in space. An explicit family of surfaces is constructed, each carrying constant curvature and two conical points. The construction gives a partial solution to the named problem. A full classification remains open, and this family marks concrete progress.
arxiv-2502-13948:
Rujuta Purohit, Ryan Hickox, and Grayson Petter hunt for the lowest-mass black holes feeding in small galaxies in a 2025 paper. The Boötes field is a well-studied patch of sky. Galaxies with low stellar mass may host black holes that barely grew since they formed in the early universe, preserving clues about how the first black holes were seeded.

The team analyzed three candidate active nuclei found by their X-ray glow, using data across many wavelengths. Confirming such faint activity is hard because star formation can mimic it. Better counts of small-galaxy black holes pin down what share of them host any black hole at all, a basic census number for galaxy evolution theory.
arxiv-2502-14048:
Karl John Villardar presents two text-processing techniques meant to make language-model systems more context-aware. Semantic Decomposition breaks a prompt step by step into a structured, layered schema that software can parse without guesswork. Selective Context Filtering then strips out the sections of context that do not bear on the task at hand.

Together, he argues, the pair can serve as a dynamic bridge between a language model and the systems around it. Responses should hang together better, and automated pipelines should waste less effort on irrelevant text. The paper is a design proposal, laying out the techniques and the uses he foresees for them in context-driven applications.
arxiv-2502-14548:
Leandro Intelisano, Heiko Damerau, and Ivan Karpov study in 2025 when a stabilizing effect for particle beams is lost in systems that use two radio frequencies. This damping effect keeps beam oscillations in check, and it vanishes when a joined mode rises out of the spread of single particle rhythms. Their work extends recent studies to the double frequency case used in large accelerators.

In one common setup, they show the threshold for loss can vanish for a standard particle spread, just as in the single frequency case. New formulas account for the voltage ratio and phase between the two systems. Beam measures in two CERN synchrotrons, plus two simulation tools, support the theory across varied filling patterns.
arxiv-2502-14748:
Sorting a mountain of documents into topics is a classic library task, and a 2025 paper by Zongxia Li and co-authors tests whether language models do it better than old topic models. Under the head's title, the study is framed as a human-in-the-loop evaluation of how much users actually learn from each approach.

Users explored two data sets with three setups: raw language model topics, language model topics with human guidance, and the classic LDA method. The model-made topics read more smoothly and won more head-to-head comparisons. But on narrow, expert corpora they came out bland and taught users little. Human guidance fixed much of that at the cost of more effort, while LDA stayed plain but effective.
arxiv-2502-14848:
Jianwen Luo and co-authors present GATE, a system that lets language models build a toolbox and keep improving it across tasks. Earlier tool-making frameworks assembled unreliable toolsets and handled one task type at a time. GATE organizes tools as a layered graph that grows and adapts as scenarios arrive, so a tool forged for one job can be refined and reused instead of rebuilt.

Tests spanned open-ended Minecraft play, agent benchmarks, and code generation on math and table problems. GATE finished Minecraft milestones up to 4.3 times faster than the best system, and beat other methods by nine to ten percent on the other suites. The authors credit the balance the graph keeps between tool count, complexity, and usefulness. Code and data are public. The work pushes agents from using fixed tools toward maintaining an evolving kit, much as experts accumulate technique.
arxiv-2502-15248:
Chandan Sheemar and four co-authors explore holographic surfaces for systems that communicate and sense at once. Merging the two jobs on one platform saves spectrum and hardware. Reconfigurable holographic surfaces can shape beams with fine resolution while also reading the environment.

The authors first derive exact accuracy bounds for estimating direction angles in three dimensions. They then pose a joint design problem: raise the data rate while lowering those error bounds. The problem is highly non convex, so they build an iterative method around simpler surrogate functions with closed forms. Simulations across settings validate the approach. The framework targets next generation systems that must talk and perceive together.
arxiv-2502-15448:
Paul Koch, Marian Schlüter, and Jörg Krüger set out MVIP, a data set for naming factory parts from many views and many senses at once. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The set joins tuned color-and-depth views with facts on each part: its traits, a plain-words note, and its broad class. Past sets give many forms, but factory tasks have their own hard marks. Training data can be scant or huge, parts can look near the same, and sizes vary. Yet the use needs near-full care in the top five picks, at low cost and time. The team gives both the set and ways tuned to those bars.
arxiv-2502-15548:
Victorita Dolean, Antoine Tonnoir, and Pierre-Henri Tournier wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on a split-domain method to solve wave equations in a waveguide, a pipe. The equations are those of Maxwell, for light-like waves. Their computations make vast, skewed systems that strain single-machine solutions. The split method cuts the pipe into strips and solves each strip, with exchanges at the cuts.

The team studies the weak scalability of the split method: does it hold as strips grow in count? Their framework weds two tools: the limit spectrum of a known matrix type, and the mode decomposition of the wave solutions themselves. It takes in waveguides of broad cross-section shape, and transmission rules of more than one kind. Numerical tests show the limit spectrum predicts the true behavior well, with few strips. The split can stay robust as the wave number climbs, at set strip choices.
arxiv-2502-15648:
Kevin Raina proposes a sharper uncertainty score for spotting out-of-place data, in a 2025 paper. Bayesian neural networks spread their bets across many settings, and their doubt should flare on inputs unlike the training set. The standard doubt split often underperforms the cruder total score, a standing puzzle.

Raina measures disagreement among the network's pre-final outputs, the logits, after a correction drawn from related work. Three scores built this way estimate the knowledge-based part of doubt directly. Across a range of detection tests they beat the usual information score clearly and match it elsewhere. Better doubt estimates matter wherever models must say they do not know, from clinics to self-driving stacks.
arxiv-2502-15748:
Reza Ameri and Behnam Afshar study the prime spectrum of hyperrings in a 2025 paper. Hyperrings generalize rings by letting sums land in sets of values. Their prime ideals can be arranged into a space with a Zariski topology, the same style of geometry used for ordinary rings. The authors prove links between the shape of that space and the algebra of the hyperring.

They also show that a strong regularity relation on such hyperrings can serve as a congruence. That lets them build a topology on the set of such relations and compare it with the Zariski one. The effect of basic relations on the topology is studied as well.
arxiv-2502-15848:
Markus Hovd and co-authors introduced in 2025 a faster algorithm for estimating drug response distributions across a patient population. In population pharmacokinetics, knowing the full spread of parameters, not just averages, guides dosing. A prior algorithm from their group was accurate but explored the parameter space in an ad hoc way, wasting cycles.

The new algorithm uses gradient information to propose promising points, cutting the cycles and runtime needed to converge. On two data sets it reached solutions matching the older method. The authors see it as a step toward robust, quick dosing decisions, while noting more work is needed to map when each algorithm wins.
arxiv-2502-15948:
Caterina Neef and Anja Richert compare a social robot with a screen-based virtual agent for long-term health monitoring at home. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Both interfaces aim to keep older adults engaged with health checks over time.

Older adults used one of the two systems on their own at home for eight weeks. They could choose which interface to evaluate. Impressions were taken at the start and the end. The robot came across as somewhat more likable. The virtual agent was judged more intelligent. The authors offer the results as a base for designing home health systems that people will keep using, weighing warmth against perceived smarts.
arxiv-2502-16148:
Shu-Cheng Chang, Fengjiang Li, and co-authors study shrink states of a bent flow on Sasaki shapes, in a 2025 math paper. Such states model pinch points of the flow as it runs. Base laws for the states had to be set first to read their traits.

Core laws fall out, and bound reads plus a plus sign for curve mass come next. Two tests mark when such a state must be cross stiff in full. Low span states with flat curve mass must match the round Einstein form. States with even Weyl curve are sphere shares at most. Shape flows gain firm pinch rules here.
arxiv-2502-16348:
S. Kiana Naghibzadeh and colleagues simulated solids that grow or melt at their surfaces in a 2025 mechanics paper. Surface growth, adding or removing mass at a boundary, drives tissue growth, freezing, and additive manufacturing, and its coupling to stress can trigger failure or pattern formation. Lagrangian simulations that track material points struggle here, needing rebuilt reference shapes and constant remeshing as the body changes.

Their method describes growth in a fixed Eulerian frame and couples it to a phase-field description of the body. A finite element solver then works on one fixed grid throughout. The approach handles large deformations without the moving-domain headaches, opening complex growth-and-stress settings to routine simulation.
arxiv-2502-16448:
Pu Wang, Yan Tian, and Yongmin Li review progress in a form of quantum key sharing that removes trust from the measuring device. Quantum key methods let two parties share a secret key with security backed by physics. The weakest point in practice is often the detector, which attackers may exploit.

Their approach uses smooth, wave-like variables that fit well with standard telecom parts. By placing the measurement in the middle, it removes all detector-side threats. The review covers the basic idea, theory advances, and lab demonstrations. It closes with the hurdles that remain for real use and where future work should focus.
arxiv-2502-16648:
Thiem Nguyen and co-authors tackle a hard learning task in a 2025 computer science paper. Their task is to pull relations from text when new relation types keep arriving. The model gets only a few examples of each new type. It must learn the new types without forgetting the old ones, and it may meet types no one has named yet.

The team borrows ideas from open information extraction, a way of pulling raw facts from text. Their model sees all pairs of items, named or not, and learns from rich written notes on each relation. Tests show it beats older methods and keeps its past skill. The work also links the task to building knowledge graphs that grow over time.
arxiv-2502-16748:
Kumar, Kanthen, and John present a study from twenty twenty-five on a unified model for skin lesion analysis. Early skin cancer spotting needs both outlining lesions and naming them. Older models do those jobs apart, wasting shared effort. Their network blends two-dimensional Gaussian splatting with a transformer U-shaped net. One model then outputs both lesion outlines and class labels. Tests run on two public skin image datasets. Five-fold checks show the model beats prior leaders on several metrics.

Segmentation and classification precision both improve in their runs. The authors pitch the dual design for clinic diagnosis support. Unified multi-task analysis is framed as the way forward. The work sets new benchmarks for automated skin checks.
arxiv-2502-17348:
Gabrielle O'Brien studies how scientists use AI tools that write code, in a 2025 paper. Researchers in many fields write programs to gather data, run statistics, and draw charts. As code-writing models spread, early users among scientists offer a glimpse of what may follow.

O'Brien interviewed scientists at a public research university and reviewed logs of their tool use. Many treated the models like a search engine for unfamiliar languages and libraries, asking for snippets and then checking them in varied ways. The paper describes those checking habits in detail. It also flags a quiet risk: choices made by the tool can slip into study settings without the scientist noticing. The findings argue for clear habits around verifying generated code.
arxiv-2502-17548:
Bernhard Mistlberger and Gherardo Vita develop an approximation for collider cross sections in a 2025 paper. At the Large Hadron Collider, predicting how often a color-neutral particle such as the Higgs boson is made requires heavy calculation. The team studies the limit where extra radiation flies nearly along the beam direction, called the collinear limit.

In that limit they prove a factorization result that writes the cross section through the new particle's mass and rapidity alone. They test the approximation on Higgs production and on Drell-Yan lepton pair production through high orders of perturbation theory, then resum the large logarithms of the limit to very high accuracy. They present the framework as the natural successor to the classic threshold approximation.
arxiv-2502-17748:
Tianyu Zhao, Mahmoud Srewa, and Salma Elmalaki tackle fairness in privacy for shared machine learning in a 2025 paper. In federated learning, data stay on user devices, which cuts central storage risk. Yet protection is uneven, and people whose data stand out face higher risk from attacks that trace data sources. Their framework aims to level that risk across clients.

The defense works on two sides at once. The server weighs each client's update by its estimated privacy risk, while each client trains in a way that curbs overfitting to its own odd data. Tests on three data sets cut privacy risk gaps by more than half at best. Model quality stayed near standard levels. Readers see privacy treated as a fairness issue, not just a shield.
arxiv-2502-17948:
Cipriani and co-authors spin neutron stars that carry a hidden passenger: dark matter. Old, fast-spinning pulsars have had eons to gather dark matter, so the team models stars where the dark part rotates on its own, either with the normal matter or against it. They vary the dark particle's mass and the star's total dark share.

The pair of rotations reshapes the star's bulk traits: its mass and size, the fastest spin before it sheds matter, and its resistance to changes in spin. Dark matter can sit in the core or spread as a halo, and each layout leaves a different mark. The results sharpen how astronomers might spot dark matter's fingerprints in real pulsars.
arxiv-2502-18348:
Frank Elavsky and five co-authors propose software that bends to each disabled user in a 2025 paper. A design that helps one person can block another, a tension they call access friction. Fixed accessibility features cannot settle every conflict in advance.

Their answer is softerware: interfaces users can meaningfully reshape themselves. The team gathered 195 ways to customize data displays around barriers disabled users face. A prototype applies a selection of those options to charts. Practitioners reviewed the approach, and blind and low-vision accessibility experts tested it in a design probe. Success, those experts said, needs accessible defaults, settings that persist, and respect for the effort each tweak costs the user.
arxiv-2502-18448:
Irina Saparina and Mirella Lapata propose a modular fix for ambiguity in semantic parsing: settle the meaning in plain words first, then parse. Language tools that turn text into queries like SQL stumble on vague or underspecified input. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Large models parse clear input well, but for vague input they favor one reading and miss the rest. The method first harvests those favored readings, then a trained fill in model finds and writes the missing ones. Training labels come from running candidate SQL to check each meaning. The approach lifts coverage and carries across data sets with varied styles and ambiguity types.
arxiv-2502-18548:
Milan Vojnovic and Se-Young Yun ask what a training method really aims at in a 2025 note on AI alignment. The method is GRPO, used to train models such as DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeekMath. It samples a group of answers for one prompt, scores them, then shifts and rescales the scores. A penalty keeps the model near a reference version while it learns.

The authors build a frame to describe where this training settles. What emerges is a way of pooling human likes that differs at root from the log pooling used in older methods. For groups of two, the setup matches plain pairwise choice, like older feedback methods. They also give exact forms for yes-no questions and for very large groups. The penalty turns out to mirror a known distance between the new and reference models.
arxiv-2502-18848:
Kerem Zaman and Shashank Srivastava (2025) build a testbed for judging whether explanation scores can be trusted. Language models now explain their answers in words, but a smooth story may not match the model's real reasoning. Many faithfulness metrics claim to catch that gap. They are usually tested alone, so nobody knows which works. The authors edit models to create matched pairs of explanations, one faithful and one not. A good metric should score the faithful one higher.

The benchmark spans four tasks: fact-checking, analogy, counting objects, and multi-step reasoning. Results varied by task and model, a warning against one-number verdicts. A filler-token metric performed best overall. Continuous scores generally beat yes-no ones, though they wobbled with noise and model choice. The authors conclude the field needs hardier metrics before explanations can be trusted in audits. Their testbed gives metric builders a common proving ground.
arxiv-2502-19148:
Zhaowei Zhang and co-authors adapt language models to each user at test time in a 2025 paper. Alignment training bakes in average tastes from static data. Real users differ by culture, values, and moment. Retraining per user is impossible.

Their Amulet method skips training entirely. Each token's decoding becomes a small online learning problem, steered by a brief user prompt. A closed-form step keeps the cost of that per-token tuning negligible. Tests across model and task mixes show clear gains in matching personal preferences. The framework offers a light path to models that bend toward the person in front of them.
arxiv-2502-19248:
René Oswald, Victor Vogt, and Stephan Schiller listen for dark matter by watching whether nature's constants hum. Ultralight dark matter could make fundamental constants oscillate gently. Two dissimilar oscillators beating against each other can reveal such wobbles. Real detectors, though, drown in restless, nonstationary noise.

Their fix pairs two nominally identical detectors and records them in step. Cross-spectra between the twins suppress spurious signals that appear in only one. The oscillators exploit a molecular vibration, extra sensitive to nuclear mass changes. Two hundred seventy-four hours of data produced the strongest current bounds on dark matter coupling to nuclear and electron mass. Improvements ran six to ten fold across two wide frequency bands. Similar bounds hold for the fine-structure constant. The paired trick, they note, scales to whole ensembles of detectors.
arxiv-2502-19448:
Dark energy drives the universe's speeding expansion, and model builders keep proposing new engines for it. James Cline writes a short comment in 2025 on a recent proposal that borrowed a time crystal model, introduced by Shapere and Wilczek in 2012, as the engine.

Cline points out a flaw: the model carries an instability that drives its energy density down to negative values. A dark energy candidate that sinks below zero, he argues, may be unfit for the job it was built for. The comment is brief and single-purpose, aimed at the earlier paper's core claim rather than at its details. It stands as a caution in the running debate over what dark energy could be.
arxiv-2502-19648:
Hyunmo Kang, Abdulkadir Canatar, and SueYeon Chung study a snag in comparing brain reads with model reads in a 2025 paper. Labs can only record a slice of neurons at once. Gauges that set brain and model side by side then rest on a thin sample.

With tools from chance matrix lore, the team shows thin samples bend those gauges in set ways. Scores come out too low as a rule, since the shapes in the data smear across the sample. Their frame ties the bend to the tone spread of the true data. Brain and model teams gain a fix for a bias built into their kit.
arxiv-2502-19748:
Suárez and co-authors model predator-prey dynamics where young predators can themselves be eaten by prey. The predator group is split by age, capturing an ontogenetic niche shift as animals grow. Roles flip with age, which adds realism and complexity at once.

Population flow follows a renewal equation in the Kermack-McKendrick style. Unlike that classic form, birth and death rates here depend on prey numbers. The team proves solutions exist, are unique, and stay positive. Sampling the fifteen-parameter space, they found two rates matter most. Those are predator maturation age and how fast prey consume young predators. Reduced versions use ordinary and delayed equations.
arxiv-2502-19948:
Yuan-Chih Yang and Hung-Hsuan Chen vary drop rates per wire in neural networks in a 2025 paper. Training tricks called Dropout and DropConnect randomly switch off neurons or links to stop overfitting. They use one flat rate for a whole layer. The authors instead give each link its own rate, set by a rule tied to the link itself. No extra learned values are added.

They test on fake and public data sets. Their method beat Dropout, DropConnect, and Standout, an older adaptive scheme. Gains came in both accuracy and toughness, the authors report. The runtime cost did not grow. Code for the method is posted in public for others to check and reuse.
arxiv-2502-20148:
Adam Wesolowski and Jinge Bao give quantum algorithms and lower bounds for three classic graph measures, in work from 2025. Eccentricity, radius, and diameter all rest on distances between points in a graph. They are basic tools for reading network shape, from roads to social links.

Their quantum algorithms find the diameter and radius of weighted, undirected graphs, along with the paths that achieve them. The run time beats classic limits in the model they use. A second algorithm estimates the diameter within a set factor, faster still. Lower bounds, proved by reduction from a minimum finding problem, show that no quantum method can do much better.
arxiv-2502-20448:
Caterina Bracci and a large team use neural networks to classify emission-line regions in galaxies, in work from 2025. Such regions show how stars and interstellar gas exchange matter and energy. Older sorting methods use one or a few line ratios, with rigid borders that fail when nebulae overlap along the line of sight.

Training spectra were simulated from photoionisation and shock models, matched to MUSE observations. Accuracy fell as noise rose, yet stayed near 80 percent at a stated signal level. Applied to the galaxy M33, the network sorted star-forming regions, planetary nebulae, supernova remnants and diffuse gas, and flagged overlaps. Its choices agreed well with traditional diagnostics.
arxiv-2502-20648:
Amarilton Lopes Magalhães, André Lima Férrer de Almeida, and Gilderlan Tavares de Araújo cut the cost of channel estimation for a new kind of wireless system, in this 2025 paper. The system uses a reconfigurable intelligent surface, a panel that shapes radio waves to improve coverage. Before data flows, the receiver must learn the channel, and doing that jointly with the data itself can beat pilot-only methods.

The authors propose a two-stage semi-blind receiver. The first stage reshapes the received signal so the combined channel and the transmitted symbols can be estimated together. The second stage splits the combined channel apart through a Khatri-Rao factorization, yielding a refined channel estimate. Simulations show accuracy matching a competing method while the computing cost drops substantially. The savings matter because these surface-assisted links otherwise demand heavy estimation work at the receiver.
arxiv-2502-21048:
A single noise pattern that fools image models on any photo can be built without any training photos, Chanhui Lee and co-authors show in a 2025 paper. Classic data-free attacks start from pure noise, which lacks meaning and transfers poorly between models. Their method mines fake semantic hints from the attack pattern itself as training proceeds.

Region sampling pulls those hints out, letting standard image transforms finally help. A weighting step stresses hard examples that the pattern barely fools. Tests on a large photo benchmark show strong cross-model transfer. The work exposes a real risk: attackers need no data at all to craft broadly effective image attacks, so defenses must assume the worst.
arxiv-2502-21248:
Vijayalaxmi Methuku and Praveen Kumar Myakala weigh the rights and risks of AI twins made while their twins still live, in a study from 2025. New tools can clone a soul's voice, acts, and lore with fine faith. Such clones can aid work, art, and keep a name past death.

The pair split these pre-death clones from post-death ghosts, since the law and the heart treat them unlike. Risks stack: split self, strain on kin, clone theft, and lore theft. As clones gain will of their own, yes, own, and blame blur. Their frame bids guard rails: keep the self whole, bind clones to clear yes, and cap their free rein. Law, they say, lags the loom.
arxiv-2503-00248:
Lukas Mayer and colleagues designed a study of what people want from AI collaborators in a 2025 paper. Five assistant agents were built to differ in how much they adapt to the human partner's actions, from stubbornly optimizing alone to actively making room for the person. Participants worked with some of the agents, rated their traits, and picked favorites, while a Bayesian model untangled how strategy drove team scores, impressions, and choices.

Considerate agents beat pure performance maximizers in preference, without actually scoring lower. Much of the pull came from fairness: people disliked agents that left them nothing meaningful to contribute, an inequality-aversion effect. Likable collaboration, the study argues, is a design target in its own right, not decoration.
arxiv-2503-00548:
Yanjun Li, Zhaoyang Li, Honghui Chen, and Lizhi Xu present a debiasing framework for video scene graph generation, in a research paper from 2025. The task builds graphs of objects and their changing relations across video frames. Bias in data skews predictions toward common relations, so rare but true relations get missed.

Their framework attacks visual bias and semantic bias at once. A memory step strengthens object features over time to fix the visual side. Semantic bias is cut by folding object features into rich triplet context in rounds. Tests show large gains over past unbiased methods on standard recall measures. The approach yields fairer graphs of complex scene dynamics.
arxiv-2503-00748:
Zihao Luo and co-authors built a lymph node finder for CT scans and a way to adapt it with few examples, in a 2025 paper. Outlining lymph nodes guides radiation therapy, but hand-labeled scans are scarce. The team first marked over thirty-six thousand nodes across 3,346 public head-and-neck scans, training a strong base model on that hoard.

Their fine-tuning trick then updates only the most critical weights, chosen on the fly, leaving the base knowledge intact. On two public test sets it beat rival few-shot methods with little labeled data. The group released the data, models, and code openly. The aim is a foundation model clinics can bend to local needs cheaply.
arxiv-2503-00948:
Jie Tian and five co-authors improve how AI turns a still image into a moving video clip. The hard part is balance: motion should look natural and match the text prompt, without warping the look of the starting image. Many current models move too little, or move in ways the prompt never asked for.

Their framework works in three stages. First, a small adapter teaches the base model to obey motion instructions better. Next, a training-free step widens the range of motion. Last, they split out the settings tied to each skill and merge them back, tuned by time step. Tests showed stronger, better-controlled motion than before. The authors call motion modeling easier than it looks.
arxiv-2503-01348:
Chen wrote in twenty twenty-five about speeding up three-dimensional stencil computation on ARM processors. Stencil methods update each point in a grid from its neighbors. They underpin fluid simulation and weather forecasting at large scale. The study targets ARM's Scalable Vector Extension, a flexible vector instruction set. A Roofline model and simulation tools guided the analysis. Software tricks like vectorization and tiling were tested.

Hardware settings were varied alongside the software changes. Vector length and cache layout both shifted performance in the tests. Power use and chip area entered the trade-off analysis too. The goal was to find balanced configurations for ARM systems. Faster stencils cut both time and energy in big simulations. That matters for disaster prediction, where speed can save lives, Chen notes.
arxiv-2503-01448:
Xiangjun Tang, Biao Zhang, and Peter Wonka generate varied human body geometry with clothing, in work from 2025. Realistic human shapes must keep fine clothing detail and true cloth body contact. Past geometry distributions model one person well but scale poorly to full datasets for learning.

Two changes fix that scaling gap in the new model design. Distributions are coded as flat feature maps instead of network weights for each person. A body model domain replaces a plain Gaussian base, with a tuned flow field on top. Training runs in two stages: squeeze shapes to a latent space, then learn that space. Pose based avatar tests beat prior methods with a large quality gain.
arxiv-2503-01748:
Alejandro Mata Ali speeds up a key calculation inside a quantum optimization algorithm, in a 2025 paper. The algorithm, shortened to QAOA, tunes settings by averaging operator values. Those operators split into sums of unitary pieces. His method computes the average in one circuit. Only a single qubit needs measuring at the end.

The trick applies to any quantum algorithm with such operators. Variational methods gain the most, in hardware and in simulators. Special care handles repeated values in the problem matrix. Several test problems in binary optimization showed the speedup in practice. Fewer circuits mean faster tuning loops for the optimizer. Simulation studies especially benefit, since classical emulation is costly. The author presents the method as a general accelerator. It removes a bottleneck shared by many near-term quantum routines.
arxiv-2503-01948:
Kun Xu and co-authors present an astronomy paper, published in 2025, counting galaxies by mass down to weights once out of reach. Their method, called PAC, cross matches a deep photographic catalog against a spectroscopic survey to measure how smaller galaxies cluster around known ones. The team sharpened the method so it no longer needs distance bins, then applied it to early data from the DESI survey.

The result is a stellar mass census spanning from dwarf galaxies a million times the Sun's mass up to giants, split between blue and red populations. Combining the clustering signal with companion measures yields the full mass function. Such a census tests how galaxies of every size form and gather their stars.
arxiv-2503-02048:
Diffusion models make fine robot motions but work too slowly for live control, and their paths can jerk. Xirui Shi and Jun Jin speed them up by marrying them to movement primitives, compact codes for whole trajectories. A consistency training trick, borrowed from image models, lets the system produce a motion in one step. An encoder-decoder holds the smooth, time-spanning code. The slow denoising chain disappears.

Tests on two standard robot benchmarks, from easy to hard tasks, beat strong rivals. Motions came out smooth and steady in time, not just accurate at the end. One-step generation cuts the wait that blocks real-time use. The design shows robot learning can borrow speed tricks from image generation.
arxiv-2503-02248:
Tong Liang and Jim Davis aim to make image sorting errors less bad in a 2025 paper. Their base is CLIP, a model that sorts images with no task training by matching them to text labels. When it errs, not all errors are equal: calling a husky a wolf beats calling it a car.

Their method, HAPrompts, asks a large language model to write class texts that heed the label family tree of each task. CLIP seems to hold such tree links in its image encoder from its text training. Across five data sets the method beat rivals on error quality. The code and prompts are shared in public.
arxiv-2503-02548:
Nayak and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on whether strings moving in a warped spacetime background behave predictably or fall into chaos. The setting is a stack of D3-branes with a twist that makes coordinates fail to commute, a playground for the duality linking gravity and quantum theory. The team studied pulsating strings that expand and contract as they move.

Perturbation math and numerics showed the twist strengthens chaos, measured by how fast nearby paths diverge. Some strings stay captured near the branes while others escape to infinity. Dispersion relations for short and long pulsating strings in a related deformed background complete the analysis.
arxiv-2503-02648:
Arpan Akash Ray and Boris Škorić design encryption that cannot be copied in a paper from 2025. Unclonable encryption uses quantum states so a ciphertext cannot be duplicated for later attack. Their scheme is the first built on continuous variables, the language of light modes. A classical cipher first scrambles the message, then an error-correcting code spreads it. Each bit becomes a squeezed light state whose squeeze direction hides in the key.

Security is proven by reducing the cloning game to a known entanglement game. The authors then add real-world noise and detector flaws to the analysis. The scheme stays robust under those imperfections. They argue current optics can implement it.
arxiv-2503-02848:
Mithilesh Nayak, Julian Thoenniss, and their co-authors plug a new solver into a workhorse method for strongly interacting electrons. Their 2025 paper implements influence functional matrix product states as the impurity solver inside dynamical mean field theory. The test bed is the single band Hubbard model, in and out of equilibrium.

The solver gives numerically exact readings for metallic states with smooth spectra at moderate cost. Narrow peaks and cold Mott insulating states strain it, needing longer time contours or larger bond sizes. Photo doped Mott systems, where light creates long lived charge carriers, showcase the method's strength in nonequilibrium steady states. Such states are prime targets for the technique, the authors argue.
arxiv-2503-03348:
Chuan Hu and five co-authors design steering control for cars shared between a human driver and an automatic system, in a 2025 paper. Their method blends nonlinear feedback control with an adaptive learning algorithm that improves itself over time. A two-degree vehicle model and a preview model of the driver set the scene. Steering authority shifts between human and machine according to how well they cooperate at each moment.

Three refinements carry the contribution: the feedback shape sharpens short-term tracking, a self-triggered rule updates the controller only when needed to save computing power, and the learning layer tunes performance online. Shared steering is the realistic middle ground for years to come, so smooth hand-offs between person and program matter for safety.
arxiv-2503-03448:
Futaba Sato studies heat flow on quantum symmetry groups in this 2025 math paper. The groups in question capture all the ways a small quantum system, described by a finite C*-algebra, can be rearranged without changing its rules. Heat flow here is a process that smooths out functions on the group over time, much like heat spreads through metal.

Sato proves three strong traits of this heat flow. It squeezes functions hard, a trait called ultracontractivity, and an even tighter grip called hypercontractivity. It also keeps a clear gap above zero in its spectrum, which means the smoothing has a steady rate. Sato then shows that two classic bounds for such groups, a Sobolev embedding and a Hausdorff–Young bound, are sharp and cannot be improved. The results firm up the basic tools used to study these quantum groups.
arxiv-2503-03548:
Milin Patel and Rolf Jung test how well deep learning detectors read LiDAR data across rough weather, inside a safety frame for self-driving. The frame, safety of the intended functionality, targets the blind spots of sensors and learned detectors. Rain, cloud, and night can all bend what a LiDAR sees.

Their 2025 paper models one such use case in simulation under many weather mixes, from clear noon to rainy night. The synthetic point cloud set runs to hundreds of frames. Pre-trained state-of-the-art 3D detectors from two open toolkits were run on the set as-is. Average precision and recall scores show how far each method bends before it breaks, data meant to guide safer design.
arxiv-2503-03648:
Kornelia Kostrzewska and Pawel Kryszkiewicz wrote this radio engineering paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on modeling how wideband amplifiers distort signals. The paper appears in Polish with an English version alongside. Real amplifiers bend loud signals, and the bend shifts when the supply voltage changes, a trick modern radios use to save power.

The authors propose an extended form of the classic Rapp model that captures this nonlinear behavior across a wide frequency range. They check the model against bench measurements of three different amplifiers. The fit holds up across the set. A model like this lets system designers predict distortion before building hardware. The authors point to sixth-generation mobile systems that are aware of their own front-end flaws as the target use.
arxiv-2503-03848:
Daniel Moura, Shizhan Zhu, and Orly Zvitia release, in 2025 work, a public dashcam set and contest for foretelling crashes. Dashcams catch real traffic strife that staged tests miss. Their set holds fifteen hundred clips, each near forty seconds, drawn from a wide range of road scenes.

Each clip is tagged with its event kind, light and weather, and scene type, from city to highway. For crash and near-crash clips, tags also mark the crash point and the first point where a sharp eye could call it. Contest models must score how likely a crash looms, graded at three lead times, the longest a second and a half out. Early, sound calls win. The set is open, with bars on ill use.
arxiv-2503-03948:
Ki Young Lee and four co-authors built a marker for a shy kind of topology in flat materials, in a paper published in 2025. The kind, called fragile topology, can be wiped out by adding plain bands, so standard markers fail to detect it. Twisted graphene sheets show it, which raised the need. Their marker works in real space, not in wave space, so it fits finite, disordered, and irregular builds.

The method turns the symmetry traits of the phase into traits of two matrices, then bends one matrix into the other to build the marker. The bending also gives a score for how robust the phase is. On a twisted graphene model and on a photonic crystal, the marker held up. The phase survived strong disorder and stacks with no clean gap, and in one case disorder brought it back.
arxiv-2503-04048:
Xiaoding Yang studies in 2025 the still states of a fluid that flows over a sloped wall, held by both weight and skin pull. The task has wide use in science and craft, from coats to drains. Still forms are set by a fixed touch angle at the wall.

Those forms solve a known energy task's core equation. Yang marks the free top by a well picked peak point to build the solves. A shoot method then runs the build, with fluid bulk as the shoot knob. The build holds for all touch angles and all wall slopes in the plane case.
arxiv-2503-04348:
Maciej Borodzik, Mark Powell, and Peter Teichner prove, in a 2025 topology paper, that two ways of saying links are alike imply each other more often than was known. They show that if links can be joined by a concordance, they can also be deformed into each other step by step. The result holds when the embedding sits in codimension at least two.

As a pay-off, every link of spheres in a sphere two dimensions higher can be fully unlinked by such a deformation, for all sizes from two up. Only the two-sphere case was known before. The proof completes older unpublished notes on stratified Morse theory, with care for the extra hurdles that appear where strands cross themselves.
arxiv-2503-04448:
Tim Engels, Ivo Adan, Onno Boxma, and Jacques Resing analyze a polling system arranged on a circle. Batches of customers land at random spots on the circle by a general rule. One server loops around the circle and serves each in turn. Two service rules are studied: one serves a batch only if it arrived before a pass, and one clears each stop fully.

For the first rule, they find the full transform of batch delay. For the second, they build a mean-value method that yields the mean delay by algorithm. Exact limits are derived for both light and heavy loads. The results can guide systems like lifts, shuttles, and ring networks where one server cycles past random demand.
arxiv-2503-04948:
Aashaq Shah, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on quality tests for new ATLAS detector parts. The ATLAS muon system at CERN is due for a Phase II upgrade. About one thousand new resistive plate chamber units will be added. They must hit their marks for hits and timing in the harsh, high rate hall of the upgraded collider.

Gas gaps for the units are made in Italy and must be tight, with no leaks. The study reports heat and cold cycle tests run in labs at Cambridge and at Frascati. Swings in heat stress the gaps as parts expand, which can open leaks. Shah sets out ways to test and boost gas tightness. Tight units leak less of gases that harm the climate.
arxiv-2503-05048:
Noé Kuhn tests a bold claim: that expected utility, economics' model of choice, is swallowed whole by active inference. Active inference casts behavior as surprise-minimizing under a model of the world. If the claim held, utility would be a special case. His 2025 paper builds counterexamples, then does the formal math. Objective functions for both frameworks are set side by side in two decision settings.

Capping the utility agent's information use makes the two match in fully seen settings. In partly hidden settings a small gap remains. Rather than a verdict, Kuhn builds a bridge: shared assumptions that let the two languages trade results. The subsumption claim survives only with its fine print showing.
arxiv-2503-05348:
Jorge Navarro and José M Zapata study how risks add up when they are not independent, in a 2025 paper on stochastic dominance. The question is when one risk can be ranked as safer than the same risk plus an added uncertain term, where that term stands for the effect of the environment. The two parts may depend on each other, which makes the ranking hard.

The pair give conditions under which the comparison holds. Part of each condition concerns the copula, the function that ties the two distributions together. They define two new forms of positive dependence for that tie. The rest concerns the added term itself, which needs certain symmetry or skew properties. Worked examples show the conditions in action. The results speak to insurance and finance, where added risks rarely arrive independently of the risks already on the books.
arxiv-2503-05448:
Duong Vo, Nelofer Syed, and Thomas Thorne propose a fast joint graphical model method for single cell RNA data. Graphical models reveal conditional links between genes. Joint models estimate networks across several related conditions at once, which exposes shared and distinct structure, a prized view in genomics and neuroscience.

Existing joint methods rely on penalties or on Bayesian priors. The new framework, JointStein, uses two target linear shrinkage of covariance matrices with formulas for optimal shrinkage strength. Simulations show it scales to large single cell datasets. Applied to glioblastoma data, it uncovers dynamic shifts in T cell network structure across disease stages. The method offers a fast alternative for large network inference tasks.
arxiv-2503-05748:
Krti Tallam writes on alignment, agency, and autonomy in advanced AI from a systems engineering view, in a 2025 paper. These three terms sit at the center of AI safety and governance, yet they lack shared definitions even for humans. Meanings differ across philosophy, law, psychology, and computing.

Tallam traces how the concepts evolved and how rival readings shape system design and rules. Case studies include driving and aircraft automation failures, a multi-agent diplomacy system, and self-learning game agents. The paper argues that urgent concern stems from AI entering high-stakes decisions. It assesses the safety challenges that agentic systems pose for oversight.
arxiv-2503-05948:
Tarusov, Ushakov and Vasiliev analyse a family of higher-spin gauge theories tied to Coxeter groups, in work from 2025. The theories live on four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, and the study works at linear order around that background. For a general Coxeter group they establish the background solution and the form of the free unfolded equations that govern the fields.

A criterion is given for when Coxeter higher-spin modules split apart cleanly, and a shifted homotopy method is lifted to the general setting. For the B2 group they classify the unitary modules, find a consistent truncation to them and sketch the dynamical content that survives.
arxiv-2503-06048:
Joshua Rozner, Leonie Weissweiler, Kyle Mahowald, and Cory Shain ask how much grammar hides in word patterns in a 2025 paper. Construction grammar holds that language is learned as pairings of form and meaning, picked up from experience. If so, the spread of words in text should carry traces of those pairings. Plain text cannot show cause, so the team used a trained language model as a stand-in for the word distribution.

They probed a RoBERTa model for patterns of statistical affinity, the pull words exert on each other. Many constructions stood out clearly in that signal. Hard cases passed too, where look-alike forms carry distinct meanings. So did schematic patterns whose slots accept whole word classes. Still, close reading suggested affinity alone may miss some constructions. The authors call it a strong but partial signal for learners.
arxiv-2503-06248:
Leidy Abril, André Moreira, José Andrade, and Hans Herrmann study Loewner evolution for trees formed by critical invasion percolation. Their 2025 paper extends the Schramm-Loewner evolution, a tool for random curves, to branching structures.

Trees pose a challenge because their driving functions must be discontinuous, and the function depends on the order in which branches are explored. Three exploration strategies were used: the invasion process itself, depth-first search, and breadth-first search. The team analyzed distributions of the driving function displacements and their spectral densities. They also tackled the inverse problem, deriving new traces from the driving functions, with a stated rate of reconstruction success.
arxiv-2503-06348:
Ashwin Pillay builds a neural score follower for live computer accompaniment of musicians. A score follower tracks where a player sits in the written music in real time. Past tools used dynamic programming, hidden Markov models, or time warping for that task. Deep learning had not been tried directly on the problem before this work.

His system, HeurMiT, learns squeezed codes of the music that hold the player's place. A MIDI augmentation kit toughens those codes against player slips. Heuristic rules join the network to link with transcription and accompaniment tools. Tests showed blazing speed but deep limits in real use. Pillay frames the work as a first probe and maps paths toward a sound neural follower.
arxiv-2503-06548:
Bruno Pinheiro and three co-authors introduce in 2025 a new yardstick for whether a device on a power grid is locally synchronized. Grid stability increasingly depends on many small devices, from solar inverters to batteries, marching in step with the network. Their measure, Synchronization Energy, grows from the complex frequency idea and the Teager energy operator applied to complex power.

Math links the measure to a device's voltage and current behavior at steady operation. Clear conditions for calling a device synchronized follow. Case studies show the measure behaving well across varied operating conditions. A local, signal-based test could let operators spot drifting devices before small mismatches snowball into grid events.
arxiv-2503-06848:
Zhenran Tang, Ruixuan Liu, and Changliu Liu put a camera in the fingertip of a robot gripper to handle tight toy brick builds, in a paper from 2025. Fixed or wrist cameras lose sight of small parts in clutter, yet brick fits demand sub millimeter care.

Their smart finger carries a cheap, sharp camera at the tool tip, so the robot sees the fit point up close as it works. Tests on brick assembly and teardown showed live fine fixes to aim errors. The slack for aim drift grew five fold over the base setup, which eased robust work in tight stacks.
arxiv-2503-07148:
A robot planner that thinks in symbols on top and in raw actions below is the design of Ali Baheri and Cecilia Alm in a 2025 arXiv paper. Long tasks under uncertainty defeat both pure planners, which cannot adapt, and pure neural policies, which cannot explain themselves.

Their hierarchy lets a classical planner lay out an interpretable chain of operators. Each operator becomes a token that steers a decision transformer writing the fine moves. The authors track how errors from both levels compound, then test in random grid worlds. The hybrid beat symbolic, neural, and earlier hybrid rivals on success and efficiency.
arxiv-2503-08248:
Mustafa Gündoğan and Mehmet Emre Tasgin propose a new receiver for quantum illumination, a method for spotting a faint target in noise, published in 2025. At room heat, in microwave and low terahertz links, strong thermal noise makes faint linked signals hard to recover after loss. Their scheme uses work extraction to turn a hard signal into an easy one.

The returned mode is measured, and that result is fed forward to a stored partner mode. The score from the stored mode then shows whether a target was present. The authors show the score matches the leading result of an ideal prior receiver, but with a linear, direct measure. Heat noise in the source can even help when it is linked before sending.
arxiv-2503-09348:
Zhoutong Ye and co-authors build a benchmark that tests whether vision-language models can combine their skills the way real tasks demand, in a 2025 paper. Such models read images and text together and shine on simple tests. Real work, though, asks them to read text in a scene, count, judge positions, and follow tangled instructions all at once, and there they stumble. MOAT gathers 1,005 hard real-world visual questions that humans find easy.

The tasks are sorted by a scheme of nine vision-language skills, so failures point at the missing skill. The benchmark is also the first to test directly how well models follow complex written and visual instructions. Seventeen leading models were tried. The best, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reached only 44 percent accuracy. The authors trace much of the gap to text-heavy reasoning habits and name the skills that bottleneck performance.
arxiv-2503-09548:
Tattwamasi Amrutam and Yongle Jiang wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five about group algebras. They ask when every part of such an algebra that stays fixed under the group must come from a normal subgroup. They call groups with that trait rigid in this sense.

The pair show that a broad class of curved, non-amenable groups has the trait. Finite products of such groups have it as well. They also prove a limit in the other direction. An endless group with the trait must be either simple and amenable, or simple in the algebra sense they define.
arxiv-2503-09848:
Giacomo Albi and Elisa Calzola build a faster method for steering crowds of agents toward a chosen outcome. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The math behind it uses Fokker-Planck equations, which track how a whole group's spread shifts over time.

The method pairs two linked problems. One runs forward, following the group, and is solved in a way that keeps steady states intact. The other runs backward and can take large time steps without breaking down. A descent step links the two until the control settles. Tests confirm the method hits its target accuracy and runs fast. The authors apply it to social cases, such as guiding opinion toward agreement in structured groups.
arxiv-2503-10248:
Idan Horowitz and Ori Plonsky compare how large language models and humans learn from repeated choices with feedback. In such tasks, people show known quirks, such as giving rare events too little weight. The authors ran models and humans through the same choice tasks to see whether the same surface patterns hide the same inner process.

On average, the models did look human-like, showing the same broad biases. A closer look broke that picture. The models leaned hard on the most recent outcomes, a strong recency bias that humans did not show. Human tricks, like switching after a surprise, were absent in the models. Similar averages, the authors warn, can hide very different minds at work.
arxiv-2503-10448:
Blood markers can track a cancer's course, but the day a patient relapses is rarely seen directly, since many leave the study first. Cleynen and co-authors build a method that reads the marker's path over time and estimates when the hidden status change happened. They frame the problem with a class of random processes that drift smoothly and jump at random moments, the marker playing the role of a stand-in for the patient's state.

An iterative regression procedure fits the change dates in continuous time, which yields the full distribution of relapse times for the group. Simulations test the method against rivals, and myeloma patient data illustrate it. The authors call the work a proof of concept.
arxiv-2503-11348:
Aissatou Diallo and co-authors present RESPONSE in 2025, a benchmark for language model reasoning in disaster situations. Commonsense reasoning about crises is a distinct challenge for these models. The data set is human-curated and partly validated by environmental engineers for realism.

It holds close to eighteen hundred instances with more than six thousand question sets. Items cover problem descriptions, missing resources, and time-sensitive solutions with justifications. Even a top model reached only about thirty-seven percent correctness on immediate response actions by human judgment. The authors see large room for improvement in crisis reasoning.
arxiv-2503-11548:
Moffat reviews how the electroweak force gets its broken symmetry, in a 2025 paper, and weighs an alternative to the standard Higgs story. In the Standard Model, the Higgs field's self-interaction shapes the masses of the weak force carriers. How strongly the Higgs couples to itself is still poorly measured. A value off the prediction would hint at new physics. Moffat surveys what experiments currently allow.

He then presents a rival theory built on finite quantum field theory. That theory is complete at high energies and needs no spontaneous symmetry breaking at all. Its vacuum value can stay at zero. He compares its particle mass predictions and vacuum stability with the standard mechanism. The paper also revisits how the Standard Model derives the W boson mass. Radiative corrections enter that result, and the measured value tests the whole picture.
arxiv-2503-11748:
Anis Maddi and four colleagues demonstrate experimentally that sound waves with complex frequencies can achieve total absorption and compensate losses. A complex frequency means the wave's amplitude grows or decays exponentially in time. Such excitation mimics gain or loss when viewed in the frequency domain.

The team excited a Helmholtz resonator, deliberately not critically coupled, with a growing-amplitude wave and still reached total absorption. In a second experiment, a decaying-amplitude signal compensated the losses of a traveling wave in a duct. The results confirm that transient complex-frequency signals can manipulate sound in ways steady tones cannot. The authors point to new routes for acoustic devices that emulate gain and loss.
arxiv-2503-12048:
Cordeiro and a team including Junior study test particles falling into a charged black hole in a gravity theory with a broken symmetry in twenty twenty-five. The Kalb Ramond field bends the rules of relativity by a set amount. The team tracked fall speed as the symmetry breaking dial turns. Signal shifts between falling and watching observers were also computed.

Tidal forces, the stretching a falling body feels, changed in both radial and sideways parts. Results were set against the classic charged hole case. The deviation equation was solved in closed form for two setups. A subtle mark of the breaking dial showed in the charged metric.
arxiv-2503-12248:
Nilupulee Gunathilake and co-authors probe a lightweight cipher for physical information leaks in a 2025 security study. Devices leak information through power use and electromagnetic radiation while they run cryptographic functions. Such side-channel attacks are growing more common and threaten small devices that cannot shield themselves well.

The target is PRESENT, a promising lightweight algorithm expected to be built into many internet-of-things devices in the future. The team investigated how robust implementations of the cipher are to electromagnetic analysis attacks that recover secret keys. Knowing where a cipher leaks before mass deployment lets designers add countermeasures while changes are still cheap and easy.
arxiv-2503-12448:
Matti Lassas published this paper in 2025. It introduces inverse problems for nonlinear partial differential equations. Such problems ask what hidden source or material produced the signals we measured. The method on show is multiple linearization. Waves are sent in, and their self-interaction inside a nonlinear medium creates new signals. Those extra signals betray the hidden properties.

Strikingly, some nonlinear cases have been solved while their linear twins remain open. Nonlinearity, usually a curse, here becomes the tool. The paper surveys results for wave-type and steady-type equations alike. It is written as an entry point for researchers coming to the field. Readers get both the core trick and a map of where it has already worked.
arxiv-2503-12548:
When a bond snaps, electrons stop marching in step, and simple models of a molecule fail. Amir Ayati and three co-authors build a solver for that hard case in 2025. Their trick is to let the electron spin wobble: each wobble gives a fresh base state, and the true state is a blend of them all.

The blend is found by a classic blend law, solved as a set of mixed states that need not stand at right angles. On the smallest test, split hydrogen, a few wobbles catch the exact ground energy. On a richer basis, a patch step is needed to pass ninety percent of the link energy. Spin as the blend's dial is the fresh move here.
arxiv-2503-12748:
Lin-Yue Li and Rong-Hua Wang study number properties of two families of polynomials built from Delannoy and Schröder numbers. These counting numbers track lattice paths, and their polynomial versions carry a power parameter that generalizes the classic forms. Their 2025 paper proves that certain weighted sums of powers of these polynomials land exactly in the ring of polynomials with whole-number coefficients. Several such integrality results are given, with alternating signs and varied weights.

Exact divisibility facts like these are the small gears of combinatorics: they certify that counts built from the polynomials stay whole. The proofs extend known results for the classic cases. The authors write for specialists in enumerative combinatorics. Their formulas add to the toolkit for path-counting problems.
arxiv-2503-12948:
Shoichi Koyama, Enzo De Sena, Prasanga Samarasinghe, Mark Thomas, and Fabio Antonacci wrote a 2025 review surveying the past, present, and future of spatial audio and room acoustics. The field aims to create immersive sound by modeling how sound behaves in space, both in physics and in human hearing. It has a long history of mixing theory with hands on invention.

The authors highlight landmark achievements and community efforts across the decades. They cover recording and playback of spatial sound, plus the simulation, modeling, analysis, and control of room acoustics. Recent advances and open problems get equal weight. The review doubles as a map for newcomers and a stock take for veterans of the field.
arxiv-2503-13048:
Haofeng Chen and co-authors build a robot skin that can feel both touch and bending at once. Their sensor uses electrical impedance tomography, a method that infers what is happening across a surface from electrical readings at its edges, needing little wiring. Bending is the hard part: it shifts the baseline readings and mixes with the signals from touch. The team pairs a neural network that classifies the surface's state with an adaptive reference scheme that separates the two effects, plus a regression model that turns readings into bending angles.

The skin itself is a magnetic hydrogel sheet that flexes with the surface beneath it. In tests, the system estimated bending angles well, told touch, bending, and rest apart reliably, and located touches far better under bending than fixed-reference methods. Live trials confirmed it can track several touches and changing angles at the same time.
arxiv-2503-13348:
Aldo Rodriguez-Puebla and co-authors revisit how galaxy growth is traced in 2025. A common trick matches galaxy counts across cosmic time to link ancestors and descendants. That trick ignores scatter in growth and mergers, and past fixes relied on models.

The authors show that dark matter halo counts change with time in a steady, known way. Using that change gives tracks where young galaxies are far smaller than the old trick suggests.
