At one early epoch, masses shrink by about tenfold compared with the standard match. Random errors in mass readings must also be handled for sound tracks.
arxiv-2503-13448:
Francesca Cappelli, Giovanni Colavizza, and Silvio Peroni reviewed in 2024 the deep learning methods that tell same-named authors apart in scholarly databases. Two researchers sharing a name can scramble credit, citations, and careers when their papers merge. The review gathers work from 2016 to 2024 and sorts it by technique, cost, and performance.

Learning models shine by fusing tidy metadata with messy text, and hybrids that mix supervision with rules balance best. Open problems remain around rare names and new authors. Libraries that clean their author records make every later bibliometric study more honest.
arxiv-2503-14148:
Simone Marchi and co-authors preview the origin of asteroid Donaldjohanson before a NASA flyby in a 2025 paper. The Lucy craft was set to pass the small body in April 2025. The rock belongs to a family born when a larger body broke apart in the inner main belt.

Fresh modeling dates that break-up to well over a hundred million years ago. On such spans, sunlight-driven forces can shift the rocks orbit and spin, and hits can scar its face. The flyby can check those tales through shape, surface, and crater counts. The same family feeds near-Earth rocks sampled by past craft, adding wider value.
arxiv-2503-14248:
Ruben Queiros, Megumi Kaneko, Helder Fontes, and Rui Campos present a method for flying networks that relay data by drone, in a research paper from 2025. Flying networks can bring wireless links where coverage is weak or gear is damaged, as in disaster zones. Keeping relay links strong while drones move is still a hard problem.

Their method, SAFnet, assigns channel width and moves the relay drone as needs shift. It uses known paths of the first drone tier to plan ahead. A search method with penalty rules guides the choices. Results come close to full search at far lower cost. The work suits planned, moving drone fleets.
arxiv-2503-14348:
The sky's red hydrogen glow maps where hot young stars ionize the gas between them, and a three-dimensional version of that map is now possible. Lewis McCallum and co-authors built it in this 2025 paper. Distances to nearby hot stars come from parallax measurements. Three-dimensional dust maps of the local Milky Way supply the terrain.

Simulated photons stream through that terrain until they ionize gas or hit dust. The result predicts the glow an all-sky survey actually sees, with good agreement in shape. The simulation underproduces the total glow and puffs its bright regions too large, which the authors discuss openly. Of the ionizing light, fifteen percent dies on dust and ten percent escapes the local volume entirely.
arxiv-2503-14448:
Ayushi Dubal and co-authors teach a learning system to shrink quantum circuits in a 2025 paper. Quantum programs built from Pauli rotations and Clifford gates often carry more two-qubit gates than the math needs, and each extra gate adds noise on real hardware.

Their method squashes each block of a circuit into a compact code, then lets a reinforcement learning agent rebuild it step by step under the machine's wiring limits. On random six-qubit tests it cut two-qubit gates by more than half compared with top heuristic tools, in under ten milliseconds per circuit. Plugged into the Qiskit compiler, it trimmed gate counts and depth by about a fifth on a standard benchmark.
arxiv-2503-14548: Tomer Milo gives a strikingly short proof of a classic inequality about the shapes of high-dimensional polytopes, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The Figiel-Lindenstrauss-Milman result bounds how vertices and faces of certain polytopes relate, with a universal constant. Milo's proof is fully elementary and pins down that constant explicitly. It sidesteps two heavy tools earlier proofs leaned on: Dvoretzky's theorem and the spherical isoperimetric inequality. The note shows a cornerstone of asymptotic geometric analysis can rest on simple means.
arxiv-2503-14648:
Kamran and co-authors study in a 2025 paper how a swimming fish's shape and stroke change the scent trail it leaves behind. Fish both spread and hide odors in their wake, and those cues guide finding food, social contact, and avoiding hunters. The study joins fluid motion with chemical transport in one model.

The team runs detailed three-dimensional flow simulations with a sharp-boundary method and an odor transport model. They compare two swimming styles: the mid-body waves of a jackfish and the whole-body waves of an eel. Two set stroke rates are tested. Odor plumes were found to track the swirling structures in the wake closely. Body shape and stroke style changed how far the cues spread and how well they were masked.
arxiv-2503-14748:
Zsuzsanna Koczor-Benda and co-authors design molecules for terahertz detection in a 2025 paper. Nanoscale junctions can convert terahertz waves into visible light. The right molecule inside the junction decides how well that works.

Commercial catalogs hold few molecules with strong conversion power. A generative neural network was used to invent new candidates. The generator was steered step by step toward active shapes. Ease of synthesis was part of the steering target as well. Sulfur-anchored single molecules are the design family used. Readers see generative chemistry aimed at a sensing gap, not just at drugs.
arxiv-2503-15448:
William Marfo and co-authors cut communication costs in federated learning for network anomaly detection in this 2025 paper. Federated setups train across many sites without pooling raw data. Traffic between sites can swamp the savings, though. Diverse client machines and networks make tuning hard. Their framework tunes batch size, picks clients adaptively, and lets updates arrive out of step. Two datasets test it: general traffic and car network traffic.

Communication time fell by over ninety percent in their runs. Detection accuracy stayed level with the unoptimized setup. A standard statistical test checked the difference claims. Security monitors are the end users of such systems. Cars add a second, harsher network setting. The paper is a distributed learning systems study.
arxiv-2503-16048:
Michael Goodale and co-authors ask what meta-learning actually installs in a neural network, and find machinery, not taste. Meta-learning was sold as giving networks human-like simplicity biases, the way children generalize language from little data. Training networks on formal languages arranged around simplicity, the team tested that story.

The models were not learning simplicity priors at all. Instead, meta-training imprinted concrete neural mechanisms, counters and similar devices, that act like cognitive primitives on later tasks. More startling: meta-training on one well-chosen formal language helped as much as training on five thousand, provided that one language forced the useful mechanisms to form. The authors draw practical lessons for cheaper meta-learning and a theoretical bridge between symbolic accounts of mind and neural hardware.
arxiv-2503-16148:
Mats Faulborn and co-authors build a theory-grounded way to measure political bias in language models, in a 2025 paper. Models now serve as simulated people, search tools, and text analysts. Bias in them can skew all those uses. Past tests leaned on a popular compass quiz that is not a valid survey tool. Prompt wording also swung the results.

Their measure draws on political science and survey design. It tests many prompt forms and lets models answer freely, not just pick from set options. A careful yardstick matters because loose tests have produced clashing claims about model leanings. The work aims to settle how bias should be measured before arguing over how large it is.
arxiv-2503-16248:
Atharv Singh Patlan and co-authors present a 2025 study of memory attacks on AI agents that move money on blockchains. Such agents read prompts, past logs, and outside feeds as one context. The team name a broad attack family, context manipulation, and its stealthiest member, memory injection: poisoned entries planted in the agent's own past. On a known open agent frame, planted lines triggered wrongful transfers and rule breaks.

A test bench of over 150 real-style chain tasks and 500 attack cases priced the risk. Memory attacks beat prompt attacks by a wide mark. Shop defenses built for prompts fell short. Agents with wallets need memory treated as hostile ground, the authors argue.
arxiv-2503-16348:
Murray Shanahan wrote a 2025 essay on the philosophy of machine minds. Modern AI systems have no body, yet people ask whether they could be conscious in some sense. Shanahan asks what picture of consciousness could fit such a disembodied system and still survive careful scrutiny.

The essay probes how subjective time and a sense of self would even show up for such a being. Its steps, questions, and answers differ sharply from our own felt experience. Shanahan finds that trying to answer honestly stretches the language of consciousness close to breaking. The attempt ends near a Buddhist idea of emptiness, where the self is not a solid thing. That landing undercuts the habit of splitting mind and world into two. The essay is short and reflective rather than technical.
arxiv-2503-16648:
Luca Di Luzio, Giacomo Landini, Federico Mescia, and Vasja Susic build axion models where a key symmetry arises on its own, in a 2025 paper. The Peccei-Quinn symmetry was proposed to solve a puzzle in particle physics, and its quality can be spoiled by extra effects. Their models protect it by design.

The protection comes from mixing two kinds of gauge symmetry, one unifying forces and one shaping flavor. They study one concrete model in detail and show it shields the symmetry to high order. It also reproduces the known pattern of particle flavors. Very light extra particles appear as a side effect, and the authors note hard open problems.
arxiv-2503-17348:
Contat and Curien study a family of random trees that arise from car parking problems, and they settle a long-standing conjecture about them. In their model, cars arrive along a street of spaces in random order, and the pattern of parked cars can be drawn as a tree. Trees that end up fully parked show special limiting behavior.

The authors prove these trees, when scaled up, converge to a self-similar random tree different from the classic Brownian tree. Along the way they confirm that a broad class of polynomial equations with a catalytic variable shares the same singularity exponent, five halves. Their probabilistic approach reveals a hidden random walk inside the tree model that does the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2503-17448:
Tanay Kibe and Pratik Roy studied a quantum energy bound in 2025 in two-dimensional field theories after a quench, a sudden change that throws the system out of balance. The bound, called the quantum null energy condition, ties energy along a light ray to how entanglement changes. A stronger primary form is expected in these theories, and it is known to limit entropy production in holographic models.

The authors test the bound in two classic quench setups, one global and one that joins two systems locally. In the global case the primary form must hold at early times and it constrains the correlation functions of twist fields in a boundary state. They also find a violation setting, which sharpens where the bound can fail. Readers get a finer map of a bound that links energy, information, and irreversibility.
arxiv-2503-17548:
Machines that solve hard picks by settling like magnets come in fixed sizes, and big asks overflow them. Matthew Burns and Michael Huang study nets of such machines in 2025, where the ask is split across a row of settlers that must agree. Their math frames the ways the row can run, from lock-step to loose talk, and bounds how surely the row lands on a sound answer.

Dice runs flesh the bounds out. Fast chatter between the machines and slow chatter rule split lands, each with its own trap. From the two the team draw shop rules for picking the split, the talk rate, and the settle heat. Their aim is a field guide for a young craft: how to grow the net without losing the settle.
arxiv-2503-17648:
Jeremy VanderDoes and Shojaeddin Chenouri wrote a 2025 paper on spotting change points in functional data. Such data arrive as curves over time, like daily counts or price paths. Analysts need to know where the pattern shifts, so each stretch can be treated as uniform. Their method builds a graph on the curves and tests for change.

The paper gives the test stats and the thresholds used to flag a shift. It also gives plain advice on how to build the graph well. Computer trials compare the method with older ones. Tests cover both small and large shifts and check how touchy the method is. Uses include foot traffic counts, asset returns, and power prices.
arxiv-2503-18048:
Table data in fields like medicine demand models that are both accurate and easy to explain. Xiaochen Zhang and Haoyi Xiong present Spofe in 2025, a self taught pipeline that pulls features from tables while keeping its reasoning open to view. It first builds teaching signals with a kernel method that can catch curved patterns plain averages miss.

Those signals are then distilled into short formulas built from multiplied terms, which people can read. A knockoff based screen with strict error control picks which features truly matter. Across many real data sets, Spofe beat rival feature pickers at both sorting and forecasting tasks. The authors say the mix of power and clarity suits high stakes work.
arxiv-2503-18248:
Naoya Arakawa and Kenji Yonemitsu wrote this 2025 physics paper on controlling spin currents with light. In the spin Hall effect, an electric current in some materials produces a sideways flow of electron spin. The pair studied atom-thin sheets of four related compounds while shining swirling light on them.

Using Floquet theory, they computed how the spin flow changes under the light in a steady driven state. The light could strengthen the spin current and even flip its direction. They trace the effect to the sheets' broken symmetry plus strong effects of the light itself. The work points to light as a knob for future spin-based devices.
arxiv-2503-18348:
Ji-Hong Li presents a fault-spotting method for underwater vehicles in this 2025 paper. The vehicles hold a fixed position with several thrusters, so one can fail while others cover for it, hiding the fault. Most detectors estimate hidden states or parameters; Li's method instead reads the vehicle's motion control error directly.

In steady operation, that error shifts in telling patterns when a thruster weakens or fails. By studying those patterns closely, Li extracts facts about the true control input, which is otherwise unknown once faults strike. That unknown input is the hard part of naming the faulty thruster, so the trick unlocks the whole scheme. Once losses are named, control can be reshaped at once. Tests on a real vehicle model back the approach.
arxiv-2503-18748:
Florian Rupp, Manuel Eberhardinger, and Kai Eckert automate balance tuning for two-player game levels in a 2025 paper. Balancing uneven levels by hand takes long testing cycles. Their setup treats balance as content generation driven by learning from simulation.

Three parts work in a loop: a level maker, a balancing agent, and a scoring simulator. The agent swaps tiles to steer outcomes toward a goal such as equal win rates. New swap-based encodings made levels stay playable while tuning ran faster. Watching swap choices revealed which tile types sway balance most. Tests in a competitive game world beat a search-based rival and extended beyond simple equal balance.
arxiv-2503-18848:
Alessandro Barone and co-authors computed a nucleon form factor in 2025 using lattice simulations of quantum chromodynamics. This axial form factor helps explain how nucleons interact weakly and how their spin is built. Together with partner form factors, it splits the axial response by quark flavour.

Such splits feed into pinning down Standard Model values from low-energy experiments, such as the proton's weak charge. The team present their result with a full error budget. Their accounting covers the steps needed to reach the continuum limit, infinite volume, and physical quark masses. The calculation used an improved fermion action with two light quarks plus the strange quark.
arxiv-2503-19348:
Amir Jalili, Feng Pan, Ai Xi Chen, and Jerry Draayer predict nuclear binding energies in two thousand twenty-five. Three deep learning models face off on the task. Recurrent nets, gated recurrent units, and long short term memory nets compete. Data come from the Atomic Mass Evaluation of twenty twenty.

Inputs span proton and neutron counts plus liquid drop terms. Shell effect terms join the feature set as well. The gated recurrent unit wins with the lowest error score. Garvey-Kelson checks confirm the predictions hold up well. Extrapolation tests near the driplines stay robust too. Deep learning thus strengthens classic nuclear models.
arxiv-2503-19748:
Ryan Martin rebuilds prior-free Bayesian inference from possibility models with exact guarantees, in work from twenty twenty-five. With no prior knowledge, analysts usually pair a default prior with Bayes' rule. Those posteriors often give only roughly valid uncertainty statements. Inferential models built as possibility measures give exact validity instead. They are not probabilities, though, which limits their direct use.

Martin takes the inner probability shadow of such a model. That shadow keeps exact coverage for credible sets in the build. Efficiency at large samples is preserved by the approximation too. Where group symmetry holds, the answer matches classic Bayes and fiducial results. A Monte Carlo method computes the shadow in practice. Worked examples show the method behaving as theory promises. Prior-free inference gains reliability without losing familiarity.
arxiv-2503-19848:
Alex Glynn proposes a simple rule to keep invented citations out of published science. Generative AI systems fabricate references, and fake entries have already slipped into peer-reviewed journals. His 2025 essay argues the fix should make a fake citation impossible to submit in the first place.

Journals, he says, should require authors to deposit the full text of every source they cite, along with the manuscript. No one can cite what they cannot produce. The idea borrows from open-science data sharing rules, court clashes over AI-filed fictions, and patent practice, where prior art is submitted in full. Glynn stresses the added work is small for authors and editors alike, while the protection is near total.
arxiv-2503-19948:
Alexander Gambashidze and co-authors teach sight-and-word models to judge which image a person would like, in a 2025 paper. The ask is whether such a model can think its way to a human taste call at the time of the test.

The team trained the models with reward-style learning on two sets of human picks. The trained models called the liked image right about two times in three, on a par with tools built just for that task. Their edge is that they show their work, in plain steps a person can read. Light reward schemes then let the models rank any images, of any shape or load. The authors say the skill can sharpen tools that turn words into images, with less hand-marked data.
arxiv-2503-20048:
Yunlong Yu, Xiang-Bin Wang, Nic Shannon, and Robert Joynt boost a quantum optimizer with a classical head start in a 2025 paper. Quantum approximate optimization can refine answers that good classical methods find first. How best to blend the two remains an open design question.

The authors build a general model covering a family of warm-start variants. For the classic MaxCut problem they derive exact formulas for the first level's expected score. Those formulas allow fair averaging over many random instances at forty to one hundred eighty qubits. A variant seeded by a leading classical algorithm beats earlier warm-start designs in their tests. The study maps where quantum refinement may add real value over classical seeds.
arxiv-2503-20348:
Felix Vogel and co-authors locate actions in videos without training anything, by listening to what pretrained vision-language models already know. Their 2025 paper introduces VideoGEM, a training-free method for action grounding: given a phrase like a person chopping onions, find where in the frame it happens. Actions are harder than objects, being verbs with fuzzy outlines.

The method adapts an attention technique from image grounding and adds three refinements. Higher model layers, where abstract concepts live, get more weight, tuned automatically per prompt. The prompt itself is split into action, verb, and object parts, each grounded separately. Across three model backbones and four video datasets, this training-free pipeline beat trained state-of-the-art systems. The result hints that foundation models already contain an action sense, waiting for the way to ask. Training-free wins matter practically: no dataset, no GPU weeks, just better questions.
arxiv-2503-20648:
Raj Sanjay Shah and five co-authors present TN-Eval in 2025, a way to judge the quality of behavioral therapy notes. Clear standards for such notes lag behind those for physical health notes, even though the notes matter for care and for the law. Working with licensed therapists, the team built a scoring guide that rates notes on completeness, conciseness, and faithfulness.

They applied the guide to notes written by therapists and notes written by language models. The guide gave steadier, clearer results than simple rating scales. Models matched human judges on two of the three scores but struggled with faithfulness. Therapist notes often missed content, model notes sometimes invented it, yet blinded therapists still preferred the model notes.
arxiv-2503-20748:
Chen Tang leads a team of nine authors in a 2025 paper that introduces UniSTD, a unified model for spatio-temporal learning. Most past models were built for one task at a time, which held back their use across fields with distinct needs.

UniSTD is a Transformer model trained in two stages. First it pretrains on plain 2D images and image-text data to build a broad base. Then joint training on spatio-temporal data tunes it for such tasks. A rank-adaptive mixture-of-experts step helps it adapt, and a new temporal part aids how it reads change over time.
arxiv-2503-20848:
Laufer, Kleinberg, and Heidari modeled how AI safety rules can backfire when they are weak and aimed at the wrong player. Their game has three actors. A regulator sets a minimum safety standard. A general-purpose AI creator builds the base technology. Domain specialists then adapt it for specific uses and share the revenue. Safety and performance both depend on what each side invests.

The first finding is a warning: weak rules aimed mainly at the specialists can lower overall safety, even though regulating use cases feels natural. The effect holds across many settings. The second finding cuts the other way. Stronger, well-placed rules covering both creators and specialists can leave everyone better off, because the standard acts as a commitment device that raises both safety and performance. The authors argue that where a rule lands matters as much as how strict it is.
arxiv-2503-21248:
Yujie Liu and co-authors build a benchmark in a 2025 paper for whether language models can do the early, creative steps of scientific discovery. Hypothesis generation had no dedicated test. The test splits discovery into three parts. Models must find inspirations, compose hypotheses, and rank them. Solved in full, those three parts would solve the whole task.

An automated pipeline mined papers in twelve fields. It pulled out questions, background, inspirations, and hypotheses, and experts confirmed its accuracy. To dodge contamination, the team used only papers from 2024 on. The pipeline can refresh itself as training cutoffs advance. Models excelled at retrieving inspirations, an out-of-distribution task. That hints they can surface novel associations. The authors offer the test as a renewable yardstick for machine-assisted discovery.
arxiv-2503-21448:
Alejandro García-Fernández and co-authors present HORIZON, a framework for sorting feature toggles driven by pricing, in a 2025 paper. Subscription software turns features on or off per customer tier. As pricing grows more tailored, the rules guarding each feature multiply through the code. Standard toggles were not built for that pricing logic.

Pricing-driven toggles must also track how much each user consumes, so limits are never crossed. Industry tools lack clear support for this need, and academic work sticks to narrow designs. HORIZON classifies the existing approaches and sets terms for fair comparison. The aim is to guide builders of subscription platforms toward toggles that respect pricing plans by design, not by patchwork.
arxiv-2503-21748:
Frank Ernesto Quintela Rodriguez and co-authors find an exact formula for how much energy can be pulled from a class of quantum systems under a restricted set of moves. The systems are bosonic, such as light or vibrating fields, governed by simple square-law energy rules. The allowed moves are Gaussian operations, the easiest to perform in labs. Their 2025 work names the prize Gaussian ergotropy.

The formula mirrors the classic result for unrestricted moves but swaps plain eigenvalues for symplectic ones, the natural spectrum for such systems. The team proves the quantity adds up cleanly across copies, so joining systems with entangling Gaussian moves gains nothing. They also bound how extractable work relates to measures of non-Gaussianity. A final part extends the frame to open systems and asks which starting state best limits energy lost to a channel.
arxiv-2503-22148:
Guansen Wang and three co-authors hunt for light dark matter through cosmic rays in a 2025 paper. If dark matter grains lighter than a proton smash together into charged pairs, they would seed extra electrons and positrons in our galaxy. Those particles gain energy as they ride cosmic winds.

Space detectors can catch the boosted particles. Reading existing data, the team capped how often such dark matter can vanish across a mass range. Future telescopes that watch faint gamma rays should add matched caps from the glow of the same events. The two routes together squeeze the space where light dark matter can hide.
arxiv-2503-22248: Xinwei Gao and four co-authors teach a car to keep its lane with constrained reinforcement learning, in work from 2025. Lane keeping balances competing goals, and hand-tuning their weights per scenario is brittle. Their setup folds the weights into the learning itself, so the agent learns the trade-offs alongside the driving policy. Tests beat standard reinforcement learning on efficiency and reliability, and real-vehicle demonstrations are reported.
arxiv-2503-22348:
Christos Charmousis and co-authors perturb black holes that carry their own scalar charge in a 2025 paper. In some gravity theories beyond Einstein's, a black hole can hold a scalar charge set independently of its mass, deforming the classic Schwarzschild shape. The team studies twisting, axial wobbles of such holes. They also build related holes in other theories by warping the metric.

One warp keeps gravity waves at light speed; another keeps the equations second order. Axial wobbles turn out to obey the classic equations, but in an effective geometry whose horizons for gravity and light split apart. Ringing tones of the hole were computed in an approximation scheme. The work maps how exotic hair changes the way a black hole shivers.
arxiv-2503-22448:
Graciana Puentes compares three ways to group data in a 2025 paper. The data come from fluid lenses, soft lenses whose shape shifts with fluid. A wave sensor read the bent light from the lenses, and each read broke into 15 shape terms. The task was to sort like reads into clusters. Three methods faced the same data set.

One method used a self-organizing map, a neural net that lays data on a grid. A second built a tree of groups step by step, and its groups matched the data well. A third split the data into five tight groups with a strong score. Judged as a whole, tree grouping plus the split method gave the most stable result. Map size and tree cut choices could swing the map-based result on their own, which made it less safe to trust alone.
arxiv-2503-22948:
Tianyang Xu and co-authors built a way to make chat models forget protected text in two thousand twenty-five. Large language models learn from huge text sets. They can memorize and repeat passages under copyright, which has sparked lawsuits. Full retraining to remove such text is far too costly. The team instead teaches the model to unlearn chosen passages.

Their method first gathers cases where the model repeats protected text. Training then swaps those outputs for fresh, plausible wording. Extra math guards keep skill on unrelated tasks from slipping. Tests show the model drops the protected passages at scale. It keeps its general language ability at the same time. The approach offers firms a practical path to legal compliance.
arxiv-2503-23148:
Hunter Meyer and six co-authors improve an X-ray imaging method in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Grating interferometry uses a fine grating to split X-rays into a fringe pattern. A sample bends that pattern, yielding three images at once: absorption, phase shift, and small-angle scattering. Such images could serve lung and breast screening and factory testing. The method assumes a perfectly even pattern, which real setups break.

Uneven grating steps and extra harmonics in the fringes leave wavy artifacts in the images. The authors correct for both flaws at once. They model several harmonics of the fringe pattern and fix the step errors. Cleaner images bring this young modality closer to clinical use. Imaging physicists are the audience.
arxiv-2503-23448:
Max Hort, Linas Vidziunas, and Leon Moonen test whether meaning-preserving code rewrites can sharpen bug-finding tools at test time. The idea mirrors metamorphic testing: a tool should give the same verdict on code that means the same. Their 2025 study first gathered published rewrite tools, finding ninety-four rewrites across twenty-eight papers. They built thirty-nine of them, then hand-checked each one.

The check was sobering: twenty-three of the thirty-nine rewrites changed code meaning, so only sixteen were safe. With those, three ensemble voting schemes were tried on a flaw data set with two language models. Accuracy did not rise. The authors warn that shared rewrites are hard to reuse safely.
arxiv-2503-23748:
Yujin Huang, Zhi Zhang, Qingchuan Zhao, Xingliang Yuan, and Chunyang Chen present THEMIS in this 2025 paper, a guard for AI models that live on phones. On-device models run offline and keep user data private, a clear win. The cost is exposure: the model file sits on the user's device, where it can be stolen or copied.

Hardware vaults called trusted execution environments can lock models away, but they are hard to scale and awkward with third-party models. Watermarking, the usual fallback, assumes skills many app developers lack. THEMIS aims for a practical middle path that works after deployment, on real devices. The paper weighs the trade-offs among protection strength, speed, and ease of use, as new graphics chips with built-in vaults begin to change what is possible.
arxiv-2503-23848:
Minghan Wang and five co-authors present a toolkit for making speech dialogue data in two thousand twenty-five. Good speech data is key for speech language models, but past sources fall short. Human takes cost a lot and raise privacy fears. Fake takes often sound stiff and false. Their system aims to close that gap.

The toolkit builds data through steps like scene setup, script writing, and voice cloning. It adds tone cues so speech sounds more like real talk. A screen tool lets users check samples, and a batch mode makes many at once. Tests show quality near human takes at far less cost. The code and sample sets in English and Chinese are free.
arxiv-2503-24148:
Yang Zou and co-authors present Trident, a design that lets many readers share battery free tags without clashes, in a 2025 paper. Tags that reflect radio waves power much cheap sensing. When several readers cover one area, stray reflections from a tag can jam a reader outside its zone.

Old fixes split access by time, which caps total flow. Trident instead splits by frequency and space. Each tag senses its channel and retunes the pitch and strength of its reply. A plan assigns pitches to readers so all can work at once. Tests raised network flow more than three fold over the time split scheme.
arxiv-2503-24248:
Weeraratne, Hunt, and Kurz write on how to pick the right count of parts in principal component analysis for health research. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The method shrinks a large data set to a few key patterns, which can aid diagnosis, care plans, and the search for new markers.

Common rules for how many parts to keep give unlike answers. One rule keeps too few, while a scree test keeps too many and harms trust in the result. The share-of-variance rule is more stable. A Pareto chart, which shows both the running share and the cut point, is their pick for the most sound choice.
arxiv-2503-24348:
Daria Rudneva and Eddy Ardonne present a 2025 math paper on categories that arise from symmetry algebras in physics. These categories encode how particles can fuse and braid, and two traits matter for their use: whether they respect a form of unitarity, and whether they carry a full modular structure.

Working through the related quantum groups, the pair computed which parameter values give each trait. Their picture rests on two stated conjectures and on number crunching. Where past rigorous work exists, their results match it fully. For the cases missing from the literature, they complete the picture. The map should guide both math and physics uses of these categories.
arxiv-2504-00048:
Cong Duy Vu Hoang and co-authors present a method that teaches small language models to turn plain questions into database code, in a 2025 paper. Businesses want this translation, called NL2SQL, to be both accurate and cheap to run. Customer-specific needs make the task harder. Their framework, Distill-C, uses a large teacher model to craft high-quality training examples. Small open models then learn from that synthetic data.

Fine-tuned small models matched or beat teacher models ten times their size. Across several hard public benchmarks, execution accuracy rose by an average of thirty-six percent over the base models. Three internal customer benchmarks showed a gain near twenty-three percent. The authors argue the approach generalizes across model families. They present it as a way to ship light, low-cost translation tools without giving up accuracy.
arxiv-2504-00148:
A team of researchers reports early tests of a new plastic film for large detectors that use liquid argon. The 2025 paper looks at a film called PVN and asks if it can shift light in the same way as a film already in use, called PEN. Such films help detectors catch faint light from rare events.

The team cast the film from a liquid mix and tested it at very low heat. The film did shift light, with speed and yield close to those of PEN. One flaw stood out: the film was quite brittle, which may limit its use. More work will be needed before it can serve in a full detector.
arxiv-2504-00248:
An electron trapped in a quantum dot absorbs light and escapes, and how readily it does so depends on the dot's inner rules. Carlos Magno Pereira and co-authors vary one rule in a 2025 study: the electron's effective mass changes with position inside the dot, dialed by a parameter in their model.

Even a small turn of that dial shifts the absorption peak and swells or shrinks its height, they find. At certain settings the trend flips, the cross-section falling as the photon energy climbs where it first rose. Transitions from the ground state also fence the dial to negative values only. The message for device builders is that mass grading in a dot is not a detail but a design lever for light sensors and other optoelectronics.
arxiv-2504-00348:
Kyle Stein and co-authors teach models from a single example in a machine learning paper. One-shot learning asks a model to spot a brand-new class from one labeled image, leaning on whatever unmarked cases are at hand, the transductive twist.

Their method splits images into mixes of latent primitives living in small pockets. A query image sharing the lone example's primitive recipe takes its label. Across feature tools and data sets, the splitting approach spread to unseen classes reliably. The framing turns spotting into recipe matching, which suits classes where marking even a handful of cases is costly.
arxiv-2504-00648:
Franco Dassi and three co-authors build error checks for a math method used on spread problems tied to stress. The model links how a solid bends with how a substance spreads through it, a pair that pulls on each other both ways. Their 2025 work asks how a user can trust the numbers such a method gives.

The team derives checks from what is left over after each run, weighted so the checks stay sound across settings. They prove the checks both flag real error and avoid false alarms. The proofs lean on split tools for the flow fields, with new steps spelled out for three dimensions. Tests in two and three dimensions show the checks track true error well. Mesh fixes guided by them should be safe.
arxiv-2504-00748:
Yunsoo Kim and five co-authors build a tool that mines medical paper summaries for cancer test data. Their 2025 paper deals with immunohistochemistry, a stain test that shows which proteins a tumour carries. Such data sit buried in the text of a huge number of abstracts.

The tool, named IHC-LLMiner, first sorts abstracts into those that fit and those that do not. It then pulls out the tumour type and marker from each fit abstract. A tuned model beat a big general model on speed and score. Of about 108,000 abstracts screened, some 30,000 were kept. The pulled data matched known web sources well and filled gaps in them. The team also posts its models and training data for free online.
arxiv-2504-01148:
Four statisticians in Puerto Rico refine a method for pulling apart the forces that shape population trends, in a 2025 paper. The method, called age-period-cohort analysis, tries to split change into aging effects, era effects, and the imprint of each birth generation. Those three forces tangle by design, which makes them hard to separate. The team builds a Bayesian version meant to handle a wide range of population and health questions.

Their setup uses a flexible prior for scale settings, tests rival ways to pin down the tangled effects, and ships in a friendly form others can adapt. They apply it to the steep fall of fertility in Puerto Rico. The case is hard to model because change came fast. Their reading stresses the momentum of generations over era effects, which pushes against the usual story for very low fertility lands.
arxiv-2504-01248:
Voice assistants in cars can state falsehoods with confidence, and checking every answer by hand is slow. Rafael Giebisch and co-authors build an automatic checker in this 2025 paper that uses large language models to grade a car assistant's answers against the vehicle manual.

They try five grading setups, mixing model ensembles and role prompts to steady the verdicts. The best setup agreed with expert judges on factual correctness more than nine times in ten, and it answered in a few seconds. Testing ran on a new data set built for the car domain. The results suggest model-based grading is a workable way to vet in-car assistants.
arxiv-2504-01548:
Sergey Norin and Raphael Steiner present a 2025 math note that settles a recent conjecture about defective graph coloring. In defective coloring, each color class may contain some edges, as long as no vertex has more than a set number of same-color neighbors. A blowup replaces each vertex of a graph with a clique, a fully linked group. A recent paper guessed that a graph's ordinary coloring number exactly equals the defective number of its blowup.

Norin and Steiner disprove the guess. They build graphs whose ordinary number beats the defective blowup number by a factor of at least 30 over 29, for infinitely many defect levels. The note is not purely negative: they also prove the two numbers never differ by more than a factor of two, so the conjecture holds up to a constant correction.
arxiv-2504-01748:
Alexis Quintana, Ignacio Negueruela, and Sara Berlanas measure how widely star birth is spread across a spiral arm of our galaxy. Their 2025 paper uses a star group called Cas OB5, which sits where the Perseus arm crosses our view. The group holds known open clusters and only mild dust dimming, which suits a pilot count.

From a wide field, the team sifted near 130,000 candidate hot stars down to about 56,000 by fitting their light. A clustering tool then found seventeen open clusters in the patch. Four of them form one linked structure, the Cas OB5 group itself. Spectra split it into two age bands, with one cluster far younger than its kin, which refines the arm's tale.
arxiv-2504-01848:
Giulio Starace and co-authors ask whether AI agents can redo published AI research from scratch, in a 2025 paper. Their benchmark, PaperBench, hands agents twenty spotlight and oral papers from a top 2024 conference. The agent must grasp the contribution, write the code, and run the experiments, with no starter files. Grading uses rubrics that break each paper into small checkable pieces, over eight thousand in total, written with the original authors.

An automated judge based on a language model grades attempts against the rubrics, and the judge itself was benchmarked. Replication is the sternest test of whether an AI understands research rather than summarizing it. The results map how far today's agents get on real science.
arxiv-2504-01948:
Manos Frouzakis and co-authors present PIMDAL in a 2025 paper on the memory bottleneck in data analytics. Database systems move huge volumes of data between memory and processors, and that traffic, not raw computation, now limits core operations such as selection, aggregation, ordering, and join.

Processing-in-memory hardware puts compute next to the data itself. The team built a data analytics library for the real UPMEM processing-in-memory system, covering all four major operators, rather than testing on simulators or partial workloads. Hardware performance metrics then show which properties of such a system matter most for fast analytics. The work maps what a data-centric machine can do today.
arxiv-2504-02048:
Giulia Roccetti and co-authors simulate how Earth would look to a far-off telescope that sees it as a single dot. Future observatories aim to read the reflected light of rocky exoplanets and judge whether they might host life. Their 2025 paper builds reference spectra and phase curves for an Earth-like planet in both plain and polarized light.

A three-dimensional radiative transfer code models real surface maps, seasonal changes, and cloud fields drawn from weather data. Fine cloud detail at small scales cut total reflectance and made the phase curve swing more. Ocean glint ruled at wide phase angles. Maps that ignore how albedo shifts with wavelength overstated some signals. Exoplanet observers get a yardstick for reading alien Earths.
arxiv-2504-02148:
Heming Zhang and a large team of co-authors build a new kind of data set for cell biology in a 2025 paper. Foundation models trained on single-cell data usually read genes as number lists, which drops the written knowledge and the signaling links between molecules that biologists rely on. The team wanted a format that keeps all three in one structure.

Their structure, the Text-Omic Signaling Graph, ties plain-language biomedical knowledge to measured gene data and to the network of signals inside a cell. From it they built OmniCellTOSG, a resource of about half a million such graphs, each summarizing a small cluster of cells. The set is meant to train graph-language foundation models that can reason about cells with context, not just counts. The authors offer it as shared groundwork for precision medicine research.
arxiv-2504-02548:
Bhattacharyya, Rybczynski, and Wlodarczyk probe speed spreads in high-force hits with odd stats. Their mark is a length-wise curb count from speed spread shares. Three roads meet on that mark: two count, one in closed form. Code runs use EPOS, FTFP-BERT, and HIJING for the first road. EPOS shows a fall trend at front and back speeds in runs. The peer two codes show a rise trend there in runs.

Closed roads use Tsallis stats and a bent flow form in the work. The flow form sits in the slack-time take for the runs. Both closed roads fit the NA61 data well in the text. Data span five force marks for bad-charge pions in hits. The fit holds at each of those force marks in step.
arxiv-2504-02648:
Raghu Arghal, Kevin He, Shirin Saeedi Bidokhti, and Saswati Sarkar model a platform that steers how a crowd learns, in a 2025 paper. People now form beliefs from two streams: signals a platform feeds them and the choices of those who acted before. The platform's designer may want welfare or may push a pet action.

The authors formalize this controlled social learning as a fresh optimization problem, mixing planning over time with private Bayesian updating by each agent. They prove the value function has a friendly shape and describe the best policies for both kindly and biased planners. In some settings the biased planner profits by fogging the signals agents receive. Even under strict openness rules, the framework shows how much steering remains possible, a warning for platform governance.
arxiv-2504-02748: Knowing how atrial heart tissue stretches and resists is essential for simulating the heart, yet standard material models are chosen in advance and may fit poorly. Peirlinck, Linka, and Kuhl let a constitutive neural network discover the material law directly from tests on healthy human atrial tissue. Trained on two-direction stretch data, the network picks the form that matches the tissue best, avoiding the limits of preset models. The authors present the approach as a step toward sharper simulation and prediction of cardiac health.
arxiv-2504-02848:
Materials scientists have oceans of computer-simulated data and puddles of laboratory measurements, and bridging the two is a standing frustration. Yahagi and co-authors propose a transfer learning scheme that translates simulation results into the experimental world using chemical knowledge.

Their domain transformation maps computed values into the space of measured ones. Two pieces of prior knowledge guide the mapping: how statistical ensembles relate the two worlds, and how the simulated and real quantities correspond. Tested on catalyst activity for the reverse water-gas shift reaction, the model won by a wide margin. It beat learning from experiment alone. Fewer than ten real data points sufficed to align the domains, where a model trained from scratch needed over a hundred. The savings could cut laboratory trial counts sharply.
arxiv-2504-02948:
Joseph Cuozzo and François Léonard chase a perfect superconducting diode in a 2025 paper. A supercurrent diode carries lossless current more easily one way than the other, like an electronic one-way valve. When such behavior can arise in a Josephson junction, and how efficient it can get, were open questions. Their junction uses a chiral nanotube, a carbon tube with a twist, as the weak link.

Within a standard theory, a magnetic field along the tube produced the diode effect, even without spin-orbit coupling. Oddly, the effect did not track the junction's anomalous phase shift. The authors found a second route: a persistent circulating current, locked by flux rules, can switch the effect on by itself. In principle that route reaches perfect efficiency. They present the result as a design rule for high-grade supercurrent diodes.
arxiv-2504-03048:
Ian Berlot-Attwell, Frank Rudzicz, and Xujie Si test a claim about language models that learn tool libraries in a 2025 paper. Such systems build and store reusable lemmas or code to solve later tasks faster. One system, LEGO-Prover, claims to learn lemmas for math proofs in this way.

The team dug into how the system truly works and found no sign that learned lemmas get reused as stored. Soft reuse, by editing stored cases, also lacked support. Once compute cost was counted fairly, the system did not beat plain prompting of the model. The authors urge tougher tests for this whole line of work.
arxiv-2504-03248:
Yuji Hirono and four co-authors build optimal observables for the chiral magnetic effect with machine learning in a 2025 paper. The effect is a current that a strong magnetic field should drive in hot quark matter. In heavy-ion collisions, its faint signal drowns in background flows that mimic it.

The team write broad observables from flow harmonics, then let an optimizer tune them for the best signal-to-background split. On simulated collisions from a standard fluid model, the learned measures beat the classic correlators by a wide margin. Background stays low while the gain holds. The method gives experiments a sharper tool for a long-sought effect.
arxiv-2504-03348:
José Fernando extends in 2025 a classic geometry theorem so that one smooth path can be threaded through many chosen points at chosen times. The old curve selection lemma says any point on the edge of a shape cut out by polynomial rules can be reached by a well behaved Nash arc. Fernando asks for an itinerary version: a path visiting control points exactly at control times.

His answer gives a sharp condition. When there are enough control points in general position, such a path exists exactly when the shape is joined by analytic paths. Polynomial paths will not do in general, since some algebraic sets hold no rational curves at all. They can work with an extra assumption, such as the shape filling full dimension. A second thread asks how well a Nash path can mimic a given rough path with the same stops.
arxiv-2504-03848:
Rupert Croft and eight co-authors set out in 2025 to use huge quasar surveys to probe the ultraviolet glow that fills the universe. Bright quasars burn a clear gap in the gas around them, an effect that reveals how strong that background glow is. Past work used only tens or hundreds of quasars, while new surveys hold far more.

The team built a model that accounts for quasars sitting in dense regions, then tested it on a simulated universe with quasars and gas formed together. Fitting the model to single quasar spectra in the test worked well. The path is open to apply it to real survey data at full scale.
arxiv-2504-03948:
Sanjoy Kundu, Shanmukha Vellamcheti, and Sathyanarayanan Aakur tackle activity recognition from a head-worn camera when the set of possible activities is not fixed in advance. Real life is open-ended, and a system must find the right label in a huge space it has only partly seen. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they propose a probabilistic search that jumps and drifts through a space of candidate labels. Common-sense structure keeps the space sensible, vision-language models refine guesses, and randomness in the search avoids checking every label.

They test the system at four levels of openness, from a fixed label set to wide-open search, on kitchen, gaze, and home activity data sets. Performance led the field in their benchmarks at each level. A clear taxonomy of openness levels is offered alongside, to help later work state exactly which problem it solves.
arxiv-2504-04048:
Shijun Liao and Shijie Qin argue that the small numerical noise in turbulence simulations carries real physical meaning, in a 2025 paper. Direct simulations solve flow equations on a grid, but rounding and grid noise always creep in. A cleaner method that holds noise near zero for long stretches gives a comparison point.

Against that clean base, the authors show sim noise acts much like heat jitter or random outside disturbance in a real flow. A fine grid then matches flow under small disturbance, while a coarse grid matches flow under large disturbance. Each result is still true to its own physics, even when summary numbers differ. The paper offers a positive reading of noise once seen as pure error.
arxiv-2504-04648:
Yulei Wang, Xin Cheng, and Mingde Ding mapped the base pattern of magnetic reconnection in a wild current sheet. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with how field lines break and rejoin in plasmas. This process drives eruptions at many scales and seems tied to turbulence. Yet the three dimensional form of it in strong turbulence was a mystery. The team built a way to find and read many small reconnection shards in one sheet.

They ran it on a top sim of flare like turbulence. Shards came out as near flat sheets laid on local flux faces. Their speeds and rates spread wide under the churn. Readers in solar physics get a first full census of reconnection in a storm.
arxiv-2504-05048:
Abughalwa, Nguyen, and co-authors work on guaranteeing private communication for every user in a network aided by a smart reflecting surface, in a 2025 paper. The surface's elements can only take coarse, quantized settings, and the channel knowledge behind them is imperfect, while an eavesdropper's location is unknown. All of this makes blanket secrecy hard.

The team jointly tunes the transmitter's beam and the surface's reflections to maximize the worst user's secrecy rate. Their algorithm reshapes the hard optimization into a sequence of solvable steps and provably settles at a local optimum with modest computing cost. Simulations with realistic settings confirm secrecy for all users.
arxiv-2504-05148:
Yasuhiro Yao, Ryoichi Ishikawa, and Takeshi Oishi fuse laser ranging with stereo cameras for real-time depth sensing, in a 2025 robotics paper. Lasers give sparse but exact distances, while stereo images are dense but error-prone. Their method runs a classic stereo matcher with a new cost term seeded by laser points. The laser data are first spread into a semi-dense map, and a consistency check rejects clashes between the two sources.

On the KITTI driving benchmark, the method reached a 2.79 percent error rate, beating the prior real-time best of 3.05 percent. Tests varied laser density, weather, and indoor scenes to show flexibility. Every step runs in parallel on a graphics processor, and no learning is involved. The authors pitch it for robots that need depth now, not after training.
arxiv-2504-05248:
Marius Almanstötter, Roman Vetter, and Dagmar Iber present a study from twenty twenty-five on reading off the constants of an equation from noisy data. Networks that learn with physics rules built in can do this task. They strain, though, when data is sparse: runs can stall, wobble, or overfit. Loss design is also a chore.

Their frame, PINNverse, recasts training as a bound optimization task. It keeps the data loss and the equation loss in live balance as training runs. A multiplier method lets it land on any point of the trade-off front. Tests on four classic models from physics and life science gave sound, true values from noisy data. The frame also helps when the forward run is costly.
arxiv-2504-05448:
Bastian and co-authors watch solar spicules with the ALMA radio array in two thousand twenty-five. Spicules are thin jets that shoot up from the Sun's surface. The team viewed a polar coronal hole on Christmas Day of two thousand eighteen, in radio, optical, and ultraviolet light at once.

Radio images caught spicules low in the Sun's outer skin, while ultraviolet views showed them reaching higher. The radio jets show as dark cuts against bright coronal glow, which lets the team gauge their hydrogen depth. Heat radiation at radio waves also gives electron density by height with few guesses about heat. The mass spicules carry up looks too small to feed the corona or the solar wind much.
arxiv-2504-05548:
Sousa, Ferreira, and Tinto calculated this forecast in twenty twenty-five for future space-based gravitational wave detectors. These detectors will sit near Earth rather than far from it. They target a middle band of wave frequencies between ground detectors and the planned LISA mission. The paper asks how precisely they could pin down steady, single-tone signals.

Using a standard precision method, the team studied three mission designs. All three located sources best at the high end of their bands. One design with far worse noise matched the others only in a narrow high band. Precision in frequency and strength also peaked in set bands that differ by design. The authors map how accuracy shifts with source position across the sky.
arxiv-2504-05748:
Tri Tung Nguyen Nguyen and three colleagues teach robots the art of listening with the face, in a 2025 paper. In conversation, a good listener nods and reacts without words; modeling that silent behavior is hard because it varies in time and form.

Rather than converting motion into dense token streams, which blur the patterns, their method compresses each sequence into a few keyframes plus the transitions between them. Interpolation refills the gaps, keeping the motion's timing while widening variety during learning. Applied to listening-head prediction in two-person conversations, the sparse code explained facial patterns better and generated higher-fidelity reactions. The authors present sparseness as a feature, not a loss.
arxiv-2504-05848:
Tommaso Favalli studies the limits of a quantum clock in a 2025 physics paper. The clock's time values come from a time measure paired with an energy operator whose levels are bounded and separate. Favalli asks how fine the clock's time steps can be, and when they can be treated as smooth.

With evenly spaced energy levels, the time measure can be a standard operator, and a clear limit on step size appears. In the general case, a broader kind of measure is needed. Adding more time states shrinks the smallest time step, and Favalli states when smooth treatment becomes fair. A final limit covers the clock's sharpness when it is used with light signals to measure distances in space and time.
arxiv-2504-06048:
Joery de Vries, Jinke He, Yaniv Oren, and Matthijs Spaan adapt a particle-based planning method to the habits of reinforcement learning. Monte Carlo tree search powers many game-playing breakthroughs but resists parallel hardware, so sequential Monte Carlo planners have grown popular; they recast control as inference and smooth action sequences with particle filters. The catch, the team argues, is that standard filter design fights the planner's real job, which is to improve the policy at the very first step. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they reshape sampling with trust-region limits on actions, handle terminal states explicitly, and improve how policy and value targets are estimated.

Their twisted variant beat baseline tree search and particle planners in both speed and sample efficiency across discrete and continuous test domains, by the authors report. The work targets robots and simulators where planning must run online under a compute budget.
arxiv-2504-06148:
Xiangxi Zheng and co-authors present a 2025 game-based test frame for the sight skills of large models that take both image and text. Fixed image tests miss how such models see and act in a world that moves and answers back. Games give a live test bed where each choice rests on what the model sees at that moment.

The frame holds five video games with more than 30 test scenes in rich, free-form worlds. Models have to interpret the screen and steer play from sight alone, much as a human player does. A ranking system that adapts to scene difficulty keeps scores fair across tasks. Top models near human scores on easy tasks but fall far behind on hard ones. The gap shows clear limits in frame-by-frame control.
arxiv-2504-06248:
Vincent Thibeault, Benjamin Claveau, Antoine Allard, and Patrick Desrosiers find hidden conserved quantities, in a 2025 preprint, in networks of coupled oscillators. The Kuramoto model tracks how rhythms sync across a network. For uniform setups, quantities that never change are well known. For messy real networks, the wiring rules that permit such constants stayed obscure. The authors attack the problem with Koopman theory, borrowed from dynamical systems. Its eigenfunctions expose the symmetries behind each conserved quantity.

From those symmetries they derive general conditions on any weighted, directed, signed graph. The conditions pick out broad families of network motifs that protect phase relations. Scanning hundreds of real networks, they find those motifs are common. So many real systems may preserve more structure than assumed. The results link wiring patterns to long-term rhythm behavior. The authors point to Koopman spectra as a next tool for dynamics on complex networks.
arxiv-2504-06748:
Sirine Arfa and co-authors present a neuromorphic computing paper, published in 2025, on running gesture recognition on a brain inspired chip. Spiking neural networks fire only in brief pulses, which saves energy, and they pair well with event based cameras that report changes instead of full frames. The target chip, SpiNNaker2, has tight memory limits, so the network must be shrunk carefully.

The team benchmarks two ways to compress the network to eight bit numbers, one applied after training and one built into training, each with its own way to scale firing thresholds. Both nearly matched full precision accuracy on the gesture task. Their plain baselines also stood up well against earlier published results.
arxiv-2504-06948:
Differential equations drive models of motion, circuits, and much more, and quantum computers may one day solve them faster. Dekuan Dong, Yingzhou Li, and Jungong Xue propose a quantum algorithm in 2025 for the steady linear kind. Their method rests on how a matrix exponential, the core of the solution, can be approached by a rational formula called a Padé approximation.

That approximation becomes a large, mostly empty linear system that quantum solvers can attack. Compared with a Taylor series route, their method needs a lower order for the same precision and scales better as order grows. Circuit details and cost counts are given, and numerical tests back the claimed edge over rival algorithms.
arxiv-2504-07048:
Avinash Kumar and co-authors present a 2025 defense for shared quantum computers. Running many programs at once lifts device use, but crosstalk from paired operations can corrupt a neighbor program. The team builds an attack that needs no knowledge of the hardware error map.

Their zero knowledge attack altered victim outputs in 40 percent of cases on commercial systems. The attack works since the victim keeps a fixed pairing and context. Their defense, QONTEXTS, switches each program across many contexts, each holding a subset of trials. Output spreads are compared across contexts to spot tainted ones. On real IBM systems, resilience rose by three orders of size and accuracy by a third on average.
arxiv-2504-07148:
Yingjie Zhou and co-authors build an AI agent that restores damaged images by reasoning step by step, in a 2025 paper. Real photos suffer mixed harm: noise, blur, compression marks, and low detail. Models trained for one harm type fail on others. All-in-one models can lose quality on some harms and still miss new ones.

Their agent, Q-Agent, uses a multimodal model to judge image quality first. A chain-of-thought plan then orders the repair steps. Older agents picked steps by trial and rollback, which wastes time and can misread the harm. Quality-guided planning skips needless repairs. The design aims for faster, sharper restoration of photos with unknown, mixed damage.
arxiv-2504-07348:
Yu-Ping Liu and colleagues build an integrated quantum memory that stores light-based qubits for just over a millisecond. Quantum networks and repeaters need such memories, but chip-scale waveguide versions had held states only for tens of microseconds. Their device is a laser-written waveguide inside a europium-doped crystal, with on-chip electric guides applying dynamical decoupling to fight spin dephasing.

Storage reached 1.021 milliseconds with an efficiency of twelve percent. That beats a plain fibre delay line at the same wait, a first for an integrated memory. The team notes that adding set magnetic fields could make such long-lived memories portable for future quantum links.
arxiv-2504-07448:
Juzheng Zhang and three co-authors improve multi-task fine-tuning in a twenty twenty-five paper. They build on LoRA, a light way to adapt large language models. When one set of adapters must serve many tasks, the tasks can interfere with each other. Merging adapters also carries cost and clutter.

Their method, LoRI, freezes one set of projection matrices at random values. It makes the other set sparse, using a mask that differs by task. That cuts the count of trainable values a lot while keeping task scores strong. The design also uses near-orthogonal adapter spaces to limit cross-task interference. Tests covered language understanding, math reasoning, code writing, and safety alignment. LoRI beat full fine-tuning in their trials.
arxiv-2504-07548:
Catherine Bandle, Simon Stingelin, and Alfred Wagner study nonlinear eigenvalue problems in one dimension where the spectrum forms an interval. They work with Robin and Dirichlet boundary rules, which fix how a solution behaves at the ends. The central question is how many solutions exist and what shapes they take.

Using phase plane methods, the authors trace the form and count of solutions across cases. Along the way they find a new type of solution that is not symmetric. Numerical examples round out the paper and show the patterns in concrete form. The work helps map a class of problems where many answers can share the same setting.
arxiv-2504-07648:
Maridi and co-authors fit several reaction outcomes of deuterons striking gold at once, in this 2025 paper. Elastic scattering, breakup, transfer, and other direct yields each carry part of the story. Fitting them one by one can hide the physics they share.

Their optical model builds its parts from the Coulomb and nuclear shares of the direct yields themselves. Run across all beam energies with data, it matched the measured values well. The authors argue the recipe carries over to other deuteron shots on heavy targets. One consistent picture, they suggest, beats a drawer of separate fits.
arxiv-2504-07748:
Alisson Rodrigues de Paula and five co-authors unveiled in 2025 a simple way to film events that last billionths of a second. Top cameras for such work reach huge frame rates but need complex setups and heavy rebuilding of images. Their method joins two mature tools: sound-based pulse shaping and a light-field camera that also records color depth.

The setup filmed laser-driven events at rates matching the best systems, with room to go far faster. It adapts easily to new pulse shapes and new subjects. A holography add-on gives depth in the same single shot. The team hopes the simple rig opens ultrafast filming to many more labs.
arxiv-2504-07848:
Akshay Gangadhar and Hiroki Sayama wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, whose text runs under a broader title on why people live society in unlike ways. It studies how inner leanings shape the path of a person's views in a shifting social network.

Each agent in the model leans one of three ways: toward the like-minded, toward the new, or toward the crowd. The team gauges how tangled each view path grows, using a Lempel-Ziv score. The results cut against gut feel: the like-seekers grow the least foretold, the novelty-seekers stay oddly boxed in, and the crowd-followers start steady then turn wild. The patterns hold across network set-ups, so the leanings, not the stage, rule the tale.
arxiv-2504-07948:
Anouar Benali and a twenty-two-author team used exascale computing to train molecular models at near-quantum accuracy. Machine learning models for chemistry are only as good as the data behind them, and the most accurate data is brutally expensive. The team stacked methods of rising precision, all sped up by graphics processors.

At the top sit quantum Monte Carlo forces, computed at a scale never reached before. Those gold-standard numbers then sharpened a foundation model for biological molecules through transfer learning. The result drove nanosecond simulations of reacting systems. The work shows supercomputers can feed learning models data once thought out of reach.
arxiv-2504-08548:
Europe's Copernicus satellites watch Earth through several kinds of eyes at once: visible light, radar, and elevation. Miguel Espinosa and co-authors train a single generative model on all three in this 2025 paper, so it can translate any one view into the others.

Their diffusion model treats each data type as a step in a sequence, steered by its own timing signal. After training, it can fill in a missing view from whichever views are given, a trick called zero-shot translation. Tests on thumbnail images from a large public set showed strong sample quality. The authors pitch the model as a foundation for later remote sensing work.
arxiv-2504-08748:
Lang Mei and co-authors survey multimodal retrieval-augmented generation in a 2025 paper. Plain retrieval-augmented generation grounds a language model's answers in searched text, cutting hallucinations, but many questions hinge on images, video, or sound that text search cannot supply.

The multimodal version retrieves across data types and feeds the model mixed evidence. The survey walks through the pipeline's components, the datasets used to build and test systems, and how quality is evaluated. Reported results beat text-only grounding, especially where seeing is part of understanding. Open problems close the tour, from aligning modalities to judging generated media fairly.
arxiv-2504-08848:
Safety filters for language models are trained mostly in English, and attackers exploit the gap with low-resource languages and mid-sentence language switching. Bibek Upadhayay and Vahid Behzadan present X-Guard, a moderation agent built for many tongues. They assembled a safety dataset spanning one hundred thirty-two languages and five million examples, each with its reasoning spelled out, and used a panel of judge models to curb single-judge bias.

The system pairs a fine-tuned translation module with a three-billion-parameter judge trained in two stages. In their tests it caught unsafe content across languages, including the code-switching tricks that slip past English-centered guards, while explaining its verdicts.
arxiv-2504-08948: Academic database research stands at a crossroads shaped by industry and by artificial intelligence. This 2025 panel proposal by Eugene Wu and Raul Castro Fernandez sets out to debate the field's future in an open forum. The document gathers summaries of earlier panels on the same question, plus position statements from the invited panelists. Views sampled from the wider data management community round out the brief. The proposal is a conversation starter rather than a study, meant to frame where database research should head next.
arxiv-2504-09048:
Yongchang Wu and co-authors present a block-wise method for rebuilding large scenes in 3D in a 2025 paper. A popular technique scatters soft 3D blobs to model a scene, but big scenes must be split into blocks, and splitting, tuning, and merging each bring flaws. Their method, BlockGaussian, plans the split by scene content.

Blocks are cut so that busy and quiet zones share the compute load fairly. Extra guide points keep each block's tuning honest against the true images. A fake-view rule cleans up floating artefacts when blocks merge. Tests on large scenes gave top scores for both speed and image quality. The whole job fits on a single graphics card with modest memory.
arxiv-2504-09448:
Lin Zhu, Xinbing Wang, and their co-authors present a Bayesian method that teaches vision models to generalize from a few examples to new kinds of data. Their 2025 paper notes that large pretrained models do well on few shot tasks within their training world, but shifts in correlation or diversity break them. Even heavy training often fails to beat a plain baseline under such shifts.

Their method aligns image and text representations, tuning only the text side. Bayesian modeling guards against overfitting the few examples, while two extra losses push the model to ignore spurious links. The gradient step is also adjusted to keep directions from clashing. Tests on few shot out of distribution tasks showed gains over standard training. The approach targets domains where labeled examples are scarce.
arxiv-2504-09648:
Guixian Chen, Jianhao Ma, and Salar Fattahi improve a classic algorithm for finding hidden structure in corrupted data. Their 2025 paper studies robust subspace recovery: from few noisy samples, some tampered with by a strong adaptive adversary, recover the low-dimensional subspace holding most clean points. Earlier methods cost too much computing or assumed friendly data distributions.

The classical RANSAC method resists outliers by sampling consensus sets, but it wastes effort and handles ordinary noise poorly. Their two-stage version, RANSAC+, pinpoints exactly where the old method fails and repairs those spots. The result is provably robust to both adversarial and Gaussian corruption, needs near-optimal sample counts, and does not need the subspace dimension in advance. It also runs faster than rival RANSAC variants.
arxiv-2504-09748:
Designing a part's inner shape by computer needs exact derivatives, and hand-deriving them for odd meshes is slow and error-prone. Zachary Wegert and co-authors automate those derivatives in this 2025 paper. Their setting pairs level-set shape design with unfitted finite elements, where the part's edge cuts freely through a fixed grid. Shape calculus for that setting is extended to edges that meet the grid's own border.

Automatic differentiation then reproduces the hand-derived formulas to machine precision at any mesh size. Even the second-derivative matrix comes out symmetric, as theory demands. The code runs in an open Julia package, on one machine or many. A graph trick spots isolated pockets of material. Engineers can now trust the optimizer's compass.
arxiv-2504-09848:
Jie Feng and a large team of co-authors survey how large language models handle space and place, in work from twenty twenty-five. Most past work looked at robots that see and move in rooms. Space skill is much wider than that. It also covers city plans, maps from orbit, and Earth science at world scale. The survey asks what links and splits these fields.

The survey first reviews how human minds grasp space and what that means for models. It then looks at space memory, stored facts, and abstract thought in the models. Last, it tracks space skill across scales, from single agents to whole cities and the planet. The path runs from memory and grasp of space to reasoning and full skill. Readers get a shared map for joint work across fields.
arxiv-2504-10248:
Collins Ogbodo, Timothy Rogers, Mattia Dal Borgo, and David Wagg teach a digital twin to move its own sensors to wherever they help most, in a 2025 paper. A digital twin mirrors a physical structure and is only as good as the data fed into it. Sensors placed once cannot follow changing conditions like new damage. The team instead frames sensor placement as a sequence of decisions and trains a reinforcement learning agent to reposition sensors as the structure evolves.

Case studies on a cantilever plate, in healthy and damaged states, show the agent learning to chase informative locations. Data quality improved, and with it the twin's accuracy in mirroring the plate. The framework keeps the twin tightly representative of its physical counterpart over time. They present it as a step toward twins that manage their own measurement strategy rather than relying on a fixed layout.
arxiv-2504-10348:
Lena Scholz and co-authors find grain boundaries in diffusion models without the need to mesh them in this 2025 work. Real crystals are patchworks of grains. The edges where grains meet can speed diffusion by orders of magnitude. To mesh such thin layers in finite element models is exact, but the cost in time and compute is far too high.

Their fix is a collapsed interface element. It folds the thickness of the edge into the math and adds the edge back as a flat surface element. Flow along the edge and flow across it are each dealt with on their own terms. Teams can model transport ruled by these edges, as in batteries and coatings, at a cost they can pay. The trick keeps the physics of the thin layer. It does not pay for that layer's volume.
arxiv-2504-10448:
A large detector team proposes in 2025 a muon detector concept for a future FCC-ee experiment. The design pairs precision drift tubes with fast plastic scintillator strips. The tubes give two-dimensional positions with fine resolution. The strips add fast timing and the coordinate along the tubes. Wavelength-shifting fibers and silicon photomultipliers read the strips out.

The authors aim for a detector that is precise, fast, robust, and cheap to build at large scale. Muons are key particles for collider physics, so tracking them well matters for the whole experiment. The concept paper lays out the design and its expected performance for the proposed circular collider.
arxiv-2504-10948:
Mohammad Najafi and co-authors release BEACON, a benchmark for counting small patterns inside huge graphs. Their twenty twenty-five paper serves a task behind fraud rings, traffic flows, and molecular studies: how many times does a query shape appear in the network? Algorithmic and learning methods both claim speed.

No shared test had let the two camps fight fairly. BEACON ships standard datasets with verified true counts, a test harness, and a public leaderboard. Ground truth is the hard part at this scale, and it is provided. Future counters can now be ranked in the open instead of each paper grading its own homework.
arxiv-2504-11548:
Juliana Bourdieu, Monica Aguero, and Marcelo Kovalsky report the first lab proof of a strange nonchaotic attractor in a common infrared laser, in a 2025 paper. The laser uses passive Q-switching with a saturable absorber and makes pulses that last just nanoseconds. In past work it was known for plain, steady pulsing or for simple chaos. Which one shows up rests on where the absorber sits in the laser.

The team tracked two values from the laser over time and used them to rebuild the shape of the pattern at work. At one set place for the absorber, the way the laser acts fits the strange pattern named above. That pattern is rich and tangled, yet it is not periodic and it is not chaotic. Such patterns may serve uses that need a wide spread of tones while the act of the laser stays easy to foresee.
arxiv-2504-11648:
