Andrew Rothstein, Minseok Kim, and Minho Woo lead a large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It builds TorbeamNN, a learned stand-in for a ray tracing code that aims heating beams in the KSTAR tokamak.

The net forecasts where electron cyclotron heating and current drive will land, for both wave modes. It runs over a hundred times faster than the lean real-time code, with no loss against the full code. Trained on KSTAR mirror shapes, it has been checked both off-line and live in shots. In live use it tracked a set height for the heating spot as the plasma shifted, with a small mean error.
arxiv-2504-11748: Christopher Xu and co-authors present a simple rolling robot in this 2025 paper. The robot, called ROCK, is a round shell with a swinging weight inside and only one motor. An uneven shell surface lets that single swinging motion steer the robot, which keeps the design simple and easy to scale. The team trained a control policy in simulation with reinforcement learning and then ran it on the real robot, which completed a rectangular path.
arxiv-2504-12048:
Text-to-video models struggle with prompts that pack in several scenes and moving cameras. The seven authors propose Modular-Cam. A large language model first reads the instruction and splits it into separate scenes plus the transitions between them. A temporal transformer inside the diffusion model keeps each scene continuous, while a module called CamOperator steers the camera work.

An adaptive ControlNet layer holds consistency across scenes and adjusts color tone as the video moves between them. Qualitative and quantitative experiments show strong multi-scene generation with fine-grained camera control. Sample results are posted on the project page. The authors present the modular split, language model for planning, diffusion for pictures, as the way to handle complex directed prompts.
arxiv-2504-12348:
Samah Hussein and co-authors rebuild three-dimensional shapes from cheap radar signals, in a 2025 paper. Millimeter-wave radars are small and affordable, but their point clouds are sparse, blurry, and full of mirror-like gaps, a poor starting point for self-driving vision. Their system, RFconstruct, attacks the problem at every level.

Two radars image crossing planes, and their streams merge into one cloud. Motion-aware fusion across time then thickens the cloud as the vehicle moves. Last, a custom encoder-decoder network turns the cloud into full shapes without needing a known bounding box. Tested against lidar-based ground truth, RFconstruct recovered the shapes of cars, bikes, and pedestrians with good accuracy. Radar-only perception inches closer to practical.
arxiv-2504-12748:
Danut-Valentin Copae, Reza Soltani, and Milan Lopuhaä-Zwakenberg study security risk diagrams in a 2025 paper. These diagrams, called attack defense trees, show how an attacker might reach a goal and how a defender can block each step. Past work often counted only the cost or harm from the attack side.

The authors add defence measures to the same picture, so both sides face limits on cost, time, and skill. They give fast methods that find the best trade offs between attack and defence values. Tests on random trees with hundreds of nodes show both methods cope well with large cases.
arxiv-2504-12848:
Lassaad Mandhour, Farah Bouhadida, and Frédéric Piéchon show that a wall between two kinds of quantum geometry can bounce particles that a plain barrier would not, in a 2025 paper. Dirac particles, whose motion locks to an internal arrow, scatter in odd ways that mirror their geometric traits.

Working with a three-band model of two-dimensional Dirac particles, the authors place regions with different Berry phases side by side. The incoming particle partly reflects and partly passes, even though its momentum is identical on both sides. No energy step is needed; the geometry alone does the sorting. The result suggests devices could steer Dirac particles by patterning quantum geometry rather than voltage.
arxiv-2504-12948:
Finding the shortest vector in a lattice underlies attacks on some codes and ciphers, and the two-dimensional case is the training ground for faster methods. Lihao Zhao and co-authors revisit it with fresh machinery. They define a new notion of a reduced basis, then build a reduction algorithm that applies the classic Euclidean algorithm across the two dimensions in an adaptive way.

On top sits a vectorised version of the half-greatest-common-divisor trick, which halves the bit-length of two vectors at once. Iterating it yields their fastest solver, with a proven running time for inputs of any shape. Experiments show at least a thirteenfold speed-up on standard-form inputs, and skipping a costly pre-conversion pays off even more on general inputs. The half-step method may serve other problems too.
arxiv-2504-13248:
Mitchell Karmen leads a large team in a 2025 report of a high-redshift tidal disruption event candidate found with the James Webb Space Telescope. In such an event, a star is torn apart by a supermassive black hole. Rates and traits of these flares tell us about the cores of galaxies and their central black holes.

All past finds sat at low redshift, since deep time-domain surveys are hard. The new candidate, in the COSMOS-Web field, lies much farther off. Its light and host traits are set out in the paper, as a rare case for the far universe.
arxiv-2504-13348:
Xiao Jin and co-authors turn rover wheel spokes into a sensing computer in a 2025 paper. A rover needs to sense the ground it crosses to move safely, yet heavy data processing drains power and slows response. Their wheel spokes are hook shaped and carry sensors that pick up shaking as the wheel rolls over terrain.

The body of the wheel itself does part of the computing, a method called physical reservoir computing. Its shaking signals become rich features for a classifier. With three sensors placed with care, the system named the terrain with 90 percent accuracy in tests. It could also flag ground it had never seen by how little it matched known types.
arxiv-2504-13448:
Daniela Ushizima and four co-authors present a virtual reality platform for exploring scientific images, in a 2025 paper. For fifty years the mouse has been the main tool for handling data, yet flat screens cramp images that are truly three-dimensional. Their platform, ASCRIBE-VR, puts researchers inside the data. It merges AI-made segmentations with immersive views of scans such as X-ray tomography and magnetic resonance images.

The tools run on common headsets and let users inspect structures at many scales, with the AI's labels close at hand. Feedback from the human explorer can loop back into the analysis. The authors aim the system at materials research, where samples hide complex inner geometry. They argue that joining machine output with human intuition inside virtual space can speed discovery, linking people with digital twins of their specimens.
arxiv-2504-14248:
Shijiao Li, Zhipeng Ma, Huajun He, and Haiyue Chen rethink traffic flow forecasts by splitting flow birth from flow spread, in a paper from 2025. Past models track how flow moves along roads, but skip how flow starts at each node in waves through the day.

Their model reads node birth waves with a multi branch match module that grows key cycles as needed. For spread, it blends wide self focus with local graph and time tools. On three real road sets it beat past models on both short and long forecasts. A lean form matched a big rival with a fifth of its weights.
arxiv-2504-14448:
Ali Arslan Yousaf, Umair Rehman, and Muhammad Umair Danish propose a new way to model risky choices in this 2025 arXiv paper. The classic account, prospect theory, explains why people fear losses more than they value gains. But its smooth curves are hard to read, and its inner parts stay hidden from the user.

The authors swap those curves for plain features guided by effect sizes, so each part of the model maps to a named habit of mind. They set out the math, show the model copies known effects like framing and loss aversion, and test it on synthetic data. Scores stay close to those of less clear models. Readers in economics, policy, and AI safety get a model of risk they can inspect and explain.
arxiv-2504-14548:
Lifeng Lin and seven co-authors attacked a known flaw of a popular 3D scene method when only a few photos are available, in a 2025 paper. The method, 3D Gaussian Splatting, builds scenes from clouds of soft blobs. With sparse views it overfits, memorizing the given photos while failing on new angles.

Their fix, VGNC, borrows a generative model that can imagine new views of a scene. Those imagined views act as a validation set. A control rule then uses them to pick the right number of blobs for the scene, no more and no fewer. Tests across several base methods and data sets showed less overfitting and better test renders. The leaner scenes also stored smaller and trained and rendered faster, the team reports.
arxiv-2504-15148: Jehyun Lee and Melissa Keranen study ways to split a complete graph into uniform layers of small pieces. Their 2025 note treats uniformly resolvable decompositions, where the edges of the graph are grouped into classes and each class holds copies of one shape. Two shapes are in play: single edges and stars with an odd number of spokes. The authors give a partial solution for the mixed case, narrowing an open question in design theory.
arxiv-2504-15348:
Sarah Libanore and four colleagues forecast how future radio and microwave surveys could constrain neutrinos that interact with each other. Self-interacting massive neutrinos would alter how cosmic structures grow on small scales. That changes the abundance of small halos, which host the galaxies driving the 21-centimeter signal from the cosmic dawn.

The team finds the HERA radio array, at design sensitivity, can improve existing coupling constraints and reach values beyond microwave experiments. Combining HERA with the CMB-S4 survey breaks parameter degeneracies and sharpens sensitivity further. Futuristic lunar interferometers could access the cleaner dark-ages signal, reaching percent-level constraints on the self-coupling. The study links particle physics to early-universe astronomy.
arxiv-2504-15448:
Yanampally Abhiram Reddy and co-authors build a live dashboard in a 2025 paper that tracks public opinion about companies on social media. Investors and policymakers watch that mood closely, but raw posts are noisy and fast-moving. Their system cleans the text first, then scores its sentiment two ways.

A rule-based scorer that handles slang and emphasis pairs with a transformer model that reads context. Merging the two aims for both clarity and accuracy. Charts then show the mood's spread over time and across firms. Real-time mood tracking could flag reputation shifts early, while the firms can still respond.
arxiv-2504-15548:
Elyas Meguellati and co-authors use large language models to clean and explain messy social media text before training detectors on it. Their 2025 paper targets hard detection problems: propaganda, hateful memes, and toxicity. Language models shine at simple classification but fade on these tangled tasks, and most prior work used them to fabricate extra training data.

Their approach instead enriches the existing set: models tidy noisy posts and attach context-rich explanations, without inflating the volume. Tests run on a persuasive meme benchmark, plus toxic comment and hateful meme collections. Better-prepared examples, the authors argue, teach small detectors more than sheer synthetic quantity.
arxiv-2504-15748:
Namitha Issac and co-authors report a likely explosive outflow in a massive star-forming cloud, in a 2025 paper. Such blasts are rare, with only six known before this one. Radio maps from ALMA show many straight streamers bursting from one center inside the cloud G34.26+0.15, matching jets seen in infrared images.

The streamers' speeds spread from rest to 120 kilometers per second and grow with distance in the pattern expected from a single explosion. The gas involved totals about 264 times the Sun's mass, and the blast energy is enormous. The authors date the event to roughly 19,000 years ago and link it to the expanding bubble of hot gas at the same spot.
arxiv-2504-15848:
Luwei Xiao, Rui Mao, Shuai Zhao, and their co-authors present a 2025 computer science paper on reading feelings in posts that pair text with images. The task is to judge the feeling aimed at one named target in the post, not the post as a whole. Past systems often miss fine visual detail and the reasons behind the feeling a post expresses.

The team built a framework named Chimera that lines up small image patches with words. It turns both wide and narrow views of the image into text, then uses a large language model to add likely causes and impressions behind the feeling. Tests on standard data sets show the method works well. The authors also note it adapts to new tasks more flexibly than some large chat models.
arxiv-2504-15948:
Gerardo Iuliano and co-authors seed flaws into smart contracts to test detectors in a 2025 paper. Smart contract bugs can drain large sums in one strike. Detector tools need fresh, varied test sets to prove their worth. Older test sets cover few flaw types and age quickly.

Their tool injects six flaw types into real contracts by pattern edits. A leading static checker then hunted for the planted flaws. It missed some of them, showing gaps in current detection. Injection rates also varied, since some contracts lacked the needed code shapes.
arxiv-2504-16048:
Power markets need prices that keep the grid safe while letting each seller act for itself. Nicholas Julian Behr and co-authors present a control method built for that tension in this 2025 paper. The method belongs to a family that steers a system toward its best point using live measurements rather than a full model. Only the link between inputs and outputs needs to be known.

Their method, named PRIME, runs in rounds based on a classic math step. It can be set up as a market, where self-interested sellers earn rewards for choices that keep the grid safe and cheap. Sellers never share their private costs or limits. The method also handles rough cost shapes, settles fast, enforces limits quickly, and shrugs off noisy readings. A test on power flow pricing shows the idea at work.
arxiv-2504-16248:
Kasia Budzik and four co-authors track the symmetries of a special class of surfaces in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The surfaces are limits of K3 surfaces, a rich family in geometry, built by a threefold orbifold step. Classic work mapped the symmetries of a cousin family, the Kummer surfaces. This paper does the same job for the new class. It finds the full group of shape-preserving symmetries that also keep a key form fixed.

The authors then locate this group inside two of the Mathieu groups, famous sporadic symmetry groups. Their method adapts lattice techniques from earlier work on Kummer surfaces. The study extends a program that links geometry to these rare groups. Specialists in algebraic geometry and string theory are the readers.
arxiv-2504-16348:
Russell Boey, Emily Kendall, Yourong Wang, and Richard Easther simulate in 2025 pairs of giant black holes sinking inside a fuzzy dark matter core. In this dark matter model, galaxy centers hold a standing-wave soliton that should drag on orbiting black holes more than normal matter would. The team ran detailed simulations of high-mass pairs inside a massive halo's core.

The pairs decayed faster than earlier estimates suggested. The drag hinged on the dark matter particle's mass: above a threshold it could solve the famous last-parsec stall, letting pairs merge. Strong drag might also muffle the gravitational wave hum that pulsar timing arrays listen for.
arxiv-2504-16448:
Shuguang Zhao and co-authors build a language model that turns doctor patient conversations into structured medical records. Their 2025 paper notes that consultation dialogues hold key clinical facts in messy form. Rule based and shallow learning tools miss deep meaning in such text. Their model, EMRModel, fine tunes a large model with a light method called LoRA. Prompts are styled like code to guide the extraction.

The team also built a realistic data set of consultation dialogues with detailed labels. A fine grained test bench for this extraction task accompanies it. The model reached an F1 score of 88.1 percent. That is a gain of about half over standard pretrained models, in relative terms. It also beat plain LoRA fine tuning. The authors present the system as a step toward usable automated record keeping from spoken care.
arxiv-2504-16748:
Yanan Zhao and co-authors build a graph learning method that needs no data augmentation and no negative samples. Contrastive learning teaches a model by pulling matching views together and pushing others apart. On graphs, making those views has meant either heavy editing tricks or special encoders. Their 2025 paper draws the views from fractional diffusion instead.

Learnable encoders follow fractional differential equations, whose order setting steers each view toward local or global structure. Two views of one graph then differ in a principled way, ready for contrast. The method works on graphs where neighbors mostly match and on those where they mostly differ. Graph learning readers get a simpler contrastive recipe with the augmentation machinery removed.
arxiv-2504-16848:
Cars that talk to the network need warning of weak connections ahead, and a 2025 paper by Sanket Partani and co-authors improves those forecasts for city driving. Their method predicts download speed for a car using data from the car ahead of it, plus patterns from the past.

The team worked with a public Berlin data set for vehicle-to-network links over 5G. They picked input traits from both the target car and the lead car after a close look at the data, then trained several machine learning models. Adding the lead car's data improved the forecasts. The gain held across model types, which suggests the lead car acts like a scout that has just driven the same stretch of road.
arxiv-2504-18048:
Zhongtian Chen and Daniel Murfet link the patterns in text data to the shape of the loss hills that a transformer model climbs as it learns. Their aim is to explain a measure of learning shape that workers use in practice, called the local learning coefficient.

First they place text distributions in a Hilbert space and split them into main modes. Cutting the small modes leaves a leaner copy that keeps the main structure. They then prove the learning measure is blind to modes below a set size. So in practice the measure reads the lean copy, not the full truth, which explains why it can be trusted.
arxiv-2504-18248:
Amirhossein Taran and four co-authors model mooring lines as true beams inside a fluid dynamics toolbox. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Floating structures ride waves while cables hold them in place. Most models treat cables as chains of lumped masses. Bending and twisting then go missing. Extreme seas punish exactly those missing forces.

Their model uses the geometrically exact Simo-Reissner beam theory. A finite volume scheme runs it inside OpenFOAM. The floating body and its lines evolve together. Bending, tension, and torsion all enter the physics. Tests against experiments and other simulations validate the setup. Offshore engineers gain a sharper tool for storm design.
arxiv-2504-18748:
Kaustubh Dhole and co-authors study how language models can answer vague best product queries, in work from 2025. Shoppers often ask for the best trail shoes without naming the traits that matter. Standard search and ranking tools struggle, since the key traits are hidden in the request.

The team proposes that models can first name the hidden traits, then reason over them to rank items. They built a data set with a four point scheme for marking the best candidates for such queries. Model based labels support the set. They then test several search and ranking methods on it and discuss use in real online stores.
arxiv-2504-18948:
Devesh Pant and co-authors build tools that read handwritten digits on paper forms, aimed at development programs in rural India. Field workers for such programs often lack smartphones or training for digital data entry, so paper forms remain common. Reading those forms by machine requires digit recognizers that work under messy real-world conditions.

The team releases a large dataset of handwritten digits and recognition models trained with metric learning, a method that teaches the model which digits look alike. The tools were deployed in a health and nutrition project that phones rural women's self-help groups with recorded advice. Phone numbers collected on paper were digitized with the system, enabling almost four million calls. Data, models, and code were released openly for others to reuse.
arxiv-2504-19348:
Vyshakh B R and Rishi Sharma model heavy quark pairs in hot nuclear matter, in this 2025 paper. Bottomonia are bound pairs of heavy quarks that form in collider crashes and then cross a soup of loose quarks and gluons. How they fade in that soup reveals the soup's traits.

Past models assumed the soup's push has no memory. The pair set up a general equation that keeps that memory and solve it by computer for one bound state. They use flow backgrounds matched to two large colliders. The balance between the pair's own time scale and the soup's time scale strongly shaped survival rates. Results are compared with collider data.
arxiv-2504-19448:
A legged robot that climbs walls on dry adhesive feet lives or dies by each step: peel too hard and the foot tears free; press too softly and it never grips. Jichun Xiao, Jiawei Nie, Lina Hao, and Zhi Li present in 2025 a framework that optimizes the whole foot trajectory and the forces along it, end to end.

Smooth three-part curves describe candidate steps for different foot shapes. A learned model predicts the forces any trajectory will produce, and a multi-objective optimizer, steered by a redundancy-aware strategy, picks the step that best trades off grip, peel force, and vibration. On the team's quadruped climber, the chosen trajectories cut peak detachment force by 28 percent and vibration by 82 percent against standard steps. The authors offer the framework as a general recipe for adhesive climbing robots.
arxiv-2504-19648:
L Casamiquela and co-authors present in 2025 the third version of a benchmark star library from the Gaia mission. Benchmark stars have firm known traits and help test the tools that read starlight. Good benchmarks let large surveys check their measures of heat, gravity, and chemical mix.

The team gathered high-grade spectra for about two hundred stars, plus the Sun, from archives and new views. With set basic traits, they derived amounts of thirteen elements tied to iron and alpha groups. Four codes that model light through gas were used to cross-check results. The library gives surveys a shared scale for chemical work on stars in our galaxy.
arxiv-2504-20148:
When a star wanders too close to a black hole it is torn apart, and the glowing disk of debris can shine for years. Guolo and five co-authors fit such an event in 2025, the long lived source GSN 069, with a fully time dependent relativistic disk model. Their fitting tool now lives inside the standard X-ray analysis software, so spectra from many dates and wavelengths constrain one evolving disk.

Seven X-ray and two ultraviolet snapshots, spanning 2010 to 2019, fit under one set of starting conditions. Long life, they find, needs no new physics: it follows when the disk's internal friction runs low, stretching its clock. The same frame covers short lived events with the dial turned up. The authors urge modelers to free that dial in every fit.
arxiv-2504-20248:
Benjamin Allen and Nicholas Hayman watch force chains shift in a still pile of grains over weeks. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Grain piles can fail in sudden slides or creep in slow motion. Past accounts of that risk lean on friction, but the web of contact forces inside a pile is uneven and ever-shifting.

They image forces between clear discs in a flat pile at set gaps over a month. Shifts come in clusters at first, then long quiet spans break the pattern. Local stress grows stronger over time, even as the pile looks settled. Heat shifts may drive some events, while ground shakes show no link. Small inner shifts may prime big slides.
arxiv-2504-20648:
Michael Ogezi and Freda Shi build SpaRE, a training set of made up visual questions that boosts space reasoning in vision language models. Such models ace captions and questions yet lag on space links that humans find easy. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Space links are rare in common image text sets, with most in a long thin tail. The team built a vast set from rich image tales in three source sets, with millions of question pairs on space links. Models trained on it gained strongly on space test sets, with a top gain near half on one known test. Scores on general tasks held strong as well.
arxiv-2504-21048:
Splitting scarce resources among many users, from bandwidth to warehouse stock, is a moving puzzle. Mohamad Hady and co-authors survey how teams of learning agents tackle that puzzle in a 2025 review. Each agent learns by trial and error while the others adapt around it.

The survey sorts methods by their core design and by the fields they serve. It maps where the approach now stands in industry-linked work. Open snags include scale, steady teamwork, and safe real-world trials. The authors chart paths for the next wave of studies. Managers and builders gain a single map of a fast field.
arxiv-2504-21248:
Reading emotions from faces in video is harder outside the lab, where lighting, angles, and motion all vary. Engel and co-authors tackle the Dynamic Facial Expression in-the-Wild dataset with transfer learning that fuses several kinds of signal.

They combine pretrained networks of three sorts. The mix joins image models from the ResNet family, a pose estimator that tracks body and face keypoints, and a general feature network, feeding a transformer classifier. The point of the fusion is to catch subtle changes in expression across time that a single stream misses. Fine-tuning these multi-modal features gave a modest accuracy gain over their baseline. The authors frame the result as evidence that borrowed, blended features help emotion recognition in messy real-world footage.
arxiv-2504-21648:
Raluca Balan and Juan Jiménez bound the growth of noise-driven waves and heat on open ground, in a 2025 paper. Their equations are stochastic partial differential equations: part physics, part dice, with the dice colored by a spatial kernel and thrown by Lévy jumps, not smooth Gaussian noise. The key ask is whether the solution's moments, its spread at high powers, stay finite.

With a classic inequality for sums of independent kicks, they cap the p-th moment of the noise integral. That cap gives clean terms under which the linear heat and wave equations hold finite moments, for three kernels. The theory then stretches to nonlinear equations with tame coefficients. Growth proves at most exponential, at a rate they name, and some cases run weakly intermittent, bursting in rare spikes. For one model they expand the solution outright and write the second growth rate in full.
arxiv-2505-00048:
Debasish Bhattacharjee and co-authors present a mathematics paper, published in 2025, defining a new way for a dynamical system to spread points apart. A point is called orbitwise expansive when nearby starting points, followed along their paths, must at some step move a set distance away from its own path. A relative version replaces that set distance with the size of the starting neighborhood.

The authors prove basic facts about these points and the sets they form, including that unions and limit points keep the property. Older notions of expansiveness from Utz and Kato turn out to imply the new one. The paper also applies the idea to systems that change over time and links it to known traits of expansive behavior.
arxiv-2505-00148:
Leah Schätzler and co-authors prove, in a 2025 mathematics paper, that solutions exist for a class of doubly nonlinear systems in domains that grow over time. Such systems model flows where both the storage term and the spreading term bend away from linearity. The moving boundary makes the problem much harder.

The team tackles the problem on domains that never shrink and whose borders are negligibly thin. They assume the energy function is convex and pushes back growth, with no cap imposed from above. A nonlinear version of the minimizing movements method constructs the solutions. Existence proofs like this are the ground floor for any later simulation or application of these models.
arxiv-2505-00448:
Fabian Woller and co-authors present a Python package for fast statistics on messy, large data sets in a 2025 paper. Real data often mix types, such as numbers and labels, and often have gaps where values are missing. Standard Python tools slow down badly on such data, which blocks live exploration tools used in biomedical work.

Their package, NApy, pairs a compiled back end with parallel threads to run tests while handling gaps head-on. In checks, it beat rival tools and plain Python versions by orders of magnitude in both run time and memory use. That speed lets analysts test ideas on the fly in interactive apps. The code is shared in public for others to use and extend.
arxiv-2505-00748:
Markus Aschwanden and Felix Scholkmann test a theory of self-organized criticality against real data in a 2025 paper. The theory says many driven systems settle into a state where events of all sizes occur, with sizes following a power law. Such patterns have been claimed for flares, quakes, fires, and more.

The pair re-examined twenty-five phenomena across fields from astrophysics to informatics, using five ways to detect events and fit the laws. Of sixty-four size distributions, about four fifths matched the model's predicted slopes well. Solar flares, earthquakes, and forest fires fit cleanly. Other cases stayed inconclusive due to background handling, narrow fitting ranges, or small samples. The paper sorts strong claims from shaky ones.
arxiv-2505-01148:
Khartov studies a wide class of probability distributions in a 2025 mathematics paper. The class, called Q, gathers distributions with a property named rational-infinite divisibility: each can be split, in a signed sense, into endlessly divisible parts. The class extends the classic family of infinitely divisible laws and is under active study.

Khartov takes up a case earlier work had not settled, where a distribution mixes a discrete part with a continuous singular part, the kind that lives on a dust-like set. He gives a test for membership when the discrete part dominates the singular part in a set sense. He also shows the condition cannot be loosened freely, works through examples, and settles an open splitting problem.
arxiv-2505-01448:
Shengkai Chen and co-authors present OpenAVS, a training-free system that segments sounding objects in video by name, in this 2025 paper. Audio-visual segmentation outlines the objects that make a video's sounds. Older systems only knew a fixed set of object types.

OpenAVS uses text as a bridge between sound and image. Foundation models turn audio into words, then match those words to picture regions. No new training is needed for fresh object names. That open vocabulary lets the system handle scenes it never saw in training. Video editing, robotics, and accessibility tools could all use sound-guided masks. The design shows how big pre-trained models can be composed, not just fine-tuned.
arxiv-2505-01848:
Light that grazes a spin hole bends in a sharp log blow up, and the hole's own ring tones fade at a rate tied to that same bend. Takahisa Igata binds the two in a 2025 study with a sum that holds in any frame. The bend's key rate, he shows, rests on marks a still eye can read in place.

Those marks are the bend of space, the rim's girth, and the spin's true turn rate at that rim. The same rate sets the ring tone's fade in the short wave edge. The bind is thus not a trick of one hole build, but a rule of the bend. Igata, the sole author, casts it as a bridge twixt lens and ring for spin holes.
arxiv-2505-01948:
Yingda Fan and co-authors predict stream water temperature at a fine scale, in this 2025 paper. Temperature can shift a lot within a short stretch of the same stream system. Fine readings help target actions that guard water quality and fish habitat. The snag is data: sensors are dense at broad scales but sparse at the fine scale where the need sits.

Their method learns at several scales at once, using graph models of the stream network. Broad-scale learning, fed by richer data, supports the fine-scale task in a shared framework. The team frames this as learning against sparsity rather than from plenty. The approach aims to give water managers sharp local forecasts even where gauges are few.
arxiv-2505-02048:
Sebastian Rassmann and co-authors argue in 2025 that plain regression beats fancy generation for medical image translation. Generative models can invent details and copy noise, which is risky in medicine. Their framework, YODA, reuses a diffusion model but samples it differently.

Standard diffusion sampling rebuilds noise along with the image. Averaging many samples cancels that noise, and the team calls this expectation-approximation sampling. Their regression variant keeps the model's first prediction and skips all refinement steps. Across five datasets, including brain MRI and pelvis MRI-CT pairs, the single-step version matched or beat full sampling. It also beat eight rival methods while running far faster.
arxiv-2505-02148:
Alexey Nekrasov and co-authors release a data set for self-driving cars in a 2025 computing paper. Cars must spot the unexpected: a mattress, a stray animal, a fallen sign. Training data for such oddities in three-dimensional laser scans barely existed. Their set, called STU, pairs laser scans with camera views and dense labels for odd objects on the road.

Objects are labeled across ranges and across time, not just in single frames. The team adapted several standard 3D segmentation models as starting baselines. Results show how hard the task remains when oddities are rare and far away. Open data and scoring code invite others to beat the baselines. Safer cars need practice on surprises before the road supplies them.
arxiv-2505-02348: Hany Gerges and Jaan Janno tackle an inverse problem for a diffusion equation with fractional time steps, in this 2025 mathematics paper. The task is to recover several hidden quantities at once from measurements taken over time. They include a scalar coefficient, the order of the time-fractional derivative, and a source term that changes with time. The pair prove the solution is unique, so the measurements pin down all the unknowns. Their proof works through the poles of the Laplace transform of the measured function.
arxiv-2505-02548:
Marta Bílková and co-authors build a logic for claims about doubt and mixed-up beliefs. Everyday lines like thinking a wallet is in one drawer rather than another, or being unsure whether a meeting is Monday or Tuesday, need a formal home. The team extends a graded modal logic with a negation that flips a truth value around one half.

They give the new logic a model theory with a finite model property and show it matches the standard one. A tableau method built on constraints can pull out countermodels from open branches. With it, they prove that checking validity in the logic is complete for polynomial space.
arxiv-2505-02948:
Giovanni La Mura and five co-authors present a 2025 paper on interstellar dust as a busy, changing place, not a dull backdrop. Dust is a small share of the mass between stars, yet it leads in blocking ultraviolet and visible light and in glowing with heat. Its grains also hold most of the heavy elements there and host rich chemistry.

Real grains are lumpy, uneven, and layered, and those traits sway how they meet light and particles. Modeling that meeting exactly is costly. The team offers a fresh build of a classic matrix method, shaped for lopsided grains and tuned to run across many processors at once. The tool aims to let astronomers match what telescopes see with what the grains must be.
arxiv-2505-03048: Michael Puls tackles a classic question about recovering shapes from integrals in this 2025 paper. The Pompeiu problem asks when a set is fully determined by the averages of functions over its moved copies. Puls studies the question on spaces formed by a group divided by a compact subgroup. Drawing on recent work in spectral analysis, he gives exact conditions for a compact set to have the Pompeiu property when the group and subgroup form a Gelfand pair.
arxiv-2505-03648:
Vladimir Fanaskov and Ivan Oseledets build a bridge between the two classic neuron styles, the threshold unit and the oscillator, inside one memory network. Oscillatory Kuramoto neurons recently beat threshold units at tasks like unsupervised object discovery, but the coupling between the two kinds was improvised. Requiring both systems to admit a Lyapunov energy function forces clean forms: Hopfield memory on the threshold side, a specific Kuramoto model on the other.

Coupled, they form a Hopfield-Kuramoto associative memory with its own energy to descend. Oscillators can even serve as a low-rank patch on the memory's weights. The note argues the two units code different things: firing intensity versus frequency-based exchange.
arxiv-2505-03948:
Paolo Malgaretti, Francesco Petiziol, and Alexander Schnell studied a quantum particle in a narrow channel in a 2025 paper. In classic physics, a particle needs heat energy to cross a barrier made by a tight squeeze. Quantum rules let it tunnel through instead, so one might expect flow to rise as the gas cools.

Their runs show a twist. As the temperature drops, quantum fixes first hold the flow back at mid-range heat, raising the bar the particle faces. Only at lower heat does tunneling win out. They chart both the settled state and the flow through the clean, narrow channel. The result warns that quantum effects can cut both ways in tiny plumbing.
arxiv-2505-04048:
Elizabeth Munch and co-authors design a data structure in 2025 that tracks a distance measure between moving shapes. Kinetic data structures keep answers updated as objects move, without recomputing from scratch. Their hourglass structure maintains the bottleneck distance, a matching cost used to compare shapes. They spell out the events to handle and the updates each one needs, for general graphs.

As a showcase, they compare summaries of flat shapes taken from every viewing direction. Those summaries come from persistent homology, a tool that records shape features across scales. The structure keeps their bottleneck distance current as shapes change. Such live tracking suits robotics and shape analysis.
arxiv-2505-04448:
Amitrajit Nag, Girish Agarwal, and Jaydeep Basu uncover hidden cavity-like modes in a two-dimensional hyperbolic metamaterial, in this 2025 paper. Such materials are built, not found: theirs stacks silver nanowires in alumina. Light inside them follows a hyperbolic rule that allows waves barred in normal matter. Most theory smooths the structure into an average medium, which is useful but hides effects born of the fine detail.

The authors show the material hosts modes that act like tiny cavities, sitting on top of its broad response. Those modes change how light travels through the stack. They also change how the material couples to quantum emitters placed near it, which matters for single-photon devices. Fine structure, the paper argues, is not noise on the average picture but physics in its own right.
arxiv-2505-04548:
Austin Lu and co-authors built a robot dummy head to speed up sound research, in a 2025 paper. Standard test heads capture sound well but cannot move. The new head blends that sound realism with robot motion, so it can move, talk, and listen much like a person.

A quiet motor lets the head serve as a moving sound source, a trait past robot platforms lacked. Tests and sound measures show the head collects high-quality audio data. Trials also show how it can help study hearing aids that focus on one voice in noise. Design files are shared openly so other labs can build their own. The authors hope the tool will make spatial sound studies faster to run.
arxiv-2505-04748:
Yihuang Xiong and Geoffroy Hautier write a practical guide to a tricky computation in a 2025 paper. The method, called delta SCF, models excited states of defects in crystals by forcing electrons into chosen levels. Paired with hybrid functionals, it can predict defect traits well. Their guide targets VASP, a widely used quantum simulation package.

They warn that such runs can fail to settle, or worse, settle on the wrong excited state without any clear sign. The guide lays out the workflow they judge sound, step by step. They test it on a hard case, the neutral silicon vacancy in diamond. Much of the advice grew from private talks with two other researchers, whom they credit. The authors hope the notes will spare others the same pitfalls and spark wider discussion.
arxiv-2505-04848:
Kevin Coulembier and Alexander Sherman prove a structural result in advanced algebra in this 2025 paper. Their setting is a symmetric tensor category, a broad framework that generalizes the world of vector spaces and group representations. Inside it, algebraic groups can be defined, and the authors ask whether the quotient of one group by a subgroup exists as a geometric object.

They show that the quotient does exist as a scheme and is built from finitely much data, under two conditions on the category. A new tool, a Frobenius kernel for group schemes in this setting, carries much of the proof. They also compare the quotient with its classical shadow and show the two agree on key geometric traits. Traits such as being affine or proper pass from one to the other. The result extends a basic construction of algebraic geometry into far more general settings.
arxiv-2505-05248:
Jose Angel Nuñez and co-authors present a 2025 method to train colon polyp detectors with fake glare. Colon cancer is a top killer, yet early polyp removal can stop it. Camera scopes miss polyps at times, so deep learning aids are in growth. A common error is that bright glare spots on wet tissue look like polyps to the model, raising false alarms.

The team builds a bank of fake glare from real training images. They mark zones where glare must never be added, then slide the fake light over fit zones. Training on the harder set gives the model more chances to err and learn. Tests show the trick improves detector scores. Better training data of this kind costs no new patient scans.
arxiv-2505-05448:
Jacob Thompson and Elizabeth Winstanley compute the stress and energy carried by a quantum field in a spinning thermal bath on anti-de Sitter space. The field is a massless, conformally coupled scalar, held in a rigidly rotating thermal state. Two independent routes lead to its stress-energy tensor. The first treats the field as a thermal gas of massless bosons through relativistic kinetic theory.

The second is full quantum field theory, with renormalization taming the infinities. Comparing the two answers tests where the gas picture of a quantum field succeeds and where it must fail. Both three- and four-dimensional anti-de Sitter spaces are covered. Rotating thermal states matter for holographic dualities and for basic questions about quantum matter in curved spacetime. The paper supplies the controlled comparison the subject needed.
arxiv-2505-05648:
Abouelenin and co-authors train the keyboard transformer behind SwiftKey under differential privacy, so the model learns from typing without memorizing anyone's words. Next-word prediction feeds on personal text, which makes privacy the hard constraint. Their 2025 work shrinks a GPT-2 style transformer to phone size and trains it in two stages: a seed model on general data, then a privacy-preserving fine-tune on typing data.

Across experiments balancing size, speed, and accuracy, the private transformer edged out the production recurrent model it would replace, with small, steady gains in next-word prediction. The cost grew gracefully in memory and run time. The team ships the model through ONNX, a portable format that eases deployment. The paper is a production report: privacy machinery, sized for a real keyboard used by millions.
arxiv-2505-05748:
Huan Yan and Junjie Hu fuse clusters by crowd weight in a 2025 paper. Grouping data by likeness is a core chore, and the merge-up kind is loved for its plain build. Its flaws are known: extra knobs to set for each new set, and merge rules that swing the end cast.

Their way needs no such knobs. It splits first by near crowd counts, reads how sub-groups touch at their rims, weighs each by crowd weight, and fuses by that weight. Four parts in all, set to hold the cast firm across sets. Data teams gain a merge tool that asks less lore up front.
arxiv-2505-05848:
Yue Yin and co-authors built RefRef in 2025, a data set for rebuilding clear and shiny objects in 3D. Standard rebuild tools presume light travels straight, so glass and mirrors break their math. Past data sets for such objects were narrow: thin glass, plain tint-free items, or backdrops set far away.

RefRef stages objects that bend and bounce light in rich ways, with ground truth to grade against. That lets each tool's failure modes show plainly rather than hide in a mixed score. The team also set a shared benchmark on the set. Better grades should push rebuild tools toward the glassy real world.
arxiv-2505-05948:
Tsubasa Umetani, Masataka Aizawa, Yuichiro Ezoe, and Yoshitaka Ishisaki search for rings around distant planets, in a paper published in 2025. No planet outside the solar system has a confirmed ring system, though Saturn-sized rings should bend a star's light in a telltale way during a transit. The team mined data from the TESS space telescope.

They cleaned and folded the light curves of 308 planet candidates, mostly large planets on short orbits around bright stars. Models with rings fit six systems slightly better, but close looks showed none was a solid ring case. For 125 planets they set firm upper bounds on ring size, which cap how common large rings can be, under a two percent rate for the biggest. A second method, watching transit depth wobble as rings tilt, may find rings in about a dozen systems.
arxiv-2505-06048:
A quantum particle swept past an avoided crossing may jump levels, and the Landau-Zener model prices that jump exactly for two levels. Malikis and Cheianov ask what happens with many levels and higher spin. They recast the classic model as a Lax equation, borrowing the machinery of integrable systems. In that frame, higher-spin versions yield scattering matrices that can be computed exactly and efficiently.

The method stretches further. Bow-tie shaped multi-level models, driven by non-Abelian gauge fields with zero curvature, also surrender their scattering matrices to algebra. The authors present new six-level and eight-level models never solved before. Exact solutions are rare anchors in quantum dynamics: simulations and experiments alike can be checked against them.
arxiv-2505-06548:
Aniruddha Roy and four co-authors test whether small open language models can write their own training instructions, in a research paper from 2025. Fine-tuning needs instruction data, but human-written sets are costly and narrow. Letting a model generate its own instructions is cheaper, though earlier work leaned on huge closed models.

Their framework adds reinforcement learning with automated feedback to the self-generation loop. They try it with three open models of modest size. The reinforcement step improved results on most tasks over earlier self-generation methods. Dataset checks confirm the gains come from the added training signal, not from more data. The authors argue this lowers the cost of aligning smaller models.
arxiv-2505-07148:
Federated learning lets phones train a shared model without sending private data to a server. The server still needs everyone's updates combined safely, and 5G users drop out constantly. Yiwei Zhang and co-authors designed a secure aggregation protocol that finishes in a single round. Base stations help with the heavy math.

Precomputation, special pseudorandom functions, and secret sharing carry the load. Even if users vanish mid-round, the sum still comes out, and no single update leaks. Tests showed strong security with far less communication and computation than older protocols. The authors target the churn of real mobile networks, where multi-round schemes stall.
arxiv-2505-07248:
Do Van Kien and Hop D Nguyen answer an open algebra question for a special class of rings in a 2025 paper. Algebraists measure how nonlinear a module's resolution is by its linearity defect, and a Koszul ring is one whose simplest module resolves in a perfectly linear way. A standing question asked whether finite defect of the residue field forces a ring to be Koszul.

The pair prove yes for a broad class: certain Cohen-Macaulay rings of near-minimal size over a field of characteristic zero. Their proof develops a full picture of the stretched rings at the heart of the class, including a complete classification in dimension one. A tantalizing conjecture gains solid ground.
arxiv-2505-07348:
Robots held up by cables can be tuned to be stiffer or softer mid-task, and a 2025 paper by Domenico Dona' and co-authors offers a method for that tuning. Cable-driven parallel robots hang their platform from several cables, and sharing the pull among cables while setting stiffness has been a two-part headache.

Their method rests on the analytic centre idea from optimization. By weighting the barrier terms that keep cable tensions in range, the stiffness of the whole robot can be steered at the same time as the tensions are spread. Simulations compare the new method with the standard one. The authors argue that live stiffness control helps these robots meet demands for both speed and precision.
arxiv-2505-07548:
Lingkun Luo, Shiqiang Hu, and Liming Chen present a diffusion based method for domain adaptation in this 2025 paper. Domain adaptation trains a model on one data source and uses it on another. A common trick labels target data with the model own guesses. Too few high confidence guesses can break the method.

Their method, called NOCDDA, uses a conditional diffusion model to make more good target samples. The diffusion model and the task classifier are trained together in one framework. A class aware noise step improves the starting noise for each class. That yields cleaner samples that carry the right class traits. Tests on five benchmarks showed strong results. The work ties image generation tightly to the final task.
arxiv-2505-08148:
Sunday Oyinlola Ogundoyin and co-authors audit the safety of custom chatbots at scale in a 2025 paper. Platforms like OpenAI's store let anyone publish tailored GPT assistants, and millions use them. Security worries have mostly been argued in theory. This team tested nearly fifteen thousand custom GPTs against seven concrete attacks, from tricking the bot into roleplay rule-breaking to leaking its hidden instructions and generating phishing text or malicious code.

Over ninety-five percent lacked adequate protection. Roleplay attacks succeeded against about ninety-six percent, prompt leakage against about ninety-two, and phishing generation against about ninety-one. A ranking system linked popularity tiers to risk, and the base models' own weaknesses were often inherited or amplified. The authors call for stronger platform safeguards and moderation.
arxiv-2505-08248:
Mitthumsiri and a large international team show that ground detectors can track the energy spectrum of cosmic rays during solar storms. Their 2025 paper concerns Forbush decreases, the dips in galactic cosmic ray flow when a solar storm sweeps past Earth. Such events matter for space weather warning, yet the spectrum's shape in space is usually measured only by satellites.

Two techniques get the spectrum from the ground. One fits the drops in count rates across a global web of neutron monitors and muon detectors, allowing the flow to vary with direction. The other reads a leader fraction statistic from a single neutron monitor. On five major storms both methods agreed, hour by hour, and matched daily satellite data where it existed. The leader fraction now runs publicly in real time. The work verifies precise spectrum watching from the ground across a wide energy span.
arxiv-2505-08348:
Yize Zhao and Christos Thrampoulidis wrote a 2025 paper explaining how language models secretly organize meaning during training. Next-token prediction is a plain objective: guess the following word. Yet models emerge with rich semantic structure inside. The authors ask what the optimization itself builds.

In a tractable model with synthetic data, training implicitly factorizes a matrix of context-to-next-word co-occurrences. Learned embeddings converge to that matrix's singular vectors, whose sign patterns encode concepts. Bigger singular values, broader concepts, are learned first, yielding a hierarchy from coarse to fine. The team turns those sign patterns into a clustering method that recovers readable categories. Checks on pretrained models found grammar classes, entity types, and topics sorted as predicted. The work links distributional semantics with modern training geometry.
arxiv-2505-09648:
Ali Alsetri, writing alone in 2025, proved a density form of the ternary Goldbach problem in a fixed residue class. The classic question writes odd numbers as sums of three primes. Alsetri fixes attention on primes that leave remainder one when divided by three.

Take any set of those primes whose relative density inside the class exceeds one half. Then every large enough odd number that is a multiple of three is a sum of three primes from that set. The proof also shows one half is the best possible threshold: below it, the claim can fail. The result tightens how sparse a prime set can be while still covering all large targets of the stated form.
arxiv-2505-09748:
Jitendra Tugnait tackles a comparison problem in network statistics: how do two similar webs of dependency differ? The setting is multi-attribute Gaussian graphical models, where each node carries several measures and links live in a precision matrix. Finding the difference graph matters more than either graph alone.

Older tools penalize the gap with a group lasso penalty. Tugnait swaps in non-convex penalties, log-sum and a clipped variant, inside a D-trace loss. Two gradient methods solve the harder objective. Theory gives conditions for finding the right links and tight estimates in high dimensions. Tests on fake and real data round out the case.
arxiv-2505-09948:
Cecilia González-Tokman and Renee Oldfield wrote this 2025 math paper on a family of random maps of the circle. The maps, of a type called Blaschke products, are picked at random at each step, and the family spreads points apart on average. The team studies how much disorder the random motion has, as measured by entropy.

The authors give a formula that can be computed for the average entropy of the family. Their work extends a classic result on fixed circle maps into the random setting. Along the way, they describe the steady chance pattern of the random system and its entropy for a broad class of such maps. The class even allows maps that do not spread everywhere and may hold an attracting point.
arxiv-2505-10048:
Rishabh Kumar Singh and Debraj Chakraborty study a shepherding problem in the plane: one fast pursuer must round up several slower, uncooperative evaders and pen them near a chosen target point. Each evader flees the pursuer with a force that fades with distance, following an inverse-square law. The authors propose two pursuer paths, a spiral and a circle, both turning at constant angular speed around the target.

For the spiral, the inward speed adjusts by feedback based on the evader farthest from the target. Under the right parameter choices, every evader settles into an arbitrarily small circular loop around the target. The pursuer ends on a circle of its own, and the authors derive when those loops are stable. For the circling pursuer they give matching guarantees plus explicit formulas for the loop sizes.
arxiv-2505-10448:
Conor Rosato and co-authors improve Bayesian sampling for costly models in this 2025 paper. Markov Chain Monte Carlo can be slow when each likelihood check is pricey and the surface is rough. Gradient help may be absent or untrustworthy in such tasks.

The team adapts subset samplers that check only part of the data at each step. A data-driven proxy stands in for Taylor expansions to screen proposals fast. A cost-aware controller adjusts the process as it runs. In a disease model task and a test task, their tuned HINTS method gave the best error for a fixed budget. Cheap subset checks plus screening made exact sampling far more efficient.
arxiv-2505-10748:
Feng Cheng and co-authors automate the design of chips that compute inside memory in this 2025 paper. The chips serve recommender systems, the ranking engines behind feeds and ads. Moving data is their main cost, so computing where data sits saves energy. But the design space is huge, with more options than atoms in many stars.

Their tool, AutoRAC, folds chip design and model design into one search. A single supernetwork holds every mixed-precision option, so candidates can be scored without retraining each. On three click-prediction benchmarks the found designs beat hand-built ones: several times faster, smaller, and far more power-thrifty. The authors say automated search can tame design spaces humans cannot browse.
arxiv-2505-10848:
Sanders and co-authors build a foundation model for mass spectrometry data in proteomics, in a 2025 paper. Proteomics studies the full set of proteins in a sample, and mass spectrometry is its main measuring tool. The spectra it produces are complex, and most software tackles one narrow task at a time. The team instead pre-train one encoder on a single broad task: reading protein sequences directly from spectra.

The learned representations then improved four other tasks, from judging spectrum quality to spotting chemical modifications on proteins. Fine-tuning the model on all tasks at once improved each task further. The work suggests one general model can serve many steps of the proteomics pipeline. That matters most where labeled training data are scarce.
arxiv-2505-11048:
Ana Mitrašinović and four co-authors revisit a 2025 claim about which galaxies are most likely to host habitable planets. An earlier study had pointed to a group of small, metal-rich, star-forming galaxies as a sweet spot for life. The team re-ran the search in the IllustrisTNG simulation with stricter filters and checks on each galaxy's past.

The stricter pass confirmed only 97 such dwarf galaxies, plus 519 unclear objects that may be flaws in the simulation. Under these rules, the claimed double pattern in habitability largely faded. Many of the confirmed dwarfs turned out to be stripped-down remains of larger galaxies. The authors argue that such odd remnants and tidal debris may still favor life, and that habitability studies should weigh the whole galactic setting.
arxiv-2505-11348:
Maryam Nowroozi proved in 2025 a finiteness result failing in an infinite tower of number fields. A theorem of Scholl says any fixed number field holds only finitely many del Pezzo surfaces with good reduction outside a fixed prime set. Nowroozi asks what happens over the cyclotomic Z5-extension of the rationals, an infinite field built by stacking layers. The prime set is the single prime above five.

For surfaces of degree three and four, the answer flips completely. Infinitely many distinct del Pezzo surfaces over that tower keep good reduction away from the one bad prime. The contrast shows how sharply arithmetic geometry depends on the ground field's size. Results of this kind test the reach of finiteness theorems proved for ordinary number fields. The paper is aimed at specialists in arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2505-11548:
Zhiyuan Chang and co-authors expose a stealthy attack on AI search systems in 2025. Retrieval augmented systems answer questions by pulling from outside knowledge bases. If those bases are open to edits, attackers can plant poisoned pages. Past attacks needed many planted pages or worked only on simple questions.

Their attack needs just one poisoned document to dominate the answers. It stays effective even on complex questions that chain several facts. That mix of stealth and reach raises the real world risk. Defenders must guard shared knowledge bases as carefully as the models themselves.
arxiv-2505-11648:
Tsutahiro Fukuhara, Junya Hara, Hiroshi Higashi, and Yuichi Tanaka make federated learning sturdier when the messages between clients and server arrive noisy or incomplete. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In federated learning, a server merges model updates from many clients. Static and missing values in that traffic can drag accuracy down hard.

Their fix learns a graph of how client parameters relate while it repairs them. Graph learning and signal restoration are solved as one joint problem. A tailored algorithm handles the problem's split shape efficiently. On two image benches, the method beat existing approaches by a few points of accuracy. The gains held under skewed data splits and noisy links. The work suits federated setups run over real, imperfect networks.
arxiv-2505-11748:
Wei Zhang and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a momentum method that uses the cube of the gradient, not just its square. Momentum helps optimisers speed up and slip past flat stalls. Most recipes use low powers of the slope signal. Their version, HOME-3, builds momentum from third powers.

Theory says the change tightens convergence bounds for both bowl shaped and smooth wavy problems. Tests across convex, smooth, and rough tasks agree: the high power version beat standard momentum throughout. The authors argue higher order momentum is an overlooked dial in training modern models, cheap to turn and broadly useful.
arxiv-2505-11948:
Arata Tomoto and Jun-nosuke Teramae settle a gap in random matrix theory, the study of how the values of huge random tables spread out. Two classic laws describe that spread for different kinds of matrices, the Marchenko-Pastur law and the elliptic law, but how they relate had stayed unclear. The team derives a formula for the spread in a family of correlated matrices that contains both laws as special cases, tying them into one picture.

These same matrices double as the wiring of a memory network, one that links pairs of patterns together. Viewed with modern eyes, that network matches the linear attention design used inside transformer models. Working from their formula, the authors find the network's stability rises and falls in a wavy pattern as more memories are stored, rather than fading steadily. The result, they argue, sharpens understanding of lopsided interactions in many high-dimensional systems.
arxiv-2505-12148:
Antonio García Muñoz refines the model of helium in the skies of distant planets, in a 2025 paper. A helium line in infrared light is a prized tracer of air escaping from exoplanets into space. Predicting its strength requires a network of reactions that make and destroy an excited helium state. García Muñoz expands that network in two directions: reactions involving hydrogen molecules and their ions, and the action of fast photoelectrons knocked loose by starlight.

He simulates the outflow of a Neptune-sized planet, GJ 436 b, with a fluid model joined to a particle-tracking model for the electrons. One reaction, Penning ionization of hydrogen, emerges as a key loss route, and its updated rate changes the predicted line strength notably. Better helium forecasts sharpen what telescopes infer about evaporating worlds.
arxiv-2505-12648:
Tengfei Liu and co-authors build a safer robot planner in a 2025 paper. Moving through busy, shifting spaces demands constant safety checks, yet learned planners rarely offer guarantees. Their framework wraps reinforcement learning with margins that adapt on the fly.

Real-time path tuning and gap analysis judge whether a route stays feasible when the robot cannot see everything. An online correction step reshapes paths to keep a dynamic safety margin while preserving control authority. Ablation tests and rival comparisons show higher success rates and faster computing. Trials on simulated and real robots confirm the planner works beyond the lab.
arxiv-2505-12748:
Li, Pang and their co-authors present TeleOpBench, a simulator-based benchmark for two-arm dexterous teleoperation in 2025. Remote control gives rich training data for robots, but hardware setups vary so much that fair comparison has been hard.

The benchmark holds thirty detailed task settings, from pick-and-place to tool use and joint work. Four control modes are built in, from motion capture gloves to vision tracking, all judged by one protocol. Mirrored tests on a real two-arm robot with dexterous hands tracked simulator results closely. The authors offer the tool as a shared yardstick for future work.
arxiv-2505-12948:
Belhaj and Bouhouch folded geometric diagrams in this physics paper from twenty twenty-five. The setting is M-theory placed on a special Calabi-Yau space built from four projective lines. Five-dimensional black branes live in that compactified world. The authors revisit the space's diagram with colored graph tools and symmetry actions.

A folding procedure then compresses the diagram into simpler known shapes. Under folding, the black brane setups reduce to compactifications with fewer shape parameters. Those reduced cases are already understood in the literature. The result ties an exotic geometry to standard ones. The paper is dedicated to the memory of the first author's mother.
arxiv-2505-13348:
Narek Maloyan, Bislan Ashinov, and Dmitry Namiot attack systems that use a language model to judge other models' answers, in a 2025 paper. Model judges scale cheaply, but poisoned inputs may bend their verdicts. The team formalized two attacks: one that flips the final decision, one that rewires the judge's stated reasoning. Both append a crafted suffix, tuned by a gradient method, to one of the answers being compared.

On a standard human-judgment dataset, two open models proved soft targets. The decision attack succeeded over thirty percent of the time, and the reasoning attack also bit often. The authors warn that judge-based evaluation pipelines carry a real security hole and need defenses.
arxiv-2505-13548:
Dmitry Nesterov offers a new form in 2025 for a family of tweaks to Einstein's gravity theory. The family, called generalized unimodular gravity, breaks part of the theory's usual freedom to pick coordinates. Nesterov builds the new form step by step through equal versions of the action, the sum that defines the theory.

The path adds time as a field of its own, in the spirit of a classic trick for the simpler parent theory. One odd fruit is that space points get linked at a distance in the action, which he probes with care. A sub-family keeps a local action and dodges that snag while holding the family's core traits. The work gives theorists a cleaner grip on how these gravity tweaks move and bind.
arxiv-2505-13948:
A robot told to find the mug it saw two rooms ago needs a memory that serves its whole mission, not just the final answer. Mingliang Zhai and co-authors build that memory-first design in this 2025 paper for embodied question answering. Observations become structured text stored in a searchable library, compared at each step to decide what to refresh.

Before the planner, the stopping judge, or the answerer acts, an entropy-based retrieval fetches the smallest memory slice that module needs. The team also built a hard benchmark of over fifteen hundred multi-target questions. Their framework beat baselines there by nearly ten points, and gained on standard sets too.
arxiv-2505-14448:
Lugo and two co-authors modeled musical sound as a complex network to study performance style in twenty twenty-five. Their subject was the bass viola da gamba, a historical bowed instrument. Audio recordings of pieces were decomposed into frequency components, which became nodes in a network of sounds.

Statistical fitting identified which distributions best describe the frequency fluctuations, revealing regularities across pieces. Network centrality measures picked out the most influential and stable groups of sounds in each piece. The largest cliques, tight groups of mutually connected sounds, marked where complex frequency fluctuations emerge. Because the same musician played the pieces, similar fluctuation patterns could be tied to interpretive style. The authors argue network modeling links large-scale statistical order in sound to a performer's personal approach, bridging scientific and musical analysis.
arxiv-2505-14548:
Bilal Islah and Ahmed Zoulati test whether federal disaster aid keeps people in their homes after hurricanes. Their 2025 paper compares storm-hit areas that received FEMA rental help with similar areas that did not. Evictions are the main outcome, with use of costly emergency credit as a second window on household strain.

Evictions rose sharply after hurricanes in places near the storm path that lacked rental aid. Where aid arrived, eviction growth was muted, and both borrowing volume and defaults fell. The pattern points to cash timing, not just damage, as a binding constraint after storms. Housing and disaster policy readers get evidence that quick rental aid works as a liquidity buffer.
arxiv-2505-14848:
George Wang, Jiaqian Hu, and Safinah Ali staff a translation agency with AI agents. Their 2025 paper presents MAATS, a system where specialist agents each police one quality dimension from a standard metrics framework: accuracy, fluency, style, terminology. A synthesis agent then merges their notes to revise the draft.

Unlike a single model correcting itself, the divided labor catches layered errors, including omissions one perspective spots and another misses. Across language pairs and base models, MAATS beat zero-shot and single-agent baselines in automatic scores and human judgment, with the largest gains in meaning accuracy, locale fit, and distant language pairs. The authors frame the design as a bridge between black-box translation and human editorial workflow.
arxiv-2505-14948:
Guessing future video frames as raw pixels hides why the world moves as it does. Hao Tang and co-authors let a language model write the motion as code instead, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their system reads a few frames into plain state lists. Code then steps those states forward and draws them back into frames.

On two test worlds, a physics sim and a balancing pole, the code path beat pixel rivals. Since states are readable, users can ask what-if and trace why a future came out as it did. The pitch is forecasts that people can audit, for watch rooms, robots, and self-driving stacks.
arxiv-2505-15048:
Yang Luo and Jian-Min Wang simulate how stars inside the disks of active galaxies feed on gas, in a 2025 paper. Disks around supermassive black holes are dense enough to form stars. Those stars can then swallow gas at high rates, growing in ways normal stars never do.

The pair ran three-dimensional models for disks of different thicknesses. They tracked how the swirl of the disk changes the flow of gas toward each star. Shearing motion, which carries angular momentum, can cut the feeding rate sharply. The authors give an approximate formula linking the feeding rate to the gas swirl and to the star's thermal mass, a ratio of its gravity reach to the disk thickness. They also weigh how fast-feeding stars push back on the disk and shape its future. The results help explain how such stars evolve.
arxiv-2505-15348:
Enric Junqué de Fortuny built the SuperEmotion dataset, set out in a 2025 report. Work on teaching machines to name feelings in text has lacked one large, shared base with a sound set of feeling types.

Older sets use mixed labels, hold few samples, or cover one narrow field. The new set joins text from many sources under one scheme. That scheme is drawn from a tested map of human feelings. Work in one field can thus be set next to work in the next. The report covers the second build of the set. It also gives first scores from a tuned modern text model, as a base mark for later work to beat.
arxiv-2505-15548:
Suvadeep Hajra wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It blames dense local links in text for the blow-up of attention scores that can wreck transformer training on long sequences.

When each token leans on many near neighbors, the attention pattern a model must fit is in effect high-rank. The lean form of self-attention can only match it by swelling its scores, and the swell grows with sequence length. Under low-precision math, training then breaks down. Tests on made-up and real language tasks back the tale: growth tracks local density, not nearness alone. Wider attention or built-in local links calm the growth.
arxiv-2505-15648:
Harmender Gahlawat and Meirav Zehavi study how to learn small decision trees when a few examples may be wrong, in a 2025 computer science paper. A decision tree sorts cases by asking a chain of questions. Small trees are easier to read, but stray examples can distort them.

The pair define two tasks, one that limits tree size and one that limits tree depth, while allowing a set number of errors. They show both tasks are hard under some measures, yet become tractable when the error count is counted as a resource. They also report results on how much the input can be shrunk in advance.
arxiv-2505-15748:
Sandeep Kumar Verma and Athulya P develop new tools in Dunkl analysis, a version of harmonic analysis shaped by reflection symmetry. They introduce a family of heat-like flows indexed by a parameter that recovers the classical Poisson flow at one setting and the heat flow at another. Using this family, they write down an explicit formula for undoing the Dunkl-Riesz potential and describe exactly which functions arise as its outputs.

The pair then defines a two-parameter potential and again pins down its inverse and range. Their method writes the inverse as a limit of truncated hypersingular integrals, concrete formulas with a small cut-off. To say how fast the formulas settle, they introduce a notion of pointwise smoothness in this setting. When a function has that smoothness at a point, the approximations converge to the function's value there.
arxiv-2505-15948:
Parth Sarin and Juan Pablo Alperin tested open-weight language models in twenty twenty-five as citation parsers, aiming at global equity in scholarly indexing. Tracking how knowledge circulates requires machine-readable citations, and research from the Global South is under-indexed partly for lack of such tools — an exclusion that reinforces itself. The pair assembled a data set of citations in plain text matched with their annotated components.

Even without fine-tuning, current language models identified citation fields with high accuracy, beating specialized state-of-the-art parsers. The smallest model tested, well under a billion parameters, parsed all fields accurately within thirty-two passes. The authors argue cheap post-training could yield small, robust parsers — and with them, fairer citation networks, better discovery, and stronger metascience worldwide.
arxiv-2505-16348:
Taeyoon Kwon and co-authors probe personalized robot help in a 2025 paper. Home robots powered by language models can tidy objects, but real help means remembering a person's own meanings and routines. The team builds an evaluation that tests two memory skills: knowing what objects mean to a user, and recalling the order of their habits.

Current agents recall simple meanings but fail to use routines when planning. Two bottlenecks stand out: too much memory at once, and clashes when several memories must combine. The authors answer with a layered knowledge graph that stores the user profile apart from raw episodes, lifting scores on both task types.
arxiv-2505-16648:
Several language models answering one medical question may do better as a team than alone. Kexin Shang, Chia-Hsuan Chang, and Christopher Yang built a framework for such teamwork. Three pretrained models took a set of medical exam-style questions. The framework pools their reasoning and lets them face each other's answers. Every model improved under the scheme. Their disagreements across questions also shrank.

The team measured how a model's confidence moves when peers push back. Confidence tracked accuracy in a reassuring way. That link matters if teams of models are to flag their own shaky answers. The work suggests hospitals could gain from model panels, not single oracles.
arxiv-2505-16948:
Dhruv Devulapalli and co-authors bound how fast quantum information can squeeze through a bottleneck, in work from 2025. Some quantum computers link two large regions through a small bridge of few qubits, and routing data across that bridge takes time.

Earlier theory gave only a trivial constant lower bound for such vertex bottlenecks. The new bound ties routing time to the regions' sizes in a strong formula, and a matching cap limits how much entanglement the bridge can build per second. For a star-shaped network, the bound says routing needs time growing like the square root of the leaf count. Free particles can hit that timing exactly, beating gate-by-gate routing.
arxiv-2505-17148:
Tristan Karch, Frédéric Kaplan and their co-authors use large language model agents to query Venice land records from long ago. Their 2025 case covers the years after the old Republic fell, when records were large and far from uniform.

Their system turns plain questions into programs that run on the records. One agent handles structured database queries, while a coding agent does harder custom work. The team sorts research questions by difficulty and maps each type to the right agent. Checks on consistency and answer quality support the approach. Results rebuilt past data on people, property and change over time.
arxiv-2505-17548:
Ding Tang and co-authors present a framework for training large language models on clusters that mix over a thousand chips from different makers, in a paper from 2025. Such mixed clusters promise more computing power, but chips differ in software, math routines, and links, so standard training tools waste them.

The framework, called H2, has three parts. A shared interface keeps the same program behavior on every chip. A direct device-to-device link library speeds talk between unlike chips. A smart pipeline plan splits the work to balance compute, memory, and transfer load. On a model with one hundred billion parameters, the system beat matched single-vendor training by a clear margin.
