The authors claim very large mixed clusters are practical.
arxiv-2505-17748:
Kerol Djoumessi and Philipp Berens make image networks explain themselves for medical scans in a 2025 paper. Such networks can outscore humans, yet their hidden logic is hard to trust in high-stakes care. Add-on explanations guess at that logic after the fact and often miss it.

Their tweak, Soft-CAM, drops a pooling step and swaps the final layer for one that builds class maps in space. The maps then are the basis of each call, not a sketch drawn later. On three medical data sets, accuracy held while explanations grew sharper in both looks and scores. Built-in clarity, they argue, suits risky calls.
arxiv-2505-17848:
Members of the NEXT Collaboration describe a large particle detector in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The detector, NEXT-100, sits in an underground lab in Spain. It hunts for a very rare kind of decay in xenon gas, which could show that a tiny particle is its own antiparticle.

The chamber holds xenon gas at high pressure and records both the energy and the shape of each event. Two planes of light sensors read the signals at each end. The detector began taking data in May of two thousand twenty-four. Early runs with argon and xenon gas ran in a stable way. The paper gives a full account of how it was built and tested.
arxiv-2505-18148:
Owen Bianchi and co-authors show that language models struggle more to find answers hidden in short documents than in long ones, in a paper from 2025. Needle-in-a-haystack tests bury one relevant passage in a sea of filler. Past work blamed position and distractor count; this study isolates the size of the passage that holds the answer.

Across three benchmarks, eleven top models, and over 150,000 controlled runs, accuracy fell sharply as the answer-bearing passage shrank. Small passages also made models more sensitive to where the answer sat. The effect survived checks for position, repeated answer tokens, and distractor volume. The authors warn that agent systems, which stitch together many small scraps of information, face exactly this weakness.
arxiv-2505-18248:
Burcu Kilic, Alper Ahmetoglu, and Emre Ugur give a robot the means to invent its own vocabulary of actions, in this 2025 paper. Planning needs symbols: named skills like push or stack that a planner can chain together. Robots usually receive those symbols from their programmers. A truly developing robot should discover them itself, plus the perceptual categories planning needs.

Their system watches objects and actions and predicts the effects an action will produce, learning with an encoder-decoder network. A curiosity module steers exploration toward the actions whose outcomes are least predictable, since those teach the most. The discovered action primitives then feed a symbolic tree search that plans manipulation tasks with one and two objects. Against two baselines, curiosity won: the robot learned more useful symbols from the same amount of flailing. It is a small model of how children turn play into concepts.
arxiv-2505-18348:
Marwa Banna, Nicolas Gilliers, and Pei-Lun Tseng give the first rate estimates for the free multiplicative central limit theorem, in a 2025 math paper. Central limit theorems describe how random sums or products settle into a fixed limit law. The additive free version was well studied, but the multiplicative one's speed was open.

They study products of many free random operators, each slightly scaled, and measure how far the product's value distribution sits from the free positive semicircle law. Their bounds, in two standard distance measures, depend only on moments of the variables. They also give a combinatorial proof of the limit theorem that extends to unbounded variables.
arxiv-2505-18648:
Sadegh Keshavarzi, Gregory Chockler and Alexey Gotsman wrote a 2025 paper on safe storage built on secure hardware. Chips like Intel SGX can shield code and state while a program runs. Once power is off, saved state can be rolled back to an old version without a trace. That breaks trust in the stored data.

The team models several failure types that can hit such systems. They set tight bounds on how much fault such storage can bear. Their method, TEE-Rex, rebuilds state after faults in a sound way. It needs no special counters or lasting safe storage. Both steady and shifting fault cases are covered.
arxiv-2505-19748:
Yilin Ye and Denis Grebenkov study how wandering particles touch a boundary over time. Their two thousand twenty-five paper works with boundary local time, a measure of that contact. They study it on wedge shapes and on rough, fractal-like curves. A key test shape is the Koch snowflake, built step by step. Angles and corners change how contact builds up.

For wedges, they find the mean contact, its spread, and the far shape of its distribution. They also write linked equations for higher moments. A multi-scale Monte Carlo method then handles complex shapes fast. It blends random walks in open space with exact escapes from sectors. The work applies to reactions that happen only at surfaces. Survival chances of particles near such walls are one payoff.
arxiv-2505-19848:
Odunayo Ogundepo and five co-authors teach language models math in African languages in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Most large models train on rich languages, leaving African ones scarce in data and compute. Adapting them takes special recipes, and the best recipe was unclear. The team ran wide experiments with ablations. They mixed translated data with synthetic data and varied when each training stage used them.

Math reasoning was the test bed, a skill that stresses both language and logic. Their results rank the adaptation strategies for low-resource settings. Clear rankings save scarce compute for the teams who need it most. The work serves researchers building language technology for under-served tongues. It also informs funders of African AI.
arxiv-2505-20348:
Steven Samuels and co-authors present a 2025 study on flaws in a very pure crystal of lithium fluoride. The team ran a cold, low-noise microwave test on the crystal. Certain modes in the crystal showed split patterns that signal a link with electron spins. Those spins point to trace magnetic flaws trapped in the crystal as it grew.

Three spin systems were read from the split patterns. Counts of fine splits and known abundances point to vanadium ions in two charge states as the likely source. Older spin studies and factory records back that read. A broader set of spots fits a fourth spin type, but its source is not yet known. The work aids use of such crystals in fine devices.
arxiv-2505-20648:
Mengmeng Chen and co-authors advance in 2025 Pareto front learning for multi-goal machine learning with a Voronoi grid twist. Front learning maps a taste vector straight to a best-trade-off solution. Past maps sample rays poorly in high dimensions and miss curved front parts.

A genetic search splits the design space into Voronoi cells for even cover. A new loss pushes both front coverage and the volume score upward. Tests across multi-goal tasks beat past front learners by clear margins. Federated learning cases show the method's reach into fresh problem types.
arxiv-2505-20848:
Luís Caires presents CLASS, a proof-of-concept programming language with strong safety guarantees, in work from 2025. CLASS is a general purpose linear language for concurrent programs. Its linear type system, rooted in linear logic and a propositions-as-types view, is meant to ensure that checked programs never misuse or leak resources, never deadlock and always terminate.

Rather than dwell on theory, the paper teaches by example in a tutorial style. Session-based programs illustrate the style, with harder cases that include thread- and memory-safe mutable data types, lazy streams and linear digital assets of the kind used in smart contracts. Correctness comes from type-checking alone in this design.
arxiv-2505-20948:
Yisen Gao and co-authors taught AI systems to suggest explanations that obey user-set limits when reasoning over knowledge graphs. Abductive reasoning works backward from observations to plausible logical hypotheses, useful in diagnosis and science. On huge graphs, though, one observation can spawn floods of redundant or off-target hypotheses, because nothing steers the generator.

Their framework, CtrlHGen, trains in two stages: first supervised learning, then reinforcement learning with rewards for following the stated conditions. To stop the model collapsing onto a few simple patterns, training data is enriched by breaking complex hypotheses into simpler parts. Softer similarity rewards keep it from overreacting to wording changes. On three benchmarks the system followed control conditions better and produced hypotheses closer in meaning to the references.
arxiv-2505-21048:
Sanskriti Agrawal and Raktim Abir write a 2025 physics paper on a measure of quantum entanglement in a system that pairs one qubit with a larger partner, a qudit. The measure, called negativity, comes from a flipped version of the state's density matrix. The authors work out the full set of values of that flipped matrix for a pure state of this kind.

They find only four values that are not zero, and just one of them is negative. That single value gives a clean route to the negativity. They then apply the result inside a proton, where they study the link between a parton's spin and its motion. There the negativity ties to a known measure of gluon spin and to a geometric angle in the state space for protons with a set light polarization.
arxiv-2505-21348:
Shunrui Li and Yang Liu uncover a topological secret inside the quantum harmonic oscillator, in a research paper from 2025. The oscillator's partition function, a workhorse of statistical mechanics, turns out to equal a Chern character, a quantity from geometry. That equality ties everyday thermal physics to a famous index theorem.

The authors read the partition function as describing a virtual bundle of quantum states over space-time. Internal energy then appears as the index theorem at work outside its usual supersymmetric home. The result suggests bosonic quantum systems carry hidden topological structure. Such links may guide new ways to compute or classify quantum matter.
arxiv-2505-21548:
Dhruv Agarwal and co-authors test whether regionally trained language models actually understand their home culture in a 2025 paper, using India as the case. Countries are building sovereign models, but fluency in a local language is not the same as sharing local values. The team scored six Indic and six global models against national surveys and community question sets.

Indic models aligned no better with Indian norms than global ones; an average American respondent matched Indian values more closely than any Indic model. In a study with one hundred fifteen Indian users, both model families Westernized or exoticized writing suggestions. Prompting and regional fine-tuning failed to fix alignment and sometimes erased knowledge. The authors blame thin culturally grounded training data and call for community-authored corpora.
arxiv-2505-21748:
John Hood, Caterina De Bacco, and Aaron Schein introduce, in a 2025 paper, a model for finding structure in networks where groups, not pairs, interact. A drug trial, a group chat, a team: real systems run on multi-way ties, drawn as hypergraphs. Their clumping and scale defeat older tools. The team's key move is to group similar units into classes and let the classes themselves form a second, hidden hypergraph.

Observed interactions are then explained by ties among the classes, compressed into low-rank form so the math stays tractable and the structure stays identifiable. On real data, from drug networks to social ones, the model predicted missing links better than state-of-the-art rivals. It also returned structures a human can read at both the unit and class level. The authors aim to make large higher-order data a routine input to science.
arxiv-2505-22548:
Changhao Song and co-authors present in 2025 Emotion-o1, a language model framework that adjusts how long it thinks based on the feeling task at hand. Long chains of thought help models read emotions, but a fixed length wastes effort on easy calls and starves hard ones like sarcasm. Adaptive depth promises a better balance.

Training distilled flexible reasoning patterns from a stronger model, then fine-tuning and reward learning polished accuracy, brevity, and form. Gains were largest on sarcasm and humor tests. The 8B model beat some much larger rivals on key tasks. It also cut reasoning length by 83 percent versus a leading baseline, showing that shorter thought can still read feelings well.
arxiv-2505-22648:
Jialong Wu and co-authors train a web agent that seeks facts on its own in this 2025 paper. Hard real problems need deep searching and step-by-step thought. Recent research agents show promise, but building one well takes a full plan.

Their plan has four stages: build browsing data, sample action paths, fine-tune the agent for a sound start, and sharpen it with reward-based learning. The agent, WebDancer, follows the ReAct style of mixing thought and action. Tests check how well it handles deep questions. The work maps a path from raw data to a working research agent.
arxiv-2505-22948:
Michael Sun and co-authors propose, in a 2025 paper, a way to teach generative chemistry models a readable grammar of molecules. Graph grammars can make molecule generation more interpretable and data efficient. But learning such a grammar has relied on expert labels or shaky rules of thumb, which limits trust.

Their method, Foundation Molecular Grammar, leans on large multimodal foundation models and their stored chemical knowledge. It renders each molecule as an image, describes it in text, and aligns the two views through prompt based learning. The induced grammar can drop into existing pipelines for molecule generation and property prediction. In tests, it did well on whether molecules can be made, how varied they are, and how little data it needs. Its chemical rules stay readable by humans, which suits automated discovery work.
arxiv-2505-23148:
Minghao Xie and co-authors simulate in 2025 why Saturn mass planets are scarce on short orbits, a gap called the hot Saturn desert. That scarcity can test ideas about how gas planets form and change. The team built a large set of made up short period gas planets around sun like and small dwarf stars, varying their starting traits.

They varied mass, glow, core share, and orbit, froze migration, and let each planet cool and lose air over long time spans. Starting mass, glow, and core share proved the main drivers of how a planet's size changes. A survivor shaped like a hot Saturn needed a narrow mix: mass below half of Jupiter, a heavy core share, and a faint starting glow. The match between those limits and theory gives planet formation models a sharp check.
arxiv-2505-23248:
Yunliang Qi and five co-authors survey ways to rebuild sharp images from blurred, low-grade ones taken from space or air. Their survey is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such sharp rebuilds are a core task in the use of far-sensed images. Scores of ways have been put forth in past years, but no full, step-by-step review had been made. The team sorts the ways into taught, untaught, and quality-check groups, and sets out the data sets and scores used to judge them. They weigh each group's strengths and flaws. A key gap: fine grain and true shape are lost when the drop in grade is large. They close with paths for new work.
arxiv-2505-23348:
Marco Caroccia and Nicolas Van Goethem analyze in 2025 a function space tied to deviatoric deformation, used in plasticity and fluid models. Such maps allow jumps and sharp edges that classic smooth tools miss. A firm grasp of their structure aids both math and materials work.

The main result names the annihilator of the space and proves a rigidity claim for maps with a fixed wave direction. A kernel projection tool joins that result to drive a blow-up method for hard limit problems. The route beats snags that blocked the fuller deformation case. Uses in integral forms and materials close the study.
arxiv-2505-23448:
Pirzada Suhail, Rehna Shaik, and Amit Sethi wrote a 2025 paper on detecting out-of-distribution inputs to a machine learning classifier. A deployed model will inevitably meet inputs unlike its training data. Safe systems must flag such inputs and express uncertainty rather than answer confidently and wrongly. The two tasks were usually handled separately.

Their framework uses network inversion, generating inputs that a trained network associates with each class. They extend an n-class classifier with an extra garbage class, seeded with random noise to represent outliers. After each training epoch the garbage class is refined with inverted examples. The combined design addresses detection and uncertainty estimation in one training loop.
arxiv-2505-23948:
Shai Chester, Rishi Mouland, and Jesse van Muiden compute scattering in a curved space in a 2025 paper on string theory dualities. They study the simplest theories where a special kind of three field coupling, called extremal, is not zero.

Those theories pair a five dimensional curved space with branes that carry gluon like modes, beside towers of graviton modes. The authors compute the coupling between the two kinds of modes. They then use it to work out the graviton exchange part of a four point function of gluon modes. That term explains why some three point diagrams blow up. For the simplest gauge theory in the set, they fix the full four point function at the order they study.
arxiv-2505-24048:
Guangtao Zheng, Wenqian Ye, and Aidong Zhang built a self guided fix for spurious bias in deep networks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a known flaw: models lean on side cues that oft ride with a class, like a backdrop, not the thing it self. Such models fail when the cue is gone. Past fixes need hand marks of which cues are false, which are dear to get and may miss the model's own traps.

Their method, NeuronTune, works after training. It probes the model's inner space to find the neurons that drive the false picks, then tunes them down. Proof backs the path. Readers get a fix that asks no outside marks of bias.
arxiv-2505-24248:
Wei-Cheng Tseng and David Harwath stress-test the speech codecs that squeeze voice recordings into compact codes. Their 2025 paper notes that these neural codecs now also serve as the word-like tokens that speech models learn from. How they hold up in noisy rooms has barely been studied.

The pair ran the codecs under varied noise and found wide gaps in how well each coped. They traced part of the gap to warped, non-linear handling of the sound signal. Checks of how each codec treats high and low tones helped explain losses in sound quality. The authors say future codec designs should be judged on noise strength, not just clean-room scores. Real-world use, from calls to voice assistants, depends on that strength.
arxiv-2505-24848:
Yang and a team including Alam and Siam set a new task in twenty twenty-five: tell when a glasses wearer is reading, from the wearer's own view. Smart glasses need such logs to give fit help in the wild. They built a set of one hundred hours of read and non-read clips.

Three feeds feed the task: the view, eye gaze, and head pose. A transformer model takes any mix of the three feeds. Each feed helps, and blends help more, their tests show. The set also sorts read kinds, like books versus screens.
arxiv-2506-00048:
Recommender systems starve when user clicks are sparse, and contrast training on graphs is one way to feed them. Aravinda Jatavallabha and co-authors apply a light contrast method in a 2025 paper. Their model, LightGCL, reshapes the user-item graph with a math tool that keeps its meaning intact. Random shuffles, used by rival methods, are avoided. Global taste signals are the prize.

Benchmark tests showed clear gains over leading models, the team reports. Fairness across popular and niche items also improved. The method resisted noise in the click data. Sparse settings are where the gains matter most. The authors pitch the approach for live shopping and media platforms.
arxiv-2506-00248: Po-Jui Chen and Piers Coleman lift an exactly solvable model into four dimensions, in a 2025 paper. The Kitaev spin liquid, defined on a honeycomb lattice, is treasured because its quantum state can be computed exactly. The authors build a four-dimensional version on an orthorhombic lattice with six sublattices per unit cell. Its free-particle surface is made of two-dimensional sheets, and flipping a flux excitation costs positive energy, suggesting a flux-free ground state like its two-dimensional cousin. Fractionalised quantum matter is not flatland-only.
arxiv-2506-00348:
Shivam Shorewala and Zihao Yang argued in 2025 that skill ratings in competitive games improve when they use not just who won, but by how much compared with expectation. Classic ratings like Elo ignore margin entirely. Existing margin-based fixes lack a principled way to fold the information in. Their method learns a curve that predicts expected margin from the rating gap, including saturation and home advantage.

The update signal is the gap between the real margin and the expected one. Tested on over thirteen thousand NBA games across a decade, the method beat standard Elo and strong Bayesian rivals. It cut prediction error, raised accuracy slightly, and reached stable ratings about thirteen percent faster, all at Elo-like computing cost.
arxiv-2506-00448:
Suhas B N and co-authors study made-up facts in AI summaries of doctor-patient talks, in a 2025 paper. Such errors can harm care and mislead decisions. Whether general error detectors work in medicine was unclear. Errors are also rare and random, which makes them hard to study.

The team built two data sets to force the issue. One removed facts from source talks to trigger false summary content. The other gathered errors that arose naturally in real summaries. General detectors struggled on clinical errors, they found. Skill on forced errors did not predict skill on natural ones. Their own fact-counting detectors, built on the forced set, carried over well to natural errors. The work adds expert-checked data and measures for safer clinical summaries.
arxiv-2506-00548:
Jiahui Geng, Thy Thy Tran, Preslav Nakov, and Iryna Gurevych present a 2025 attack on multimodal language models. Such models read images and sound as well as text, and their guards focus on text. The team's method hides the banned instruction inside an image or a sound clip. The model reads the hidden order as if it were a normal input, and the guard misses it.

Their crafted files are tuned so the model's inner code matches the target order. Mixed with plain text, the files work even better. Tests on four known models gave the top attack success rates, above 80 percent on one large model. The team also grades replies by quality and fit, not just success. They test guards against the trick as well. The work warns that each new sense a model gains opens a new door.
arxiv-2506-00748:
Translation tools can warp facts about gender when they move between tongues that mark gender and tongues that do not. Pardis Sadat Zahraei and Ali Emami build a test set for that warp in a 2025 paper. Their set holds 3,950 hard scenes across six languages, such as Persian and Finnish, that leave gender open.

Four major systems all slid into stereotypes on the set. Each one reached for male pronouns when a role hinted at status, some four to six times more than female ones. A mid-size open model, retrained on the new set, shed most of those errors. It went on to beat the big closed systems. The work shows targeted data can fix biased output.
arxiv-2506-00948:
Frederique Bassino and co-authors show in 2025 that a classic group task on matrix groups over the rationals takes linear time on the mean case. The head gives that form of the claim. The task asks if a word in group steps equals the plain unit.

Time is counted in bits, since big whole numbers swell as counts grow. The linear claim holds for both raw words and cut down words picked at chance. It then flows to nilpotent and chain like groups for free. No method can beat linear time here, in worst or mean case, the team also shows.
arxiv-2506-01148:
Orchid Chetia Phukan and seven co-authors join two kinds of sound traits to sort heart murmurs: coded traits from a learned audio codec, and classic traits of tone. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The team holds the two kinds fill each other's gaps. The coded traits catch fine sound marks, such as shifts of rhythm. The tone traits hold the form of the sound's waves, such as its spread of energy, which is key for heart sounds. Their frame, BAOMI, fuses the two by a bandit-based focus. An agent gives more weight to the heads that count most in a multi-head focus net. Tests back the join.
arxiv-2506-01348:
Yeping Jin, Lauren Wise, and Ioannis Paschalidis harden the Cox survival model against the possibility that the data do not follow the assumed distribution. Survival analysis predicts time to an event, from death to machine failure. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team wraps Cox regression in distributionally robust learning. The ambiguity set is a ball around the data, measured by Wasserstein distance. Duality turns the worst-case problem into an ordinary regularized fit, computable with modern conic programming. Guarantees on finite-sample behavior accompany the reformulation.

Simulations and real case studies favor the robust version on both accuracy and stability. Misspecification and small data perturbations hurt it less than traditional fits. The paper targets clinical and reliability settings where the cost of a brittle survival curve is real.
arxiv-2506-01448:
A large team led by S Smit and M Bluschke studied a three-layer copper oxide superconductor in two thousand twenty-five. Such trilayer cuprates hold the record for the highest transition temperatures, yet why they work so well stays unclear. Using fast light-based tools, the team probed charge order and pairing layer by layer.

They found charge order on the inner layer, which also hosts a large pairing gap and strong particle coherence despite being underdoped. The outer layers showed larger gaps than in simpler cuprates. Model work backs a picture where the layers boost each other. That interlayer effect may explain the record performance of this family.
arxiv-2506-01548: Antoine Bret argues that the Vlasov equation cannot fully describe collisionless shocks. His 2025 paper rests on one contrast: the equation conserves entropy, while a shock does not. That clash means a key shock trait lies outside the equation reach. Bret suggests a rigorous theory of such shocks may need to work at the Klimontovich level, one rung finer. The note is brief and sets a conceptual boundary for plasma theory rather than reporting new simulations.
arxiv-2506-02048:
Muzsai, Imolai, and Lukács train a language-model agent to crack cryptographic puzzles. Their training ground, Random-Crypto, generates fresh Capture The Flag challenges on demand, giving reinforcement learning a stream of tasks with exact right answers and many reasoning steps. They fine-tune a Python-equipped Llama model with a group-based reinforcement method inside a secure sandbox.

The trained agent solves far more unseen challenges than before, and the gains carry over to two outside tests: a public CTF benchmark spanning crypto and beyond, and a 135-question cryptography quiz. Breakdowns credit the improvement to better tool use and steadier step-by-step reasoning. The authors offer the generator as a rich practice field for security-minded agents.
arxiv-2506-02148:
Arjun Bagchi, Supratik Biswas, Astha Kakkar, and Saikat Mondal wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five about flat space cosmologies. These are time-based forms of three-dimensional flat space with no cosmological constant. Each one has a horizon, much like the edge seen in some black hole models.

The authors study small changes made by a scalar field around these forms. They work out the tones at which the field fades, treating the horizon as a hard wall. They also link their results to the flat limit of a known black hole case. From those tones, they build a value used to test older answers in the field.
arxiv-2506-02248:
Matt Nagle and co-authors measured skin stiffness and direction traits in living people in 2025. Skin is elastic, springy, and stretched unevenly by natural tension, with fibers that give it a grain. Good data on that grain in living skin are scarce and cover few ages.

Elastic waves sent through the skin gave readings from seventy-eight volunteers aged three to ninety-three. A Bayesian model weighed age, sex, and skin tension. A new grain measure, based on the oval shape of the angular data, proved more robust than the classic ratio. Grain strength grew slowly with age, and stiffness rose in a straight line along the natural skin lines. Men had stiffer skin on average, while tension shifted both measures.
arxiv-2506-02348:
Bower and co-authors report long-term position tracking of the Galactic Center magnetar PSR J1745-2900 with the Very Long Baseline Array. New measures join ten past epochs to give twenty-five epochs and forty-one measures over 1,984 days. A magnetar near the centre of our galaxy can test motion around the central black hole, Sgr A-star.

Proper motion is now fixed to within about two percent. Acceleration limits sit near what an orbit around Sgr A-star would allow at most. A hidden companion model can fit the positions, but pulse period data rule it out. No change in the magnetar's apparent size was seen, so the scattering path stayed steady over the watch.
arxiv-2506-02448:
Baoyu Liang and co-authors build VidEvent, a large dataset for teaching AI to understand events unfolding in video, in a 2025 paper. Events have structure, layers, and logic that current systems grasp poorly. The team define a task: pull an event script from a video and use it to predict what comes next.

The dataset holds over 23,000 carefully labeled events drawn from movie recap videos, with detailed structures, broad hierarchies, and logical links between events. A meticulous annotation process kept quality high. Baseline models with published scores give future work a yardstick. The authors argue the resource can push video understanding from labeling clips toward following stories, and they release the data and tools publicly.
arxiv-2506-02748:
Arabhavi and co-authors reported survey results on planet-forming disks around very low-mass stars and brown dwarfs in two thousand twenty-five. Such disks are lighter than those around Sun-like stars and may evolve faster. The James Webb telescope can now read their inner gas in fine detail.

The team analyzed infrared spectra of ten disks around objects from a fiftieth to about a seventh of the Sun's mass. All showed molecular emission, and most showed a silicate dust feature. Carbon-rich gases were found in every source, with larger hydrocarbons in nearly all. Oxygen-bearing gases appeared less often. Trends link richer carbon to weaker dust and lower disk mass, consistent with fast inward drift of solids.
arxiv-2506-03048:
Yang Zhang and six co-authors report a new pattern in a crystal in a twenty twenty-five paper. The crystal is a ferroelectric, a solid whose tiny electric charges point in set ways. Past work found swirls of these charges, but a helix, a corkscrew form, had stayed out of reach.

With imaging at the scale of single atoms, the team found polar domains that line up in a helix at a larger scale. From one domain to the next, the charge turns in the same sense, like steps on a spiral stair. Both right-hand and left-hand forms show up. The find gives a new route to helical order and handedness in such crystals.
arxiv-2506-03248:
Zachary Claytor and Jamie Tayar harvest star rotation rates from the background of an old space telescope's images, in a 2025 paper. The Kepler mission's huge pixels blended many stars together, contaminating its light curves. A reprocessing project separated the blends, yielding clean brightness records for over four hundred thousand background sources.

The authors trained a neural network on synthetic spotted-star light curves to read rotation periods directly. Applied to the new curves, it returned periods for over thirty-two thousand sources, about ten thousand of them brand new, plus hundreds of pulsation frequencies from red giant oscillations. Checked against known values, the network's periods agreed excellently. A warning came with the harvest: comparing foreground and background pairs showed many supposedly known periods may belong to the wrong star.
arxiv-2506-03348:
Peter Graham and Davide Racco re-examine a famous limit on the QCD axion in a 2025 paper. The catalog record names only Racco; the byline printed with the text lists both authors. The axion is a proposed particle that could solve a puzzle in nuclear physics and form dark matter.

A standard argument says pattern limits from the early universe rule out a heavy axion paired with fast cosmic inflation. The authors show the limit melts when one coupling in the underlying theory is small. Then the axion's key scale shrinks after inflation, muting the forbidden patterns. They check that the rescue does not overproduce axions in the process. Large regions of theory space, long thought closed, reopen.
arxiv-2506-03448:
Bimsara Pathiraja and co-authors improve image editing tools when a request names one object among many in 2025. Past tools edit a single bold object well. They fail in busy scenes with many things. The team first builds a hard test set from real photos with named objects. Top tools, trained on millions of cases, score poorly on it.

Their model, called RefEdit, trains on a pipeline that makes fake edit examples. It used only twenty thousand examples, far fewer than rivals. Yet it beat large base models on the new test. It also did well on standard tests, near closed tools. Data and model files are shared for checks.
arxiv-2506-03648:
Yan Huang, Yu-Tian Li, and Wen-Gao Long sort the real solutions of a classic equation in a 2025 paper. The Painlevé I equation has solutions that can wave, split, or blow up along the number line. The team studies the large slope regime at the points where a solution crosses zero.

Using a complex method for wave like problems, they expand key multipliers in full detail. Those expansions sort solutions into three types by their acts at the zeros. They also solve the link between far left behavior and the sites of zeros on the right. A phase map in two inputs sums up the results, and simulations back the theory.
arxiv-2506-03948:
Myung-Chul Jung and Nojoon Myoung study tiny bubbles in graphene, a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon, as possible building blocks for quantum bits. When graphene is strained into a bubble, the strain acts like a magnetic field and traps electrons in a quantum dot. Stretching the bubble into an ellipse changes that trap, and the authors ask how the shape change shifts the trapped energy levels.

Working on paper rather than in a lab, they compare a single dot with a pair of dots. The two setups react to stretching in opposite ways. Levels in a single dot shift most when the bubble is stretched along one axis. Levels in a double dot shift most under stretch along the other axis. The authors say this split behavior matters for tuning graphene qubits, since shape could serve as a control knob.
arxiv-2506-04048:
Gabriele Magrini, Federico Becattini, Giovanni Colombo, and Pietro Pala film flight with event eyes for wild watch in a 2025 paper. Plain film tools blur at fast, small flight and lose the quarry in the frame. Event eyes give swift, crisp reads with no blur, a fit for such hunts.

Their set holds tagged birds, bugs, and drones with box marks and track tags. Off-beat flight paths of wild things drive the set's form, the team notes. Ways to read the rush streams frame the next part of the work.
arxiv-2506-04148:
Sairam Pamulaparthi Venkata, Valentina Balbi, and Michel Destrade lead a team showing that wrinkles in a soft auxetic membrane can be programmed to appear, spread, merge, and vanish as pulling increases. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Auxetic materials widen when stretched, the opposite of ordinary matter. Their membranes could serve robots, aircraft, and medical devices.

The trick is grading the material: stiffness and the auxetic ratio vary across the disc. Edge tractions then wrinkle chosen regions in a chosen order. A classic tension-field theory models the behavior inside commercial software. The simulations confirm nonstandard wrinkle patterns on demand. Beyond the device promise, the study validates the theory for graded materials generally. Programmed wrinkling could tune grip, flow, or optics on soft surfaces. It turns an instability engineers usually fight into a feature.
arxiv-2506-04248:
Julio Cesar Jaramillo Quiceno, of the Universidad Nacional de Colombia, sets out a new q-deformed form of the Heisenberg algebra in a two thousand twenty-five paper. That algebra lies at the heart of quantum theory. It links where a thing is and how it moves. In past work, many in physics put forth such changed forms, each with a deformation parameter, q.

Quiceno first looks at the old forms by Wess, Schmüdgen, Wess and Schwenk, Gaddis, and others. He then sets out a new algebra built from parts tied to place and speed. Its rules use real counts and three functions of q. With the right picks, the new form gives back the plain old algebra. It also gives back a few known changed ones. So one set of rules can hold what were once split, stand-alone ideas.
arxiv-2506-04348:
Six authors refine light contrast calls for rocky planets in 2025, in part two of an Earth-as-planet study. Next-scope eyes will soon read Earth-like worlds near home stars, yet past contrast calls rest on plain world builds. Their 3D light runs add true shade maps, split clouds, and waft shapes drawn from Earth reads.

Plain builds miss Earth's full play, above all in light lean, the runs show. Thin cloud builds bend soak lines in water bands, which can skew air chem reads. Contrast calls drop by half against plain builds, and lean reads may serve better.
arxiv-2506-04448:
Mohammad Sadi and co-authors pick out single spin states in a crystal defect in a 2025 paper. The host is hexagonal boron nitride, a flat crystal prized for quantum sensing. Its boron gap defects can be read with light, but close spin lines blur the reads.

The team made round polarized microwaves with a cross shaped guide and a chip. Round waves let them drive just one spin jump at a time, up or down. Light based tests proved the pick worked, and field strength changed how clean the pick stayed. A cleaner pick should sharpen how well such crystals sense faint magnetic fields.
arxiv-2506-04648:
Liu and fourteen co-authors sped up video generation in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Diffusion models make fine video but run slowly, and attention is the bottleneck. Shrinking numbers to FP8 and skipping weak attention links each help alone. Bolted together without joint training, though, quality crumbles.

Their design trains the two tricks together from the start. A shared three-dimensional tile size serves both compression routes. Sensitivity shifts across denoising steps, so the scheme adapts step by step. A custom kernel built on FlashAttention exploits modern graphics hardware. Attention ran about seven times faster, and full generation about five times. Quality on the standard benchmark held steady.
arxiv-2506-04848:
Dávid Javorský, Ondřej Bojar, and François Yvon wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It releases MockConf, a dataset of student interpreters at work, built to teach machines the art of translating speech on the fly.

Simultaneous interpreters render speech into another language seconds behind the speaker, long before sentences end. Text translation corpora cannot capture that dance, with its shortenings and simplifications. MockConf holds seven hours of mock conference recordings in five European languages, transcribed and aligned at word and span level. The authors also release InterAlign, a web tool for annotating such long parallel material. They propose evaluation metrics and run a first automatic alignment baseline. The package is public, aimed at researchers who want machines to interpret, not just translate, with all the mess that involves.
arxiv-2506-05348:
Wang and co-authors let their virtual building blocks be born anywhere, at any time. Rebuilding moving 3D scenes for novel-view video usually starts from a fixed set of Gaussian blobs in a canonical pose, warped by a deformation field; complex motion breaks that scheme. Their method, FreeTimeGS, instead allows each primitive to appear at an arbitrary moment and place.

Each blob also carries its own motion function, drifting into neighboring regions as time passes, which trims redundancy. The result is a flexible four-dimensional representation that bends with the scene instead of fighting it. On several benchmark data sets, the rendering quality beats recent methods by a wide margin. The authors provide a project page with examples.
arxiv-2506-05448:
Benedikt Seidl and co-authors study whether groups of cold gas clouds can survive being swept by hot galactic winds, in a paper from 2025. Such winds blow out of galaxies and can shred cold clouds. Past work found a size limit for a lone cloud to survive when cooling is included.

The team ran three-dimensional simulations of many round clouds at once, in patterns closer to real interstellar gas. Groups of clouds could survive together even when each lone cloud would be destroyed. Tight packing, small gaps between clouds, and breaking into pieces all helped survival. The authors propose a new survival rule based on the group's total mass and how much of the wind's path the clouds fill. A shared threshold value fits their tests.
arxiv-2506-05548:
Thin sheets of carbon, wrapped in boron nitride, can act in odd ways when a gate tries to set their charge. Maffione and co-authors chase the source of that odd act in a 2025 study. Their rig lets them twist the wrap layers while the device runs, a rare level of control.

The twist angle, they find, works like a switch for the odd act. When the two wrap layers sit at a mid range angle, the gate can fail to bite and the charge can lag in loops. Shift the angle a bit and the act fades. The angle between the wrap layers, not the pattern they make with the carbon, runs the show. The map gives labs clear rules to make the effect show up on cue.
arxiv-2506-05948:
Rathnakaran and Asoka Biswas wrote this 2025 physics paper on a heat engine built from spins. A normal engine runs between a hot bath and a cold bath. Their quantum Otto engine swaps the cold bath for a measurement step, so it runs with a single heat bath.

The machine holds two pairs of spins. One pair does the work, while the second, helper pair is measured to draw off heat. Links between the pairs let the measurement basis tune the performance of the engine. Running in finite time, the engine still delivers real power. With local control of the helper pair, its efficiency can even pass the standard quantum Otto limit.
arxiv-2506-06048:
Haripriya Harikumar and Santu Rana propose in 2025 TRUST, a method that makes a classifier's confidence scores more honest at test time. Standard tricks like dropout often fail to separate predictions worth trusting from shaky ones, which the authors blame on noisy classifier weights that blur fine-grained statistics.

Their method optimizes at test time to correct for that noise, producing a score with a clean property: remove the lowest-scored samples and accuracy rises steadily. That monotonic behavior makes the score practical for triage, letting a system abstain on exactly the cases it should. The method outperformed standard baselines in their tests.
arxiv-2506-06148:
Yan-Xiao Wang and Yin Zhong map the phases of a chain model that mixes topology with electron interaction in this 2025 physics paper. The model is the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, a line of sites with alternating link strengths, here filled to one quarter with spinless electrons that repel or attract their neighbors. Which ordered state wins depends on the settings.

The authors diagonalized the system exactly with twisted boundary conditions and cross-checked with a mean-field picture. Strong attraction yields a plain band insulator with no topological character. For middling attraction, a bond-order wave, where links alternate in strength, appears when the link imbalance is large enough. Elsewhere a charge-density wave, where electrons bunch on alternating sites, takes over. The phase boundaries meet at sharp points the team pinpoints. The work shows how topology and ordering compete in one dimension.
arxiv-2506-06248:
Pourcel, Basu, Ernoult, and Gilra extend a brain-like learning method so it can handle inputs that change over time. The method, equilibrium propagation, trains energy-based models by letting them settle, but its math covered only fixed inputs. Their 2025 work rebuilds the method on a broader action-based frame that follows the whole path of the system.

Different end conditions then give different learning rules, and many turn out impractical to build. One known family, Hamiltonian echo learning, falls out as a special case. The authors show it is the only version they found that keeps the traits that make the method attractive for hardware. Those traits are forward-only running, few passes at any model size, and learning from local signals alone.
arxiv-2506-06348:
Vassiliki Mancoridis and co-authors teach spaceborne sensors to spot methane plumes by borrowing strength from airborne ones. Methane packs a strong warming punch, so fast leak hunting matters for climate action. Airborne imaging has a head start, with neural nets that sift true plumes from false bright spots.

Their 2025 work builds a plume classifier for the EMIT space mission, then refines airborne trained models with transfer learning. That beats a space only model. A second trick, an image translation method called CycleGAN, warps space data to look airborne. Classifiers then run on the warped data directly, which gave the best plume finds of all.
arxiv-2506-06448:
Vaastav Anand and three colleagues present a 2025 systems paper on a chicken-and-egg problem in cloud computing research. New ideas for microservice systems need realistic test systems to prove themselves, but real production systems are closed, so researchers settle for toy examples or simulations. The authors propose building test systems from distributed traces, the call records that large internet firms have released.

Their system, Palette, first compresses a trace into a causal model capturing which services call which, in what order, with what timing and branching odds. From that model it generates full benchmark systems that mirror the original's scale and behavior. The authors argue trace-grown benchmarks can replace the hand-built stand-ins the field relies on.
arxiv-2506-06548:
Three physicists track how a swirling packet of electrons changes when an uneven electric field disturbs it, in a 2025 theory paper. These packets carry orbital angular momentum and have a vortex shape, with a hollow core where the wave vanishes. They draw interest across optics and electron physics.

The field in the study breaks the round symmetry of the packet. Working to first order in perturbation theory, the team computes how the wave and its density evolve. The field can reshape the packet and spoil its neat form. In one clear effect, the single line of zeros along the axis splits into many separate nodes across the sideways plane. Such results matter for labs that steer twisted electrons through real, imperfect fields.
arxiv-2506-06648:
Gabriel Luis Dizon revises predictions for primordial black hole mergers in this two thousand twenty-five astrophysics paper. Primordial black holes, formed in the early universe, might make up some dark matter, and their binary mergers are a target for gravitational wave detectors. Merger rates are suppressed by a factor involving the expected local count of neighboring black holes. Recent clustering results let Dizon rebuild that count so it varies with the binary's mass ratio.

For broad mass distributions, the suppression largely disappears for binaries with extreme mass ratios. Rates rise for distributions favoring lighter average masses, most visibly by extending the low-mass end of the detectable constraint windows. The author projects consequences for the future Einstein Telescope and LISA observatories, in both resolvable mergers and the stochastic background. Clustering becomes testable at lower abundances than expected, though three-body channels remain future work.
arxiv-2506-07348:
Pablo Moraes and co-authors describe a pocket race car that drives itself by camera alone, built for the FIRA twenty twenty-five Autonomous Cars Challenge. The UruBots team's compact electric car, about the size of a radio-controlled model, must navigate varied tracks and dodge obstacles in real time.

A convolutional neural network reads the camera feed and outputs steering and throttle directly. It was trained on more than ten thousand images gathered for the project. On the track the car finished in under thirty seconds, holding roughly zero point four metres per second while avoiding obstacles. The paper lays out the mechanical build, the electronics, and the learning pipeline as a reference for other university teams.
arxiv-2506-07448:
Nguyen-Hien and co-authors argue that language models need a richer account of their own uncertainty. Today's safety practice mostly rejects answers flagged as unsure. That blunt rule treats all doubt alike, though some doubt can be cleared up and some cannot. The team urges a Bayesian frame that sorts doubt by its source.

With doubt sorted, a model and its user can act in fitting ways. They can ask a clarifying question, fetch outside facts, or sharpen the prompt. Doubt that cannot shrink can still be flagged plainly. The authors say this active stance would beat passive refusal in high stakes uses, and make systems more open about their limits.
arxiv-2506-07548:
Weiqiang Jin and co-authors teach teams of game agents with a curriculum that adapts as they improve, in a 2025 paper. Most multi-agent training holds the opponent's strength fixed, which the authors call meta-stationarity, and they show it traps learning in shallow strategies. Their framework, CL-MARL, raises or lowers difficulty online using win-rate signals.

A scheduler reads momentum and recent returns to keep the steps smooth, with no hand tuning. Because a moving target scrambles credit for rewards, a new advantage method compares each agent against counterfactual teammates. On hard StarCraft battle maps the system reached a 40 percent win rate, ahead of five rival methods, and peaked faster.
arxiv-2506-08048:
Zheng Han and five co-authors teach surgical overlays to bend with the body, in a 2025 paper. In augmented reality surgery, a scan-based model of the patient’s organ is projected onto the live view to reveal hidden vessels and tumors. Breathing, gas inflation, and cut ligaments all deform the organ, and a stiff overlay soon points at the wrong spots.

Physics-based finite element models bend plausibly but run too slowly for the operating room. The team instead learns deformation from data, guided by biomechanics and by prompts the surgeon can give during the case. The model aims to track large shape changes in real time. Reliable bending overlays could make image-guided surgery trustworthy in the soft-tissue cases where it is needed most.
arxiv-2506-08348:
Wenhan Yao, Fen Xiao, Xiarun Chen, Jia Liu, YongQiang He, and Weiping Wen present Pureformer-VC in a 2025 paper on voice conversion. The task swaps the tone of any voice into any other voice for speech tools. Past contest based methods struggle to split speech parts cleanly and rebuild them in a natural way.

Their encoder uses conformer blocks to split content, style, and speaker traits apart. A decoder built from zipformer blocks then restyles the speech toward the target voice. Training leans on a variational split plus a triplet test that sharpens speaker gaps. A style transfer step with shared weights lifts decoder quality further. Tests on two multi speaker sets match top subjective scores with better hard metrics.
arxiv-2506-08448:
Hyakka Nakada and Shu Tanaka work in 2025 on how to recast hard choice problems into a form that quantum annealers can solve. Those machines handle problems written with yes or no choices and pair terms only. Real problems in machine learning often have higher order terms and dense links, which the standard recasting tricks cannot handle.

The pair model the target with sums of a simple bent line function. That form can mimic any curve, and it also has an exact match in the pair term form the machines need. They prove the match holds and set out a step by step build. A clear, general route from messy problems to machine ready form would widen what quantum annealers can be tried on. The paper gives the math base for such a route.
arxiv-2506-08748:
Ivo Mihov and Nikolay Vitanov craft light pulses that widen a quantum transition's response far beyond the usual limit, in a 2025 paper. Driving a two-state system harder normally broadens its spectral line; smooth pulses broaden it less, and one exotic shape even narrows it. That narrowing wins headlines, but some jobs want the opposite: fat lines ease off-resonance excitation.

The pair present two families of pulse shapes whose broadening outruns even the rectangular pulse at equal energy. Runs on IBM's quantum hardware back the designs. Deliberately sloppy excitation becomes a tool where precision is the enemy. The catalog of pulse shapes now spans narrowing, tame broadening, and this superbroadening.
arxiv-2506-08948:
Alessandro Fregosi and co-authors measure how a thulium-doped ceramic behaves as a laser material at two microns. Such lasers serve medicine and sensing, and a quirk called cross-relaxation can nearly double their efficiency. The team built a three-mirror folded cavity and timed how the ceramic absorbs pump light and emits laser light.

The laser reached a slope efficiency of 73 percent, a figure that let the team extract the cross-relaxation strength. Rate equations modeled the system under steady and pulsed pumping, and their solutions matched the lab readings closely. The fitted cross-relaxation value matched the measured one, showing the effect runs near its theoretical best. The work certifies the ceramic as a sound laser medium.
arxiv-2506-09048:
Yuxin Dong and co-authors ask what a task vector really is, inside a language model that learns from examples in its prompt. Task vectors compress a demonstrated task into one internal representation that can be reused, speeding inference. Why they emerge, and where they fail, was unclear.

The authors propose the Linear Combination Conjecture: a task vector acts like a single demonstration blended linearly from the originals. In linear transformers trained on triplet prompts, the vectors emerge exactly as the conjecture predicts. It also forecasts failure on mappings of high rank, which tests on real models confirm. Saliency checks and parameter pictures round out a rare case of a mechanism understood, not just observed.
arxiv-2506-09448:
A research team adds dynamic vocabulary to an open speech recognition model so it stops fumbling rare words, in a 2025 paper. Whisper-style foundation models transcribe general speech well but miss names and terms absent from training. Contextual biasing fixes this by hinting likely words, yet most biasing methods train from scratch and lose the foundation model's knowledge.

The team bolted an existing biasing method onto OWSM version 3.1 with the model's weights frozen. Training needed only a small dataset because the base knowledge stayed intact. On a standard LibriSpeech test set, errors on the biased words fell by nearly twelve points. Overall word error rate improved by about a point too. The system also ran slightly faster than the unbiased baseline. The authors present the recipe as a cheap upgrade path for open speech models.
arxiv-2506-09648:
Mattia Rosso and colleagues hunted for scaling laws for uncertainty in deep learning in a 2025 paper. It is well known that accuracy improves predictably as data and model size grow. Whether a model's uncertainty, its own sense of how unsure it is, follows similar tidy laws was unknown, especially for today's huge over-parameterized networks where classic guarantees break down.

Across vision and language tasks, the team measured several uncertainty estimates from approximate Bayesian methods and ensembles. Tidy scaling patterns did appear, both for familiar test data and for shifted data, as dataset and model sizes varied. Such laws let builders forecast how much data a target confidence level needs, instead of discovering it by expensive trial.
arxiv-2506-09848:
Khatua and co-authors examine a cobalt compound whose atoms form a honeycomb, hunting for exotic magnetic behaviour, in a 2025 physics paper. Honeycomb magnets are prized because competing forces on few neighbours can melt magnetic order into a liquid-like state. Most work uses a smaller spin; this compound's cobalt ions carry a larger spin, three halves, which opens a different route to the same physics. The crystal has no mixed-up atom sites to muddy the picture.

Heat and magnetisation data showed a sharp kink near fifty-five degrees above absolute zero's minus range, marking the onset of long-range order. Neutron beams mapped the order, and muon probes felt the local fields inside. Both fixed and flickering fields coexisted, the authors report. Computer calculations of the electron structure round out a portrait of a magnet that orders yet keeps moving.
arxiv-2506-10148:
Panagiotis Batakidis and Ioannis Gkeneralis present a 2025 mathematics paper building a quaternionic version of toric geometry. Toric geometry studies spaces with many circle symmetries; here the circles are replaced by quaternionic spheres, acting on spaces of dimension a multiple of four. The authors work out when such local symmetries can exist and how to classify them.

Two invariants do the classifying: a combinatorial characteristic pair and a cohomological Euler class, which together pin down the action up to homeomorphism. The team also imports a class of fibrations into this setting and proves a quaternionic Arnold-Liouville theorem for them. Orbit spaces turn out to be special affine manifolds with corners, classified by a quaternionic analogue of the classic Delzant theorem.
arxiv-2506-10848:
Qingyan Wei and colleagues speed up diffusion language models with staged sampling, in work from 2025. Diffusion models write many tokens in parallel, which cuts delay versus word by word models. Fixed sampling plans waste that edge by treating each step the same way through the run.

Their SlowFast plan swaps between explore and speed stages as the text forms. Three rules guide when and where tokens can lock in with trust. A cache link cuts repeat compute across steps for extra speed gains. Tests reached over fifteen fold speed up on one model with tiny score loss. Cache pairing pushed gains far higher and beat a strong classic model on flow.
arxiv-2506-11648:
Hiroya Watanabe, Hiroaki Kusuno, and Yoshiyuki Tagawa showed in 2025 that a container's converging shape speeds an impact-driven liquid jet; the catalog title appends a journal name. Dropping a partly filled container makes a focused jet shoot from the surface, a classic classroom effect. Whether narrowing walls boost the jet was open.

In a flask-shaped container the jet ran up to about one point six times faster than in a straight test tube at the same impact speed. Solving for the pressure impulse field matched the measured surface speeds. The boost comes from how narrowing changes flow rate and the impulse gradient along the axis. Uses range from ejecting thick liquids to needle-free injection.
arxiv-2506-12148:
Chiara Di Bonaventura and colleagues argue that fixed test sets give a false picture of how well models detect hate speech, because abusive language keeps changing. Slang shifts, words gain or lose hostile meanings, and reclaimed terms move between groups. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team ran two experiments in which hate speech data evolved over time. They tested a wide set of language models under both the usual fixed benchmark style and a time-aware style that respects when each example was written.

Scores from the two styles did not line up. Models that looked strong on the fixed tests could look weaker once timing was honored, and the ranking of models shifted. The authors call for benchmarks that are rebuilt around time, so safety claims about hate speech detection rest on language as it is used now, not as it was used years earlier.
arxiv-2506-12248:
Jennifer Grannen, Siddharth Karamcheti, Blake Wulfe, and Dorsa Sadigh present ProVox, a framework for robots that work with people, in a research paper from 2025. Partner robots must learn a person's goals and tastes fast. In shared settings, people can also teach robots new skills and concepts as they work, so the robot should plan ahead rather than wait.

ProVox lets users state preferences and expected behavior before physical work starts. A language model planner, shaped by that profile, guesses intent from context and robot skills. It then suggests helpful actions early. The design aims to cut the burden on the user. Tests probe how well the robot personalizes its help.
arxiv-2506-12648:
Curtis Fox, Aaron Mishkin, Sharan Vaswani, and Mark Schmidt study, in a 2025 paper, how the smoothness of a problem shapes the speed of simple search methods. Most theory uses one global smoothness value, yet real problems have calm regions where bigger steps are safe. Many local rules have been tried, but their rates are hard to compare across methods.

The authors offer a simple joint view of global and local smoothness that depends only on the problem itself. Under that view, line search clearly beats fixed step sizes. In some cases plain descent with line search even beats faster fixed-step methods. Gains also appear for several other step rules and for random and coordinate methods.
arxiv-2506-12748:
Cotăescu wrote this work in two thousand twenty-five, on Dirac's theory with mass and an axial chemical potential. The Dirac equation tells how massive fermions act. He solves the equation in full, with no rough guess work.

From the solve, he gets the mode spinors and the projection operators, which give the spectral form of the main conserved operators. He sets out the odd partner of the Pryce spin operator for the first time. With the rest, it sets the spin and polarization operators for a particle and its antiparticle, in the free case and with the potential in place. When he quantizes both cases, he gets two distinct operator algebras. In them, those tools take canonical forms. He can then build statistical operators, each kind with its own vortical chemical potential.
arxiv-2506-12848:
Tiny, fleeting hand movements can betray feelings people hide, and Hao Xu and co-authors present their entry to a 2025 challenge on reading them. Micro-gestures are subtle, brief, and small in range, which makes them hard to spot in skeleton tracking data. The team starts from a known video model that turns poses into three-dimensional heat maps.

Three upgrades follow. A topology-aware skeleton layout fits the challenge dataset and captures finer motion. A revised time processing step smooths the motion record. Word embeddings of the gesture labels add extra supervision that helps the model generalize. The system reached about sixty-seven percent top accuracy on the hidden test set, ranking third on the official board.
arxiv-2506-13148:
Ryszard Staruch and co-authors adapt large language models to fix grammar with the smallest possible edits, in this 2025 paper. Decoder models shine at fluent rewrites but overshoot when teachers want minimal change. The adaptation problem was little explored.

A new training schedule attuned to error rates lifts the models' minimal-edit skill. Their system set a state-of-the-art single-model score on the standard BEA test. The team also detokenized the common training sets to look like natural writing, and found errors lurking in them. Training on the cleaned data changed results measurably. Code is released for replication.
arxiv-2506-13348:
Mae Younes and Adnane Boukhayma render shiny surfaces better in twenty twenty-five. Gaussian splatting produces new views of a scene fast and well. Reflective scenes remain hard, because mirror-like surfaces create sharp, high-frequency highlights. Inverse rendering in such settings strains the standard representation.

Their method, TextureSplat, gives each Gaussian primitive its own texture map. Normals and material properties vary across the primitive's local space. That extra representation power targets exactly the specular detail that breaks simpler models. A unified material texture atlas lets the graphics hardware accelerate rendering at test time. The approach is geometrically and physically grounded. Readers in computer graphics get splatting that can handle the chrome and glass of real rooms.
arxiv-2506-13648:
Wouter Schuttert, Mohammed Iqbal Abdul Rasheed, and Bojana Rosic present neural networks that respect the curved geometry of material property tensors, in a 2025 paper. Traits such as heat conduction in composites vary due to material mix and manufacturing. These traits are modeled as tensors that live on a curved space.

A stochastic treatment must keep both the tensor structure and spatial symmetries. Splitting tensors into strength and orientation parts parameterizes uncertainty. That uncertainty must then pass through a physics model, which needs a fast surrogate. Standard networks break the geometry, so the authors design manifold-aware ones. The work targets reliable forecasts of composite behavior.
arxiv-2506-13748: Maya Thompson, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, shows that a graph count for surfaces can be built up from near-tree parts. The count is a polynomial tied to graphs drawn on surfaces, in pure math. She uses step rules that cut or shrink one edge at a time, for a broad form of the count on pseudo-surfaces. With those rules she proves the near-tree form. Past counts of the same kind then fall out of her main result as special cases.
arxiv-2506-14048:
Madox McGrae-Menge, Jacob Pierce, Frederico Fiuza, and Paulo Alves show how to teach machine-learned plasma models to respect basic physical symmetries. Their paper came out in 2025. Plasma is hot ionized gas, and its full behavior is expensive to simulate, so researchers build smaller learned models from simulation data.

Their trick is data augmentation: they expand the training data with transformed copies that obey known symmetries, such as changes of reference frame. Models trained on the enriched data recovered the correct fluid equations and pressure closures more accurately. The approach also removed false patterns tied to one particular frame and needed less data overall. It beat both unaugmented learned models and standard theoretical closures on simulations of magnetic reconnection.
arxiv-2506-14148:
Long-Vu Hoang, Tuan Nguyen, and Tran Huy Dat show that sound scattered off an object can reveal what the object is, without touching or photographing it, in a 2025 paper. When a sound wave hits an object, the echo carries traces of its shape and material. Their case study is hair: judging its type and moisture from echoes off a head with a hair sample.

They compared four learning strategies, from fully supervised networks to fine-tuned foundation models. The best, a self-supervised model tuned end to end, reached nearly ninety percent accuracy. Because no camera is involved, the method protects privacy and works in the dark. The authors see wide potential wherever inspection now depends on images, from personal care to industry.
arxiv-2506-14948:
Mohna Chakraborty, Lu Wang, and David Jurgens build a framework for testing how language models reason about moral choices. Models are now used in settings that demand moral judgment, yet their reasoning often stays shallow and drifts from human values. The authors ask whether giving models an explicit moral structure improves their decisions.

They benchmarked twelve open models on four moral datasets, using prompts grounded in value systems, ethical theories, and thinking strategies. Reasoning with structure beat answering directly, in both accuracy and coherence. Prompts built on first principles and on a scaffold joining Schwartz's values with care ethics gave the strongest gains. The team also showed that a large model's moral skill can be distilled into a small model through training, with no added cost when the small model runs. They present the framework as a scalable path toward models whose moral reasoning people can inspect and trust.
arxiv-2506-15148:
Scoring a tracker that follows many moving objects is harder when the tracker also admits its own doubt. Yuxuan Xia and co-authors generalize a leading score for that case in this 2025 paper. Their metric charges separately for location error, doubt mismatch on found objects, missed objects, false alarms, and identity switches.

The score rests on the older GOSPA family and keeps its readable break-down of costs. Computing it exactly is an assignment problem, and a relaxed version still counts as a true metric while running in polynomial time. Simulations show the score behaves as intended across tracking scenes. The authors pitch it for radar and surveillance systems that report uncertainty, which most modern trackers now do.
arxiv-2506-15248:
Hamant Kumar and Neeraj Kumar Tomar introduce a new space property in topology in this 2025 paper. Building on Q-star closed sets, they define Q-star normality, a weaker form of the classic normality property for topological spaces.

The paper then uses a second family of sets, Q-star-g closed sets, to characterize both the new spaces and classic normal spaces. Preservation theorems follow, showing which constructions keep the new property when spaces are mapped or combined. Work of this kind refines the ladder of separation properties in topology, giving mathematicians finer tools to sort spaces that classic terms lump together.
arxiv-2506-15348:
Benjamin Enriquez and Khalef Yaddaden recast a deep algebra theory in category terms in 2025. Double shuffle theory links two ways of multiplying special values in math. A geometric approach by Deligne and Terasoma frames those links through harmonic products. The authors seek a cleaner base for that construction.

They define a bimodule that carries a factorization structure. Such a structure is shown to yield an algebra map on its own. Both harmonic products of the theory then fall out of the frame. A categorical base may make a hard theory easier to extend and teach.
arxiv-2506-15548:
Junyan Jiang and co-authors unify music tasks by treating labels as music itself. A chord chart, after all, can be written as notes. Their 2025 paper frames both understanding and generation as music-for-music sequence modeling: chord reading in, melody out, and so on.

The design runs two pretrained language models, one for the source music and one for the target. A light adapter links them, so the heavy models stay frozen. Across chord recognition, melody generation, and drum track generation, the method beat task-built rivals. Code, demos, and weights are public. Music AI readers get a cheap way to turn one strong model into many music skills.
arxiv-2506-15948:
Connor Ding and co-authors examined in 2025 the tension between information and computing cost in modern compression methods that use non-linear transforms. They compare two image approaches: neural fields that store a scene in network weights, and splatting methods that fit many simple blobs. Each wins on different axes, from compactness to speed and readability.

A textual transform they introduce compresses images to extremely low bitrates while pleasing human viewers, and doubles as a denoiser. A final contribution upgrades a classic universal compressor so whole families of methods inherit its guarantees. The authors argue these trade-offs reach beyond compression into classification and generative AI. The work maps how to balance resources against performance when data must shrink.
arxiv-2506-16048:
Kang, Desai, Jia, and Lucia present WAMI, a compiler path that turns MLIR programs into WebAssembly without flattening away high-level structure. WebAssembly keeps gaining features such as garbage collection and stack switching, but most compilers lower programs to a low-level form first and lose the chance to use them. MLIR keeps several levels of abstraction, yet its WebAssembly output has relied on the LLVM backend and inherited its limits.

WAMI adds WebAssembly dialects inside MLIR that mirror the high-level features directly, so code generation stays modular and each language front end need not redo the work. A case study uses stack switching to show the flexibility. On standard benchmarks the generated code ran at most 7.7 percent slower than LLVM-based output, and faster in some settings.
arxiv-2506-16148:
Monalisa Dubey and twelve co-authors present a close study of a Type IIP supernova in this 2025 paper. The star, SN 2018pq, exploded at the edge of the galaxy IC 3896A, and the team tracked it with fast cadence brightness measures and low resolution spectra.

Its bright plateau phase lasted about ninety-seven days, a normal span for its class, and its brightness sat in the normal range. The fall from plateau to the late phase ran steeper than usual. Spectral modeling with a radiative transfer code showed a normal Type IIP event. Light curve fits point to a red supergiant parent star, though two methods disagree on its mass, one giving about eleven solar masses and the other fourteen to sixteen.
arxiv-2506-16248:
Michael Foltýn and co-authors study light play in single bismuth particles in a 2025 paper. Bismuth bits have drawn note for heat and light driven chemistry uses. The team made round particles across a wide size range and read their build and optics one particle at a time with electron microscopy.

Each particle held local surface plasmon resonances, the light modes that make metal bits shine and heat. Changing size slid those modes from near infrared up to ultraviolet light. The modes stayed stable across that whole span. With low cost, body safety, and rust resistance, bismuth looks fit for large scale plasmonic work.
arxiv-2506-16348:
Cedric Möller and Ricardo Usbeck extract structured facts from text with a lean, old-fashioned strategy that beats giant generative models, in this 2025 paper. Closed information extraction reads a sentence and returns triples, subject, relation, object, drawn strictly from a known catalog of entities and relations. At full scale the catalog holds millions of entities and hundreds of relations, so guessing freely is hopeless.

Their system, DISCIE, takes the discriminative route: it classifies and links, using the types of the entities involved as a strong hint about which relations are plausible. That type information lifts accuracy most on rare, long-tail relations, the usual failure zone. Running smaller models, DISCIE matched or beat far larger generative systems while costing less to operate. The lesson for builders of knowledge bases is unfashionable and useful: constraints, well used, outperform size.
arxiv-2506-16448:
A home-grade brain wave emotion reader is built by Tri Duc Ly and Gia Ngo in a 2025 arXiv paper. Dry sensors and cheap headsets now put EEG in homes. Their net reads feeling scores on three axes: pleasantness, arousal, and control feel. Kernels at many scales pull traits from the wave stream. One new kernel learns from four brain zones at once.

The model beat a known past best, TSception, across score gauges. Runs stayed steady across repeats of the tests. Home emotion tools gain a stronger core from the design.
arxiv-2506-16548:
Arjun Dosajh and Mihika Sanghi test a method for making a language model forget sensitive facts, in work from 2025. Large language models can memorise training text, which raises privacy and copyright risks. Erasing set facts after training is hard because the models answer in open-ended ways.

The pair applied an adaptive method that steers the model's inner states away from the facts to be forgotten. They tested which layers of the model respond best to the erasure. Their entry placed fourth on the contest board for both a small and a larger model size. The work was part of a shared task on unlearning factual knowledge. Such methods could help model owners remove private data without full retraining.
arxiv-2506-16748:
Arjo Chakravarty, Michael Grey, Viraj Muthugala, and Mohan Rajesh Elara plan paths for crowds of robots moving in open space. Steering hundreds of agents without collisions is a known hard problem: exact methods stall beyond a few dozen robots, while grid-bound methods behave poorly in continuous space.

Their framework starts from a fast rule-based planner and then polishes the routes with a safety-aware smoothing step that shortcuts bends the way a pulled string straightens. A backup solver based on safe time intervals repairs any collisions the smoothing creates. In tests with more than five hundred agents, the method ran in real time and produced routes close to the best known lengths. The authors offer it as a building block for warehouse and swarm robotics.
arxiv-2506-16948:
Aashaq Shah, Thomas Adolphus, Yingchang Zhang, and Oleg Brandt test greener gases for particle detectors. Resistive plate chambers track particles in physics labs, but their standard gases warm the planet strongly. The ANUBIS experiment will run a large gas volume, so its footprint matters. The team ran small chamber prototypes with a one-millimeter gap on varied gas mixes.

Current draw and detection efficiency were logged for standard and altered mixes. The goal was to hold detector performance while cutting climate harm. Low-impact mixes are cast as a workable near-term swap, with fully green gases as the long goal. Results also serve large chamber systems at other collider labs and beyond.
arxiv-2506-17048:
Noël Hallemans and co-authors review how battery factories could control electrode making in real time, in a 2025 paper. Electrodes are among the costliest parts of a lithium-ion battery, yet plants still set conditions mostly by trial and error. Once a recipe is fixed, the line is rarely steered as a whole to hold it.

Drawing on methods used in other film and sheet industries, the authors map where sensors and feedback loops could help. Live control could cut cost, waste, and carbon output while raising yield and speed. They also lay out the hard parts, such as measuring wet coatings fast enough to act.
