The paper serves as a guide for makers who want smarter, steadier production lines.
arxiv-2506-17148:
John Anderson, Sanchit Chaturvedi, and Cole Graham study shock formation in one dimensional flow laws in this 2025 paper. Conservation laws govern things like traffic and gas flow. Smooth waves can steepen over time until a shock forms, where values jump sharply. The authors ask whether that process is stable under small changes.

They show that waves close to a shocking simple wave still form a shock nearby. The shock appears at a close place and time. They also describe the edge of the region where the smooth solution exists. The exact form of a typical shock is given with a precise expansion. A companion paper uses these results to study what happens as viscosity fades to zero.
arxiv-2506-17248:
Zequn Yang, Hongfa Wang, and Di Hu build a fast way to measure how different data types interact inside a multimodal system, in a 2025 paper. A photo and its caption, for instance, may repeat each other, add unique facts, or combine into something new. Knowing which is true, for each single sample, helps engineers improve such systems.

Their estimator, LSMI, rests on pointwise information theory. It first measures the most tractable interaction, redundancy, then extends to the rest with an efficient entropy method. Tests on fake and real data check its accuracy and speed. Uses include sorting samples and guiding how models teach each other.
arxiv-2506-17748:
Chatterjee, Goel, and Chakraborty present HIDE, a fast way to catch language models making things up, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Models often state falsehoods in a confident tone, and checking several answers per question is slow and costly.

Their idea is that a hallucination shows up inside the model as a split between how it represents the question and how it represents its own answer. They measure that split with a statistical independence test applied to the model's hidden states during a single generation, needing no extra training. Across four question answering sets and six open models, HIDE beat other single-pass detectors by about twenty-nine percent on average and rivaled slower multi-pass methods. The tool could make chatbots safer to deploy.
arxiv-2506-18148:
Diyam Akra, Tymaa Hammouda, and Mustafa Jarrar present QuranMorph, a word-by-word morphological annotation of the full Quran checked by human experts. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Arabic language technology needs gold-standard texts, and the Quran is a central one. Automated tagging risks errors that careful handwork avoids.

Three expert linguists tagged every token, over seventy-seven thousand in all. Each word got its dictionary base form from a large linked Arabic lexicon. Fine-grained part-of-speech labels came from a forty-tag scheme. The rich annotation lets the corpus link outward to many language resources. Base forms connect verses to dictionaries covering millions of tokens. The corpus is open and public through a university lab site. It serves both language engineers and scholars of the text.
arxiv-2506-18448:
Quang Nguyen and co-authors build a team of AI agents that finds grasps from spoken requests in a 2025 paper. Telling a robot 'pick up the red mug behind the box' is easy for people and hard for software, especially in clutter with no task-specific training.

Their system, GraspMAS, splits the job among three agents. A planner breaks down the request, a coder writes and runs vision code, and an observer judges the outcome and sends feedback for another pass. On two large data sets the team beat prior language-driven grasp methods without any fine-tuning. Tests on simulated and real robots confirmed the approach works off the page.
arxiv-2506-18548:
Jingwei Kang and co-authors rebuild the theory of click models for the carousel interfaces that now fill search and shopping apps. Click models predict which results a user will examine and choose, and the standard taxonomy grew up around single ranked lists and older graphical models. Neural click models and grid or carousel layouts do not fit that scheme. Their 2025 paper proposes a new foundation.

The authors name three fundamental design choices, stated as mathematical properties, that fix which statistical patterns, and so which user behaviors, a model can express. Every known click model, graphical or neural, for lists, grids, or carousels, can be placed by those choices in one taxonomy. The scheme also shows designers which behavior a planned model could never capture before they build it. The authors offer it as the base for the next generation of click models.
arxiv-2506-18748:
Uslu, NaderiAlizadeh, Eisen, and Ribeiro wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with given names shown in fuller form in its text. It speeds learned resource sharing in multi-user wireless networks by smart starts for the dual values.

State-augmented graph nets can learn sharing policies that beat the old dual climb, by treating the dual values as live inputs. The catch is slow settling at run time. A second graph net learns to guess near-best dual starts from past runs. Training also samples dual values from the real descent path, which sharpens the main net. On a power control case the full scheme wins by a wide margin in tests. A convergence proof and a strong bound on bad luck excursions close the paper.
arxiv-2506-18948:
Dakang Cen, Zhiyuan Li, and Wenlong Zhang work on backward problems for fractional wave equations in a 2025 paper. The task is to rebuild the starting state of a wave from its final state, a notoriously unstable job. Real sensors also give only scattered point readings clouded by random noise.

Their numerical frame runs on uneven time grids and assumes little smoothness in the solution. A regularization step tames the noise from scattered points. Error bounds balance grid error, noise level, and point count, and they guide an up front choice of the tuning value. Test runs show the method recovers the start state with good accuracy. The work serves sensing tasks in imaging and geophysics.
arxiv-2506-19448:
Udit Raj, Slobodan Maletić, and Sudeepto Bhattacharya present a 2025 study of group links in plain networks through a shape lens. Most network math stops at pairs, yet real systems meet in threes and more. The team lift a bare link web into a clique complex, where full groups become blocks. On that lift they build a strength-weighted table of block neighbors. Two gauges follow: a global hub score for blocks and a local degree score.

A layering process then grows the complex step by step, and persistent homology reads which shapes survive the growth. All gauges fall back to the classic ones when blocks are mere edges. Ecology and cell webs, rich in group acts, are the target fields.
arxiv-2506-19648:
Fernando Miguelez, Urtzi Ayesta, Josu Doncel, and Maria Dolores Ugarte study how fresh data are in queue systems. Their 2025 paper uses the Age of Information, a score for staleness. Most past work assumes packets arrive with zero age. In real networks, packets often wait before they even enter the system under study.

They derive a formula for average age when packets start with some age. It equals the standard age plus a fix term tied to how packet age links with gaps between departures. If those are unrelated, the fix is just the mean starting age. When the link is unknown, they give firm bounds. Tests cover forwarding, tandem, and retrial queues, plus a chain of queues not solved before.
arxiv-2506-19748:
Aman Pandey and Chanchal Kundu build new math tools in a twenty twenty-five paper. Their topic is fractional inaccuracy, a way to measure how far a guess sits from the truth. They extend that idea to cases with many variables at once. To do so, they use copulas, which are tools that capture how variables move together.

The authors define two new measures, one based on plain copulas and one on survival copulas. They set bounds for these measures and study how they act under known orderings. They then define two more forms from related copula types and check like properties. Readers in statistics get a single frame that joins several earlier ideas.
arxiv-2506-19848:
Long Xing and co-authors present ScaleCap in a 2025 paper, a captioning scheme that grows richer as more compute is spent. Big vision language models skew detail, lavishing some image parts and skimming others. They also invent objects that are not there, a language side bias.

Two parts fight those biases as the caption builds line by line. A question engine asks image specific questions and folds the answers into the text. A contrastive rater then weeds out invented lines at the sentence level. More budget means more questions, so detail grows in a balanced way. Alignment tests back the gains, and 450,000 images were captioned in the scale run.
arxiv-2506-19948:
V Vanlaer and co-authors listen to a massive star's vibrations to weigh how fast its core spins compared with its surface, in a 2025 study. The twelve-sun pulsator HD 192575 shows split frequency multiplets whose asymmetries encode rotation and structure. Fresh TESS observations sharpened the frequencies, and the team remodeled the star and inverted the symmetric splittings for its spin profile.

Nearly every acceptable profile spun slower than four-tenths of a cycle per day, with the core turning less than twice as fast as the envelope, a mild difference. Matching the observed asymmetries proved fussy, depending heavily on which modes were which. The authors call the work the first detailed rotation inversion for this class of star.
arxiv-2506-20048:
Sungee Hong and co-authors lay down principles for evaluating whole return distributions of policies from offline reinforcement learning data. Judging a policy by its average return hides its risks. Distributional evaluation promises a fuller picture instead.

The classic fitted evaluation method needed a distributional upgrade. Few such methods existed and none shared a framework. The authors state guiding principles for building them soundly. Several new methods follow, each with convergence backing. Older methods gain theoretical justification in the same frame. Simulations include control tasks and Atari games. The new methods beat rivals across the tests. The work serves safe policy screening from stored play logs.
arxiv-2506-20448:
Tom Oosterloo and co-authors watch a young radio galaxy's jets stir the cold gas around it in a 2025 paper. The galaxy, PKS 0023-26, hosts a bright active nucleus and wide clouds of molecular gas. With the ALMA telescope array, the team mapped carbon monoxide lines across the radio source and beyond. Three line maps together reveal motion, heat, and density.

Gas motion was strongly disturbed only in the central kiloparsec, and mildly near the northern lobe. Yet other scars ran wide. Line ratios along the radio axis showed extreme conditions unlike the calm outer gas. No carbon monoxide signal appeared at the core itself. Gas seemed wrapped around the northern lobe, as if the jet's shock had shredded and pushed clouds aside. The authors note the galaxy hands only a small share of its energy to the gas as motion. The imprint shows instead in gas state and placement.
arxiv-2506-20648:
Vivekanand Mohapatra bounds dark matter annihilation using the universe's dark ages radio signal, in his 2025 arXiv paper. Before the first stars, the hydrogen 21-centimeter line should show a clean absorption dip, free of messy astrophysics. If dark matter particles annihilate, the injected energy heats and ionizes the gas, shrinking or erasing that dip.

Modeling the gas's thermal and ionization history turns the expected signal into a limit on the annihilation rate per unit mass. Even after folding in uncertainties from future moon-based experiments and cosmology, the bound beats space-telescope constraints for light dark matter below about ten giga-electronvolts.
arxiv-2506-21048:
Salvatore Capozziello, Giuseppe Meluccio, and Jonas R Mureika link two ideas about the limits of measurement to black holes in a 2025 paper. Modified uncertainty principles stretch Heisenberg's rule at very small or very large scales. Non-local gravity theories, which smear gravity's action over a region, also change how black holes behave.

The authors argue the modified principles are not free inventions; they arise as effective shadows of non-local gravity. Matching the two views pins down numbers that were free before and yields shared laws for black holes beyond Einstein's theory. Black holes thus become a test bed where quantum limits and gravity meet.
arxiv-2506-21548:
Dmitry Shishkin, Ealeal Bear, and Noam Soker read, in a 2025 paper, the shape of a burst star's husk and the kick of its core. The husk, S147, shows two big ears face to face. Ears most times cone out; these lie flat. The team holds that two jet pairs, close in aim, blew each ear. A line through two bright X-ray zones adds a last axis, for a full point-mirror form. In their tale, jets that made those zones gave a first kick to the neutron star. The ear jets then gave a twin kick. Each ran near 450 kilometers per second, a vast kick.

Such jets could stir gravity waves that today's ears could catch in our Galaxy. The shape dates the husk at 23,000 years.
arxiv-2506-21648:
A large team of researchers offers a 2025 review of system design for planet and deep space missions. The paper gathers ideas for gear that must work far from Earth, where old Earth based fixes often fail. It spans Mars, Titan, small space probes, and rovers, and draws on work from space, electrical, and planet science.

Five areas get close attention. They include Mars position systems with tight accuracy and reef style platforms for the seas of Titan. Other areas are close orbital meeting methods with heat shields and small CubeSat designs for asteroid trips. Power systems for Mars rovers that deal with dust round out the set. The authors present these as paths for future missions.
arxiv-2506-21748:
Liav Hen and co-authors use diffusion models to design metasurfaces, flat optical parts built from tiny structures that steer light. Their 2025 paper attacks inverse design: given the light pattern you want, find the geometry that makes it. That search is hard because structure and optical response relate in a tangled, nonlinear way, and hand tuning gets stuck easily.

A physics simulator first generated training pairs of geometries and their scattering patterns. A conditional diffusion model then learned to propose a structure and height from a target pattern at a chosen wavelength. Once trained, the model designs new parts directly, replacing slow expert search with learned generation for these light-bending surfaces.
arxiv-2506-21848:
Sorting news stories by topic is usually handed to giant neural networks that nobody can inspect. Duo Zhang and Junyi Mo offer LinguaSynth, a transparent alternative that feeds five kinds of language signals into a plain logistic regression. The signals cover word choice, sentence structure, named entities, word meaning, and whole-document meaning, each computed openly.

On the classic twenty-newsgroups benchmark the system reached about eighty-five percent accuracy, beating a strong word-count baseline by over three points. Pulling the features apart showed that structure and entity signals did the disambiguating work that raw word statistics miss. The authors argue the result challenges the assumption that deep black boxes are required for strong text classification, at least where interpretability and low cost matter.
arxiv-2506-21948:
Yichuan Liu and Yingzhou Li present in 2025 a solver for optimization tasks where no slope data are available. Their method, UPOQA, suits problems that split into parts, a common shape in science and engineering. It builds stand-in models for each part from sampled values and searches inside a trust region that respects the split.

Fresh parts of the design include a near projection step, better handling of part sizes, and a search for a good start. On eighty-five standard test problems, the solver needed far fewer costly function calls than rivals. The gain grew when high precision was demanded, and tests on quantum problems confirmed its practical worth.
arxiv-2506-22148:
Joshua Goulton and Milena Radenkovic ask whether Switzerland's trains could carry avalanche warnings to villages the networks cannot reach, in a 2025 paper. Delay tolerant networking ferries data by physical movement, storing and forwarding at each encounter. Disaster zones and high valleys are exactly where such store-carry-forward tricks earn their keep.

The team simulated the entire Swiss rail network as a data mule backbone in a standard opportunistic network simulator. Two classic routing protocols faced off: Epidemic, which floods copies everywhere, and PROPHET, which forwards by predicted contact likelihood. Alerts started either in dense cities or in sparse mountain regions. The rail system delivered robust connectivity in both settings. The authors conclude that national transport infrastructure, already moving on schedule, can double as an emergency communication skeleton for infrastructure-poor terrain.
arxiv-2506-22548:
Alireza Allahyari is the lead author of a 2025 paper that tests a change to general relativity using flickers from black hole systems, with three co-authors named in the byline. The change adds cubic terms for how space curves. Two coupling values set its size, though one term could in principle be removed by redefining fields. Since matter is taken to couple to the metric in the usual frame, both terms stay in play.

The team computed flicker rates for a corrected spinning black hole and compared them with data from a known system. A Bayesian analysis then bounded both coupling values in set ranges. Those bounds are tighter than past limits from the early universe and from the speed of gravity waves. The work shows how steady flicker patterns can probe gravity theory.
arxiv-2506-22748:
Binyamin Stivi, Vishnuu Mallik, Lamberto Dell'Elce, and Aaron Rosengren set out in 2025 to rebuild the paths of old Earth satellites from public tracking data. The records are rough and have long gaps, so long-range forecasts often drift. They aimed to recover a starting state that stays true to the physics over decades.

Their method smooths the orbital values, sorts them into groups, and keeps only a set that hangs together well. That filtered set yields a starting state with far better forecasts than raw records give. They tested it on a satellite launched in the nineteen sixties into a high orbit. The rebuilt path matched its fall back to Earth in 2020 within a day.
arxiv-2506-23148:
Shuzhen Lv and Philip Zhang count patterns in permutations and find that many different-looking arrangements occur equally often, in this 2025 paper. A permutation is an ordering of numbers. A mesh pattern decorates a small pattern, here the orders 123 and 132, with shading rules. Those rules forbid extra points in certain regions of the diagram. Two patterns are equidistributed if, across all permutations, they appear the same number of times.

For shadings arranged with a particular mirrored symmetry, 126 joint equidistributions were conceivable and earlier work had settled most of a simpler family. Lv and Zhang prove 112 of the 126, using clever one-to-one correspondences, recurrences, and generating functions. Along the way they bank 562 further results for other shading styles. Several distributions turn out to be counted by the unsigned Stirling numbers, an old sequence from a different corner of combinatorics.
arxiv-2506-23448:
Teruyuki Kitabayashi and Aya Shimizu present a 2025 cosmology paper completing the test kit for a class of inflation models. Warm inflation keeps the early universe bathed in radiation while it expands. Judging such models needs three numbers from the infant sky, and the third, the running of the spectral index, had only rough formulas before.

The authors derive an exact general expression for that running in warm inflation, with no approximations. They then apply it to warm natural inflation, a version tied to a particle physics favorite. The new number sharpens the lower bound on that model's symmetry-breaking scale. With all three sky numbers in hand, the model can be fairly weighed against telescope data. The formula also serves other warm variants.
arxiv-2506-23648:
Zhe Liu and co-authors built MReg in 2025, a model that grades a leaking heart valve from ultrasound video. Color Doppler scans are a key tool for this diagnosis, but grades can depend on the user. Past smart tools did not match clinic workflow well.

The model treats grading as a regression task, since the grades form an ordered scale. A feature step copies how a sonographer reasons, picking out and boosting the telling signals. A mixture-of-experts module then sums features by grade level. Trained on nearly nineteen hundred in-house cases with three grades, MReg beat both weakly guided video tools and standard classifiers. Code was released with the study.
arxiv-2506-23748:
Nam Anh Nguyen and Arnold Reusken analyze the error of a computer method for a heat-like flow that moves maps between curved spaces, in a 2025 paper. The head describes the case as corotational, where the map spins with the flow. Such flows model liquid crystals and other materials whose local direction evolves over time.

Their scheme uses standard finite elements in space and a semi-implicit step in time, leaving a linear problem to solve at each step. For smooth solutions they prove the best possible error rates, leaning on an energy bound that mirrors the true flow's energy loss. Computer tests confirm the theory. The work gives users of this scheme a firm sense of its accuracy.
arxiv-2506-23848:
Quentin Labriet and Loic Poulain d'Andecy present a 2025 math paper on a quantum group. The group is a deformed version of a classic matrix group. The authors study operators that link representations of the group. Such operators are the tools that split or join symmetry spaces. Their formulas use a family of special polynomials tied to the deformed setting.

One set of operators, called holographic, is written through those polynomials. The dual set gives a deformed form of classic Rankin-Cohen operators. The modules are built on polynomial spaces, with a twist: the variables do not commute. Links to joining coefficients are given through a second polynomial family. Algebra readers get explicit formulas where past work often stays abstract. Explicit forms let others compute with the operators rather than just prove they exist.
arxiv-2507-00048:
Thomas Deucher and co-authors build a shared digital twin for self-driving labs in a 2025 paper. Machine learning guides automated experiments at several research sites at once. Shared data standards let those separate labs help each other learn faster.

The twin runs on an online simulation platform with FAIR data handling throughout. FAIR means data stay findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable for all partners. Dispersed teams run their own optimization tasks independently on their own equipment. Raw results flow into one central database shared by the group. Shared analysis tools and models then improve for everyone who contributes. Readers see how labs can pool data without pooling their benches.
arxiv-2507-00148:
Deepu Benson and five co-authors study how hard Boolean functions get when inputs may be unknown. Each query can answer zero, one, or unknown, and the output may be unknown only when the revealed bits cannot settle it. That hazard-free extension mirrors parallel hardware that must not guess. The team proves an analogue of Huang's sensitivity theorem inside this model.

Deterministic query cost of the extension is at most quadratic in its randomized cost and quartic in its quantum cost, beating the best bounds for plain Boolean functions. An exponential gap in decision tree size also appears. General conversion methods from plain trees to hazard-free ones are shown optimal.
arxiv-2507-00348:
Guldemir, Olukoya, and Martínez-del-Rincón proposed a defense in twenty twenty-five against a quiet problem in malware detection: malware families change over time, and entirely new ones appear. A detector trained on yesterday's families can miss tomorrow's.

Their method trains an autoencoder, a network that squeezes data into a compact code, using a triplet rule that pulls same-family samples together and pushes others apart. A clustering step then groups the codes, and samples that land outside every known cluster stand out as possible new families. The team tested the approach on Android malware and on Windows program files. It improved the detection of new families over earlier methods on both sets. The authors present it as a practical way to keep detectors honest in a threat landscape that never sits still.
arxiv-2507-01048:
Ricardo Vargas and co-authors describe version two of a public data set of oil well events in 2025, using team framing for a long author list. Bad events in wells can cause losses, spills, and deaths. Early detection with machine learning has proved its worth. The first version came from Petrobras in 2019, due to a lack of public data.

The set holds time series data labeled by experts. It has grown through joint work and is a base reference in the field. The new version changes the structure and adds more labeled cases. The article details the set so new users can join the effort. The aim is earlier detection that allows fixes in time.
arxiv-2507-01248:
Tianxiong Zhao, Daisuke Noto, Xia Li, Tomás Trewhela, and Hugo Ulloa test the rules that describe how grains of mixed sizes sort themselves in flowing sand-like material, in a 2025 paper. When a mix of big and small grains is sheared, the sizes separate, and formulas link the sorting speed to the local flow. Those formulas were built on simpler tests with steady shear, leaving their reach in doubt.

Using computer simulations that track each grain, the team sheared mixtures across a wide range of rates. The known scaling held only in a middle band of flow strength. It broke down both in slow, near-still flow and in fast, crash-heavy flow. As a result, standard flow models predicted the wrong sorting speeds there. The authors argue that broader laws are needed to cover sorting across all these regimes.
arxiv-2507-01448:
Arnd Behring, Kirill Melnikov, Ivan Novikov, and Giulia Zanderighi refine Higgs boson predictions in 2025. A tight cut on jet energy had seemed to cause huge corrections in one Higgs production mode. That raised doubts about how well theory could predict the rate.

The authors show the corrections come from soft, near-parallel radiation, which a shower model handles well. They merge that shower treatment of the Higgs decay with high-order corrections to production. Predictions improved markedly even under the tight cut. Remaining uncertainty, driven by decay modeling, sits at roughly five to seven percent.
arxiv-2507-02048:
Nicolás Bernal, Jacinto Neto, Javier Silva-Malpartida, and Farinaldo Queiroz study light dark matter in a 2025 physics paper. Dark matter may be made of particles far lighter than most searches assume. Their model ties the particles to a force that acts on muons and tau particles but not electrons. The team asks what an early era ruled by matter would change in the picture.

Such an era would alter how many particles froze out in the young universe. The right leftover amount can then come from a wider range of masses and couplings. The authors map the space that future machines could test. Planned projects named in the paper may probe much of that space within years.
arxiv-2507-02148:
Zijie Cai and Christopher Metzler benchmark how well single-image depth estimation works underwater, where the numbers it returns must be true distances. Water attenuates and scatters light, distorts color, and clouds the view, and verified underwater depth data are scarce. Models trained on land data face a steep domain shift.

The team tested leading vision foundation models, zero-shot and fine-tuned, on the real FLSea and SQUID datasets. Large land-trained models performed poorly below the surface. Fine-tuning one model on a synthetic underwater version of an indoor dataset, rendered with a physical image formation model, improved results across every benchmark. The study details where current models fail in the sea.
arxiv-2507-02448:
Si-Pei Wang and Lie-Wen Chen extend a nuclear interaction model in a 2025 paper. The model feeds simulations of heavy-ion collisions and neutron star studies. Their upgrade adds more momentum terms and density terms, which lets the force bend in more flexible ways, including non-monotonic shapes for the symmetry part.

They build several versions tuned to lab data, theory results, and neutron star limits, with set slopes for symmetry energy. The versions then predict matter traits and star sizes for comparison. Readers get tools that may extract the dense matter recipe from collision data with less bias.
arxiv-2507-02648:
Aspen Hopkins, Isabella Struckman, Kevin Klyman, and Susan Silbey sort harms and fixes across AI supply chains, in work from 2025. AI products now come from chains of outside models, data, and tools. Those chains lack the spare parts and clear breaks that let normal supply chains isolate faults fast.

Stakeholders in the chains face growing and varied risks as roles spread wider. The analysis maps who takes part, what harms they face, and where harm starts. Market shape and power gaps shape which fixes stay within reach for each party. Four fix types are named: recourse, repair, reparation, and prevention. A health care case shows how chain position shifts the likely response to harm.
arxiv-2507-03048:
Henzinger and co-authors present a way to watch whether a machine-learned system treats people fairly while it runs, in this 2025 paper. Such systems now make choices about people in many fields, and bias can creep in unseen. Their method works even when the system's inner model is unknown.

The team built a language for stating fairness rules, such as equal treatment across groups. Watcher programs then track a stream of system choices and report a running fairness score after each step. The score comes with a proven error bound that shrinks as more events arrive. A test version shows the approach can run in practice.
arxiv-2507-03248:
Wenhao Lu and co-authors present OpenSN, an open library for emulating low-earth-orbit satellite networks on the ground. Constellations such as Starlink are joining the core of the future internet, and new routing ideas need a fair test bed. Older emulators based on Mininet strain to mimic real distributed software.

Their 2025 paper builds each node as a container, so true routing programs can run inside. The design trims wasted steps when links are made, which lifts speed and lets one machine host more nodes. A key-value store keeps user settings apart from container control, easing new features. The authors argue the mix of speed, scale, and openness makes OpenSN a strong lab tool.
arxiv-2507-03648:
Du and co-authors pull apart a popular way to cut training costs for language models: pruning the training data down to a small, high-value subset. Most pruning methods bundle two choices, how each example is represented and which algorithm picks the subset. The paper varies each part on its own to see which one drives results. Theory and experiments point the same way: better representations, such as training gradients, lead to better subsets under any selection rule.

Selection rules, by contrast, trade wins across settings, and none leads everywhere. The team also finds that rules built for the same stated goal can pick very different examples, which warns against trusting a method's label. For practitioners, the lesson is to spend effort on representations first. The study's value is its clean split, which gives later work a shared way to compare pruning ideas.
arxiv-2507-04148:
Saeed Alaei and four colleagues study refund mechanisms for a single buyer who is unsure what an item is worth, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Buyer and seller share a model of the value, but the buyer learns the truth only after receiving the item. A seller can offer refunds, partial or random, when the buyer is unhappy.

Randomized refund schemes are common in practice, yet the authors focus on deterministic ones. They characterize optimal mechanisms as virtual value maximizers. The characterization covers both continuous and discrete type settings. Using it, plus bounds on menu size complexity, they build efficient algorithms. The algorithms find optimal and near-optimal deterministic mechanisms for sellers.
arxiv-2507-04548:
Renato Cordeiro Ferreira and co-authors tell in a 2025 paper how they built a voice tool that spots low blood oxygen. The state, where blood holds too little oxygen, can creep up in lung ills. Their tool hears it in how a person speaks.

The team built the same design twice, in two runs, and logged what broke each time. Data hunts, training, and live use each taught hard lessons, which the paper sets out in full. Such a log is gold for the next crew that tries voice as a vital sign. Health tech teams gain a frank build tale, flaws and all.
arxiv-2507-04848:
Émilie Charlier, Pierre Popoli, and Michel Rigo build one machine that writes numbers in infinitely many bases in this 2025 paper. Cantor bases write real numbers using a sequence of different bases, a flexible generalization of decimal. Usually the machine depends on the chosen base.

Their approach flips the setup. A single transducer, built for one fixed number, accepts the base sequence as input and outputs the expansion. Under assumptions about the special Pisot numbers inside the base, only a finite part of the machine ever matters. The result unifies computations across a whole family of numeration systems. It deepens the theory linking automata and number systems.
arxiv-2507-05348:
Sumi Kim and co-authors test star blast feedback on small galaxies in a 2025 paper. Giant elliptical galaxies host swarms of small satellite galaxies. How hard dying stars blow back shapes how many satellites form and how they look.

Eleven giant hosts were simulated twice from like starts: once with strong mechanical winds, once with weak heat-only feedback. Hosts barely changed between runs. Satellites split hard: weak feedback made about five times too many mid-size satellites against sky counts. Those extra satellites also sat too compact and metal-poor. The match of the strong-wind run backs firm feedback in galaxy models.
arxiv-2507-05448:
Martin Schüle asks what it means to say a large language model understands words, in a 2025 paper. Systems such as ChatGPT can write and chat in ways that look human, which tempts people to credit them with real grasp of meaning. Critics reply that the systems only juggle patterns, with no true sense behind the words.

Schüle narrows the debate to meaning at the level of single words and full sentences. He looks inside the models at how they store and build their picture of language. He then sets that picture beside classic theories of meaning from Frege and Russell. The result is a more careful view: the models show some marks of meaning, yet fall short of full human understanding in clear ways.
arxiv-2507-05548:
Owen Henderschedt, Jessica McDonald, and Songling Shan prove a case of a long-standing guess about coloring graphs. In a total coloring, both the points of a graph and the lines joining them get colors, and neighbours — including a point and its own lines — must all differ. The Total Coloring Conjecture caps the colors needed at the largest number of lines at any point, plus two, but the guess has resisted proof in general.

The team settles it for very dense graphs. For any fixed margin, once a graph is large enough and every point touches at least half the other points, with a little room to spare, the cap holds. Density, in other words, gives enough structure to force the coloring through.
arxiv-2507-05848:
Dries Van De Putte and co-authors present a software pack for reading glowing dust bands in space, in this 2025 paper. Clouds near bright stars emit aromatic infrared bands, carried by small carbon grains. The team's tool, PAHFIT, splits a spectrum into band parts, dust glow, gas lines, and starlight.

Using JWST views of the Orion Bar, they tuned a pack of band settings for such clouds. The tool then fit both the Orion spectra and spectra from a star-forming ring in another galaxy, with errors of only a few percent. Their measures trace how the band carriers change between harsh and sheltered zones.
arxiv-2507-06248:
Mustafa Altın and Ahmet Kazan study soliton surfaces in four dimensions in a 2025 geometry paper. Their surfaces are tied to the Betchov-Da Rios equation, a model with roots in vortex dynamics. They describe the surface using a parallel transport frame, which avoids the twists of classical moving frames.

The authors derive how the frame changes along the surface and extract its main invariants: two basic quantities plus Gaussian curvature, mean curvature, and torsion measures. With those in hand they prove when the surface is flat, minimal, or of special conformal types. A worked example with projections into three dimensions illustrates the theory.
arxiv-2507-06848:
Labeling every pixel of an image by hand is expensive, so weak supervision learns from image-level tags alone. Joëlle Hanna and Damian Borth take a different route in 2025, reading the attention maps inside a vision transformer as the segmentation signal itself.

Their transformer carries one special token per class and trains with random masking, which pushes each token to own its class. At test time the attention maps of the tokens for the predicted classes are merged into draft masks. Those drafts beat rival methods on standard and specialist data sets, and a segmentation model trained on them nearly matched fully supervised results. The method needs no external activation-map machinery.
arxiv-2507-07248:
Jean-Philippe Corbeil and co-authors present a benchmark for medical risk in language models in this 2025 paper. Models are entering health care fast, yet safety tests mostly check general risks or the clinician's view. Real users range from patients to doctors, with very different skill levels. A wrong answer can harm health directly. The team built MedRiskEval, a benchmark tuned to medical risk. Its new part, PatientSafetyBench, holds 466 samples across five risk categories, written from the patient's side.

They ran open and closed models through the new set plus older safety data sets. The point is to catch failures that clinician centered tests miss: advice a patient might follow without a doctor's filter. The authors call the work a first foundation for safer medical deployment. They argue that risk review must mirror who actually asks the questions.
arxiv-2507-07348:
James Chapman, Kedar Karhadkar, and Guido Montúfar help learning agents adapt to new worlds from few tries in a 2025 paper. Agents trained in one set world often fail when world facts shift. Training in many worlds helps, but data across worlds can be scarce. Their test bed is a Markov process whose rules bend with context facts, such as mass or slope.

A new Bellman equation bakes context into the value math. The team prove it gives a close first-order guess of the value learned across many worlds. From it they draw a data growth trick for set worlds: fake new cases that teach the shift. Tests in sim worlds show the trick lifts scores on new contexts. The work suits robot and game teams that can train in one world but must act in many.
arxiv-2507-07448:
Otso Kinanen and co-authors investigate a toolchain to speed up the work cycle in quantum software development, in a 2025 paper. Quantum computing promises change across science and industry, but developers face scarce hardware, heavy simulation costs on classical machines, and a complex stack.

These limits make an efficient workflow hard. The authors explore using remote computing power in a smart way to ease the move between local runs and larger remote resources. Lowering that barrier could improve how developers test and iterate. The paper speaks to tool builders for a young software field.
arxiv-2507-07648:
Qi Gao and Yuan Wan compute the live motion of a polaron, a particle dressed in lattice vibrations, in this 2025 paper. The standard approach sums over every path the particle could take, a sum that explodes in size. Their method squeezes that sum into a compact network form called a matrix product state.

A flow equation builds the squeezed form step by step. Benchmarks in one dimension match known results for the polaron's energy spectrum. The team then pushes into two dimensions, where older methods struggle, and reports the spectrum there. They also simulate how polarons wander and spread in both settings. The method could open other hard dynamics problems to exact study.
arxiv-2507-07748:
Peizhang Shao and co-authors survey how large language models are being used in law. Their 2025 review sorts the field through two lenses at once. One lens is legal reasoning, and the other is the roles and terms of legal work. New transformer models can read context and draft arguments, which lets them take on tasks that older tools split apart. The review maps gains in search, prediction, and dispute work.

It also names hard blocks: made-up facts, weak grounds for answers, and poor fit across legal systems. Gains in training tricks are weighed next to risks in fairness and trust. The authors close with open fronts, such as thin data in some areas of law.
arxiv-2507-07848:
Dispoto, Bonetti, and Restelli offer a way to turn a skilled but opaque computer agent into a simple rule set in twenty twenty-five. Agents trained by trial and error can master games and trading tasks. Yet no one can easily see why they pick one move over another. Simple rules are clear, but they often play worse.

The new method learns from records of the skilled agent at work. It weighs not just what the agent did, but how much better that move was than the rest. Tests on classic control tasks and on a trading task worked well. The simple rules kept much of the skill while staying easy to read.
arxiv-2507-08148:
Some magnets arrange their spins in swirling multi-wave patterns whose handedness and direction order are hard to read with neutrons. Erik Kirstein and co-authors turn to polarized light, using two forms of dichroism to dissect the layered antiferromagnet Co1/3TaS2. At middle temperatures one signal exposes a striped phase with three-state directional order.

At low temperature and high field the other signal stands alone, marking a purely chiral, non-coplanar state. In between, a phase carries both orders at once, and microscopy maps the domains directly. A theory built on four-spin interactions explains the cast of phases, making the compound a rare stage for tunable spin textures.
arxiv-2507-08248:
Jason Kahei Tam, Murilo Gustineli, and Anthony Miyaguchi report their entry to a fungi naming contest that gives very few sample photos per species. Fungi are hard for vision models: species look nearly alike, while one species varies a lot. The contest dataset was built for that few-shot test.

The team tried several transformer vision models, image augmentation, and balanced sampling. They also fed in text data about the species. Language models asked to name fungi cold did far worse than vision models. Pretraining on fungi images and careful sampling drove their best score. Their entry placed mid-pack in the final private ranking. The report is candid that headroom remains. It maps what helped for other teams facing rare-species data.
arxiv-2507-08548:
Alen Adamyan and four colleagues teach a video tracking model to manage its own memory, in a 2025 paper. The Segment Anything Model 2 follows objects across video by storing past frames in a memory bank. Hand-written rules decide what enters that bank, and they struggle with distractors, occlusions, and fast motion.

The team frames memory control as a sequence of decisions and hands it to a reinforcement learning agent. In a test setup where each video got its own agent, the learned control beat the base model by a wide margin. Its gains were more than three times those of the best hand-crafted rules. The authors read that gap as untapped potential inside the memory bank itself. Learned memory policies, they argue, deserve a place beside rule-based tuning in tracking systems.
arxiv-2507-08848:
Calum Corrie Imrie and co-authors adapt a safety assurance method so it can vouch for learning systems that act by trial and error, in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning suits robots and vehicles whose surroundings defy tidy models, but safety-critical use demands proof, not just good averages. Existing safe-learning tricks add constraints during training, yet they do not build a structured safety case across the system's whole life.

Their adaptation, AMLAS-RL, extends a supervised-learning assurance method into an iterative cycle for reinforcement learning. A running example, a wheeled vehicle driving to a goal without collisions, shows the steps. The framework generates assurance arguments stage by stage, so gaps surface early. The authors aim it at engineers who must convince regulators, not just themselves, that a learning component is safe.
arxiv-2507-09048:
Thomas Fauchez, Geronimo Villanueva, and colleagues describe a tool linking climate models to telescope observations in a 2025 study. Three-dimensional climate models predict conditions on distant planets, but observers see spectra, the light signatures of an atmosphere. Turning model output into fake spectra lets teams compare theory with real data on equal terms.

Their module folds full atmospheric and surface information from climate models into spectral simulations. Case studies include a rocky planet in the TRAPPIST system. The tool is free for the research community to use. It helps planners judge which planets deserve scarce telescope time and what signals to expect.
arxiv-2507-09348: Fatemeh Maleki and a co-author sort out, in a short 2025 paper, parts of weak logic systems. The systems in view accept fewer rules than the classic intuition-based logic. The part studied here keeps only the if-then links and drops the rest of the language. For most of the known systems of this kind, the authors pin down exactly what that if-then part looks like. The result is brief and stated at a high level, with no data or tests.
arxiv-2507-09448:
Pramod Chunduri, Yao Lu, and Joy Arulraj built Tracer in 2025, a video database system that re-identifies objects across networked cameras with adaptive query processing. Finding the same car or person across many cameras serves traffic watch and security, but the search is costly. The leading system filters by place and time, yet its accuracy fades on large networks because each camera's history is local.

Tracer picks the best camera to process at each step, guided by a recurrent network trained on long-term links between cameras. A probabilistic search model speeds queries while holding the high recall that critical uses demand. Readers get a smarter way to hunt through camera networks: let the system learn where an object is likely to surface next instead of scanning in a fixed order.
arxiv-2507-09548:
Ashok, Kris, and Ganesan record the buzz of a coin vibration motor and find it far less steady than its job suggests. Such motors drive phone alerts and precision actuators, and engineers assume a clean hum that grows with voltage. Accelerometer traces do rise on average as voltage climbs, but moment to moment they wander.

Waveforms show swelling and fading amplitude, drifting pitch, and random deviations that worsen at high drive. Pressing the motor or its mount mid-run reshaped the pattern, proving the output depends on starting conditions and contact, not voltage alone. The authors warn that fine control of miniature actuators must reckon with this built-in nonlinearity.
arxiv-2507-09648:
Traffic science rests on fundamental diagrams, curves that relate density, flow, and speed, yet building them from modern trajectory data is harder than it looks. Zhengbing He and Cathy Wu note that the standard measurement framework, Edie's definitions, demands regions of the road where traffic is stationary and uniform. With full trajectory datasets now common, the missing piece is a systematic way to find those qualified regions. Their method does exactly that, using parallelogram-shaped patches of the time-space diagram that match how traffic states actually sit.

An open-source tool wraps the method for researchers and practitioners. It can turn any large time-space record of vehicle paths, measured or simulated, into a fundamental diagram automatically. The authors present this as a long-needed bridge between rich new data and a classic theory. They suggest it will also help test car-following models against clean, comparable measurements.
arxiv-2507-09948:
Models that predict how a chip design will perform often fail on designs unlike their training set. Zijian Ding and co-authors attack that gap with synthetic data. Their system, Iceberg, expands both machine-written programs and rough labels for unseen settings. A companion model learns in context from true and near labels together. The recipe targets high-level synthesis, where code becomes hardware.

Pretraining on the synthetic pool lifted accuracy sharply when adapting to six real applications with few examples. Offline design search also improved on two test sets. The gains show fake data can teach real generalization when the labels are handled with care. Code is openly shared.
arxiv-2507-10048:
Benedict Gerlach, Marie Anastacio, and Holger Hoos study the efficiency of training robust decision trees. Their 2025 paper deals with a simple pipeline for adversarially robust trees, at a time when trustworthiness and sustainability both matter.

The pipeline has three stages. First, the perturbation size is chosen automatically for each dataset by a simple new algorithm, and it can be estimated from smaller models, which saves a lot of time. Second, leading adversarial training methods are trained and compared on time and adversarial accuracy. Third, the robustness of each model is certified, and the time that step takes is measured as well.
arxiv-2507-10348:
Yichen Li and co-authors argue that federated learning across unlike models should share features, not just answers. Their 2025 paper concerns training many private models of different shapes on separate data, then pooling their knowledge without moving the data. The usual pooling step teaches the global model from the others' output scores, but with unlike architectures that knowledge turns biased and training wobbles.

Distilling the richer internal features instead compensates for the bias, the authors show, and stabilizes the joint training. The result is a steadier recipe for the realistic case where hospitals or firms bring different models to the same table. Privacy keeps the data home; the method makes the sharing work.
arxiv-2507-10448:
Yingqian Wu and co-authors build a multi-agent system for financial analysis in a 2025 paper. Financial reports span macro trends down to single firms and need heavy data work. Single models tuned on simple questions cannot cover that range. Companies split such work across departments, and the team copies that pattern.

FinTeam assigns four language model agents distinct roles. A document analyzer, an analyst, an accountant, and a consultant cooperate in sequence. Each agent was trained with targeted financial expertise. Test tasks came from real online investment forums. Reports covered macro, industry, and company analysis levels. Human judges accepted FinTeam reports at a rate above baselines. Gains also showed on two financial benchmarks. Specialist agents, the authors argue, beat one generalist model. The project code is shared for further work.
arxiv-2507-10548:
Mingxian Lin and co-authors built a test set for robots and AI agents that must act in the world, in this 2025 paper. Vision-language models do well on still images, but acting step by step in a scene is harder. Their dataset holds more than three thousand language-guided tasks in realistic virtual settings made with a game engine.

Each task pairs first-person views with instructions, actions, and plain-language reasons for each step. Tasks cover finding the way, moving objects, and multi-stage goals. Top commercial models scored below twenty percent success with no training. After fine-tuning on the data, a smaller open model improved a lot across all task types.
arxiv-2507-10648:
Karthik Yadavalli and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a grid of simulated light curves for stars that shed their outer layers and then explode. Such stars end as bright supernovae whose light changes with time. The shape of that light reveals what the star threw off.

The team ran a known radiation transport code to make nearly two thousand light curves. They varied the mass distribution, the velocity profile, and the mixture of the ejected material. A compression tool built on stellar evolution models kept the grid both flexible and true to life. Set beside three known supernovae, the grid produced close and realistic matches. The velocity profile influenced the light most. The share of nickel-56 alone influenced the total light less, though it could affect the colors. From the curves, the team could read back the key traits of the explosion.
arxiv-2507-10948:
Andrew Newman and a large team catalog 37 embryonic galaxy clusters found not by their galaxies but by shadows in intergalactic gas, in a paper from 2025. Their survey maps hydrogen absorption in three dimensions at redshift 2.5, when the universe was young. Finding dense regions this way skips the bias of needing bright galaxies first.

Simulations say 85 percent of the finds will grow into full clusters, and nearly all the rest into groups. Their masses and numbers match mock surveys. The team also re-examined the known proto-supercluster Hyperion and found a new outlying piece of it. Gas behavior there fits a simple physical model, hinting that black hole feedback has not yet disturbed the whole structure. The catalog multiplies the known sample tenfold.
arxiv-2507-11448:
János Végh published this theoretical neuroscience paper in 2025. It rebuilds the physics of how a neuron holds its resting membrane potential, the stable voltage across its membrane. Végh argues that classic textbook models lean on untested assumptions. His replacement starts from the fact that biology moves charge with slow positive ions, not electrons, and folds in recent experimental findings that the older picture leaves out.

From those first principles he derives the resting potential directly, rather than as a weighted mix of ion reversal potentials. He also defines an equivalent thermodynamic electric field for discussing ion channels and their selectivity. A simple electrical-thermodynamic control circuit, he argues, sets the resting voltage and keeps it robust through growth and evolution. The model claims to resolve old puzzles about heat absorption and leakage current in nerves.
arxiv-2507-11948:
Carlo Baronio and four co-authors train Kevin, a model that writes fast graphics-chip code, by reward across many turns of work. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Writing such code, called kernels, is hard and key to how fast smart systems run. Experts write, run, read the speed, and rewrite. That loop gives clear rewards: is the code right, and how much faster is it? The team builds a training recipe that learns across the whole loop, with care for long paths and for which turn earned the reward. Kevin beat its base model by a wide mark on right code, and sped past the base frame, past a top rival too.
arxiv-2507-12348:
Ben Gripaios and Khoi Le Nguyen Nguyen sort out which gauge theories lose strength at high energy, in a 2025 math and physics paper. Such theories, called asymptotically free, sit at the heart of the standard model of particles. The team focus on theories whose matter is made only of fermions, the class that holds electrons and quarks.

Their proof rests on a fact they establish about the labels used to sort particle states: two key measures both rise strictly as any label grows. That fact caps the list of free theories for each force type, so the full set can be written down in tables. At most two labels can be nonzero, and none can pass four. The tables give other researchers a ready map for building and testing new theories.
arxiv-2507-12548:
Petit Rosas and Torres Bobadilla proposed in 2025 a fast way to evaluate Feynman integrals for Monte Carlo event generators in particle physics. Their method integrates the differential equations that these integrals obey, with a new strategy for handling branch cuts inside a numerical scheme. The integrator works in double and quadruple precision.

Tested on one- and two-loop five-point integrals with many complex scales, it ran far faster than existing tools. One-loop cases took about milliseconds and two-loop cases a few hundred. Applications include a radiative return process in scalar QED and top quark pair plus jet production. On-the-fly computation in generators is the goal.
arxiv-2507-12648:
Jeongwoo Lee and three co-authors argue in a 2025 study that small jets on the Sun may seed the kinks seen in the solar wind. Space probes have found many sharp bends in the wind's magnetic field, called switchbacks, and their source is still debated. The team used sharp images and magnetic maps from a solar observatory in California. They studied spicules, the thin jets that shoot up all over the Sun's surface layer.

The jets rose from bright threads that sit on open field lines of one magnetic sign, as a switchback source would need. The jets came in clusters, and the gaps between them matched the time gaps between switchbacks. They also form often enough for probes to catch many. The team notes the jets differ from larger coronal jets in clear ways.
arxiv-2507-12948:
Weiqiu You and co-authors present, in 2025, a method that checks each step of a language model's reasoning using only the steps already verified. Early mistakes in a reasoning chain can poison later judgments, so checking a step against the whole chain often fails. Their framework scores steps one by one in order.

Each score comes with a statistical guarantee rather than a hard yes or no. On four benchmarks the method set a new best score, and on very long synthetic chains it caught propagated errors far better than rivals. The authors offer it as a sturdier way to audit machine reasoning before trusting the final answer.
arxiv-2507-13348:
Six researchers in China teach a vision language model to ask for sharper images only when needed in a 2025 paper. Such models read images as long token strings, which costs compute. Most scenes, the team found, can be read well at a quarter of the usual sharpness.

Their model starts with a small image and judges if it suffices. If not, it sends a special token to request the full image. Reinforcement learning trains that choice, with a judge model scoring answers and a penalty keeping requests in check. Tests show strong skill on text heavy tasks while saving many tokens on easy ones.
arxiv-2507-13448:
Jenny Wan and co-authors confront simulations of baby galaxies with the Webb telescope's first hard counts in this 2025 paper. At cosmic noon, when the universe was a few billion years old, faint satellite galaxies swarm around bigger ones. How many survive depends on how tides shred their dark matter cradles, a process modelers set by hand.

The team compared satellite counts from recent Webb surveys at redshifts one to three and a half against dark-matter-only zoom simulations. The biggest wobble in the forecasts came from assumptions about how fast cradles dissolve. Letting galaxy toughness vary swung the predicted satellite numbers by a factor of about three and a half. Within that range the telescope data matched the standard model well. The data even hint cradles live at least as long as fluid simulations suggest. The authors offer their framework for sharper tests ahead.
arxiv-2507-13548:
Error correcting codes built from two circulating blocks are old favorites, but decoding them past a modest error load was out of reach. Oren Dubin and two co-authors present in 2025 fast decoders for two such families, one built from Sidon sets and one from cyclic codes. The decoders repair up to a square root sized share of errors.

A bridge found in earlier work turns the first family into Wozencraft codes, an even older design, while keeping both distance and decoding speed. That yields the first explicit Wozencraft code decodable from square root errors. The authors also mark where the bridge fails for the second family. The limits, they note, guide the next constructions.
arxiv-2507-13648:
Seungjun Moon, Sangjoon Yu, and Gyeong-Moon Park present EPSilon in two thousand twenty five. Hybrid avatars pair SMPL meshes with neural radiance fields. The mix renders people well but runs very slowly in practice. Deforming each sampled point to the mesh costs the time.

Most sampled points sit in empty space and add nothing. Empty ray omission drops rays that cross only void. Empty interval omission trims unoccupied spans along each ray. Quality holds while sampled points fall to under four percent. Inference runs about twenty times faster than before.
arxiv-2507-13848:
Piotr Bentkowski and Tomasz Gubiec model how like-minded clustering of health behaviour can backfire in epidemics, in work from twenty twenty-five. People split into those who follow anti-epidemic steps and those who do not. Spread rates depend on the behaviour of both the sick and the healthy person. The team runs a standard spread model on two kinds of fake social networks. One kind tunes how often the two groups mix, with little clustering.

The second kind adds triadic closure, so friends of friends link up often. When sick followers cut spread a lot, more group split can raise infections among followers. That paradox appears only in the clustered networks, not the plain ones. Local clumps let behaviour amplify spread inside the follower group itself. More social distance thus fails to protect when clustering runs high. Network shape must enter plans for behaviour-based controls.
arxiv-2507-14148:
Pugliese and co-authors locate a cheap light sensor indoors using a single ceiling LED and smart reflective surfaces. Indoor positioning by visible light is attractive because lights are already there, but a lone anchor cannot fix a position. The trick is the reflectors: each can be switched and steered, bouncing light so its path lengths betray the sensor's position. The team derives the best estimators for the direct and bounced distances, and replaces a slow grid search with a closed-form solution.

Those distances feed a weighted least-squares locator whose weights come from the theoretical accuracy limits the authors derive. A steering strategy keeps the reflectors aimed as the estimate improves. In simulations, the method reached near-theoretical accuracy in few iterations and tolerated misaligned reflectors. For warehouses, hospitals, and malls, the paper sketches positioning piggybacking on lighting with minimal new hardware.
arxiv-2507-14548:
Guanglian Li analyzes a multiscale computation method in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. Some materials vary on a tiny scale that defeats plain simulation. Multiscale finite elements build that fine detail into coarse elements. Oversampling enlarges each coarse patch to cut boundary errors.

Li studies the interpolation error of two classic oversampling variants. The setting allows rough, wildly oscillating coefficients with no scale gap. His analysis leans only on the smoothed limit problem and its accuracy. It skips the fine corrector functions and their cell problems entirely. The error bound mixes mesh size and period size in a clean form. Minimal smoothness of the limit solution suffices. The result sharpens theory for a widely used simulation family.
arxiv-2507-14648:
Stallrich and co-authors strengthen a classic experiment design trick in a 2025 statistics paper. Foldover designs mirror an experiment's runs to cancel confusion between main effects and interactions. The method sits inside many standard screening and response surface designs.

The team shows foldover does more than clean up effects. It also creates degrees of freedom for a variance estimate that does not depend on which model is picked. They sort those into pure error and fake factor types. A fast construction algorithm then builds designs that sharpen the power to spot main effects. Simulations and a 20-run chemical example show gains when the usual sparsity rules fail.
arxiv-2507-14748:
Patrik Reizinger and five co-authors study skill learning in reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper, through the lens of policy diversity. Self-supervised methods that learn skills by mutual information also learn a view of the world, but how that view is shaped in such methods was not well understood.

The team focus on one method, Contrastive Successor Features. They prove it can get back the true features of the environment, up to a linear change. The key is the inner product form of the features and the spread of skills. The result ties skill diversity to views that can be identified.
arxiv-2507-14948:
Shubham Agarwal and Martin Muser heat a classic friction model and find it apes thick fluid flow as well. The model lines atoms on springs over a wavy floor, a toy for dry rub and stuck films. Warm runs show a slow creep phase twixt fast flight and full spread, as goo films show. Its spread pace flips from odd to plain heat law near the heat peak of the toy.

One lore fix falls in their read: thin flow under shear need not mean shear cut the hills. Shear-born drops can set the pace, with hill cuts a side show. Past fits of a famed flow law to data may thus be chance hits. Rub and rheology teams share one toy moral.
arxiv-2507-15048:
Hanfeng Chen and Maria Elena Filippin model how a central bank digital currency changes monetary policy and household welfare. Their 2025 paper builds a New Keynesian economy where the new currency competes with bank deposits. Banks hold market power, so the contest between the two forms of money shapes interest margins across the economy.

When households value the digital currency more, the effect is mildly expansionary: bank power weakens and deposit spreads shrink a lot. Deposit flight stays modest, so fears of banks being hollowed out look overblown in the model. Paying interest on the currency under a standard rule adds little welfare, but an optimized rule adds much more. Gains grow with the currency's benefit to users. The authors show the design details, not just the launch, decide the payoff.
arxiv-2507-15348:
Dmitriy Tsarev and co-authors explore, in a 2025 theory paper, quantum sensor networks built from bright solitons, self-held light or atom waves. Measuring several unknowns at once with quantum tools can beat classic limits. The authors set a general limit for such networks, covering both plain and non-linear schemes.

They focus on special shared states, called N00N states, tuned for multi-value sensing. As a source, they propose a three-mode soliton Josephson junction, a small atomtronic circuit. Its ground state shifts sharply from a smooth wave to a mix of Fock states that nears the target state. Even with weak losses, the circuit can near the best allowed accuracy. The work opens paths toward quantum sensors built as networks.
arxiv-2507-15448:
Junmin An and Jon-Lark Kim extend the theory of frames into finite number systems. Frames are redundant coordinate systems that keep signals stable under loss. Recent work carried them from real and complex numbers into finite fields. The authors add Galois inner products, which unify the usual real and complex ways of measuring angles.

With that tool they define Galois frames, their Gram matrices, and their operators. The special case of equiangular tight frames gets a full treatment. The team then characterizes when self-dual codes over these fields give rise to such frames. Explicit families are built from constacyclic codes with the same self-dual trait. The work links coding theory and frame design in the finite world. Such frames may serve channels where symbols live in finite alphabets.
arxiv-2507-15848:
Markus Bachmayr, Matthieu Dolbeault, and Polina Sachsenmaier present a 2025 paper on fast ways to solve equations that change over time. When the full grid is too large, a low rank form can store the answer in a much smaller shape. The hard part is picking the rank so the answer stays right without growing too large.

Their scheme runs step by step and trims small parts at each stage with a soft threshold rule. They prove the rank stays close to the best rank one could pick. A time based Schrödinger case is worked out in depth, and changes for heat type problems are also given. Tests back up the claims.
arxiv-2507-16148:
Jindong Wang, Yutong Mao, Xiao Liu, and Wenrui Hao, writing for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, learn models of Alzheimer's progression for each patient with operator learning. Alzheimer's is a varied disorder of nerve decay. Models that forecast paths for each person stay limited in spite of gains in care. Standard models set the dynamics in advance. This frame learns them from data.

The path learns disease operators for each patient straight. The operators govern how amyloid, tau, and nerve decay markers evolve across the brain over time. With Laplacian eigenfunction bases, it builds neural operators that are aware of geometry. They catch complex brain dynamics from scans, markers, and clinical data over time. Set in a digital twin frame, it allows forecasts for each person. Applied to Alzheimer's data, it hit high accuracy across markers.
arxiv-2507-16348:
Mikhail Drugov and Dmitry Ryvkin design contest prizes for a world of unknown luck in a 2025 economics paper. In a rank-order tournament, effort responds to the prize ladder, but the designer usually must guess the noise distribution. Here the only knowledge is an upper bound on its entropy, its randomness budget.

The robust scheme guarantees the best worst-case lowest effort. It pays every rank except the last, with a distinctly larger top prize, and asymptotically the prizes follow the harmonic sequence while the implied noise turns exponential. The ladder is steeply unequal for small fields, softening toward a Gini of one half as the field grows.
arxiv-2507-16448:
Zbigniew Palmowski, Lewis Ramsden, and Apostolos Papaioannou wrote a 2025 paper on ruin risk for insurers over a finite time span. Their model is a discrete time risk process where claim sizes are steered by a Markov chain, a system that hops between states. In the classic model without that steering, a famous ballot theorem gives the ruin chance directly.

The chain's memory breaks the classic argument, since the steps are no longer freely swappable. The authors show a general ballot result still holds under the chain's steady state, giving a clean formula when the starting surplus is zero. For any starting surplus, they build a method on multivariate Lagrangian inversion. That yields formulas for hitting times and a Seal type expression for the finite time ruin chance.
arxiv-2507-16648:
Eleon Bach, Yann Disser, Sophie Huiberts, and Nils Mosis (2025) prove a hard limit on a classic optimization method. The active-set method moves along constraints, choosing at each step which one to engage next: the pivot rule. The authors show that for every fixed exponent above zero, maximizing a convex objective of a simple power form under linear constraints can force the method through exponentially many steps. This holds no matter which pivot rule is used.

Their test objectives sit arbitrarily close to linear ones, where the method becomes the famous simplex method. The special case of exponent one gives the lower bound for convex quadratic maximization, the paper's catalog title. The proof rests on a new extended formulation, built recursively from deformed products, which projects onto a polygonal approximation of a parabola. It improves the best earlier bound, which needed polynomial objectives of growing degree.
arxiv-2507-16748:
Jingni Wu and Amir Zeldes study how small linking words share work with other signals, in a 2025 paper. Discourse markers like but, then, and since hold texts together. Many carry several meanings at once. Other phrases can do the same linking job, and both kinds often appear side by side.

Working in a rich discourse framework, the authors grade how many senses each marker holds. They then test whether murkier markers attract more numerous or more varied helper signals. Murky markers did draw a wider variety of helpers, but not a greater total count. Genre also shaped the patterns strongly. The findings matter for teaching machines, and people, to read links between clauses correctly.
arxiv-2507-17048:
Zheting Jin and Sohrab Ismail-Beigi explain how praseodymium doping locks charge order into three dimensions in a cuprate superconductor. The host is YBCO7, and density functional theory finds the lowest-energy praseodymium layouts for barium-site and yttrium-site swaps. At the barium site the smaller ion pulls neighbors inward. That breathing distortion pins charge-stripe walls to the dopant columns and aligns them along the c axis.

Yttrium-site dopants push outward instead and fail to pin the stripes. Monte Carlo simulations show stripe order growing with the dopant's own structural order, matching past experiments. The authors give design rules for engineering electronic order by ionic substitution.
arxiv-2507-17148:
Dongyi Yang, Chenxi Sun, and Jianwei Zhang hunt axion dark matter through a spin dependent force in a 2025 paper. Axions, feather light hypothetical particles, are prime dark matter suspects, and their touch on electrons may fake a tiny magnetic field.

Sensitive atomic magnetometers could read that field. Because local axions swarm densely, the scattering signal swells far past single particle hopes. The team derive coupling limits two orders tighter than before at low axion mass. With a magnetometer now in development, the reach should pass even star based bounds. The method can also map local dark matter clumps.
arxiv-2507-17448:
Situo Zhang and co-authors present a new computer model for chemists in 2025. The model works backward from a target drug or compound to the steps that could make it. Most older tools match set patterns. This one is trained to show its steps in plain form, so a person can check the plan.

Tests use a common set of past reactions. The model scores higher than older tools, with and without extra search steps. Experts who did not know its source also judged its plans sound. The team then used it to rebuild long routes for real drugs and for a type of surface coating. The aim is trust in plans that labs could run.
arxiv-2507-17548:
Lingxiao Tang, He Ye, Zhongxin Liu, Xiaoxue Ren, and Lingfeng Bao published this paper in 2025. It strengthens a language model's ability to reason about code: predicting what a program will print, or whether a given line will run. Such reasoning underpins debugging, generation, and repair tools.

The team blames two faults for weak results: poor training data and the limits of plain supervised tuning. Their framework, CodeReasoner, builds training sets focused on the core execution logic of Python programs. A first tuning stage injects execution knowledge distilled from a stronger teacher model. A second stage applies reinforcement learning to sharpen reasoning and generalization. The resulting seven-billion-parameter model beat prior methods by wide margins on three benchmarks and matched a leading commercial model on key tasks. Scaled up, it passed that model everywhere. Ablations confirmed each stage earns its place.
arxiv-2507-17848:
Lijun Wu, Dong Hao, and Zhiyi Fan give a way to explain the calls of a graph neural network, a model that learns from linked data. Such models act as black boxes, and past ways to explain them miss how nodes sway each other inside the network.

Their frame, GraphEXT, splits the nodes into groups and treats the graph shape as an outside force on the game between them. A fair share value, adapted to that force, scores each node by what it adds as it moves between groups. On fake and real data the method beat past ones on how truly its reasons matched the model's calls.
arxiv-2507-17948:
Nine authors present VERIRAG, a system that audits summaries of science studies, in this 2025 paper. People who gatekeep public information often lack deep training, so they lean on AI systems that cite sources. Standard systems treat all cited proof as equal, however weak the methods behind it.

VERIRAG instead checks source papers for flaws in their statistics and methods, using a taxonomy of rigor the authors built. Their test set holds 1,730 summaries with hidden flaws modeled on retracted papers. The system beat baselines by a wide margin on their main score. The authors frame it as a copilot that leaves an audit trail for human editors.
arxiv-2507-18248:
Ines Frajtag and co-authors test how well a face-point tool holds up under surgical lights. Face maps guide robots and vision tools in brain, eye, and face surgery, but bright lamps and odd head tilts can throw them off. Their 2025 test rig moves a robot arm round a fixed head model while lamps and model stay put. The tool in view is a wide-used face mesh tracker.

Under surgical light, point finds get more true at wide yaw and pitch than in plain light. Spread of the reads grows too, since some points land off mark. The team weighs what the trade means for use in live care. A tool that gains at hard angles but wobbles on select points needs guard rails before the ward.
arxiv-2507-18348:
Sarridis, Koutlis, Papadopoulos, and Diou built a free tool kit in twenty twenty-five to test ways to cut bias in image models. Bias can make such models unfair and weak on new data. Past work used split tools and unlike tests, so fair checks were hard.

Their kit, VB-Mitigator, holds twelve known bias-cut ways and seven test data sets in one place. New ways, sets, scores, and models can be plugged in with ease. They give best steps for fair tests and a full score match of top ways. The kit aims to speed work toward fair image models for all.
arxiv-2507-18948:
Hui Jiang and co-authors film molecules at the crossroads where excited states switch paths, in this 2025 paper. Those junctions, called conical intersections, steer how molecules shed light energy. Events there are over in femtoseconds and shift atoms by tiny amounts.

The team combine mega-electron-volt electron diffraction with a super-resolution inversion method. The pairing beats the usual diffraction limit on fine detail. Both electron cloud and nuclear motions come into view at the junction. Sub-angstrom sharpness lets them watch bonds bend and break in real time.
