Shunyu Wu and six co-authors tackle data valuation for time series foundation models: judging which training series actually help, so poor data can be dropped and good data credited. Classic influence methods collapse under the size of these models and ignore the time structure of the data.

Their lightweight method, LTSV, uses in-context finetuning, which theory suggests approximates the influence function at a fraction of the cost. A sample's value is estimated from how the model responds when it is included in context. Efficient, time-aware valuation matters because foundation models are only as good as the vast, uneven corpora they absorb during pretraining.
arxiv-2511-11948:
Zachary Couvillon and Anwesh Ray count elliptic curves whose division fields overlap in prescribed, unexplained ways, a phenomenon called entanglement. Such overlaps change the Galois groups that control a curve's arithmetic, and knowing how common they are shapes conjectures across number theory.

Curves are drawn from one-parameter families coming from genus zero modular curves, and techniques from the geometry of numbers and sieve methods produce asymptotic lower bounds ordered by naive height. For entanglements between the two- and three-division fields, and between the two- and five-division fields, the counts grow at least like explicit powers of the height bound. Entanglement, once an exotic exception, gets a population estimate.
arxiv-2511-12348:
Mostafa Nozari and three co-authors work on small subnetworks that must both communicate and sense where a target is, a pairing known as integrated sensing and communication. Sensing and data traffic compete for the same limited resources, so picking which subnetworks should sense at each step matters.

Their low-complexity algorithm selects sensing nodes in rounds, using the spatial spread of the deployment to refine the set and raise localization accuracy. Simulations reach very fine accuracy in a few rounds under simple noise, with a large gain over the best benchmark at the same sensing budget. They also measure the trade-off: fewer sensing rounds raise throughput but lower precision.
arxiv-2511-12548:
Wenzhang Du proposes CAO, an optimizer that adapts to curvature only where curvature matters most, to speed training in sharp, uneven regions of a loss landscape. First-order methods are reliable but slow in such regions. CAO periodically sketches a low-rank picture of the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, using products that avoid forming it in full.

Gradients are then corrected inside that sketched subspace, while all other directions keep the plain first-order step. Theory restores the standard convergence guarantee for smooth non-convex losses, with a wider stable step range, and faster contraction under an added growth condition. On image benchmarks with residual networks, the method reaches a set loss level far earlier than Adam, with final accuracy matched.
arxiv-2511-12948:
Jinwoo Park works out the theory for borrowing statistical strength across time series that keep changing. Locally stationary series drift slowly, so a regression fitted in one period may mislead in another. Locally linear smoothing handles the drift better than the classical local constant estimator. Park proves uniform convergence for the multivariate version under strong mixing, splitting the error into variation, smoothing bias, and a new term caused by the local stationarity itself. That extra term turns out smaller than in the older benchmark, which explains the method's edge.

On top of the theory, Park builds transfer learning estimators for the realistic case where the series of interest is sparsely observed but related series are dense. A smoothly varying bias function links them, with a local temporal adjustment for stability. Simulations and an analysis of international fuel prices support the predictions.
arxiv-2511-13548:
Siyang Cheng and 9 co-authors present ForgeDAN, an evolutionary system that crafts jailbreak prompts against aligned language models. Jailbreaks try to slip past safety training and draw out harmful output, so testing them is part of defense work. Earlier auto-generators mutated prompts narrowly and judged success with fragile keyword checks.

ForgeDAN mutates text at character, word, and sentence levels for wider variety. A similarity-based fitness score rewards prompts that stay on topic while pushing toward the harmful goal, and a language model judge checks both compliance and harm to cut false alarms. In tests it beat leading methods on success rate while keeping prompts natural and hard to spot.
arxiv-2511-13748:
Dennis M. Heim presents a classical particle model whose coarse-grained behavior, he argues, is the Schrödinger equation. Companions move on a line under Newton's laws with an ordinary force: each pays a cost for mismatched signed inverse gaps to its two neighbors. A binary polarity carried by each particle is what makes still states with nodes stable in his construction.

Finite chains in the model settle into the stationary densities of a boxed particle and a harmonic oscillator, and they develop double-slit fringe patterns. In the smooth limit Heim derives the Schrödinger equation, with the wave function carrying two real fields rather than standing as a basic object. The claim is presented as a construction to be judged on its stated mechanics.
arxiv-2511-14048:
Zifan Wang, Georgios Pantazis, and Sergio Grammatico study games where players must act under uncertainty they do not fully trust. Each agent guards against distribution shifts inside a Wasserstein ball around the data, and each may pick its own level of caution. A penalty built from a Lagrangian formulation enforces those heterogeneous robustness limits.

The authors show the robust Nash equilibrium problem equals a finite-dimensional variational inequality with a strongly monotone mapping, under stated assumptions. They then design an equilibrium-seeking algorithm and prove its average regret shrinks with more iterations, reaching any preset accuracy. Simulations back the theory, offering a principled way to compute equilibria when players fear different amounts of model error.
arxiv-2511-14248:
Hongju Lee, Youngjun Park, Jisun An, and one co-author forecast neighborhood-level Airbnb trends with help from language model embeddings. Short-term rentals strain local housing, so planners need early warning of where revenue and bookings are heading. The framework predicts revenue, reservation days, and reservation counts one to three months ahead using a sliding window.

Instead of modeling single listings, it builds a representation of each region that merges listing features with accessibility and human mobility data. Tables are converted into text prompts, and a language model turns them into regional embeddings for sequence models. On Seoul data the method roughly halved forecast error against conventional baselines.
arxiv-2511-14648:
Lane Boswell and Ying Cao give a hands-on guide to testing whether a quantum system is entangled, meaning its parts are linked so that measuring one fixes the other. Entanglement sits at the heart of quantum information science, the field that joins quantum mechanics with information theory. The paper focuses on one math tool for the test, the Schmidt decomposition.

The authors show how to apply the method step by step and how to read the result. A system that needs more than one Schmidt term is entangled, while a single term means it is not. The piece serves as a clear teaching entry point for students meeting entanglement tests for the first time.
arxiv-2511-14948:
Jaro Meyer, Frédéric Giraud, and four co-authors tackle a practical filming problem: cameras of very different kinds rarely record in perfect sync. Their system, RocSync, aligns video streams to within a few milliseconds without relying on built-in hardware sync. It uses a custom LED device that the cameras can all see.

Mixed setups are the hard case, combining pro and consumer cameras, color and infrared sensors, and units with or without sound. RocSync is built to be cheap and general enough for field work where controlled capture is not possible. Good sync matters for three-dimensional reconstruction, pose tracking, and scene analysis, and the paper shows a workable route for real-world shoots.
arxiv-2511-15348:
Cornelis van der Mee develops the scattering theory of a wave system whose diagonal carries a zero where the standard theory expects only plus and minus ones. The system is the matrix form of the AKNS equations, a backbone model for nonlinear waves, now with a single zero entry in its signature matrix. Scattering theory reads a potential from how waves bounce off it, then inverts that reading to solve evolution problems.

Van der Mee builds both directions, direct and inverse, for potentials that fade fast enough at infinity. The time evolution of the scattering data follows, and through it the initial-value problem for a coupled long-wave and short-wave system is solved. Extending the transform to the zero-entry case widens the family of solvable wave equations.
arxiv-2511-15448:
Vincent Astier and Thomas Unger study signatures of hermitian forms, algebraic objects that generalize familiar notions like length and angle, over a broad class of rings called Azumaya algebras. A signature records sign-like information at each ordering of the base ring. Choosing those signs in a consistent, natural way is the central problem the authors address.

An earlier method worked for a narrower class of algebras. Astier and Unger show the same approach extends to Azumaya algebras with an involution, a symmetry that flips elements in a structured way. The result gives total signatures that vary continuously over the real spectrum, the space of all orderings of the base ring.
arxiv-2511-15648:
Finn Münnich, Szymon Cygan, Théo André, and Anna Marciniak-Czochra extend the theory of pattern formation in systems where some components diffuse and others stay put. Such mixed systems, written as reaction-diffusion equations coupled to ordinary differential equations, can show instabilities and sharp jump patterns absent from classic models. Past theory covered only one diffusing component, leaving richer cases open.

With several diffusion scales, new instability routes appear, including ones driven by a coupled non-diffusing and slowly diffusing pair. The authors give simple sufficient conditions for diffusion-driven instability with any number of components and classify all sources in the smallest three-component case. Some sources vanish under a common reduction. Jump patterns far from equilibrium are also proven to exist.
arxiv-2511-15948:
Raphael Ruschel, Hardikkumar Prajapati, Awsafur Rahman, and B. S. Manjunath introduce Click2Graph, an interactive system that builds video scene graphs from a single user cue. A scene graph lists objects and their relations, such as a person holding a cup, over time. Existing generators run as closed pipelines with no human guidance, while promptable segmentation models accept clicks but do no relational reasoning.

From one click or bounding box, Click2Graph segments and tracks the subject, discovers interacting objects on its own, and predicts subject-object-relation triplets that stay consistent over time. A discovery module proposes objects conditioned on the subject, and a classification head reasons jointly about entities and predicates. Tests on a standard benchmark establish a strong user-guided foundation.
arxiv-2511-16348:
Wen-Hao Jiang, Ruiwen Ouyang, and Ye-Ling Zhou survey models of neutrino mixing built on modular S4 symmetry that predict the trimaximal TM1 pattern. The survey is framed by the JUNO experiment's precise new measurements of the mixing angle and the solar mass splitting. In these models the pattern comes from leftover symmetries after a flavor symmetry breaks.

The authors explain how vacuum alignment of modular and flavon fields produces the TM1 pattern, then present three models that reach it by different building strategies within the same symmetry structure. Because the strategies differ, the models predict different links between the lightest neutrino mass and the effective mass probed in neutrinoless double beta decay. Future decay searches could therefore tell the three models apart.
arxiv-2511-16448:
Anne E Blackwell, Joel N Bregman, and Sophia Chan Davis survey metals in the hot gas of 26 galaxy groups and clusters with the XMM-Newton telescope, asking where that enrichment came from. The observed metal levels exceed what today's visible stars could have produced, even though clusters are nearly closed systems that keep their metals.

Measuring radial metallicity profiles and comparing them with the stellar fraction, the authors fit a tight relation with small scatter. Closed-box chemical models using updated supernova yields still underpredict the gas metallicity, and the shortfall grows where the stellar fraction is low. The gap requires an early enrichment population distinct from visible stars. Three systems break the trend with steep gradients and low metallicity, which the authors read as late-forming systems enriched only recently.
arxiv-2511-16548:
Guanchen Wu and six co-authors present CLOZE, a framework that grows medical ontologies by mining clinical notes with large language models. Ontologies organize diseases and their relations for research and care, but they lag behind practice; clinical notes hold rich, current observations yet are unstructured and private.

CLOZE works zero-shot, with no extra training or labeled data: the model extracts medical entities from notes and slots them into the hierarchical ontology, capturing complex relations between concepts. Protected health information is removed automatically to preserve patient privacy. Experiments show the extensions are accurate and the approach scales, making it a cost-efficient way to keep medical knowledge bases current and more useful for downstream clinical and research tools.
arxiv-2511-16648:
Ignacio Magaña Hernandez and Katelyn Breivik ask how the gravitational wave event GW190814, famous for its extreme mass ratio of about one to ten, could form through ordinary isolated binary evolution. Using the COSMIC population synthesis code with a backpop sampling technique, they map the observed event back to the starting conditions of its progenitor stars.

The progenitors turn out not to be unusual compared with massive star populations in the Local Group. The dominant pathway has the first mass transfer phase pass through a common envelope and the second stay stable. The decisive ingredient is the natal kicks at compact object birth. A small first kick keeps the binary bound, while a large second kick, aimed in the orbital plane toward the center of mass, pumps up eccentricity and shortens the merger time. Such lucky kicks occur in about a fifth of randomly oriented cases.
arxiv-2511-16848:
Feliciano Pedro Francisco Domingos and seven co-authors determine the sex and age of European lobsters from sound alone, a non-invasive trick with direct value for fisheries and aquaculture. Lobsters produce buzzing and carapace vibrations, recorded here with hydrophones in concrete tanks at Johnshaven, Scotland. The question is whether those sounds betray whether the animal is male or female, juvenile or adult.

Mel-frequency features fed a battery of deep and machine learning models. Age classification topped ninety-seven percent accuracy for most models, and sex classification exceeded ninety-three percent for all but one. The results show supervised learning can extract age- and sex-related signatures from lobster bioacoustics. That opens a passive acoustic monitoring route for conservation and farm management that never handles the animals and could run on edge devices underwater.
arxiv-2511-17048:
Wenzhuo Sun and four co-authors introduce RoomPlanner, a framework that turns a short text prompt into a full three-dimensional room. Earlier systems needed hand-designed layouts or panoramic images to guide them. RoomPlanner instead plans the layout itself, so a brief description is the only input a user must supply.

A chain of language-driven planners first expands the prompt into detailed descriptions of each object and the background, then seeds three-dimensional point clouds. Arrangement rules then shift objects until the layout has no collisions and leaves usable space. A new camera-path sampling method speeds up the final rendering, keeping total generation under half an hour. Experiments show rooms that look realistic, beat prior methods on speed and quality, and stay editable afterward.
arxiv-2511-17148:
David Solano and five co-authors quantify how extreme heat affected mortality in Catalonia, Spain, between 2012 and 2022, and what made the risk worse. They linked daily death records across 379 basic health areas with weather, air pollution, and socioeconomic data for the summer months. They then fitted hierarchical Bayesian models that account for patterns across space and time. More than 210,000 summer deaths fell in their complete sample.

Extreme heat and heatwaves both raised mortality even after adjusting for pollution and social factors, with effects appearing a few days after exposure. High ozone levels added risk, and the combination of extreme heat with high ozone was worse than either alone. Areas with greater income inequality and older populations also saw higher mortality. The authors argue adaptation plans should pair heat warnings with air quality management and equity-focused measures.
arxiv-2511-17348:
Ilaria Brivio and nine co-authors introduce POPxf, a data format for publishing theory predictions in particle physics. Many predictions, especially in effective field theory, are polynomials in the model's parameters, yet they are often shared in ad hoc tables that hinder reuse. POPxf encodes such polynomial observable predictions in a structured, machine-readable form, recording all assumptions and metadata.

The format, developed on behalf of the LHC Higgs and Effective Field Theory working groups, handles errors and correlations flexibly enough to capture effects that depend on the parameters themselves. The authors aim at three practical gains: predictions others can reproduce, easier global fits that combine many measurements, and smoother reuse of results under new models. A public archive hosts the spec. The paper is infrastructure work, meant to standardize how theory reaches lab analyses.
arxiv-2511-17448:
Yuqi Li and seven co-authors harden vision-language models against adversarial attacks by distilling robustness from two teachers at once. Single-teacher distillation transfers limited knowledge, converges slowly, and struggles to balance clean accuracy against robust accuracy. Their framework, MMT-ARD, fuses two teachers with complementary roles, one preserving clean features and one enhancing robust ones, so the student model learns both kinds of knowledge together.

A dynamic weighting strategy, driven by teacher confidence, focuses training on the hardest adversarial examples, while an adaptive sigmoid weighting curbs bias between the teachers and balances transfer across modalities. On ImageNet and zero-shot benchmarks, the method raised robust accuracy and zero-shot accuracy for a standard vision transformer student, and trained more than twice as fast as single-teacher approaches. The authors offer multi-teacher fusion as a scalable route to safer multimodal models.
arxiv-2511-17748:
Daniel Myrén, Zeeshan Afzal, and Mikael Asplund warn that flexible energy use in smart grids can be turned into a weapon. Aggregators control many batteries, chargers, and other flexible loads at once, so an attacker who seizes that control could shift large amounts of power suddenly.

The authors study attack plans that aim to break the grid's first swing of stability after a sudden change. They find that a lot of power is needed, yet current flexible capacity could in principle be enough to threaten a national grid. The work urges stronger guarding of aggregator systems.
arxiv-2511-17848:
Zhihui Tian, Ethan Suwandi, Tomas Oppelstrup, Vasily Bulatov, Joel Harley, and Fei Zhou speed up simulations of grain growth in materials, where a network of crystal grains changes over time. Graph neural networks model such networks well, but they struggle with the large cells needed for realistic structures.

Their design compresses space with a reversible convolutional autoencoder, then lets a graph network evolve the squeezed version. For the largest mesh tested, memory use and running time drop by more than a hundredfold compared with a graph only baseline. Accuracy and long term behavior improve as well, aiding realistic microstructure studies.
arxiv-2511-18148:
Shixiao Liang, Chengyuan Ma, Pei Li, and seven co-authors detect freeway crashes in real time, at the level of a single lane, using only sparse vehicle telematics data. Traditional crash reports arrive late and rarely pinpoint the lane, creating safety risks and economic losses while responders wait.

Offline, they grid past trajectories into spatial cells, learn normal vehicle intentions, and set an alert threshold from official crash records. Online, each cell accumulates risk from odd transitions, speed deviations, and risky lateral moves. On Wisconsin data the system identifies most crashes with accurate lane localization and very few false alarms, sometimes minutes early.
arxiv-2511-18248:
Wei Zhen Teoh tackles joint forecasting of player movements in team sports. Predicting each athlete alone is not enough: a useful forecast must give sets of paths that can happen together as one plausible play. Standard scores grade each agent's best single guess and can crown models whose joint futures make little sense as a team. Teoh argues this blind spot has shaped the field's designs for years.

The proposed model, CausalTraj, is built to produce jointly probable forecasts while respecting the arrow of time, using a likelihood-based design. Teoh also argues for judging models on the coherence and interpretability of whole multi-agent scenarios, not only per-agent accuracy. For analysts, coherent joint forecasts promise more realistic simulation of how a play unfolds.
arxiv-2511-18348:
Qingzheng Gao, Xiao-Jin Liu, Zhi-Qiang You, Zheng Li, and Xingjiang Zhu recheck the radio spectra of pulsars, the spinning remains of dead stars. Old wisdom held that most pulsar spectra follow a simple power law, a straight fall with frequency. The team test that claim on the largest clean set yet, with data for close to nine hundred pulsars.

A Bayesian model check, backed by classic tests, finds curved or broken shapes are the norm. A broken power law fits three in five pulsars, while the simple law fits just over one in ten. Dozens show a peak near a gigahertz, and fast spinning pulsars curve often. The old view, they show, was a quirk of the stats method then in use.
arxiv-2511-18448:
Shaoyu Liu, Jianing Li, Guanghui Zhao, Yunjian Zhang, and Xiangyang Ji build EventBench, a test suite for models that read event camera streams. Event cameras report pixel change as it comes, not frames, which suits fast motion and harsh light. Multimodal models have grown strong here, but no shared test yet spans their full skill range.

EventBench stands out in four ways. All raw streams and task prompts are open. Tasks span reading, naming, and space reasoning across eight scores. It adds 3D space tasks, a first for this field. A training set tops a million event text pairs. Scores across models show where event based reading lags and where it leads.
arxiv-2511-19048:
Teodor Kostić and six co-authors test if two spectral lines that probe two heights in the Sun's air can pin how sideways flows change with depth. Horizontal flows near the surface drive much of solar weather's seed motion. One line views the photosphere; a second, magnesium line views the temperature minimum layer above it.

Feasibility is checked in a simulated solar atmosphere from the MURaM code, where true flows are known at four depths. Correlation tracking follows the line of sight magnetic field inferred from synthetic polarimetric views of both lines. The tracked flows are then matched against the true height dependent speeds. Two eyes at two heights may yield a depth profile of surface flow.
arxiv-2511-19148:
P. Rivière-Marichalar and six co-authors observe the young star HL Tau to trace where the chemistry of planet-forming disks comes from. Disks inherit material from their birth cloud, but heat and light can rework that material. Comparing the disk with its surrounding envelope shows how much chemistry is preserved and how much is reset.

New NOEMA telescope data target four sulfur-bearing and related species: CS, H2CO, H2S, and SO2. Maps of the detected emission reveal where each molecule sits and how it moves. Column density ratios differ sharply between disk and envelope, especially for CS against H2S, pointing to real chemical change during disk formation.
arxiv-2511-19248:
Md Akil Raihan Iftee and five co-authors expose a security hole in federated learning, where client models adapt to local data at test time. That on-the-fly personalization helps with shifting data, but it also opens a door: a compromised client can feed poisoned inputs and send harmful updates that spread through shared training.

Their attack framework, FedPoisonTTP, works under grey-box knowledge. It builds a stand-in model from probing queries, crafts poisons that look like normal data, and tunes them to slip past common adaptation filters. On corrupted vision benchmarks, a few bad participants sharply drag down test-time performance for the whole system.
arxiv-2511-19448:
Juri Zach and Peer Stelldinger introduce PuzzlePoles, cylindrical visual markers that machines can read from any side. Autonomous systems rely on known marker patterns that cameras recognise for setup and location fixes, but flat markers fail when viewed edge-on or from behind. The PuzzlePole wraps the PuzzleBoard pattern, with its distinctive puzzle structure, around a pole, so recognition and pose estimation work across the full circle of viewing directions.

The pattern's uniqueness supports accurate location and orientation while tolerating partial blocking, since a visible slice can still identify the pole. The design adapts to many uses, from robot navigation and live mapping to tangible interfaces that people handle. The authors present the marker as a flexible addition to the sensing toolkit for autonomous systems.
arxiv-2511-19648:
Manil Shrestha and Edward Kim present two hybrid algorithms for answering questions that need several hops across a knowledge graph. Each hop multiplies the possible reasoning paths, Recent systems lean on repeated language model calls to link entities and rank paths, which is slow and can leave answers ungrounded in the graph. The first algorithm spends a single model call to predict the sequence of relations the answer needs, then executes that plan with a breadth-first search, so every answer is verifiably grounded.

The second removes the model entirely, scoring edges with a small neural network that fuses text and graph embeddings. It runs more than a hundred times faster with competitive accuracy, the authors report, while the planned search reaches near-perfect accuracy on their tests. Together the pair offer a choice between maximum grounding and maximum speed.
arxiv-2511-19748:
T Rouabhia and A Boumali solve the Kemmer oscillator exactly in the curved spacetime of a steadily accelerating observer. The Kemmer equation describes spin-one particles such as vector bosons, and its oscillator version adds a special interaction borrowed from the Dirac oscillator. The work uses Rindler coordinates, the frame of constant acceleration where a seeming temperature arises. The authors first build eigenvalue equations like those of a simpler scalar theory in the same coordinates.

Adding the oscillator interaction through a momentum swap yields a closed-form energy spectrum. Acceleration changes the oscillator's length scale, shifts the discrete energy levels, and lifts degeneracies that flat space would keep. When acceleration is sent to zero, the standard flat-space Kemmer oscillator spectrum returns, as it must. The exact solution gives a tractable model of bosons under extreme acceleration.
arxiv-2511-19948:
Bradley E Schaefer tests a popular idea about where normal Type Ia supernovae come from. The symbiotic idea says the exploding white dwarf's partner must be a red giant with a heavy wind. That claim makes sharp predictions that can be checked in remnants, old images, spectra, and early light from many past explosions.

Schaefer gathers tests covering many normal supernovae of this type: searches for leftover red giants, pre-eruption images, hydrogen and helium lines, radio and X-ray signals, and early brightening. None of the tested systems shows the needed red giant companion. He concludes that symbiotic systems make up, at most, a tiny fraction of normal Type Ia progenitors, far too small to measure.
arxiv-2511-20648:
Man, Wang, Zhang, and co-authors teach vision-language models to locate objects in 3D. Their 2025 paper presents LocateAnything3D with a Chain-of-Sight recipe. Language-vision models describe flat images well but rarely judge depth. Multi-object 3D detection from one camera stayed a specialist task. Their method recasts detection as next-token prediction.

The model first reports 2D detections like a visual chain of thought. Distance, size, and pose estimates follow in order. Objects are handled nearest first, easing early ambiguity. Each box factors into center, dimensions, and rotation. That ordering ranks facts by stability and learnability. Open-vocabulary and visual prompting abilities survive intact. On the Omni3D benchmark the model set a new best score. Its 49.89 average precision beat the prior champion clearly. The margin was over fifteen points absolute. Zero-shot tests on unseen categories also held up well.
arxiv-2511-20748:
Kanako Narita and colleagues report in 2025 a blind hunt for line-emitting galaxies in the ALMA Lensing Cluster Survey. The survey pointed the ALMA radio array at 33 galaxy clusters, whose gravity magnifies faint galaxies behind them. Magnification typically runs about fourfold, reaching thirtyfold in extreme cases. A blind spectral scan avoids the target-selection biases of earlier surveys.

The search found seven line emitters, including one shining in ionised carbon at redshift 6.071, deep in the early universe. Four emit carbon monoxide at redshifts 0.8 to 1.1, though three are multiple lensed images of one galaxy. Lensing let the sample reach molecular gas masses about ten times below previous blind-survey limits, and most emitters follow known scaling relations. The bonus was a CH signal from a galaxy at redshift 1.142, the first such detection from an individual galaxy at cosmological distance in a blind survey.
arxiv-2511-21048:
Jingtao Guo and Yuyi Mao count crowds in 2025 using Wi-Fi signals, without cameras and without pooling anyone's raw data. Channel state information from Wi-Fi reveals how bodies disturb the radio environment, but every site differs, and sharing sensing data across sites raises privacy risks. Their FedAPA system trains federated models at each site. Instead of averaging all clients' prototypes with fixed weights, it weights peer prototypes by similarity, so each client receives a personalised global prototype suited to its environment.

Local training mixes classification with contrastive learning that aligns local with global knowledge, and the authors supply a convergence proof. In a real distributed test across six environments with up to 20 people, FedAPA beat multiple baselines across the board. Accuracy rose by at least 9.65 percent, the F1 score by 9 percent, and mean absolute error fell by 0.29 people. Communication overhead dropped by 95.94 percent, making the approach cheap to run.
arxiv-2511-21148:
Two shapes with the same area are equidecomposable if one can be cut into finitely many pieces that reassemble into the other, as in Tarski's 1925 circle-squaring puzzle. Mark Mordechai Etkind, Sigrid Grepstad, Mihail Kolountzakis, and Nir Lev prove in 2025 that such reassemblies can be done with measurable pieces in two modern settings. Their tool is the measurable Hall theorem of Cieśla and Sabok, which turns an abstract matching into a measurable one.

First, any two measurable sets of equal measure that are bounded remainder sets, meaning their counting error stays bounded, for one irrational direction vector are equidecomposable using only lattice translations. Second, when two cut-and-project sets sit at bounded distance, their defining windows are equidecomposable the same way. For one-dimensional sets, a separate argument even makes the pieces Riemann measurable, a stronger niceness condition.
arxiv-2511-21248:
Irene Schimperna, Lea Bold, Johannes Köhler, Karl Worthmann, and Lalo Magni examine when a controller steered by a learned model can be trusted, in 2025. Model predictive control plans moves by simulating the future, and data-driven Koopman models are popular stand-ins for the true physics. The catch is approximation error: the surrogate is never exact, so stability guarantees can evaporate unless the error is controlled.

Schimperna and her coauthors prove that control with end-point terminal conditions stays recursively feasible. It also settles to its target when the model's error obeys a proportional bound, growing at most linearly with state and input size. They show kernel-based Koopman models, built by the kEDMD algorithm, meet that condition for a broad class of nonlinear systems. A numerical case study confirms the framework, though the authors flag its cautious constraint tightening as a drawback.
arxiv-2511-21448:
Rebeka Tóth, Tamas Bisztray, and Richard Dubniczky build a richer trap for deceptive email in 2025. Phishing and spam now arrive polished by large language models, and detectors need training data that captures the manipulation, not just the message. Their dataset sorts mail into phishing, spam, and legitimate. It flags whether a human or an LLM wrote each item. It also labels each item's emotional appeal, like urgency, fear, or authority, plus its underlying motive.

Tóth and her coauthors benchmarked several LLMs at spotting those emotional and motivational cues, found their reliability moderate and uneven, and used the best model to annotate the full collection. They also generated rephrased versions of the emails, meaning preserved but wording changed, and graded a leading LLM against expert labels on both versions. Detection of phishing proved strong, while telling spam from legitimate mail remained a persistent weakness.
arxiv-2511-21548:
Wen-Tai Hsu studies how long a wandering particle stays trapped inside a network of narrow tubes, in 2025. The domain is built from a finite graph: thin tubes along its edges and small chambers at its vertices, in two or three dimensions. Narrow passages act as entropic barriers, so the diffusion lingers in one chamber for ages before hopping onward, a phenomenon called metastability.

Hsu identifies a whole sequence of characteristic time scales, one per vertex, and characterizes the process at intermediate scales and at the first critical scale where hopping begins. The analysis leans on the narrow escape problem, estimating where a particle exits a chamber and how long escape takes given that exit point. Those estimates stand as results of independent interest for diffusion in bottlenecked domains, wherever geometry alone creates long trapping times.
arxiv-2511-21648:
Tianchen Zhao decides when symmetries of a special surface survive its degeneration, in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. K3 and Enriques surfaces are central objects of surface classification. Their arithmetic versions live over local fields, where a surface has good reduction if it extends to a smooth model over the ring of integers. A finite group acting on the surface may or may not extend to that model.

Zhao gives a criterion for extendability. It is read off from the group's action on the second ℓ-adic cohomology, the surface's topological fingerprint in this arithmetic setting. The result generalizes work of Chiarellotto, Lazda, and Liedtke on Galois actions on K3 surfaces. A corollary follows: a symplectic linear action always extends when the residue characteristic does not divide the group's order. Zhao ties the good reduction of Enriques surfaces to that of their K3 double covers, so results transfer between them.
arxiv-2511-21848:
Leonardis and colleagues build a computer simulation of a mouse reaching with its front leg, aiming to understand how brains control bodies. Starting from motion-capture of mice reaching for a water droplet, they register movements onto a musculoskeletal forelimb model with nine muscle actuators in the MuJoCo simulator. An imitation learning system then learns to reproduce the recorded reaches by trial and error.

GPU acceleration with JAX let training run at more than one million steps per second across parallel simulation copies. The key experiment added realistic limits on how large the control signals could be, mimicking what real muscles can do. With those naturalistic constraints, the simulated muscle activity predicted the real electrical signals measured from the animals' muscles, called EMG, noticeably better than unconstrained versions did in the comparisons reported. Control constraints, they argue, are a critical ingredient for modelling biological movement.
arxiv-2511-22148:
Rahman and colleagues examine a weak point in quantum federated learning. Many quantum devices train a shared model without pooling their private data. Most existing frameworks quietly assume all clients are alike. Real clients differ in their data, their encodings, their hardware noise, and their computing power. The team sorts this variation into two kinds, data heterogeneity and system heterogeneity. Quantum methods promise speed and scale from effects like superposition and entanglement.

They trace how the differences slow training, destabilize it, and drag down model quality. They then grade the known fixes and spell out where each one falls short. A case study shows that tackling the variation head-on is workable in practice. The authors close with open problems for making the approach robust on real, mixed hardware. The message is that heterogeneity must be designed for, not assumed away.
arxiv-2511-22348:
Jia, Ling, Bai, Zhao, and Zhai are computer engineers in Beijing and Hong Kong. They schedule neural networks onto AI accelerator chips by gradient descent instead of search. Deployment choices interact awkwardly: how each layer is tiled onto the hardware and which adjacent layers are fused into one execution both change memory traffic, energy, and latency. Existing tools optimize them separately or by slow heuristic search. FADiff builds a single differentiable cost model predicting energy and latency for mappings and fusion strategies alike, folding the discrete choices into a loss so gradients can explore the joint space.

As one continuous optimization, the framework finds joint strategies layer-wise methods miss, with substantial energy-delay product improvements over prior tools. The analytical model keeps sensitivities explicit, so designers see which choices drive cost. The approach scales where combinatorial search stalls.
arxiv-2511-22548:
Lattanzi and colleagues measure a molecule astronomers may soon hunt for in space. Thionylimide, HNSO, mixes sulfur, nitrogen, and oxygen, and its bent cis form was recently detected in a Galactic Centre cloud. The higher-energy trans form had never been characterised at high resolution. Using a free-space spectrometer with a hollow-cathode discharge source, the team produced trans-HNSO in the laboratory and recorded its rotational spectrum.

They assigned 104 transitions between 200 and 530 gigahertz, fitted to a root-mean-square deviation of 40 kilohertz, matching high-level quantum chemistry predictions closely. The trans form sits only slightly higher in energy. Its larger dipole makes its lines more than five times brighter than the cis form's at equal abundance. That is a strong incentive to search. The measurements provide the rest frequencies telescopes need, and may let astronomers test whether quantum tunnelling reshuffles the two forms in cold clouds.
arxiv-2511-22748:
Osmanov asks where a galaxy-spanning civilization would park its structures. On the Kardashev scale, a Type-III civilization harnesses a whole galaxy's energy, and Dyson-style megastructures are technosignatures astronomers might actually spot. Osmanov considers megastructures orbiting a galaxy far from its center, where the galaxy's own radiation fades to the level of the cosmic microwave background. The structure is not swamped by galactic light.

For a Milky Way-like galaxy, he estimates where a solar-mass megastructure would need to sit: the orbit's radius exceeds the galaxy's radius by several times. The energetics work out kindly: even lifting a solar mass into such an orbit poses no energy problem for a Type-III civilization. Detectability is addressed too: such objects could betray themselves through microlensing, and the angular resolution required looks promising for instruments. The paper extends the Dyson sphere idea from stars to whole galaxies.
arxiv-2511-22848:
Del Gaudio, Ghimenti, and Ganguli show how fast, temporary synaptic changes can rescue memories already lost. Their model is a continuous Hopfield memory, the classic network storing patterns as attractors, augmented with rapid short-term associative plasticity strengthening synapses between co-active neurons, then decaying. Using the cavity method, they map the boundary between retrieval and the forgetting spin-glass phase as memories accumulate.

Capacity barely moves: plasticity yields only marginal gains in storable memories. The drama is above capacity. Dynamical mean field theory and simulations show the combined dynamics descending an energy landscape over neurons and synapses, dipping near recently visited patterns, like a trampoline under a ball. Without plasticity, retrieval attempts swing toward a stored memory and escape; with it, the sagging landscape traps them there. An optimal plasticity time constant maximises the rescue, a mechanism with obvious resonance for working memory.
arxiv-2511-23048:
Volkov and colleagues report the first detection of a ground level enhancement, a sudden surge of cosmic-ray particles at Earth's surface caused by a solar flare. They used neutron detectors built for a different job. Their instruments belong to the NEVOD complex in Moscow and were designed to study extensive air showers, the cascades sparked by high-energy cosmic rays. An upgrade added channels that track the neutron flux.

The event, catalogued as GLE 77, followed an X-class solar flare on November 11, 2025, and both NEVOD arrays, PRISMA-36 and URAN, registered the jump starting at 10:15 universal time. In five-minute averaged data the counting rate peaked 20.1 percent above background on PRISMA-36 and 24.8 percent on URAN, close to the 21 percent rise at the nearby Moscow neutron monitor. This supports adding such air-shower detectors, 108 of them at NEVOD, to the global monitoring network.
arxiv-2512-00148:
Galaxies like the Milky Way formed inside dark matter halos shaped by both cosmic and local physics. Jonah Rose and a large team introduce the DREAMS Project in 2025, a suite of one thousand and twenty-four simulations. Each run zooms in on a Milky Way-mass halo with cold dark matter.

Every simulation uses its own initial conditions and its own mix of cosmological and astrophysical parameters. Comparing the runs shows which outcomes depend on physics choices and which are robust. The suite gives astronomers a context for the real Milky Way and a way to measure how uncertain their conclusions are. A suite this large turns single-simulation anecdotes into statistics that can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-00448:
The rough Bergomi model captures how market volatility actually behaves, but calibrating it is notoriously hard. Changqing Teng and Guanglian Li propose a computational framework for efficient calibration in 2025, using Wasserstein distance. The model's non-Markovian structure causes both pricing and calibration difficulties.

The authors aim to enhance simulation as well as calibration in one framework. Wasserstein distance measures how far the model's implied distributions sit from market ones, giving calibration a clear target. Faster, reliable calibration makes a realistic volatility model usable on a trading desk, not just in research papers. Wasserstein distance is borrowed from optimal transport, where it measures earth-moving cost. Rough volatility matches market data better than smooth models, which motivates the effort. For a desk that must mark its book each day, the gain is trust. The model can be fit to the tape fast, and the fit can be checked with care.
arxiv-2512-00748:
Ke Liu, Shangde Gao, Yichao Fu, and Shangqi Gao tackle a hard truth in medical imaging in a 2025 paper. When experts outline organs or tumors in a scan, they often disagree. Boundaries can be fuzzy, and each rater brings their own judgment to the task.

Older methods tried to produce one single outline, hiding that spread of opinion. This team models the segmentation task probabilistically, with several raters in mind. Their approach keeps the diversity of expert views instead of averaging it away. It can also adapt to a particular rater's style, which helps doctors get outlines that match how they work.
arxiv-2512-00948:
Benedikt Kantz and six coauthors let people query knowledge graphs in plain words in a 2025 paper. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities, but querying them usually takes a special query language, a question-answering system, or a visual editor. Each route demands skills many users lack.

Their approach has users describe a prototype graph in natural language, then edit it visually. Constrained language models turn the words into a draft query graph that follows the graph's ontology. The user then fixes the draft by sight before running it. Joining language with visual editing could open graph data to far more people.
arxiv-2512-01048:
Maya Varma and four coauthors present TRoVe in a 2025 paper on video-language models. These models handle temporal tasks, questions about how a scene changes across frames. Yet recent work suggests they often lean on static cues, like background or a single object's look, instead of real change.

TRoVe discovers error-inducing static feature biases in such models. It hunts for the frozen features that trick a model into wrong answers on temporal questions. Exposing those shortcuts matters for safety and science uses, where change over time is the whole point. A model that ignores motion should not be trusted with surveillance or sports video.
arxiv-2512-01148:
Hamza Tahboub, Weiyan Shi, Gang Hua, and Huaizu Jiang present SocialFusion in a 2025 paper on social AI. Understanding social interactions from visual cues is fundamental for an AI that behaves competently around people. Powerful pretrained vision-language models do well at many tasks, yet they struggle to learn several social perception tasks at once.

Training them jointly often causes negative transfer, where learning one task hurts another. SocialFusion addresses this social degradation in pretrained models. Fixing it matters for uses like reading group photos, classroom scenes, or workplace video. A socially competent model must keep many social skills at once.
arxiv-2512-01248:
Junyuan Zhang and a large team present TRivia in a 2025 paper on table recognition. Table recognition turns a picture of a table into a structured form like HTML or Markdown. It is a core part of document parsing, and it has long relied on supervised learning with labeled examples.

Recent work fine-tunes vision-language models on those labels at scale. TRivia instead fine-tunes such models in a self-supervised way for table recognition. Learning without hand-labeled tables could make document tools cheaper to build for new languages and layouts. Accurate table extraction underpins search, finance, and research tools that read documents.
arxiv-2512-01348:
Sayantan Dey, Alireza Alaei, and Partha Pratim Roy tackle reading handwriting in scarce languages. Tools for neat printed text are strong now. Hand-written text at the scale of a full page is much harder. The task is worse for tongues like Hindi and Urdu with few digital aids.

Scripts in those tongues link letters in ways that foil simple cuts. The team works on page-level reading for such scripts. Their aim is robust optical reading that needs fewer aids. Better tools would open books, forms, and notes in those tongues to search and study.
arxiv-2512-01748:
Stella Etuk and Ashraf Matrawy add sensitivity-aware privacy to language model training. Models can memorize training text, which risks leaking private facts. Differential privacy adds noise to guard that data. Classic methods add the same noise to all parameters.

Uniform noise wastes privacy budget on low-risk parts. Their SA-ADP method scales noise by sensitivity. Sensitive parts get more guard, dull parts get less. That split aims to keep model quality higher at the same privacy level for downstream tasks. Sensitivity scores come from the training data itself, so no hand-made list of private fields is needed before the method can run.
arxiv-2512-01848:
Jinghan Jia, Nathalie Baracaldo, and Sijia Liu make large reasoning models safer with reinforcement learning. Reasoning models write out thought chains. That helps math and logic a lot. It also creates new safety risks inside the chain itself. Unsafe acts can hide in middle steps while final answers look clean.

Training past supervised fine-tuning is their route. Reinforcement signals reward safe reasoning, not just safe endings. The team aims to lift reasoning skill and safety together. Safer chains matter as reasoning models move into health, law, and finance work. Reward design targets the chain, not just the answer, which is where the paper locates the new risk in reasoning models.
arxiv-2512-01948:
Deep research agents are AI systems meant to write analyst-level reports by searching, reading, and synthesizing sources on their own. A 2025 paper from the OPPO AI Agent Team asks how close these systems are to being genuinely useful, rather than merely impressive on question-answering tests.

Most existing agents were validated on benchmarks of short answers, while the harder job of writing a full report went largely unmeasured. The benchmarks that do test reports suffer from fuzzy tasks and subjective scoring, which hides real user needs. The authors' assessment aims to ground the field in what people actually ask research agents to produce.
arxiv-2512-02148:
The flavors of quarks and leptons follow a pattern no one fully understands, and theories that explain it invoke symmetries broken at enormous energies. Anna Chrysostomou and four co-authors show in 2025 that breaking such a flavour symmetry in the early universe could ring gravitational waves loud enough to hear.

They use a flavour gauge group as their working example, with symmetry breaking at scales far beyond any collider's reach. A phase transition at those energies would leave a gravitational-wave signal that future observatories might detect. That turns an untestable high-energy idea into an observational target, one of the few handles on physics at such extremes.
arxiv-2512-02248:
A pulsar's flicker can be unfolded to remove the smearing caused by interstellar gas, a trick called cyclic deconvolution, but only for the right pulsars and telescopes. Jacob Turner evaluates in 2025 the prospects for the technique across a sample of hundreds of pulsars with fast spin periods.

Using the cyclic figure of merit, he rates the chances for many telescope and frequency combinations. He finds the most promising frequency range sits at low frequencies, making observatories like uGMRT, LOFAR, and the MWA the best-suited instruments. A clear prospect map tells observers where cyclic spectroscopy can realistically deliver ultra-sharp views of pulsar emission.
arxiv-2512-02748:
Philip Schaten and co-authors add live streaming to BART, a toolbox for magnetic resonance imaging reconstruction. Interactive real time MRI needs modular parts that pass data along a pipeline without pausing. Rebuilding images while the scan runs lets operators adjust on the fly.

A new protocol streams multidimensional arrays into BART's reconstruction algorithms. Demonstrations use radial FLASH imaging, mixing iterative reconstruction with dynamic coil compression and gradient delay correction. Live, modular reconstruction could shorten scans and improve imaging for moving organs, children, and guided interventions. Live views let a tech move the scan while the child still lies still, which cuts the need for a second pass in most cases.
arxiv-2512-03048:
Austin Spizzirri argues that AI alignment should grow well formed agents rather than stamp values into them. Encoding fixed human value content hits a specification trap, he argues. That trap joins the is ought gap, deep value pluralism, and an extended frame problem into one structural instability.

His syntropic frameworks paper proposes process based, multi agent, developmental mechanisms instead. Agents would become reasons responsive through growth, not through frozen rules. Philosophical groundwork of this kind shapes how labs and lawmakers frame the alignment problem before technical choices harden. Fixed lists of right and wrong age fast in a world that shifts. Growth based frames may age with more grace than rule books cast in stone at one point.
arxiv-2512-03148:
Two models of strongly linked electrons may in fact be one. Yuting Bai and Philip Phillips prove that claim in this 2025 work. One model is the Hatsugai-Kohmoto model with momentum mixing, and the other is the Hubbard model with a twist.

Their proof shows the first model equals the twisted Hubbard model. They then use a known result that a twist does not change bulk physics. So the two models share the same bulk behavior in the charge sector. The result can simplify study of these hard electron systems. Charge behavior is often the part experiments probe first, so the proof has direct value.
arxiv-2512-03348:
Dark matter might slowly decay over cosmic time. Javier Juarez Jimenez and Ana Avilez-López forecast how well future surveys can test that idea in this 2025 work. They focus on two numbers: the share of dark matter that is unstable, and its decay rate.

Their forecasts use redshift-space distortions, patterns in galaxy positions caused by motion. They apply a Fisher matrix method with data expected from Euclid and BOSS. Clear forecasts tell survey teams what precision to aim for. They also show whether decaying dark matter can be told apart from the standard model. Redshift distortions are already measured by surveys, so forecasts rest on proven data types.
arxiv-2512-03548:
Aircraft that take off vertically must tilt into forward flight smoothly. Zexin Lin and co-authors present a learning-based control method in this 2025 work. The tilting rotor shifts the center of gravity and thrust direction during transition.

Current methods control altitude and position separately. That split causes strong vibration and limits adaptability. A learned controller that handles the coupled dynamics could smooth the transition. Safer transitions matter for air taxis and delivery drones now in development. Learning control can adapt to each aircraft, rather than one fixed model for all, which matters as tilting designs vary between makers.
arxiv-2512-03648:
Emma Brink examines a new kind of group cohomology that grows out of condensed mathematics, a framework built by Clausen and Scholze. Cohomology is a tool algebraists use to measure the shape and twists of a system. In the condensed setting, groups that vary smoothly get their own derived tools. Brink's 2025 arXiv paper asks how this new version compares with older ones.

She finds the condensed version is often finer, picking up detail the classic tool misses. Still, for a broad class of groups, the classic version with solid coefficients can be rebuilt inside the condensed world. That bridge lets results pass between the two frames. The paper also revisits core parts of condensed math with care for size issues in set theory. It lays out a sheaf framework that keeps large sites safe to use.
arxiv-2512-03748:
Many future devices, from magnetic memory to brain-inspired chips, depend on magnetic fields that vary across tiny structures. Orlando D. Cunha and colleagues show in a 2025 quantum sensing preprint how to photograph those fields with full direction information. Their tool uses nitrogen-vacancy centres, atomic defects in diamond that respond to magnetism, mounted on an ordinary commercial microscope.

The team adapted the microscope to run a pulsed measurement protocol that reads the shifts of all four defect orientations. From those shifts they rebuild the stray-field vector above microfabricated permalloy structures with several stable magnetic states. Images resolve details near half a micrometre across a wide field of view, and each acquisition takes only a few minutes. The authors present the setup as a practical, scalable way to inspect complex magnetic devices routinely, rather than a one-off laboratory demonstration.
arxiv-2512-03848:
Heart imaging is usually split among separate programs: one outlines anatomy, another classifies disease, a third drafts clinical text. Hania Ghouse, Maryam Alsharqi, Farhad R. Nezami, and Muzammil Behzad unite those jobs in PULSE, a 2025 medical imaging preprint. Their multi-task vision-language framework learns all three skills inside a single architecture built on self-supervised representations.

A multi-scale decoder reconstructs anatomical segmentations, while shared global features support diagnosis and grounded report generation. Training balances several objectives at once, covering region overlap, pixel-level fidelity, and boundary quality. Because the model learns task-invariant features of the heart, it generalises across datasets and imaging types. It can also adapt to a new modality with only a few examples. The authors present PULSE as a step toward a foundation-style system for cardiac analysis that hospitals could scale.
arxiv-2512-04148:
Charged leptons like the electron are usually assumed to barely mix with heavy fermions. J. de Blas and colleagues show the mixing could reach twenty percent without breaking any rule, in a 2025 preprint. The loophole sits in effective field theory. When mixing effects cancel at tree level in the leading operators, or are suppressed by tiny lepton masses, experiments lose their grip.

Using a model that realises this scenario naturally through symmetries, the authors check every current direct and indirect constraint. The limits turn out so mild that, given the present lower bound on heavy fermion masses, theory itself supplies the strongest restrictions on the mixing. They then forecast future sensitivity at the high-luminosity LHC and the proposed FCC colliders. Hadron machines leave theory in charge, but FCC precision could finally measure the mixing squared to per-mille accuracy.
arxiv-2512-04248:
Generating a convincing 3D indoor scene is easy one view at a time and hard across views, where furniture slides and walls disagree. Shaoheng Fang and co-authors present MVRoom in a 2025 computer vision preprint, a pipeline for controllable scene generation built on multi-view diffusion. A coarse 3D layout is the control signal throughout.

The design has two stages. First, new representations bridge the layout and consistent image-based conditioning signals. Then an image-conditioned stage generates the views, using a layout-aware epipolar attention mechanism to keep them in agreement. An iterative wrapper repeats the process to build scenes with varying object counts and complexity, supporting text-to-scene building. Experiments show high-fidelity results, beating state-of-the-art baselines quantitatively and qualitatively, and ablations confirm the key components earn their place.
arxiv-2512-04448:
Jianglin Ma, Ben Yao, Xiang Li, and Yazhou Zhang ask whether ACL, long the top venue in language technology, still leads its field. Submissions to AI conferences have exploded in the language model era. Growth brought worries about plagiarism, thin reviewing, and rigged bidding. Most evidence so far is anecdote and interviews. Their 2025 arXiv paper replaces stories with ten years of hard numbers across seven leading conferences.

The study builds a four-part bibliometric frame: conference scale, citation counts, how impact spreads, and sway across venues and journals. A new metric, Quality-Quantity Elasticity, tracks how citation growth answers acceptance growth. The data span 2014 to 2024, the decade of deep learning's rise. Their findings chart which venues grew, which kept quality, and where impact thinned as volume soared. The results give the field a factual base for reform debates.
arxiv-2512-04548:
Ngo Phuc Duc Loc uses gravitational waves to limit how many ultra-light regular primordial black holes could have filled the early universe. Primordial black holes are born from dense patches in the infant cosmos. Regular ones lack the singular core of standard holes, which changes how long they live. If the lightest of them once ruled the cosmos, their evaporation would leave a hum of induced gravitational waves. His 2025 arXiv paper turns that hum into a bound.

The chain runs from early ripples that differ between matter kinds to waves stirred at second order as the holes vanish. Limits on extra relativistic energy, drawn from nucleosynthesis and the microwave background, cap how strong that wave sea can be. Loc works the scheme out in full for the Simpson-Visser space. The result trims the allowed share of ultra-light regular holes.
arxiv-2512-04948:
Arkady Tseytlin and Zihan Wang review a subtle question about the supermembrane, a hypothetical sheet-like object in eleven-dimensional physics. The membrane's action, the formula that governs its motion, keeps part of the theory's overall symmetry as a symmetry on the membrane's own three-dimensional world. Unlike the string case, there is no simple spinning-membrane formula that captures this directly, so the authors build one step by step in a fixed gauge.

They construct a version of the action with the smallest amount of the symmetry and set it beside the full version tied to eleven dimensions. The two do not match in general, for a reason rooted in how the membrane's particles must be described, though they agree in four and five dimensions. One-loop scattering calculations confirm the split: the answers coincide in the lower dimensions and part ways in eleven.
arxiv-2512-05448:
Chen-Hui Niu and a large team of co-authors identify the most restless fast radio burst source known, and locate it inside the expanding wreckage of a supernova. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of radio energy, mostly seen once and never again. This source, designated FRB 20190520B, has stayed persistently active across roughly four years of watching — a first. It lets astronomers track how its dispersion measure, the delay imprinted by free electrons along the path, evolves over time.

The dispersion is falling steadily, at a rate far beyond any previous burst measurement and orders of magnitude beyond pulsars. A decline that large and consistent points to the burst sitting inside a dense, expanding ionized medium, most plausibly a young supernova remnant whose shell thins as it grows. The finding ties at least one repeater's home to the aftermath of a stellar explosion.
arxiv-2512-05648:
Igor Shilov and seven co-authors study how to keep dangerous knowledge out of a language model. Filtering training data is costly, and a few mislabeled harmful items can still teach a model risky skills. Earlier work routed such knowledge into a set-aside part of the network, so it could be cut out later. Their 2025 paper improves that idea with a method called Selective Gradient Masking.

The masking is strict: examples from the target domain may update only their dedicated parameters, and nothing else. The team tested the method by removing one language from a bilingual model, and biology knowledge from a model trained on Wikipedia. With noisy labels, it kept wanted skills while forgetting targeted ones better than filtering or the earlier routing scheme. It also resisted attempts to restore the removed knowledge by further training, needing about seven times more steps than a rival unlearning method.
arxiv-2512-06048:
Sahil Garg's paper is a field report from the front line where generative AI meets cybersecurity operations. An AI pipeline that cannot continually adapt becomes a liability. Garg draws lessons from running production grade generative systems for defense. Retrieval level adaptation refreshes what the model can look up; model level adaptation changes the model itself. The two complement each other inside a complete system, and the paper offers practical guidance on using each.

Best practices target robustness, precision, and auditability. Open research directions are flagged where current systems remain fragile. Practitioners get an actionable map of what breaks. An honest production account is worth more than another benchmark.
arxiv-2512-06248:
Cheng Cheng and Jinqiu Yang build a stricter way to grade code written by large language models, with a sharp eye on safety. Tools that write code can boost a programmer's speed, but they can also slip flaws into software. Old grading schemes lean on one score that compares new code with a sample answer, and that score can miss real faults and reward shallow matches.

Their framework, CFCEval, adds a fresh test set built to avoid overlap with training data. Grading covers four sides. It checks how well the code is written, whether it can fix known flaws, and whether it still works after the code is reshaped. It also checks how well the code matches what was asked. A new score tracks human judgment more closely than the old one. The study gives teams a fuller way to check code tools before they trust them.
arxiv-2512-06348:
Xiaoyu Ma, Likun Zhang, and Christopher Wikle build a model for extreme weather that strikes many places at once. Floods, heat, and storms rarely hit a single spot; their joint pattern across space and time shapes true risk. That pattern can shift as climate drivers change, so a fixed model may miss how extremes team up or drift apart.

Their model, a conditional form of a variational autoencoder, lets big climate indices steer the inner code behind weather fields. A convolutional network in the decoder blends those indices with the spatial ties in the data. Tests on simulated fields show it copies real patterns well and recovers how joint extremes vary, at low cost once trained. It also offers a simple test for whether the extreme pattern depends on a climate driver. When it does, users can run what if trials to price the change in joint risk.
arxiv-2512-06448:
Takaaki Tateishi and Yasuharu Katsuno tackle a hard corner of a common business task: rewriting old enterprise software in a modern language. Companies hold vast systems in PL/I, an aging language, and want them in Java. The snag is the macro procedures: small programs that spit out PL/I code as text. A translator must match what the generated code does, not just what the macro says, and language models often stumble there.

Their fix, called templatization, runs the macros symbolically, treating unknown values as named placeholders, and turns the result into code templates. Those templates become the bridge handed to a language model, which fills them in as readable Java that a team can maintain. In an early trial, translation through templates gave Java matching the macro generated code. It aims at legacy systems too big to rewrite by hand.
arxiv-2512-06748:
Zhichao Dong and five co authors extend quantum key distribution so many users can share one uplink at once. Quantum key distribution lets parties grow a secret key whose safety rests on physics, a building block for a future quantum internet. Sharing it among many users under attack is the hard part. Their system uses a non orthogonal access scheme with continuous variable states of light, peeled apart by a quantum successive cancellation receiver.

The authors bound the key rates users can achieve and the information an eavesdropper could gain, in closed form, under collective attacks. A power allocation algorithm then tunes each user's signal to maximize the total secret rate, with a guarantee of settling at a locally best point. In simulations the shared scheme beat an orthogonal rival by a clear margin, served many users at once, and stayed robust as turbulence and distance varied.
arxiv-2512-06848:
Sepyan Purnama Kristanto, Lutfi Hakim, and Hermansyah build a small, low-power system that watches drinking water for germs and sudden changes in quality. Two kinds of evidence usually sit apart: microscope images show the organisms themselves, while chemical sensors track fast shifts in the water. Their framework, AquaFusionNet, joins both streams in one model light enough to run on cheap edge hardware.

A gated attention step lets the model learn how what the microscope sees lines up with what the sensors report at the same moment. The team trained it on a new set of annotated water micrographs they assembled, since public sets for drinking water are scarce. Run for six months at seven sites in East Java, Indonesia, the system caught contamination events with high accuracy while drawing little power. Joining the two views also cut failures caused by dirty lenses, cloudy water, and uneven light.
arxiv-2512-07648:
Georges Bouzerar and Maxime Thumin wrote this 2025 physics paper on superconductivity in flat-band systems. Flat bands, where electrons barely gain energy by moving, may host very hot superconductivity. Disorder is the usual enemy of such states, wrecking them in ordinary materials.

The authors test that enemy on a two-dimensional Lieb lattice model. In conventional superconductivity, disorder slashes the critical temperature fast. The drop is steep and linear as disorder grows from zero. Flat-band superconductivity behaves strikingly differently in their study. For weak off-diagonal disorder, its critical temperature falls only quadratically. That gentle slope means the state shrugs off fluctuations and localization. Purity has long been a hard barrier when making new superconductors. If flat-band compounds forgive impurities this well, synthesis gets far easier. The authors frame the result as good news for materials hunting. Robustness, not just peak temperature, becomes a design asset.
arxiv-2512-07748:
Alan Kahan, Pablo Viñas, Torsten Zache, and Alejandro Bermudez wrote this 2025 quantum physics paper. The Jackiw-Rebbi model is a classic field theory in one space dimension. Its soliton waves can bind fermion states that carry fractional electric charge.

The authors design a trapped-ion simulator to realize that model in the lab. Ions near a structural transition zigzag in a plane, playing the scalar field's role. Their inner states encode spins, linked by sound waves. A zigzag coupling pattern completes the Yukawa-coupled Dirac picture. Most studies freeze the soliton and let fermions move on it. This work instead lets the full system push back on itself. A Born-Oppenheimer step reveals how fermion back-reaction can pin the kink in place.  Quantum spreading and localization of the kink both emerge in that treatment. Today's ion machines could seek the signatures.
arxiv-2512-07848:
Di Zhu, Chen Xie, Ziwei Wang, and Haoyun Zhang wrote this 2025 paper on predicting harm in city car crashes. New York City logs well over a hundred thousand collisions a year. Knowing which crashes will injure people guides prevention and response.

Their pipeline, RaX-Crash, favors small, explainable models over giant ones. It merges three linked city tables holding tens of millions of records. A unified feature design lives in partitioned storage for the training. Compact tree ensembles, a random forest and a gradient-boosted model, learn the patterns. Small language models, fed text summaries, enter as a comparison arm. On a test set held out by time, the trees win clearly. The language models trail far behind both ensembles in accuracy. Simple class weighting lifts recall of fatal cases at a modest cost. Importance analysis names human vulnerability, timing, and location as top drivers.
arxiv-2512-08048:
Chandler Timm Cagmat Doloriel and colleagues, machine learning researchers, posted a systematic study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is continual test time adaptation, where a model must keep adjusting as new, shifted data streams in. Many recent methods use masked image modeling to stay stable, but each fixes one masking family and varies only how masks are chosen.

Their testbed, called Mask to Adapt, holds the selection strategy and losses fixed while varying the masking family itself. They compare spatial masks, which hide patches or pixels, with frequency masks that hide bands of image frequency. On patch based transformer models, spatial masking built stable representations over long streams while frequency masking collapsed badly. On convolutional networks the gap vanished, and for some fine grained tasks frequency masking became competitive. The study turns those contrasts into design guidance.
arxiv-2512-08348: Laurence Carassus and Miklos Rasonyi, mathematicians who work on finance models, posted a paper on arXiv in December 2025. They study an investor who seeks the best expected payoff, yet also judges the result against a reference entity. That comparison can change what counts as best. A personal equilibrium is a strategy that stays best under this self check. The authors prove such an equilibrium exists in a multistep market model that is generically incomplete, under suitable technical assumptions.
arxiv-2512-08448:
Liyi Gu, Keigo Fukumura, Jelle Kaastra, and a large international team of X ray astronomers posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. During a 2024 campaign led by the XRISM satellite, the active galaxy NGC 3783 launched an ultrafast outflow at a fifth of light speed. The launch coincided with the sharp decay of a bright soft X ray and ultraviolet flare, all within half a day.

The outflow shows narrow iron lines with modest spread, pointing to a dense clump of gas as its source. Weaker outflow hints appear through the whole flare, their speeds climbing over about three days, as if the clump rides inside a larger stream. Radiation pressure cannot drive this acceleration. The outflow motion instead mirrors solar coronal mass ejections, the great eruptions of the Sun corona. That resemblance implicates magnetic driving, likely reconnection near the accretion disk, behind both the launch and the flare.
arxiv-2512-08748:
Stefania Perciballi describes an upgrade to the inner tracking system of the ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. The three innermost layers will be replaced during the next long shutdown. The new detector uses wafer scale pixel sensors, made in a modern imaging process, thinned greatly and bent around the beam pipe into a truly cylindrical shape.

Only two sensors per layer are needed, held by minimal supports, and air cooling replaces water cooling. That change cuts the material per layer to a small fraction of the current value, which sharpens tracking. A new sensor variant improves charge collection speed while keeping fine spatial resolution, very high detection efficiency, and strong radiation tolerance. Large prototypes show wide active area and very low fake hit rates. Timing tests on a small structure reach tens of picoseconds in resolution.
arxiv-2512-08848:
Lucas Hataishi proves that the Drinfeld center, in unitary form, of a unitary tensor class can be rebuilt as a class of unitary bimodules for a canonical algebra object. That result extends a theorem of Mueger to the non fusion case, where the category need not be finite. The proof uses a monadic reconstruction method suited to the unitary and operator algebra setting.

The author then applies the result to express factorization homology through operator algebra based extensions of symmetric enveloping algebras. Actions of Drinfeld doubles of compact quantum groups also enter the description. The work connects abstract category theory with operator algebras and topological field theory tools.
arxiv-2512-09648:
Mateusz Kupper and colleagues present Optyx, a Python library for building networked quantum computers that mix matter qubits with photonic links. Future large-scale quantum systems will likely network stationary qubits through light, but current software targets either gate-based chips or linear-optical devices alone. Hybrid systems are left without a unified tool.

In Optyx, users build experiments that combine qubit registers, discrete-variable photonic modes, lossy channels, heralded measurements, and real-time feedback. The library compiles these descriptions through the ZX and ZW calculi into optimized tensor network forms, then executes them with contraction schedulers. Benchmarks on exact multi-photon circuit simulations show tensor network contraction beating permanent-based methods by orders of magnitude for low-depth circuits and entangled photon sources. Loss and distinguishability are handled natively. The authors present Optyx as a high-performance simulator and a prototyping environment for photonic network experiments.
arxiv-2512-09748:
The Euclid Collaboration reviews what its space mission should reveal about dark energy and modified gravity. Euclid was designed to probe how gravity drives the expansion of the universe and the growth of structure. That gives it a chance to test whether general relativity fully holds, or whether the standard cosmological model needs revision. The review gathers pre-launch forecasts predicting how tightly Euclid data will pin down the parameters of competing models.

Euclid relies on two probes: weak gravitational lensing, which maps how light bends, and galaxy clustering, which traces how galaxies group. The forecasts cover time varying dark energy, changes to how perturbations grow, specific modified gravity theories, and extensions involving neutrinos and a possibly varying fine structure constant. The review also weighs how nonlinear clustering, simulations, and relativistic corrections affect the predictions. Overall, Euclid can sharply constrain these models, or possibly catch the standard model failing.
arxiv-2512-09948:
Phil Attard gives a Monte Carlo algorithm for quantum statistical mechanics when the phase space weight is complex. Complex weights break the usual Metropolis sampling recipe, which needs positive probabilities. His algorithm applies generally across quantum statistical problems. The method builds on the Wigner-Kirkwood expansion, a systematic way of adding quantum corrections to classical phase space.
