Reliable semantic tags support corpus studies of how language is used across cultures.
arxiv-2601-09748:
José Ulloa Araya documents, in Spanish, how to run a full Bitcoin node on Linux. His 2026 arXiv paper covers installation, configuration, and day-to-day use. The work starts from compiling the source code by hand and ends with full synchronization with the network.

The paper walks through the technical phases and the main files Bitcoin Core creates. It also tests, empirically, what key settings do: txindex, prune, dbcache, maxmempool, and maxconnections. A full node verifies the chain without trusting anyone else. A clear Spanish guide widens who can take part in that verification.
arxiv-2601-10248:
Laura Grigori, Daniel Kressner, Nian Shao, and Igor Simunec fix a flaw in fast Krylov tools. Krylov tools build a base for a large space step by step. A random form builds that base fast and with a sound shape. But it warps a key link.

The matrix it yields should match the one from the plain path. In the random path, it oft does not. That gap can slow or spike the solve. The team give a fix that brings the link back. They show it on eigenvalue tasks and on functions of a matrix. The fix keeps the speed and the shape.
arxiv-2601-10448:
Naeem Ramzan and Muhammad Tufail Khan grade the look of ultra HD video sent in layers. New codecs pack video into a base layer and a boost layer. Here the base is VVC, a new top codec. The boost is LCEVC, a light add on layer. A third form uses AI in the codec.

Grades from math scores miss how a clip looks to a viewer. The team use human grades. Viewers rate each form on the same clips. That gives a true rank of the layered forms. The work helps broadcasters pick a form that looks best per bit.
arxiv-2601-10548:
Xizhi Liu, Jie Ma, and Tianming Zhu study a core question in extremal graph theory. Given a small graph F, they ask how many copies of F a large graph can hold as induced subgraphs. The inducibility of F is the best share such copies can reach as the host graph grows. Turán graphs, built from balanced complete parts, are the test case here.

The paper works out the inducibility for this family of graphs. The result adds exact values to a problem where few are known. Such values show which host shapes pack the most copies of a pattern. The work will interest readers in combinatorics who study how local patterns fill large networks.
arxiv-2601-10648:
Joseph Rowan, Buu Phan, and Ashish Khisti study a one-shot coding problem for broadcast messages. One source is encoded a single time and sent to many decoders. Each decoder hears the message through its own noisy channel. The send counts as a success if at least one decoder recovers the source well enough.

The setup uses codebook diversity, meaning the decoders do not all rely on the same codebook. A distortion limit sets how close a recovery must be to count. The problem fits alerts and beacons that must reach someone, anyone, on the first try. The analysis helps engineers judge when one broadcast is enough.
arxiv-2601-10748:
Jun Li and co-authors present AnyECG, an ECG foundation model for broad health profiling. AI methods that read electrocardiograms can spot many heart and non-heart conditions. But most research trains a separate model for each single disease. That split misses how diseases cluster in one patient. It also rarely forecasts future risk.

AnyECG is described as an evolved foundation model, trained to read ECGs as a whole. A single model that profiles many conditions could triage patients faster. It could also flag risks before symptoms grow. The work targets clinics that want one ECG tool with a wide view of health, not a shelf of narrow ones.
arxiv-2601-10948:
Maria G. Sousa, Everton M. C. Abreu, Albert C. R. Mendes, and M. J. Neves study heat and statistics in noncommutative phase spaces. Noncommutative models tweak the rules of position and momentum. They carry a Planck-scale parameter, which makes them semiclassical: close to classical physics, with a whisper of quantum gravity. Such models attract interest as a path toward quantum gravity.

The authors analyze the thermostatistics of Yukawa and Lee-Wick potentials in this setting. They examine negative heat capacities, a strange trait where a system cools as it gains energy. Self-gravitating systems show that trait classically. Seeing how it survives noncommutative tweaks tests the reach of both thermodynamics and Planck-scale models.
arxiv-2601-11548:
Tao Hu tests the Frank-Wolfe method under inexact oracles in this preprint. The 2026 work deals with optimization over convex sets. Frank-Wolfe avoids projections by using a linear minimization oracle. In practice, both gradients and oracles can be inexact.

Hu asks how much error the method can tolerate. For smooth nonconvex functions, a convergence guarantee is given. The rate blends a 1 over root k decay term. An added delta term prices the oracle's inexactness. The study also weighs the oracle's cost against projection. Linear minimization is often far cheaper per step. The results tell users when cheap steps still converge.
arxiv-2601-11848:
Savvas Petridis, Michael Xieyang Liu, Alexander J. Fiannaca, Carrie J. Cai, and Michael Terry study how people brief AI for long jobs. As AI can work for minutes or hours alone, prompts grow into long, full specs. Briefing a human for long work is not the same task.

They set two images side by side: a compass and railway tracks. One hints at a goal with room to roam, and one hints at a fixed path. Their study asks which image fits how users think. The answer can shape tools for long AI work.
arxiv-2601-12048:
Pooneh Afsharijoo, Pedro D. González Pérez, and Hussein Mourtada prove a family of partition identities. Partitions split a whole number into parts. Their identities use partitions in three colours. Rules on the parts come from famed past identities.

Those rules link to the Rogers-Ramanujan and Andrews-Gordon identities, and to recent wider forms of them. The new forms tie partitions to surface singularities of type Ar. Such links often reveal deep ties between counting and geometry. The proofs add a new branch to that story.  The three colour case is the new core of the work.
arxiv-2601-12348:
Haris Khan and Sadia Asif build generative AI agents for content that users can control and that stays protected. Generative tools have changed creative work. Yet users lack fine control over output, and output lacks proof of origin once made.

Their multi-agent frame splits the work among agent roles with set tasks. It adds watermarking in the generation step itself, not as an afterthought. Past multi-agent tools chase quality alone. A built-in mark plus control could aid trust and rights in AI media.  Marks made at birth of a work are hard to strip.
arxiv-2601-12648:
Nafiz Imtiaz Khan, Kylie Cleland, Vladimir Filkov, and Roger Eric Goldman ask whether AI can log training cases for doctors. Radiology trainees must log each procedure case they perform, by hand. Manual logging eats time and invites errors and gaps. The team test whether large language models can automate that documentation.

They evaluate how well models extract case details for the log. They also identify which procedure types are hardest to extract. A final question is how such a tool would fit clinical workflows. If AI logging proves reliable, trainees could spend more time learning. If certain case types fail often, those need human checks. The study weighs feasibility before any replacement of manual work.
arxiv-2601-12748:
Bin Xie and four co authors work on process reward models for reasoning tasks. These models score each step of a reasoning chain, not just the final answer. They have achieved strong results on complex reasoning problems. Their bottleneck is the cost of process level supervision, since human step labels are dear.

A widely used alternative estimates step rewards by Monte Carlo sampling. It defines a step reward as the chance that a policy reaches the right answer from that step. Such estimates are noisy, though, and noise can mislead training. The team pursue noise aware learning for these models. Cleaner step signals could make reasoning training both cheaper and better.
arxiv-2601-13048:
Srividya Ravikumar, Abhinav Anand, Shweta Verma, and Mira Mezini probe how state space models hold long range links in data. Such models score well on long chain tasks. Most past work, though, judged them by score alone and not by how they work inside.

The team runs what they call the first full study of kernel sense in one such model, S4D. They train it on a real task, the hunt for flaws in source code that could aid attacks. They then read the trained kernels to see what spans the model keeps or drops. For builders, the study shifts talk from raw score to clear cause. It shows which long links the model truly uses.
arxiv-2601-13348:
M. Karen Shen, Jessica Huang, and co-authors sort AI chat bot addiction into three kinds. News of heavy chat bot use has raised fears of a new addiction. Yet the state is poorly grasped. Teams lack a clear account of why users get hooked, what marks show, and what forms it takes.

The team names a frame called the AI Genie phenomenon. In it they set three kinds of heavy tie. One is escapist role play. A next is pseudo social company, where the bot fills a friend slot. The last is epistemic rabbit holes, long hunts for facts that never close. A clear sort is a first step to care that fits each kind.
arxiv-2601-13448:
Sofiane Tanji, Samuel Vaiter, and Yassine Laguel make fair machine learning both fair and Pareto sound. Fair tools oft waste skill. A model can be made more fair yet leave a group worse off than it need be, with no gain for a next group. That waste is called Pareto inefficiency.

Old fixes that keep Pareto sound lean to one view of fair. They bend poorly when the fair aim shifts. The team's frame is two level. One level sets the fair aim. The next finds the best model for it in a Pareto sound way. For teams that must show both fair and no waste, the split is the point.
arxiv-2601-13548:
George Wang and Daniel Murfet set up patterning as the twin task of interpretability. Interpretability works back from a trained net to how it acts past its train data. It picks the net's inner parts apart to read its rules.

Patterning runs the next way. Given a wished form of wide act, what train data yields it? Their tool is susceptibilities, marks of how out comes shift when the data spread is nudged a bit. Such marks can point to which data taught which act. For teams that must shape a model's acts by data picks, a twin task with its own tools is a fresh lever.
arxiv-2601-13848:
Corrado Possieri designs stabilizing controllers from input-output data alone in 2026. The setting is continuous-time, linear, time-invariant systems. Classic design needs measures of how inputs and outputs change over time. Those derivatives are hard to measure or estimate well in practice.

Possieri's framework is derivative free, as the title states. Filters process the data to yield a parameterization of the system dynamics. From that form, a stabilizing controller can be built. Such data-driven control suits plants where models are poor but data is rich. The plan needs no state data, which is a plus on real plants. Plant teams can use it when good state reads are hard to get.
arxiv-2601-13948:
Nikita Kuzmin, Songting Liu, Kong Aik Lee, and Eng Siong Chng protect speaker identity in live voice apps in 2026. Streaming speaker anonymization hides who is talking as the audio flows. This real-time case remains underexplored next to offline methods. Neural audio codecs give superior speaker feature disentanglement, keeping words clear while voice traits split off.

Codecs can pair with causal language models for streaming tasks. That pairing can enhance linguistic fidelity and prompt control. Their Stream-Voice-Anon aims to raise the utility of real-time anonymization. Users could then speak in public apps without giving away their voiceprint.
arxiv-2601-14048:
Sahabub Jahedi and co-authors hunt dark matter through a rare kind of interaction in 2026. Lepton flavor violating interactions involving dark matter remain largely unexplored. Flavor violation means a lepton changes type, like a muon becoming an electron. The team studies these interactions in effective field theories.

They analyze astrophysical photons and positrons produced from dark matter annihilation. Telescopes can search for those products as indirect detection signals. A systematic study maps which interactions could leave a visible trace. Null results still teach us where dark matter cannot hide. The scan is broad by design, so gaps in past work stand out. It sets a clear base for the next round of sky hunts.
arxiv-2601-14148:
Meng Li, Tong Xie, Zuodong Zhang, and Runsheng Wang tackle aging and variation in AI chips in 2026. As CMOS technology pushes to the nanoscale, aging effects grow more pronounced. Process variations also increase, posing significant reliability challenges for AI accelerators. Traditional guardband design uses pessimistic timing margins for safety.

Those margins sacrifice significant performance and computational efficiency. They render older approaches inadequate for high-performance AI computing demands. The team pursues cross-layer evaluation and design optimization for reliable accelerators. Chips that age with grace would serve data centers for longer. The full-stack view joins chip wear to code and task plans. That join is where most of the lost speed can be won back.
arxiv-2601-14248:
Tehreem N. Hai, Kristen B. W. McQuinn, and eight co-authors report new data on a small, quiet galaxy in this 2026 paper. The galaxy is Canes Venatici C, a dwarf in the nearby Local Volume. Dwarf galaxies like it are low in mass. This one has stopped forming stars, yet it sits far from big neighbors.

Finds like this are on the rise, and they test a common view. That view says a dwarf's present surroundings are the main cause when it stops forming stars. The team used the Hubble Space Telescope to take fresh data on this case. Their study checks what the new data say about that claim.
arxiv-2601-14348:
Dominik Stammbach and a team from Princeton and Stanford study legal search tools in this 2026 paper. AI tools are often pitched as help for public agencies with heavy workloads. Public defense is a hard case. A constitutional right to counsel meets complex law, huge caseloads, and tight resources there. Defenders work under steep strain.

Yet hard facts on how AI tools serve this work are scarce. The abstract cuts off as the authors set up that gap. Their title names the topic plainly: legal retrieval for public defenders. Readers get a study framed around the real search needs of defense teams, not generic legal tech claims.
arxiv-2601-14448:
Abdullah Enes Doruk presents a perception method for self-driving cars in this 2026 paper. The field is shifting from sparse object detection to dense 3D semantic occupancy prediction. Occupancy maps say which parts of space are filled and by what. Such maps help vehicles face long-tail safety cases, rare scenes that still matter.

Current voxelization methods, which chop space into small cubes, carry flaws. They demand excessive computation. Their fusion of sensor inputs is brittle and static, and it breaks down in dynamic settings. GaussianOcc3D answers with Gaussian-based adaptive multi-modal prediction. Readers get a design meant to keep occupancy maps fast and robust on real roads.
arxiv-2601-15048:
Mingcheng Nie, Ruoxi Chong, and a team of co-authors make the case for a new radio waveform for 6G. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the physical layer, the level where signals are shaped for the air. Work to standardize the sixth generation of wireless has just begun.

Current systems fall short of the goals set for 6G. The authors put forward OTFS as a candidate waveform. OTFS shapes signals in the delay-Doppler domain, a view that suits fast motion. The paper is an invited survey of the path toward making it a standard.
arxiv-2601-15248:
Dennis Scheidt gives a hands-on guide to imaging with a single pixel. His 2026 arXiv tutorial deals with single pixel imaging and compressive sensing. Instead of an array of sensors, the method uses one bucket detector, a simple photodiode, to sample a patterned light field.

That design is cheap and works where sensor arrays do not. It suits odd wavelengths and noisy settings, where it can gather signal well. The tutorial walks through how the method works in practice. It is aimed at readers who want to build or use such a camera.
arxiv-2601-15648:
Manujith K. Michel and Varadharaj R. Srinivasan extend derivations to algebras in a 2026 arXiv paper. A derivation is a map that obeys a product rule, like differentiation does. An iterative derivation comes with a family of higher maps that mimic higher derivatives. The authors start with such a map on a field. They ask when it extends to a central simple algebra over that field.

They prove the extension works under one condition. The field's characteristic must not divide the exponent of the algebra in the Brauer group. The Brauer group classifies such algebras up to a natural equivalence. Conditions of this kind decide when local structure lifts to richer settings. Algebraists use these results when they move tools from fields to the algebras built over them.
arxiv-2601-15748:
Junle Pei and four co-authors build a general theory of quantum entanglement in particle decays in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is the decay of a particle-antiparticle pair. Each particle carries the same spin, denoted S. Each then decays in sequence into a two-body final state. The angles of those decays carry information. Entanglement between the pair can be read from them.

The authors call their framework universal. It aims to cover arbitrary spin, not just one case at a time. A single formalism lets experiments compare results across particles. Collider teams increasingly test quantum effects in decay data. A universal tool helps them speak a common language. The paper is theoretical, aimed at particle physicists.
arxiv-2601-16048:
Wan-Peng Sun and nine coauthors sort fast radio bursts by their light shape. Their 2026 preprint uses the CHIME burst list, its second full list. Bursts are oft split into those that repeat and those seen once. It is not clear if the two groups are truly two kinds. The team lets the data sort bursts with no fixed labels.

They join a map tool with a clump search to group the bursts. The groups rest on the form of each burst in light and tone. Clear groups would hint at more than one birth path for bursts. Weak groups would hint at one wide kind. The work gives a fresh, data led view of this split.
arxiv-2601-16148:
Remy Sabathier and three coauthors build still mesh forms that move in time. Their 2026 preprint sets out ActionMesh, a tool for 3D forms in motion. Past top tools are hard to use in real work. They need long set up, run slow, or give weak forms. A form ready for film or game use must be clean at once.

ActionMesh gives such forms in one forth pass. No long post work is needed to clean the mesh. Fast, clean forms help teams test acts and scenes with speed. The tool aims at real work flows, not just lab demos. It joins time based spread maths with mesh output.
arxiv-2601-16648:
Francesco Guidi, Jingfeng Shan, Mehrdad Saeidi, and their co-authors study how machines learn to act. Their 2026 preprint sets out a design for self-run agents. The design copies two ways that the human brain learns. One way links cues in the world with what tends to follow them.

Most built systems learn only from gains and losses after an act. Human brains also let cues sway a choice before the result is known. The authors join both styles in a single frame for learning from rewards. They argue that this mix can lead to wiser acts. The work speaks to the design of robots, smart cars, and like tools.
arxiv-2601-16848:
Jaume Anguera Peris and Joakim Jaldén plan AI at the edge of phone nets. Edge AI runs tasks near cell towers, not in far clouds. That nearness cuts lag for apps that can't wait. It also suits apps with tight power and size caps. Their 2026 preprint builds chance models for such edge nets.

Those models size how much gear a net zone needs. Many cells share the load in their frame. Right-size plans keep lag low with no waste. Phone firms can use the math to place gear. Such plans grow key as AI moves to the edge.
arxiv-2601-16948:
J. R. Bermejo-Climent and a team of six co-authors hunt a faint mark from the cosmos' birth. That mark is called primordial non-Gaussianity. It would show the first bits did not spread in a pure bell form. The Quaia quasar set gives a vast map for the hunt. Their 2026 preprint adds a fresh gauge to that hunt.

The gauge tracks how mean red shift wobbles across the sky. Those wobbles tie to how galaxies clump with mass. Big-scale clump bias can then bound the birth mark. Fresh gauges add cross-checks for a key cosmic hunt. They also use Quaia's map in a new way.
arxiv-2601-17348:
Srikant Panda, Sourabh Singh Yadav, and Palkesh Malviya audit how vision-language models describe people with disabilities. These models pair images with text for many public tasks. The authors look at person images where disability is present. They find a pattern worth care. Models can start with facts seen in the image. Then they shift to claims the image does not support.

That shift adds guesses about a person's life or limits. Such guesses can harm and mislead at scale. An audit names the flaw so it can be fixed. Better rules would keep descriptions tied to what is seen. The work serves builders of fair image tools.
arxiv-2601-17548:
Narek Maloyan and Dmitry Namiot map prompt injection flaws in agentic coding assistants. Tools like Claude Code, Copilot, and Cursor now write and run code with file and shell access. Skill-based designs widen that reach. The authors run a systematic analysis of the flaws. They sort risks across skills, tools, and protocol layers.

A coding agent tricked by injected text can harm a whole project. It could leak keys, break builds, or ship bad code. A clear map of attack paths helps teams guard each layer. The work serves builders of AI coding tools. It also guides firms that let agents touch live code. Safety must grow with agent power.
arxiv-2601-17848:
Marcos V. de S. Silva, Manuel E. Rodrigues, and C. F. S. Pereira ask if odd black hole mimics can live in a changed theory of gravity. Their 2026 preprint studies black bounces in three dimensions. A black bounce is a shape that acts like a black hole but has no single point of infinite density. The shapes were first found in general relativity. The team works in f(R) gravity, where the rules of gravity are broadened.

They check whether the known bounce shapes still solve the new equations. They also find what kind of matter could hold such shapes up. Each new solution tests how far the idea of a black hole can stretch. Results guide the search for signs that gravity differs from Einstein's version.
arxiv-2601-17948:
Z. Asmaee and K. Azizi compute quantities that reveal the spin structure inside heavy baryons. Their 2026 preprint studies tensor form factors of decuplet hyperons. The particles in view are the Omega-minus, Sigma-star-plus, and Xi-star-minus. Form factors encode how a particle's insides respond to probes. Tensor ones carry news about spin and internal dynamics that simpler factors miss.

The team works within QCD sum rules, a method that ties particle traits to the theory of quarks and gluons. Results for these rare particles are hard to get in the lab. Theory values guide both experiments and lattice studies. The work adds data points for some of the least known members of the baryon family.
arxiv-2601-18048:
Moisés Bravo-Gaete, Jhony A. Herrera-Mendoza, Julio Oliva, and Xiangdong Zhang construct a new family of black holes. Their 2026 preprint gives exact solutions in five dimensions. The holes rotate, carry electric charge, and live in a Lifshitz spacetime, a setting where time and space scale at different rates. The spacetime solves Einstein's equations joined to a dilaton, two Abelian gauge fields, and axionic scalars, with two added Chern-Simons terms.

Exact solutions are rare and valuable in gravity research. They let scholars test ideas about charge, spin, and horizons without numeric fog. A Lifshitz background also links gravity to condensed matter models. The new family widens the map of known black holes.
arxiv-2601-18248:
Mohammad Aghaie and Ryosuke Sato use a toy model to test a bold claim about a famous puzzle. Their 2026 preprint deals with the strong CP problem. A recent claim by Ai, Cruz, Garbrecht, and Tamarit holds that there is no such problem, once limits are taken in a new order. The order in question swaps the volume limit with the sum over topological sectors. Aghaie and Sato examine the claim critically through one-dimensional quantum mechanics of a particle on a ring.

A ring model keeps the theta-vacuum structure but drops the clutter. If the claim fails on the ring, it fails in spirit. Simple models are sharp tools for testing grand claims. The paper is a careful check on a hot idea.
arxiv-2601-18448:
Lloyd Austin Courtenay warns of a leak that can spoil studies which sort bones and shells by shape. Shape work first lines up all forms with a shared fit, so that size and tilt do not skew the chart. Teams then teach a model to sort the lined up forms into groups. The snag is that the shared fit is done on all forms at once, before the split into train and test sets.

That early blend lets facts from the test set seep into the train set. A model can then look sharp in tests for the wrong cause. Courtenay sets out how the leak works and why it counts for shape based claims. The fix is to keep the fit and the split apart, so each test stays fair. Shape fields that now lean on smart models need that care to keep their finds sound.
arxiv-2601-18748:
Aiya Kuchukova, Santosh Vempala, and Daniel Zhang study how fast a dice-walk through packs of hard balls settles to a fair spread. A pack of balls that can't share space is a clean model for stuff that takes room. To draw a fair pack at chance, a walk swaps one ball at a time to a new spot, if the spot is free. How fast that walk forgets its start is the key ask.

The team prove the walk is fast in a wide range of pack depths. Their proof builds new tools that stretch two famed tricks from the world of set counts to the world of space. Those tricks track how one part of a pack leans on the rest. The same tools work for a wide class of point sets with push-apart pairs. Fast walks serve sims in chem and bio.
arxiv-2601-19048:
Han-Hung Lee and three co-authors build a system that creates whole virtual worlds users can steer. World generation feeds games, simulation, and robotics, but three walls block it: control, scale, and speed. Past end to end models had too little data, while object by object methods fixed the resolution and lost detail on big scenes.

Their framework, NuiWorld, aims to clear all three walls at once. Users should be able to shape the world, grow it large, and get it fast. Worlds that obey their makers would serve game design, training sims, and robot practice grounds alike.
arxiv-2601-19348:
Yanhao Sun and five co-authors recheck a quantum key scheme as real devices push it out of its ideal mode. Continuous variable quantum key distribution lets two parties grow a secret key with security backed by physics. A newer two way version resists excess noise better and looks practical.

Real devices, though, are imperfect, and the light field slips from one clean mode into a spread of modes. The team analyzes the scheme in that continuous mode regime. Security claims must survive the move from ideal math to real optics, and this work checks that they do.
arxiv-2601-19448:
Binyan Xu and four co-authors defend neural networks at test time by auditing inputs from outside the model. Backdoor attacks plant hidden triggers that flip a model's answer on cue. Old test time defenses diagnose from inside, repairing the model or hardening inputs, but they stay tangled with the poisoned weights.

Their paradigm uses a vision language model as an external auditor of what comes in. An outside judge is not bound by the victim model's corruption. The shift from internal repair to external audit may hold up better as attacks grow more advanced.
arxiv-2601-19548:
Jan Keim and Angelika Kaplan write about a quiet problem in software projects: knowledge gets scattered. What a system is meant to do may sit in requirements files. Why it was built that way may live in diagrams, code comments, or old documents. As the system changes over years, these pieces drift apart and stop agreeing with each other.

The authors set out a vision for automating the care of this architectural knowledge. Machines would gather the spread-out pieces, link them, and keep them in a structured form. Developers could then find and use the knowledge when they need it. Keeping records in sync should slow architectural erosion, the slow decay of a design. The paper is a roadmap for tools that treat design knowledge as something worth managing on purpose.
arxiv-2601-19648:
P. F. Dias, F. M. Zimmer, N. G. Fytas, and M. Schmidt study a model of magnetism on a honeycomb grid. The Ising model treats each site as a tiny magnet that points up or down. Neighbours influence each other through couplings of different strengths and signs. Here the first and second neighbours favour alignment, while third neighbours favour opposition.

That mix is called frustration, since no arrangement can satisfy every bond at once. Frustrated systems can settle into unusual phases, neither fully ordered nor fully random. The authors investigate which phases win as conditions change on the honeycomb lattice. The honeycomb shape matters in real materials such as graphene-like magnets. Phase diagrams from models like this guide the hunt for new magnetic materials.
arxiv-2601-20148:
Marcus Emmanuel Barnes, Taher A. Ghaleb, and Safwat Hassan present LogSieve, a tool that shrinks build logs from continuous integration systems. Logs are key for finding why a build failed or slowed down. But their growing size makes both human reading and automated analysis slow, costly, and energy-hungry.

Most earlier work on log reduction targets neat system logs, not the noisy text that build pipelines produce. LogSieve is task-aware, so it keeps the lines that matter for the analysis at hand. Smaller, cleaner logs would let language models scan build failures at lower cost and with less noise.
arxiv-2601-20448:
Zhiyu Chen, Minhao Liu, and Yanru Zhang present TimeCatcher, a forecasting framework for time series that refuse to sit still. Lightweight models based on simple networks forecast well by catching stable trends and seasons. But they rest on an assumption of local calm, so they err on long forecasts of wild series, above all when abrupt swings occur.

Such swings are common in domains like web traffic monitoring. TimeCatcher uses a variational framework that is aware of volatility, so it can brace for unstable stretches. Forecasts that admit when the ground is shaky serve planners better than calm lines through stormy data.
arxiv-2601-20548:
Kahraman Kostas and Rabia Yasa Kostas review how machines learn to identify Internet of Things devices, and where that work goes wrong. Their paper looks hard at the identification process, from the choice between unique and class-based methods to feature extraction and evaluation metrics. Data heterogeneity across devices is a recurring problem.

They name specific errors in past studies, such as improper data augmentation and misleading session identifiers. From these they build a guideline for more reproducible, generalizable security models. Device identification underpins network defense, so cleaning up its methods has practical weight. None of the fixes call for new gear. Most call for more care in how a study is set up and run.
arxiv-2601-20848:
Weixin Chen, Li Chen, and Yuhan Zhao build fairness controls that can change after training. Their 2026 paper concerns recommender systems. Most fairness-aware methods fix the fairness demand at training time. They offer little flexibility afterward. In the real world, different stakeholders want different fairness levels. Those demands also shift over time. Retraining for each new demand is prohibitive.

The authors propose a single-train framework for post-training fairness control. One trained model serves many fairness settings. Users can dial the requirement up or down without new training. That design cuts cost and speeds response to new rules. The paper appears in the companion proceedings of the 2026 Web Conference. It targets platforms that must answer to varied fairness demands at once.
arxiv-2601-21348:
Thuy Phuong Vu and co-authors study memorization in diffusion models from a fresh angle. These models can copy training images too closely, which is a problem when new output should match the data's pattern without cloning it. Most fixes change the data or the model itself.

The authors instead look at the denoising process, the step-by-step cleanup that builds each image. Viewing the model as part of a wider pipeline changes where control can be applied. Their angle suggests new ways to dial memorization up or down. That control matters for privacy and for fair use of training data.
arxiv-2601-21548:
Irene Ambrosini and seven co-authors train silicon neurons to play air hockey, a game that punishes slow reactions. The puck moves fast, so choices must land in a split second. Their system uses a compact network of spiking neurons on a mixed analog-digital chip.

Hardware and learning rules were designed together from the start. Training by trial and error reaches solid puck play in very few trials. Few-trial learning matters because real robots wear out and cannot practice forever. The demo shows brain-like chips handling a task where speed, not size, is the whole challenge.
arxiv-2601-21748:
Lin Li and Jiongmin Yong study a control problem where the cost of a decision is itself defined recursively. Their setting is stochastic linear quadratic control, a workhorse model where a system moves with noise and the goal balances performance against effort. Here the cost functional comes through backward stochastic differential equations.

Those equations live in a space where well-posedness, whether a solution exists and is unique, is a subtle issue. The 2026 preprint adopts a framework in which the problem is correctly stated, then works through the control theory on that basis. Results of this kind underpin applications from finance to engineering, where today's cost depends on how future uncertainty will be judged, not just on averages.
arxiv-2601-21948:
Neural decoding tries to rebuild what a person saw from their brain activity, a central problem for brain-computer interfaces. It also promises insight into how the brain represents the visual world. The 2026 preprint behind this entry argues that current methods miss a basic mismatch in granularity.

Human vision and deep vision models work at different levels of detail. Deep models chase semantic invariance, recognizing the same object across many changes, while early human vision keeps fine spatial detail. The authors frame this as deep models with shallow alignment to the brain. Closing that gap could improve both decoding accuracy and our scientific picture of how seeing is organized in the cortex.
arxiv-2601-22148:
Daniel Hawtin and Padraig Ó Catháin study the symmetries of q-graphs, a generalization of graphs built from finite vector spaces. In a q-graph, the vertices are the one-dimensional subspaces of a vector space over a finite field. And the edges are a chosen subset of two-dimensional subspaces.

Symmetries of such objects, the transformations that leave them unchanged, reveal their structure and connect them to finite geometry and coding theory. Their 2026 preprint analyzes those symmetry groups for regular q-graphs, where every vertex behaves alike. q-analogues translate classical combinatorics into a richer finite setting, and their symmetry results feed designs, codes, and network-like structures used across discrete mathematics.
arxiv-2601-22548:
Dani Roytburg, Matthew Bozoukov, and co-authors sanity-check the claim that model judges favor their own work. Past studies found that models, acting as judges, rate their own outputs higher. Their 2026 preprint notes that this self-love is hard to split from plain test confounds.

A skewed test can fake narcissism where none exists. The team sort which biases the vanity claim truly explains. Clean measures matter: judge bias can warp training and leaderboards at scale. The work is a caution and a cleaner yardstick. It asks the field to measure twice.
arxiv-2601-22848:
Camilo Carvajal Reyes and Felipe Tobar build a generator for time series, data that unfold over time. Their method uses flow-based models, which learn to turn noise into realistic series. To keep sampling fast, the work happens in a smaller latent space, a compressed view of the data.

The key addition is a push for symmetry in that latent space, taught by adjusting a pre-trained encoder. Fair synthetic series help test forecasts and train models when real data are scarce. Symmetry keeps the fake series true to how real ones shift and stretch.
arxiv-2601-23248:
Ioannis Anagnostides, Ioannis Panageas, Nikolas Patris, and Tuomas Sandholm prove slow-convergence bounds for a leading online learning algorithm. Follow the Regularized Leader is the premier method for online optimization. Its behavior in potential games, though studied for decades, remained poorly understood.

The authors show it can take exponential, even doubly exponential, time to reach a Nash equilibrium. The result holds for two-player potential games, any permutation-invariant regularizer, and even tiny learning rates. Such bounds redraw expectations for learning in games. Vanishing learning rates do not rescue the algorithm in the proof, which closes a common hope for practitioners.
arxiv-2602-00248: Varun Srivastava and colleagues test how showing uncertainty on thematic maps affects trust. Prior views split: some say openness builds trust, others say it breeds confusion. In a between subjects experiment with 161 participants, uncertainty shown at low, medium, and high levels generally reduced trust, with larger cuts as uncertainty rose. Maps ruled by low uncertainty, however, did not differ much in trust from maps with no uncertainty shown. Showing uncertainty also made readers question data accuracy more.
arxiv-2602-00648: Hao Ma and colleagues rethink audio compression at extremely low bitrates. Waveform-based codecs lose key content there and produce harsh artifacts and distorted meaning. Their new approach shifts the goal from signal fidelity to task use. It pairs a sense of meaning at the sender with generative synthesis at the receiver. The model rebuilds general audio at 0.275 kbps with high fidelity. The authors report it still carries speech that can be understood far below that rate, beating current neural codecs on quality and meaning.
arxiv-2602-00848: Ziwei Gong and colleagues introduce Factuality-Controlled Generation, a method letting users set truth rules with queries. Models face a trade-off: shorter but highly factual replies, or richer but potentially less accurate ones. Each use needs its own balance. They propose judging FCG on two fronts, respect for truth rules and response detail. They train models on the FCG task with synthetic data, and show this training greatly lifts both rule respect and detail.
arxiv-2602-00948: Mingxi Zou and colleagues replace lone backtests with a shared market game where trading plans live or die together. In FinEvo, each plan acts as a learning agent that reads past prices and news, built from rules, deep nets, reward learning, or language models. Across the group, plans spread, change, or fade through choice, new ideas, and outside shocks. Tests with shocks and live news give steady, repeatable runs with varied ends, as plans rule, fail, or team up based on rivals.
arxiv-2602-01048: Yuhang Guo and Houyu Zhou ask how to place a hall so no group bears far more travel pain than the rest, when folk may game their stated spots. Each group's pain is its total or worst trip to the nearest hall, scaled by weights. That one aim folds in old aims like least total pain, least worst pain, and group-fair variants. For one hall, they give two game-proof plans with tight worst-case bounds, BALANCED and MajorPhantom, matching known tight bounds for old aims.
arxiv-2602-01148: Jiaxuan Zou and co-authors map the bounds of latent chain-of-thought, where models think in smooth vectors, not words. Such models shine at search yet flop at sums, a puzzle the team traces to choice sureness. High sureness drives exact runs but chokes search, while low sureness frees search but piles up slips. A symbolic index gauges that sureness and steers the trade, and the team proves staged learning is a must, since direct training fails on data drift.
arxiv-2602-01248: Douglas F. Watson builds the Riemann Xi-function from plain Markov cycles, with no primes or Euler products in sight. Starting from finite, local, reversible Markov hops on discrete cycles, he takes a scaling-limit trace kernel with an exact theta-series form. A log kernel from that limit lands in the Polya frequency class, yielding a canonical Laguerre-Polya function by classification. At a self-dual scale, a completion map makes the kernel match the classic theta kernel, which Mellin-maps to the Riemann Xi-function.
arxiv-2602-01548: Da-Chuan Tian and co-authors estimate photometric redshifts by classification, giving well-calibrated probability curves. Their network splits redshift space into ordered bins, optimizing a continuous ranked probability score, keeping redshift's ordinal nature, giving uncertainty. Unlike fits giving single point values, classification captures multi-modal posteriors born of color-redshift degeneracies. On a record spectral sample from DESI and SDSS, it beats Random Forest, XGBoost, and neural regression on DESI Legacy and Pan-STARRS. Deep optical photometry plus mid-infrared coverage proves essential for high precision across the range.
arxiv-2602-01848: Salaheddin Alzu'bi and colleagues fix agentic frameworks for long tasks, where orchestration turns brittle and traces hide failures. Their ROMA framework decomposes goals into subtask trees run in parallel, while aggregation compresses and validates intermediates to control context. Four roles separate orchestration from model choice: Atomizer, Planner, Executor and Aggregator, giving transparent traces and letting systems mix models and tools by cost and capability. On SEAL-0 with GLM-4 it beats Kimi-Researcher by nearly ten percent on web evidence, and on EQ-Bench DeepSeek-V3 matches leading closed source models.
arxiv-2602-02048: Umberto Domanti and colleagues ask whether semantic network organization relates to idea novelty in large language models, against humans. Generative AI in creativity support tools must interface two black boxes, mind and machine. Standardized tests went to ChatGPT-4o and 81 psychology students, split by creativity. The expected relationship held between ChatGPT-4o and higher creative humans, yet despite a more rigid network, ChatGPT-4o proved more original than lower humans. The authors attribute this difference to human motivation and model hyperparameters, advancing artificial creativity research.
arxiv-2602-02548:
Xiaoce Wang and 5 co-authors replace one-shot coordinate prediction with stepwise tool use for screen agents, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents that click by predicting coordinates generalize poorly across screen sizes and shapes. Coordinate-free options need more training data than exists.

ToolTok models screen operations as a sequence of progressive tool calls, in line with human interaction habits. Each tool is a learnable token embedding. An anchoring mechanism grounds every tool in related concepts, giving a helpful head start so embeddings can be learned from little supervision. A three-task curriculum, from token definitions through text-guided selection to simplified visual pathfinding, teaches a pretrained model the tool meanings step by step. The four-billion-parameter system beat models of like size and rivaled one nearly sixty times larger, using under one percent of rivals' training data.
arxiv-2602-02648:
Yasamin Panahi and 3 co-authors show that topology can force quantum critical behavior in strongly disordered materials, in work posted to arXiv in 2026. Quantum criticality under strong quenched randomness, frozen disorder in the material, resists theory's control. Their lever is average symmetry: translation symmetry that survives only on average while on-site symmetries remain exact.

Systems under average Lieb-Schultz-Mattis constraints cannot simply settle into a trivial state, the authors argue. Without symmetry breaking or intrinsic topological order, some local operator correlations must decay slowly, in two distinct patterns tied to exact and average symmetries. The authors verify both patterns in a random-singlet spin chain and in disordered free-fermion critical states in one and two dimensions. Surprisingly, the anomaly argument reveals critical correlations that decades of study on those very systems had missed. Reading the effect in the lab looks feasible, they add.
arxiv-2602-02748:
Noam Goldberg and 1 co-author map exactly when robust scheduling under budgeted uncertainty is tractable, in a 2026 paper. One machine must sequence jobs whose processing times vary within a budget of total deviations. A job counts as tardy if any allowed scenario finishes it late, and the goal is minimizing tardy jobs. The problem is NP-hard in general.

Parameterized complexity gives the map. Against the robustness budget itself, the problem is W-one-hard yet solvable in XP time. Against the number of distinct due dates, it stays NP-hard even with only two due dates, but becomes pseudo-polynomial when that number is bounded. One common due date reduces the problem to a robust knapsack variant the authors solve in polynomial time. Against the number of jobs with nonzero deviations, the problem is fixed-parameter tractable. Each natural parameter draws its own border between feasible and hopeless.
arxiv-2602-02948:
Reconstructing hidden quantities from noisy measurements, with honest doubt, is the goal of Jack Michael Solomon and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Such inverse problems appear across science and engineering. Point figures alone are not enough when decisions depend on how confident the rebuilding is.

Their architecture, vsPAIR, pairs two variational autoencoders. One encodes the observations. The other encodes the quantity of interest, using sparse codes that concentrate information into identifiable factors. A learned map connects the two latent spaces. Tests cover blind inpainting, computed tomography, and recovering a heat formula's starting state. The system solved all three while giving interpretable, ordered doubt figures at fast use speed.
arxiv-2602-03048:
Spending training computation where it helps most is the idea behind a 2026 paper by Zhiyuan Yao and 9 co-authors. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves language model reasoning. Standard methods give every training example the same rollout budget, wasting effort on examples the model has already mastered or cannot yet use for learning at its current stage.

Their algorithm, CoBA-RL, estimates each task's potential training gain with a capability-oriented value function. A heap-based greedy strategy then allocates rollouts to the highest-value samples and recalibrates as capability evolves. The method explicitly balances exploration against exploitation. Experiments across challenging benchmarks showed consistent generalization improvements. The authors argue that quantifying sample training value is pivotal for efficient post-training of language models.
arxiv-2602-03348:
Low-dissipation numerical schemes for shock-capturing are compared head-to-head by Shaoshuai Chu, working with 1 co-author. Hyperbolic conservation laws govern compressible flows such as gases, and numerical dissipation, machine smearing, can blur contact and shear waves. Several schemes aim to reduce that smearing relative to the classic Harten-Lax-van Leer family, but their trade-offs in score, strength, and cost have lacked a unified comparison across orders and systems.

Schemes considered include contact-resolving, flux-splitting, and central-upwind variants, extended up to fifth order in finite-volume and finite-difference systems. Tests solve one and two-part Euler formulas for gas motion. Investigated schemes showed comparable dissipation levels, with only subtle differences on selected benchmarks. Trade-offs among wave detail, shock strength, and computational cost are highlighted as practical guidance for solver selection.
arxiv-2602-03648:
Can developers trust a language model to write infrastructure code that is secure? Ehsan Firouzi and 2 co-authors test GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash on that question in a 2026 paper. They examine two skills: spotting security smells in existing Infrastructure as Code, and generating fresh scripts for vulnerable scenarios.

On small Stack Overflow snippets the models catch at least 71 percent of smells with a general prompt, and more with guided step-by-step prompting. On complete GitHub projects, detection is weaker, though guidance recovers much of the gap. Generation fares worst: only about 7 percent of scripts for vulnerable scenarios come out secure. An explicit instruction to write secure code helps one model noticeably and the other barely.
arxiv-2602-03848:
Donghae Seo and 2 co-authors unify two constructions in fractional quantum Hall physics inside one category-theoretic framework in a 2026 paper. Quantum Hall hierarchies build new phases from parent states, while anyon superconductivity emerges when doped quasiparticles condense. Both are formulated with modular tensor categories that keep the conserved electric charge explicit.

Doping is handled by a generalized stack-and-condense procedure: an auxiliary topological order is stacked on the parent, and the doping quasiparticles then condense. If the condensation preserves charge symmetry, the result is a hierarchy state; if it breaks the symmetry, an anyon superconductor results. The framework reproduces every known anyon superconductor from field theory and predicts new ones, including a charge-2e example from the Laughlin state.
arxiv-2602-03948:
Bibhabasu Mandal and 1 co-author study private estimation on networks where only node degrees are shared. Sensitive relationship data often reaches analysts as degree summaries, which still leak information about individual links. Their 2026 paper works with the beta model, the standard statistical model for such summaries.

They derive finite-sample lower bounds on estimation error under local and central differential privacy. Simple estimators they propose nearly achieve those bounds. The results cover ordinary graphs and extend to hypergraphs, where links join more than two nodes. Experiments on synthetic and real communication data confirm the theory's predictions about the privacy-accuracy trade-off.
arxiv-2602-04248:
Search that forgets teaches agents nothing between problems. Hao Lu and 4 co-authors give Monte Carlo tree search a memory in their 2026 framework, Empirical-MCTS. Standard search discards successful reasoning patterns after each instance, unlike human solvers who accumulate know-how.

Two mechanisms close the loop. A meta-prompting optimizer refines the search's own criteria from pairwise feedback during local exploration. A memory agent curates a global repository that acts as a policy prior for future searches. The dual loop turns stateless inference-time search into continuous, non-parametric learning, letting an agent's experience compound across problems.
arxiv-2602-04348:
Erin Claire Carson argues that sloppy arithmetic is fine when the problem is already sloppy. Her 2026 paper looks at mixed precision computing, where parts of a calculation run at different accuracies on modern hardware. The question is where low precision is safe.

When grid, sensor, or approximation errors already dominate, rounding error from low precision may cost nothing measurable. Carson studies how these error sources interact in matrix computations. Balancing them on purpose lets scientists choose precisions that speed computing without visible accuracy loss. Worked examples from matrix algebra show the promise, timely as hardware more and more rewards mixed precision.
arxiv-2602-04448:
In a 2026 paper, Jiacheng Liang and 3 co-authors tackle safety problems in Mixture-of-Experts language models. These models route each input to a small subset of expert networks. That routing can let standard safety training appear to work while leaving risky experts unchanged.

Their method, called RASA, first finds the experts most often activated by successful jailbreak attacks. It then fine-tunes only those experts while holding routing fixed. A later step keeps routing consistent with safe contexts. Across two model designs and many attacks, RASA gave near-perfect resistance and less over-refusal. It also preserved general ability on standard knowledge and math benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-04648:
Alessandro Leanza and 3 co-authors add eyes to a back-support exoskeleton in a 2026 paper on adaptive assistance for industrial lifting. Such devices reduce spinal load, but help must arrive at the right moment and match the task.

Their system combines first-person vision, wearable gaze tracking, and grasp detection to gate assistance. A state machine tracks task progress, and a variable controller adapts torque to posture and object state. Fifteen participants lifted loads under three conditions: no device, device without vision, and device with vision. Vision-guided help arrived earlier and stronger. Users reported less physical demand and greater fluency, trust, and comfort, and preferred the vision mode.
arxiv-2602-05048:
Planning with a human partner means not knowing everything: objects, goals, and intentions can all be missing. Zeyu Fang and 2 co-authors built a system for asking the right questions in that situation in this 2026 artificial intelligence paper. An agent that asks too much wastes time; one that asks too little plans blind.

Their method, MINT, grows a symbolic tree of possible human-AI interactions and uses a neural planning policy to estimate how much each knowledge gap clouds the outcome. Self-play then tunes the agent's questioning strategy, and a language model searches the tree's reasoning to draft the best queries. The authors prove a return guarantee for the approach. On three benchmarks with unknown objects of rising realism, MINT-based planning reached near-expert results while asking only a few questions per task.
arxiv-2602-05148:
Fine-tuning a large model cheaply usually means assuming the weight update is low-rank, as in LoRA. Songtao Wei and 8 co-authors question that assumption in this 2026 machine learning paper. When a task spreads its singular values fairly evenly, a low-rank update may simply not have room to express what needs to change.

Their method, CoSA, borrows from compressed sensing instead. Weight updates are written through fixed random projection matrices and a compact learnable core, so the update lives in a low-dimensional code without being low-rank. The authors analyze the scheme formally as a synthesis process, proving updates can be encoded compactly and mapped back through the projections. Across ten tasks and five models from the RoBERTa, Llama, and Qwen families, CoSA matched or beat leading parameter-efficient methods, which the authors read as a more expressive route to adaptation.
arxiv-2602-05248:
Melting hides energy: while ice turns to water, temperature stays pinned even as heat pours in. Zhiang Xie, writing alone, resolves that information loss in this 2026 atmospheric physics paper. He introduces a latent temperature, the path the system would have followed without the phase change, and lets energy conservation speak about it.

A rigorous duality emerges between the total latent heat released during melting and the accumulated amount by which the latent temperature exceeds the melting point. The duality is exactly a one-dimensional Wasserstein distance between the two temperature paths, priced by a surface dissipation timescale and the melt energy. Applied to ice-sheet surface melting, the timescale reads directly from radiative and turbulent heat loss. That same setup derives the empirical Positive Degree Day law from first principles and predicts realistic degree-day factors from the surface energy balance, no hand calibration needed.
arxiv-2602-05348:
The Bc meson, made of a bottom quark and a charm quark, is a rare probe of how heavy quarks bind. Na Cai and 2 co-authors calculate how often it would be produced when photons strike protons in this 2026 particle physics paper. The framework is nonrelativistic QCD factorization, the standard theory for heavy quarkonium production.

Besides the dominant direct channel, where a photon and a gluon fuse, the authors add resolved contributions where the photon first fluctuates into partons, giving gluon-gluon and quark-antiquark starting pairs. They compute total cross sections and momentum distributions for four collider setups, from the retired HERA to the planned LHeC, FCC-ep, and EIC. The direct channel leads everywhere, but the gluon-gluon resolved channel corrects it by around ten percent where most events land, at low transverse momentum, and grows in importance as collision energy rises. The quark channel is negligible.
arxiv-2602-05448:
Picking the best few items from a long list is costly when each check means asking a large model to compare several items at once. Sheshansh Agrawal, Thien Hang Nguyen, and Douwe Kiela offer BlitzRank, a zero-shot ranking method built on tournament graphs. Each group comparison yields many pairwise wins and losses, and the method stores them all in one shared preference graph.

By closing the graph under chains of wins, BlitzRank infers extra orderings without paying for more model calls. The authors also give rules for knowing when the top items are already certain, and a greedy plan that asks for the most useful comparisons next. When preferences form cycles, the method groups tied items into tiers instead of forcing a false order. Across fourteen test sets and five models, it matched or beat rivals while using far fewer tokens.
arxiv-2602-05548:
GRPO has become a standard way to draw out reasoning from language models, yet its exploration and difficulty handling are still weak. Zhiqi Yu, Zhangquan Chen, and 3 co-authors trace both problems to a hidden symmetry in how group-relative advantages are assigned. Correct and incorrect attempts in a group receive weights that mirror each other in a strict way.

That symmetry has two costs. At group level, unsampled actions stay untouched, which blocks exploration of new correct solutions. At sample level, the method favors medium-difficulty items and ignores how training needs shift over time. Controlled experiments show that softening the symmetry helps exploration but can add instability, and that a curriculum from easy to hard items boosts learning. The authors build these lessons into Asymmetric GRAE, which tunes exploration incentives and difficulty focus as training proceeds. Across seven benchmarks it improved GRPO and its variants.
arxiv-2602-05748:
Knowing whether one specific example trained a model is a sharp privacy test, and membership inference attacks try to pass it. Amit Kravchik Taub, Fred Grabovski, Guy Amit, and Yisroel Mirsky propose LeakBoost, which actively interrogates a model instead of reading static scores like loss or confidence. Given a candidate input, it synthesizes an interrogation image tuned to amplify differences in internal activations between members and non members.

That probe image is then judged by an existing membership detector, unchanged. Across image classification data sets and architectures, adding LeakBoost raised detection quality sharply at low false positive rates, where privacy attacks matter most. A sensitivity analysis found deeper layers and short, gentle optimization give the strongest leakage, and gradient based detectors gain the most. The authors present the method as a modular add on for auditing privacy leakage.
arxiv-2602-05948:
Robots that must spread out, one per node of a network, solve the classic dispersion problem. Himani, Supantha Pandit, and Gokarna Sharma add a twist of place: each robot has a color, and it must settle on a node of its own color. The graph is anonymous, connected, and undirected, its nodes colored from a small palette, and the robots start placed arbitrarily.

When only one color exists, the new problem reduces exactly to classic dispersion. The authors develop several deterministic algorithms with guaranteed bounds on both time and the memory each agent needs. They also prove an impossibility result and a lower bound that no deterministic algorithm can beat. To their knowledge, this is the first treatment of location aware dispersion, a problem where robots are not interchangeable. Guarantees on memory matter because simple robots carry little of it.
arxiv-2602-06248:
Deleting sensitive or copyrighted material from a trained language model is called machine unlearning, but checking that the knowledge is truly gone is hard. Patryk Rybak and 3 co-authors present REBEL, a system that hunts for leftovers. Standard checks use tame questions, which can mistake surface silence for real forgetting.

REBEL evolves adversarial prompts, breeding new attacks from ones that partly worked. On two standard benchmarks, it pulled supposedly forgotten knowledge back out of models, with success rates far above fixed test prompts. The results span many unlearning algorithms. The authors warn that current methods may offer only a thin layer of protection.
arxiv-2602-06548:
Motion models usually learn one skeleton at a time, so a model trained on humans cannot animate a dog or a robot. Mingxi Xu and 9 co-authors present NECromancer, a universal motion tokenizer that works directly on arbitrary BVH skeletons, the standard format for motion capture data. It learns motion separately from body structure.

Three parts make it work. A graph encoder reads each skeleton's joints, rest poses, and topology. A topology-agnostic tokenizer compresses motion into discrete tokens that mean the same thing across bodies. A large data set gathers BVH motions across many skeletons. The token space supports cross-species transfer, composition, denoising, generation, and text-based motion search, with high-quality reconstruction under strong compression.
arxiv-2602-06948:
Jean Kaddour, Srijan Patel, Gbètondji Dovonon, Leo Richter, Pasquale Minervini, and Matt J. Kusner ask whether AI agents can predict their own success. They elicit success probability estimates from agents before, during, and after task execution, and find universal overconfidence: some agents that succeed only 22 percent of the time predict 77 percent success. The gap between belief and performance is the paper's central finding.

Counterintuitively, pre-execution assessment, made with strictly less information, often discriminates success better than post-execution review, though the differences are not always significant. Adversarial prompting that reframes assessment as bug-finding achieves the best calibration. The work suggests that asking agents to look for their own flaws, rather than to judge themselves after the fact, may yield more honest uncertainty estimates.
arxiv-2602-07048:
Sumin Kim and nine co-authors use language models as semantic risk managers for prediction market trading. Prediction markets tie event series to plain-language descriptions, yet robust lead-lag links are hard to find. Their hybrid screener runs in two stages. First, a statistical stage uses Granger causality to pick candidate pairs, each with a leader and a follower, from market-implied probability series. Second, a language model stage re-ranks those pairs by asking if the direction allows a plausible economic transmission mechanism, judged from event descriptions.

The team scores ranked pairs with a fixed trading protocol that turns link quality into realized profit and loss. On Kalshi Economics markets, the hybrid beat the statistical baseline. Win rate rose from about 51 percent to about 55 percent. Average losing trade size fell from about 649 dollars to about 347 dollars, driven by filtering fragile links prone to big losses.
arxiv-2602-07348:
When a liquid drop meets a deep pool, it may merge fully or only partly, and the neck between drop and pool oscillates as it does so.  Manas Ranjan Behera and three co-authors run axisymmetric simulations across drop shapes to generalize the mechanisms of partial coalescence.

They map the boundary between partial and complete coalescence against Weber, Ohnesorge. Bond numbers, which capture inertial, viscous, and gravitational effects, and they trace neck oscillations to the upward liquid column that pinches off through inward horizontal momentum.  Fluid dynamicists get a phase diagram and a mechanism that organizes a messy, shape-dependent phenomenon.
arxiv-2602-07448:
Balloon-borne telescopes need highly stable images, and Sunrise III carries a dedicated system for that job.  A large team led by Thomas Berkefeld describes the wavefront correction and image stabilization system developed for the telescope, and its results were measured during integration and the 2024 science flight.

A correlation tracker and fast tip-tilt mirror handle rapid stabilization. A six-element Shack-Hartmann sensor measures defocus, coma, and other low-order aberrations for correction by an active secondary mirror.  The system targets 0. 005 arcsecond stabilization precision and tight focus stability.  Solar experts get the engineering record behind sharp images from the edge of space. Sharp images from a balloon platform demand exactly this kind of steady control.
arxiv-2602-08048:
Diffusion language models make text by side-by-side cleaning, but falsehood finders built for one-way models do not transfer well, since truth evidence appears, drifts, or self-corrects across cleaning steps. Arshia Hemmat and three co-authors offer TDGNet, which treats finding as learning over changing token-level focus graphs.

At each step, the method thins the focus graph, updates per-token notes by message passing, and pools path-wide evidence with time focus. Tests on two diffusion models across question-answering benchmarks show steady AUROC gains against output-based, latent, and static-graph baselines, at single-pass cost and modest overhead. The work shows that for diffusion models, when evidence appears matters as much as what appears.
arxiv-2602-08748:
Algebraic Bieri-Strebel groups arise from polynomials, and tree-pair representations offer a concrete way to picture their elements. Lewis Molyneux revives a previously discovered construction method for such representations. His arXiv paper also exhibits a class of higher-order groups that admit no tree-pair representation at all.

Together, the two results show there is no maximum degree beyond which every higher-degree polynomial group must have a tree-pair representation. Readers get both a tool and a limit: a construction for many groups, plus proof that the construction cannot extend to all of them.
arxiv-2602-08948:
Big reasoning gains from sampling hundreds of answers waste enormous compute. Chen Jin and three co-authors propose CoRefine, a tiny controller that decides when a language model should stop, recheck, or try a new angle. The controller, a 211,000-parameter network sitting atop a frozen model, reads the model's confidence across its full reasoning trace.

It averages just 2.7 refinement steps per problem, cutting tokens roughly 190-fold against 512-sample baselines while staying competitive on accuracy. When it confidently halts, it is right 92.6 percent of the time, showing confidence dynamics carry real signal. A tree variant balances exploration and exploitation for serving and verifier-friendly deployment.
arxiv-2602-09148:
Fair order means earlier events should be handled first, but flawed clocks make that hard: stamps from unlike clients in the same short window cannot always be trusted. Muhammad Haseeb and six co-authors embrace the doubt instead of fighting it. Their tool, Tommy, compares noisy stamps by odds using a stats model of per-clock sync error.

Odds-based comparison can loop, so global order is tricky. The authors map ordering to an old ranking problem from social-choice theory, yielding sound ways to reason with looping comparisons. Tommy then gives a partial order of events, with far better fairness than a Spanner TrueTime-based baseline. The work offers a practical route to fairer distributed systems.
arxiv-2602-09348:
Two central qubits sit in an environment formed by a transverse-field Ising chain, which is driven across its quantum critical points and repeatedly reset to its starting state at random times. A 2026 paper led by R. Jafari, with three co-authors, asks how that resetting reshapes entanglement and quantum discord between the qubits. The environment is not a passive bath here, but a driven system whose own history matters.

In strong coupling, entanglement and discord revive inside the interval bounded by the Ising critical points, though the revivals fade as resets grow more frequent. Weak coupling instead gives steady decline, and with resets the correlations fall in oscillations whose period lengthens as reset rate or ramp time scale shrinks. Revival peaks also decay exponentially with reset rate for one measure, while discord shows no clean scaling. The study maps how control over an environment can tune quantum correlations.
arxiv-2602-09448:
Training dense retrievers increasingly relies on synthetic queries, but past methods generate one query per document and judge quality alone. Xincan Feng and three co-authors study multi-query synthesis systematically in their 2026 paper, uncovering a tradeoff: high-quality queries help in-domain tasks, while diverse queries help generalization to new domains. Controlled trials across four benchmark types and three embedding models trace the diversity benefit to query complexity.

The link is strong: complexity, approximated by content words, closely tracks how much diversity helps. The authors formalize this as the Complexity-Diversity Principle, stating that query complexity sets the optimal diversity level. Two strategies follow: synthesize multiple queries for high-complexity tasks, and weight training by content words for existing data. Both lift out-of-domain performance on reasoning-heavy benchmarks, with compounded gains when combined.
arxiv-2602-09748:
When an attacker mounts a model extraction attack, selected data points are put to a black-box machine learning model as queries in order to uncover its parameters. Daan Otto and three co-authors note that rising demand for explanations may add counterfactual queries to the usual factual queries. Their 2026 paper studies linear models under three query types: factual, counterfactual, and robust counterfactual.

For any query set, novel mathematical formulations describe the classification regions where the unknown model's decision is known, without recovering any parameters. Bounds on the number of queries needed to extract parameters follow for counterfactual queries under arbitrary norm-based distances. With differentiable distance measures, the full model can be recovered from a single counterfactual query. With polyhedral distances, required queries grow linearly with data-space dimension, doubling for robust counterfactuals. Distance choice and counterfactual robustness thus shape model security.
arxiv-2602-09948:
Discrepancy theory asks how evenly items can be split among colors, and its classical tools assume the quantity being split adds up neatly. A 2026 paper led by Tatiana Rocha Avila, with two co-authors, studies what happens when it does not. Recent work extended the theory to non-additive functions, motivated by fair division, but many classical methods fail there.

The authors focus on coverage functions in a sparse setting that mirrors the classical Beck-Fiala setup. The same setting covers matroid rank functions and graph edge coverage. Assuming each item touches only a few elements across all functions, they prove a constructive bound. It grows polynomially with that sparsity, the number of colors, and the logarithm of the item count.
arxiv-2602-10348:
Stepped-wedge designs stagger treatment roll-out over time for practical and ethical reasons, but standard analyses use parametric models with linear covariate tweaks and preset correlations. A 2026 paper led by Liangbo Lyu, with one co-author, proposes new estimators for causal average effects in stepped-wedge designs. They sharpen precision through machine-learning-based covariate tweaks for complex outcome-covariate links. Quadratic inference functions learn patterns as they go.

Consistency and asymptotic normality hold under mild conditions needing only squared-error convergence of nuisance estimators, even with model misspecification. The paper gives an account of when minimal asymptotic variance is reached. The estimator never cuts efficiency versus an independence working correlation and handles treatment-effect variety by exposure and date. Simulations and reworkings of two real studies show the methods.
arxiv-2602-10548:
Yigang Qin and EunJeong Cheon bring labor theory into computing design in a 2026 paper for the CHI conference. Human-computer contact research has renewed its focus to labor and the political economy of computing, yet it rarely engages labor theory deeply. The paper traces Labor Process Theory from Marx and Braverman through Burawoy and later thinkers.

The authors survey HCI writings on labor, mapping its themes and its conceptual, tested, and design plans. From the theory they draw directions for research and practice. They urge distinguishing labor from work and linking practice to value production. They also urge studying management rather than only workers, analyzing consent and legitimacy, looking beyond the point of production, and making alternative institutions. The goal is structural analysis, not just better interfaces for current jobs.
arxiv-2602-10948:
Palash Dey and four co-authors study the parameterized hardness of a common subgraph problem in a 2026 paper. Given two graphs and a size threshold, the question asks for a common subgraph on at least that many vertices with no isolated vertices. Every part must therefore have at least two vertices. The variant arises in graph theory and machine social choice.

The authors show the problem is NP-hard and give a fixed-parameter tractable recipe parameterized by the size threshold. A study across structural settings yields a complete dichotomy of parameterized results. It covers vertex cover number, maximum degree, treedepth, pathwidth, and treewidth of one or both graphs, for single and combined parameterizations. The paper maps exactly where the problem becomes tractable and where it stays hard.
arxiv-2602-11448:
Interpretable image classifiers should explain themselves in human concepts, but flat concept lists ignore levels. Nghia Nguyen and two co-authors propose Layered Concept Code and Pursuit, a frame that induces a levels of concept codes and recovers concepts by layered sparse coding. Standard sparse coding can predict correctly while explaining inconsistently with the levels.

Given a semantic levels, a geometric construction builds the code levels, and sufficient terms for recovery follow when true concepts form a rooted path. Layered coding reliably recovers those codes where standard coding fails. Tests show better concept precision and recall at competitive scores, with larger gains when training samples are scarce. Levels thus makes accounts more faithful.
arxiv-2602-11748:
Effective test-time scaling needs models that can generate, verify, and refine several reasoning hypotheses inside one continuous context. Futing Wang and eight co-authors diagnose why that in-context search stays shallow. Longer reasoning paths cover more states, but their sampling probability decays exponentially during autoregressive generation. The authors name this trap the Shallow Exploration Trap. Broader coverage demands longer trajectories that the model rarely samples.

Their recipe, Length-Incentivized Exploration, explicitly rewards length coupled with a redundancy penalty. That maximizes state coverage in two steps. Tests across different model families show the method effectively encourages in-context search. It improves in-domain task scores by about 4 percent on average. Out-of-domain benchmarks gain about 3 percent, showing that rewarding longer, non-redundant search pays off beyond the training distribution.
arxiv-2602-11848:
Logic statements can be calculated with algebra if statements are transformed into poly form. Pelle Brooke Borgeke continues a series on the PBNF transform, a version of propositional calculus in which algebraic polynomials serve as symbols for links, here named operators. Moving to a dual space yields poly families, another shape of or-based boolean normal form, named Polynomial Boolean Normal Form.

Only one law of reasoning is used: the rule of substitution. Different poly sets can be chosen from the house of PBNF depending on statement form, making sums simpler. The approach can also find new theorems and extend older ones, including results by Church and Barkley Rosser on duality. The paper thus offers an algebra toolkit for logic reasoning with a single proof rule.
arxiv-2602-11948:
Muon, an optimizer that updates weight matrices along approximate polar factors of gradients, performs strikingly well at scale, yet theory lags behind. Antoine Gonon and two co-authors show that standard explanations fall short even on simple strongly convex quadratics, where single-step comparisons and worst-case bounds miss the real behavior. Understanding Muon, they argue, needs more than local proxies and pessimistic guarantees.

Their analysis surfaces two effects that simple quadratics already reveal. First, approximation error in the polar step can qualitatively change discrete-time dynamics, improving reachability and finite-time performance, an effect practitioners exploit when tuning Muon but theory treats as mere accuracy loss. Second, the objective's structure shapes finite-budget constants beyond conditioning alone. Any general theory of Muon must either include these ingredients or explain why they do not matter in practice.
arxiv-2602-12048:
Breaking time-reversal symmetry alone does not guarantee one-way transport, a subtlety this paper clarifies for quantum spin-Hall devices.
