One is driven by the immune system attacking the body itself, covering celiac disease, a skin condition, and a nerve condition affecting balance. The third covers gluten sensitivity, where neither allergy nor self attack explains the symptoms. The paper compares how each form starts, looks, and spreads through populations.
europmc-pmc3311548:
Yuan, Cohen, Ravel, Abdo, and Forney compared ways of pulling DNA out of human associated bacteria, in a 2012 study. Reading microbe communities without growing them first always starts with extracting DNA, and a poor method can distort which species seem present. The team ran six common procedures on eleven bacterial species, alone and in an even test mixture.

Every method skewed the apparent mix of species away from the true even balance. Methods that smashed cells open with tiny beads, or used an enzyme that digs through bacterial walls, came closest to the truth. All six methods repeated well across workers and days. The authors advise that studies of human samples build in bead beating or the enzyme step to crack tough cells open.
europmc-pmc3329548:
Hospodsky and colleagues showed that people themselves fill indoor air with bacteria, in a 2012 study. Breathing in certain airborne bacteria can spread infection or worsen asthma, yet where indoor bacteria come from is poorly understood. The team sampled air and dust in a university classroom, both while it was occupied and while empty. They compared the bacteria with those outdoors, in ventilation ducts, and in floor dust.

With students present, the air carried far more particles and bacterial genomes, up to about a hundred times more in the larger particle size range. The bacteria matched types living on human skin, noses, and hair. Stirred up floor dust was a major source, though direct shedding from bodies contributed too. The findings mean people in shared rooms inhale microbes shed by current and earlier occupants.
europmc-pmc3349748:
Hemetsberger and colleagues investigated how the maize smut fungus Ustilago maydis disarms its host during infection. They focused on Pep1, a small protein the fungus secretes into plant tissue, and searched for the plant component it acts upon.

Pep1 turned out to bind and inhibit POX12, a maize peroxidase involved in generating reactive oxygen species for defence. Fungal mutants lacking Pep1 triggered strong oxidative bursts and were blocked early in infection, while the intact effector kept the plant's alarm quiet. The work identifies suppression of the oxidative burst as a decisive early step in establishing this fungal disease.
europmc-pmc3364948:
Jeon and colleagues showed that a probiotic bacterium, Bifidobacterium breve, teaches the gut immune system to calm inflammation. They compared two intestinal strains in mice and found that only B. breve, not Lactobacillus casei, generated regulatory T cells of the Tr1 type that produce the calming signal interleukin-10 in the large intestine.

The effect ran through CD103-positive dendritic cells, which responded to the bacterium via the TLR2 and MyD88 pathway by releasing interleukin-10 and interleukin-27. Those signals drove T cells to become interleukin-10 producers expressing cMaf, interleukin-21, and Ahr. Feeding B. breve eased colitis in susceptible mice, an effect lost when interleukin-10 was absent.
europmc-pmc3386248:
Jones and a large team argued in 2012 that the resting brain's network layout keeps shifting rather than sitting still. Brain scans at rest show linked regions forming modules, but the flickering of those links has blocked their use as disease markers. The team built an atlas of regions from nearly nine hundred older adults.

Tracking links over sliding time windows proved the modular pattern is genuinely unsteady. Comparing Alzheimer patients with matched healthy peers, the team found the difference lay in how long the default mode network lingered in certain strong states, not in average link strength. That dwell time, they propose, may underpin scan findings across early memory disorders.
europmc-pmc3564748:
Lucy Turner and colleagues summarized a Cochrane review in Systematic Reviews in 2012 on the CONSORT Statement, a checklist meant to improve how randomized trials are reported. Poor reporting hides how a trial was run, so readers cannot judge its results. The question was whether journals that endorse the checklist publish trials described more completely than journals that do not.

The review gathered fifty evaluations covering 16,604 trials and scored reports against items from the CONSORT checklists. Across most comparisons, endorsement came with better reporting: sixty-nine of eighty-one analyses favored endorsing journals, and five outcomes improved by a margin the authors counted as clear. Gains were uneven, trials per analysis were often few, and many evaluations were judged weak. Even so, nothing suggested endorsement does harm, so the balance favors journals adopting the standard.
europmc-pmc3578748:
Donald Shepard, Eduardo Undurraga, and Yara Halasa estimated the burden of dengue across Southeast Asia in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. Dengue, a mosquito-borne fever, hits the region hard, but patchy reporting hides its true scale. Numbers that leaders can trust are needed to rank dengue against other health problems and to fund control work fairly across countries.

Gathering reports from surveillance, the World Health Organization, and published studies for twelve countries, the team corrected for underreporting and priced each episode from a review of cost studies. For 2001 to 2010 they estimate an average 2.9 million episodes and 5,906 deaths a year. The yearly bill came to about 950 million dollars, with 214,000 disability-adjusted life years lost, a rate above seventeen other conditions named for comparison. Prevention and vector control costs were left out, so the true bill runs higher.
europmc-pmc3594748:
J. Ross Chapman and colleagues identified a guardian of one DNA repair route in Molecular Cell in 2013. When both strands of DNA break, a cell must choose: stitch the ends back together, or trim them and use a matching template. Proteins 53BP1 and BRCA1 fight over that choice by controlling the trimming step, called resection. A third protein, RIF1, turned out to be the missing enforcer on the 53BP1 side.

Mice without RIF1 failed at the antibody-shuffling task that needs direct joining, and at fusing broken chromosome ends. RIF1 is called to breaks by marked 53BP1, and without it broken ends were over-trimmed. In cells lacking BRCA1, removing RIF1 also stopped the toxic mis-joining that a class of cancer drugs provokes. The division of labor is tidy: the pair blocks trimming early in the cell cycle, and BRCA1 later lifts the block so template repair can run.
europmc-pmc3636048:
Aurélie Kapusta and colleagues measured how much of our non-coding RNA is built from jumping genes, in PLoS Genetics in 2013. Long noncoding RNAs regulate genes across vertebrates, but where they came from was murky. Transposable elements, DNA chunks that copy themselves around the genome, were the suspects. Comparing human, mouse, and zebrafish, the team catalogued these elements inside mature lncRNA transcripts and in the switches that control them.

More than two thirds of lncRNAs carried transposable element pieces, making up about thirty percent of human lncRNA sequence, while protein-coding transcripts rarely did. Some element families were strongly enriched, and the mix differed by species. In humans, the embedded pieces evolve more slowly than chance, a sign of real function, and they supply about thirty thousand starting, splicing, or ending signals. Jumping genes, the authors conclude, are founding architects of this RNA class.
europmc-pmc3651348:
Weaning is one of the hardest weeks in a pig's life, Campbell, Crenshaw and Polo explain in a 2013 review in the Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology. Piglets leave the sow and face body, social and housing shocks at once. The strain hits the gut and the immune system, cutting health, growth and feed intake, above all in the first week after weaning. Farms have eased some harms with better housing, feed and handling.

The review sets out what the stress does inside the gut: its shape, build, working and immune defences. Those gut changes then drive the farm-level losses that follow, in growth, intake, sickness and death rates. By tying gut facts to output facts, the piece gives pig producers and vets a base for sharper plans to get piglets through weaning with less loss.
europmc-pmc3653748:
Tiny sacs shed by cells into blood carry a rich load of RNA, Huang and a large team show in a 2013 BMC Genomics study. The sacs, called exosomes in the text, may let cells talk to each other and may yield blood markers of disease. The team sequenced RNA from sacs in three human blood samples. They also tested library kits from three makers, building 14 libraries and reading 101.8 million sequence pieces.

Short RNAs called microRNAs made up over 42 percent of raw reads and 76 percent of reads that could be placed, with 593 kinds found. The five most common kinds took near half of all placed microRNA reads. Other RNA kinds turned up too, plus 185 candidate new microRNAs. Each kit caught some RNAs better than others.
europmc-pmc3734448:
Claire Verraes and a large group of co-authors wrote a review in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2013 on antimicrobial resistance in the food chain. Bacteria on food that resist antibiotics are a direct risk to people who eat the food. Resistance genes in harmless bacteria are an indirect risk, since disease bacteria can pick those genes up.

The review maps three routes by which resistance reaches food. One is antibiotic use on farms selecting resistant bacteria. Another is resistant bacteria added on purpose during food making, such as starter cultures. The third is cross-contamination during processing. Raw foods carry the highest risk because nothing kills the bacteria before eating. Heat and other killing steps lower the risk, while weak treatments can leave stressed cells alive and more able to pass resistance on.
europmc-pmc3751348:
Loris Lopetuso, Franco Scaldaferri, Valentina Petito, and Antonio Gasbarrini wrote a review in Gut Pathogens in 2013 on commensal Clostridia, a major group of gut bacteria. These rod-shaped bacteria settle in the gut of breastfed infants in the first month of life and live close to the gut wall. That position puts them at the center of gut function.

The review sets out how these bacteria help control the gut's physical, metabolic, and immune processes, in dialogue with other resident microbes. It also covers what happens when the microbe mix shifts into an unhealthy state, a change tied to several gut disorders. The authors argue that the group's key role could be used to prevent and treat such shifts, and to shape drug effects.
europmc-pmc3763548:
Wafa B'chir and nine co-authors reported a study in Nucleic Acids Research in 2013 on how stress switches on autophagy genes. When cells face stress, such as starvation or a clogged protein-folding compartment, a signal through the factor eIF2-alpha cuts general protein making but boosts one regulator, ATF4. Autophagy, the cell's self-eating cleanup, rises at the same time.

The team showed that the eIF2-alpha/ATF4 path directly drives a program of autophagy gene activity under amino acid starvation and compartment stress. Two kinases and the factors ATF4 and CHOP are all needed to raise genes that build and run the autophagosome, the cleanup sac. They sorted the genes into three classes by how they depend on ATF4 and CHOP, and showed that mixed binding lets the response scale with stress strength.
europmc-pmc3764148:
Julia Salzman and four co-authors reported a study in PLoS Genetics in 2013 on circular RNA. Most RNA messages are straight lines, but thousands of genes also make circle-shaped transcripts, and at many genes the circle is the main form. The team used an improved computer method to find and compare these circles.

They found widespread circular RNA in the fruit fly and estimated that human circles may reach about one percent of the number of standard RNA molecules. Using data from the ENCODE project, they showed that which genes make circles differs by cell type. So do how much circle each gene makes relative to its straight form, and even the splice patterns of the circles. The authors conclude that circle making is a built-in, regulated part of gene expression.
europmc-pmc3765848:
Hongen Zhang, Paul Meltzer, and Sean Davis presented a software package called RCircos in BMC Bioinformatics in 2013. Circos plots draw genome data in circles, showing how regions relate across chromosomes. The original Circos tool runs in Perl and needs extra file preparation, which makes it awkward to combine with R, the statistics environment many genome researchers use.

RCircos rebuilds the approach using only packages that ship with base R. It supports the standard Circos two-dimensional track types: scatter, line, histogram, heatmap, tile, connector, link, and text label plots, each with its own function. All inputs are simple data frames, so results from other R pipelines can flow straight in. The authors offer it as a simple, flexible base for building complex genome figures.
europmc-pmc3775148:
Jordan Vacheron and eight co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2013 on plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, helpful bacteria that live on roots. These bacteria boost plant growth by direct and indirect means, and a key route is reshaping the root system itself.

Their signals, including plant hormones, increase side-root branching and root hair growth, which improves nutrient uptake. They also change root function and the physiology of the whole plant. How their signals trigger plant responses is only partly known. The review stresses the ecology of the root zone: soil conditions and other microbes shape which bacteria thrive and how strongly they act. Grasping those community effects, the authors argue, is a prerequisite for farm strategies built on these bacteria.
europmc-pmc3780648:
Rafael Lugo-Huitrón and five co-authors wrote a review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2013 on quinolinic acid, a neurotoxin the body makes itself. The compound comes from the kynurenine pathway, the main route for breaking down the amino acid tryptophan. It is normally present in tiny amounts in the brain and spinal fluid.

Quinolinic acid switches on NMDA receptors, and its breakdown enzyme saturates fast, so extra amounts keep stimulating those receptors and can kill nerve cells. The review argues that receptor activation alone cannot explain its toxicity. The authors describe its wider targets: pre-synaptic receptors, energy failure, oxidative stress, transcription factors, the cell skeleton, behavior changes, and cell death. They tie the compound to a range of human neurological diseases.
europmc-pmc3885448:
Caiyun Xuan leads a team of co-authors in a breast cancer microbe study in PLoS One, with the record dated 2014. Most breast cancers have no known cause. Microbe imbalance has been tied to obesity, diabetes, and colon cancer, so the team ask if breast tissue microbes shift with cancer.

Gene sequencing compared tumor tissue with matched healthy tissue from the same patients. One bacterium ran high in tumors, another in healthy tissue, and their levels moved in opposite ways in healthy tissue but not in tumors. Total bacterial load was lower in tumors, and lower still in advanced disease. The pattern marks a disturbed breast microbe mix in cancer. Whether microbes help cause the disease stays open, but the link merits study.
europmc-pmc3917348:
Diana Urrego, Adam P. Tomczak, Farrah Zahed, Walter Stühmer, and Luis A. Pardo review, in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2014, how potassium channels help control the cell cycle. Potassium channels are pores that let potassium ions cross the cell membrane. Cell division is tightly controlled in healthy tissue, and its failure is a hallmark of cancer, so every layer of that control matters.

The review explains the ways channels can shape division, from setting membrane voltage to changing cell volume at key steps. It then walks through specific channels that show these effects in action. The picture that emerges is of channels as working parts of the division machinery, not bystanders, which also makes them possible targets for slowing unwanted cell growth.
europmc-pmc4034148:
Ryan T. Kendall and Carol A. Feghali-Bostwick review fibroblasts, the cells that drive scar-like build-up in organs, in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2014. Fibroblasts are the most common cells of connective tissue and its main builders. Under lasting injury and inflammation they turn into myofibroblasts, heavy producers of matrix that can also contract and pull wounds shut.

The review traces where these activated cells come from, a wider set of sources than once thought. It covers the signals that wake them, from cytokines to growth factors, and their twin roles in healing and in disease. The same cells shape inflammation, new blood vessel growth, and even tumour progress in nearby cancers. Current care for fibrosis leans on broad immune-damping and anti-growth drugs. The authors survey newer therapies that aim at fibroblast biology itself, with the goal of stopping build-up while sparing normal repair.
europmc-pmc4051748:
E. Bethan Davies, Richard Morriss, and Cris Glazebrook pool trials of online help for student mental health, in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2014. Depression and anxiety are common at university and drag on study and social life. Many students never reach a professional. Their fluency with digital tools makes web programmes a tempting route.

Seventeen randomised trials met the entry rules, most testing website programmes, many built on cognitive behavioural therapy. Fourteen trials gave data fit for pooling, covering close to eighteen hundred students. Effects on depression, anxiety, and stress were small but leaned positive against control groups. Reporting quality was middling, samples were small, and skewed data clouded several results. The authors back self-guided online therapy as a viable option while warning that the proof is fragile.
europmc-pmc4105248:
Jeffrey D. Galley, Michael T. Bailey, and colleagues tested whether even a short social stress can disturb the bacteria living on the colon's inner lining in mice. Their study appeared in BMC Microbiology in 2014. Gut bacteria shape host health, and earlier work showed long stressors shift faecal populations, but lining communities matter more for immunity.

Mucosa-associated bacteria sit close to immune tissue, so changes there carry weight. The researchers exposed mice to a social stressor and profiled the colonic lining community, noting that mouse strains differ in anxiety and stress hormone responses. Stressor exposure did reshape the community, cutting lactobacilli in particular. Because lactobacilli are considered beneficial, stress-driven losses of them could have real health implications, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc4196248:
Nita G. Forouhi and a large European team split saturated fat into its parts in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology in 2014. Saturated fat as a whole is tied to type 2 diabetes, but the individual fatty acids in blood may not all act alike. The EPIC-InterAct study gave a chance to test each one against later diabetes.

The study covered 12,403 people who developed diabetes and a comparison group of 16,154, drawn from 340,234 Europeans. Blood saturated fats made up 46 percent of plasma phospholipid fat. Even-chain types, such as palmitic acid, came with higher diabetes risk. Odd-chain types, found largely in dairy fat, and very long chain types came with lower risk. The authors argue diet advice should treat these fats separately, not as one block.
europmc-pmc4237348:
Bruce J. Walker, Ashlee M. Earl, and ten co-authors released an assembly repair tool called Pilon in PLoS ONE in 2014. Sequencers can now read hundreds of bacterial genomes in a day, but the draft assemblies they produce carry errors and gaps. Fixing them by hand cannot keep up.

Pilon takes a draft assembly plus paired sequencing reads and polishes it automatically. It corrects single letters, repairs wrongly joined stretches, and fills gaps, and it calls variants from small changes up to large insertions, duplications, and deletions. On both single-set and two-set chromosome genomes it produced longer, cleaner assemblies with fewer errors than rival tools. Its variant calls matched the best callers, while also catching the big changes others missed. The team reports it already improves thousands of assemblies.
europmc-pmc4251848:
Janus Christian Jakobsen, Christian Gluud, and three co-authors set stricter rules for judging meta-analyses in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. A meta-analysis can look decisive while resting on too few patients, many outcomes, or biased trials. Journals lacked a shared procedure for deciding when pooled results deserve belief.

Their eight-step procedure starts by reporting both fixed-effect and random-effects results, taking the more cautious as the headline. It then demands checks for heterogeneity, adjustment of significance thresholds for the number of main outcomes, and a calculation of how many patients the question truly needs, tested by trial sequential analysis. Bayes factors, bias probes, and GRADE quality ratings complete the pass. The authors built the steps from Cochrane and GRADE practice, aiming for valid claims of benefit, harm, or futility.
europmc-pmc4275948:
Emmanuelle Anthoine, Leïla Moret, Antoine Regnault, Véronique Sébille, and Jean-Benoit Hardouin reviewed how researchers choose sample sizes when they validate new health questionnaires. Their review appeared in Health and Quality of Life Outcomes in 2014. A questionnaire that asks patients to report their own health must be tested on enough people, or its scores cannot be trusted.

The team searched for validation studies of new patient reported measures published over a recent span and recorded how each study set its size. Practices varied widely, and many papers gave thin reasons for the numbers they used. The review gives scale builders a picture of common practice and a push toward firmer, stated grounds for sample size.
europmc-pmc4309448:
Gerardo Cárcamo-Oyarce, Putthapoom Lumjiaktase, Rolf Kümmerli, and Leo Eberl watched single cells slip out of bacterial biofilms in a soil microbe. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2015. Quorum sensing, the chemical census bacteria take of their own numbers, is usually cast as a tool for group coordination.

In young biofilms of Pseudomonas putida the signal molecules were made unevenly, by chance, and acted mainly on the cell that made them. The signal switched on production of soapy compounds that loosened the cell's grip, and induced cells wandered out of their colonies alone. The escape looks asocial rather than cooperative, which recasts what quorum sensing is for at the start of a biofilm.
europmc-pmc4350348:
Lorenzo Galluzzi and a large group of co-authors propose a cleaner way to classify cancer immunotherapies. Their paper appeared in Oncotarget in 2014. Immunotherapy had grown from a promise into approved treatments, with many regimens in trials alone or beside standard drugs, and the usual split into passive and active treatments no longer fit.

Even supposedly passive antibodies lean on the patient's immune system, so the authors sort treatments instead by whether they target a specific tumor antigen or act broadly. The scheme covers antibodies, vaccines, cell transfers, and immune checkpoint drugs. A shared language helps trial designers combine treatments sensibly and helps readers compare results across a crowded field.
europmc-pmc4352848:
Anurag Mathur and colleagues built a tiny human heart system for drug testing and reported it in Scientific Reports in 2015. Drug projects often fail because animal tests predict human harm poorly, and heart harm drives about a third of safety withdrawals. Their system grows heart tissue from human induced pluripotent stem cells, which are adult cells reset to a stem-like state, inside a small perfused device.

The tissue stayed alive and working for several weeks, with cells aligned as in real heart muscle. Flow through the device could be predicted by computer models, like blood flow in small vessels. Drug tests on the system gave strength values closer to whole-tissue data than tests on loose cells did. Such systems could screen drugs for heart risk earlier and with human cells.
europmc-pmc4383848:
Mohammadreza Hajjari and Adrian Salavaty reviewed a long non-coding RNA that promotes cancer, in Cancer Biology and Medicine in 2015. Long non-coding RNAs are RNA molecules over 200 letters long that never become proteins, yet they regulate genes in many ways. One of them, HOTAIR, acts as an oncogenic molecule in several cancers, including breast, stomach, bowel, and cervical cancers. Its level in tumors may thus serve as a marker for diagnosis or a target for therapy.

HOTAIR works largely by guiding a silencing complex, PRC2, to genes it shuts down, reshaping which genes are active in the cell. The review describes how HOTAIR itself is regulated, how it interacts with that complex, and how it feeds into cell pathways in each cancer type. Blocking such an RNA is a fresh drug idea the review helps map.
europmc-pmc4410648:
Franck Giacomoni and a French team built Workflow4Metabolomics, an online workbench for metabolomics, in Bioinformatics in 2015. Metabolomics measures the small molecules in samples at scale, and its data demand heavy processing: cleaning, statistics, and chemical annotation. New algorithms appear constantly, in many programming languages. The platform gathers them in one collaborative place, built on the Galaxy system, so modules can be chained into full workflows and run from a browser.

Tools can be tested on reference data sets before users trust them on their own. Private accounts give each researcher a workspace. The whole framework can also be downloaded as a virtual machine for local installation. The French bioinformatics and metabolomics infrastructures maintain it. Shared plumbing, the authors argue, lets a fast-moving field compare and reuse methods instead of rebuilding them.
europmc-pmc4436848:
V Peter Collins, David Jones, and Caterina Giannini reviewed pilocytic astrocytoma in Acta Neuropathologica in 2015. These brain tumors, recognized as a distinct kind more than seventy years earlier, are classed as low grade and most patients live long after treatment. Many need only surgical removal, and they rarely turn into aggressive cancers, though some look deceptively like more dangerous gliomas under the microscope.

Genome-wide sequencing changed the picture of their cause. Nearly all cases carry a single fault in one signaling route, the MAPK pathway, which controls cell growth. The most common fault joins part of one gene, KIAA1549, to the active part of another, BRAF, creating a fused protein that drives growth. Rarer partners and related faults in growth receptors also occur. The review uses these markers to sharpen diagnosis and sort hard cases.
europmc-pmc4448148:
Anoek Zomer and a team of co-authors watched vesicles spread cancer behavior inside living tumors, reporting in Cell in 2015. Most cancer cells release extracellular vesicles, tiny packages holding proteins, lipids, and RNA. Lab dish work showed that taking up such vesicles can change a cell, but proving this inside a body is hard because receiver cells cannot be told from others.

A genetic switch solved that problem: cells that took up vesicles changed color permanently. Aggressive tumor cells' vesicles were taken up by tamer cells in the same tumor and in distant tumors, and carried RNA messages linked to movement and spread. Filming inside living tissue showed the receiver cells then moved more and spread more readily. Tumor cells, the authors argue, share spread-promoting cargo across the whole body.
europmc-pmc4472748:
Ron Pinhasi and a large team of co-authors pinpointed the best source of ancient DNA in the human skull in PLoS ONE in 2015. New sequencing methods let researchers read whole genomes from fossils, but most bones hold very little surviving DNA of the original individual. The dense petrous bone, part of the skull base around the ear, was already known to preserve more DNA than other skeletal parts.

Comparing three areas inside petrous bones from archaeological skeletons across Eurasia, the team measured how much original DNA each gave, plus read lengths, damage patterns, and total yield. The region around the inner ear gave the richest yields. Samples also came from hot climates, where preservation is usually poor, and still produced usable DNA. The finding gives archaeologists a precise spot to sample, so scarce fossil material can be drilled where it counts most.
europmc-pmc4494348:
Alberta Di Pasquale, Scott Preiss, Fernanda Tavares Da Silva, Nathalie Garçon, and Diane Harper reviewed vaccine adjuvants in Vaccines in 2015. Adjuvants are substances added to vaccines to strengthen the immune response to purified antigens that alone provoke too little reaction. They have been used for more than ninety years, starting with aluminum salts and oil-in-water emulsions, chosen by trial rather than theory.

As knowledge of how the immune system senses pathogens grew, adjuvant design became deliberate. The review traces that history from the nineteen-twenties to the present. It explains how adjuvants ignite the innate response at the injection site. It also explains how they steer the adaptive response that follows, shaping its type, size, and quality. Continued safety monitoring keeps their benefit-risk profile favorable, the authors conclude. New adjuvant systems target diseases older vaccines could not touch.
europmc-pmc4496048:
Vasco Elbrecht, Florian Leese, and Mehrdad Hajibabaei tested whether DNA counts can stand in for animal counts in PLoS ONE in 2015. Metabarcoding identifies species in a bulk sample by sequencing a standard gene fragment, a fast way to survey ecosystems such as streams. Whether read numbers reflect how much of each species was present, though, was disputed, because the copying step can favor some species and tiny specimens may vanish.

Their protocol extracts DNA from whole bulk samples, copies the barcode fragment once, and sequences directly. In one experiment, stonefly specimens of known types spanning a wide biomass range showed how specimen size shapes read counts. In another, dozens of freshwater invertebrate species of similar size were recovered together. The authors weigh primer bias and detection limits and judge where abundance claims from sequence data are justified.
europmc-pmc4570748:
Claudia Lennicke and four co-authors review hydrogen peroxide as a signal inside tumor cells, in Cell Communication and Signaling in 2015. Hydrogen peroxide is best known as a bleach-like reactive chemical, yet cells make it deliberately. At the right dose and place it flips switches on enzymes and gene regulators by reversibly oxidizing sulfur atoms, steering growth or death decisions.

Cancer cells run hotter than normal ones: they produce more hydrogen peroxide and keep a shakier redox balance, which shapes their surroundings and the immune attack on them. The review charts where the peroxide is made, how it is cleared, and which pathways it drives toward growth or cell death. Those sources and switches, the authors argue, are candidate drug targets.
europmc-pmc4588148:
Irene Salinas and Brian Dixon review the immune defenses of fish surfaces, in Biology in 2015. Teleost fish, the great bony fish group, meet the microbe-rich water world through skin, gills, gut, and nose. Each surface carries its own lymphoid tissue, stocked with B and T cells tuned differently from their blood counterparts.

Vaccination and infection studies show these surfaces mount their own adaptive responses. Antibodies appear in gill, gut, and skin mucus after surface exposure. In rainbow trout, a dedicated antibody class, IgT, and its B cells dominate all surface tissues and answer in compartments, surface by surface. The review gathers a field the authors note is far thinner than its mammalian counterpart.
europmc-pmc4622648:
Marije B. Overdijk and colleagues' 2015 study centres on how the antibody drug daratumumab kills blood cancer cells. The drug targets CD38, a marker on multiple myeloma cells, and was in clinical development. Macrophages, immune cells that eat targets, crowd the tumours involved. The team asked whether eating by macrophages drives part of the drug's effect. The work appeared in mAbs.

Live imaging showed macrophages quickly swallowing several tumour cells in a row once the drug coated them. The effect held across myeloma and Burkitt's lymphoma cell lines, in mouse and human macrophages, and in mouse tumour models. Cells from eleven of twelve myeloma patients were eaten this way. Eating thus ranks as a fast, strong, and clinically relevant part of how the drug works.
europmc-pmc4653248:
Toshiaki Watanabe and colleagues published the 2015 English version of the Japanese Society for Cancer of the Colon and Rectum guidelines for colorectal cancer treatment. Colorectal cancer is the leading cancer killer of women in Japan and the third among men. Many new treatments had appeared in recent decades. The guidelines appeared in the International Journal of Clinical Oncology.

A guideline committee reviewed the evidence and debated contested questions, grading both evidence strength and recommendation strength for each answer. The aims were to cut treatment gaps between hospitals, avoid both needless and insufficient treatment, and help clinicians and patients understand each other. Because the guidance weighs Japan's insurance system and real practice, it serves as a bedside reference for consent talks and for choosing each patient's treatment.
europmc-pmc4703848:
Phelim Bradley, N. Claire Gordon, Timothy M. Walker, and a large team predicted antibiotic resistance from bacterial genomes in Nature Communications in 2015. Standard resistance tests take days for fast-growing bacteria and weeks for tuberculosis. The team's software, Mykrobe predictor, reads raw sequence data and reports species and resistance in about three minutes on a laptop. It works by comparing sequence fragments against a graph built from known bacterial diversity.

For Staphylococcus aureus, its calls across twelve antibiotics matched lab testing closely on an independent set of 470 isolates. For tuberculosis, on 1,609 isolates, it caught most resistance, though gaps in genetic knowledge limited it. Traces of rare variants helped flag the most resistant strains. The team also showed the approach can run on new portable sequencing machines. Faster resistance answers could steer treatment days earlier than culture allows.
europmc-pmc4722848:
Christian Wehrenfennig, Giles E. Eperon, Michael B. Johnston, Henry J. Snaith, and Laura M. Herz measured charge movement in a new solar material, in Advanced Materials in 2014. Perovskite solar cells, built from organolead trihalide compounds, had rocketed from about ten percent efficiency to over fifteen in a very short time. Why the material performs so well was unclear. The team used light-based methods to track charge speed and survival times in the material.

Their measurements found high charge mobilities paired with unusually long carrier lifetimes. That pairing lets charges travel beyond the depth at which light is absorbed, exactly what a good solar absorber needs. The films were made by cheap solution processing, the route that makes perovskites attractive for low-cost clean energy. By naming the traits behind the record efficiencies, the study gave cell designers concrete targets.
europmc-pmc4732148:
Francisco Javier Ordóñez and Daniel Roggen built a deep learning system that recognizes human activities from wearable sensors, in Sensors in 2016. Activity recognition usually depends on hand-designed features extracted from sensor streams, a craft bottleneck. Their framework pairs convolutional layers, which learn features from raw signals, with recurrent LSTM layers. The recurrent stage tracks how movements unfold over time. It needs no expert feature design and fuses sensor types naturally.

On two datasets, one from a public challenge, the system beat competing deep networks lacking the recurrent stage, by four percent on average. Tests with single sensor types also worked, though fusion helped. The authors probed which design settings matter most, offering tuning guidance. For assistive technology, from fall detection to rehabilitation support, automatic feature learning lowers the cost of each new application.
europmc-pmc4749248:
Arnold and ten colleagues measure the current burden of swallowing problems after acute stroke in 570 consecutive patients at a specialist centre. Using a standard bedside screen, they find dysphagia in 118 patients, or 20.7 percent, and it persists to discharge in half of them.

Stroke severity, not the stroke's location, predicts the problem. Affected patients develop pneumonia far more often, at 23.1 percent against 1.1 percent, stay longer on monitored beds, and reach home far less often. At three months they show worse outcomes and higher mortality, 13.6 against 1.6 percent. Severe dysphagia needing tube feeding stands out as a strong marker of death.
europmc-pmc4907448:
Ambika Satija and co-authors tracked plant-based diets and type 2 diabetes in three large United States cohorts in 2016. The combined groups held 69,949 women in one nurses' study, 90,239 in a second, and 40,539 men in a health workers' study, all free of chronic disease at entry. Diet scores were built from food questionnaires repeated every two to four years.

Plant-heavy eating was split into healthful and unhealthful versions, since fries and soda are plant-based too. Healthful plant patterns tied to lower diabetes rates, while unhealthful ones did not help and could harm. The lesson is quality within the plant kingdom, not plant share alone. Diet advice gains a needed shade of care.
europmc-pmc4978148:
Krzysztof J. Gorgolewski leads a large team introducing BIDS, a standard layout for brain imaging data. Their paper appeared in Scientific Data in 2016. Tens of thousands of MRI studies have mapped the brain without harm to subjects. Yet labs each filed their data their own way, which made sharing and reuse slow and error prone. The Brain Imaging Data Structure fixes folder names, file names, and the sidecar notes that describe a dataset.

The standard builds on formats that common software already reads. It codifies what most labs already do informally, and it captures the metadata that standard processing steps need. Automated pipelines and quality checks can then run on any compliant dataset. The authors present BIDS as plumbing, not science, but plumbing the field lacked. They argue shared structure is what turns single lab data into a common research resource.
europmc-pmc5150648:
Keisuke Katsushima and a large team of co-authors targeted a non-coding RNA in brain tumors, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Glioma stem cells renew themselves and seed glioblastomas, and the Notch signaling pathway keeps them in that stem-like state. The team searched for cancer-specific parts of that pathway.

They found that Notch activation switches on a long non-coding RNA called TUG1 only in the stem cells. TUG1 works in two places at once: in the cell body it soaks up a small RNA that would push differentiation, and in the nucleus it helps silence differentiation genes. Blocking TUG1 with tailored antisense strands, delivered into veins with a drug carrier, forced the stem cells to mature and strongly curbed tumor growth in mice.
europmc-pmc516448:
I. C. McManus, A. Keeling, and E. Paice followed British doctors for twelve years in BMC Medicine in 2004. They asked whether the stress, burnout, and career satisfaction doctors show around age thirty could have been predicted earlier. The candidate predictors were learning styles and personality. Both were measured when those doctors applied to medical school in 1990 or studied there.

Questionnaires traced the cohort from application through training into practice. Approaches to work were forecast by study habits and learning styles recorded years earlier, at application and in the final year. Views of workplace climate and workload reflected both work habits and current stress, while stress, burnout, and satisfaction themselves tracked personality traits measured five years before. The authors read working life as stamped early by stable personal differences.
europmc-pmc5261648:
Torvid Kiserud and a broad team of colleagues built the World Health Organization fetal growth charts in PLoS Medicine in 2017. Poor fetal growth predicts death and illness around birth and may raise the risk of common adult diseases, yet doctors lacked one chart set meant for worldwide use. The study followed low-risk pregnancies in ten countries, from Argentina to Thailand, in women without known limits on fetal growth.

Of the women recruited, 1,387 took part, each with seven planned ultrasound scans; 8,203 measurement sets passed quality checks. Median pregnancy length was 39 weeks and median birthweight 3,300 grams, but both varied by country. Indian babies were smaller than the rest even after accounting for pregnancy length, and the largest gap in pregnancy duration between countries was twelve days. The charts cover estimated fetal weight and standard ultrasound measures, and the authors stress that healthy growth still differs around the world.
europmc-pmc5315048:
Pooja M. Tiwari, Komal Vig, Vida A. Dennis, and Shree R. Singh reviewed gold nanoparticles in medicine in Nanomaterials in 2011. Gold particles at tiny scale are easy to make, easy to coat, and easy to track in the body. They also seem less toxic than many other metal particles. Coating, or functionalizing, the particles lets them carry cargo to set cell types.

The review gathers the main coating methods and the jobs they open up. Coated gold can haul drugs and genes into cells, light up tissues for imaging, and serve in sensors that spot disease marks. Their large surface for their size and their strong light effects suit these tasks. The authors note low cell harm in early tests. They also warn that much more work is needed before wide clinical use is safe.
europmc-pmc5374548:
Shifu Chen, Tanxiao Huang, Yanqing Zhou, Yue Han, Mingyan Xu, and Jia Gu built a cleaning tool for gene reading data in BMC Bioinformatics in 2017. Raw reads from fast machines carry slip errors, stray adapter bits, and bubbles from the flow cell. Clinic work needs those flaws counted and, where apt, fixed. Most past tools profile quality but cannot correct errors.

Their tool, AfterQC, uses the overlap of paired reads as its key trick. Where the pair overlaps, a mismatch flags a bad base to cut or mend, and adapters show their seams. The tool spots flow-cell bubbles, trims ragged ends, and drops reads laced with long single-letter runs. It checks strand bias by word patterns, then writes clean data plus a visual HTML report. Batch runs with many cores at once suit the large sets of modern labs.
europmc-pmc5405248:
Antonina A. Votintseva leads a large author group in a 2017 study in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology on fast gene testing for tuberculosis. Standard testing grows the germ in the lab, which takes weeks, before drugs can be matched to the strain. Reading the germ's whole genome gives drug resistance and strain data at once, but it has rested on those slow cultures. The team pulled germ DNA straight from patient spit samples.

The germ was found in every sample where DNA extraction worked, and most gave enough data to predict drug response, always matching lab results. On one machine the full run took under two days; on a small portable reader, key answers came in hours. The authors say same-day results could speed care and tracking of spread.
europmc-pmc5459448:
Tjørve and Tjørve review the many forms of the Gompertz growth model and add unified versions. Their article appeared in PLoS ONE. The Gompertz model fits growth across biology. It serves for animals, plants, bacteria, and tumors. Only the logistic model rivals its use. Countless re-parameterisations crowd the literature. Different fields evolved diverging traditions. Parameters often resist direct comparison. The authors sort the forms into two types.

Type I forms carry an inflection-time parameter. Type II forms carry a starting value instead. The Gompertz-Laird is one common variant. Seven re-parameterisations receive review here. The authors then propose unified versions of both forms. In them, the growth constant means relative growth rate. Absolute-rate variants are also given. These unified models sit inside the Unified-Richards family. Their parameter sets compare across models without conversions. Users gain fast access to every shape parameter.
europmc-pmc5592248:
Shi and co-authors, with the RSV Global Epidemiology Network, estimate a disease burden in The Lancet. Their target is respiratory syncytial virus, a top cause of lung infection in young children. The study updates older global figures with a much larger data set.

For 2015, they estimate 33.1 million RSV lung-infection episodes in children under five. About 3.2 million led to hospital admission. In-hospital deaths came to about 59,600. Total deaths could reach 118,200 once community deaths count. Babies under six months made up about 45 percent of admissions and deaths. A mother's vaccine or antibody shots could cut that burden a lot. Readers get national and regional numbers for planning.
europmc-pmc5627048:
Blandin Knight and co-authors review early detection of lung cancer in Open Biology. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer. Timing decides the odds starkly. Small stage I tumors, cut out early, see five-year survival near 70 percent.

Most patients get no such chance. About three quarters arrive with advanced disease. One-year survival for stage IV disease sits near 15 to 19 percent. The review surveys routes to catching tumors sooner. Imaging and screening programs form one strand. Blood and breath biomarkers form another. The biology of the earliest lesions guides the search. Cells that repair airways may seed the tumors. Challenges get plain treatment as well. Readers see both the progress and the distance left in shifting lung cancer diagnosis earlier.
europmc-pmc5668948:
Gardner and co-authors present a software and survey study in Genome Research. It introduces MELT, the Mobile Element Locator Tool. Mobile element insertions form about a quarter of human structural variants. When they disrupt genes, they can cause disease. Most large sequencing projects still skip finding them. MELT was built for the 1000 Genomes Project to close that gap.

Tests on real and simulated data favored MELT over prior tools. It won on speed, scale, specificity, and sensitivity. Run modes suit both local machines and cloud systems. The team mapped insertions in modern humans and chimpanzees. Ancient Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes were included too. Patterns differed across lineages for several stated reasons.
europmc-pmc5670148:
Stubbs and co-authors report metabolic studies in Frontiers in Physiology. They test drinks that supply ketones from outside the body. Ketogenic diets raise blood ketones but are hard to follow. Drinks offer a simpler route to ketosis. Healthy volunteers joined three randomized studies. Drinks contained a ketone ester or ketone salts.

Both drinks raised blood ketone levels within hours. The ester reached peaks nearly three times the salt peak. Levels returned to baseline in three to four hours. Eating first lowered the peak by about a third. All drinks lowered blood glucose, fatty acids, and triglycerides. Electrolytes stayed in the normal range. Repeated drinks or steady infusion held levels up for nine hours.
europmc-pmc5702448:
Lee and co-authors review drug resistance in a virulent form of Klebsiella pneumoniae. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. This germ causes lung and urinary tract infections. A stronger form emerged in the mid-1980s. It strikes younger, healthier people. It can spread to the liver and eyes.

Most such strains stayed drug-sensitive at first. That picture is now changing. Some strains pair strong virulence with resistance. Strains that resist carbapenem drugs have been found. The review covers spread patterns worldwide. It explains what makes the strains so virulent. Resistance mechanisms get detailed coverage. Recent isolates from China raise concern. The authors urge a fast global response.
europmc-pmc5751248:
Costantini and co-authors review how omega-3 fatty acids affect the gut microbiota. Diet shapes each person's gut community over the long term. Fiber effects are well studied, while fat effects are less clear. The review gathers the few adult studies on omega-3 supplements.

Those studies show a drop in Faecalibacterium after omega-3 intake. Bacteroidetes and butyrate making Lachnospiraceae tend to rise. Like shifts appear in bowel disease, where omega-3 may push back toward balance. Animal work links omega-3, gut microbes, and immunity in gut wall health. A gut-brain path is also covered.
europmc-pmc5753348:
Kalvari and co-authors present Rfam release 13.0, a database of non-coding RNA families. Each family is shown by an alignment, a shared structure, and a statistical model. Release 13.0 shifts the resource to a genome centered approach. It annotates a non-redundant set of reference genomes with RNA families.

The release adds 236 new families, for a total of 2,687. The website gains faceted text search and new structure views from R-scape. A fresh workflow for literature curation is described. A pipeline that builds families from RNAcentral data is also set out.
europmc-pmc5786548:
Durgeau and co-authors review advances in aiming CD8 T cells at cancer. These killer T cells spot tumor antigens and destroy the cells that show them. Checkpoint drugs that release T cell brakes have shown survival gains in melanoma and lung cancer. CD8 cells that carry the PD-1 marker seem central to those gains.

The review covers how killer cells bind and kill their targets. Adhesion molecules that firm up the contact get close attention. It also covers neoantigens, fresh targets born of tumor mutations. Patients whose T cells target neoantigens often respond better, they note.
europmc-pmc5798848:
Dignon and co-authors present a computer model of protein phase separation. Some proteins gather into liquid-like droplets inside cells. These droplets form soft compartments without a membrane. Their sequence helps decide when they form.

The team builds a coarse-grained model, with one bead per amino acid. They test it on the FUS and LAF-1 proteins. The model maps phase diagrams and shows how mutations and chain length shift them. Readers get a flexible tool for probing how protein sequence controls droplet behavior. The results also fit a classic theory for how polymers separate.
europmc-pmc5805548:
Chen and co-authors review inflammation across the body's organs. Inflammation is the immune reply to germs, damage, or toxins. Brief bouts heal tissue. Long bouts drive disease in the heart, liver, lung, brain, and gut.

The review covers causes, shared signal pathways, and how bouts resolve. Pathways named include NF-kappaB, MAPK, and JAK-STAT. Each pathway is drawn with its main triggers and effects. Later sections treat each organ's own pattern of response. Markers that flag active inflammation get their own survey. Readers get one frame for a process behind many chronic diseases, from arthritis to cancer.
europmc-pmc5851248:
Wu and Tymianski review a smarter way to protect the brain in stroke, aimed past the NMDA receptor. Their review appeared in Molecular Brain. These receptors drive the excitotoxic death of starved neurons. Blocking them outright failed in trial after trial. Stroke remains a leading cause of death and disability worldwide.

The receptors also carry survival signals the brain needs. Newer drugs cut only the death-signaling wiring downstream. That spares the receptor's helpful work and its side effects. The pair map the cascades that decide neuron fate. They argue the wider window could finally deliver neuroprotection.
europmc-pmc5858448:
van Kempen and co-authors summarise a systematic review on noise and health. Their article appeared in an environmental health journal. The review fed into new WHO noise guidelines for Europe. It covered noise from road, rail, and air traffic, plus wind turbines. The team found 600 relevant references from 2000 to 2015. Only 61 studies allowed exposure-response estimates to be worked out.

The strongest evidence linked road traffic noise to ischaemic heart disease. Pooling seven long-term studies gave a risk rise of 8 percent per 10 decibels. Evidence on stroke, diabetes, and obesity was far thinner. The authors rated that evidence from moderate to very low. They call for more long-term studies of better quality.
europmc-pmc5890448:
Misaghi and co-authors give a comprehensive review of osteosarcoma. Their article appeared in SICOT-J. This rare bone tumour strikes 3.4 people per million yearly. It ranks third among cancers in adolescence. Five-year survival sat near 20 percent for decades. Added chemotherapy in the 1970s lifted it sharply. Rates now pass 65 percent for classic cases.

The review sorts the types of osteosarcoma and their features. Clinical and tissue traits are analysed in turn. Diagnosis and staging methods are set out clearly. Treatment history runs from amputation to limb salvage. Current care and future directions close the survey. Readers get the full arc of a changing field.
europmc-pmc5897348:
Fan and co-authors build a guided nanozyme for tumour catalytic therapy. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Nanozymes are materials that act like natural enzymes. Steering them inside the body remains a challenge. The team made nitrogen-doped porous carbon nanospheres. These spheres show four enzyme-like activities at once. All four regulate reactive oxygen species in cells.

A ferritin coat guides the spheres into tumour cell lysosomes. There they boost reactive oxygen generation in a targeted way. Human tumour grafts in mice shrank notably, the team reports. Off-target activity is the core problem this design tackles. Ferritin guidance offers a general targeting strategy, they argue.
europmc-pmc5939048:
Li and co-authors report that CRISPR-Cas12a cuts single-stranded DNA in two distinct ways. Their letter appeared in Cell Research. Cas12a is an enzyme from a type V-A CRISPR system. Guided by a single CRISPR RNA, it cuts double-stranded DNA targets. Its action on single-stranded DNA was less well understood. The team used FnCas12a on short, labelled single strands.

They find cleavage sites near the 22nd base from the paired end. No PAM sequence was needed for this cis-cleavage. They also found a trans activity once the enzyme complex forms. The activated complex chopped separate single strands into tiny pieces. Cleavage of single strands ran slower than of double strands.
europmc-pmc5979948:
Agmon and co-authors model how lipid peroxidation during ferroptosis changes membrane properties. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Ferroptosis is a form of regulated cell death. It is marked by a build-up of lipid hydroperoxides. How those peroxides actually kill the cell stayed a puzzle. The team built molecular dynamics models of lipid membranes. They fed known ferroptosis features into the models.

The simulations probe the physical fallout of peroxidation, they report. Membrane traits shift as oxidised lipids gather. From those shifts they form hypotheses about cell death. The work links chemistry to membrane mechanics. It aims to explain the final step of ferroptosis.
europmc-pmc5993148:
Koppula, Zhang, Zhuang, and Gan review the amino acid transporter SLC7A11 in cancer metabolism. Their review appeared in Cancer Communications. Cancer cells often raise nutrient transporters to meet their needs. SLC7A11 swaps cystine in and glutamate out of the cell. That flow feeds glutathione production and guards against oxidative stress. It also shields cells from ferroptotic death. Many human cancers overexpress this transporter.

New work gives it a wider role, the authors note. It shapes glutamine use and nutrient dependence in cancer cells. How the transporter itself is regulated is also covered. Open questions for the field are flagged. Targeting it may open new cancer treatments.
europmc-pmc6028448:
Sztupinszki and co-authors move a cancer test to newer data. Their research article appeared in NPJ Breast Cancer. The test measures homologous recombination deficiency, or HRD. Faulty HRD repair leaves scars across the genome. Such tumors may respond well to certain drugs.

The first HRD scores came from SNP arrays. Sequencing has now largely replaced those arrays. The team built an R package called scarHRD. It derives the same scar scores from sequencing data. Scores from both methods matched well in breast tumors. Correlations ranged from 0.73 to 0.87 by measure. The new scores also separated BRCA mutant cases clearly. Readers get a bridge from old array tests to modern sequencing.
europmc-pmc6030848:
Waterhouse and co-authors update the SWISS-MODEL modelling server. Their article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The server builds protein models by homology. It compares a sequence with known related structures. Such models help close the gap between sequences and structures.

The server now models protein complexes as well. It handles both same-chain and mixed-chain assemblies. Given the partner sequences, it infers the full structure. A new engine, ProMod3, powers the modelling. A new method also estimates local model quality. The service is free for all users. Readers get a guide to a long-running automated tool. It serves researchers who lack deep computing expertise.
europmc-pmc6034748:
Goldenberg and co-authors review TROP-2 as a cancer target. Their article appeared in Oncotarget in 2018. TROP-2 is a protein first found on trophoblast cells. It is raised in many solid cancers. Normal tissues show much lower levels.

The protein helps regulate growth, invasion, and spread. It also plays roles in stem cell biology. That profile makes it a drug target. The review focuses on antibody-drug conjugates. One drug links an anti-TROP-2 antibody to a toxin. It showed strong activity in animal models. It also helped patients with advanced breast and lung cancers. Urothelial cancers responded in early studies too. Readers get a survey of a rising precision medicine target.
europmc-pmc6037748:
Clark and co-authors compare genetic tests for sick children. Their meta-analysis appeared in NPJ Genomic Medicine. Genetic diseases are a leading cause of childhood death. Finding the cause fast can change care decisions. Three test types compete for first-line use.

The review covered 37 studies with 20,068 children. Genome sequencing found a cause in 41 percent. Exome sequencing reached 36 percent. Chromosomal microarray reached only 10 percent. Sequencing also changed care more often than microarray. Testing parent-child trios beat testing children alone. Hospital-based reading outperformed reference labs in the data. The authors back sequencing as a first-line test. Readers get pooled numbers to guide testing choices.
europmc-pmc6055048:
Liu and co-authors review the link between an RNA mark and cancers. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology. The mark is called m6A and sits inside messenger RNA. It is the most common internal mark of its kind. Special proteins write, erase, and read the mark.

Writers place the mark on RNA strands. Erasers remove it again, making the system reversible. Readers bind marked sites and steer the RNA's fate. They affect splicing, export, stability, and translation. In cancers, these regulators can drive cell growth and spread. The review covers solid tumors and blood cancers. Leukemia, brain, lung, and liver cancers all feature. The authors flag the mark system as a drug target.
europmc-pmc6105748:
Foyer reviews reactive oxygen species as signals that regulate photosynthesis. Her review appeared in Environmental and Experimental Botany. Photosynthesis pours out reactive oxygen in abundance. Such molecules were once read as pure damage. Opinion has shifted toward their signaling value.

Oxygen signals flow from chloroplast to nucleus. They adjust gene programs as light changes. Antioxidants like glutathione and ascorbate shape the messages. Some chloroplasts seem specialized for signaling duty. Protein tags add further control layers. Slow drops in output once blamed on damage may be regulation instead. Readers get a redox view of how plants tune their engines.
europmc-pmc6116548:
Xu and co-authors present a research article on astragaloside IV, a compound from the herb Astragali radix, and lung cancer. Immune cells inside tumors can take an M2 form that helps cancer spread. The compound was known to slow lung cancer invasion. Its effect on those immune cells was not known.

The team grew macrophages in the lab and pushed them toward the M2 form. The compound blocked that shift. It also cut the invasion and new blood vessel growth of lung cancer cells. In mice, it slowed tumor growth and spread. The authors link the effect to the AMPK signaling pathway.
europmc-pmc6192448:
Jolley and co-authors present an article in Wellcome Open Research on open-access bacterial population genomics. The PubMLST.org website hosts curated databases for over 100 microbial species and genera. They merge sequence data with where samples came from and what traits they showed. The software behind the site is called BIGSdb.

The authors describe how BIGSdb grew from 2010 to June 2018. It supports gene-by-gene analysis, from single genes to whole genomes. Uses include tracking outbreaks on maps and watching vaccine targets for change. One scheme surveys meningococcal vaccine antigens to warn of falling vaccine efficacy. The article shows how shared, open databases turned typing schemes into full population genomics.
europmc-pmc6224348:
Watkins and co-authors review talk therapies for PTSD. PTSD can follow a traumatic life event. It is often chronic and disabling. In 2017 two major guideline sets were published. One came from the VA and Defense Department. The other came from the American Psychological Association. The review appeared in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience.

The authors first compare how each guideline was built. They then discuss therapies both sets strongly recommend. Prolonged Exposure is one of them. Cognitive Processing Therapy is another. Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy is the third. Each therapy addresses trauma memories or related thoughts directly. Each has a large evidence base. The authors close with implications and future directions.
europmc-pmc6227248:
Rogawski and co-authors studied gut germs and child growth in poor settings. Gut infections in early life can stunt growth. The team used precise molecular tests on stool samples. The data came from the MAL-ED cohort study. It appeared in The Lancet Global Health.

The team tested for 29 gut pathogens with PCR. Samples came from children in their first two years. Sites spanned seven low-resource settings. Both diarrhoeal and normal stools were tested. Length was measured each month. The authors linked specific pathogens to growth faltering. Some germs harmed growth even without diarrhoea. The work shows why broad pathogen control matters. It goes beyond treating diarrhoea alone.
europmc-pmc6244748:
Ellis, Lin, and Tartar review the immune side of wound healing. Their review appeared in Current Dermatology Reports. Normal skin healing moves through four phases. Blood clotting comes first, then inflammation, growth, and remodelling. Immune cells, skin cells, and deeper skin cells trade signals at each step. Chronic wounds stall when those signals go wrong.

Neutrophils arrive first at the wound bed. When they die and are cleared by macrophages, the wound shifts toward repair. Blood vessels grow and soft repair tissue forms. Fibre making cells then reshape that tissue into scar. The authors name the shift from inflammation to growth as the key turning point. If inflammation runs unchecked, scars form badly or wounds stay open. The review sums up what helps or blocks that shift.
europmc-pmc6295048:
Lee and co-authors measure how common gestational diabetes is across Asia. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first found in pregnancy. It raises risks for mother and baby. The team searched four databases for studies from Asia.

They kept 84 studies that met a quality score. The pooled rate for Asia was 11.5 percent of pregnancies. Rates varied a lot between studies and places. Past gestational diabetes was the strongest risk factor. A heavy baby in a past birth also raised risk. High body weight, family diabetes, and high blood pressure mattered too. The results help clinics plan screening in the region.
europmc-pmc6302548:
Benjamin and co-authors find a drug pairing that starves cancer cells of energy. Their study appeared in Cell Reports. Fast-growing cancer cells dump lactate through two transporters, MCT1 and MCT4. The old blood pressure drug syrosingopine blocks both transporters. Metformin blocks a key mitochondrial enzyme.

Used alone, each drug has limited effect. Together, they trap lactate inside the cells. That block halts a step that restores NAD+, a molecule glycolysis needs. Energy output then crashes, and cancer cells die. Adding NAD+ or its precursors partly rescued the cells. The team proposes this pairing as a new cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc6324048:
Nilsson and co-authors describe UNITE, a database for identifying fungi from DNA. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. It targets the ITS region, the formal fungal barcode. About one million public fungal ITS sequences are offered. They cluster into roughly 459,000 species hypotheses. Each cluster gets a permanent identifier for clear reference.

Curators have improved the data over fifteen years. More than 275,000 fixes and notes were added. Recent work redesigned handling of unclassifiable groups. The system now plugs into the GBIF taxonomic backbone. Many parallel classification schemes can run at once. UNITE feeds several metabarcoding pipelines with reference data. It exchanges data with all major fungal sequence bases.
europmc-pmc6335848:
Coley and co-authors teach a neural network to predict chemical reaction products. Their paper appeared in Chemical Science. Chemists usually predict outcomes by training and intuition. A reliable computer method could speed that work. It could also flag side products early. The team framed each molecule as a graph. Atoms form the nodes of the graph.

Their graph-convolutional model learns from past reactions. It takes reactants, reagents, and solvents as input. It then predicts the major product formed. The approach covers a broad range of organic reactions. It can validate routes that planning software suggests. That raises confidence before any lab work begins. The authors present it as a step toward automated reaction checks. It supports, rather than replaces, chemist judgment.
europmc-pmc6382748:
Prasad and co-authors review TDP-43 protein in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience. TDP-43 normally handles RNA and DNA tasks in cells. In ALS, clumps of altered TDP-43 appear in the brain and spinal cord.

Almost all sporadic ALS patients carry these clumps, even without a TDP-43 gene fault. The review explains how the protein misfolds and piles up. It covers the gene changes that can start the process and the cell harm that follows. ALS has no cure, so each step in this chain matters. The authors map targets where drugs might break it.
europmc-pmc6438948:
Rugo and co-authors report extended follow-up of PALOMA-2, the phase 3 trial of palbociclib plus letrozole as first treatment for advanced ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. Postmenopausal women who had no prior systemic therapy for advanced disease were randomized two to one, 444 to the combination and 222 to letrozole with placebo.

After a median follow-up near 38 months, median progression-free survival reached 27.6 months with palbociclib against 14.5 months without it. Every subgroup benefited, the gain carried into later therapy lines, and chemotherapy was delayed from 29.9 to 40.4 months. Side effects matched the known profile and quality of life held steady, supporting the pair as standard first-line care.
europmc-pmc6445148:
Zhang and co-authors show that the long non-coding RNA Neat1 acts as a common helper for inflammasomes, the alarm complexes of innate immunity. At rest Neat1 sits in nuclear paraspeckles. When macrophages meet a trigger signal, it leaves those bodies, moves to the cytoplasm, and binds the NLRP3, NLRC4, and AIM2 inflammasomes.

Bound Neat1 speeds inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 processing, and it stabilizes mature caspase-1, raising interleukin-1β output and pyroptotic cell death. Low oxygen raises Neat1 as well, explaining part of hypoxia's inflammatory effect. In mouse peritonitis and pneumonia, animals lacking Neat1 mounted markedly weaker inflammation, marking the RNA as a shared control point.
europmc-pmc6470248:
Schäfer and Schwarz test whether psychology's published effect sizes can still anchor interpretation, comparing 900 effects drawn from ordinary publications against 93 from pre-registered ones. Cohen's benchmarks, or comparison with past literature, remain the standard ways to call an effect small or large. Both yardsticks wobble badly in the data.

Median effects in the ordinary literature reached r = 0.36, while pre-registered work, shielded from publication bias and questionable practices, sat at r = 0.16. Inflation has therefore corrupted the comparison pool. Effects also varied enormously between sub-disciplines and study designs, defeating any single benchmark. Many more pre-registered studies are needed before honest reference values exist.
europmc-pmc6472148:
Salehi and co-authors update the evidence on apigenin, a flavone found across fruits and vegetables, with the focus on work in living animals and humans rather than test-tube effects. Flavonoids as a class mop up free radicals, calm inflammation, and fight viruses, and apigenin is among the most studied members.

Findings in living systems are sorted by illness: diabetes, amnesia and Alzheimer's disease, depression and insomnia, and cancer all receive sections. One cited study used 20 milligrams per kilogram and reported better spatial learning plus brain and vessel guarding. Food intake data close the review, letting readers weigh how much people truly take in from food against the doses used in tests.
europmc-pmc6551848:
Baldwin, Reuben, Newbury and Danese test whether two ways of measuring childhood maltreatment pick out the same people, writing in JAMA Psychiatry. Studies often rely on adults recalling childhood harm years later. Others record the harm as it happens, through officials, carers or interviews at the time. Their review pools every study that held both measures for the same individuals.

Sixteen studies covering 25,471 people went into the meta-analysis. Agreement between the two measures was poor. On average, 52% of people with recorded childhood maltreatment did not report it later, and 56% of people who did report it had no matching record. The two methods largely identify different groups, the authors conclude, so findings from one cannot stand in for the other.
europmc-pmc6617248:
Cummings and co-authors take stock of the Alzheimer drug pipeline for 2019. Their review appears in Alzheimer's & Dementia: Translational Research & Clinical Interventions. Few treatments exist for Alzheimer disease. Drug programs in this field fail at a high rate. Watching the pipeline shows where development is heading.

The authors searched ClinicalTrials.gov for all drug trials in progress. They counted 132 agents in trials. Twenty-eight agents sat in phase 3, and 74 sat in phase 2. Thirty more were in early phase 1 testing. Ninety-six agents aimed to modify the disease itself. Amyloid was the top target, in 40% of those programs. Tau drew 17 programs. New biomarkers, earlier patient groups, and adaptive designs marked recent trials.
europmc-pmc6636548:
Pyzik and co-authors review the neonatal Fc receptor and question its narrow name. Their review appears in Frontiers in Immunology. The receptor was first tied to antibody transfer to newborns. It actually works throughout life and across the body. It binds IgG antibodies and albumin. Binding rescues both proteins from breakdown. That recycling keeps them circulating far longer. The receptor also ferries IgG across cell barriers.

Newer work shows a direct immune role as well. The receptor helps present antigens from IgG immune complexes. That shapes responses to infection and vaccination. Drug designers now target the receptor deliberately. Some therapies extend antibody half-life through it. Others block it to clear harmful antibodies.
europmc-pmc6688448:
Nastase and co-authors give a tutorial on intersubject correlation for shared brain responses. Their article appears in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience. One person's brain activity can model another's. That trick measures shared information across brains. It works during naturalistic, dynamic experiences. No set response model is required. Speaker-listener coupling becomes measurable this way. Perception and recall can be compared head-on. Standard fMRI designs struggle with such richness.

The tutorial develops the method's logic. Questions the approach can answer are mapped. Spatial patterns and network estimation extend it. Pitfalls in method receive thorough treatment. Best practices are spelled out in full. The authors aim at access for newcomers. Social neuroscience is the target field.
europmc-pmc6708248:
Peng and co-authors review neoantigen vaccines, a new form of cancer treatment. Neoantigens are proteins made only by tumor cells, never by healthy tissue. They arise from the many mutations that build up in cancer cells. Because they look foreign, the immune system can be trained to attack them.

The review covers how computer tools find neoantigens from tumor DNA. It then surveys vaccine types, from nucleic acid and peptide shots to cell-based ones. Early trials suggest the vaccines are safe and can work. Pairing them with checkpoint drugs or radiation may work even better, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc6754748:
Lombardo and co-authors lay out big data approaches to autism's heterogeneity. Autism is diagnosed from behavior. Beneath that one label sits wide variation between and within people. Grasping that variation matters for care and for research. Small studies and simple case-control designs are poorly suited to the task.

Big data, the authors argue, must be broad, deep, and rich. Broad means large samples. Deep means many levels of data on the same people. Such data test whether autism is better seen as a spectrum or as several autisms. A model's worth is judged by what it explains. The paper offers organizing principles for this shift.
europmc-pmc6836748:
Pham and co-authors review the quinolone antibiotics in MedChemComm. Quinolones are a major family of bacteria-killing drugs. They arose in the early 1960s, starting with nalidixic acid, reported in 1962. Early members acted on few bacteria and were poorly absorbed. Later chemistry fixed both flaws, making them key treatments in clinics and hospitals alike.

The review follows the family's development and how the drugs attack bacterial DNA machinery. It covers their use against community and hospital infections. Safety gets a full section. Joint pain limits use in children, and recent reports link the class to aortic rupture in older patients. Rising resistance also narrows where they can still be used.
europmc-pmc6883848:
Mauger and co-authors report a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on how RNA shape controls protein output. Messenger RNAs fold into structures as they are read. Whether that folding helps or hinders protein production was unsettled, tangled as it is with codon choice. The team attacked the question two ways, with modified building blocks and with designed sequences.

Fitting detailed production data to kinetic models, they showed more structured coding regions lengthen an mRNA's working life. The effect held apart from codon usage. Across 130 test messages for two proteins, higher output tracked with stronger structure. The findings matter for natural gene control and for designing therapeutic mRNAs.
europmc-pmc6950048:
Bouaïcha and co-authors review microcystins, liver toxins made by cyanobacteria. Their review appeared in Toxins. Microcystins are the most widespread class of cyanobacterial toxins. They are also the class most often blamed for poisoning events. Studying them is hard because the family is hugely varied in structure.

At least 279 microcystins have now been reported, and the authors tabulate them all. Some structures were proven after full chemical isolation. Others rest on tentative matches from sensitive instruments. About a fifth of the list may arise from changes after the toxin is made, in nature or during sample handling. Reported toxicities vary widely, even for the same compound. The review ties structure to harm.
europmc-pmc6962448:
Wang and co-authors identify the protein that lets bone sense mechanical load. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Bone reshapes itself to match the forces it bears, a rule known since Wolff's law. A built-in gauge, or mechanostat, was predicted but not found.

Mice lacking the force-sensing protein PIEZO1 in bone-forming cells lost bone mass and suffered spontaneous fractures. Their bones also stopped responding to unloading, showing the sensor drives the crosstalk. Under load, PIEZO1 works through a partner, YAP, to switch on two collagen types, II and IX. Those collagens in turn tune the bone-eating cells that clear old bone. The authors name PIEZO1 the skeleton's major mechanosensor, and a possible target against disuse bone loss.
europmc-pmc7095448:
The Coronaviridae Study Group of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses formally classifies the new coronavirus and names it SARS-CoV-2, in Nature Microbiology. The group is responsible for virus classification and naming in this family. It assessed where the tentative 2019-nCoV belongs using family trees, taxonomy, and past practice.

The virus forms a sister branch next to the SARS coronaviruses of humans and bats within one species, Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus. The group also proposes a naming pattern for individual isolates, giving host, place, isolate, and date.
