It urges study of viruses at the species level, not only of the pathogens causing immediate harm, to prepare for future spillovers from animals.
europmc-pmc7118348:
Russell and co-authors estimate how deadly COVID-19 was, using the outbreak on the Diamond Princess cruise ship, in Eurosurveillance. The quarantined ship held a closed group where nearly everyone was tested, even people with no symptoms at all. Counts from China at the time were skewed by missed cases and by deaths that had not yet happened.

After adjusting for the delay between a case being confirmed and death, they put the ship's case fatality ratio at two point six percent. Its infection fatality ratio came to one point three percent. Adjusting further for the older ages of the passengers gave estimates for China of one point two and zero point six percent. The gap between the two ratios shows how many infections never became confirmed cases at all.
europmc-pmc7171048:
Zhang and co-authors survey insomnia among medical staff during the COVID-19 outbreak in China. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Psychiatry. Staff were recruited from hospitals, including frontline workers treating infected patients. A questionnaire sent through the WeChat program gathered the data. It asked about sleep, mood, anxiety, and stress tied to the outbreak.

The team set out to measure how common insomnia was in this group. They also looked for the social and psychological factors linked to poor sleep. Worry about infecting family, friends, and colleagues weighed on many staff. The authors connect quarantine and isolation duties with fear, loneliness, and anger. Their findings show why hospitals should watch staff mental health during a major outbreak.
europmc-pmc7176648:
Ou and co-authors test whether a gut bacterium can protect the brain in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in Nutrition & Diabetes. The bacterium is Akkermansia muciniphila, a common resident of the human gut. It is known to support the gut lining and improve insulin response. Alzheimer's involves amyloid buildup in the brain and loss of memory skills.

The team gave the bacterium to APP/PS1 mice, a standard Alzheimer's model. Mice ate either normal chow or a high-fat diet. Treated mice kept a healthier gut barrier than untreated ones. The authors measured amyloid pathology and thinking skills in the animals. Their results suggest gut microbes may influence brain disease. The work links diet, gut health, and memory in one testable path.
europmc-pmc7189648:
Perera and co-authors develop blood tests for antibodies to SARS-CoV-2. Their report appeared in Eurosurveillance in March 2020. Counting past infections helps estimate how severe the disease is overall. It also shows how close a population is to herd immunity. Such counts must happen fast enough to guide decisions.

The team built an ELISA test for IgG and IgM antibodies. The test targets the binding region of the viral spike protein. They checked it against 200 blood donor samples as negative controls. None crossed the cutoff lines they set. Samples from other coronavirus infections showed little cross-reaction. The assays are suited to large population surveys. Public health teams gain a tool for tracking the pandemic's true reach.
europmc-pmc7258448:
Liu and co-authors analyze the first 365 confirmed COVID-19 cases in Shenzhen, China. Their report appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. Shenzhen is a city of 13 million people near the early outbreak center. Many residents had links to Hubei Province. The first local cluster came from a family that had traveled to Wuhan.

Most patients, 91 percent, had a clear exposure at first. Over time, more cases had no clear source. That shift pointed to growing community spread. The share of infected children rose from 2 percent to 13 percent after late January. Family spread likely played a part. Mean incubation was about six days. The authors call for urgent steps to break local transmission chains.
europmc-pmc7282048:
Prüst, Meijer and Westerink review what micro- and nanoplastics may do to the brain. Their review appeared in Particle and Fibre Toxicology. Tiny plastic particles are now everywhere in the environment, and humans and animals inevitably take them in. Studies show the particles can reach the brain, but how many arrive, and what harm they cause, is poorly known.

Drawing on studies in several species and in cell cultures, the authors find signs of oxidative stress, which can damage cells and raise the risk of neuronal disorders. Exposure also inhibited an enzyme that nerve signals depend on and changed neurotransmitter levels, which may explain reported behavior changes. They call for systematic comparisons across particle types, sizes, and doses to pin down the real risk.
europmc-pmc7294848:
Samavati and Uhal argue that ACE2, the doorway SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter cells, does far more in the body than serve the virus. Their perspective appeared in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. ACE2 normally protects the heart and lungs. Working through a partner receptor called MAS, it reduces acute injury and slows scarring in lung tissue.

Infection may disable that protection. When the virus occupies ACE2 in airway cells, the balancing system tips toward the harmful arm of the renin-angiotensin pathway, amplifying damage across the body. The authors discuss exploiting this balance as therapy: boosting the protective ACE2 and MAS route, or blocking the proteases the virus needs to get inside. Both ideas follow from the receptor's normal physiology.
europmc-pmc7295848:
Jiang and co-authors review the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway and its outsized role in cancer. Their review appeared in Molecular Biology Reports. The pathway influences many cell processes, and when it stays switched on it helps tumors grow, spread, and survive. The authors catalogue how the pathway goes wrong in different human cancers.

Overactivation is tied to tumor formation, cell proliferation, invasion, metastasis, stem-like behavior, and drug resistance, plus effects on the immune surroundings of the tumor. Drugs blocking the pathway have entered clinical trials, helped by strong laboratory results. As single treatments, though, their benefit so far is limited. The authors argue combinations of targeted therapies are more likely to deliver real gains for patients.
europmc-pmc7445748:
Duranti and co-authors study how a gut bacterium, Bifidobacterium adolescentis, makes GABA. GABA is the main calming signal chemical in the brain and links to anxiety and depression. Some gut microbes can make it and sway the gut-brain axis.

The team scanned genomes of more than 1,000 bifidobacterial strains. That screen marked B. adolescentis as a model GABA maker in the human gut. Gut data also tied its levels to mental disorders. Tests of 82 strains found two strong makers, named PRL2019 and HD17T2H. Feeding these strains to rats raised GABA output in the body. The results point to a role for this species in gut-brain talks and in mental health.
europmc-pmc7450548:
Bai and co-authors review markers that predict who gains from immune checkpoint drugs. These drugs opened a new era in cancer care, with lasting gains in some tumors. Yet most patients do not benefit, so better selection tools are urgent.

Early markers came from molecules inside tumor cells. Work then widened to cells and molecules in the tumor surroundings. Blood and whole-body host markers joined the list. High-throughput sequencing sped the search and pushed the field from single markers to combined sets. The authors see merged models as the future. Such models blend data on tumor and host interplay. They could turn immune therapy into a precise, patient-fit treatment.
europmc-pmc7460848:
Cimmino and co-authors review how bisphenol A, or BPA, may drive human disease. BPA builds polycarbonate plastic used in food packs, medical devices, and thermal paper. It can leak into food, drink, air, and soil.

BPA builds up in human tissues and acts like a hormone. It binds estrogen receptors, which can shift body weight and tumor growth. Through another receptor, GPR30, it may sway metabolism and cancer spread. Binding to androgen receptors may impair male fertility. Several gene factors join its action on fat, liver, and heart systems. Gene-level marks, such as DNA methylation, add lasting effects. The review gives a broad map of these harm paths.
europmc-pmc7506548:
Yu and co-authors review the NF-kappaB pathway as a drug target for cancer and inflammatory disease. The pathway has two arms. The canonical arm fires fast and fades fast, driving inflammatory genes.

The non-canonical arm starts through a few TNF receptor family members. It runs slow and long, since it needs new protein making. It shapes immune cell growth, lymphoid organs, and steady immune balance. Ubiquitin tags control both arms with care. When control fails, inflammation diseases and cancers can follow. Blocking the pathway has long tempted drug makers. The review sums up how each arm is regulated. It then weighs clinical work on blockers and where they may help most.
europmc-pmc7538848:
Riddell and co-authors test how long SARS-CoV-2 stays infectious on common surfaces at varied heat. Heat was the main factor they changed across the tests they ran. All of the tests ran in the dark to remove any effect of light.

Surfaces were held at three set heat levels for the length of each test run. Half-life at the lowest heat ranged from one point seven to two point seven days. At the highest heat it fell to just a few hours of time. Viable virus lasted up to twenty-eight days at the lowest heat level. That held for glass, steel and both kinds of banknotes tested. At the highest heat, some surfaces cleared the virus within one day. The results inform cleaning and risk control steps for shared public spaces.
europmc-pmc7545148:
Nurk and co-authors present HiCanu, a genome assembler for high-fidelity long reads. Accurate assemblies underpin most genome analysis work. New PacBio HiFi reads are long and highly accurate.

HiCanu adapts the Canu assembler for HiFi data. It uses homopolymer compression and overlap error correction. It also filters false overlaps with care. Tests focused on hard regions of genomes. These included duplicated segments, satellites and gene variants. For human genomes at 30× coverage, allele recovery beat prior tools. One assembly reached an NG50 of 77 Mbp. It also resolved 337 of 341 validation clones.
europmc-pmc7555448:
Sies presents a commentary on the concept of oxidative stress. The term names an imbalance favoring oxidants over antioxidants. It can disrupt redox signaling or cause molecular damage.

The commentary sets out basic features of this global concept. Defense rests mainly on antioxidant enzymes and their partners. Outside compounds play a smaller role in defense. Biomarkers of damage exist for many molecule classes. They cover protein, lipid, carbohydrate and DNA damage. Practical uses in health and disease are outlined. The author warns against oversimplified claims in translation. The piece gives a concise guide to a wide field.
europmc-pmc7654748:
Ogando and co-authors compare two related coronaviruses growing in lab cells. They use Vero E6 cells, a standard line for virus work. One virus is SARS-CoV-2, the cause of COVID-19. The other is the older SARS-CoV.

SARS-CoV-2 made more viral RNA inside cells, yet about 50-fold less live virus came out into the fluid. Both viruses caused much the same cell damage on much the same timing. Three known drugs blocked both to a like degree. With repeated passage, SARS-CoV-2 gained changes in its spike gene that altered its plaques.
europmc-pmc7683248:
Lu and co-authors review wearable health devices and their place in care. Wearables track body signals and activity round the clock. They promise a steady stream of data for diagnosis and treatment. Past reviews stressed consumer gadgets, so this one targets clinical use.

The team screened 960 papers and kept 82 for close study. Devices exist for the head, limbs, and torso. Uses fall into four groups: health monitoring, chronic disease care, diagnosis and treatment, and rehab. The authors find real promise but flag limits in proof and design. They call for stronger clinical tests before wide uptake.
europmc-pmc7710148:
Griss and co-authors present a resource for comparing pathways across large datasets. Omics studies list hundreds of changed genes and proteins. Pathway analysis turns those lists into clear biological stories. Mixing data from unlike omics types or species makes this hard to do well.

The tool, ReactomeGSA, plugs into the Reactome pathway database. It works through a web page and through an R package. It gives explicit support for single-cell RNA data. As a test, the team merged five cancer studies and studied B cells in tumor immunity. B cells showed opposing effects in unlike cancers, a result that shows the tool's reach.
europmc-pmc7734048:
Cheng and co-authors review the gut microbiota's role in colorectal cancer. Imbalance in gut microbes, called dysbiosis, tracks closely with this cancer. The gut community is so large and active that some call it a forgotten organ. Several bacteria now stand out as candidate drivers of the disease.

Named suspects include Fusobacterium nucleatum, Escherichia coli, and toxigenic Bacteroides fragilis. Their routes to cancer span inflammation, toxins that damage DNA, oxidative stress, and biofilms. Microbial products can also speed or slow tumor growth. The authors cover clinical uses of gut profiles and fresh ideas for prevention and treatment based on them.
europmc-pmc7737948:
Gold and co-authors describe adults in hospital with COVID-19 in Georgia. Data came from eight Georgia hospitals for March 2020. In all, 305 patients with confirmed COVID-19 were included. Records gave age, sex, race, health history, and outcomes in hospital.

Most patients, 61.6%, were younger than 65 years, and 50.5% were female. Where race was known, 83.2% were non-Hispanic Black patients. That share topped the group's share of all hospital stays. Over a quarter, 26.2%, had no known high-risk traits. After adjustment, Black patients were not more apt to need a ventilator or to die. The authors urge prevention aimed at the hardest-hit groups.
europmc-pmc7784348:
Wei and co-authors review vasculogenic mimicry in tumors that lack oxygen. Vasculogenic mimicry is a newer found way for tumors to gain blood supply. It differs from the classic route that uses vessel lining cells. Here tumor cells themselves form the channel walls. The pattern shows up in many aggressive cancers.

The authors focus on the hypoxic tumor microenvironment. Low oxygen is a common trait of fast-growing tumors. They explain how such conditions favor the formation of these tumor-lined channels. The process counts as a new model of vessel formation in aggressive disease. Understanding it may point to new ways to cut tumor blood supply.
europmc-pmc7803748:
Sartori and co-authors review how skeletal muscle grows and shrinks. Muscle is the body's protein store. It also helps control sugar and fat balance. Muscle loss worsens the outlook in cancer, organ failure, and infection. It also marks unhealthy aging.

Cells police their own parts through quality systems. These systems tune contractile proteins and cell organelles. Gene programs adjust them to food and surroundings. Stress from force, oxidation, or low energy feeds into shared pathways. Those pathways settle how much protein and organelle mass turns over. The authors sum up new findings in this network. Knowing these controls could yield targets for treating muscle loss.
europmc-pmc7829348:
Mohammad and Thiemermann review metabolic endotoxemia and its role in body-wide inflammation. The gut wall normally blocks bacterial lipopolysaccharide, or LPS. Diet changes can weaken that wall. LPS then leaks into the blood.

Blood LPS switches on the TLR4 receptor. That triggers release of inflammatory signals. The result is low-grade inflammation that does not quit. This state feeds many chronic diseases. Obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease can all raise gut leakiness. Diet and drug steps may seal the gut again. The authors survey those options in detail. Cutting this slow inflammation is the shared goal.
europmc-pmc7875348:
Yinda and co-authors report a research study on a mouse model of severe COVID-19. The mice were bred to carry the human ACE2 receptor under a keratin promoter, known as K18. The team infected these mice with SARS-CoV-2 and tracked how the disease developed.

Infection caused fast weight loss and a dose-dependent lethal course. The authors report high levels of viral RNA in the upper and lower airways. Lung tissue showed interstitial pneumonia much like that seen in severe human cases. Immune cells moved into the lungs, and pro-inflammatory signals rose. Virus also appeared in parts of the brain in some animals. The team presents the model as a tool for testing treatments against severe disease.
europmc-pmc7942748:
Meinecke presents a study of consumption, or tuberculosis, in classical antiquity. The work began as a doctoral dissertation at the University of Michigan. Its subject is how Greek and Roman writers knew and described the wasting disease. Meinecke warns that the word tuberculosis is used loosely here. No test for the bacillus is possible in ancient sources, so the term means consumption as the lay reader knows it.

The arrangement is chronological, as the topic demands. Hippocrates is cited from the Littré edition, and Galen from Kühn's. The original Greek and Latin texts are left out for reasons of cost and space. Interested readers can find them with ease, he notes. The study builds a careful record of ancient views on a major killer. It serves both classicists and historians of medicine.
europmc-pmc7946148:
Ruhräh presents a biographical study of John Ferriar, a doctor and man of letters who lived from 1761 to 1815. Ferriar was the son of a clergyman, the Reverend Alexander Ferriar. He was born at Oxnam near Jedburgh on November 21, 1761. His early years passed near Alnwick. Edinburgh was the natural place for his degree, taken in 1781 with a thesis on smallpox.

He married in 1782 and began practice at Stockton-on-Tees. Three years later he moved to Manchester. There he joined the founders of its Literary and Philosophical Society. From then on he split his time between medicine and literature, Ruhräh writes, serving both with devotion. His output was large and much of it fine. The study recovers a British literary doctor of real range.
europmc-pmc7984248:
Chen and co-authors present a review of porphyrin-based metal-organic frameworks for medical use. Porphyrins are ring-shaped molecules with fine light and electric traits. Alone, they are unstable in body-like conditions and quench their own glow. Metal-organic frameworks are sponges of metal and linker molecules with vast inner surface. Joining the two may keep the strengths and lose the flaws.

The review sorts the designs into three kinds. Porphyrins can sit inside a framework, form the framework's links, or join it as a composite. Synthesis routes for each kind are set out. Medical uses lead the second half: tumour therapy and biosensing above all. Light-driven treatments gain from the pairing in clear ways. The authors close with the hurdles that remain for clinic use. The paper maps a young material class with care.
europmc-pmc8043748:
Colombo and co-authors show that gut microbe products push amyloid plaque growth in Alzheimer's disease. The gut microbiome was known to modify the disease, but the messenger was missing. The team worked with Alzheimer's model mice, some raised germ-free. They measured short-chain fatty acids, the metabolites gut bacteria release. Germ-free animals carried far less amyloid plaque and lower fatty acid levels.

Adding fatty acids back restored plaque growth in germ-free mice. In colonized mice, supplementation made plaques worse still. Microglia, the brain's immune cells, changed their gene activity in response. ApoE expression rose sharply. More microglia gathered at plaques, yet each held less amyloid inside. The authors name these fatty acids as key gut-brain messengers. Modulating them may offer a new handle on the disease.
europmc-pmc8052448:
Lindskrog and co-authors sort non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer into molecular subtypes tied to outcome. Tumors that look alike under the microscope behave very differently. The team ran an integrated multi-omics analysis on 834 patients. Transcript data did the first sorting. Chromosome stability and immune infiltration added further layers.

Four transcriptomic classes emerged, labeled 1, 2a, 2b, and 3. Both the classes and chromosomal instability predicted outcome independently. Class 2a tumors carried p53 disruption and APOBEC mutations, and fared worst. Class 2b tumors drew heavy immune infiltration. More immune cells there meant fewer recurrences. The team then validated the classes in 1,228 further samples. A single-sample classifier makes the scheme usable in future trials. Surveillance and treatment could finally be tuned by subtype.
europmc-pmc8115348:
Bottery and co-authors argue that antibiotic resistance is a community property, not just a trait of single species. Lab tests judge one pathogen alone in a dish. Real infections embed pathogens in mixed microbial crowds. Neighbors can shield, feed, or fight the target species. Those interactions bend how antibiotics bite. They also bend the selection that breeds resistance.

Gene swapping between species spreads ready-made resistance fast. Beyond that, daily interactions shift which mutants gain ground. A treatment that wins in pure culture may fail in a crowd. The strength and direction of selection can flip with company. The authors map the routes by which this happens. They then list the studies the field most needs. Ecological context, they insist, belongs in stewardship plans. Ignoring the crowd invites nasty surprises in the clinic. Resistance plans must think like ecologists.
europmc-pmc8125348:
Liebl and Hofmann review the p53 pathway and its breakdown in colorectal cancer. The protein p53 stands guard over the genome. Stress signals free it from its keeper, MDM2. It then orders repair, cell arrest, senescence, or death. Few guardians matter more against cancer. In colorectal tumors, that guard is often gone or corrupted. The gene TP53 is mutated in 43% of these cancers by the review's count.

Most such mutations swap a single building block. They kill the guard's normal work in one stroke. Worse, many mutants gain new, tumor-friendly tricks. Stemness, invasion, and spread all get boosts from them. Tumors without TP53 mutations often break its regulators instead. Genes like ATM and DNA-PKcs fail in smaller shares. The review closes with drugs that target p53 itself. Reactivating the guard, or exploiting its loss, drives the search. Trials are only the first chapter.
europmc-pmc8226948:
Candelli and co-authors examine how lipopolysaccharide and gut microbes interact in inflammatory bowel disease. Lipopolysaccharide coats Gram-negative bacteria and can trigger sharp inflammation. It can also drive slow, chronic inflammation from inside the gut.

Food and gut microbes supply a steady internal source of it. The gut wall and its lymphoid tissue meet that supply first. Both shift toward an inflammatory pattern under its push. Microbe diversity falls, and regulatory T cells lose ground. Those changes mirror what doctors see in bowel disease. The review traces the loop and where it might be broken.
europmc-pmc8301948:
Yuan and co-authors test kaempferol against ferroptosis in oxygen-starved neurons. Kaempferol is a plant compound known to guard brain cells. The team modelled stroke-like injury by cutting oxygen and glucose, then restoring them.

Injury lowered SLC7A11 and GPX4, two guards against ferroptosis. Cell antioxidant stores such as glutathione also fell. Kaempferol turned on the Nrf2 pathway. That raised the SLC7A11 and GPX4 defence line again. Cell death dropped in their assays. The work links a dietary compound to a named death pathway. It hints at a stroke therapy angle. Microscopy and protein assays backed the cell death readings.
europmc-pmc8443448:
Molteni and co-authors chart illness length and symptoms in UK school-aged children with SARS-CoV-2. In children, infection is often silent or mild and short. Lasting illness had been reported, but its rate and shape were unclear.

The study drew on the COVID Symptom Study app, where adults reported for children aged 5 to 17 years. The team measured how long illness lasted and which symptoms ruled. They split results for ages 5 to 11 and 12 to 17. Children who tested negative served as a matched comparison group. The data set held reports on over a quarter of a million children. Findings help frame what families and schools should expect.
europmc-pmc8660748:
Thong and co-authors set out causes and treatment options for cancer-related fatigue. This deep tiredness hits many survivors during and after treatment. It is often missed by care teams and left untreated. The authors review what drives it and what helps.

No single treatment stands as the gold standard. Several options show benefit, from drugs to added therapies. Exercise holds the strongest evidence so far. It can prevent or ease fatigue during active treatment and after it ends. The review weighs drug and non-drug paths side by side. It gives clinicians a plain guide to a common but neglected problem.
europmc-pmc8744548:
Jurcau and Simion review neuroinflammation in brain ischemia and in injury after blood flow returns. Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide. Even with better vessel reopening, patients face added harm when flow returns. Inflammation sits at the center of that harm.

In the early phase, immune cascades kill cells and break the blood-brain barrier. Swelling and bleeding can follow. Later, the same pathways help repair tissue and restore function. The review sorts the cell types and steps in each phase. It also covers treatment attempts in cells, animals, and patients. Future therapy ideas close the account.
europmc-pmc8746448:
Neufingerl and Eilander review nutrient intake and status in adults on plant-based diets versus meat-eaters. Health bodies now urge diets richer in plants and lower in red meat. The team pooled observational and trial studies from 2000 to 2020. In total, 141 studies were included, mostly from Europe, Asia, and North America.

Protein intake ran lower on plant-based diets but stayed within advised levels. Fiber, folate, and vitamins C and E ran higher. Vitamin B12, vitamin D, iron, zinc, and iodine ran lower. Vegans had the lowest B12, calcium, and iodine intake. The review gives a balanced base for diet planning.
europmc-pmc8796548:
Gao and co-authors review brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, in Alzheimer disease and its drug potential. Synapse faults are a core trait of the disease and grow as it advances. BDNF supports the plasticity that learning and memory need. Its loss links to amyloid buildup, tau changes, inflammation, and neuron death.

How faulty BDNF signaling drives the disease is still not settled. The review first maps the gene's structure and the factors that control it. It then weighs BDNF as a diagnostic marker in patients. Therapies that target the factor form the last part. The authors see real promise but clear gaps in mechanism.
europmc-pmc8926248:
Milbury and co-authors present the validation behind FoundationOne CDx, a genomic test for solid tumors. The assay reads 324 cancer genes at once. US regulators cleared it as a companion diagnostic. It matches patients to 28 approved drug therapies. It reports small variants, copy number changes, and rearrangements. It also reads tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability. One bloodless test thus replaces many single checks.

Validation had to prove the results trustworthy. The team measured detection limits and blank limits. Precision and agreement with other methods were tested. Each variant class faced its own checks. The evidence base tops 30,000 test results. Clinical validation tied findings to real treatment labels. The authors argue the test meets a high standard. Reliable profiling, they say, is what precision medicine stands on.
europmc-pmc8929548:
Brown and co-authors issue expert recommendations for indoor light that supports sleep and health. Light through the eyes steers body rhythms. It shapes alertness, hormones, and mood as well. Modern indoor life gives too little day light and too much night light. A new international standard now quantifies light's nonvisual effect. It centers on melanopsin, the pigment in special retinal cells. The panel expresses advice in that standard's measure.

Daytime, evening, and nighttime each get target levels. The values use melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance. The rationale draws on human sensitivity studies. Circadian, hormone, and alertness responses all inform the numbers. The authors relate their advice to existing standards. Practical guidance for homes and workplaces follows. The framework is meant for designers and practitioners. Better light, they argue, is preventive medicine.
europmc-pmc9021448:
Mou and co-authors trace how gut microbes may harm the brain through long-term inflammation throughout the body. A disturbed gut community can inflame the gut lining and leak signals into the blood. The review follows those signals to the blood-brain barrier, the shield that guards the brain. Inflammatory messengers can weaken that shield and let harmful factors through.

Once the barrier leaks, brain inflammation, nerve cell loss, and faster brain ageing may follow. The authors link this chain to Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis. They present the barrier itself as a marker and a possible target for treatment.
europmc-pmc9024848:
Néron and co-authors present IntegronFinder 2.0, updated software for finding integrons in bacterial genomes. Integrons are gene-swapping platforms that often carry antibiotic resistance genes. The new version runs faster, handles draft genomes and metagenomes, and adds functions for very large datasets. The team applied it to more than 20,000 complete genomes to map where integrons occur.

They also scanned close to 4,000 Klebsiella pneumoniae genomes, a major hospital pathogen. Its integrons held 165 gene families, most tied to drug resistance, plus the largest mobile integron in their plasmid database. The tool is free and open source.
europmc-pmc9262248:
Emran and co-authors review multidrug resistance in cancer, its molecular mechanisms, and ways around it. Resistance is a major obstacle to effective cancer treatment. It can be present from the start or acquired during therapy. Chemotherapy fails in most resistant cases.

Drivers include altered genes and epigenetics, stronger drug efflux pumps, and blocked cell death. Low oxygen and autophagy inside tumors also foster resistance. The review explains resistance genes and the controls that switch them on. It then covers lab approaches to inhibit, bypass, or reverse resistance. Options range from immune prevention to microparticles and nanomedicine. The authors argue that grasping the mechanisms is the first step to better strategies.
europmc-pmc9668748:
Gandal and co-authors map gene activity changes across the whole cerebral cortex in autism spectrum disorder. Brain disorders of this kind lack clear tissue marks. Molecular work had found gene shifts in frontal and temporal cortex. Whether the shifts stop at those zones was unknown.

The team sequenced RNA from 725 brain samples in total. The samples spanned 11 cortical areas from 112 donors. Donors with autism were set against neurotypical controls. Gene changes proved wide across the cortex, not local. The shifts ran in a front to back slope pattern. Primary visual cortex showed the largest gaps of all zones. Normal gene gaps between regions also faded in autism brains. Single-nucleus data pinned shifts to excitatory neurons and glia. Rare and common risk variants met in shared gene modules.
europmc-pmc9925748:
Werba and co-authors use single-cell RNA sequencing to study chemotherapy effects in pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a complex tumor setting that drives growth. Deep single-cell work on how that setting responds to therapy was lacking. The team sampled fresh human tumors before and after chemotherapy.

Samples held a mix of basal and classical cancer cell types. They also held distinct fibroblast and macrophage groups. Both cancer types responded to chemotherapy in like ways, with no shift toward a basal program. Cell-to-cell signals fell after treatment, notably TIGIT signals to cancer cells. TIGIT stood out as the main inhibitory checkpoint on CD8 T cells. The authors warn that chemotherapy may aid resistance to immunotherapy.
fichte-vocation-man-1848:
The Vocation of Man, Johann Gottlieb Fichte's Die Bestimmung des Menschen of 1800, is his most widely read book. William Smith's English translation of 1848, the first in the language, is the text here. Fichte wrote it for readers beyond the schools, in dialogue form, as a journey of one mind through its own doubts.

Doubt speaks first, stripping the world to a show of images. Knowledge answers, showing the mind its own laws at work in that show. Faith speaks last, and carries the speaker to duty, freedom, and trust in a moral order. The three voices move like acts in a play. No other work of Fichte's reaches the heart so directly.
french-constitution-1848:
France wrote a new constitution in 1848 after the February Revolution toppled King Louis-Philippe. The charter founded the Second Republic in the springtime of the peoples, when thrones shook across Europe. Its makers tried to join a strong executive to the widest democracy France had known.

The text grants the vote to all adult men, the first full manhood suffrage in French history. It creates a president elected by the people for four years, facing a single elected assembly. In December 1848 the voters chose Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte as president. Within four years he seized full power in a coup and strangled the republic his office came from. The constitution remains the charter of 1848's hope and of its winter, the republic that elected its own destroyer.
frus-1861-d148:
On 22 August 1861, William Dayton sent a further report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 148 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late August found Dayton watching French yards and ports for Southern orders. Confederate buyers sought ships and arms where they could. His report belongs to the quiet counter work that kept such goods from sailing under French colors. Southern buyers in France worked through banks and brokers, hard men to track. Hard men to track were tracked all the same, by consuls, clerks, and patience. Tracked all the same, by patience and proof.
frus-1861-d248:
James Shepherd Pike reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 18 August 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 248 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d48:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 31 May 1861. The dispatch is document 48 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Britain had now declared its neutrality and granted the South the rights of a belligerent. Adams had to accept that step while blocking any move beyond it. His end of May report shows the care with which he drew that line in talk with British ministers. Adams treated the belligerent grant as a fixed fact and fought on the ground beyond it. Beyond that line lay recognition, and on that line Adams would not yield an inch.
frus-1862-d148:
Dated 22 September 1862, Document 148 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It forms one link in the long chain of orders and reports that bound Washington to its legation in Britain during the Civil War.

On that same date Lincoln issued his first Emancipation Proclamation, warning that enslaved people in rebel states would be freed on 1 January. The step changed what the war was about in foreign eyes. Seward's mail to London in these days went out as that news began its slow trip across the sea.
frus-1862-d248:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, sent William L. Dayton a dispatch on 2 January 1862, printed as Document 248 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris, the Union's voice at the court of Napoleon III.

The new year opened with French, British, and Spanish forces gathering in Mexico, a move Washington watched with deep distrust. Dayton's standing task was to defend Union interests without pushing France toward the Confederacy. Seward's January letters set his envoy's line for a year in which Mexico and the war would stay tightly linked. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d348:
Document 348 opens the file of France's minister in Washington: a letter dated 7 December 1861 from Henri Mercier to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The catalog title spells his name Merrier. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mercier represented Napoleon III's France in the Union capital, a post of great delicacy during the Civil War. December 1861 was the Trent crisis month, and every foreign envoy in Washington watched the Anglo-American quarrel closely. Mercier's letters to Seward form the French counterpart to the British file in this volume. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d448:
Baron Friedrich von Gerolt, the Prussian minister in Washington, received this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 May 1861. It is Document 448 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, one of its earliest papers.

Gerolt was the dean of Washington's diplomatic corps, long resident and deeply read in American affairs. In May 1861 the war was a month old, and Seward was setting the terms on which foreign governments would deal with the rebellion. A note to Prussia's minister in those weeks belonged to the first framing of the Union's case. The case ran: one nation, a domestic revolt, no foreign hand welcome. The letter reaches back to the spring when all the volume's later files began.
frus-1862-d48:
16 April 1862 is stamped on a letter Seward got from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 48 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d548:
Dated 27 September 1862, this note from Roest van Limburg to Secretary of State William H. Seward was printed after its successor in the volume's Dutch file. It is Document 548 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The slight disorder of dates is a window on how the volume was made. Papers were gathered by subject. They were printed as the files came together, not in perfect time order. Van Limburg's late-September note dealt with the standing questions between his government and the United States. Read with the note of 29 September, it shows the Dutch legation working steadily through the autumn. Meanwhile Antietam and emancipation remade the setting. All Washington diplomacy was done in that new setting.
frus-1862-d648:
Robert H. Pruyn, the American minister to Japan, dated this dispatch 15 May 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 648 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed among the papers on Japan. Pruyn had stepped into the job only weeks before.

Ministers abroad wrote on a set rhythm, sending news, requests, and accounts of their talks with local rulers. Pruyn's letter is part of that steady flow from the Japan legation. For readers today, it shows American ties with Japan in their first years. A handful of men ran them, writing letters that took months to cross the Pacific.
frus-1863p1-d148:
In a week the ship news ran the Union's way, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 8 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London, and a dispatch from him sits just before this letter in the volume. The letter is document 148 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's April letters kept the press on while the ship news ran the Union's way. He had to hold the gains without crowing, since Britain's pride was a force of its own. This letter is Washington's word in a same-week cross with London. It shows the secretary's care with tone, the skill that matched Adams's own and made the pair so strong.
frus-1863p1-d248:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 24 July 1863. The letter is document 248 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d348:
Washington's business with Britain on 31 December 1862 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 348 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Notes on this route often dealt with single ships, single cargoes, or single men. Small cases mattered, because each one tested what neutrality would allow. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d448:
A letter of 6 April 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 448 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1863p1-d48:
On 25 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to James M. Mason for the second day in a row. Memminger ran the Confederate treasury; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 48 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Back-to-back letters from a treasury chief point to deals that would not wait. The South's credit in Europe hung on cotton and on faith that the new republic would last. Memminger's sheets to Mason fed that work. With its twin, this letter shows Richmond's money men writing in haste in the fall of 1862, as costs rose and the purse shrank.
frus-1863p1-d548:
In the flow of wartime mail, F. W. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 3 June 1863. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them.
frus-1863p1-d648:
The 26 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d148: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on November 20, 1943, two days before Cairo and eight before Tehran. The letter is Document 148 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It was among the last written approaches to a man the president had never met, from the middle of the journey itself. The record gives the date and the two leaders' names. The letter is preserved in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d248:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 22 November 1943, at three in the afternoon, open the Sextant Conference's staff work. Admiral Leahy proposed, and the chiefs agreed, that Britain's General Sir Alan Brooke chair their meetings during the conference.

The first business was order of work. Far East operations would be taken early, so the Chinese theater could be studied before Europe, and the chiefs adopted the agenda in paper C.C.S. 404/1. General Marshall read out Stilwell's brief note of Chiang Kai-shek's views, and the chiefs set times to study it and to meet the Generalissimo and his advisers the next day. They also settled conference procedure on the Quebec model, and took up relations with Soviet and Chinese military representatives.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d348:
Harry Hopkins sent a secret telegram from Tehran on 30 November 1943 to Ambassador Kirk at Cairo, addressed through him to Frank Shea of the information services. It answers a query about the background material meant to accompany the Cairo communiqué.

Shea had noted that the communiqué placed the conference only somewhere in North Africa. He asked whether the background stories could name Mena. Mena is the suburb by the Pyramids where the meetings were held. Hopkins' answer is firm: strike out or hold for later release every reference to the Mena House, to the villas occupied by any member of the party, or to Mena itself. Color stories about trips to the Pyramids and the Sphinx are allowed, so long as nothing hints at where the conference sat. The Cairo dateline stands, and the communiqué text is unchanged.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d448: An editorial note stands at Document 448 of the Cairo-Tehran volume. The State Department's historians wrote it long after the events described. Such notes supply background, clarify names, and link related papers. The volume itself gathers the record of the 1943 Cairo and Tehran conferences. There the Allied leaders argued over invasions, borders, and the postwar map. The note is a brief pause where the editors guide the reader.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d48: On October 20, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, while the foreign ministers sat in Moscow. The message is Document 48 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. London and Washington watched the Moscow talks closely, since their results would set the agenda for Tehran. The catalog record gives the date and the two names and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series as part of that anxious, hopeful week.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d548:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote again to President Roosevelt on January 16, 1944. His letters that winter ranged across the whole war, from invasion timing to relations with Moscow. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Churchill believed in working by correspondence, and his messages often arrived like small essays: argument, history, and pressure in one package. Roosevelt received more of them than any other correspondent. Mid-January found the alliance in the demanding space between deciding and doing. For readers, this letter is another stroke in the written partnership that directed the Western war effort from day to day.
frus-1944-quebec-d148:
Santa Maria airfield is the narrow subject of this State Department briefing paper, prepared for Quebec in September 1944. The American Army Air Corps was building a second Azores airfield on the island of Santa Maria, in Portugal. Washington had negotiated the facility directly with Lisbon, using Pan American Airways as a commercial cover for the government's interest.

The paper advises Roosevelt not to raise the airfield with Churchill. If Churchill raised it, the president should make clear the deal stood apart from the Anglo-Portuguese agreement of 1943 and the old alliance of 1373. The Air Corps expected to operate the field directly. No question of postwar civil aviation control, the paper stresses, was involved.
frus-1944-quebec-d248: Morgenthau gave Roosevelt his recommendation on French lend-lease at Quebec on September 15, 1944, in a single sentence: for the time being, postpone taking any action. Roosevelt had referred Hull's discretion proposal to him two days into the conference. The memorandum bears the president's endorsement in reply: "Approved: F. D. Roosevelt." Morgenthau telephoned Hopkins to report the recommendation.
frus-1944-quebec-d48:
Emory S. Land, the War Shipping Administrator, wrote to President Roosevelt on September 1, 1944. Land ran America's wartime merchant shipping program, the largest shipbuilding effort in history. His message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Shipping was the alliance's scarcest resource, and its division between theaters and allies was a standing argument that Quebec would revisit. A message from the shipping chief to the President in the conference's run-up carried tonnage, priorities, and hard numbers. For readers, it shows the material foundation beneath the leaders' strategy, counted in ships rather than speeches.
frus-1945-50-intel-d148: On 29 April 1946, the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers) put a memorandum into the files. It is document 148 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff. Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings.
frus-1945-50-intel-d248:
A memorandum from the Deputy Director (Wright) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 4 November 1947. It stands as document 248 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d348:
Formal minutes cover a meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Committee, held on 16 June 1948. It is document 348 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The pages give the meeting in the plain form staff used at the time: a topic, the sense of the talk, and the result. Staff in other offices then worked from this record, treating its lines as the settled word. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d48:
Minutes of the 168th meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 20 November 1945. The numbered meetings show a standing body grinding through the department's business week by week. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A numbered run of minutes lets readers watch an institution think over time. The 168th meeting took up the department's affairs with the intelligence question at its height. What the committee agreed, deferred, or sent upward shaped the State Department's final position. The volume prints several of these committee records. Together they give the State side of the story an official spine that the letters alone would lack.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d148:
Mikolajczyk's resignation made the Polish question much more acute, Stettinius wired the President on 25 November 1944. His telegram is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It reads the fall of the one London Pole who could deal with Moscow.

Mikolajczyk fell, Stettinius explains, because his own government would not back his program of settling the territorial issue with the Soviet Union. Without him, the London government has no basis at all for talks with Moscow or with the Lublin Committee. Washington must expect the Soviets to move fast, raising the Lublin body into Poland's sole authority. That body, Stettinius notes, is backed by Moscow but has very little support inside Poland itself.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d248:
Roosevelt asked Stalin to join the war on Japan in this message of 4 October 1944. Sent through Ambassador Harriman in Moscow, the excerpts printed in the Malta and Yalta volume carry the heart of it. General Deane had already delivered the allied chiefs' statement on the Far East war.

The President says he accepts completely the assurances Stalin has given on the point. The three countries, he writes, are waging a successful war against Germany together. They can join with no less success against Japan. That nation, he is sure in his heart, is as great an enemy of Russia as she is of America's. The short message is part of the long courtship that brought the Soviet Union into the Pacific war.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d348:
Secrecy gave way to publicity in this American draft of a first press release for the Yalta Conference, dated February 6, 1945. The draft announces that the President, the Soviet Premier, and the British Prime Minister are meeting in the Black Sea area. Their stated purpose: to concert plans for finishing the defeat of the enemy and building firm foundations for a lasting peace.

The talks, it says, had not passed the early stages, yet showed unity of purpose, frankness, and friendship. Meetings ran day and night, starting with military reviews of all the European fronts. The draft is the public face the conference chose for itself, mid-stream.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d448:
Greece had asked and heard nothing, and this British paper of February 10, 1945, takes up its case. When the Hungarian armistice was signed, Moscow let Czechoslovak and Yugoslav representatives join the Hungarian control commission. That let them deal with questions touching their own governments. Greece sought like facilities in Bulgaria.

On January 23, the Greek government, backed by Britain's Moscow embassy, asked the Soviet government for the same standing. No reply, the paper notes pointedly, had yet been vouchsafed. London's concern is plain between the lines: Greek claims on Bulgaria, above all reparations, risked being shut out of the room where Bulgaria's fate was run.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d48: Another Churchill message reached Roosevelt on 9 January 1945, continuing the daily pace of that month. It is document 48 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. By mid-January the correspondence concerned a journey already set in motion, and each new letter added detail to plans that ships and aircraft were about to carry out.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d148:
British Minister John Balfour added an agenda item in a letter to Acting Secretary Grew dated June 1, 1945. The letter is document 148 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It follows up his letter of May 29, which had delivered the British list of subjects for the summit.

Foreign Secretary Eden asks him to say this. In view of Stalin's message about the surrendered German naval and merchant ships, the British propose adding a new item. It would go in the Germany section of the agenda. The item reads simply: disposal of the German fleet and merchant ships. A note adds that Grew passed the substance to Truman on June 5. The small addition put one of the war's tangible prizes squarely on the Potsdam table.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d248:
A briefing paper favored trusteeship for Eritrea in a paper dated June 30, 1945. The paper is document 248 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Eritrea, Italy's oldest Red Sea colony, was among the territories the peace settlement would dispose of.

The United States favors an international trusteeship over the former colony, the paper states. Its data section traces Eritrea from the purchase of Assab in 1869 to its role as the base for Italy's attacks on Ethiopia in the 1890s and again in 1935. The colony held some 600,000 people in 1931, few of them Europeans. Ethiopia has historic claims to the region, which blocks her from the sea, but handing it to Ethiopia outright might endanger the Italian population and clash with the Atlantic Charter. The dilemma ran on for years after the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d348:
Aboard the cruiser Augusta on July 12, 1945, the American delegation drafted a working paper on a German import program. It proposed that the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States order their commanders to push one step in the Control Council. The step was a single program of minimum imports for Germany as a whole.

The paper calls for fair sharing of supplies between zones, so Germany's total import bill shrinks. Ration scales and standards of need would be the same in every zone. Buying and paying for imports would be shared, on terms set in the Control Council, and early outlays repaid as a first charge on German exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d448:
Greek elections come up in Grew's memorandum of a conversation with Lord Halifax on July 10, 1945. The British ambassador had called that afternoon, and the Greek item is third on the record. Halifax discussed Grew's recent aide-mémoire on supervising the Greek plebiscite and elections. On several points, London was in accord with Washington.

Britain agreed on approaching the Greek government, and in time the Soviet and French governments. But London did not concur in the American recommendation on the sequence of plebiscite and elections. That, Britain felt, was a matter for the Greek government itself to determine. Grew offered detailed discussion with his officer Kohler, which Halifax declined for the time.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d48:
Only an extract survives in print of Churchill's telegram number 64 to President Truman, sent from London on June 1, 1945. It is document 48 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The surviving passage comes from a busy day when Churchill was also pressing Truman to move the Big Three meeting to an earlier date.

In the printed lines, Churchill reports that he has spent the last few days forming Britain's new and, in his words, very complicated government, and that the work is now done. He stresses that nothing in the British election will keep the three major powers from meeting at the earliest possible date. The rest of the telegram is left out of the published volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d548:
John Balfour, the British minister in Washington, wrote to Assistant Secretary of State Will Clayton on June 21, 1945. His letter is document 548 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It answers a U.S. note of April 18 about landing rights for U.S. air lines.

Balfour says Britain has no wish to oppose the United States in gaining landing rights in any country. Britain, he adds, is bound by the deals reached at Chicago in December 1944. He cites the interim civil aviation pact, under which each state may set routes and airports in its land. Charges for their use must be fair and no higher than for its own planes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d648:
Ambassador Winant sent a personal and secret plea on Palestine from London on July 8, 1945. Addressed to the Secretary of State, it is document 648 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Winant writes of his deep concern over the situation.

Winant reports a visit from Dr. Chaim Weizmann, the Zionist leader, two days before. Weizmann had done much good in Palestine after Lord Moyne's killing, but was now ill and worn down. His only recent word from Churchill was a brief note putting a settlement off to a peace conference. A world Zionist conference was set to meet in London at the month's end. Weizmann told Winant he would feel bound to resign his post if no advance had been made by then. Winant stresses this was no threat, but the despair of a tired man who feared a more militant policy would follow him.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1048:
Stalin answered President Truman's coal memorandum from Berlin on July 29, 1945. He confirms that he has received the July 27 paper. He also has the copy of Truman's directive to General Eisenhower on German coal exports.

The question of using German coal to meet European needs, Stalin writes, will receive proper study. Washington will be told the Soviet view when it is formed. Stalin adds one caution. Steps to export German coal must not stir disturbances inside Germany, a risk Truman's own directive names. Avoiding such trouble, he says, serves all the Allied governments.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1148:
Poland's President Bierut wrote to President Truman on 23 July 1945, three days after the joint letter he had signed with his prime minister. A second appeal so soon kept up Warsaw's pressure. The summit was deciding Poland's border and standing that week.

Bierut led the government the Soviet Union had installed and backed. He wanted the United States to treat that government as Poland's rightful rulers and to deal with it as such. A letter to a president is the highest channel a foreign leader can use. This one is part of Warsaw's drive for American acceptance, pressed while the talks could still shift.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1248:
President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on 25 July 1945. The two men exchanged notes through the whole Churchill week at Potsdam. This one came on the prime minister's last full day at the talks.

The count in London the next day would end Churchill's leadership. Neither man wrote as if the partnership were ending; the work went on to the final hour. This message belongs to that last day of joint business. It is part of the closing set of letters between the president and the prime minister who had led Britain through the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1348:
The acting secretary of state sent instructions to John Winant, the American ambassador in London, on 16 July 1945. That was the day before the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill, and Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945 formally opened. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

London was Washington's closest partner and its first sounding board in 1945. Instructions sent on the eve of a summit set the line an ambassador should hold with the host government. Readers can use this message to see what Washington wanted London to know. To do. As Truman and Byrnes set out for Germany and the talks with Stalin began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-148: An editorial note placed after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume adds the editors' guidance at a packed point in the files. Such notes in Foreign Relations volumes cite sources and tie papers together. They may also admit where the record is silent. This one helps readers judge the strength of the evidence around it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-48:
A United States delegation memorandum sets the agenda for the foreign ministers' meeting of July 21, 1945, at noon. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Five items of business are listed in order.

First came the date for formally setting up the new Council of Foreign Ministers. The Big Three had left that choice to the ministers the day before. German economic questions came second, on the subcommittee's first report after days of work. Poland came third, on the liquidation of the London government and the carrying out of the Yalta agreement. Fourth came the same Yalta declaration as applied to liberated Europe and the satellite states. The U.S. was presenting a new paper spelling out the steps it believed should be taken there. Italy and the other satellites closed the list.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d748:
Document 748 is a proposal the United States delegation tabled at Potsdam on July 21, 1945. It dates from the conference's fifth day. By then each side knew the others' opening lines. New texts were drafted to probe and to trade. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Mid-conference proposals carry the marks of contact. They answer points made across the table. Readers can line this text up with rival drafts of the same week. The comparison shows bargaining as a written duel. The document adds one dated step to the path from first claims to the final protocol.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d848:
Document 848 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 16, 1945. It was drafted before the conference formally opened. Teams arrived in Germany with paper ready for the first sessions. This draft was kept in the delegation files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A pre-opening draft shows the summit before the summit. Staff had war-gamed the talks and written for them. Readers can measure the plan against the event. The document honors the foresight, and the misses, of the planners. It opens the working-paper run at its true start: in the quiet days when everything was still expected to go as written.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d948: Seymour Rubin wrote to his deputy Covey Oliver on July 29, 1945, about a British worry over Soviet republics filing separate reparation claims. Rubin had read the Department's telegram passing the idea to Pauley. He reports it has not happened so far. The Soviet Union seems set on treating its claims as a whole. In any case, Rubin argues, the zonal plan now taking shape makes the question moot. Soviet and Polish claims would be met from the eastern zone, plus a set amount from the west.
frus-1948v02-d548: An editorial note in the 1948 Germany and Austria volume sums up a June 1948 letter exchange. General Clay told Marshal Sokolovsky on June 18 that currency reform for the western zones would start on June 20. Berlin was not included. Sokolovsky replied on June 20 that the reform was illegal and split Germany. Clay answered on June 21, denying that Berlin lay in the Soviet zone. The note points readers to the printed texts of each letter.
frus-1950v01-d148:
NSC 68/4, a top secret report to the President from the National Security Council, is the record here. Dated December 14, 1950, it carries the amended NSC 68 program into force as a working guide. The President's directive orders a joint State-Defense review to speed the build-up.

The report states that the Korean invasion gave the appraisal new urgency. Chinese entry into the war raised the danger further. Forces once planned for 1954 were now due by June 30, 1952. Political, economic, and psychological action would proceed under a military shield. The paper's logic drove budgets and alliances for the rest of the decade.
frus-1977-80v06-d248:
An editorial note in Volume VI of the 1977-1980 series prints the hotline exchange of December 29, 1979, on Afghanistan. Carter's message calls the Soviet invasion a clear threat to peace. He writes that Soviet forces were used to overthrow the Afghan government and install a new one. He urges prompt withdrawal. He warns that ties built over many years could be undone. Acting Secretary Christopher sent the texts to Moscow on December 30.

Brezhnev's reply of the same date rejects Carter's account. He says Soviet forces entered at the Afghan government's request. The note thus pairs charge and denial at the moment detente broke.
gao-gaoreports-b-298248:
Triple H Services protested an Army Corps award for grounds work in GAO decision B-298248, dated August 1, 2006. The winner was B.R. Mowing. The site was Berlin Lake in Berlin Center, Ohio. Work held grass cuts and clean work for blocks and grounds. The firm said the winner's bid was skewed in price. It also hit the fitness call for the winner.

GAO denied the protest. The record did not back the skew claim. Prices by task did not show a key skew that would harm the state. The fitness call was also left to stand. GAO does not undo a fitness yes sans strong proof of flaw. No such proof was made.
gao-gaoreports-b-306748:
Moving costs for border staff who live abroad are cleared in this GAO decision, B-306748, dated July 6, 2006. Customs and Border Protection set a new rule for its border posts. Staff posted in the United States must live in the United States. Some staff lived in Canada or Mexico. They faced moves to keep their jobs.

GAO raised no bar to paying the move costs. The agency found that U.S. homes help its border staff do the mission well. Its pay and costs funds may cover the moves if the agency so chooses. The ruling helps agencies weigh staff costs that flow from a rule the agency itself imposed.
gao-gaoreports-b-310548:
Cornell Companies, Inc. lost its protest. That ruling is B-310548, dated December 3, 2007. The Federal Bureau of Prisons sought halfway house services in El Paso County, Texas. The award went to Dismas Charities, Inc. Cornell fought a weak mark on its bid. It said the mark broke the call's score points. It said talks should have flagged the mark.

GAO denied the protest. The facts behind the mark sat inside the score points. So the mark was fair to give. The mark was no grave flaw in the bid. It did not block the bid from meeting the call or from a fair shot. Small flaws need not be raised in talks.
gao-gaoreports-b-316048:
A health aid letter is ruled a rule in this GAO opinion, B-316048, dated April 17, 2008. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services wrote to state health chiefs in 2007. The note dealt with the State Children's Health Insurance Program. That plan funds care for kids in poor homes. Two senators asked if the note is a rule under the Congressional Review Act.

GAO held that it is. The Review Act asks shops to send rules to Congress before they bite. It asks for a copy to the Comptroller General as well. The note must take that path before it can take hold. Form does not rule; a note with rule force is a rule.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-248:
Social Security Administration, GAO-05-248 of March 2, 2005, reviews a plan to help people on disability aid get back to work. The agency paid about $75 billion to about 8 million people ages 18 through 64 in 2003. Few of them used state rehab help or made it back to a job. A 1999 law made a new path: the Ticket program.

Each ticket works as a voucher for job help. Holders can take it to state rehab teams or to new approved work networks. Tickets rolled out in three waves from February 2002 to November 2003. GAO finds the plan's own groundwork thin; sharper plans could make it work, the title holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-348:
Military Personnel, GAO-05-348 of April 26, 2005, asks why troops still fall into cash traps in time of war. Trips to Iraq and Afghanistan strain the purse of each home left behind. Deep debt can cost a troop a security pass, draw blame, or end a career. Pay has risen and aid plans have grown. Yet young troops, most of all, still tell of cash woe.

GAO asks how far war trips drive that woe. It asks if a sound frame grades the aid plans in place. It asks if young troops get the cash craft class the rules demand. More acts are owed, the title says.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-548:
Joint training across the services is the aim of a Defense Department program reviewed in GAO report GAO-05-548, dated June 21, 2005. Modern operations mix commands, services, and civilian agencies more than ever. The Training Transformation Program is meant to ensure that forces meet joint work in training, not first in combat. Full operation is due by 2009. GAO gave an overview and flagged early management troubles.

The department has set clear leadership roles for the program. It has launched three linked efforts to train people, units, and staffs for joint missions.  The first full program check was due later in 2005. Two problems stand out early. Partners do not all grasp the vision behind the change in the same way. Winning their full buy-in will take steady contact and coordination. GAO said both points need continued focus as the network of training tools is built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-748:
Medicaid financing is the subject of GAO-05-748, a report from June 28, 2005. The program covered nearly 54 million low-income people. It cost $276 billion in fiscal year 2003. Some states hire consultants who get paid only if federal payments rise. GAO checked how wide that practice is, whether the claims fit the law, and how well the claims are watched.

GAO found that most states have used such consultants on a wide range of projects. Claims from those projects are not always in line with federal law or policy. That mismatch can weaken the program's fiscal integrity. State and federal oversight of the claims was limited. GAO urged tighter federal watch over this work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-148:
Lead in drinking water is the hazard behind GAO-06-148, a report issued on January 4, 2006. High lead levels in the District of Columbia's tap water in 2003 raised national concern. Lead leaches into water from corroded pipes and home plumbing. The Environmental Protection Agency's lead rule sets testing and treatment duties. GAO reviewed the agency's data on the rule and asked whether the rule itself needs change.

GAO also asked how much school and child care water gets tested for lead. Its findings point to gaps in the data the agency holds. Without timely, complete data, the agency cannot judge how well the rule works. GAO urged better data checks and tighter parts of the rule. It named lead monitoring, review of treatment changes, and plumbing standards. It also urged the agency to use existing data to gauge lead in school water.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-348:
War memorials abroad rest on careful books as well as stone. In GAO-06-348 (March 1, 2006), GAO audits the American Battle Monuments Commission for fiscal years 2005 and 2004. The Commission was created in 1923. It runs 24 American military cemeteries on foreign soil and 25 federal memorials, monuments, and markers.

GAO acted under 36 U.S.C. 2103. It judged whether the statements were reliable and controls were sound. GAO gave the statements a fair-presentation opinion, in all material respects. It also found the Commission kept effective control over reporting and legal compliance. Still, the audit notes weak points, such as controls over computer systems. Readers get the full audited accounts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-648:
Checks on doctors who treat veterans are examined in GAO report GAO-06-648, issued on May 25, 2006. The Department of Veterans Affairs must confirm that over 36,000 physicians in its facilities hold proper credentials. It also grants each doctor privileges that define what care the doctor may give. GAO reviewed files at seven medical facilities against selected credentialing and privileging rules.

GAO found that the files met all four credentialing requirements that were reviewed. The files also met four of the five privileging requirements. The fifth rule, using data on a doctor's past performance in privilege choices, was a problem at six of the seven facilities. GAO said that part of the process needs improvement to keep care safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-248:
At land border crossings, a fingerprint program was meant to confirm who enters the country. GAO found strain at those posts in GAO-07-248, a report dated December 6, 2006. The US-VISIT program records foreign visitors at air, sea, and land entry points. It checks prints against watch lists and logs arrivals. GAO visited 21 land crossings on both borders. It reviewed entry setup, exit plans, and links to other border programs.

Entry screening stood at 154 of 170 land crossings, GAO found. Border officers said the prints improved identity checks. But computers slowed or froze at 12 of the 21 sites visited. At 9 of those sites, staff did not always report the faults. Exit tracking at land borders was still untested and undefined. A planned shift from 2 prints to 10 could crowd small, aging posts. GAO urged better fault reporting and clear measures of impact.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-48:
Military families who skip the managed care plan can struggle to find a doctor, and GAO-07-48, dated December 22, 2006, looks at their access. The Defense Department runs care through TRICARE. Members who enroll use contractor-built provider networks. Those who do not must rely on a fee-for-service option or a preferred provider plan. Some reported that civilian doctors would not take them on.

A fiscal year 2004 defense law told GAO to study the issue. GAO read the department's survey results and spoke with officials and contractors. It traced how access gets measured for the nonenrolled group. It listed what blocks doctors from joining in and what fixes were under way. It also checked whether the department had done the steps the law required. The report maps a quiet gap in a huge health system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-448:
Missile defense progress is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-448, issued March 14, 2008. The Ballistic Missile Defense System is the Defense Department's largest research program, funded at $8 billion to nearly $10 billion a year.
