GAO must grade the Missile Defense Agency's work each year. Block 2006, the second block of the build, closed in December 2007.

The agency fielded more gear, including land-based interceptors and upgraded Aegis ships, and met most test goals. But fewer assets were fielded than planned, and block costs rose by at least $1 billion. Work pushed into later blocks hides the full cost, and too few tests exist to prove how the fielded system performs. GAO recommended full block cost estimates with outside checks, and richer tests. The department agreed on cost estimating and partly on tests.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-548:
Older workers and one-stop career centers are studied in GAO report GAO-08-548, dated April 21, 2008. Americans age 55 and older will reach 30 percent of the population by 2025, and more will keep working than in past generations. The Labor Department points to one-stop centers as the link between these workers and employers.

GAO surveyed one-stops across the country. About 71 percent took more than one step to link older workers and employers outside the senior community service program. Staff training for helping older workers ranked among the most effective steps. The department runs outreach such as National Employ Older Workers Week but knows little about results. GAO also warns that federal performance measures may discourage centers from serving older workers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-748:
For 11 years, auditors could not give the full U.S. government books a clean verdict. GAO-08-748, dated June 17, 2008, details the control flaws behind that streak, based on the audit of the fiscal year 2007 statements. It also tracks fixes promised in past years.

Agencies still cannot square shared deals between each other. The combined books do not always match agency books, stay in balance, or follow standard rules. Gaps between the stated deficit and agency records go unexplained. GAO adds 10 new fix proposals. The Treasury and the budget office mostly agreed with the findings.
hume-enquiry-human-understanding-1748:
David Hume published An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding in 1748 in London. Hume, a Scottish philosopher, recast the hard arguments of his earlier Treatise in a clearer, shorter form. The Enquiry became his most read statement of empiricism, the view that knowledge rests on experience.

Hume argued that we never see causes, only events following each other, yet the mind expects the pattern to hold. He tested miracles, free will, and belief in God against that standard and found them wanting. His calm, polite style carried radical doubts. The book still sets the terms for debates on reason, belief, and what the mind can know.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
Georg Ebers turns to a servant's loyalty in Volume 6 of In the Fire of the Forge, his romance of old Nuremberg. Ebers lets Biberli, the faithful attendant of Heinz Schorlin, argue against his master's newest plan. A friar has just left, and Heinz is again drawn toward entering a monastery, a step Biberli fears more than any battlefield danger in this volume.

Chapter V gives the servant a blunt, funny case for marriage instead. Even a wife far below Heinz in rank, he argues, would keep his master in the world where he belongs. He recalls the knight dancing with Eva Ortlieb while onlookers praised the pair. Then his tone hardens: respectable people now point at the Ortlieb sisters and repeat a scoundrel's slander. Honor, love, and gossip pull the knight three ways.
israeli-declaration-independence-1948:
Israel's Declaration of Independence was proclaimed in Tel Aviv on May 14, 1948, and the hosted text is the declaration in full. It opens with the Jewish people's bond to the land. There they were born as a nation, and there their faith and culture took shape. Exiled by force, they kept faith with the land through long centuries abroad.

In modern times they returned in growing numbers. Pioneers revived the Hebrew tongue and built towns, farms, and a working economy. The text grounds the new state in the United Nations vote of November 1947 calling for a Jewish state. It declares Israel open to Jewish return and promises full equality to all who live there. It also calls on Arab neighbors to choose peace. War began the next day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-jacob: Aaron ben Jacob ben David haKohen, a French ritualist of Narbonne, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He suffered in the expulsion of the Jews in 1306 and emigrated to Majorca. There, before 1327, he composed Orhot Hayyim, the Paths of Life, a ritual work of great merit. Its first part treats daily prayers, the Sabbath, and the festivals. The entry calls it a compilation of Talmudic laws rather than an original system. Ethical and doctrinal chapters, absent from Jacob ben Asher's code, add to its value.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abodah-zarah-id:
'Abodah Zarah, meaning idolatrous worship, names a treatise of the Mishnah, Tosefta, and both Talmuds. It has five chapters in the order Nezikin. Its laws govern how Jews should act toward idolatry and idolaters.

Rules bar trade with heathens near their festivals and ban selling goods for idol use. Other rules guard against cruel shows and risky contact. Stories sit among the laws, such as elders in Rome asked why God does not destroy idols. The Gemara adds history, ethics, and much detail on Greek and Roman life. It also preserves accounts of Jewish martyrs under Hadrian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-bar-hil: Abraham bar Hillel was one of the few Hebrew poets in Egypt. He lived in the second half of the twelfth century. His Megillah Zutta, finished in 1176, tells a key episode of Jewish history in Egypt in fine rimed prose. Poems at the start and end show him to be a skilled maker of verses. The entry stresses the work's worth because so little writing by medieval Egyptian Jews survives. It came to light only in 1896, in the Cairo genizah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-nior: Abraham of Niort was a Talmudic commentator in France in the second half of the fourteenth century. Niort now lies in the department of Deux Sèvres. Isaac de Lattes, in his chronicle Sha'are Zion, calls him a notable scholar and a commentator on the Talmud. His home town's name is spelled in several forms in Hebrew writing. Gross identifies those forms with Niort, the Latin Niortium, and the entry rests on Gross's Gallia Judaica.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adret-13848: Adret was a noted Spanish-Jewish family. Its men are known from the thirteenth to the fifteenth century. Spanish texts write the name Adret in all cases. Some writers give Adereth, and the entry says that form is wrong. The name most likely comes from a place. It may be the village of Les Adrets in France, or a town in Spain. The list of kin runs to nine men. Two took new names at forced baptism in Barcelona in 1391. One was a victim of the Valencia court in 1487.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-ahai-b-raba: Aha b. Raba, a Babylonian amora and son of Raba b. Joseph, was a contemporary of Amemar II. and of Ashi, and died in 419. During the last five years of his life he filled the rectorate of the academy at Pumbedita. The entry records this career in brief, naming his father, his contemporaries, and his final office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akrish-isaac-b-:
Isaac b. Abraham Akrish was a scholar, book-lover, and editor. He was born in Spain about 1489 and died after 1578. He was among the exiles of 1492 who settled first at Naples. Driven out again in 1495, he wandered for years, though lame in both legs. At Cairo he tutored the children of David ibn Abi Zimra for about ten years.

His library was seized at Candia in 1553, the year of the burning of the Talmud. At Constantinople he at last found rest, under rich patrons. There, about 1577, he edited two sets of old documents. They hold the history of the exilarch Bostanai, letters between Hasdai ibn Shaprut and the Khazar king, and Profiat Duran's sly letter, long misread as a defense of Christianity. The entry credits Akrish with saving several such treasures of Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-micha:
Michael Solomon Alexander was the first Anglican bishop of Jerusalem. He was born of Jewish parents at Schönlanke, in Posen, in May 1799. He died at Belbeis, in Egypt, on November 23, 1845. His training was strictly orthodox. At sixteen he was teaching Talmud and German. In 1820 he moved to England as a private tutor. He married a Miss Levy of Plymouth in 1821.

Reading the New Testament led him to baptism, on June 22, 1825, at Plymouth. There he had served as reader to the Hebrew congregation. In Dublin he taught Hebrew and was ordained in 1827. He then worked for a society that sought to convert the Jews. From 1832 to 1841 he held the Hebrew chair at King's College, London. In 1841 he was made bishop at Jerusalem. He died of heart disease on a journey home, after nearly four years in the post.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkalai-moses-b: Moses ben David Alkalai wrote Hebrew school books in Turkey. He lived in the nineteenth century. With his father David he turned a Hebrew history into Judaeo-Spanish. That book came out at Belgrade in 1859. He wrote a work on the laws of meals that same year. A Hebrew grammar by him came out in 1860. A book on arithmetic followed in 1867.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amadia-amadiah-: Amadia is a town in Asiatic Turkey north of Mosul. It sits in the vilayet of Bagdad. The entry calls it the birth town of David Alroy. He was the false messiah of an earlier entry. In 1163 the town held about a thousand Jewish families. That count comes from a book of sorrows. In 1895 the town held 1,900 Jews. They owned about 150 houses there. Their trade dealt chiefly in gall-nuts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anab-grape-1448: Anab is a city in the hills of south Judea. Its name means grape in Hebrew. The book of Joshua lists it in Judah's share. That list is found in chapter fifteen. From Anab Joshua drove out the Anakim. That deed is told in chapter eleven. The town keeps the same name to this day. One work on the land of Palestine is cited.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anna-in-greek-w:
Anna is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Hannah, and the entry covers two women who bear it. The first is the wife of Tobit, of his own kin. The entry notes that pious Jews of old praised marriage within the kin as a merit.

The second Anna is the prophetess of Luke, chapter 2. Daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, she had been a widow for eighty-four years after seven years of marriage. She spent night and day in the Temple in prayer and fasting. When the infant Jesus was brought in, she gave thanks for the hope of Jerusalem's redemption. The entry pairs her story with Simeon's, told just before it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apollonius-or-a:
Apollonius Molon was a Greek rhetorician and anti-Jewish writer who flourished in the first century before the common era. His father's name, Molon, sets him apart from an older namesake, Apollonius Malachos. Around 75 B.C. he was still praised as a master of speech.

Born at Alabanda in Caria, he moved to Rhodes, where Cicero and Julius Caesar both sat among his pupils. Josephus, though, treats him only as a leading and harmful foe of the Jews. At Rhodes he took up the Jew-hating ideas of the Stoic Posidonius, the entry says. From there he spread wild charges, that Jews worshiped an ass in their Temple and killed a fattened Greek each year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aryeh-loeb-ben-:
Aryeh Loeb ben Asher ranks here among the most eminent Talmudists of his age. Born in Lithuania at the close of the seventeenth century, he died at Metz on June 23, 1785. He served as rabbi in Pinsk and then led the academy in Minsk. In 1765 Metz, then one of Europe's great congregations, called him as rabbi, and a royal decree confirmed the choice in October 1766.

One quarrel marks his Metz years. At Pentecost the congregation customarily paused the Torah reading for the hymn Akdamut. The rabbi ordered the reader to go on, trustees defied him, and a violent scene drove him from the synagogue. He never entered it again except to preach four times a year, yet he kept the post until death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-astarte-worship:
Astarte was the Phoenician form of an old Semitic mother-goddess. In Arabia she was Athtar, and in Babylonia Ishtar. The Old Testament calls her Ashtoreth. Solomon is said to have built a high place for her near Jerusalem. Josiah removed it in his reform. At Zidon she was the chief god of the city, paired with Baal.

Wherever she was worshiped, Astarte was a goddess of fertility and sexual love. The entry asks whether her worship among the Hebrews was always a foreign import. It notes how seldom and how vaguely the Old Testament names the cult. Jeremiah and Ezekiel still attest forms of it in their day. The prophets' campaign against Baal and Astarte, the entry says, had a deep effect on the moral life of Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aussee-2148:
Aussee is a town in Moravia, Austria. It had a Jewish community in the seventeenth century. In 1622 Emperor Ferdinand II. gave the town to Prince Karl of Lichtenstein, on terms that only Catholics might live there. Even so, a synagogue was ordered built in 1688 by the dean of Müglitz.

That synagogue was destroyed in 1722, after a strange clash. A Catholic priest entered during the eve of Yom Kippur service and began a mission sermon. The congregation's officers put him out when he would not leave. He charged them with assault. After a long lawsuit the court ordered the synagogue torn down and none built in its place. Three men were branded with a hot iron and exiled. A fourth, aged seventy-four, was set to work on a Catholic church. Only in 1783 could the Jews build a true synagogue again.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-shalisha-2: Baal-shalisha is a place named in the second book of Kings and in the Talmud. Eusebius took it for Baithsarisa, fifteen Roman miles north of Lydda. The entry calls that match uncertain. Much favors instead the ruins of Serisiyyah, on the western side of the Ephraim hills. Another candidate is Kefr Thilth, somewhat to the northeast. One firm fact comes from the Talmud. Fruit ripened earlier at Baal-shalisha than anywhere else in Palestine, a point that mattered for the rules on first fruits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bagdad-2348:
Bagdad, capital of the Turkish vilayet of that name, stands on both sides of the Tigris in lower Mesopotamia. Arabic tradition says the Abbassid calif Abu Ja'far Manṣur founded it in the middle of the eighth century. The entry argues that he rebuilt an older Persian town, since a Babylonian Bagdad is named in the Talmud. Jews settled there freely and soon formed a quarter of their own, near Sura and Pumbedita.

The long entry follows the community through califs, bans on dress and riding, and times of favor at court. It notes Karaite disputes in the city streets and the siege by Tamerlane in 1400. Travelers' reports close the account: Benjamin II. found 3,000 Jewish families in 1847, with nine synagogues and trade with India largely in Jewish hands. Local tombs tied to Joshua, Ezekiel, and Ezra end the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-banoczi-joseph-:
Joseph Bánóczi was a Hungarian scholar born at Szt. Gál, in the county of Veszprém, on July 4, 1849. He studied at Budapest, Vienna, Berlin, Göttingen, and Leipsic, then in Paris and London. In 1878 he became a privat-docent of philosophy at Budapest. He joined the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in 1879 and the royal board of education in 1892.

Bánóczi also served the Jewish community for years. He taught at the Budapest Jewish Theological Seminary from 1877 to 1893 and led the normal school for teachers from 1887. With W. Bacher he helped save the schools of the Transylvanian Sabbatarians who had turned to Judaism in 1868. His books include a study of Kant on space and time, Hungarian versions of Lewes, Schopenhauer, and Kant, and, with Bacher, the "Hungaro-Jewish Review" of 1884-90.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barrientos-isaa: Isaac Barrientos is named only as an author, otherwise unknown. The entry states plainly that he is certainly not the same man as Daniel Levi de Barrios, with whom he might be confused. His one recorded work is "Theologia Natural Contra los Atheos, Epicureos, y Sectarios del Tiempo," printed at The Hague in 1725. Nothing is given of his birth, home, or death. The whole notice rests on the single bibliographic record cited from Kayserling's bibliography of Spanish-Portuguese Jewish authors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-peter-pere:
Peter Beer was an Austrian school reformer born on Feb. 19, 1758, at Neubydzow, in Bohemia. He died at Prague on Nov. 8, 1838. Trained in Bible and Talmud, and unusually in German and Latin too, he began teaching at age twenty-one.

At Prague's Jewish school from 1811, Beer rebuilt how Hebrew, Bible, and religion were taught. The entry places him well ahead of his time as a backer of deep reform. His textbooks on Bible history and religion served Jewish schools for years, in edition after edition and in several tongues. One of his later books was a prayer book meant for educated women of the Jewish faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ii-j-j:
Benjamin II, whose real name was Joseph Israel, was a Rumanian traveler born in Moldavia in 1818. He died at London on May 3, 1864. After losing his small fortune in the lumber trade, he took the name of the famed Benjamin of Tudela. Late in 1844 he set out to search for the Lost Ten Tribes.

His road ran through Egypt, Palestine, Persia, India, and Afghanistan, and later to Algeria and Morocco. His books tell of eight years in the East and three years in America. Critics doubted his tales, but scholars of rank backed his plain and truthful account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berenice-former: Berenice, once called Hesperides, was a city of the Cyrenaic Pentapolis in North Africa. Jews settled there, as in the other towns of Cyrenaica, from the time of Ptolemy the First. Though they held the rights of citizens, they formed a body of their own. Unlike other places, they had no ethnarch at their head. They ran their affairs through their own archons instead. A Greek inscription dated to 13 B.C. names the nine Jewish archons of the city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-max-p: Max Bernstein, born May 13, 1854, at Fürth in Bavaria, was a German author who wrote under the pseudonym Silas Marner while practising law at Munich. The entry lists his comedies, among them "Cœur-Dame," "Mein Neuer Hut," and "Ritter Blaubart," and his dramas "Dagmar," "Ruth," and "Gold." It also names his short story collections and notes that, though popular with general readers, his works drew little notice from critics and literary historians. His wife was the author Elsa Bernstein.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beziers-formerl:
Béziers is a town of France in Hérault. Jews lived there from very early times. Councils of 506 already show Languedoc communities. Under the Visigoths they suffered violent persecution. Conditions eased after 732 under the Carlovingians. The viscounts of Béziers treated Jews kindly. Jews even held public office as bailiffs.

In 1160 a bishop ended a cruel Holy Week custom. Stoning Jews gave way to a yearly payment. The thirteenth century brought darker days. Béziers was stormed in 1209 during the Albigensian crusade. Two hundred Jews died in that massacre. Later councils added fresh restrictions. The entry also names Béziers' many scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-biztha-3348: Biztha was one of the seven eunuchs of Ahasuerus. Esther's first chapter is his only setting. The king commanded the seven to fetch Queen Vashti. She was to be brought before him. That is the whole of the entry's fact. It is a single sentence long. No other deed or fate is recorded for Biztha.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bocara-abraham-: Abraham b. Moses Bocara was rabbi of the community of Leghorn Jews at Tunis. He died in 1879. His book Ben Abraham treats hard problems in religious law. A relative, Jacob Bocara, had it printed at Leghorn in 1882. The entry adds only that several other writings by him survive in manuscript form. It gives no account of his life, birth, or training.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonsenyor-astru: Astruc Bonsenyor was a physician in Barcelona. He was a grandson of Astruc Bonsenyor, dragoman of Jaime I. of Aragon. He was also the father of Judah Bonsenyor. In the year 1334 he was granted the privileges his grandfather had enjoyed. That is the whole entry: three short facts of family, trade, and royal favor, with no works, birth date, or death date given for this later Astruc at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bratzlav-or-bra:
Bratzlav, or Braslavl, is a town in the government of Podolia, Russia. It stands on the right bank of the southern Bug. It was founded in the fourteenth century and passed among Poland, Lithuania, Russia, and the Tatars.

In 1479 Tatar conquerors slew more than 600 inhabitants there, among them 400 Jews. In 1551 local Jews defended the town bravely against the Crimean khan. The worst year was 1648, when Chmielnicki massacred all the Jews of Bratzlav. Later plots brought fresh cruelties on the town's Jews. In 1895 Jews numbered 2,460 there, 39.2 per cent of the whole population by the entry's count.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bury-st-edmunds:
Bury St. Edmunds was a Suffolk town built around a monastery whose ruins still stand. Under Abbot Hugh, from 1173 to 1180, the abbey fell deep into debt to Jewish lenders. The sum passed 3,025 pounds, and the sacristan William guarded Jewish deeds and money in wartime. A blood charge arose there in 1181 over a boy named Robert.

Abbot Samson, who took office in 1182, cleared the abbey debt within twelve years. On March 18, 1190, fifty seven Jews were slaughtered at Bury. Samson then won their expulsion from the town. The entry ends with Moyse Hall, a building once thought a synagogue. A careful inquiry, it says, found no good evidence for that claim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-camel-3948:
Camel is the well known ruminant native to Asia and Africa. Its Hebrew name, gamal, matches forms in Assyrian, Aramaic, Arabic, and other tongues. Bible passages place camels chiefly with the desert peoples around Israel. They formed part of the patriarchs' wealth and served as beasts of burden. David kept a special officer over his camels, named Obil.

Israelites were barred from eating camel, as Leviticus and Deuteronomy state. The entry collects Talmud notes on camel teeth, hair, and habits, plus Aramaic proverbs about the animal. One proverb says the camel asked for horns and lost its ears instead. A final point defends the gospel saying about a camel and a needle's eye against the reading rope.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carmi-4048: Carmi was the title of a small Hebrew review issued at Adrianople. It ran for some months in 1882 under the editorship of Baruch Mitrani. The hosted entry is very brief. It gives the place, the year, and the editor, and it cites Franco on the Jews of the Ottoman Empire. It does not describe the review's contents, its writers, or why it stopped, so readers learn the basic facts of its short life and nothing more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-catarivas-shema: Shemariah Catarivas was a Talmudic writer of the eighteenth century. He came first from Tiberias. In 1750 he went to Tunis as an alms collector, after a stay in Algiers, and settled there. He won a name for scholarship and piety. He was a close friend of Abraham Cohen Baberrebi, an old rabbi of Tunis. That rabbi's grandson printed Catarivas' Zeker Ẓaddiḳ at Leghorn in 1843. The work comments on the first two orders of the Mishnah. Responsa by Catarivas also appear in another Leghorn volume from 1842.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coen-josef-di-m:
Josef di Michele Coen was one of the Jewish boys of Rome baptized under Pope Pius IX. Born in 1854, he was apprenticed to a shoemaker in 1864. Sent to deliver shoes at a priest's house, he was seized and dragged to the Casa dei Neofiti and held there for baptism. Papal officials refused to give him back despite his father's protests.

France's ambassador protested hard, but Rome answered that the boy chose conversion himself. He was baptized on Sept. 29, 1864, with a string of new names. His sister died from the shock, his mother lost her mind, and his father fled Rome. Only in 1870, after the papal government fell, was Coen freed and returned to his mother at Leghorn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-colmar-german-k:
Colmar, chief town of Upper Alsace, Germany, held a large Jewish community at the start of the thirteenth century. The town's rulers favored the Jews, who kept their own quarter and a synagogue, lost to fire in 1279. When Emperor Rudolph I besieged Colmar in 1285, citizens blamed the Jews and drove them out on that false charge.

Meir of Rothenburg, the town's rabbi, was held for a ransom of 1,500 marks and refused to let it be paid, dying in prison. Jews returned, then faced a ritual murder charge in 1292. The year 1348 proved fatal, as the Black Death charge found believers on the council. Later sections trace tight rules on Jewish residence, a banishment in 1512, and slow return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cordova-4648:
Cordova, a city in Andalusia, Spain, had Jewish residents as early as the eighth century. They lived in a quarter called the Juderia. One gate, Bab al-Yahud, later became the Almodovar gate. Jews traded there in silks and slaves. Under Moorish rule they shared in the life of the academy, studying philosophy, grammar, math, botany, and music beside Moors.

The article follows the community through its peak and its fall. It names the diplomat Ḥasdai ibn Shaprut and describes a synagogue with Hebrew verses and an Arabic dedication. Later sections cover decline and expulsion. Readers get a rich city portrait drawn from chronicles and local records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cremieux-mordec: Mordecai ben Abraham Crémieux was rabbi at Aix, in Provence. He was born at Carpentras in 1749. He died on May 22, 1825. His one named work is Ma'amar Mordekai, the Treatise of Mordecai. It comments on the Oraḥ Ḥayyim part of the Shulḥan 'Aruk. The book came out in two parts at Leghorn in 1784. The entry is brief. It gives his town, his book, and his dates, then lists six standard sources where more can be sought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dagobert-4848: Dagobert was a king of France who reigned from 602 to 638. About 629 he decreed that Jews who would not convert by a set date must leave his lands or die. A Jewish historian records that many changed their faith and large numbers were slain. The entry questions the story's scale. Cassel reads it as a local persecution, aimed at certain persons. It was not even carried out with rigor. A council at Rheims a year later simply renewed older canons on Jewish matters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-jacob: Jacob's son David was rabbi of Szerezow, in the government of Grodno, Russia, and one of the most influential rabbis of Lithuania at the end of the eighteenth century. He wrote "Ḥomot Yerushalayim" (The Walls of Jerusalem), published at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1807. The book is a commentary on one part of the Shulḥan Aruk code, covering the Oraḥ Ḥayyim section from its beginning through the laws about tefillin, the phylacteries worn in prayer. The short entry rests on three printed catalogues and biographical collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deiches-or-daic:
Deiches, also spelled Daiches, is a Polish Jewish family name known since the seventeenth century. Members of the family live in Russia and Austria. The entry warns that family ties between them can be fixed in only a few cases. Since many came from Cracow, that city may be the family's home place.

The article then gives short lives of its leading members. Eliezer Deiches, born at Wilna in 1797, served as dayyan there from age twenty-nine until his death in 1881. He eased ritual burdens for others while living strictly himself. Elijah Judah Deiches led large schools in Lithuania, then moved to Jerusalem. Israel Ḥayyim Deiches, born in 1850, studied Talmud at Kovno.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-simon-5:
Simon Deutsch was an Austrian Hebraist and revolutionist who died at Constantinople on March 24, 1877. As a young man in Vienna he studied Hebrew and, with A. Kraft, catalogued the Hebrew manuscripts of the Imperial Library. In 1848 he sided with the revolution. When it collapsed, he escaped to France.

In Paris, Deutsch built a successful business career. After the fall of the Commune he was denounced as a Communist, arrested, and held in the Orangerie prison at Versailles. Only the Austrian ambassador's efforts saved his life. He died at Constantinople while there on business, though his body was buried in Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dobsewitch-dobs:
Abraham Baer Dobsewitch, son of Joseph Ezra, was a Russian Hebraist and exegete born at Pinsk on Oct. 17, 1843. At thirteen he had already written a commentary on the Canticles. He taught Hebrew at Yekaterinoslav from 1861. He died at New York on Jan. 14, 1900.

At Kiev, Dobsewitch tutored the sons of Brodski and other wealthy families. He moved to the United States in 1891 and wrote for Hebrew and Yiddish papers there. His chief book, Ha-Mezaref, printed at Odessa in 1870, gives rational readings of Aggadah passages. Later books attacked rival critics by name. Manuscripts on the Masorah and on Samaritan texts stayed unpublished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dubnow-simon-se:
Simon Dubnow was a Russo-Jewish historian born at Mstislavl, in the government of Mohilev, in 1860. He finished district school in 1877. Moving from town to town, he tutored for a living. In 1880 he settled in St. Petersburg and began to publish.

Dubnow wrote first for Russki Yevrei and Razsvyet, then moved to Voskhod in 1882. His studies of Shabbethai Zebi and of the Frankists appeared there in 1883. A long history of Hasidism ran in Voskhod from 1888 to 1893. He also gathered unpublished papers from community record books. Since 1890 he has lived at Odessa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-b-menah: Eleazar ben Menahem was a Palestinian scholar of the fourth century. He belonged to the fourth amoraic generation. Few rulings and still fewer homilies carry his name. The entry gives two of his readings of Scripture. On a psalm that speaks of God's Edens, he notes the plural form. Each pious soul, he says, has its own place in Eden. On a verse in Genesis he reads Abraham's road back from Egypt. Abraham retraced his path, Eleazar says, to pay the debts he owed from the trip down.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-escapa-also-jos:
Joseph ben Saul Escapa was rabbi of Smyrna in the first half of the seventeenth century. He was probably born at Uskup, in European Turkey, the place behind his name. He first led the rabbinate and school at Salonica. At Smyrna he shared the post, then held it alone after his colleague died. David Conforte reported seeing him at about one hundred years old.

Escapa taught Shabbethai Zebi, and later excommunicated him. His chief work, Rosh Yosef, comments in detail on the four Turim of Jacob ben Asher. One part appeared at Smyrna in 1658, another in 1659. His responsa were printed at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1709 as Teshubot Rosh Yosef.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezbon-5948: Ezbon is a name given to two men in the entry, and nothing beyond their family places is stated. The first was a son of Gad and father of one of the Gadite families, from Genesis. In Numbers the same slot reads Ozni instead. The second was a son of Bela, son of Benjamin, from First Chronicles. No deeds, dates, or places are attached to either man. The entry is a short genealogy note, fixing two family links and one clash between the lists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-feder-tobias-gu:
Tobias Gutmann Feder was a Polish poet and grammarian born at Przedborz about 1760. He died at Tarnopol, Galicia, in 1817. He worked in turn as preacher, proofreader, cantor, and teacher. He admired Elijah Wilna deeply and, like him, fought Hasidism and mysticism with a sharp pen. One judge named him Ben Ze'eb's heir as a grammarian.

His Bayit Ne'eman, an essay on truth, appeared at Berlin in 1794. Kol Nehi mourns Elijah Wilna in 1798. Other works attack modern Bible criticism and a rival's Proverbs version. Zemir Arizim mocks the Hasidim and their wonder rabbis. His Purim parody in the Zohar's style, Zohar Hadash le-Purim, shows his gift for mimicry. Letters and poems of his were printed at Lemberg in 1877, long after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischer-karl-61:
Karl Fischer, a Christian censor of Hebrew books at Prague, was born at Lichtenstadt, Bohemia, on July 5, 1755. He died at Prague on Jan. 22, 1844. He rose from assistant to successor of the imperial censor Leopold Tirsch. He knew the Semitic languages and their writings well. That shows in his notes to a rabbinic dictionary of 1818 and to a Rashi translation of 1833.

He also wrote to Rabbi Eleazar Flekeles in Hebrew. His fair dealing shows most in his book on the Talmud, issued at Vienna in 1883. He also served for a time as librarian at Prague.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-forty-the-numbe:
Forty, next to seven, is the number that occurs most often in the Bible. In Talmudic writing it often serves as a round number. It can stand for the vague word many, and so it became a symbolical number. Forty years were seen as the height of a man's life. From that, forty years came to stand for a generation. 

Forty days of rain brought the Flood, and forty days embalmed Jacob. Moses went without food on Mount Horeb for forty days, and so did Elijah on his wanderings. The spies spent forty days in Canaan. Forty years cover the desert wandering, the reigns of David and Solomon, and Philistine oppression. In the Talmud, forty is the age of reason. Hillel, Johanan ben Zakkai, and Akiba all began their work at forty. Each is given a life of 120 years, three forties in one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fresco-moses-63: Moses Fresco was a Turkish Talmudist born at Constantinople in 1780. He died there in 1850. In 1839 he followed Samuel Ḥayyim as chief rabbi of the Ottoman empire. He wrote a collection of responsa printed at Salonica in 1818. Its title means the hands of Moses. The entry says that book is much quoted by the rabbis of the East. The notice is very short and gives no other facts of his life or work. One short source line closes it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gedallah-6548:
Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan the scribe, came from a noble and godly house. Nebuchadnezzar made him governor of Palestine after the conquest. He set his seat at Mizpah. Scattered Jews soon gathered round him there. He urged them to stay loyal to Babylon, lay down arms, and rebuild their ruined towns through farm work.

Baalis, king of the Ammonites, plotted his fall. He sent Ishmael, of royal seed, to kill him. Johanan warned Gedaliah, but the governor would not believe it. At a feast Ishmael slew Gedaliah, the Chaldean guard, and the Jews with him. The remnant then fled to Egypt in fear. A fast in Tishri still marks his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ghazzati-nathan:
Nathan Benjamin Ghazzati, a Shabbethaian prophet born at Jerusalem in 1644, died at Sofia in 1680. He studied Talmud and Cabala under Jacob Hagis, then settled at Gaza. When Shabbethai Zebi came to Gaza, Ghazzati bound himself to the man claim. He called himself the risen Elijah, sent to clear the Messiah path.

In the spring of 1665 he foretold that the Messiah would come in glory the next year. He spread the fame by letters to great communities in Europe. Jerusalem rabbis banned him in 1666. At Venice in 1668 he was forced to confess in writing that his prophecies were made up. He kept up his work in secret all the same.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldfaden-abrah:
Abraham Goldfaden was a Hebrew and Yiddish poet. The entry calls him the founder of the Yiddish drama. He was born at Starokonstantinov, Russia, on July 12, 1840. He finished the Jitomir rabbinical school in 1866. He then taught in government schools for nine years. In 1875 he started a Yiddish humorous weekly at Lemberg.

His stage career began at Jassy in 1876. There his play "The Recruits" opened the first regular modern Yiddish theater. He built the stage himself and wrote the piece. He also composed its music and trained the actors. Russia banned Yiddish theater in 1883, ending his tours. His plays number about twenty-five. "Shulamit" and "Bar Kochba" are named the most popular.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gracian-zerahia:
Zerahiah ben Isaac ben Shealtiel Ḥen was a physician, philosopher, translator, and Hebraist. He flourished near the end of the thirteenth century. He was born at Barcelona or at Toledo. About 1277 he went to Rome. All his works were written there before 1290. His native tongue seems to have been Arabic.

He wrote philosophical commentaries on Proverbs and Job. The Proverbs work was finished Nov. 28, 1288. He also commented on hard passages of Maimonides' "Moreh." His translations from Arabic into Hebrew were many. They cover Aristotle's Physics, Metaphysics, and De Anima. They also cover Averroes, Avicenna, Al-Farabi, and Galen. Most were made for Shabbethai ben Solomon in 1284.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gunzburg-david-:
David Günzburg, Baron, was a Russian Orientalist and communal leader. He was born at Kamenetz-Podolsk on July 5, 1857. Tutors at home trained him, among them Adolph Neubauer and Senior Sachs. At twenty he took the candidate degree at St. Petersburg University. He studied Arabic poetry under Ahlwardt at Greifswald in 1879-80. He edited Moses ibn Ezra's "Tarshish" and wrote studies on metrics.

Günzburg championed Jewish art with zeal. With Stassov he published "L'Ornement Hébreu" in 1903, showing ornament from Syrian, African, and Yemenite manuscripts. His library ranked among Europe's largest private ones. It held many rare books and manuscripts. He served as trustee of the St. Petersburg community and on many learned and civic bodies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hahn-joseph-yus:
Joseph Yuspa Hahn, born at Frankfort-on-the-Main in the later sixteenth century, was a German rabbi who died there on April 3, 1637. His father Seligmann taught him well. The name Hahn came from the family house, "Zum rothen Hahn." His chief work, "Yosif Omeẓ," came out only in 1723.

That book treats prayer, the high points of religious life, schooling, charity, morals, and the civil calendar, all in a popular style. On teaching, Hahn holds that a child must learn at its own pace and grasp, and that Bible, not Talmud, suits a child unfit for deep study. The book also tells of the Fettmilch riots, the Jews' expulsion from Frankfort in 1614, and their return in 1616. Hahn founded a burial society and served as acting rabbi when the post stood empty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hammerstein-osc:
Oscar Hammerstein, born at Berlin on May 8, 1848, was an American theatrical manager. Schooled at Berlin, he emigrated in March 1863 and settled in New York. He made cigars, then turned to journalism as editor of the "United States Tobacco Journal." He also invented cigar-making machinery that changed parts of the trade. In 1883 he entered the theater as manager of the old Thalia.

From there he built or ran a string of New York houses: the Harlem Opera House, the Columbus, the Manhattan Opera House, the Olympia, the Criterion, the Victoria, and the Belasco. In 1903 he was building the Drury Lane Theater. He also wrote musical works of his own, among them the musical comedy "The Kohinor" of 1894 and the opera "Santa Maria" of 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harburger-heinr:
Heinrich Harburger, born at Bayreuth in Bavaria on Oct. 2, 1851, was a German jurist. He studied at the gymnasium in his home town and at the University of Munich. He took his doctor of law degree there. He then rose through the Munich courts as judge and as state attorney.

In 1896 he became an honorary professor at Munich. In 1899 he joined the court of appeals as a senior judge. The entry notes that he was the first Jew in Germany to serve as attorney at a court of appeals. He wrote on criminal law and on gifts in law, and he belonged to the Institute of International Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hawk-7348: Hawk renders a Hebrew word for a bird listed among the unclean birds in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. The term may cover any of the smaller day-hunting birds of prey. Such birds are common in Palestine. The entry names two kinds of kestrel as very common there. It also names the hobby and the Eleonora falcon. In Job, the hawk spreads its wings toward the south. That line points to the travels of smaller migrant birds. A Talmud note says the hawk kills small birds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hess-michael-76:
Michael Hess, born in Stadt-Lengsfeld on April 9, 1782, was a German educator and author, and brother of Mendel Hess. Trained for the rabbinate at Fürth, he went to Frankfort in 1804. There he taught the young Baron James von Rothschild.

In Oct. 1806 Hess became principal of the Philanthropin, a new Jewish school at Frankfort. He held that post for forty-nine years. He also preached at the school hall and backed Jewish rights and radical reform. His pamphlets treated religious teaching, moral training in early childhood, habit, and honor as a motive in education. He died at Frankfort on Feb. 26, 1860.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirschberg-erns: Ernst Hirschberg, born March 8, 1859, at Königsberg, East Prussia, was a German statistician. Educated in his home town, he graduated in 1882. Soon after, he joined Berlin's city statistical office. He rose there to assistant director in 1902 and director in 1903. He also headed the statistical bureau of Charlottenburg. The government gave him the title of professor. His listed works treat worker insurance, old-age insurance, bread price figures, the social state of Berlin's working classes, and jobless insurance with poor relief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-honig-israel-ed:
Israel Edler von Hönigsberg, born at Kuttenplan, Bohemia, in Oct. 1724, was an Austrian tobacco maker. He was the first Austrian Jew to be ennobled, the entry notes. Son of a poor merchant, he learned Bible and Talmud from his father. At fifteen he had to join the family business.

On trade trips Hönig learned the tobacco business, then little known in Austria. In 1752 his family took the Prague tobacco lease and spread it to several provinces. War contracts brought him two imperial patent letters. In 1783 he gave up his contract early at Joseph II's wish and took state posts. Hereditary nobility came in 1789. He died at Vienna on Jan. 19, 1808.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hurwitz-hyman-7:
Hyman Hurwitz was a professor of Hebrew and author born in 1770 who died in 1844. A native of Poland, he mastered Bible and Talmud at home. He then moved to England and picked up English fast. Christians hired him to teach in an academy, where he added science and classics.

Friends helped him open a school for Jewish youth, the Highgate Academy, in 1799. His Introduction to Hebrew Grammar appeared in 1806, and a fuller grammar ran to a third edition in 1841. His Hebrew Tales drew from the ancient sages and spread into many tongues. He left teaching in 1821. A few years later he took the Hebrew chair at University College, London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-ghayyat-isa:
Isaac ben Judah ibn Ghayyat was a Spanish rabbi, Bible commentator, philosopher, and liturgical poet born at Lucena in 1038. He died at Cordova in 1089 and was buried at Lucena. Some call him the teacher of Isaac Alfasi, others his fellow pupil. His own pupils included his son Judah and Moses ibn Ezra.

After Joseph ha-Nagid died in 1066, Ibn Ghayyat took his place as rabbi of Lucena and held it until death. He wrote a handbook of festival law, later printed as Gates of Joy. His note on Ecclesiastes survives only in quotes. His greatest work was in liturgical poetry. His hymns fill the prayer book of Tripoli under the title Lips of Song.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-8148:
Isaac, second patriarch, was the child of a miracle: Sarah, long childless, was ninety at his birth and Abraham a hundred. His name means laughter, for both parents had laughed at the promise. Circumcised at eight days, he was bound on the altar at Moriah and spared when a ram was offered instead. At forty he married Rebekah, and after twenty childless years her twins Esau and Jacob were born.

Famine drove him to Gerar, where he passed Rebekah off as his sister, then prospered at farming until the Philistines, envying him, stopped up his father's wells and drove him out. Rabbinic tradition adds that God stamped Abraham's features on Isaac's face, ending slanders about his paternity, and credits Isaac with instituting the afternoon prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-iturea-8348:
Iturea is the Greek name of a province drawn from Jetur, a son of Ishmael in Genesis. The province itself is named only once in Scripture, in Luke. Its people, the Itureans, appear in Eupolemus as a tribe David conquered, and then in Strabo, Pliny, and Josephus. The entry places them in the Mount Lebanon region.

An inscription of about the year 6 tells how Aemilius Secundus was sent by Quirinius against the Itureans in Mount Lebanon. In 38 Caligula gave Iturea to Soemus, called king of the Itureans. When Soemus died in 49, his kingdom was folded into the province of Syria. After that, the Itureans served Rome as soldiers. Inscriptions name an Iturean wing and an Iturean cohort, each styled Augusta, in the Roman army.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-publicat:
Jewish Publication Society of America is a society for printing and spreading works that teach the principles of the Jewish religion. Based in Philadelphia, it was founded on June 3, 1888, the third body of its kind in the United States. Membership stood at 1,071 after the first year and reached 4,700 by 1903. Each member gets a copy of each book, and more than two hundred thousand volumes had gone out by then.

The society issues four or five books a year: histories, essays, poems, lives, and fiction, some turned from German, French, and Hebrew. Its biggest tasks named here are an English form of Graetz's History of the Jews in six volumes and a new English Bible, of which only the Psalms had appeared by 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jolowicz-heyman:
Heymann Jolowicz was a German preacher and author born on Aug. 23, 1816, at Santomischl in Posen. He studied at the University of Berlin and preached at Marienwerder, Kulm, and last at Köslin. He belonged to the far Reform party and spoke his views without fear. On retiring he settled at Königsberg and gave talks in 1864 and 1865 on the growth of Judaism and its services.

He also founded a bold Reform congregation with Sunday services and a German prayer order, though it did not last. As a writer he was busy from his student years. His works include a translated and noted Book of Kusari, poems of the holy past, a many-tongued book of eastern poetry, and a history of the Jews in Königsberg. He died at Königsberg on Jan. 31, 1875.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-jaco: Joseph ben Jacob of Pinczow was a Lithuanian Talmudist of the seventeenth century and a pupil of Zebi Hirsch of Lublin. In 1687 he became rabbi at Kosowi and was then called to Syeltzy. War drove him out in 1702, when Swedes held the area for a time, and he lived at Hamburg until 1706. He went back to Syeltzy, but sickness in 1710 forced him out again. At Berlin he published Rosh Yosef, his notes on several treatises of the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judenschule-sch: Judenschule, in Latin schola judorum, was the usual German word for a synagogue in medieval times. It seems to appear first in a charter of Frederick II of Austria in 1244. That charter set a fine of two talents for willful harm to a synagogue. The name school came from the old practice of using the synagogue as a schoolroom. Italian Jews likewise call the synagogue scuola, and Slavic lands use shkola. In England the Ashkenazim say shool. The sexton in some places was even called the school singer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalir-eleazar-m:
Eleazar Ḳalir was one of the first and most fruitful of the payyeṭanim, the poets who wrote hymns for the liturgy. He signs his father's name in the acrostics of his poems. His own home and dates long puzzled scholars, who placed him in Italy, Babylonia, or Palestine, at dates from the late seventh to the late tenth century.

The entry sorts the legends told about him, among them a tale that his teacher Yannai, jealous of his skill, caused his death by a scorpion. Modern study points to Palestine and, most likely, to the second half of the seventh century. Ḳalir filled the liturgy with hymns drawn from Talmud and Midrash, in a bold and dense Hebrew that later critics faulted. Still, his forms set the pattern for hymn writers for centuries, and more than 200 of his hymns stand in the festival prayer books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaulla-9248: Kaulla is the name of a Württemberg family. The entry praises its love of country and its good works. Jacob Raphael Kaulla heads the list. He was a German court banker born at Buchau. He died at Hechingen on May 1, 1810. In 1806 the king of Württemberg gave him and his kin full rights of citizenship. The grant honored the family's service to the land in hard times. A later member, Leopold von Kaulla, moved the family foundations to Stuttgart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kisch-9348:
Kisch is the name of a family of some distinction. It migrated in the sixteenth century from Chiesch in Bohemia. The founder of the family lived in Prague in the eighteenth century. Its members are now spread throughout Europe.

Abraham Kisch was a Prague physician and one of the teachers of Moses Mendelssohn. Driven from Prague in 1745, he later returned as physician of the community. He also directed the Meisel Hospital until 1763. Alexander Kisch, born at Prague in 1848, was a rabbi and writer. Enoch Heinrich Kisch, born in 1841, practised as a balneotherapist at Marienbad. He edited journals on balneology. Hermann M. Kisch, born in 1850, became postmaster-general of Bengal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kolisch-sigmund: Sigmund Kolisch, an Austrian poet and historical writer born at Koritschan in Moravia on Sept. 15, 1817, studied at the University of Vienna. His subjects were classical philology, history, and philosophy. After a short stay in Italy in 1847 he joined the Vienna revolution of 1848. When imperial troops won, he fled to Germany. Twenty years in Germany, France, and Italy followed before his return to Vienna in 1868. His works include small novels, a book on Kossuth and Metternich dated 1850, and a tragedy dated 1875.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kulke-eduard-95:
Eduard Kulke, an Austrian author born at Kostel in Moravia on May 28, 1831, died at Vienna on March 20, 1897. He trained at polytechnics in Vienna and Prague and taught for some years. Settling in Vienna, he gave himself to writing. Tales of Moravian ghetto life soon won notice and placed him next to Leopold Kompert among ghetto writers.

Plays and Wagner essays widen the picture. Kulke published tales dated 1869 and 1871, a tragedy on Korah dated 1873, and memoirs of his friend Hebbel dated 1878. As a music critic he championed Wagner with heat in books dated 1883 to 1890. Later he changed his mind and broke with the Wagner camp.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lenchitza-polis:
Lenchitza, called Leczyca in Polish, is a district town in the government of Kalisz, Russian Poland. In 1904 its Jews numbered about 2,000 out of 9,044 people. Rabbi Ephraim, author of "Olelot Efrayim," who died in 1619, was born there.

On April 20, 1639, members of its Jewish community faced a ritual murder charge after a Christian child was found dead in nearby woods. A tramp's forced claim blamed the Jews. Local judges tortured many on the rack, and two men, Lazar and Maier, were quartered. Monks displayed the child's remains and drew pilgrims. Later, 300 Jews died under General Czarniecki, and seven were burned in 1710.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levin-lewis-cha: Lewis Charles Levin, an American politician and writer, was born at Charleston, South Carolina, on Nov. 10, 1808. He died at Philadelphia on March 14, 1860. As a youth he taught school in Mississippi and studied law. A duel wound drove him from that town. He practiced law in several states, then settled in Philadelphia in 1838. There he edited the "Temperance Advocate" and spoke for the temperance cause. He helped form the Native American party in 1843. He sat in Congress from 1845 to 1851.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-libowitz-nehemi: Nehemiah Samuel Libowitz, a Russian Hebrew scholar and author, was born on Jan. 3, 1862, at Kolno. He studied Talmud under his father and read works of criticism on his own. In 1881 he came to the United States and settled in New York. There he divides his time between business and letters. His chief work gathers material for a life of Leon of Modena. It came out at Vienna in 1896 and again at New York in 1901. He also wrote sharp pamphlets against two named scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loans-10048:
Loans explains how lending worked in ancient Israel and in Talmud teaching. Loans of money or grain were acts of favor by the rich to people in need, not a way to fund trade. The Bible makes it a duty to lend to a poor fellow Israelite and to take no interest.

Talmud teaching ranks lending above giving, since a loan in time can save a person from begging. Lenders must not press or shame a debtor who cannot pay. Debtors who can pay must not delay. Debts from loans were wiped out in the year of release, a rule that later led Hillel to act so lenders would not hold back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstamm-saul:
Saul Löwenstamm, rabbi of Amsterdam, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. Born at Rzeszow in 1717, he wrote under a name drawn from his book Binyan Ariel. He served as rabbi in Hungary and then at Dubno, following his father-in-law. In 1755 he moved to Amsterdam after his father's death. He died there in 1790.

The article describes Binyan Ariel as a three-part work of notes on the Pentateuch, the Five Scrolls, and Talmud passages. He also wrote notes on the Shulhan Aruk, the Mishnah, and many poems and approbations. Much of his energy went to the study house his father had founded, which gained a new home in 1778. The entry ends with his son Jacob Moses succeeding him, a picture of rabbinic Amsterdam in the eighteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machpelah-10248:
Machpelah, the field and cave Abraham bought for a family burial place, is described in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. The name's meaning is unclear, though the old translations render it the double. The field lay near Mamre, or Hebron, and belonged to Ephron the Hittite. Abraham paid four hundred silver shekels for it.

The article lists who was buried in the cave. Sarah came first, then Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob. Josephus mentions the tombs without using the name Machpelah. From the twelfth century, travelers began visiting the cave. Benjamin of Tudela describes six sepulchers shown to visitors for a fee. He tells of an iron door, lit candles, and two empty caves before the tombs. Samuel ben Samson counted twenty-four steps down a narrow passage in 1210. The entry blends Bible, Josephus, and pilgrims' reports into one site history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manchester-1034:
Manchester, the Lancashire manufacturing city, receives a Jewish community history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. About 25,000 of its 543,969 people were Jews. That made it the second largest Jewish community in the British empire. Jews began settling near Shudehill and Long Millgate about 1780.

The article starts with two brothers from Liverpool, Lemon and Jacob Nathan. They founded the first synagogue in the upper room of a house. Lemon Nathan became its first president, and a cemetery opened at Pendleton in 1794. A charity for winter relief followed in 1804. The congregation moved to Halliwell Street in 1824 and built its own synagogue. A schism in 1856, after Rabbi Schiller-Szinessy's appointment, produced a Reform congregation. Gustav Gottheil then led the old congregation for thirteen years before leaving for New York. The entry traces a community built, split, and reunited within three generations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-adolf-bern:
Adolf Bernhard Marx, a German writer on music, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn. Born at Halle on May 15, 1799, he was meant for the law but gave up a legal post to study music in Berlin under Zelter. He died at Berlin on May 17, 1866, after decades of teaching and editing.

Marx helped found a leading Berlin music journal in 1824 and, with Kullak and Stern, the Berlin music school of 1850 that became the Stern Conservatory. His own compositions faded, and a quarrel over them ended his close friendship with Mendelssohn. His books lasted better: a four-volume treatise on composition, a life of Beethoven, and a study of Gluck and the opera.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medini-hayyim-h:
Hayyim Hezekiah Medini was a Palestinian rabbi who built an encyclopedia of Jewish law. Isidore Singer and M. Franco profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Jerusalem in 1833, son of Rabbi Raphael Eliahu Medini, and took his rabbinical diploma at nineteen. He spent thirteen years on a rabbinical court at Constantinople and was called in 1866 as chief rabbi to Kara-Su-Bazar in the Crimea. He returned to Palestine in 1889, and from 1891 acted as chief rabbi of Hebron.

His books of responsa and Talmudic studies appeared steadily. But the entry crowns one work, “Sede Hemed,” an encyclopedic collection of laws and decisions arranged in alphabetical order. Twelve volumes of it had appeared at Warsaw since 1890. It is the kind of lifetime reference work that makes the name of a scholar permanent. The entry treats it as the center of his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-zeb:
Menahem ben Zebi was a German rabbi. He died, probably at Posen, in 1724. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 enters him through the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. S. Waldstein. He had studied under two noted teachers. One was R. Heschel. The other was Aaron Samuel Kaidanover. Kaidanover wrote the "Birkat ha-Zebah." The entry lists three books by Menahem. All three carry his name worked into their titles.

The "Zinzenet Menahem" was printed at Berlin in 1719. It explains difficult passages of the Haggadah. The "Lehem Menahem," Bread of Menahem, collects his responsa. It also explains Talmudic passages. The "Ta'ame Menahem" comments on Rashi's Pentateuch commentary. No incident of his life survives in the notice. The notice rests on two sources. One is Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue. The other is Azulai's "Shem ha-Gedolim." A bibliography and a shelf of books stand in for a biography.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-albert-10:
Albert Meyer, a Danish tenor born at Sorö in Zealand on October 29, 1839, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer, published in 1906. He began in the chorus of Copenhagen's Royal Theater in 1860, studying under H. Rung, before war service in 1864 interrupted his start.

A concert on his return paid for a year of study under Lamperti in Milan, and from 1866 he sang as soloist at the Folketheatret. In 1873 he turned to teaching, publishing a singing method grounded in the physiology of the voice and opening his own Copenhagen school. He also conducted the synagogue chorus from 1882 and compiled its Sabbath melodies in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minden-lob-b-mo:
Löb ben Moses Minden, born Judah of Selichow in Lesser Poland in the seventeenth century, was a cantor and poet who took his name from the town where he sang. Herman Rosenthal and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He served as ḥazzan at Minden-on-the-Weser and died, very old, at Altona or Hamburg in 1751.

His Shire Yehudah set Hebrew songs beside German translations with music, opening with drinking-song lines addressed to dear brothers and companions. An epilogue printed at Amsterdam in 1696 scolds rabbis who let people chatter through services, a cantor's complaint from inside the pulpit. A second songbook, Zemer wa-Shir, was printed at Frankfurt in 1714 by Solomon London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monis-judah-109:
Judah Monis was Harvard's Hebrew instructor for thirty-seven years — and a convert who kept the Jewish Sabbath all his life, as Crawford Howell Toy and Frederick T. Haneman write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Algiers about 1683 and educated, it is said, in Italy, he reached Boston early in the eighteenth century. His first firm record is his baptism, in College Hall at Cambridge, in 1722.

At the baptism Monis preached and printed his own confession of faith, then threw himself into his new religion's cause — while never giving up Sabbath observance. Harvard appointed him in 1722; he resigned in 1759, on his wife's death, and withdrew to Northborough, where he died a few years later. The entry weighs Hannah Adams against Harvard's historian Quincy for his dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moser-moses-110:
Moses Moser was a German merchant best remembered as the closest friend of the poet Heinrich Heine. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1796, he trained for business in Berlin and worked as assistant to the banker Moses Friedländer. He later served as confidential cashier to Moritz Robert.

Moser had real talent for mathematics and also studied philology. With Gans and Zunz he helped found the Society for the Culture and Science of Judaism. Heine valued his ability and character, called him a living appendix to Nathan the Wise, and sent him many intimate letters. Their closeness lasted until 1830, and the entry preserves a figure known mainly through his famous friend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-silas-mey:
Silas Meyer Moses was a Bombay banker who rose to president of the Bank of Bombay. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in Bombay on November 23, 1845, he was educated there and was related to the Sassoon family. As a young man he went to China for David Sassoon and Company.

In 1880 Moses returned to Bombay and became manager of the bank. When his uncle Solomon Sassoon died in 1894, he took his place as a director and on the Port Trust. In 1897 he was elected president of the bank, the first member of the Jewish community to reach that post. He also sat on the legislative council of the Bombay presidency.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-myers-asher-isa:
Asher Isaac Myers was an English journalist born in London in 1848 and dead there in 1902. Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Trained in the clothing business, he became joint proprietor of The Jewish Record in 1868. A year later he joined The Jewish Chronicle, the paper that made his career.

Under Dr. Benisch, Myers managed the Chronicle's business, and at Benisch's death in 1878 he inherited a share of it. As joint owner and acting editor he raised the paper to the first rank of Jewish journalism. He also helped found the Jewish Workingmen's Club in 1872. His house became a center of Jewish intellectual life in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nesvizh-11448:
Nesvizh was a small town in the government of Minsk. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town stood already in the thirteenth century. The census of 1897 counted 8,446 people there. Of those, 4,764 were Jews, well over half.

Market gardening was a common trade among its Jews. The town held 650 Jewish artisans in that count. Day laborers among them numbered 110 more. A Talmud Torah taught 120 pupils there. Day schools served forty-three boys and fifty-eight girls. Charities ran a dispensary and free-loan funds for the poor. Eight synagogues served the town's Jewish life. Fire struck Nesvizh hard in that census year, 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nimrod-11548:
Nimrod was a son of Cush and a mighty hunter. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, Wilhelm Bacher, and the Editorial Board wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His kingdom held Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh. Those cities stood in the land of Shinar. His name became a proverb for hunting skill.

Rabbinic lore makes him the first great rebel. His name is read as, he who made all rebel. He first taught men to eat meat, tales say. Adam's skin coats, stolen down the line, empowered him. Beasts crouched before him in those coats. He is blamed for urging the Tower of Babel. He threw Abraham into a furnace, says tradition. Esau slew him at last, two hunters made jealous. Critics match him with Gilgamesh or with Marduk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-obed-edom-11648:
Obed-edom was a Gittite in whose house the Ark rested. Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, Schulim Ochser, and the board wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Ark had been kept at the house of Abinadab. It stayed with Obed-edom for three months in all. Then it was borne to the City of David.

God blessed Obed-edom and all his house, the Bible says. Rabbis taught that he lit a candle by the Ark. He lit it twice each day, at dawn and at dusk. They said his blessing took the form of many children. His wife and eight wives of his sons bore young. Other men of this name kept the Temple gates. One played the harp as the Ark was moved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orabuena-11748:
Orabuena was a Spanish family of Navarre, in Spain. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It thrived in the thirteen and fourteen hundreds there. Many of its men were rabbis or tax farmers. A like named family, Buenahora, may have been kin.

Juze Orabuena stands first in the line, a chief rabbi. He was doctor and aide to the king of Navarre. He was born at Tudela in the mid thirteen hundreds. The king set him a wage and a grant for life. His son Judah took his place as rabbi in 1408. Judah rode oft with King Charles the Third himself. He drew a grant of gold from the king each year. A third Judah served as rabbi at Tudela in 1348.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pagay-josephine:
Josephine Pagay was an Austrian actress born at Vienna. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She died at Berlin on November 18, 1892. At the age of fourteen she first took the stage. Her first part was Cupido in a famed light opera.

That first work was Orpheus in the Underworld, a hit piece. Her brisk speech, her wit, and her gifts won all hearts. She scored great wins in the works of Offenbach. She won in works by Suppé, Millöcker, and Strauss too. She shone in the farces of Kaiser and of Costa. She stood at the height of her fame for two decades. In the mid eighties she left the stage all at once. She then lived in quiet at Berlin till her death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-patto-pato-benj:
Benjamin Dias Patto was a Spanish preacher and teacher in Amsterdam. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Patto studied under Saul Levi Morteira, a leading rabbi of the city. He was killed in April 1664.

Patto helped edit Morteira's sermons for print in 1645. He became the first teacher at Abi Yetomim. That school served orphans and opened in Amsterdam in 1648. A colleague's epitaph for him confirms that he was murdered. He also wrote a Spanish poem for a martyr named Bernal. The poem was printed in a memorial volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pilegesh-hebrew:
A pilegesh was a concubine known to ancient Hebrew law. Emil G. Hirsch, Schulim Ochser, and the Executive Committee wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the house she held a wife's standing. Her person was held as sacred as a wife's.

Barren wives gave their maids to their husbands. Sarah, Leah, and Rachel all did this in Genesis. Her sons ranked equal with the wife's sons. The outrage at Gibeah cost Benjamin thousands of men. Later kings kept concubines out of sheer luxury. Solomon alone is said to have kept three hundred.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-kaim-122:
Kaim Pollak was a Hungarian writer born at Liptó-Szent-Miklós in 1835. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He learned Talmud in his home town, Presburg, and Sátoralja Ujhely. In 1858 he went to Prague and heard Rapoport lecture. He then taught at Jewish schools in three towns.

Pollak kept his last school post until a pension in 1902. He wrote school books of many kinds. His geometry book for public schools reached eight editions. In 1880 he brought out a full Hebrew-Hungarian dictionary. He turned works of Gabirol into Hungarian. He also gave Hungarian readers a book on Israel's past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-presbyter-12348:
Presbyter is a Greek title for an elder in a community. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. From Moses to Talmudic times, elders formed a standing body. In Greek they were called the Gerusia. The word presbyter itself shows up late, though. It is not found before the first Christian years.

Still, the title must have been in use before then. The Christian office of presbyter was taken straight from Judaism, they say. A list of officers of a Jewish town in Cilicia proves the point. It names synagogue heads, priests, and presbyters side by side. The article sorts out who these elders were and what they did.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-purim-12448:
Purim is the Jewish feast of lots, kept each year in Adar. Kaufmann Kohler and Henry Malter wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It falls on the fourteenth day of the month. In Shushan it was kept on the fifteenth as well. It marks the rescue of Persia's Jews from Haman's plot. That plot sought to wipe them out in one blow.

The Book of Esther tells how the feast was founded. Mordecai and Esther set it as a national feast, it says. The writers leave the book's own tale to a sister article. Here they treat the feast as it grew after its founding. Customs, foods, gifts, and noise fill the later account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ramah-ramath-or:
Ramah is a Hebrew word meaning height. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word forms part of many place names in Palestine. Several different towns were also called simply Ramah.

The article works through those towns one by one. It places one Ramah in Asher and one in Naphtali. A third lay in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. King Baasha fortified that town, and King Asa tore the works down. A fourth Ramah is linked to Samuel's home. The entry helps readers keep same-named Bible places apart. It matches old names to sites known in 1906.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rehumai-i-rab-1:
Rab Rehumai was a Babylonian amora of the fifth generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied under Raba b. Joseph b. Hama. He also put questions to Abaye.

The article is best known for the tale of his death. He always went home on the eve of the Day of Atonement. One year study at Mahoza held him too long. His wife waited, then wept at his failure to come. Legend says heaven punished his neglect with death. The roof where he sat fell in and killed him. He died on that same holy eve. The entry joins Talmud teaching to a warning tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rieger-paul-127:
Paul Rieger was a German rabbi and historian born on July 4, 1870. Isidore Singer and Hermann Vogelstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Dresden. He studied at Breslau and Berlin universities.

The article says he also studied at Jewish seminaries in both cities. His Breslau thesis treated crafts in the Mishnah. Its title asks about their technology and terminology. He served as rabbi at Potsdam from 1896 to 1902. Hamburg's Temple congregation then called him as rabbi. With H. Vogelstein he wrote a history of Rome's Jews. That work filled two volumes in 1895 and 1896. He also wrote a small pamphlet, Hillel und Jesus, in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenfeld-leopo:
Leopold Rosenfeld was a Danish composer born in Copenhagen on July 21, 1849. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He spent six years in a counting-house before his father let him study music.

At the Copenhagen Conservatory from 1872 to 1875, Rosenfeld focused on composition. A scholarship in 1881 let him travel abroad, and in 1889 he became a professor. He wrote many piano pieces and more than thirty booklets of songs. His orchestral piece Henrik og Else won great favor in 1885. He also wrote a guide to teaching singing, Om Textsang.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ruth-rabbah-cal:
Ruth Rabbah, also called Midrash Rut, is a homiletic commentary on the Book of Ruth. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It belongs to the Midrash Rabbot, covering all five scrolls.

Eight sections carry the reader through Ruth verse by verse. Some verses get a literal reading, others an allegorical one instead. A long introduction of separate proems stands before the commentary proper. Its spirit is that of the Palestinian teachers of legend and sermon. Its main sources include the Jerusalem Talmud and Bereshit Rabbah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salvador-franci:
Francis Salvador was a patriot of the American Revolution who died on August 1, 1776. Cyrus Adler and L. Hühner wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He came of the wealthy London Salvador family, once Jessurum Rodriguez.

Salvador inherited great wealth, increased by his marriage dowry in London. Then the Lisbon earthquake and the Dutch East India failure swept it away. About 1773 he emigrated to South Carolina, leaving wife and children in England. Within a year he had bought considerable lands in the colony. He threw himself heart and soul into the American cause there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-solo:
Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel ben Solomon of Falaise, a tosafist of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. In French he was called Sir Morel. Rabbinic books often cite him by that name. He studied under Judah Sir Leon of Paris and Isaac ben Abraham of Sens.

In 1240 Samuel took part in the famous Paris dispute. The baptized Jew Nicholas Donin had stirred up that attack on the Talmud. Samuel also wrote tosafot, or notes, on several Talmudic tracts. His notes on Abodah Zarah were printed with the text. He wrote rulings on points of ritual law as well. Meïr of Rothenburg and other leading rabbis cite those rulings often.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schapira-herman:
Herman Rosenthal and Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Hermann Schapira. He was a Russian mathematician. Schapira was born in 1840 at Erswilken, a small town in Lithuania. He died at Cologne on May 8, 1898. Trained for the rabbinate, he held a rabbinical post at twenty-four. Then he turned the rest of his life to secular science.

Schapira studied at Odessa and at Berlin's Gewerbeakademie. After years in trade, he returned to study at Heidelberg. He took his doctorate in 1883 and taught mathematics there. He still loved Hebrew literature all his life. He edited the Mishnat ha-Middot from a Munich manuscript in 1880. He was also an ardent Zionist from the start. On a Zionist lecture tour he caught pneumonia at Cologne and died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwerin-gotz-1:
Gotthard Deutsch and Eduard Neumann wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Götz Schwerin. He was a Hungarian rabbi and Talmudist. Schwerin was born in 1760 at Schwerin-on-the-Warthe. He died on January 15, 1845. He studied at the yeshibot of Presburg and Prague. In 1796 he settled in Hungary as a private scholar at Baja.

In 1812 Schwerin became rabbi of Szabadka, and in 1815 of Baja. His house became the district's center of learning. In 1827 Hungary's communities elected him chief rabbi of the country. He could summon parties and compel their appearance. No ritual official could be appointed without his consent. Thousands of disputes passed through his hands. He used his power with unbending justice. He also gave the sermon its due place in worship. His grandson Samuel Kohn wrote his life in Hungarian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shema-13548:
Shema is the first word of the verse Jews recite as their confession of faith. Kaufmann Kohler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord. At first the Shema was that single verse from Deuteronomy.

In the liturgy it grew to three full portions. The first commands love of God and teaching children. It also commands words on arm, head, and doorposts. The second promises reward for obedience and warns of punishment. The third gives the law of fringes as a reminder. The entry shows how one short verse became the center of Jewish prayer, morning and night, across the centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sifre-zuta-the-:
Sifre Zuta, the Small Sifre, is a distinctive midrash on the book of Numbers. Wilhelm Bacher and S. Horovitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. It holds special interest for the study of Jewish law. Weiss questioned its authenticity, but wrongly, the entry argues.

Medieval authors knew it under two other titles as well. To separate it, one work calls the big Sifre Rabbati instead. The small Sifre itself has not survived whole. A later writer notes it was already lost in his day. Earlier authors still quoted it in their books. Samson of Sens used it on Mishnah orders. Many fragments live inside the Yalkut Shim'oni on Numbers. Brüll gathered and compared those fragments for scholars. The entry tells how a lost book is rebuilt from quotations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-moritz-al:
Moritz Alexander Simon was a German banker and philanthropist born at Hanover in 1837. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked in his home town with the banking house of Ezechiel Simon. After some years in New York he founded his own bank. In New York he saw the misery of poor Jewish immigrants.

Simon came to see the Jewish question as a social one in part. In 1893 he opened a school at Ahlem near Hanover. It trained boys in farming and in handicrafts. By 1905 it had trained about 170 pupils. He left the school 750,000 dollars in his will when he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spektor-isaac-e:
Isaac Elhanan Spektor was a Russian rabbi and author born in 1817. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Rosh, in the government of Grodno. His father, a rabbi with Hasidic leanings, first taught him. The boy soon won fame as a prodigy, an ilui.

At thirteen he married and settled with his wife's parents. He studied under Benjamin Diskin, who ordained him as rabbi. When his wife's dowry was lost, he had to earn a living. In 1837 he became rabbi of tiny Sabelin in poverty. His pay was five Polish gulden a week there. He died at Kovno on March 6, 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stieglitz-juliu:
