In the Nagoya region nearly everyone lived within a short drive of all three facility types. In the northern Higashimikawa region, coverage collapsed, with only about a third of residents within reach of a hospital, and elderly coverage ran lower still. Transit access split the same way. The maps quantify a familiar rural penalty and show officials exactly where medical deserts persist.
plos-pone-0357048:
Samir Regmi and colleagues dunked seven rice varieties, including local Nepalese landraces, under deep water for ten days to learn which survival strategy works when fields flood completely. Their 2026 trial measured survival after a recovery week along with shoot growth, leaf greenness, and chlorophyll, comparing two philosophies: race upward for air, or sit still and save energy.

Sitting still won. The landraces that barely elongated kept their leaves green and survived best, while the fastest stretcher piled up growth underwater and then died at the highest rate. Statistical grouping cleanly separated the patient conservers from the reckless escapers. Two local varieties emerged as promising breeding material, and the study confirms energy thrift, not heroics, as the trait flood-prone rice needs.
plos-pone-0357448:
Rachel A. Roston, Nicholas J. Tustison, and A. Murat Maga published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on aligning medical images when anatomy is strikingly abnormal. Registration, warping one image to match a template, underpins modern morphometrics, but standard tools align by brightness alone and fail when organs are rearranged. Their label-informed approach lets experts supply segmentations declaring which regions correspond, guiding the warp by biology rather than pixels, inside a widely used open ecosystem.

The demonstration was dramatic: mouse embryos lacking a key developmental gene develop severe spinal curvature scrambling their organs, and ordinary registration failed to match them to a normal template. With label guidance, the knockout embryos registered properly, restoring correspondence organ by organ, raising the power of measurements drawn from the alignment. The method is offered as a general fix for developmental and comparative studies, where the interesting subjects are those breaking ordinary registration.
plos-pone-0358248: Xiong and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on teaching computers to name Chinese dishes from photos. Many dishes look nearly alike, so the task is fine-grained. Their learning method sharpens how the system separates one dish class from its close rivals. The test set is CNFOOD-241, a large named collection. Better dish naming helps calorie apps and menu tools read a photo correctly.
plos-pone-0358348:
Linan Sun, Boyang Fu, and Wenwen Liu built sentiment into stock portfolio design, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Investor mood moves markets, sometimes beyond what company facts justify. The team used the Black-Litterman model, a standard portfolio framework, and wove investor sentiment into how portfolios are constructed.

Sun's sentiment-aware portfolios aim to ride the crowd's emotions profitably rather than be blindsided by them. The Black-Litterman model is a natural home for this, since it already blends market data with investor views. Adding a measured mood signal tests whether sentiment can be used with discipline, not just chased. Fund managers and researchers gain a worked example of behavioral finance applied inside a mainstream tool.
plos-pone-0358648:
Jian Zhang and three colleagues trace how university teaching becomes joined up professional and entrepreneurship skill, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Five hundred eighty-four students rated their courses, teachers, drive, and campus resources, plus what they had truly taken in from the experience. The authors arranged the factors as a process: resources go in, students build understanding, drive turns it into behavior, and results emerge at the end.

Teacher competence, course content, engaged students, and links with enterprises all associated positively with integrated outcomes. The pathway ran mainly through instructional practice, the lived quality of teaching, which acted as the key middle step. Policy support showed no direct association at all, surfacing only through indirect routes. The authors advise universities to spend less faith on policy declarations and more on the classroom processes and industry links that the data truly connect to learning.
plos-pone-0359348: Zhao and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tracking desert spread on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. They combined two satellite signals: surface albedo, how bright the ground is, and a glow from plants that shows how green they are. Watching both over time maps where land is turning to desert. The plateau feeds major Asian rivers, so its land health matters far beyond its borders.
plos-pone-0360048:
Masayuki Kato and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on hospital hygiene. After gastrointestinal endoscopes are cleaned by automated reprocessing, germs can remain or return. The authors run microbiological surveillance, regular germ testing, in routine clinical practice, in a prospective randomized study design.

Endoscopes are hard to clean because of their long, narrow channels, and lapses have caused infections worldwide. Surveillance after reprocessing checks whether routine cleaning in real hospitals, not ideal ones, keeps scopes safe. Infection control teams and endoscopy units are the readers who must decide how much testing is enough.
pmc-10048148:
Sallam published a systematic review in 2023 on what ChatGPT, the conversational AI built on a large language model, can do in health care. The review gathers published studies and reports on the tool's use in teaching, research and everyday medical practice. It weighs hopeful findings against the worries raised about accuracy and safety.

Across the collected work, the tool helped with tasks like drafting, summarising and answering study questions, while authors kept flagging errors and bias as live risks. A balanced map of promise and concern is useful as hospitals and schools set rules for AI use.
pmc-10496548:
Yu Gao and co-authors test a methylene blue nanoemulsion cream on the slow-healing wounds of diabetic mice. Diabetic wounds linger because blood vessel growth stalls and cells die off. Methylene blue already helps in other diabetes-linked ills, and the nanoemulsion form aims it at the skin.

Their 2023 study compares treated and untreated diabetic mice, with cell tests in high sugar beside them. Treated wounds closed faster and grew more vessel markers tied to fresh blood supply. Dying cells thinned out in the treated tissue. In the dish, the cream sped cell migration and lifted survival proteins while trimming death signals. The team reads the gain as repair driven through vessel growth and oxidative calm.
pmc-10503448:
Shan Cong and co-authors sort gut tumors by how their cells burn fuel, in a 2023 study. Tumor cells vary widely in their energy habits, and those habits tie to outlook and to drug response. Such links had not been shown for cancers of the stomach and bowel.

Using gene and clinical data for more than two hundred fifty fuel linked genes, the team built four metabolic subtypes. One subtype had the worst outlook and a gene pattern tied to drug handling. Other subtypes leaned on sugar pathways. The subtypes also tracked with response to chemotherapy and with tumor traits. The authors propose the typing as a guide for therapy and prognosis.
pmc-10655348:
Tingwen Cai and co-authors test whether the hormone erythropoietin can save bone cells from steroid damage, in a 2023 study. Steroids can starve the hip bone's head of blood, killing the bone-forming cells and collapsing the joint. In dishes, the hormone shielded those cells from a steroid that normally drives them to self-destruct.

Treated cells showed less of the death machinery: lower levels of two executioner proteins and of a stress signal called STAT1, with a guard protein raised instead. In rats with the hip disease, the hormone cut the share of empty bone pockets left by dead cells. The authors suggest the hormone, best known for making red blood cells, could be developed into a treatment for this hip condition.
pmc-10655448:
De Castro Araújo Neto and six co-authors adapted a professionalism scale for pharmacists into Brazilian Portuguese and tested how well it works, in a study published in twenty twenty-three. The scale, based on Hall's framework, measures the attitudes and habits that mark a true professional.

The work ran in three stages. First the team translated the scale and adjusted it for Brazilian culture. Then experts from different regions checked that each item still made sense. Finally, six hundred Brazilian pharmacists completed the adapted scale. Statistical analysis grouped the thirty-nine items into six themes, matching the design of the original. Agreement checks scored above the accepted bar, and the themes held together reliably. The authors say the Brazilian version is ready for use in studies of pharmacist training and professional growth.
pmc-10656448:
Ying-Yu Chen and co-authors measure skin hydration with light in this 2023 study. Dry skin weakens the barrier and can spark inflammation, yet the standard electric test reads only shallowly and bends with room humidity. Their method shines a spread of wavelengths on skin and reads the bounce.

Absorption numbers from the light tracked the electric standard closely across hydration states. Scattering and absorption together flagged boosts from wet pads and face masks. The setup is fast, touch-free, and simple, suiting long monitoring runs. The authors also link the reads to skin sensation. They offer the method as a handy clinic and lab tool.
pmc-10657148:
Seven authors, led by Asma Guedria, assess in 2023 how parents and children in Tunisia fared in mind during the COVID lockdown. Most early work on the pandemic's mental toll covered the public or health staff, not families at home. Their survey reached over five hundred parents of children under eighteen in May 2020.

Parents filled forms on worry, burnout, and their children's anxious traits. Mothers made up most of the sample. The team scored general worry with a standard seven point scale and parenting burnout with a set tool. It then hunted for traits tied to stronger parent worry, to guide support in future lockdowns.
pmc-10657448:
Turcin Saridogan and a large team of co-authors published this study in 2023. It tests a targeted drug, futibatinib, in breast cancers with changes in a growth factor receptor family called FGFR. The drug locks onto all four members of the family and cannot be shaken off.

The team grew nine patient-derived tumors in mice, each with a different FGFR change, and dosed them with the drug. Three of the nine shrank or stalled. The strongest response, a lasting shrink of more than 110 days, came in a tumor with a changed and multiplied FGFR2 gene. Lab work confirmed that adding that change to normal breast cells made them grow faster and answer the drug. Database checks show such changes appear in only a few percent of patients.
pmc-10675648:
Junhyung Moon and co-authors build a smarter way to estimate energy burned in exercise, in this 2023 study. Lab calorimetry gear that measures energy use is scarce, so wearable sensors are an appealing stand-in. Their method counts energy spent during a workout and during recovery afterward. That recovery burn is called excess post-exercise oxygen consumption.

Thirty-two healthy adults did aerobic sessions at low and high effort. The team fed body traits, effort level, and heart rate into machine learning models. Tracking ran until each person's metabolic rate settled back to rest. Estimates tracked the true values very closely, with low error. Fitness tools could use such a method for fairer calorie counts.
pmc-10687448:
Shiwei Sun and co-authors present a 2023 study of machine learning models that call how hard a keyhole adrenal gland surgery will be. Scan traits, read by a method called radiomics, join clinic facts in the models. Cases from one hospital split into train and test sets, with a fresh later set kept for a hard check.

Key scan traits were picked by a shrink method and rolled into a score. Many model types were built and set side by side on accuracy, balance, and curve reads. The best pick is shown with per-trait weight charts, so doctors can see what drives each call.
pmc-10688048:
Cheng Luo and co-authors present a meta-analysis, printed in 2023, on the two rival ways to reopen blocked heart arteries when the kidneys are also failing. Patients with both coronary disease and chronic kidney disease face bypass surgery or a stent procedure, and trials disagree on which serves them better over time. The team pooled every randomized trial they could find under standard review rules, five trials covering nearly twelve hundred patients.

In the long run the stent group fared worse on major heart and brain events and needed repeat procedures far more often than the bypass group. The authors read the pooled evidence as favoring surgery for durable benefit in this doubly burdened group, while noting how few trials exist.
pmc-10689948:
Petrosyan and co-authors check the safety and strength of wild licorice roots in Armenia. Licorice root is prized in folk and modern remedies. The team gathered roots from forests in five regions of the country. Tests weighed heavy metals in the extracts and gauged the helpful plant compounds inside.

Metal levels stayed under the limits set by regulators in every sample. Levels of flavonoids, tannins, and pigments shifted a lot with the soil of each region. All five extracts showed clear antioxidant power in a lab test of rival reactions. The study is the first of its kind for Armenian wild licorice, and backs its careful use.
pmc-10691048:
Yiran Zhou and co-authors study how subtypes of a TP53 gene mutation affect pancreatic cancer, in a 2023 paper. The molecular traits of this cancer are well described, but how detailed mutation subtypes shape progression was unclear. The team focus on cancers already changed by a KRAS mutation.

They include 639 patients treated at a Shanghai hospital from 2019 to 2021. Gene changes are analyzed and linked with clinical traits and outcomes. One TP53 subtype, the missense type, tied to poor cell differentiation in KRAS-mutant cancers. The title frames this as a gain-of-function trait in small tumors. Survival models weigh the effect.
pmc-10691148:
Congping Li and five co-authors trace a chain that links cigarette smoke to a form of cell death in lung disease. Their 2023 study concerns chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, where smoke drives steady lung damage. The death pathway is ferroptosis, which runs on iron and oxidized fats. The team hunt for the switch that turns it on.

In smoke-exposed mice, lungs showed damage, stress chemistry, and ferroptosis signs together. In lung cells, smoke extract cut survival and the cell's main protective enzyme while raising damage markers. Silencing a gene called GNPAT blunted the death pathway. The team show smoke lowers a regulator, SIRT4, which in turn strips a chemical tag from GNPAT and lifts its level. Restoring GNPAT undid parts of the rescue. The chain offers new drug targets for smoke-driven lung disease.
pmc-10692048:
Naswandi Nur and five co-authors clone in 2023 an acid-loving lipase from a bacterium found in tempeh, the fermented soybean food. Lipases split fats and serve many industries, and acid-stable ones suit biodiesel making. The source strain, Micrococcus luteus EMP48-D, had been pulled from tempeh earlier.

The team copied the lipase gene into Escherichia coli and read its code: 1,356 letters spelling a protein of about 40 kilodaltons. The enzyme worked best under acid conditions and favored certain fatty acids. This is the first cloning of a lipase gene from this bacterial species. An acid-tough fat splitter from a food microbe could feed greener fuel production.
pmc-10693048:
Guohui Li and co-authors characterise two pear enzymes that gate lignin and stone cell formation in fruit, in work from twenty twenty-three. The enzyme family converts a core amino acid into cinnamic acid. That step opens the path from primary to secondary metabolism. Three family genes are found in the pear genome search. Two are produced as pure proteins for lab testing.

Both proteins act strictly on the intended amino acid substrate. Neither touches a close cousin amino acid in the test tubes. Kinetics differ modestly between the two pear enzymes in vitro. Raising or silencing one gene shifts stone cell and lignin content in fruit. A regulator protein binds the promoter switch of the second gene. Lignin control points for pear breeding come into view.
pmc-10693548:
Oscar Kirstein and a large team show in 2023 that spraying insecticide inside homes changes not just how many mosquitoes live, but their ages. The dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti must survive long enough for the virus to mature inside it. In a trial in Merida, Mexico, targeted indoor spraying was tested against no spraying.

The team dissected 813 female mosquitoes over nine months after spraying. Sprayed homes held far more young, never-bred females at one and three months. Survival curves dropped in the sprayed group, so fewer females lived long enough to pass on virus. The age shift faded by six months. The authors say this double effect, fewer and younger mosquitoes, should count in judging spray programs.
pmc-10694148:
Hongqiao Yang and six co-authors test whether a seizure drug can shield the brain in the first day after a burst aneurysm bleeds. Their 2023 rat study targets early brain injury after subarachnoid hemorrhage, the phase that sets the prognosis. Two villains drive it: oxidative stress and pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death.

Rats given perampanel after the bleed scored better on nerve tests, with less brain swelling and neuron loss at 24 hours. Both oxidative stress and pyroptotic death fell. The drug also revived a protective pathway built on the SIRT3 enzyme and its FOXO3 partner. When a blocker shut that pathway down, every benefit reversed. The team read the pathway as the drug's mechanism, and a candidate route for future stroke care.
pmc-10694948:
Removing Helicobacter pylori bacteria can change how early stomach cancer looks through a scope, but the effect on mixed-type cancers is unclear. Yoshitaka Tokai and co-authors study patients whose early gastric cancers mixed two cell types. They compare magnified scope images, taken with narrow-band light, between patients who had the bacteria removed and those who had not.

The study covered 124 patients treated at one cancer hospital. In cancers dominated by the differentiated type, scope findings for that type showed in every patient either way. The team also examined the surface layer over the cancer under a microscope. Their goal is to help doctors read post-treatment scope images with fewer mistakes about the cancer's true makeup.
pmc-10695948:
Xuan Gu, Hailin Zheng, and Chi-Shing Tse study how nature contact shapes emotion control in city youth in a 2023 paper. Time in nature lifts mood, but the inner path was unclear. The team surveyed young adults living in urban China. They asked how often the youth meet nature, directly or through media.

The sample held 2,097 adults aged 18 to 35 years. Feeling close to nature carried the link to emotion skills. That closeness helped youth rethink bad feelings in a calm way. It also cut the habit of hiding feelings from others. Love of natural beauty changed the strength of some links. The authors draw lessons for schools and city planning.
pmc-10696048:
Water leaves the land through soil and plants, a flow called evapotranspiration, and its shifts can tip a region toward drought. Sheng Hong and co-authors track that flow over forty years in China's Southeast River basin, using a global land model fed by satellite data. The basin covers the country's wet southeastern coast.

The flow rose significantly across the four decades, by about two and a half millimeters per year. Plant transpiration made up nearly three quarters of it. Greener vegetation, measured from orbit, tracked the rise closely and explained a tenth of the increase since 2000. Where the flow rose, a standard drought index fell, in a strong spatial mirror pattern. The authors name rising evapotranspiration a trigger of the region's seasonal droughts.
pmc-10696748:
Vu and six co-authors measure combined diabetes and hypertension burden in Vietnam across survey waves, in a study from twenty twenty-three. National risk factor surveys from twenty ten, twenty fifteen, and twenty twenty-one supply data. Adults aged twenty-five to sixty-four are the focus. Comorbidity prevalence, trends, and correlated factors are estimated.

Comorbidity reaches about three point nine percent by twenty twenty-one. That is over eight times the twenty ten level. Men, urban residents, and older people change the most. Body mass and clustered risk behaviors correlate strongly. Integrated care for the two conditions is urged.
pmc-10696848:
Rio and co-authors compare severity scores for trauma patients in intensive care. Such scores guide who needs ICU admission and help predict death risk. Yet little was known about how well the indices perform for those two jobs in trauma patients specifically.

The retrospective cohort study reviewed trauma cases treated in an ICU. It scored each patient with several severity indices and checked the scores against real admission and death outcomes. Head-to-head results show which index sorts risk most accurately. Better scoring could sharpen triage, family talks, and use of scarce ICU beds after severe injury.
pmc-10697048:
Shenhe Jin and co-authors summarize in 2023 the newest trial news on a class of antibody drugs for B-cell lymphoma, shared at a major European blood conference. These drugs are built to grab a T cell with one arm and a cancerous B cell with the other, dragging the killer cell onto its target. Several versions aim at the same pair of markers.

Updates covered three drugs in hard-to-treat large B-cell lymphoma that had returned or resisted care. Response rates ran from about half to three quarters of patients, with complete responses in a large share. Many complete responders stayed free of disease a year on. The main side effect was a feverish immune reaction, common but rarely severe. One drug also shone as first treatment for high-risk patients, paired with standard chemotherapy.
pmc-10698048:
Zhenni An and co-authors present a 2023 study on how family resources shape geography grades, and whether creativity carries part of that effect. Family capital covers the books, support, and expectations a home provides. The authors surveyed 1,268 high school students with questionnaires on family capital and creative behavior, then matched the answers to class geography scores.

Family capital predicted higher creativity and higher grades. Creativity in turn predicted better geography results on its own. Statistical mediation tests showed creativity partly channels the family effect into achievement. In plain terms, richer home resources seem to spark inventive habits that pay off in class. Schools might narrow gaps by training creativity directly in students whose homes offer less.
pmc-10699048:
Chen and seven co-authors use genetics to test whether the diabetes drug metformin lowers cancer risk. Reports have hinted at protection, but ordinary studies cannot prove cause. Mendelian randomization uses inherited gene variants as a natural experiment to get closer to causal answers.

Across 26 cancers, only one link stood firm: metformin use tied to much lower odds of HER-positive breast cancer. Other cancers showed only modest hints. A two-step analysis suggested testosterone levels carried about a quarter of the protective effect. Repeated checks with other methods agreed. The authors present metformin as a candidate preventive for that breast cancer type.
pmc-10701748:
Kitty Wu, Aditya Raghunathan, and Robert Spinner report an unusual nerve case: a woman with ten years of worsening leg pain and tingling on top of the foot. Scans showed several vague nodules along the superficial peroneal nerve in the midleg. At surgery, the team found six separate fatty tumors studded along a ten-centimeter stretch of the nerve and one branch. The growths clung to the nerve with no clean plane between them.

Because the tumors could not be peeled away safely, the surgeons removed that nerve segment. Lab study confirmed multiple fatty tumors outside the nerve, with signs of past injury. Four months later the patient's pain was gone and normal activity had resumed. The authors place the case within the known classes of fatty nerve lesions. Its clustered pattern, they note, fits those classes poorly, and its cause remains unknown.
pmc-10702048:
Merijn Rijk and co-authors lay out a plan to predict bad outcomes after chest infections in this 2023 protocol paper. Lower respiratory infections are everyday fare in family practice, yet spotting who will crash is hard. These infections also raise the near-term risk of heart trouble, which tangles prognosis further.

Two models are planned from linked Dutch health records. One forecasts hospital admission or death within a month. The other forecasts new cardiovascular trouble within three months. Candidate clues span symptoms, vital signs, lab values, medicines, and history. The team will build the models with a regularized regression method and test them in fresh cohorts. The goal is sharper decisions at the front desk of care.
pmc-10704648:
George Lagoumintzis and George Patrinos reviewed how food advice could be shaped to each person, in two thousand twenty-three. Each body reacts to food in its own way, based in part on its genes. That idea sits at the heart of personal food plans.

Their review brings three fields into one frame. One field reads genes, one reads the small chemicals the body makes, and one reads the germs in the gut. The authors show how the three affect each other and shape food needs. They also note blocks in the way, since many diseases involve many genes at once. The goal is diet plans that fit one person, not all people.
pmc-10706048:
Melis Gönülal, Sinem Karaca, and Didem Didar Balcı present a 2023 dermatology case report on a rare inherited skin disorder of the face. Keratosis pilaris atrophicans faciei roughens and thins the skin around hair follicles, mostly on the cheeks and brows, and can leave lasting marks. Light-based treatments help, and lasers under six hundred nanometers have the best record.

Their patient was treated with a 585-nanometer diode laser built on a newer semiconductor pumping technology. According to the authors, no earlier report describes this laser type being used for the condition. The short report adds the device to the short list of options for a stubborn, disfiguring disorder with few proven treatments.
pmc-10706148:
Meng-Yan Wang and co-authors review what is known about TGF-beta2, a signaling protein long treated as a twin of its better-known sibling. Their 2023 review argues that the second family member has its own expression pattern, activation route, and jobs in the body. It steers cell growth, movement, and specialization.

Mice lacking the protein develop striking defects across many organs, above all in the heart and vessel system. Faulty signaling from it is tied to tumors, eye disease, heart disease, immune disorders, and movement system problems. The review gathers the spread of findings into one map. The authors aim to spur work that treats TGF-beta2 as its own target, not a stand-in for the first family member.
pmc-10706248:
Małachowicz, Krasnov, and Wenne compare how two Baltic cod groups answer salt change in a 2023 study. Western cod live in saltier water than eastern cod, and both groups have crashed in recent decades. Gill tissue from lab-exposed fish was read on a gene chip after salt was raised or lowered. Four hundred genes shifted with the change.

The shifting genes cluster in immunity, metabolism, cell death, and tissue structure. Crucially, the pattern split by subpopulation: the same salt swing drove different gene answers in west and east fish. The authors say salt handling in Baltic cod is a layered trait, and each group needs its own care plan as seas freshen.
pmc-10706948:
Hyung-Mun Yun and co-authors test a plant flavonoid as a driver of bone-forming cell growth, in this 2023 paper. The compound, trifolirhizin, comes from the root of Sophora flavescens, a plant long used in traditional medicine. The team isolated it at high purity and fed it to bone precursor cells. It caused no cell toxicity at working doses.

Treated cells showed stronger bone enzyme activity and higher levels of key bone markers. A master bone switch, RUNX2, rose in the cell nucleus, along with major growth signals. Among stress kinases, only JNK switched on. The cells also migrated more, built more internal scaffolding, and laid down more mineral. The authors propose the compound as a candidate plant medicine for bone diseases like osteoporosis.
pmc-10707148: Figueira and co-authors frame plant polyphenols as a missing piece in the inflammation puzzle in a 2023 editorial. Knowledge of chronic disease keeps growing fast, from cancer and diabetes to brain decline. Yet core questions about how these ills work stay open. Inflammation sits at the center of that unknown. The piece points to polyphenols, the plant compounds found across fruits, tea, and wine, as an underplayed part of the story and a lead for closing the gap.
pmc-10707548:
Ivan Abičić and co-authors examined how reflux reaching the throat and voice box shows up in children, and whether a digestive enzyme found in tissue tracks with the standard scores. Diagnosis of this condition, called laryngopharyngeal reflux, rests on a symptom questionnaire and an examination score. Some researchers suspect the enzyme pepsin, carried up from the stomach, irritates the throat and swells the tonsils.

The team tested saliva and tonsil tissue from child patients for pepsin and compared results with the two scores. Children whose tonsils tested positive tended to score higher on both measures, though the gaps were not statistically firm. The authors call for larger studies to pin down what the trend means for diagnosis and care.
pmc-10707648:
Grace Nanyunja and a large team piloted a support link scheme in Uganda in two thousand twenty-three for people at risk of tuberculosis. Staff at four health centres screened adults who came for TB tests. Those who qualified were referred to a local office that signs people up for state support schemes, with travel costs paid by phone.

Of those screened, most people qualified for at least one scheme, and most accepted a referral. Yet only a small share ended up enrolled in the end. Surveys show many who went to the office were turned away. The study shows where the chain breaks and what to fix.
pmc-10708048:
Foamed plastic parts save weight and material, but their hidden bubble structure decides whether they survive a crash or snap. Piotr Szewczykowski and five co-authors dissect microcellular polyamide moldings reinforced with glass fiber in 2023. Thin and thick pieces are scanned with electron microscopy and X-ray tomography. The pictures are checked against molding simulations, and two polyamide grades at thicknesses from two to eight millimeters are compared.

Thin samples proved weak; thick ones performed excellently, and the imaging shows why: bubbles shrink as wall thickness grows. The authors tie each mechanical result to the structure that produced it. For car parts molded this way, they conclude, thickness is a structural decision, not just a shape. Foam, measured honestly, explains itself.
pmc-10709448:
Ruimin Lu, Qinglin Zhang, and Chang Guo present a 2023 chemistry paper on a reaction that can produce every mirror-and-twist variant of a product on demand. Controlling a molecule's three-dimensional shape is central to making natural products and drug candidates. Their method attaches an allyl group next to a carbonyl using imidazole-based starting materials, with nickel and iridium catalysts steering the outcome.

By choosing the leaving group and the handedness of each catalyst, all six isomeric products become accessible, each in high yield and with excellent selectivity. The team proved the method's worth by building two natural products in chosen handed forms. They also completed a variable-shape synthesis of a marketed pain drug. The authors offer the protocol as a blueprint for divergent synthesis, where one route fans out into many related compounds.
pmc-10709648:
Mohamed Morsy and co-authors built and tested a new material that can sense humidity, in work published in 2023. The material mixes three parts: a manganese compound, tiny carbon dots, and a plastic-like polymer. The team made the mix and then checked its size, shape, and chemical makeup with standard lab tools.

Tests showed the grains were well under 30 nanometres wide, which fits the nano scale. Images showed a fibrous form, with the polymer spread across most of the surface. The team then exposed the material to air with moisture levels from low to near full. It reacted in about two minutes and reset in under four minutes. Such a sensor could serve farms, factories, and health care.
pmc-10709848:
Living near a busy road brings noise and fumes, and hearing may pay part of the price. Xingxing Chen and co-authors studied more than thirteen thousand Chinese adults aged sixty-five and over in 2023, using a national longevity survey. They compared hearing loss across distance bands from major roadways.

Hearing problems affected about thirty-eight percent of the group. Risk rose in steps as homes got closer to major roads, with those within fifty meters showing higher odds than those beyond three hundred. The link grew stronger for people exposed to carbon monoxide pollution and for those who often opened their windows. The authors urge care in housing placement and window habits for older adults near traffic.
pmc-10710248:
Yi Ji, Jialin Gu, Hongqun Zhang, and Houxi Xu present a 2023 study hunting for marker molecules in colon cancer. MicroRNAs are tiny molecules that tune gene activity, and their patterns shift in cancer. Finding the key ones could aid early diagnosis and treatment.

The team mined two public gene datasets and found fourteen microRNAs changed in both. Software predicted the genes those molecules target, and a network map singled out three key microRNAs. Lab tests on patient samples confirmed the pattern. A large cancer database gave the same answer from independent data. The authors also probed links between the three markers and immune cells inside tumors, plus markers used to guide immune therapy.
pmc-10710348:
Hanno Hoven and co-authors present a 2023 study on how work history shapes later access to care. People in weaker social spots often report barriers to doctors, above all to specialists. The team asked whether rough patches in a past career leave lasting marks. They used a large European survey of 31,616 people aged 52 to 80 in 25 countries, with full career records.

Career traits linked to later reports of care given up for cost. The link was weaker for care missed due to scarce services. Patterns held for men and women, and after accounting for current income, wealth, and health. Country-level quality of care did not change the links. The authors call for work on why old career scars still shape care access.
pmc-10710448:
Saddam Hussain Khan and co-authors scan chest images for COVID-19 in a 2023 medical imaging paper. Diagnosing the infection from CT slices is tricky because labeled examples were scarce and the telltale patterns are subtle shifts in texture and brightness at lesion edges.

Their framework builds a boosted convolutional network around blocks that split, transform, and merge image features, enriching the channels that carry fine detail. Transfer learning and multipath residual connections stretch the limited training data further. The authors report the design catches the faint irregularities of infected slices more reliably than plainer networks, aiming at faster triage support.
pmc-10710648:
Naoki Nitta, Tadateru Fukami, and Kazumichi Yoshida report in 2023 a rare case of high-grade brain tumor spread through bone marrow. Spread outside the nerve system is rare for such tumors, and full marrow spread is rarer still. A thirty two-year-old man gives the case its course.

Return lesions in the brain were cut and radiated after his first tumor care. Back pain and blood faults then led scans to find tumor in spine, pelvis, and thigh bones. Marrow biopsy proved grade four tumor cells had invaded the marrow. The patient died twelve days after the second admission, which marks the grim pace.
pmc-10710948:
Alexei Antonov and four co-authors reviewed in 2023 what is known about Moyamoya disease and its effects on the mind. In this rare disorder, the main arteries inside the skull slowly narrow and close. A web of small backup vessels grows in their place. The disease mostly harms the blood supply of the brain, but its wider effects reach mood and thought.

The review covers how common the disease is, how it develops, its signs, and how doctors find it. It then turns to outcomes such as weak memory and thinking, mental disorders, and quality of life. Care for those outcomes remains hard, the authors note. They close by pointing to open questions and paths for future research on support for patients.
pmc-10712048:
Jie Meng leads a team that pools trials of diabetes drugs and mind function. Their pooled study from twenty twenty-three deals with DPP-4 inhibitors. Type two diabetes raises the risk of mind decline.

Four data bases were searched from the start to a set date. Six clinical trials with thousands of patients were pooled. Mind state scores were compared across the drug groups. The drug class linked in general to score gains. Spread between studies was measured with standard tests. Sensitivity checks dropped one study at a time. Bias checks rounded out the analysis.
pmc-10712148:
Dorothy Thomas and co-authors ask what helps or blocks violence screening in Uganda's HIV clinics in a 2023 study. People with HIV face more gender-based violence, which can sink their care. Thirty providers from twelve clinics sat for deep talks.

Clear rule books, state training, site classes, and peer backing helped staff screen and refer. Yet referrals stayed rare. Staff doubted the worth of the places referred to, funds ran short for clients and sites, and social norms made clients shy away. The team says plans should build on the helps and break the blocks.
pmc-10712248:
Yifang Huang and five co-authors map how body weight relates to death risk in Chinese patients with high blood pressure, and how age bends that relation, in a 2023 study. The cohort was huge: over two hundred thousand hypertensive adults in a Shanghai management system, followed until death or the end of 2018.

The weight-mortality curve formed a U, with the lowest risk at a body mass index around twenty-six to twenty-seven, above the textbook normal range. Being underweight carried about fifty percent higher early-death risk than normal weight. Flexible statistical models let the curve's shape shift with age rather than assuming one size fits all. The findings join the obesity-paradox debate with unusually strong numbers, and they caution against one weight target for every hypertensive patient.
pmc-10712348:
Xiaodong Wang and co-authors report a 2023 study of COVID-19 in Chinese children who had received a stem cell transplant. These children have weak immune systems after treatment, so a new virus posed a sharp risk. The study follows children in the first year after transplant during a recent outbreak in China.

The team reviewed records for two hundred forty-seven young patients. None had been vaccinated against the virus, and none had caught it before. Infection was confirmed by a standard gene test, and illness severity was graded by set rules. The most common underlying disease in the group was a blood disorder called thalassemia major. The authors record symptoms, lab and scan results, treatments, and outcomes, giving transplant teams a clear picture of how the illness behaved in this fragile group.
pmc-10712948:
Stewart Heitmann and co-authors build a yardstick for the heart risk of new drugs, in a 2023 paper. Many drug classes can trigger fatal rhythm faults by disturbing heart muscle cells, so safety checks are required before human trials. Older checks focus on one ion current, though risk turns on four. The team simulated a hundred thousand varied heart cells to find how blocking those currents leads to stray beats.

They call that link the axis of arrhythmia. Tested on 109 drugs, it matched known clinical risk labels with accuracy near ninety percent. The authors say drug makers can use the axis to judge a new compound's risk from its channel-blocking profile alone, without animal tests.
pmc-10713648:
Volkan Kizilgoz measures kneecap height on MRI scans in a 2023 paper. The Blackburne-Peel index gives a standard ratio for patellar height. X-ray values are known, but MRI norms were less settled.

One hundred forty-eight knee scans were re-measured for the study. An adapted version of the index suited the MRI images. Results were split by sex and by age groups. Correlations with age were tested across the sample. The overall mean index came out near 0.80 in the sample. Readers in orthopedics gain reference values for judging kneecap position on MRI.
pmc-10714148:
Kei Oyama, Yuji Nagai, and Takafumi Minamimoto give a hands-on method in 2023 for placing designer switches into a monkey brain zone. Such switches let scientists turn a wide brain area up or down with a drug, which helps map what the area does. The target here is a folded front zone linked to planning.

Older ways to reach folded zones were slow or gave loose control over where the switch spread. Their method uses brain scans taken before surgery to aim shots given by hand with a plain syringe. A mild virus carries the switch code into the cells. Clear steps matter: other labs can copy the aim and spread, which makes primate brain maps more alike across sites.
pmc-10714448:
Laura Huey Mien Lim and co-authors chart twenty-five years of asthma emergency care in Singapore and project its future, in a 2023 paper. Asthma attacks send many people to emergency rooms and hospital wards, yet city-wide trend data were scarce. The team gathered national registry records covering hospital stays and deaths over twenty-five years, plus emergency visits over fifteen. They hunted for stretches where rates held steady and modelled the rest.

Hospital stays hovered near eighty episodes per hundred thousand people from 2003 to 2019. The authors split the timeline at change points to read the trend cleanly. They then built a forecast model that mixes future population size with the latest stable rates. The projection runs to 2040, giving health planners a sense of the asthma load ahead and where services may strain.
pmc-10714548:
Hang Xu and a large team found a sugar-handling enzyme that helps prostate cancer grow in a 2023 study. Cancer cells rewire their fuel use, and blocking that wiring can kill them. The team screened a family of enzymes that start sugar breakdown and landed on one, ADPGK.

That enzyme was the only one in its family both raised in prostate tumors and tied to worse survival. In lab and animal tests, raising it sped cell growth and spread, while blocking it slowed both. It works by binding a partner protein and switching on a growth path, which lifts sugar burning. The authors name the enzyme as a target for new prostate cancer drugs.
pmc-10715748:
Mailani Dwi Hidayati and colleagues published a small cross-sectional study in 2023. They studied people with asthma triggered by house dust mites. Mite allergens can damage airway linings with protein-cutting activity. The body has natural blockers against that activity. Two blockers are alpha-one antitrypsin and cystatin C. The team asked whether their levels differ in asthma.

The study compared ten patients with ten healthy volunteers. Blood tests measured blocker activity and blocker amounts. Most measures showed no clear difference between the groups. One measure did differ. Cystatin C blocking activity was higher in patients. The authors present a narrow, careful result. Larger studies would be needed to explain what it means.
pmc-10716248:
Kug Jin Jeon and three co-authors teach deep learn tools to call true touch tween jaw drain and back tooth from flat X-rays. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Flat films are the stock first read past back tooth pulls, but true touch needs a cone scan. Nine hundred one teeth were read by both ways to set truth, near half in touch.

Three learn tools were built and graded on truth, hit, and miss marks. The best hit near four fifths true in whole, with high marks on both touch and clear calls. The team pitch it when cone scans can not run.
pmc-10716848:
Milan Plećaš and co-authors survey parasitoid wasps in oilseed rape fields in Serbia in a 2023 study. Oilseed rape is a major crop for oil and animal feed, and it draws many insect pests. Most past work on its parasitoids came from western, central, and northern Europe.

Over two years the team sampled thousands of primary and secondary parasitoid specimens. The survey aimed at the wider wasp community, not only wasps tied to known crop pests. Flowers rich in pollen and nectar may draw many other species into the fields. The records fill a southern Europe gap and help growers judge the natural pest control these wasps may provide.
pmc-10716948:
Emily Hladkowicz and four co-authors ask frail older adults what matters after surgery in a 2023 study. Older patients have surgery often and face rough transitions from hospital to home. Their own priorities for that handover are rarely the starting point for improvement work.

Twelve adults aged sixty-five and older with clear frailty signs took part in phone interviews. All had stayed in hospital for planned surgery and then gone home. Thematic analysis built five themes from their accounts. Support from family and services loomed large, captured in the title's quote about not coping alone. The findings give discharge planners a patient-centered checklist. Better transitions may prevent the setbacks that send frail patients back to hospital.
pmc-10717148:
Marta Wróblewska-Zierhoffer and co-authors counted second cancers in Polish patients treated for a melanoma of the eye, in a 2023 study. Uveal melanoma is rare, and whether its patients face unusual rates of other cancers matters for follow-up care. The team reviewed six hundred and forty-four patients registered at a Poznań center between 1991 and 2017, checking department records and the regional cancer registry.

One in five patients, one hundred and twenty-six people, had an additional primary malignancy. In most, it appeared after the eye tumor; in over a third, before. Skin, breast, and lung were the commonest sites. By the study's close, most of these patients had died, and deaths from the second cancer outnumbered deaths from spread of the eye melanoma. The rate is higher than most groups report, and settling whether these patients are predisposed to particular cancers needs a larger database.
pmc-10717448:
Eleven authors review equity in headache care worldwide in this 2023 paper, the second part of a series. Headache disorders are common and disabling everywhere, yet organized care and modern drugs reach patients very unevenly across countries.

The review compares headache services in low, middle, and high income countries under a tiered service model. Barriers repeat across settings: few trained staff, low awareness, cost, and weak policies. Drug safety and access to new treatments are covered, with attention to pregnancy and child health. Telemedicine is offered as one lever for equity, since remote visits cut travel and waiting where internet access allows.
pmc-10717748:
Bingyu Wang and co-authors tested electrical acupoint stimulation in brain aneurysm surgery in a 2023 trial. Clipping an aneurysm through the skull can cause sharp swings in blood pressure and heart rate, risking rupture. High opioid doses calm that stress but bring vomiting and slow waking.

Forty-two patients were randomised to real or sham stimulation at three acupoints, from before anaesthesia to the end of surgery. The real group needed less of the opioid remifentanil. Blood pressure and heart rate were lower at key surgical moments, brain injury markers were lower, and a protective enzyme was higher. The method may protect the brain, they conclude.
pmc-10718448:
Ramia Zakhour and co-authors study HPV vaccine hesitancy among parents in Lebanon in this 2023 paper. HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection and a cause of cervical cancer. The vaccine is safe and effective, yet many parents hold back.

Questionnaires went to parents at two public and two private schools near Beirut. Of 306 replies, 185 parents knew of the vaccine, and most of them had not given it or planned to. Parents against the vaccine more often called vaccines needless or unsafe. Mothers and daughters were more open than fathers and sons. A missing doctor recommendation was a top stated reason for refusal. Cost and faith views mattered little.
pmc-10719248:
Swapping magnesium into a nickel iron oxide makes it split water better, report Nyemaga Malima and co-authors in a 2023 study. The team cooked up thin sheets of the mixed metal ferrite without solvents, tuning the nickel to magnesium balance across the full range.

One blend needed far less extra voltage to release hydrogen than the pure nickel version, and another blend led on the oxygen side. The sheets kept the same crystal structure throughout, so the gains came from the local chemistry around the nickel atoms. The authors present the materials as cheap, green candidates for clean hydrogen production.
pmc-10719348:
Maryam Ghahremani and Mahmoud Shahabadi give a sharp way to read wave modes in light chain guides. The study appeared in 2023. Such guides have stacked three-part forms and lossy stuff in their mix. Past reads need hunt for mixed roots on a mixed plane, which is slow and fault prone.

The new way pairs shop solver output with set math steps that stay in real values. It gives the mixed wave count with top care, even with light and stuff loss in play. A one-cell trick lets fine grids run on thin compute. Two test cases, one metal-like and one glass-like, matched past lab and math reads well.
pmc-10719648:
Children with middle ear infection often wait months for specialist care in Australia's public hospitals. Ali Altamimi and co-authors used an ear, nose, and throat telehealth service in 2023 to ask whether those waits harm children's behavior. Parents of forty-five referred children filled in a standard questionnaire on strengths and difficulties, and the team compared children seen within their target wait with those seen late.

Between a quarter and two fifths of the children scored in the borderline or abnormal range. Children seen late scored worse on emotional, conduct, peer, and total problem scales. Longer waits in days also tracked with more internalizing problems, such as anxiety and withdrawal. The authors call for changes to current practice.
pmc-10720048:
Masayuki Mishima and Kei-ichi Sugiyama weigh how to test mid-size peptide drugs for DNA damage. Their 2023 paper sits at a rule boundary: small chemical drugs must pass genotoxicity tests, while large biologic drugs skip them. Mid-size peptides, a rising drug class, borrow traits from both sides, and some carry unnatural amino acids that standard thinking never covered.

The authors argue the small-drug rulebook mostly fits, since these peptides are built and dosed more like chemicals. But they propose a few changes to the standard test set where peptide traits make the usual assays mislead. The paper is guidance for developers and regulators meeting this in-between class.
pmc-10725648:
Simone Ferretti and co-authors weigh, in a 2023 review, a back-path robot cut for prostate cancer and its hard points. The known cut is the gold path for local disease. The back path, from 2010, comes through the Douglas space and spares the front frames that hold pee control and sex force. Trials and pooled reads show a clear early gain in pee control, with like short and long cancer marks. One fear dogs the path: more cut-edge tumor finds, called margins, in the piece out.

That fear rests on thin proof, the review holds. Past reads clashed new back-path hands with old front-path pros. Fresh reads back the path as safe past low risk. Fine points for skill close the piece.
pmc-10725748:
Davina Wildemeersch and co-authors set out the PERISCOPE trial protocol in this 2023 paper. About one in ten surgery patients develops persistent pain after the operation. That pain is often nerve like and hard to treat. Finding high risk patients before surgery could focus preventive care where it matters most.

The trial will enroll 560 adults having planned surgery. Each completes a short holistic screening questionnaire before the operation. The study tests how well the answers predict persistent pain later. It also seeks the best cutoff score for entering a high vigilance care program. Other outcomes cover pain course and care use after surgery. The design is pragmatic, run inside normal hospital flow across surgical groups.
pmc-10725948:
Chiara Tomasoni and co-authors show in 2023 how acute myeloid leukemia bends the bone making plans of marrow support cells. This blood cancer floods the marrow with stalled young cells, wrecking normal blood making and reshaping the niche that shelters it. Stromal support cells supply that niche, giving rise to fat and bone forming cells.

Growing normal stromal cells beside leukemia cells in dishes, the team saw the support cells start down the bone path but fail to finish it. An early bone marker rose while late bone genes stayed silent. Normal blood stem cells caused no such stall, and the effect needed direct cell contact. Tracing the signal, the authors found leukemia switches on the Notch pathway inside the stromal cells, and that this activation drives part of the block. A marrow niche so skewed may help explain why leukemia thrives where healthy blood should form.
pmc-10726348:
Gebauer, Jensen, Rafehi, and Brockmöller test in twenty twenty-three whether drug shuttle proteins in cell membranes care about a molecule's handedness. Many drugs come in mirror forms, and the body often handles them differently, but membrane transport was little charted. The team measured uptake of many paired mirror forms through three related cation shuttles in cells.

Two shuttles showed strong handedness preferences for several compounds, often in opposite directions. The third was less picky, though it favoured one mirror form of one drug clearly. Combining a shuttle with a liver enzyme in the same cells added the two preferences together. The authors say transport handedness is real but sharply compound-specific, shaping drug levels in the body.
pmc-10728048:
Jee Young Lee, Ye Jun Lee, and Gyu Min Kong describe a surgical fix for a hip implant that would not seat in a 2023 case report. A 72 year old man had two stage revision surgery for an infected hip replacement, using a modular tumor style implant. Two months later the hip dislocated, and after a manual fix it dislocated again.

At the next revision, a dual mobility bearing was chosen to lower the risk. But the tight soft tissue around the joint blocked seating of the head into the socket. The team solved it by placing the head into the socket first, then assembling the stem part of the implant around it.
pmc-10729148:
Yuzo Suzuki and a large team test a blood ratio as a death risk marker in a rare lung disease. Their study from twenty twenty-three covers idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis. This progressive scarring disease mainly attacks the upper lobes. No established prognostic markers existed for it before.

Two hospital cohorts supplied just over one hundred twenty patients. White blood cell counts were checked at diagnosis and one year later. The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio tracked mortality risk after adjustments. Age and known severity measures were accounted for statistically. A simple blood ratio could help doctors judge urgency. Cheap routine tests gaining prognostic value matters for rare diseases. Larger studies can confirm the marker strength.
pmc-10729248:
Oula Norman and co-authors study in 2023 what collagen thirteen does in the lung and in lung scarring disease. Lack of this protein in people causes a muscle nerve illness with breathing trouble and low lung capacity. Cell scans also mark it in fat-storing lung cells tied to scar healing.

Stain tests placed the protein in wall cells of the air sacs in mouse lung, with faint marks in human scarred lung. Mice lacking the protein had larger lung capacity by more than ten percent. The team then gave such mice a scar-inducing drug to test whether lack of the protein raises risk of stiff lung disease.
pmc-10735448:
Jennifer Wolff, Diane Echavarria, and Laura Gitlin describe a study on advance care planning for older adults with memory loss, seen in primary care. Such planning lets people state their values and wishes for future care before they can no longer decide. Family caregivers often lead daily care but are left out of these talks.

The program, called SHARE, paired two hundred seventy-three patients with their caregivers in a trial. Half were offered a guided planning talk with trained staff. The report shares six-month results from caregiver surveys. It also covers ethics, readiness to decide for a loved one, and a tool to check the quality of recorded talks.
pmc-10735548:
Monika Oczkowska, Ellam Kulati, and Michal Myck compare how income relates to well-being in old age in Germany and Poland, in a 2023 study. The neighbours differ sharply in welfare design and in outcomes: far more older Poles report trouble making ends meet, and material and social deprivation past sixty-five runs about twice the German rate. The authors match regional and personal data to ask whether local quality cushions low income.

Early findings show the income-well-being link much stronger in Poland, and strongest of all among people in poor health. Where public services cannot be relied on, personal resources carry more weight. Oddly, controlling for local conditions changed the link in neither country, which suggests the nation-wide system, not the region, sets how much income matters. The study frames welfare context as the backdrop against which money buys well-being, or fails to.
pmc-10735648:
Laura Samuel and co-authors study food aid access for adults with disabilities in a 2023 paper. People with disabilities face more food insecurity and more barriers to enrolling in the SNAP food program. State rules on enrollment ease vary, and their effect was the question.

Using a national survey of low-income households, the team linked state policy traits to participation and food insecurity. Broad eligibility rules tied to higher participation among low-income people in the models. Results for the disability subgroup are detailed in the paper. The work argues that paperwork design is itself a health policy lever.
pmc-10735848:
Lisandra Mendoza and co-authors check a dementia rating tool in Hispanic older adults, a group where good measures are scarce. The tool, a modified Clinical Dementia Rating scale, rates daily function through a structured interview with someone who knows the patient, with no thinking tests involved. The team compared it against a standard activity scale in 260 people, some healthy and some with mild impairment, testing in each person's main language.

Different raters agreed well on the tool's scores, and the agreement held whether the interview ran in English or Spanish. Scores also matched the comparison scale closely, a sign the tool measures what it claims. The authors conclude the modified scale is a valid, reliable way to track function in Hispanic patients, which matters most in the early stages, when treatment can help most.
pmc-10735948:
Five authors test a loving-kindness meditation program for older adults in this 2023 study. Meditation is known to aid stress control, but whether this practice, which directs warm wishes to oneself, family, others, and all humanity, works for a socioeconomically diverse older group was open.

Fifty-nine adults were split into two groups under a waiting list design, with the second group starting later. Outcomes were tracked at baseline, after the course, and after journaling and rest periods. The program proved feasible and acceptable: fifty-four finished, and every participant rated the practice as good or better. Scores for both feasibility and acceptability ran high, supporting wider trials of the approach.
pmc-10736048:
Five authors study how Covid hit care staff in assisted living homes in a 2023 survey of chiefs. One hundred twenty-nine chiefs from a big aging study gave counts and talk views. Staff lack, pay for sick time, and staff worry form the core strain marks.

Homes that gave memory care saw more staff lack when guards sent sick staff home. Pay strain for time off and staff worry also tracked with gaps at work. Talk themes name lead acts toward staff, staff harm, and staff quit risk as the live threads.
pmc-10736148:
Leslie Hasche and co-authors published this education paper in 2023. It describes a university course on intergenerational justice: fairness between age groups, and within them, across a lifetime. Public debate often pits generations against each other over budgets, climate, housing, and care. The course instead teaches students to analyze those fights through justice theories. Versions of it have run for over nine years, for graduate students and older lifelong learners alike.

Sessions mix theory with activities that bring age groups into direct contact and problem-solving. Topics range from politics and ecological justice to health care and employment. Instructors and former students share which strategies worked to unsettle ageist assumptions. The authors argue that such courses do double duty. They teach a neglected branch of social justice, and they build real connections across ages. That makes the format a promising tool for gerontology education and for softening generational conflict narratives.
pmc-10736248:
Farida Ejaz and co-authors describe a hard start to a prevention trial in this 2023 conference paper. The team worked with Utah Adult Protective Services on a phone-based service for caretaker neglect. They focused on cases that had been closed as unclear, since neglect often came back in that group.

The plan was to link both victims and caretakers with local services that could meet their needs. That support, they hoped, would cut repeat reports of neglect over time. In practice, signing people up for the study proved very hard. Their account is useful for teams who run trials with adults at risk and the staff who serve them.
pmc-10736348:
Peiyuan Zhang and co-authors factored in 2023 a comfort scale for people dying with dementia. The fourteen-item scale is widely used to judge end-of-life care in nursing homes, but its shape when family or staff answer was little tested. The team read 476 answers, from staff and family of long-stay residents with moderate to severe impairment in Indiana and Maryland homes, at the start of a federal trial.

Three clusters rose for both answer kinds. Distress items like restlessness and fear grouped first. Dying signs like choking and gurgling grouped second. Serenity, calm, and peace formed a well-being third. Some pain items straddled two groups. The team reads the scale as sound, with three true dimensions of the dying experience.
pmc-10736548:
Jennifer Sauer and co-authors report a 2023 AARP research project on the economic cost of menopause. Many women pay a lot to ease symptoms like hot flashes, night sweats, brain fog, and mood swings. Some cut work hours or leave jobs when symptoms grow severe. The project set out to measure that burden.

The first phase held six online focus groups with US women aged forty and older. Groups were split by stage of the transition, from early change to post-menopause. Themes matched past research: symptoms disrupt daily life, and treatments do not always help. Later phases of the project build on these talks with wider surveys.
pmc-10736648:
Jennifer Lister and co-authors test whether hearing loss changes how depression and thinking skills relate in older adults, in a 2023 study. All three problems are common in later life, and hearing loss is the strongest fixable dementia risk in midlife, while depression leads in late life. The sample held 65 adults averaging 74 years.

Two hearing tests, mood scores, and two thinking tests were measured in an ongoing study of early decline. Neither hearing nor thinking scores alone predicted depression. The pairing did: a significant interaction showed the depression-thinking link bending with hearing level. The authors say ears may quietly shape the mind-mood connection, and hearing care could matter for both.
pmc-10736748:
Jacklyn Kohon, Katsuya Tanaka, Dani Himes, and co-authors map heat risk for older adults in Portland, Oregon, in this 2023 study. Extreme heat hits low-income older adults and people of color hardest. Risk grows with rented housing, no air cooling, chronic illness, and living alone.

The team built two risk indexes for the Portland area. One used area-level data drawn from regional records, and the other used survey answers collected after the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome. The two maps of risk did not line up well. Only one area ranked among the most at risk on both, and it held the region's largest cluster of age- and income-restricted rental housing. The authors argue that heat aid should target the people and places in most need rather than spread evenly, which makes relief both fairer and cheaper.
pmc-10736848:
Kening Jiang and co-authors link hearing loss to fatigue in a 2023 survey study. Tiredness tracks with worse thinking, weaker bodies, and lower quality of life. Straining to hear may drain energy, but past studies drew mostly on clinic patients, who may feel that drain more than most.

The analysis covered 3,031 middle-aged and older adults in a national United States survey from 2015 to 2018. About one in four had hearing loss by a standard tone test. Those with hearing loss were about twice as likely to report feeling tired on most days, or nearly every day. The link held after many health and social factors were counted.
pmc-10736948:
Lingming Chen and co-authors link anxiety to indoor falls among older adults living at home, in a research paper from 2023. One in three seniors falls each year, and mental factors behind falls are underexplored. The study followed 359 adults aged sixty-five to ninety-five in central Massachusetts.

Anxiety was scored at the start, and falls were logged on monthly calendars with follow-up interviews. Rates ran near forty-one indoor and forty-six outdoor falls per hundred person-years. Each extra anxiety point raised indoor fall odds by about six percent, even after adjusting for health and history. Outdoor falls showed no such link. The authors suggest anxiety screening in fall prevention.
pmc-10737048:
Ad Maulod and his three co-authors, publishing in 2023, study how family caregivers in Singapore live with filial piety, the cultural duty to respect and care for older relatives. Policy in many Asian societies leans on this duty, and earlier work shows that meeting its expectations can protect a caregiver's mental health while failing to meet them can harm it. The team interviewed 34 caregivers of older people with physical limits, chosen to span good and bad experiences.

They find the same duty felt very different depending on the caregiver's situation. Those with hard experiences described care as sacrifice, expected and owed, with little freedom to choose. Those with good experiences described care as love grown from a close bond, backed by strong family support. The authors argue that calling care natural hides this gap and discourages burdened caregivers from seeking help. They urge policies that support both sides.
pmc-10737148:
Kathleen Unroe, John Cagle, and Mary Ersek describe a trial called UPLIFT, from twenty twenty-three. The trial tests a way to improve care for nursing home residents with mid to late stage dementia. Two staff in each home get special training and serve as palliative care leads. All other staff get basic training in comfort care as well.

Sixteen nursing homes take part, and the trial ends in twenty twenty-five. The leads screen residents and bring in outside comfort care doctors and nurses when needed. The authors report real problems, such as leads leaving their jobs. They also note hard talks with the regular medical teams.
pmc-10737348:
Clio Cheng and Vivian Lou test health messages for wearable robots in a 2023 study of older adults in Hong Kong. Soft robots that aid weak muscles could help elders live at home longer. Take-up depends on how the pitch is framed and what users value.

A trial with 154 adults aged fifty to seventy-four varied two message traits. Some pitches stressed gains, others losses; some spoke of near gains, others of far ones. Age, gender, and muscle risk did not move intent to use. Two cultural values did: stress on self-direction and on group bonds of equals. A third value, duty to the group, changed how message frames worked. Culture, the authors say, must shape robot pitches.
pmc-10737448:
Takashi Amano and co-authors ask whether knowing one's dementia diagnosis brings more social support, and whether the gain varies by race. In theory, a clear label should help a person draw the support they need. Hard proof, above all across racial and ethnic groups, has been thin.

Their 2023 study uses the Health and Retirement Study, with thousands of person-year records for people with dementia. Knowing the label was tied to more informal support and more formal support overall. The formal support gain did not clearly appear for non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic groups, though. The authors read this as a sign that the benefits of diagnosis are not shared evenly.
pmc-10737548:
Jennifer Schrack, Amal Wanigatunga, and Nancy Glynn frame, in a 2023 symposium paper, new ways to read movement as a sign of health in older adults. How much people move, how much energy they burn, and how well they move have long foretold health and long life. Past work stressed speed and effort level. New work aims to sharpen these measures, drawn from lab tests and from motion sensors worn in daily life, to sort risk with more care.

Five talks in the session use large United States groups. One links heart rhythm shifts, activity, and thought health. One ties hand and body motor skill to brain size on scans. Others tie activity amount and spread to dementia, and match effort measures to heart outcomes and death. The set shows how fine movement data can flag risk early.
pmc-10737648:
Ferdinand Delgado and co-authors examine how severe Alzheimer's dementia changes the link between executive function and falls. Their 2023 study uses data from several hundred older adults with intact thinking, mild impairment, or dementia. Executive function covers planning, attention switching, and related skills tested by standard tasks.

An unexpected pattern emerged. Among people with Alzheimer's dementia, worse executive scores went with a lower reported history of falls. The authors note that few falls were reported for the severe group, which may reflect less walking or less reporting rather than true safety. In people without dementia, some tests did track fall history as expected. The finding warns against reading fall risk in advanced dementia with tools built for healthier adults.
pmc-10737848:
Needing daily help does not strain every wallet or spirit equally, and Lei Chen asks how age bends the strain in a 2023 California study. The data merge a 2019-2020 state survey of long-term services and supports with a health interview survey, covering two thousand thirty people who need such care.

Young and middle-aged participants struggled most to make ends meet. Middle-aged and older ones rated their health worst, while the young reported the severest psychological distress. Difficulty with household tasks, and piling up several kinds of difficulty, meant more financial strain and more distress, and both links ran significantly stronger for the young. Chen argues the findings cut across the usual aging and disability silos: support networks should be coordinated for people of all ages, not split by birthday.
pmc-10737948:
Julia Toman, Charity Lewis, Victora Sanchez, and Michelle Arnold studied what older Black women know and believe about hearing care when they come to an ear, nose, and throat clinic for help. Older Black adults in the United States face known barriers to care, and Black women often report past bad experiences that breed mistrust of providers.

The team mixed two methods: interviews with fifteen women and a hearing beliefs questionnaire completed by eighty-six. The interviews surfaced experiences of racism in health care, the role of religion in seeking help, and a strong sense that treating hearing loss matters. The surveys matched: women showed little stigma about hearing aids and little resistance to treatment. The authors say clinics can refer such patients to audiology with confidence.
pmc-10738048:
Christian and co-authors check whether racial gaps in end-of-life care persist among older Americans with like access to care. Their 2023 study uses Medicare claims from 2021 and asks who chose hospice care, who talked with a doctor about end-of-life wishes, and who got formal planning services. Hospice quality was scored from family survey star ratings.

Black, Asian, and Hispanic patients were each less likely than white patients to choose hospice. Patients who were not white also landed more often in low-rated hospices, even within the same zip code as white patients. In those hospices they got fewer visits in the last days of life. The team found no large gaps in recorded planning talks. They urge the Medicare program to keep watching these trends.
pmc-10738148:
Jessika Dayrit and three co-authors study childhood trauma among US veterans in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Harmful events in childhood, called adverse childhood experiences, shape health for decades. Most research covers the general public, not those who served in the military. The team used survey data from a national health system run by the CDC. Their sample held more than seven thousand adults, weighted to match the population.

They compared veterans' later health by how many adverse experiences they reported. Risk climbed in steps. Those with four or more such experiences had about four times the odds of poor outcomes as those with none. The analysis accounted for income and education. The findings argue for trauma-aware care in veteran health services.
pmc-10738248:
Melinda Heinz and Frank Houghton apply a place-and-health model to Irish Men's Sheds, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Sheds are shared workshops where older men meet, make things, and talk. The model asks how a place, its meaning, and its social life support well-being. Talks were held with thirty-seven members aged sixty-five and over in County Limerick.

Welcome and fairness stood out most in what the men said. Members stressed that each man who walks in should feel wanted and should be seen for what he can offer. Men who lived alone said the shed eased loneliness. Readers see the social side, more than the benches and tools, as the core health gain.
pmc-10738448:
Dylan Serpas and co-authors examine how disability traits shape experiences of ableist slights among middle-aged and older adults. Small daily slights add up to real health burdens. Their pattern across disability types was unexplored.

Over two hundred adults with disabilities answered online surveys. Most reported mobility or physical conditions. They rated how visible their disability appears to others. Experiences of subtle discrimination were recorded in detail. Mental health symptoms were measured alongside. Younger middle-aged adults showed stronger harm links. Visibility changed how often slights were reported. The findings refine support for aging disabled adults. They also guide anti-bias training in care and work and care settings.
pmc-10738748:
Tina Kilaberia, Yuanyuan Hu, Edward Ratner, and Janice Bell explored how older adults used technology during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a study published in 2023. Digital tools spread fast in those years, but how the shift felt for older people was less clear. The team mixed a survey with in-depth interviews.

Eighteen older adults took part, split into high and low scorers on a standard technology-use survey. Nearly all needed help from family, friends, or paid services at some point. Those with stronger skills ordered goods online more often and used health portals more. Several in the lower group described thinking difficulties that held them back. Two themes ran through the interviews: many ways to get things done, and simply getting through it. Support, the authors imply, matters as much as the tools.
pmc-10738948:
Allie Schierer and co-authors follow long term care choices among older adults in a 2023 study. As thought and body fade, older people must pick between a care home and help at home, and a web tool exists to guide that planning.

Nearly three hundred adults who used the tool were surveyed over eighteen months. Two thirds changed their plan at least once. Early rounds flipped most, then choices settled with time. Swings clustered around shifts in family carers, the COVID period, and health turns. The team urge doctors to revisit the choice every six to twelve months.
pmc-10739048:
Ling Xu and Minjaal Raval published this gerontology study in 2023. It reports on a program that pairs Asian American grandparents with their grandchildren for guided life review, six weekly hour-long talks held in person or remotely. Such bonding matters in Asian families and supports grandparents' health. The paper focuses on the grandchildren's side, analyzing the written reflections that twelve of them filed after each session.

The grandchildren described strong positives: feeling closer, learning their grandparents' life stories, and engaging more. They also shared what helped the talks flow, including taking notes, using the manual's guiding questions, and bringing in translators. Difficulties came up too, such as over-explaining, language gaps, and topics that felt too broad. The authors judge the program promising for strengthening ties between generations.
pmc-10739348:
