Fengqi Jiang and co-authors chart three decades of research on adeno-associated virus vectors for gene therapy in a 2023 bibliometric study. The small virus became gene therapy's favorite delivery truck for its safety and efficiency. Six thousand papers from 1991 to 2022 map the field's growth.

Output climbed steadily, with the United States producing most papers and the deepest citation record. A handful of authors and one specialist journal anchor the literature. Hot topics now cluster on gene editing, gene structure, and CRISPR pairings, plus virus therapy for specific inherited diseases. The map shows a field maturing through widening international cooperation.
pmc-10739448:
Mary Janevic and co-authors test whether older adults in an underserved city area will take health lessons by podcast. Podcasts are cheap, warm, and easy to replay, yet health programs for older adults seldom use them. Their 2023 trial sits in Detroit, where community coaches teach self-care skills to mostly Black older adults. Six podcast episodes, with a peer host and community guests, pair with the group meetings.

Eight trial board members, a mix of older adults and staff, heard the first three episodes. All said the episodes were fun, fit their lives, and taught the skills well on a five-point scale. Warm host chat, a can-do tone, and true stories won praise. More kinds of voice were asked for. Full trial grades on change will come later.
pmc-10739548:
Philip Greulich reviews, in a solo 2023 paper, how math models can help stem cell research when they are used with care. Cell biology now uses models in a fast-growing share of its papers. Too often, the model is a gloss: it is fit after the fact to back a result staff already had. That use adds little and can even mislead. Greulich argues that a model earns its place when it answers a sharp question or foretells the result of a process.

The review lays out when to model, how to set one up, and how to read its output with care. Two traps get stress: fit that hugs the data too tight, and claims of broad laws that outrun the proof. The guide is aimed at lab staff who want more from a model than a stamp.
pmc-10739848:
Yong Du and co-authors study aroma formation in Daqu, a starter used for a strong aroma style of Chinese liquor, in a 2023 paper. The hot phase of its fermentation is thought to be the key time for aroma. Yet how substances change during that phase was little known.

The team paired chemical profiling with microbe sequencing across the hot phase. Profiles after five and nine days looked alike, and amino acid paths stood out. Some aroma compounds rose while esters fell. Dozens of microbe genera took part, through core energy and amino acid pathways. The work maps how microbes drive aroma.
pmc-10740048:
Saba Khursheed and ten co-authors wrote this 2023 review on silver nanoparticles made by living things, and their promise for fish farming. Silver particles kill bacteria, viruses, and fungi, and making them with plants or microbes avoids harsh chemistry. Fish farms battle constant infections and water quality problems, so a green antimicrobial draws real interest.

The review covers how the particles are made, how they fight germs, and how they can clean water by helping remove pollutants and heavy metals. It then turns to the obstacles: unclear rules, questions of long-term safety for fish and eaters, and the particles' own footprint in water systems. The authors judge the potential high but the evidence unfinished. They map the research still needed before farms can adopt the particles with confidence.
pmc-10740148:
Magdalena Zemelka-Wiacek and Marek Jutel review where allergen immunotherapy stands and where it heads next. Their 2023 review notes a paradox. The treatment is over a century old, yet it remains the only allergy therapy that can cure rather than merely suppress symptoms. So it keeps a central place in modern care. Its current reinvention runs through personalized and precision medicine.

Five engines drive the change, the authors argue: mobile health tools, component-resolved diagnostics that pinpoint the exact allergen molecule, newly validated biomarkers, advanced data management, and next-generation preparations of the therapy itself. The review gathers the key advances in each area and sketches what future treatments may look like when they combine.
pmc-10740848:
Andreia Garcês and Isabel Pires review what is known about drug-resistant bacteria living inside Europe's wild carnivores, in this 2023 review. Resistance is usually seen as a hospital and farm problem. Wolves, foxes, otters, and bears, though, can carry resistant strains too.

Wild meat-eaters meet these drugs through tainted food and water, contact with farm stock and pets, and human activity in their home ground. Once they carry the strains, they hold the germs and move them across wide landscapes. That harms wild nature, makes guarding species at risk harder, and can loop back to people through shared ground and through germs that pass from beasts to humans. The review gathers the proof spread across Europe, species by species. Its point: keeping watch on wildlife belongs in any serious plan against drug resistance.
pmc-10741048:
Roberto Bava and co-authors present a 2023 study on whether a bergamot fruit extract can shield honeybees from a common insecticide. Bee losses from pesticide poisoning are a serious problem for beekeeping, and poor nutrition weakens bees' defenses and detox systems. The extract is rich in plant polyphenols with known protective effects.

Caged bees were fed measured doses under controlled conditions. The insecticide alone, at a set dose, killed all twenty bees in a cage within a day. Groups that also received the extract were tracked for survival and other signs. The study tests whether a dietary supplement can blunt a pesticide's harm, a route that could matter for managed hives near farmland.
pmc-10741548:
Marcela Tenorio and co-authors present BENDI, a set of game-like touchscreen tasks for measuring young minds in children with Down syndrome. Standard cognitive testing matters for diagnosis and for designing help, but good tools are unevenly available across rich and poor countries. The battery turns four classic experimental tasks into games probing self-control, attention, motor skill, and memory for context. It was tried with 68 Chilean children from 20 months to 12 years old.

Consistency checks rated the tasks adequate to excellent. Their internal structure and their agreements and disagreements with other measures matched theory, and scores rose with age as expected. Because the games lean little on language or local culture, the authors hope they can travel to other countries without heavy adaptation, widening access to fair cognitive assessment.
pmc-10741648:
Renata Markiewicz and co-authors review the protein reelin and its role in schizophrenia in a 2023 paper. Genetic studies tie reelin to mental health, and reduced reelin expression may limit dendrite growth, disturb new neuron formation, and wire brain circuits wrongly. Those changes could feed the thinking problems seen in the illness.

Reelin also shapes synaptic plasticity, the strengthening and weakening of connections that underlies learning. The review gathers what is known about this signaling path in schizophrenia. A clear neuronal marker could in time support earlier diagnosis and more targeted treatment for a complex disorder.
pmc-10741748:
Maria Waltenberger leads a team on focused radiation for spine metastases. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses a boost at the same time concept. It deals with cancer folks with few spread sites.

Cases at one center over near a decade were reviewed. Most got the boost plan in five dose sessions. Local control rates at one and two years were high. Spine break freedom was also high at those marks. Bone weakness raised break risk by a lot. Just one grave late side effect was seen.  Survival rates were also tracked after the boost care.
pmc-10741948:
Eirini Tomara and co-authors review tongue tie and breastfeeding in a 2023 paper. Tongue tie means the band under a baby's tongue is short or tight. The limit on tongue movement can make feeding painful or ineffective. Some dyads end feeding early when the problem goes unaddressed.

Experts still dispute how the condition should be defined and graded. Cutting the band is one option, but when to cut lacks shared rules. Some argue diagnosis should rest on anatomy alone, others on feeding impact. The review urges support for mothers facing feeding trouble either way.
pmc-10742048:
Parigi leads a team checking cancer rates in bowel disease patients under tight modern management in a 2023 cohort paper. Inflammatory bowel disease raises cancer risk, especially in the colon. Treat-to-target care plus regular surveillance is the modern standard.

Two Milan centers followed thousands of patients for about twenty thousand patient-years. Cancer incidence matched the general population overall. Gut cancers were commonest, with colon cancer slightly above expected rates. Cancers under surveillance were mostly caught at early stages. Deaths were few, and most were cancer-related. The authors credit the management strategy for the low, early-caught burden. Structured follow-up appears to pay off. Long-term vigilance remains essential.
pmc-10742448:
Patients with certain inflammatory muscle diseases carry antibodies against a protein called Ro52, and Akira Yoshida and co-authors ask whether the pattern of that response splits patients into meaningful groups. They studied 122 patients with anti-synthetase antibodies and 34 with anti-MDA5 antibodies. The key split was whether Ro52 antibodies appeared alone or together with the broader Ro/SSA response.

The lone pattern was the most common in both diseases. In the anti-synthetase group, either Ro52 pattern went with a characteristic skin sign. In the anti-MDA5 group, the lone pattern marked patients who arrived with failing breathing and who survived less well overall. The authors suggest the lone response could help stratify patients, while candidly noting that its added value over simply testing Ro52 was not evident in their data.
pmc-10743148:
Mohammed Alassiri and co-authors test an immune peptide in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis in a 2023 paper. The model, called EAE, mimics central nervous inflammation and myelin loss. PEPITEM is a peptide that blocks immune cells from crossing vessel walls. Female mice get it after the first signs of disease appear.

Treated mice show milder disease, the team reports. Fewer T cells enter the spinal cord, and levels of myelin and nerve proteins shift in spinal tissue. Two cytokine signals in blood and cord also fall. The authors suggest PEPITEM could calm inflammation in multiple sclerosis with fewer harms than synthetic drugs.
pmc-10743248:
Shamaila Masood and co-authors pack a desert plant extract into a skin gel and test its protective powers. The plant, Leptadenia pyrotechnica, has long been valued in folk care. The team brewed extracts in five solvents and measured how well each mopped up free radicals.

The methanol extract scored best, clearing 85.5 in a hundred of radicals in the test. Chemical assays and liquid chromatography confirmed rich phenolic content. They folded that extract into a carbomer emulgel and tracked its pH, spread, and feel over 90 days at several storage heats. Sun-protection readings came from a light-based method. The gel held up well, backing its use in skin care.
pmc-10743648:
Salim Sazzed and co-authors built a tracer for actin threads in cell tomograms in a 2023 paper. Actin forms a messy web that holds a cell's shape and drives its crawling. In cold electron scans the web runs in all directions amid noise and blind wedges, so hand tracing is slow and machine tracing is hard.

Their tool, Struwwel Tracer, grows short thread bits from seed points along the densest paths. A pruning map lets users judge which bits look real. Good bits then fuse step by step into long curved threads. On fake scans of a cell finger it scored high marks at all noise levels. On a real mouse cell scan its threads matched the known web well.
pmc-10744148: Mamoru Shibata wrote a 2023 essay on the push for tailored care in migraine, a disease of repeated severe headache attacks. Migraine ranks among the top causes of years lived with disability worldwide. Yet care still rests on broad trial and error for most patients, and Shibata asks what leaps are still needed before treatment can be matched to each person's own pattern of illness.
pmc-10744248:
Vladimir Kozlov and co-authors made a family of palladium complexes in 2023 and tested them against cancer cells. Metal complexes are a major hunting ground for new chemotherapy drugs, and ligand design decides much of their power. Their ligands pair two different donor groups in an unsymmetrical pincer shape.

The complexes formed readily both in solution and, notably, with no solvent at all, a greener solid-phase route. Standard spectroscopy and X-ray methods confirmed the structures. In cell tests, the complexes killed several solid and blood cancer lines strongly. One variant stood out and also triggered cell death in a drug-resistant leukaemia line, marking this complex type as promising.
pmc-10744848:
Umberto Lucia and co-authors view cancer growth through thermodynamics in this 2023 Europe PMC paper. Their tool is the constructal law, used here to study resonant heat transfer in cancer cells. The key quantity is the ratio of a cell's volume to its surface area.

They argue that cancer cells seek more surface area to shed heat more easily. As malignant cells begin to migrate and the tumor spreads, that expansion ratio falls. From this, they deduce that good therapy should control ion transport so as to raise the ratio and limit spread. The view favors anti-migratory and anti-invasive treatments over those that only slow cell division.
pmc-10745448:
Giulia Gorla and co-authors set out a workflow for studying measurement error in small near-infrared devices, in a 2023 paper. These pocket tools are spreading into many fields, but their accuracy and reliability get little attention. Errors in such data are complex, and the steps used to clean the signals can change them.

Their workflow is meant for labs that work with varied samples and tools. As a test case, they used solid pills and tablets, the kind drug labs handle daily. A variance-splitting method helped them spot which tool factors drive error. They also show how to sum up error patterns in images and a single index, so teams can judge cleaning steps fairly.
pmc-10745648:
Lorcan Mason and co-authors review how sleep and nutrition shape injury risk in adolescent athletes, in work from twenty twenty-three. Sleep drives growth, repair, and immunity, all vital for young athletes. Teen athletes sleep far less than guidelines advise, near six hours a night on average.

Adolescence shifts sleep timing later while raising sleep needs above the general public. Poor sleep hurts physical and mental performance, slows recovery, and raises injury risk. Nutrition interacts with sleep in that recovery load. The review gathers the evidence on both factors together, a pairing often studied apart. It sets groundwork for trials on sleep and diet plans that protect young athletes.
pmc-10745848:
Coal carries trace metals that end up in ash and air, and Bożena Karbowska and co-authors measure five of them in European coal. Their 2023 study compares samples from Poland with samples from a Russian deposit in the Kuzbass Basin. Thallium was read by a sensitive voltammetry method; the rest went through flame atomic absorption.

The non-European coal held about four times more thallium than the Polish coal, peaking at 0.636 milligrams per kilogram against 0.055. It also averaged more cadmium and zinc, while iron sat near 15 milligrams per kilogram in all samples. Thallium levels did not track the other metals. The authors note that such metals persist and build up in living things, which makes coal dust emissions worth watching.
pmc-10747548:
Germana Esposito and co-authors explain why Lake Avernus, an Italian volcanic lake wrapped in myth as a gate of Hades, turned red in March 2022. Their 2023 report starts from the lake's long record of color changes. The cause, found only lately, is a rotation of cyanobacterial blooms fed by natural nutrients and human pollution.

Their fast detection strategy fused satellite and drone views with on-site sampling and lab analysis. The red came from a bloom of a toxin-making cyanobacterium. From that strain the team isolated fourteen members of a peptide family, seven of them new to science. The paper also probes why the coloring comes and goes in cycles, and what the toxins mean for the lake.
pmc-10747648:
Matthew Donohue and co-authors extend a mass-based potency test to bird flu vaccines. Their 2023 study deals with flu vaccine strength checks, which now rest on a diffusion test that needs matched sera and standards. In a fast pandemic, shipping those parts stalls release. Their method, CombE-IDMS, reads potency by mass tools with no antibodies or reference stock, and past work matched the standard test on seasonal vaccines.

Here the test faced pre-pandemic H5N1 and H5N8 materials, plain and boosted, after forced stress by heat, acid, oxidation, and freeze-thaw. Results tracked the standard test across all stress forms. The authors pitch it as a rapid backup for pandemic supply.
pmc-10748148:
Jianlin Huang and four co-authors design in 2023 a miniature eight-port antenna array for 5G phones that work below six gigahertz. Phone frames leave little room, yet multi-antenna systems need many ports for fast links. Their element pairs a shaped radiator with three split-ring resonators on the metal frame.

Each element measures just 6.8 by 7 by 1 millimeters. Bandwidth spans 1.7 gigahertz, covering three major 5G bands at once. Tests cover one-hand grip effects, current flow, and tuning choices. Efficiency runs from forty to eighty percent, and port isolation beats twelve decibels. Link capacity estimates reach the mid-thirties in bits per second per hertz. The array suits slim handsets that need wideband reach.
pmc-10749448:
Valentina Migliorati, Paola D'Angelo, and Francesco Sessa redraw how salt ions dress themselves in water. Plain models spread water evenly around chloride and iodide ions, like rings on a target. Their 2023 study instead tracks the ions' lone pairs, the electron clouds that grip water hardest.

A subset of first-ring waters binds tight to those pairs, forming a tetrahedral dress. A new score, tied to grip strength, splits the first ring into a tight inner set and a loose outer set. The loose set is barely stirred by the ion's charge. Lone pairs, long ignored, turn out to run the show. The picture should sharpen how chemists model salt water.
pmc-10749948:
Brindley Hapuarachi and co-authors review in 2023 whether exercise can make tumors respond better to immune therapy. Exercise helps people with cancer live longer and feel better, and in mouse studies it slows tumor growth. Tumors full of active immune cells are called hot, while tumors that shut immune cells out are called cold and tend to resist immune drugs.

The review explains how exercise frees immune cells into the blood, changes the signals around a tumor, and may fix its blood vessels. Early proof from animal work suggests training can shift a cold tumor toward a hot state. The authors stress that human trials must now test the idea, since it could extend immune therapy to patients whose tumors now resist it.
pmc-10750048:
Murillo and co-authors report how tagging antibodies with biotin sharpens an optical biosensor in a 2023 paper. Biotin, a small vitamin, locks onto the protein streptavidin with unusual strength, and that grip is a workhorse connector in biotechnology. Interferometric biosensors read binding events as shifts in light, and their sensitivity sets what they can detect.

The team attached biotin to an antibody against a common lab protein at several ratios and tracked how the labeling aged. Swapping the plain antibody for the tagged one improved detection of the target protein four-fold. The setup also stood comparison with ELISA, the standard lab assay. Tagged antibodies brought steadier, more repeatable sensing layers, and a design bonus: any biotin-tagged antibody can plug into the same sensor frame, so one instrument can retarget many analytes.
pmc-10752348:
Lu Pan and six co-authors published a software paper in twenty twenty-three presenting Ursa, an automated toolbox for single-cell multiomics analysis. Single-cell data have exploded, but many biologists lack the coding depth to analyze them. Ursa wraps six automated workflows into one R package covering genomics, transcriptomics, epigenetics, proteomics, immunomics, and spatial data.

After quantification, the package runs quality control, dimension reduction, clustering, trajectory inference, and gene-set enrichment with minimal user effort. Results arrive as ready outputs rather than raw code homework. The authors aim to close the expertise gap so bench scientists can exploit their own data. Ursa is freely available from a public GitHub repository for anyone to install.
pmc-10753548:
Whitehurst and Hall watch sapphire's raw ingredient crystallize by a route nobody had seen, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Corundum, crystalline aluminum oxide, is grown industrially with molybdenum oxide flux. What takes place inside that layered system was unobserved till now. This work is the first direct look at it.

Direct observation brought three steps to light for the team. An intermediate compound forms where the layers touch. It forms at moderate heat in the run. That layer then melts as the heat rises more. In the end it decomposes into corundum at higher temperature. The yield is pale bluish-gray crystals. Their color was gauged with care by the team. The authors name this the molten intermediate decomposition mechanism. The reagents match decades of flux growth practice in the field. So past syntheses used this same hidden pathway, and did not know it.
pmc-10753748:
Suryyia Manzoor and co-authors present a 2023 study on a magnetic catalyst that cleans polluted water under visible light. The composite joins tungsten disulfide and a vanadium compound on iron oxide particles, so a magnet can pull it back out after use. Three targets were tested: a cancer-linked dye, a common weed killer, and Escherichia coli bacteria.

Lab checks confirmed the crystals, shapes, and heat behavior of the material. Under visible light for three hours, it broke down about 96 percent of the dye and 98 percent of the weed killer at their best pH levels. Scavenger tests pointed to hydroxyl radicals doing the damage. The study also measured how strongly the catalyst suppressed the bacteria.
pmc-10755748:
Anna Scheeder and five co-authors watch drug carriers meet bacteria at single-cell scale in a 2023 paper. The carriers are fusogenic liposomes, fat bubbles that can merge with cell walls. They may ferry antibiotics into hard-to-reach Gram-negative bacteria. How each carrier acts on a cell was poorly known.

The team used sharp microscopes to film carriers on two bacteria types. Carriers merged with the outer wall of Gram-negative cells. On Gram-positive cells they mostly stuck or slipped lipids inside. Longer wall sugars made full merges less likely in the first type. Merged lipids weakened the wall and let a second drug work. The work shows bulk tests miss key single-cell effects.
pmc-10758648:
Marano wrote in twenty twenty-three an editorial on patients who develop both stomach and colorectal cancers as separate diseases. Colorectal cancer is the most common second cancer in stomach cancer patients, and the reverse also holds. Better tests and treatments mean more patients live to face a second cancer. Marano discusses a recent study of such dual cases. It compared cancers found at the same time with those found months apart.

Cases found later fared better than cases found together. Stomach cancer stage strongly shaped outcomes in the study. Surgery to remove stomach and colon tumors predicted longer survival. Many second cancers appear within five years of the first. Marano urges early detection, surgery when feasible, and close follow-up. Larger studies are still needed, he concludes.
pmc-10772248:
Walid Al-Qerem and co-authors check whether two Arabic asthma surveys can be trusted, in a 2023 study. Asthma is common and weighs heavily on daily life. Arabic tools exist to rate symptom control and quality of life. But few studies had tested whether those tools measure well.

The team gave both surveys to 314 adults with asthma, most of them women. They used two forms of factor analysis to see how the questions grouped. One survey fit a three-part pattern and the other a single score. Sound tools matter because doctors and researchers rely on the scores to judge care. The study gives Arabic-speaking clinics a tested base for both surveys.
pmc-10772348:
An antifungal drug picked from the medicine cabinet kills only the tumor cells that carry two broken copies of a gene, in a 2023 study by Yenal B. Lakes and co-authors. The tumors are cutaneous neurofibromas, skin growths that appear in nearly every person with neurofibromatosis type 1, sometimes by the thousand, with no approved drug treatment.

The team built the tumors' cell model from a patient's stem cells, editing the second gene copy to mimic how the tumors lose it. Those precursor cells were screened against a library of approved drugs. The antifungal econazole killed the double-mutant cells while sparing single-mutant ones, and its cream form triggered death in mouse and human tumor grafts too. The repurposed drug earns further testing.
pmc-10827848:
Rocco Pizzarelli and co-authors test a growth factor in a mouse model of autism in a 2024 paper. The mice lack the Neuroligin 3 gene and show the social deficits seen in autism spectrum disorders. No current drug eases most such symptoms, so new options are needed.

The team gave the mice IGF-2, a protein that crosses into the brain and aids cognition. Treatment reversed the faults in social interaction and in telling new mice from familiar ones. Usual synaptic signals in a key hippocampus area did not change, yet cells grew more excitable. The authors flag IGF-2 as a candidate tool for social deficits, pending more work on how it acts.
pmc-10837848:
Jia-Li Yu, Zhen Li, Bo Zhang and colleagues report a young Chinese woman with Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease, a rare self-limiting inflammation of the lymph nodes, in 2024. She had recurring fever and swollen neck nodes, and a biopsy confirmed the diagnosis.

Her blood showed raised inflammatory markers including IL-6 and interferon gamma, signs of past or recent cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus exposure, and shifts in T cell counts. Steroid treatment brought relief. Alongside the case, the authors review how viral infection and autoimmune responses may drive the disease, with T cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells releasing cytokines that inflame the nodes. The review aims to help clinicians recognise this often-missed condition.
pmc-10852048:
Julio Plaza-Diaz and co-authors introduce, in a 2024 editorial, a research collection on the molecular machinery of obesity and its partner diseases. Obesity is growing worldwide and counts as a major health concern. Its causes braid diet, behavior, schooling, and genes.

The editors highlight pathways inside fat cells that govern how they mature. Two signaling chains and their crosstalk help decide whether fat tissue expands. Obesity then drags other illnesses with it, from high blood sugar and blood fats to heart disease. Framing obesity as a molecular disease, not a character flaw, guides the collection. The editorial maps the mechanisms the gathered papers explore.
pmc-10985548:
Chee San Tong and ten co-authors study how two cell skeleton nets, actin and microtubules, move as a group and talk to each other, in a paper from 2024. That teamwork is key to cell shape and motion, yet its rules are hard to pull apart.

Using waves that travel across the cell skin in mast cells, the team found one bridging protein acts early to start actin waves. When microtubules shrink, they free that bridge, which then seeds new actin growth nearby. Loss of the bridge blocked waves and hurt cell split and travel as well.
pmc-10990248:
Maria Edwards and co-authors test whether a high-fat, low-carb diet can be used safely in adults healing from a brain injury. Their study, dated 2023 in its own text, draws on animal work that hints ketosis may limit further harm to the brain. Human proof was thin, so the team ran a small trial of whether the plan can work at all.

Patients in the weeks after a brain injury were offered six weeks of the diet, with added fats from a set source. The goal was to lift a blood marker of ketosis past a set line and hold it there. Some patients were tube-fed and some ate meals, with matched products for each path. The team logged how well the diet was kept and every ill effect that came up.
pmc-11225448:
Infertility weighs heaviest where large families are the norm, and Emily Groene and co-authors survey women seeking treatment in Dodoma, Tanzania, in a study whose text is dated 2023. One hundred sixty-eight women aged eighteen to forty-nine answered questions and had their medical records reviewed to sort the cause of their infertility: ovarian, tubal, uterine, or male and other factors.

The causes did not sort neatly by age, behavior, or history. One link stood out: about thirty-one percent of the women carried a diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease, and those women had nearly double the prevalence of tubal-factor infertility after adjustment. The team also asked what blocks treatment, distance, cost, and knowledge among them, and compared barriers across the women's home regions. The authors press for prevention of pelvic infection as infertility policy.
pmc-11532548:
Li and colleagues propose in 2024 a federated learning design for judging credit risk without pooling private financial data. Federated systems train locally and merge models centrally, but communication costs balloon with uneven data like default records. Their method adjusts the model's receptive field during feature extraction. It also builds a fusion scheme that blends local and global features with fewer transmissions.

In experiments, the design kept accuracy while cutting communication rounds by about four-fifths. Dynamic kernels allocated weights to suit varied default patterns. The authors present the framework as a cheaper path to privacy-preserving credit scoring.
pmc-11536948:
Zheng and co-authors test a medicinal fungus extract against stomach cancer cells. Stomach cancer is among the most common digestive cancers. Once it spreads, standard treatments lose much of their power. Poria cocos, known as Fu Ling, is a classic Chinese medicinal fungus. The team treated cancer cells with varied extract doses. Assays measured growth, movement, and invasion through barriers.

Treated cells grew, moved, and invaded less than untreated ones. Gene checks tracked changes tied to a shape-shifting process cancer uses to spread. The extract pushed cells toward ferroptosis, an iron-driven death. Mouse tumors confirmed slower growth in the body. The work supports the fungus as a candidate for deeper study.
pmc-11539548:
Rungtiwa Jirawiwatsaree and Chidsanu Changsiripun test whether clear dental retainers spoil chewing. Their 2024 study follows 30 patients who got upper and lower clear retainers after braces came off. Some patients eat while wearing such trays, yet the effect on chewing was unknown.

At delivery, at three months, and at six months, each patient chewed test food with and without the trays. Sieve tests sized the chewed bits, and a survey scored how well foods could be eaten. Bits were larger with trays in at the first visit, a sign of weaker chewing. That gap faded by three and six months. Bit size fell over time in both modes, as patients adapted to the trays.
pmc-11547848:
Mattia Battistin and eight co-authors coated zinc oxide with chitosan in 2024 to make a safer, greener sunscreen filter. Bare zinc oxide blocks ultraviolet light well but can act as a photocatalyst and stress skin cells. Binding it to the natural polymer chitosan used a gelation step that steadied the particles. Tests confirmed the coating and mapped heat behavior, charge and particle size across acidity levels.

The coated powder stayed stable near neutral and mildly alkaline pH, and its light-driven activity dropped. It harmed cultured skin cells less than the bare oxide, above all at higher doses. It also gave higher sun protection and UVA scores than plain zinc oxide. Stronger protection from less oxide promises cost and environmental gains. The team plans dose tuning and wider safety tests.
pmc-11571648:
Oluwaseyi Somefun and co-authors ask young people themselves how to raise vaccine acceptance among their peers. Hesitancy among young adults was a stubborn barrier during the COVID-19 pandemic. Rather than guessing, the team held focus groups and interviews with 165 young adults in Nigeria, South Africa, and Zambia.

Participants described deep frustration with how vaccine information had reached them. Their recommendations were practical: build communication aimed at youth, in formats and channels they actually use. Put vaccine education into school lessons and community programs. Offer alternatives to injections, which some fear. And let trusted public figures carry accurate information, since official voices alone lacked credibility. The authors say these youth-designed fixes are directly usable by health programs. Their broader point is that young people should sit at the table as partners in health strategy, not just receive its messages.
pmc-11572648:
Ghada Araji and her team sift in full the lack of vitamin B12 in sick folk on wash care for failed kidneys. They take in risk traits, finds, side ills, and care. Their 2024 review takes up a big care theme for folk with end-stage kidney ill.

Told rates of lack run from twenty to ninety in each hundred, which shows how hard a find is here. Sick folk on wash care face lots of food gaps: Those gaps come from curbs on food, poor soak-up, and loss of food goods in care. The review looks at proof in hand on what drives lack in these sick folk. It weighs hard finds, side ills that may come, and care picks too. The team aims to give a round tool for school folk, care staff, and state heads on a food flaw that draws scant heed.
pmc-11573148:
Kengo Tejima and co-authors present a 2024 method that fixes two known flaws of single-cell RNA sequencing in solid organs. The technique reads gene activity cell by cell, but cells differ in total transcript count, and tearing tissue apart triggers stress genes. Both flaws distort the picture, worst in mixed solid tissues.

Their fix is a computed coefficient, a weighting factor specific to each cell type. The team reports factors for 76 cell types across 10 solid organs. With the weights applied, rebuilt bulk profiles from single-cell data matched real bulk data far better. The factors also improved the unmixing of bulk samples. Strikingly, they tracked aging progress, hinting at diagnostic use. The paper gives solid-tissue studies a needed correction tool.
pmc-11573848:
Mami Takeoka and co-authors report a 2024 study of premature babies whose lung-related heart strain seemed cured but was not. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia, a chronic lung disease of very early birth, can raise pressure in the lung arteries. Ultrasound suggested the pressure problem had resolved in ten such children.

At a median age of about two years, the children underwent heart catheterization, the definitive test. Ultrasound measures had indeed improved since the newborn period. The catheter told a different story: half the children still had mildly raised lung artery pressure. Imaging also showed narrowed small lung arteries and, in some, early emphysema signs. The authors warn that a clean ultrasound can hide lingering disease and argue for catheter checks in follow-up.
pmc-11575448:
Gena Kedir, Akeberegn Gorems Ayele, and Workineh Shibeshi test a tree bark extract for pain and inflammation relief in rodents, in a research paper from 2024. Acacia seyal bark is a folk remedy for pain in Ethiopia, but lab proof was missing. The team made an alcohol extract of the stem bark.

Three doses were tested in standard pain and swelling assays. The extract cut writhing in the chemical pain test strongly. On the hot plate test it lengthened reaction time, showing a central pain effect. It also shrank paw swelling and slowed lump growth in chronic tests. The results back the folk use and call for deeper study.
pmc-11575548:
Samantha Hollands and seven co-authors wake a silent gene cluster and map how it builds an unusual peptide antibiotic scaffold, in this 2024 paper. Curacozole is a small ring-shaped peptide from a Streptomyces bacterium, dressed with azole rings and one flipped amino acid. Its biosynthetic genes sat cryptic, switched off, in the genome.

Forcing production of a rare transfer RNA flipped the cluster on. Deletion studies trimmed it to seven essential genes. The pathway proved tolerant: six edited precursor peptides still processed into new curacozole variants, including versions swapping the signature ring for indole or hydroxylated variants. Test-tube work assigned the enzymes that form the azole ring. A neighboring gene, long conserved but puzzling, turned out to be an iron-dependent hydroxylase that edits one phenylalanine in the precursor, the phenylalanine-specific step of the title. The authors highlight how engineerable such peptide pathways are.
pmc-11576548:
Alwa Hussien Aladia, Samar Hamdan, and Ahmad Alkheder report an infant case of a rare genetic disorder in this 2024 paper. The disorder blocks the body's making of cholesterol and causes many birth defects. The patient, a boy less than a month old, was born in Syria.

He showed a small head, unusual facial features, joined toes, and defects in several organs. He also suffered severe vomiting, poor feeding, and low blood salt. Tests found very low cholesterol, and gene tests confirmed the diagnosis. A cholesterol-lowering drug, used in an experimental way, eased his irritability and was tolerated well. The authors stress early recognition, and note theirs is the first documented case in Syria.
pmc-11576948:
Mingzhi Li, Young-Hwa Choe, and Chao Gu study in 2024 how a green image shapes what clothes buyers choose. Green claims now loom large in the world fashion trade. The team mines buyer notes on a big Chinese shop site to hear views in buyers' own words.

Scraped notes were sorted by a topic tool into three themes: felt quality, felt worth, and sense comfort. Survey checks then weigh how buyers rate green wear next to plain wear. Green wear scored high on felt quality, worth, and plans to buy and buy again. The team urges firms to stress green cloth and green make steps.
pmc-11577948:
Yuying Li and co-authors build a prediction tool for the pneumonia that stalks elderly patients through hip fracture surgery when their hearts are already failing. The combination is common and dangerous: a broken hip, an acutely failing heart, and lungs primed for infection around the operation. Their 2024 paper gathers 535 such patients from one hospital's records across three years.

Statistical screening picked the risk factors that matter, among them accompanying lung disease and the blood's hemoglobin and albumin levels. The team shaped them into a nomogram, a paper calculator for bedside risk. Standard checks of discrimination, calibration, and clinical usefulness judged the model, and importance analysis showed which variables carried the prediction. The study goes further, following survival itself to name the factors that govern prognosis after the pneumonia question is settled.
pmc-11578648:
Hugo Andrade and co-authors map where rare lizards of Brazil's sandy coast plains may live now and in a warmer future. Their 2024 study covers seven lizard species found only in these restinga habitats. Barely a sliver of the original habitat remains. The team builds range models from three methods and tests two paths for future climate, one mid-level and one harsh, late in this century.

The models show each species' fit range shifting as the climate warms. Three named species share much of their future range with each other. The team also checks how much of the future range falls inside strictly protected areas today. That check shows whether current reserves will still guard these lizards later. The study gives planners a clear view of where protection must move or grow to keep pace with change.
pmc-11579748:
Uma Sankar Mandal and co-authors report a nickel-based recipe for building two families of ring-shaped molecules prized in drug design. The targets are medium rings joining two benzene units through oxygen, a shape found in real medicines such as the antidepressant doxepin. Making such rings in one controlled step has been difficult.

By tuning the reducing agent and solvent, their reaction can be steered to either of two product families, a divergent trick. It delivers the rings in high yield, with the right shape and orientation, and tolerates many chemical decorations on the starting materials. The team proved the route by making doxepin and its close relative nordoxepin. Computer modeling backed the proposed mechanism, and docking tests explored how the new molecules might bind biological targets. The authors present the method as a predictable, scalable path to a scaffold family that medicinal chemists value.
pmc-11582448:
Adriana Vizuete and co-authors tested two drugs that might shield the brain during early inflammation, in a study published in 2024. Brain inflammation shifts immune cells toward a sugar-burning mode called aerobic glycolysis, which can harm neurons. The team triggered inflammation in animals with a bacterial toxin and watched the shift unfold. One drug dialed down the sugar burning, and the other blocked an inflammation sensor.

The sugar-blocking drug reversed the metabolic shift, calmed inflammation markers, and improved the animals' behavior. The sensor-blocking drug quieted a chain of inflammatory signals and lowered glucose uptake in the brain. Both results support the idea that the sugar-burning shift really occurs early in brain inflammation. The authors propose that tuning immune metabolism could become a route to protect the brain after injury.
pmc-11585148:
Frank Reichenberger leads a team of seven authors in 2024 in proposing a screening routine to catch lung involvement early in rheumatoid arthritis, without any radiation. People whose arthritis comes with certain antibodies face real risk of interstitial lung disease, yet no settled screening exists for it.

Their protocol layers three safe tests: breathing function tests, an ultrasound scan across the chest wall, and a graded exercise test of heart and lungs. Together these can flag early scarring before symptoms force the issue. The authors present the plan as a practical way to watch a known danger closely and cheaply.
pmc-11585248:
Christiana Kyvelidou and co-authors study how embryo fluids affect immune cells in a 2024 paper. Before an embryo implants, it releases a mix of molecules into its surroundings. Those signals may shape how the mother immune system responds. The team collected spent culture media from human blastocysts and tested them on dendritic cells, which help direct immune responses.

Protein tests found a wide range of cytokines and growth factors in the media. Media from embryos that failed to implant raised activation markers on the immune cells more strongly. Treated cells released low levels of cytokines yet could still activate naive T cells. A key enzyme activity fell after treatment. The authors conclude that embryos actively signal to immune cells around them.
pmc-11585548:
Jinxin Zang and eight co-authors tracked antibiotic use in eastern China in 2024 by testing wastewater, spanning the end of the zero-COVID policy. Samples came from five treatment plants in January and February of 2021 and 2023. Lab methods measured 27 antibiotics, and the team compared wastewater estimates with local prescription records. The policy ended in December 2022, and a case surge followed.

Twenty-three antibiotics turned up in the water. Estimated use in 2023 ran from about sixfold to over thirtyfold higher than in 2021, matching the prescription data. The spike likely mixes real infection treatment with misuse during the surge. The authors warn that heavy antibiotic use breeds resistance, and that wastewater checks offer a fast public view of drug habits. They urge study of the surge's long-term effects on resistance.
pmc-11585948:
Anning Zhu and six co-workers wrote a 2024 study on air pollution and hospital stays for high blood pressure in Lanzhou. Dirty air is a known health risk, but its link to this cause of admission is less studied. The team used city data from several years. They counted close to fifty thousand such admissions.

Two gases raised the risk of admission soon after high exposure. The effect of one showed up a few days later. Other pollutants showed mixed or no links, and dust measures showed none. Effects split by sex and age in sub-group checks. The results add a local case for cleaner air.
pmc-11587448:
Julia van Kraaij and co-authors present a 2024 interview study on why nursing work feels like a tug-of-war. Forty-three nurses and managers in Dutch hospitals described their work environment for a study of nursing as a complex system. Four themes emerged from the transcripts.

Direct care for patients remains the heart of the job, and nurses bend flexibly to keep hospitals productive. But that bending has a price: tasks and rules set elsewhere shrink nurses' autonomy, and rigid organizational structures decide how they may shape their own work. Nurses struggled to balance bedside care against the surrounding demands. The authors argue the fix is systemic: more autonomy, supportive management, and structures that flex back.
pmc-11587648:
Drug hunters need lots of flu enzyme to work with, and bacteria offer a cheap factory if the enzyme stays active. Fatemeh Sadat Shariati and co-authors build a shortened flu neuraminidase in gut bacteria in this 2024 study. Three host strains were tried, and a standard lab strain won. The team then tuned feed strength, temperature, and timing with a statistical design.

The best recipe, mild temperature and a three-hour induction, more than doubled output to 7.6 micrograms per milliliter. The purified enzyme, at 48 kilodaltons, cut its test substrate with strength close to a natural cholera enzyme. The flu drug oseltamivir blocked it as expected. The authors pitch the system for cheap, safe enzyme supply.
pmc-11589148:
Yao and four co-authors built a prediction tool in twenty twenty-four to flag COVID-19 survivors likely to keep lung damage three months after infection. Lingering lung abnormalities are common after hospital care, and spotting high-risk patients early could guide follow-up.

The model drew on five hundred one patients treated at two centers between mid twenty twenty-two and early twenty twenty-three. Two hundred forty of them received chest scans at three months, and a third showed lasting abnormalities. A stepwise method picked the clinical and lab measures that mattered most. The resulting score separated high-risk from low-risk patients with strong accuracy, and its risk estimates lined up well with reality. The authors package it as an easy chart for bedside use. They suggest it can steer who gets closer lung monitoring after COVID.
pmc-11590348:
Jie Li, Meng-Meng Chen, Bingqiang Zhang, and Yi Zhao search for new markers of preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy syndrome. Their 2024 study focuses on G protein-coupled receptors, a large family of cell surface switches. The disease lacks good early tests and firm treatments, so fresh markers carry real weight.

Using a network method that groups genes by shared patterns, the team flagged two receptors as central: CCBP2 and GPR87. Lab tests then showed that both slow the growth, movement, and invasion of trophoblast cells, the placental cells whose failure sits at the heart of the disease. The authors offer the pair as candidates for diagnosis and for future drug work.
pmc-11591748:
Chaoyong Wang and co-authors test how volcanic activity affects microbial growth in shale in this 2024 paper. The study site is the Qiliao section in Chongqing, China. Organic carbon in the shale was richer at the top of the layer than at the bottom. That pattern suggests volcanic input shaped biological growth over long periods.

Lab cultures received volcanic ash leachate at seven dilutions. A ciliate species changed its growth clearly against the control at several strengths. A cyanobacterium made chlorophyll most efficiently at the strongest leachate level. Element analysis compared nutrients from ash with those from other weathered rocks. Ash delivered a distinct nutrient mix that favored some microbes. The work links deep time volcanic events to the microbes that seed organic rich shale.
pmc-11593148:
Shalika Rana and co-authors ferment legume seeds with a food-safe fungus to raise their store of health-linked compounds. Their 2024 study treats soybean, chickpea, green pea, and red kidney bean with Aspergillus sojae, a fungus used in food making. Under attack, plants brew defensive chemicals that also interest nutrition science.

Each bean sprouted its own signature defense compound after treatment, and all carried more total polyphenols than untreated seeds. Soybean led on total content. Lab tests showed stronger antioxidant action in the treated beans. Treated red kidney bean strongly blocked two enzymes tied to blood sugar control. Treated soybean best blocked a fat-digesting enzyme. The authors see controlled fermentation as a way to upgrade everyday legumes.
pmc-11593248:
Bezawit Ketema and co-authors test ways to raise screening uptake for chronic diseases in south-central Ethiopia in a 2024 study. Screening catches diseases such as high blood pressure and cervical cancer early, yet uptake stays low despite national guidelines. The team compared routine care with a bundled offer plus outreach messaging.

Facilities offering several screenings at once, paired with behavior-change communication, lifted uptake sharply. Gains reached eighteen points for cervical screening, forty-four for blood pressure checks, and twenty-three for blood sugar checks, with smaller gains for breast exams. The comparison used a difference method over baseline and end-line surveys. Bundling services, the authors argue, beats single-disease offers for drawing people in.
pmc-11593748:
Sebastian Jungkunz studies bias by vaccine state in the COVID-19 years in a 2024 paper. Vaccine rules split folk into camps with hard feels. Jungkunz ran a set tale test in Germany with 6,100 adults in late 2021. Each read a short tale of a person whose vaccine state was set by lot. They then rated warmth and bias toward that person. Their own vaccine state and how strong they felt it were logged.

Bias ran high among the vaccinated toward the unvaccinated. The reverse bias ran low. Warmth gaps hung on how strong a person felt their own state. Folk with weak state feel showed no in-group tilt at all. Strong feel fed bias on the vaccinated side alone. Jungkunz reads the split as lopsided: one camp drove the rift more than the other.
pmc-11596948:
Adamantia Kontogeorgi and co-authors review 3D printing in assisted reproduction in a 2024 paper. Printing tools promise to reshape fertility care. Evidence for their real value in care needed gathering. A systematic review followed set rules for such work.

Forty-eight papers on printing and reproduction were taken in. Bioprinting follicle cultures and artificial ovaries leads the findings. Decellularized matrix inks copy the ovarian setting well. Young eggs matured inside such builds in studies. Uses in the womb include growth factor delivery systems. Stem cells are aimed at scarred or thin linings. Plain printing serves training simulators and custom tools. Microfluidic platforms add fine control to lab work. The review keeps promise apart from proof shown. Care for female infertility is the main gain so far. Use in the clinic stays early but speeds up.
pmc-11598148:
Ming Xie and four co-authors detect heads in crowded scenes in a 2024 paper. Busy images hold many small, overlapping heads, a hard case for standard detectors. Their method builds on a popular real-time detector family and adds two modules. One fuses features with context and scale adjustment, and the other applies attention within convolution. Both aim at stronger detection across sizes.

They also replace the standard overlap measure with one that keeps final boxes tight and non-overlapping. The system reached high average accuracy on complex scene tests. Training loss settled quickly as well. The authors present the method as both fast and accurate for crowded head detection.
pmc-11599748:
Maxwell and co-authors produced the first global map of carbon stored in the soils of tidal marshes, at a fine scale of thirty meters. Marshes are threatened coasts that lock away large amounts of carbon in their waterlogged soils. Knowing how much carbon they hold, and where, is vital for protecting them and for counting nature's help against climate change.

The team trained their model on soil data from 3,710 sites worldwide. Landscape traits and a global map of marsh extent filled the gaps between samples. The top meter of marsh soil holds about 1.44 billion tonnes of carbon, with a third of it in the United States. The map gives conservation planners a concrete basis for action.
pmc-11599848:
Ryan Leow and co-authors check whether a heart measure called Yeo's index predicts bad outcomes in a valve disease. The disease, rheumatic mitral stenosis, narrows the heart's mitral valve after rheumatic fever. Yeo's index combines two ultrasound measures and was designed to spot severe narrowing.

The team studied 297 patients followed for a median of just over six years. Nearly half reached the combined bad outcome of death, heart failure admission, valve treatment, or stroke. A lower index stayed tied to that outcome even after other factors were counted, driven mainly by the need for valve treatment. Among patients without a prior irregular heartbeat, the index also predicted new cases of it. The measure may help doctors time care for this valve disease.
pmc-11600648:
Jingya Yu and co-authors survey sleep quality in women with gestational diabetes in a 2024 multi center study. The condition is the most common pregnancy complication worldwide. Poor sleep is common in this group, yet most research asks how sleep disorders cause the diabetes rather than how these women actually sleep.

Nearly four hundred women at four hospitals in Chongqing, China completed sleep and anxiety questionnaires in mid twenty twenty two. Average sleep scores sat in the poor range borderline, and close to half reported poor sleep quality. Many slept under eight hours. Regression models identified factors tied to worse sleep.
pmc-11600848:
Five authors, led by Bining Zhao, test in 2024 whether a ketogenic diet eases egg cell loss in mice with a syndrome that blocks ovulation. The syndrome is the top cause of such infertility, and the low carb, high fat diet had already helped one mouse model. The team used a second model, driven by a hormone blocking drug.

Mice on the diet for three weeks gained blood ketones and lost weight, with better ovary function. Cell tests used the main ketone body to mimic the diet. The diet quieted a DNA alarm pathway tied to cell death in egg support cells. The work names a route for the gain.
pmc-11600948:
Problem-based learning asks students to learn medicine by working through cases, and peer teaching asks them to teach each other along the way. In this medical school's primary care course, clinical problem-based sessions ran online, with peer teaching added to lift motivation. Gustavo Salata Romão and co-authors surveyed 378 students from the first through seventh semesters with a 14-item questionnaire about the format.

The study reports the students' perspective on learning from classmates in the virtual room. The authors frame the findings as guidance for schools weighing how much peer teaching belongs in online clinical teaching.
pmc-11603048:
Pin-Ching Hu and co-authors compare treatments for an advanced lung cancer stage in a 2024 study. Stage IIIA/N2 non-small cell lung cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, and guidelines for its standard treatment remain controversial. In particular, whether surgery belongs in the plan is still debated after years of research.

Using the Taiwan Cancer Registry, the team studied 2,237 patients. They compared survival across treatment strategies, including trimodal therapy that combines three approaches, and across surgical methods. Registry-scale survival data give doctors firmer ground for a decision that trials have not settled.
pmc-11603148:
Weiwei Yang and co-authors build a single cell map of the immune mix in osteoporosis. Their paper from 2024 notes that bone loss rises with age, yet the immune cell cast inside weak bone was poorly known. Naming the cell groups that push the bad bone setting could open new care paths.

One macrophage group showed a hot, M1 like state, switching on cytokine and bone eater paths and talking to bone eaters through a named signal pair. A neutrophil group ran the same paths with a high trap score. A memory T group voiced several swelling signals. A B cell group grew in share in the disease group with bone eater paths on. The map ties immunity to bone loss.
pmc-11603648:
Lingzhi Sang and four colleagues published a workforce study in two thousand twenty-four on why rural health workers in China think of quitting. Primary care clinics struggle to keep staff. The team used two-factor theory, which splits job factors into hygiene factors and motivators, to see what drives the wish to leave.

Over one thousand one hundred rural workers answered structured questionnaires. Workers rated hygiene factors higher than motivators, both only middling overall. The wish to quit sat below the scale midpoint. Status, salary, and personal progress linked most strongly to staying intent. Social support carried part of the effect of incentives, the model showed. The authors suggest managers reward progress and status, not pay alone.
pmc-11603848:
Esengul Ekici and Kadir Ozdel studied how fear of anxiety itself links obsessive symptoms and anxiety, in this 2024 paper. People with obsessive-compulsive disorder vary in symptom type, from harm fears to contamination and symmetry needs. The team surveyed 170 patients with the disorder.

Perceived threat from anxiety sat between lasting anxiety and two symptom types: harm and unacceptable thoughts. It played little role for contamination or symmetry symptoms. Momentary anxiety showed few links, apart from the contamination type. The authors say the fear of feeling anxious may keep some symptom types going. They suggest care plans tailored by symptom type that target this fear.
pmc-11603948:
Han Xia and five co-authors build a diagnostic model in two thousand twenty-four to tell two chest tumor types apart. Mediastinal lymphomas and thymic epithelial tumors can look alike on scans, which makes diagnosis hard for less experienced radiologists. The authors test whether a model, and a human-machine mix, can help.

They gathered contrast CT scans from two centers, with about ninety patients each. A model combining clinical and image features beat junior and senior radiologists on an outside test set. Pairing each reader with the model raised accuracy for all three readers. The gains were largest for the least experienced reader. The authors present the hybrid system as support for, not a replacement of, human judgment.
pmc-11604148:
Bauri and colleagues report that tuberculosis care on a remote Papua New Guinea island held steady through the pandemic. Daru Island battles drug-resistant TB, and COVID-19 strained its small health workforce. The team reviewed program records for 3,751 patients from 2017 through 2022.

Case reports fell nearly thirty percent from 2019 to 2021, then recovered. Active case-finding stopped during the worst years. Still, treatment success stayed high: about eighty-seven percent for normal TB and eighty-four percent for drug-resistant cases. The authors credit years of system strengthening and community trust built before the crisis.
pmc-11604948:
Abel Saldivia-Tejeda and co-authors test gentler farming for maize in Mexico's dry highlands. Rain-fed maize there suffers from erratic rain and poor yields under plowed, bare-soil methods. Conservation farming keeps beds unplowed and soil covered, and may rotate maize with other crops. Their 2024 study runs two trials plus tests on seventeen farmers' fields over many years.

In one trial, maize on lasting covered beds beat plowed yields by more than seventy percent. In the other, gains were small and not firm. On farms, bed maize again beat plowed yields by about seventy percent. A maize-bean rotation was the most profitable in trials, while plain bed maize won on farms. The authors back the method for the region.
pmc-11605248: Li Wu, Huiying Wang, and Ruzhi Zhang reported a rare skin case in 2024. A man aged twenty-three had patches of lichen sclerosus on his left arm for seven years. The patches spread slowly to his upper arm and shoulder blade, in a band that followed Blaschko's lines. The condition is a long-term, immune-linked skin disorder that most often affects genital skin. Cases away from that area are rare, above all in men, and this case caused no itch or pain, which made it hard to name.
pmc-11605548:
Tabei and five co-authors report a case of metastatic brain tumor from parotid cancer in a 2024 paper. The patient was a man in his thirties with recurrent HER2-positive parotid carcinoma on chemotherapy. A brain lesion in the left frontal lobe was treated with focused radiation.

The lesion shrank at first, then grew back, and new lesions appeared in other lobes. Further focused radiation was given at each stage. Later scans suggested spread along the brain's lining, and drug treatment into the spinal fluid was used while whole-brain radiation was avoided. Disease later returned with swelling and headaches, and care turned to comfort. The authors expect such cases to rise.
pmc-11605848:
Luming Wang and co-authors compared three ways to remove large tumors from the chest in 2024, using records from their own hospital. The tumors sat at the front of the chest and measured five to ten centimeters across, a size where the best approach is still debated.

The study covered 159 patients treated from 2018 to 2022. Two groups had camera guided surgery through small cuts, from below the breastbone or between the ribs. The third group had the breastbone opened. The camera groups lost far less blood, about a third as much, and needed pain drugs for a like span after surgery. The team also split patients by whether the tumor had grown into nearby organs.
pmc-11606048:
Arash Rahimi and co-authors test which body measures best flag metabolic syndrome in adults in southern Iran. Their 2024 study draws on a large cohort with near twenty-seven hundred adults aged thirty-five to seventy. Body mass index, the stock measure, can miss how fat is spread. Eight measures in all were scored, from waist size and waist-to-height ratio to newer shape and volume indices drawn from waist and hip.

Waist-to-height ratio, a roundness index, and a belly volume index flagged the syndrome best in both sexes. A body shape index tied least to metabolic traits. The authors back the top three as sharper clinic tools and call for shared rules on their use.
pmc-11606148:
Paul Daniel Crane and co-authors chart a rare autoimmune disease in Colorado in a 2024 study. Stiff person syndrome brings growing muscle stiffness and painful spasms, and it may affect only one or two people per million. Hard counts are scarce because cases are missed and firm diagnostic rules are new.

The team searched health records from a large Colorado system for 2012 to 2022. They counted new and total cases in adults and applied published diagnostic criteria to check the labels. Sound counts help plan clinics for a disease most doctors never see, and they show how much case definitions change the picture.
pmc-11607248:
Aden Kittel and three co-authors map research on virtual reality in sport in a 2024 review. Headsets and 360 degree video can place athletes inside lifelike scenes. Coaches hope such tools can train the mind side of performance. Skills like reading play and choosing moves are the focus.

The team searched four databases for studies up to early 2024. Fifty seven studies met their rules for inclusion. Most appeared after 2020, showing a fast growing field. Decision making was the skill studied most often. Most work measured skills once rather than training them over time. Head mounted displays were the most common tool. The authors chart gaps for future sport science to fill.
pmc-11607348:
Working memory often falters early in multiple sclerosis and drags down quality of life. The nine authors use a data-driven hidden Markov technique on magnetoencephalography recorded during a visual-verbal n-back task. Patients and healthy controls performed the task while the method extracted spectrally defined brain networks and their timing. Two network changes stood out in relapsing remitting patients.

First, an early theta prefrontal network tied to encoding and attention switched on less strongly in patients. Its weakness tracked poorer accuracy and slower replies. Second, a frontoparietal beta network active 300 to 600 milliseconds after each stimulus ran stronger in patients treated with benzodiazepines. That network resembles the classic P300 marker, and the boost matches the known beta effect of those drugs. The authors offer the extracted networks as candidate markers for tracking working memory decline.
pmc-11607448:
Omid Yazdanpanah and three colleagues train one neural network to predict how bridge parts ride out earthquakes. Engineers test bearings and piers with costly hybrid simulations, and each new setup usually needs fresh calibration. Their model blends attention with the Mamba sequence architecture to follow long shaking records.

It learned from 141 tests across bearings, piers, and loading speeds. Predictions matched measured hysteresis curves with correlations up to nearly ninety-nine percent. The model also captured leftover deformation after shaking. Reliable prediction could cut the number of physical tests a bridge design needs.
pmc-11607948:
Hye Young Jin and co-authors test a simple blood score for liver scarring in young patients in this 2024 study. The score, called APRI, combines a liver enzyme level with the platelet count, and it tracks scarring well in adults with fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems.

The team reviewed records of 115 children and teens with the disease, aged about seven to nineteen, and compared the score with liver stiffness measured by a scan. The score ran higher in the group with abnormal stiffness and rose along with stiffness, but the link was weak, and its accuracy for flagging abnormal stiffness was modest. The authors call for larger studies across wider scarring levels to find sharper noninvasive markers for young patients.
pmc-11608048:
Deep neck infections can turn severe fast, yet severe cases are rare and poorly summed up in past reports. Ling Jin and six co-authors review five such cases treated in their own unit. Their 2024 report lays out how each case was found and handled.

All five patients were diagnosed with neck scans plus direct checks during surgery. Cultures grew mixed germs, most often Klebsiella and other gut-type bacteria, along with germs that thrive without air. Three patients had diabetes, and three had spread of the infection toward the chest. Care mixed surgery to open and drain the area, daily dressing changes, and targeted drugs. Stays ran long, at an average of 35.8 days, and all five patients recovered.
pmc-11608248:
Ajil Nair and co-authors build a family of glowing molecules that shine in both liquid and solid states, in a 2024 paper. Most fluorophores glow in one state and dim in the other. Dual-state emitters are prized for sensors and displays. Their plug-and-play design starts from a simple pyrimidine core. Two aryl arms attach at chosen positions.

Swapping those arms tunes color and brightness in a predictable way. Ten derivatives were made and fully characterized. Crystal structures and theory backed the design rules. Absorption, emission, and energy gaps all shifted with the arms. Materials chemists gain a modular kit for light-emitting molecules. The approach may extend to other core scaffolds.
pmc-11608348:
Luis Silva and co-authors tested gut germs and insecticide resistance in malaria mosquitoes in a 2024 study. The germs a mosquito carries sway its growth, mating, and defense. Whether they also sway how well insecticides kill was the open point here.

Larvae of two mosquito colonies, one spray-hardy and one spray-prone, were dosed with four strains of Pseudomonas germs. All four strains stayed in the adults for life. Infected mosquitoes were more likely to survive insecticide, but the size of the boost hinged on the host colony. The host-dependent twist warns that spray plans must weigh local germ mixes.
pmc-11608448:
Ming-Shyan Lin and co-authors (2024) asked whether a blood protein called galectin-3 tracks fatty liver in the general community. Fatty liver, or hepatosteatosis, can progress to scarring and cancer. Galectin-3 is already tied to liver inflammation and fibrosis. The team reanalyzed data from a community health screening program covering 766 adults. Ultrasound scans judged liver fat, and blood tests measured the protein. The analysis adjusted for age, sex, body size, and other risks.

About a third of the group had moderate to severe fatty liver. Those with the condition carried clearly higher galectin-3 levels than those without it. Higher levels stayed linked to higher odds of fatty liver after adjustment. The risk climbed further when a high protein level came with a raised ratio of two liver enzymes. The authors propose galectin-3 as a helpful blood marker for this common condition.
pmc-11608548:
Allister Irvine and co-authors argue that urinary tract infections in the United Kingdom are treated half-blind, and survey the rapid tests meant to fix that, in a 2024 review. Diagnosis usually starts from symptoms alone, because the gold-standard culture takes at least three days and no point-of-care test yet identifies the pathogen and its antibiotic weaknesses reliably. The result is guesswork prescribing, which feeds antimicrobial resistance and worse outcomes.

The article highlights new point-of-care devices in development that promise to name the causative bacteria quickly and accurately at the bedside or pharmacy counter. Each still needs clinical studies to prove its utility. The authors say adopting such tools would let general practitioners and pharmacists prescribe with evidence instead of habit. They frame better UTI diagnostics as a concrete, near-term lever for antimicrobial stewardship in everyday practice.
pmc-11608848:
Christopher Finlay and three co-authors ask whether satellites can track slow magnetic changes made by the oceans in this 2024 paper. Ocean water moving through Earth's field creates a faint magnetic signal of its own. That signal carries clues about ocean flow, heat, and salt.

The team used detailed computer models of the oceans to predict the signal at satellite height. They weighed it against stronger sources, such as the field from Earth's core and fields from the upper air. On time scales of months to years, the ocean signal stands out at fine scales. The authors argue that current and future survey satellites could pull it out and watch it over time.
pmc-11610348:
Liang Yu and Liang Cheng test whether close biochemical monitoring and tailored nutrition help female weightlifters cut weight before competition, in a 2024 randomized trial. Making a weight class can drain strength and health. Twenty-eight lifters from Sichuan were split evenly: one group got personal diet plans, weekly consultations, and supplements guided by blood tests, while the other kept its usual routine through the cut.

By the fourth week the supported group showed lower muscle damage markers and kept higher testosterone and hemoglobin than controls. The control group's damage marker rose as its hormone levels fell. Monitoring plus feeding, the authors conclude, blunts the cost of the cut.
pmc-11610548:
A 58-year-old man with advanced lung cancer saw his tumor vanish under drug treatment before surgery, in this 2024 case report by Mingjin Xu and co-authors. His cancer was stage IV squamous cell lung cancer with a rare EGFR exon 20 insertion, a change that usually blunts drug response. Scans and gene tests mapped the disease, including a spot on one adrenal gland.

Four rounds of chemotherapy plus an immune drug shrank the main tumor and cleared the adrenal spot. Surgeons then removed the lung tumor and found no living cancer left, a complete response. He stayed on the immune drug afterward, with no relapse or immune side effects at 9.4 months. The case hints this combo can convert some inoperable cases.
pmc-11611148:
Msaad Guerfali and co-authors track how probiotic feeding reshapes metabolism in Mediterranean fruit flies bred for release, in a 2024 study. The sterile insect technique floods fields with sterilized males that mate without producing offspring. Probiotics in the larval diet raise the quality of those males. What changes inside the fly was unclear.

Gas chromatography and mass spectrometry profiled fly extracts across three life stages. The Vienna 8 strain, a workhorse of medfly programs, was used. Metabolic shifts followed the probiotic diet stage by stage. Better males mean fewer needed per hectare of crop. Pest control programs gain chemical evidence for the diet upgrade. The work also models insect-diet-microbe links.
pmc-11611748:
Pratibha Bhalla and Ondine Cleaver open a 2024 article collection on the cells that line every blood vessel, arguing they sit at the center of vascular and metabolic disease. This single cell layer, they note, acts almost like a hormone organ, releasing factors that steer blood flow, pressure, and clotting. When overactivated, the same cells can falter and harm the tissues they serve.

The collection gathers reviews and studies on how these cells fail in conditions from diabetes to brain disorders, and on how repairing or regrowing them might treat disease. One review covers how surgery and anesthesia can breach the blood brain barrier in older patients. The editors present vessel lining repair as the future of therapy in this field. The issue aims to map targets for that work.
pmc-11611848:
Manjunathachar and co-authors build a two part vaccine against cattle ticks. Ticks trail only mosquitoes as disease carriers for people, and they top the list for animals. Chemical sprays are failing as ticks grow resistant. The vaccine pairs two tick proteins: one guards the tick's iron balance, the other powers its muscles.

Silencing both genes cut tick counts sharply and all but wiped out egg laying and hatching. Ovaries of treated ticks showed warped cells. In cattle, three shots raised strong antibodies that lasted months. The authors pitch the cocktail as a green pillar of tick control, easing spray use on farms.
pmc-11612448:
Chao Liu and co-authors analyze, in a 2024 paper, the reliability of subsea control systems, which operate equipment on the sea floor. Because failures in such systems are costly, the analysis aims to find weak points early. The authors combine two methods: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis, known as FMEA, and a Fuzzy Fault Tree Approach, known as FFTA.

FMEA first lists the potential failure modes of each part, their causes, and their effects, and a risk matrix ranks how much harm each mode can do. FFTA then builds a fault tree that divides the system into subsystems and components, and finds the smallest combinations of failures that can cause a top-level failure. Fuzzy set theory supplies failure probabilities where exact figures are unavailable. The results identify the high-risk failure modes that most need preventive protection and regular testing.
pmc-11612848:
People of African ancestry who offer to donate a kidney are often asked to take a genetic test for APOL1, a gene linked to kidney disease risk, during their donor evaluation. Gordon and co-authors studied how donors, recipients, and community members felt about a chatbot called Gia that explains the test before a clinic visit. They ran ten focus groups in two United States cities with fifty-four participants of African ancestry, then surveyed them.

Five themes came out of the talks. Participants liked using the chatbot before seeing the kidney doctor, and many said it made them more willing to take the test. Cost was a worry, since the price of testing could sway a candidate's choice. Views on chatbots in health care varied, and personal barriers such as access could limit use. The groups were receptive to adding the chatbot to donor evaluation.
pmc-11613648:
Lőrincz and Nagy look for a cheaper way to compute how strongly molecules attract each other, without losing accuracy. High-grade quantum chemistry methods give excellent energies, but reaching their full accuracy needs huge sets of helper functions centered on atoms, which inflates cost. A rarely used fix places helper functions off the atoms, floating where the attraction actually happens, though setting them up is fiddly.

Their scheme spreads a double layer of floating centers between the two molecules, with several functions at each. Matched with a modest atom-centered set, it equalled or beat much larger standard sets while using fewer functions, with errors of a few tenths of a calorie unit. The gain held for complexes up to 72 atoms.
pmc-11613948:
Christopher Lwanga and co-authors follow babies exposed to HIV but not infected in a 2024 multi-country study. Such children, born to mothers with HIV, are hospitalized and die more often than unexposed peers. Why they fare worse is unknown, which blocks targeted help.

The team reanalyzed a cohort of hospitalized children aged 2 to 23 months in Uganda, Kenya, and Malawi. Among 1,486 children, the 217 exposed-uninfected ones faced about double the risk of dying in hospital and in the month after admission. Wasting and stunting were also more common in that group. The authors call for work on the drivers of the gap.
pmc-11615248:
Xichun Liu, Pengfei Guo, Qiufan Yu, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It presents a way to tag proteins with fluorine atoms at one exact spot, so that shape changes inside the protein can be watched with a scanning method.
