Proteins often change shape when they bind metals or partner molecules, and that shape change switches their function. The team used an enzyme to attach fluorine markers at the tail end of a protein, then read the markers with fluorine NMR. Tests on three proteins showed the tags could report shape changes both near and far from the tail. In one case, the tail itself acted as a switch that keeps cobalt levels in balance inside the cell.
pmc-11615548:
Diabetes prevention classes rarely reach Chinese immigrants in the United States, where language, food access, and health knowledge all raise the risk. Lu Hu and co-authors lay out a trial in a 2024 protocol that rebuilds the class around the community's culture. One hundred fifty adults at risk will be split into two groups.

The active group gets short prevention videos in their own language a few times a week, coaching calls from bilingual staff, and ten weeks of farm produce through a community agriculture program. Weight is the main yardstick at three and six months. Two yearly cohorts are already enrolled, and results will show whether the tailored model works.
pmc-11615648:
Mohammad Javad Boozhmehrani and eleven colleagues pool studies on a surgical choice for children with lung hydatid cysts, in a 2024 review. The parasite-driven cysts demand surgery, and after removing one, surgeons either fold the remaining cavity shut, capitonnage, or leave it. Which is safer for children was unsettled.

Thirteen studies entered the meta-analysis. Overall complications ran high, but folding the cavity cut them sharply: twenty-four percent against fifty-eight percent without. Cure rates also favored the folding technique, about eighty-four against sixty-five percent. Cyst size, patient age, publication date, and surgery type all influenced complication rates. The authors recommend capitonnage as the preferred technique for pediatric lung hydatid disease. They call for long-term follow-up studies and trials combining surgery with drug therapy.
pmc-11616148:
Soichi Inai and co-authors report a brain malformation case with lasting weakness after surgery in this 2024 paper. The patient was a 21 year old woman with headache, right limb weakness, and language trouble. Scans showed a cavernous malformation with swelling in the frontal lobe. Her weakness grew despite medical care, so emergency surgery followed.

Weakness usually follows surgery when nearby tissue or veins are damaged. Here scans showed no such damage. Tissue tests instead found dense neutrophil infiltration, a sign of noninfectious inflammation. Swelling grew again a week after surgery, and weakness persisted. Steroid treatment brought rapid recovery over ten days. She left hospital free of symptoms on day twenty, with no recurrence.
pmc-11616748:
Thu-Thao Thi Huynh, Minh Trong Quang, and Hoang Danh Nguyen report a plant genome sequence in a 2024 paper. The plant, Syzygium zeylanicum, belongs to the myrtle family. Its chloroplast genome, the small DNA circle that runs photosynthesis, had never been fully read before.

The genome runs to about 159,000 letters and follows the classic four-part layout of its kind. It holds 85 protein-coding genes, 37 transfer RNA genes, and eight ribosomal RNA genes. Family tree analysis placed the species closest to a relative, Syzygium acuminatissimum. The authors offer the sequence as a base resource for future work on the group's evolution and conservation.
pmc-11617248:
The germs in a COVID-19 patient's gut shift their drug resistance during treatment, while those in the throat hold steady, in a 2024 study by Elizaveta V. Starikova and co-authors. Resistance genes as a whole, the resistome, are a public health worry that the pandemic threw into relief.

Swabs and stool samples were read with a panel covering nearly five thousand resistance genes. Throat resistomes looked much alike across patients and barely changed over time. Gut samples fell into two distinct patterns only loosely tied to gut community types. About half the patients switched pattern within a week of therapy, most moving to the less diverse one. The contrast shows how unevenly treatment pressures act on the body.
pmc-11617848:
Tae Sung Kim and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on red blood cell transfusions for critically ill patients in South Korea. Guidelines favor holding transfusion until hemoglobin falls low, yet practice varies. The team followed 307 anemic, non-trauma patients admitted to intensive care through emergency departments at five university hospitals.

Just over half received transfusions, and nearly half of those had hemoglobin at or above the usual trigger level. High lactate, fast heart rate, and low blood pressure often drove the decision instead. Death rates and hospital stays did not differ between transfused and non-transfused groups. The authors urge wider guideline use and criteria tuned to each patient.
pmc-11618748:
Sultan Alharbi tested in a solo 2024 study whether full contrast staining during a liver cancer procedure predicts a good response. The procedure delivers drug-loaded beads through an artery to a solitary liver tumor, starving and dosing it at once. During the first session, doctors can see on X-ray whether the contrast fully stains the tumor.

Forty-one patients were reviewed and split by whether full staining was seen in the first session. Full staining appeared in 22 patients, a little over half. Both groups had one or two sessions in pursuit of a complete response, judged by standard tumor criteria. Traits like a well-defined tumor and super-selective delivery were tied to staining in the report. Readers get a sign visible mid-procedure that may tell the team, on the spot, that the treatment is likely to work.
pmc-11619148:
Eko Pangarsa and co-authors report a breast cancer case where hormone therapy, not chemotherapy, led the treatment in a 2024 paper. The patient, a thirty-six-year-old premenopausal woman, had luminal breast cancer that had flooded her bone marrow, a rare and dangerous spread called disseminated carcinomatosis of the bone marrow. It appears in well under one percent of metastatic cases and has no official treatment guideline.

Standard practice leans on chemotherapy, with its heavy toll, since the situation is life-threatening. This team instead opened with endocrine therapy plus a CDK 4/6 inhibitor, a drug that brakes cancer cell division and pairs with hormone treatment in this cancer type. The case shows the gentler first line in action from diagnosis in 2020. Single cases cannot set policy, but they can widen the options doctors dare to try.
pmc-11619248:
Akihisa Kawajiri and co-authors find a reserve pool of immune cells that can become many kinds of helper, in a 2024 study. The cells are memory like CD4 T cells that arise on their own as the body keeps its balance. Past work sorted them into set helper types, but one plain subgroup's role was unknown.

In cell poor settings, the whole pool could turn into three helper kinds and drove mild, lasting swelling, while fresh cells gave a strong single kind response. Gene reads showed the plain subgroup is a raw, uncommitted pool. It can multiply fast and supply all three kinds, with resident guard cells holding one path in check.
pmc-11621748:
Carolyn Kousky, Galen Treuer, and Katharine Mach draw lessons for home insurance as climate risks grow, in a paper from 2024. Storms, floods, and fires now strain the market that helps owners rebuild after disaster. The authors build three edge case futures for Florida and trace how choices made in the next few years could play out over the next fifteen.

Each future links near term rules on rates and aid to later risk, home prices, loans, and town wealth. The point is that a fix that calms the market this year can raise harm or cost down the road if it keeps building in risky spots. The authors call for choices that weigh long term safety and fair shares of cost, not just short term calm.
pmc-11622148: Emmanuel Mazinis and Vasilios Thomaidis present a rare case that joins two unlike faults in one patient, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The teeth show short root anomaly, with roots far shorter than normal, plus missing teeth and wide pulp chambers. The same patient has transverse hemimelia, a limb that ends partway. No past proof links the tooth fault to the limb fault. Shared gene, womb, and metabolic paths hint one hidden cause may sit behind both.
pmc-11622448:
A drug that couples an antibody to a cell-killing payload, called T-DXd, has shown strong results against cancers that display the HER2 protein. Eight clinicians in Athens report in 2024 how it worked in their own clinic for gynecological cancers. They review ten patients with advanced uterine, ovarian, or cervical disease. All had already passed through several earlier treatments, a median of four lines. The drug was given by infusion every three weeks.

Half the patients saw their tumors shrink, including two who had received an earlier HER2 drug. One more held stable at twelve weeks. The middle time before the disease advanced again was 5.4 months. The authors present the series as real-world support for the drug in these cancers.
pmc-11622748:
Ridvan Sivritepe and three co-authors ask how well medicine knows dynapenia, the age-related loss of muscle strength that no single disease explains. Their 2024 review defines the condition against its better-known cousin: mass can look adequate while strength and function fade. The condition is common in older adults and carries heavy consequences, from disability and falls to hospitalization and death.

The authors walk through causes and care. Oxidative stress, failing cell batteries, and chronic inflammation feed the decline. Diagnosis rests on function tests: grip strength, a timed stand-and-walk, and a short performance battery. Treatment is a package rather than a pill: exercise, nutrition, selected drugs, management of other conditions, and fall prevention. Their message is hopeful and practical. Caught and treated as its own condition, dynapenia can be pushed back, preserving independence and quality of life in old age.
pmc-11623948:
Talita Choudhury and co-authors probe how genes and a mother's diabetes combine to cause heart defects at birth, in a 2024 mouse study. About one percent of babies are born with such defects, and a mother's diabetes is a known risk. The team focused on embryos with one weak copy of the Notch1 gene. Earlier work showed the mix raised defect rates.

The harm centered on the lining cells of the growing heart, where cushions that form valves failed to shape well. Cell tests showed stress plus the weak gene jointly scrambled gene networks. Raising a defense enzyme against that stress did not rescue the hearts. The authors warn that antioxidant plans alone may fail in babies with this gene risk.
pmc-11624748:
Bernardi and co-authors compared two operations for a detached retina with tears along its lower half, in a study published in 2024. When the retina peels away, surgery must press it back and seal the tears. The standard fix removes the eye's gel and fills the eye with gas. Some surgeons add a band around the outside of the eye for lower tears, where gas support is weakest. Whether that band improves results was the question.

The team reviewed past cases of one defined tear pattern, breaks in the lower arc of the retina. One group had the gel surgery with gas alone. The other had the same surgery plus the encircling band. They compared how often the retina stayed attached and how vision recovered. A clear answer helps surgeons choose for a tricky pattern where gravity works against the repair.
pmc-11625548:
Yao Xiao and co-authors link parents' education to depression risk in college students through brain connectivity, in this 2024 Europe PMC study. Over three hundred sixty students without mental illness history completed depression assessments and resting-state brain scans. Their parents' education levels served as the socioeconomic measure.

Students whose parents had more education tended to report fewer depressive symptoms. A connectivity pattern, drawn mostly from the default mode and ventral attention networks, predicted symptom levels in new data. That pattern also sat between family background and symptoms, suggesting brain network organization is one route by which early-life advantage shapes mental health at college age.
pmc-11626948:
Eleven authors trace a heart harm chain in sepsis in a 2024 mouse and cell study. Germ toxin in blood fires body-wide flare and wounds the heart by wrecking cell power hubs. A guard protein, Dusp1, fades in that state, and a sugar-path enzyme is cast as the hand that strips it.

Mice bred with the guard cut or raised in heart cells, plus mice with the enzyme cut, went through toxin shots. Heart scans, power hub checks, and dock runs map the chain link by link. The chain marks both proteins as drug aims for sepsis heart care.
pmc-11628748:
Juan Gao and nine co-authors tested a new plant-derived compound for stroke injury in a 2024 study. After a blocked artery starves the brain, immune cells in the brain drive a wave of inflammation that widens the damage. A compound from a traditional Chinese herb showed promise, but its role in this injury was untested.

In dishes, the compound calmed inflamed immune cells and nudged them toward a healing mode. In mice, it eased brain inflammation in both a chemical model and a real stroke model where an artery was briefly blocked. Gene reading pointed to a two-part signaling axis that the compound restrains. Silencing that axis is known to cool the inflammasome, a protein machine that fans inflammation. The authors present the compound as a candidate stroke drug, with animal-stage evidence so far.
pmc-11628948:
Melyda and co-authors weighed the costs and benefits of two hormone treatments after surgery for endometriosis, in a 2024 study tied to the PRE-EMPT trial. Endometriosis is a painful condition where womb-like tissue grows outside the womb, and pain often returns after surgery. The trial compared long-acting hormone options, a coil or an injection, against the daily combined pill.

Four hundred and five women at thirty-four British hospitals took part and were followed for three years. The pill cost about five hundred and thirty-three pounds more per woman and gained a small edge in quality of life. That trade worked out near seventeen thousand pounds per healthy year gained, close to the usual funding limit. Other measures leaned toward the long-acting options, leaving the choice finely balanced.
pmc-11629148:
Yang and co-authors set foot force maps of sound young, sound old, and sugar hosts side by side. Force and shear on the sole split by zone in the reads. Hosts sat still and walked in the test spans for maps. In sum, 20 young, 16 old, and 15 sugar hosts took part. Still stands span flat, front-back slope, and side slope forms. Walk reads span force sums, peak force, and shear marks.

The sole split in zones: big toe, small toes, and three front pads. Arch side and heel zones cap the sole map in the set. Old hosts showed high still force in mid-front and heel zones. Front-back shear rose there too in the old set reads. Sugar hosts give the third arm for the age tale.
pmc-11629648:
A diabetic child's blood can turn acidic in ketoacidosis, a crisis that sometimes announces the disease itself. Nagham Alsolaimani and five co-authors compare in 2024 one hundred forty-seven such crises at a Saudi center, splitting children whose diabetes was new from those already known. Records covered five years.

Newly diagnosed children were younger and arrived after longer symptoms, with the classic thirst and urination dominating. Known patients more often showed vomiting and belly pain, and their crises were fewer. Middle childhood carried the heaviest load in both groups. The authors blame delayed recognition for the new patients' worse entries. They call for public awareness so the disease is caught before the crisis.
pmc-11630248:
Akira Yasuhara and co-authors study a tiny aluminum comb in 2024 that traps light waves at its surface. Such plasmonic crystals guide light below the wavelength scale, which suits sensors and chips. The team carved the crystal from large aluminum grains with a focused ion beam, keeping the metal's quality high.

They read the crystal with two electron-beam tools. One charts how the waves' energy varies with motion, including modes hidden from light. The other catches the light the crystal emits, mapping the same modes from the other side. Together the tools gave the full picture, covering both shining and dark modes. The authors commend the paired approach for nanophotonics work.
pmc-11631348:
Jonas Thiele and co-authors argue in 2024 that brain-based prediction studies should prize explanation over raw score. Many studies forecast intelligence from brain wiring with real accuracy but little insight into how the brain works. In a registered study of 806 healthy adults, with a second sample for checking, they tested which connections forecast general, stored, and fluid intelligence.

Which kind of intelligence and which task during scanning both mattered a lot. Many different sets of connections could forecast well, spread across the whole brain. That breadth fits and extends older theories that stress certain regions. The authors urge future studies to map predictive features with care rather than chase top scores alone.
pmc-11631948:
Making a metal sheet just one atom thick is hard, because metal bonds pull equally in all directions. Alexei Preobrajenski and co-authors find a way to grow nearly freestanding 2D gold layers. They form gold monolayers on an iridium surface, then slip boron atoms underneath, between the gold and its support.

The buried boron lifts the gold into suspended single-atom sheets patterned with tiny hexagons and triangles. On bilayers it produced regular fields of nanodots instead. Microscope images, X-ray spectra, and calculations together show the boron drives the patterning. Freed from the substrate, the gold's electronic bands shift to a truly 2D character. The films also survive heat well, which opens them to catalysis studies.
pmc-11632048:
Liujun Zhou and seven co-authors track prescriptions of antibiotic combinations that the World Health Organization does not recommend, in a 2024 study. Fixed-dose combinations pack two antibiotics in one pill, and unapproved mixes can fuel drug resistance. The team mined prescription records for intensive care patients in six major areas of China from 2013 to 2019. Over fifteen million prescriptions were screened, covering nearly one and a half million patients.

About six percent of patients received a non-recommended combination at least once. The yearly count of such patients rose over the period, even as their share shifted. Trends were also broken down by drug and by hospital. The numbers give regulators a baseline for curbing products that add resistance risk without proven benefit.
pmc-11633048:
Xin Liu, Jun Wan, Ming Wei, Yanan Tong, and Zhaomin Yao test whether edaravone can shield placental cells in preeclampsia. The condition brings high blood pressure and organ damage in pregnancy, with poor placental function causing lasting low oxygen in placental tissue. Edaravone is a strong antioxidant used against other diseases and injuries. The team checked placenta tissue from women with and without preeclampsia, then modeled low oxygen in a human trophoblast cell line.

Key proteins tied to hypoxia and the PI3K/AKT pathway ran higher in preeclampsia placentas. Edaravone kept treated cells alive, cut cell death and reactive oxygen species, and countered activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway. The authors propose pathway inhibition as a treatment lead.
pmc-11633548: A journal cover feature from 2024, tied to work by Hyung Tae Lim, Tae Ho Shin, and co-workers, spotlights a fuel cell layer that moonlights as an oxygen store. In a solid oxide fuel cell, a lanthanum-doped ceria layer sits at the cathode. The featured study gives that layer an extra role: it soaks up oxygen ions when they are plentiful and releases them when the cell runs short. That buffering lifts performance and durability at high current, and it maps how oxygen pressure spreads inside the device.
pmc-11634048:
Aldenise Ewing and co-authors examine racial disparities in colorectal cancer screening and the role of online medical record use. Their 2024 cross-sectional study uses data from a national survey in the United States.

Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the country, and screening lowers the risk. Screening rates nearly doubled for some adults in the early 2000s, yet they stay lowest among younger adults, safety-net patients, and the uninsured. Online medical record systems may be an underused tool to promote screening. The study tests whether record use differs by race and whether it connects with getting screened.
pmc-11634148:
Mengxuan Cao and thirteen colleagues published an imaging study in two thousand twenty-four on predicting stomach cancer's return after surgery. Recurrence shapes a patient's outlook, yet doctors lack sharp tools to foresee it. The team taught a deep learning model to read CT scans taken before surgery.

Records came from over two thousand eight hundred patients treated at two centres. The model's scan score was blended with clinical features into a combined signature. It separated patients who relapsed from those who did not with strong accuracy in training and in two check groups, one at another centre. Survival curves split clearly by the signature. The authors offer it as an aid for planning follow-up.
pmc-11634948:
Zahid Hussain and four co-authors test how steel-free bars grip concrete in beams, in a 2024 study. The bars are made of glass fiber plastic, which does not rust like steel. Building codes set how far two such bars must overlap to pass force safely, but the code ignores the grip boost from stirrups, the loops that cage the bars. The team built sixteen beams and loaded them to test overlap lengths and stirrup spacing.

Stirrups clearly raised the bond strength, cut slipping, and let the concrete take more splitting stress. One pairing of overlap and tight stirrups lifted capacity by over half against no stirrups. The US code overrated plain bond but played safe with tight stirrups. A newer Canadian rule came closest to the test values.
pmc-11635248:
Christina Stuart and co-authors test whether walking on the day of lung surgery speeds recovery. Their 2024 prospective study spans six hospitals in one health system, from 2019 to 2023. Early movement is standard advice after many operations, yet its weight after lung resection had little hard study.

Just over a thousand patients who had a lung segment or lobe removed formed the cohort. About forty-two percent walked on surgery day itself. That group suffered fewer complications across the board: lung problems, wound infections, bleeding, and heart issues all ran lower. Adjusted models were used to check that the walkers were not simply the healthier patients. The authors argue for making same-day walking a firm target after lung surgery.
pmc-11636048:
Hai-Peng Tang and co-authors compile everything known about a prized Chinese mint. Mentha haplocalyx has long flavored food and folk medicine, used for colds, coughs, fever, indigestion, asthma, and flu. The review sweeps botany, traditional uses, nutrition, chemistry, and tested health effects, drawing on four major literature databases.

Chemists have found terpenoids as the lead active family, alongside flavonoids, phenolic acids, and polysaccharides. Lab and animal studies report protection for nerves, relief of asthma and inflammation, better blood sugar control, and antibacterial and antioxidant action. The plant also supplies fiber, amino acids, minerals, and vitamins. The authors close with the herb's commercial promise and the research still needed.
pmc-11638648:
Di Huang and co-authors review how an old alcohol drug, disulfiram, might be retooled against cancer with nano delivery, in this 2024 paper. The drug is safety-approved and shows anti-tumor and immune-boosting effects. Trials so far, though, disappointed, largely because the drug reaches tumors poorly.

The review catalogs the drug's cancer-fighting routes, including its immune paths. It then surveys carrier systems built to ferry it: particles, gels, and other vehicles, each answering a delivery hurdle. The authors close with pairings that join the revived drug with modern immune therapy, and they sketch the trials that could prove the idea in patients.
pmc-11638748:
Takuya Nakai and Shigeo Fukunishi present a case report, published in 2024, on redo hip surgery in a man aged eighty-five. More than twenty-five years earlier he had received a Lübeck hip replacement, a metal implant with a spongy surface meant to mimic natural bone. Such implants often serve well for years, but the stem can crack as a late problem.

Scans showed two breaks in the thigh bone around the implant plus a broken stem, with the lower part still firmly fixed. Surgeons replaced the upper thigh bone and fitted a new stem built for that purpose. The authors present the approach as an effective fix for an older patient whose old implant failed in this complex way.
pmc-11638948:
Researchers use in 2024 hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry to watch how RNA strands stop a brain protein from clumping. Clumps of TDP-43 mark several degenerative brain diseases. RNA binding is known to block clumping, but the shape changes behind that guard were unknown.

Exchange patterns show RNA shields the protein's RNA-grabbing domains and the linker between them. At high salt, one natural RNA sequence loses its guard while a repeat sequence keeps it. The loss aligns with a salt-driven shape shift in the bound protein. Domain contact changes emerge as the key mechanism. The work may guide RNA-based drugs that keep the protein soluble in diseased brains.
pmc-11639548:
Penghui Zhang and four colleagues study what makes pelvic organ prolapse return after surgery and build a risk chart, in a twenty twenty-four paper. Prolapse, where pelvic organs slip down, harms quality of life through bladder, bowel, and pain problems. The team followed eighty-seven women after a laparoscopic fix for three years. Twenty-two saw the prolapse return.

Older age, more past births, and one pattern of pelvic muscle contraction raised the risk in full models. Keeping the uterus was among the factors weighed. Blood markers tied to tissue stretch were also tested. The chart built from these factors aims to help doctors warn and follow the women at highest risk.
pmc-11639948:
Scan reports often note surprise findings that have nothing to do with the reason for the scan, and researchers lack one shared way to define them. Jacob Pilegaard Mølstrøm and co-authors reviewed the literature in 2024 on incidental findings in FDG PET/CT scans, a type of whole body imaging used in cancer care. They searched three major databases and sorted how each study worded its definition.

Of thousands of papers screened, sixty-five met the bar for the review. Most definitions spoke of tracer uptake in tissue, and many added that the finding lay away from the scan's target or that the patient had no symptoms. No single wording ruled the field. The authors propose a common definition built from the traits they found most often.
pmc-11640048:
Zhichen Guo and co-authors studied a skeleton steering protein in mouth cancer tied to a virus in a 2024 paper. The protein, called Mena, helps cells move, and the team asked what it does in oral cancers that carry HPV16. Database analyses and tissue staining compared virus positive and virus negative tumors. Cell and mouse experiments then tested Mena's effect on invasion and spread.

Mena levels were lower in virus positive tumors, and there its links to spread were weak. In virus negative tumors, higher Mena tracked with lymph spread, stage, and a shape shifting program in cells, and with worse survival. Experiments confirmed Mena drives migration and invasion. The twist: the virus suppresses Mena, which in turn blunts the cancer's spread in virus positive cases.
pmc-11640148:
Ines Serratosa and co-authors review robotic lung surgery after pre surgery drug treatment in a 2024 study. For locally advanced lung cancer, chemotherapy alone or with immune drugs is now common before surgery. The drugs can shrink tumors, but they may also make the operation harder. The team checked whether outcomes after robotic surgery held up.

Records covered 253 patients from 2019 to 2024, of whom 23 had drug treatment first. That group had longer operations, about 250 minutes against 221. Rates of switching to open surgery were much the same. Long air leaks after surgery were more common in the treated group. The authors read the record as harder surgery with broadly kept outcomes.
pmc-11640348:
Michael Davis and Rosalia Simmen report on a long cattle breeding study in a 2024 paper. Starting in 1989, Angus cattle were bred in two lines, one for high and one for low blood levels of a growth hormone called IGF-I. The team used decades of records to estimate how strongly that trait and growth traits pass from parents to calves.

Records ran into the thousands for most traits, covering birth weight, later weight, weight gain, and height. The growth hormone trait proved moderately heritable, and so did the weight traits. The study also measured how the traits move together, which tells breeders what happens to growth when they select on one trait. In later years the lines were picked by feed cost traits instead. The results give cattle breeders firm numbers for planning selection programs.
pmc-11640548:
Alberto Carturan, Sonia Morè, Antonella Poloni, Serena Rupoli, and Erika Morsia survey the hunt for immune-based and targeted treatments for myeloproliferative neoplasms, blood cancers where immunotherapy has lagged. Checkpoint drugs transformed lymphoma care and engineered T cells transformed other blood cancers. These slower myeloid cancers have resisted similar breakthroughs.

The obstacles are plain: no universal surface marker to aim at, wide variation between patients and subtypes, and an immune system already distorted by the disease itself. Trials now test sharper JAK inhibitors and other targeted agents. The review maps what is running and what might finally crack these cancers. Progress has been slow but the pipeline is real.
pmc-11640648:
Elena Sandri and colleagues compared lifestyle and nutrition in Spain during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Their 2024 cross-sectional study used a health habits scale with many items. Data came from over twenty thousand people during the pandemic. A smaller group of about four thousand answered after it. The scale covered food, activity, sleep, and self-rated health.

Exercise time rose slightly after the pandemic ended. Fried food, juice, and alcohol intake all fell. Ultra-processed food and soft drink use rose instead. Coffee and energy drink use rose sharply. Sleep quality, body image, and self-rated health slipped a little. The authors say unhealthy food habits remain deeply rooted. They call for public steps to protect mental and physical health.
pmc-11641248:
Chunxia Zhou and co-authors test whether ultrasound treatment improves seaweed sugars from Sargassum, in this 2024 study. These long sugar chains are drawn from the seaweed with alkali, acid, or hot water, giving three starting samples. Each sample then got an ultrasound pass. The team measured chain makeup, size, and chemical content for all six versions.

All samples held the same nine sugar units, in varied shares. Ultrasound shrank the chain size in every sample. After treatment, the samples blocked a diabetes-linked enzyme more strongly and fought oxidation better. One treated sample led on enzyme blocking, another on oxidation defense. The treated samples also slowed sugar-damage products on proteins more. The authors say ultrasound offers a simple boost for uses in food and medicine.
pmc-11641648:
Researchers review in 2024 how single-cell analysis can map the cell types that drive asthma in fine detail. Asthma is a long-term lung disease with many forms shaped by genes and environment. Mixed immune responses blur the picture when whole tissue is read at once.

Single-cell RNA sequencing reads each cell alone, sorting types and states with care. Recent asthma studies find new immune cell subtypes and clusters with hinted roles in disease. Cells in focus span dendritic cells, eosinophils, lymphocytes, mast cells, and more. The review weighs what the method has shown and where it still falls short. Sharper cell maps could point to treatments tuned to each asthma form.
pmc-11641748:
Hanin Wattad and colleagues lay out a roadmap for genome editing in a non-model organism. Their 2024 paper centers on the giant freshwater prawn Macrobrachium rosenbergii. CRISPR editing is harder outside standard lab species. Genetic variation runs high, and sex chromosomes and repeats raise off-target risks. The team had earlier adapted editing to prawn embryos and cultured cells.

Here they built a genome annotation pipeline for the prawn. The pipeline trains on genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data together. It predicts gene models well enough to guide knockout design. Sequencing showed frequent variation in genes on normal and sex chromosomes. The paper faces those challenges directly with practical steps. It aims to make editing workable in other non-model species too.
pmc-11641948:
Shifa Shahid and nine co-authors published a dental development study in twenty twenty-four on the protein-cutting enzyme ADAM10 and tooth enamel. The enzyme snips around a hundred different substrates, and the enamel-forming ameloblast cells produce it. Whether enamel actually needs it was the open question.

Because deleting the gene everywhere is lethal, the team removed it only in ameloblasts of mice. The animals grew discolored teeth with softer enamel. Enamel density and volume dropped in both incisors and molars, and the orderly rod pattern unraveled toward the surface, leaving gaps and bent rods. The enzyme also cuts known enamel and cell-contact proteins. The study proves ADAM10 is essential equipment for building sound enamel.
pmc-11642048: Stergios Boussios, Matin Sheriff, and Saak Ovsepian wrote on the molecular biology of cancer and how malignant cells interact with emerging therapies. Their 2024 article opens by noting that cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide. World Health Organization data reported in 2020 ranked it second globally, with about ten million deaths.
pmc-11642148: Eduardo Martin-Sanz introduces a special issue of a journal in an editorial from two thousand twenty-four. The issue gathers work on vestibular disorders, conditions that affect the inner ear system that controls balance. Such disorders can cause dizziness and vertigo, and they remain hard to diagnose and treat well in daily clinic work.
pmc-11642248:
Natasha Priya Dyal, Robert Orenstein, and Sandhya Rani Nagarakanti report a spine bone infection caused by a mouth germ that near never harms. The germ, Neisseria sicca, lives in the throat of most people and is waved off as dirt when it shows in a test. Their 2024 case is a 62-year-old man with fever and back pain. Scans showed bone infection at two chest spine bones.

A first drug round failed, and his pain grew. Needle samples from the bone, read with full tests, named the germ. Due to its tame fame, the team sampled again, and the germ showed twice from a clean site. That proof set the drug: a vein drug first, then a pill kin. Pain eased fast, scans near cleared, and by late 2023 the infection was gone. Past print held just four such cases.
pmc-11642348:
Matthias Heinzl and co-authors test a blood fat as a flu warning sign in a 2024 study. HDL, the so called good cholesterol carrier, also fights inflammation. Low levels mark poor odds in bacterial infection and sepsis, but its role in flu was unclear. The team read records of 199 patients hospitalized with flu over two seasons at one center.

Most patients were men, and deaths in hospital formed the key outcome. HDL levels on record were weighed against inflammation markers and survival. A cheap, routine blood value that flags risk early could help wards sort who needs close watching. The flu setting extends a sepsis lesson into viral illness, where triage tools are thinner.
pmc-11642448:
Yidi Zhan and co-authors study a moth protein that carries scent signals for both sexes. Moths use scents to find mates of their own kind, and carrier proteins in the antennae grab those scent molecules. Most work on such proteins covers how males sense female scents.

The team found twenty carrier genes in this moth and saw that one, called PBP1, is made mostly in the antennae. Lab tests showed it binds strongly to the female scent and also to a male scent. The authors argue that this dual role helps keep kinds apart when they breed. The finding could aid pest control tools that steer moth behavior.
pmc-11642648:
Chunhao Tao and co-authors build, in 2024 work, a one-step lab test that both finds a pig virus and names its strain. The virus cuts sow births and fills piglets' lungs, and it comes in two great types, one of which splits into five lines that all roam China. Knowing the line guides farm control.

Seven probe sets were built: two aimed at a shell gene to split the types, and five at a second gene to name the lines. Packed into two pools, the test ran true, with tight repeat scores and reach down to a few copies per drop. On more than a thousand farm samples it matched the check method well. All found cases proved to be one line, proofed by letter reads.
pmc-11642948:
Andrea Lear and co-authors review death records of sheep and goats in Tennessee to find what kills them most. Records came from two state labs over five years, covering animals brought in for postmortem exams. Small farm ruminants matter to the state's farm economy and face many diseases. The 2024 study weighs age, sex, season, and county in its analysis.

Internal parasites were the top finding in both species. Young females were most at risk, above all in summer. Pregnancy loss diseases came next, though most had no found cause. Goats showed brain disorders among top findings; sheep showed lung infections. Age mattered in most patterns. The authors say teaching farmers to spot and act on these diseases early could cut losses.
pmc-11643348:
Ailong Jiang and colleagues review the models physicists use to describe the structure of liquid metals. Metallic materials face rising demands for strength, lightness, and catalytic and electrochemical function, and advanced materials are designed from the melt. High-temperature X-ray diffraction has built broad agreement that short- and medium-range ordering exists within metallic melts, with clusters and links that persist above the melting point.

But the test extremes obscure basic traits, and debate goes on. Simple models are the usual way to make such complex systems clear. The review proceeds from transient models, pictures of fleeting local structures, to heat-based statistical models that treat the melt as a balanced mix of configurations. The physical image behind each model and its uses are carefully covered. The assumed liquid structure carries into predictions of how the metal sets.
pmc-11643448:
Wojdat and Piwowarczyk studied how to prepare the surface of tungsten carbide so it bonds strongly to steel with adhesive. These hard carbides are prized for cutting tools, but joining them by brazing or welding can cause stress and cracks, so glue bonding is an attractive option. The team compared modern treatments, laser micro-texturing and low-temperature plasma, with grinding, blasting, and etching, then measured bond strength with shear and pull-off tests.

Both modern treatments raised joint strength by about half compared with grinding. Plasma treatment gave average shear strengths around 30 to 32 megapascals, depending on the gas used, and laser texturing gave the best result at about 34.5 megapascals. The authors conclude that surface engineering of this kind can make adhesive joints a reliable way to assemble carbide tools.
pmc-11643548:
Klaudia Morawska and co-authors compared, in a 2024 study, how well potassium sensors hold up as temperature shifts. Such sensors help track potassium in blood and water, and solid-contact designs need a middle layer to keep their signal steady. Heat and cold can throw that signal off.

The team built five sensor types with unlike middle layers, from charged plastics to carbon tubes and metal oxide grains. Each was tested at 10, 23, and 36 degrees for sensitivity, range, and drift. Sensors with a mixed carbon and oxide layer, and one with a perinone plastic, resisted heat shifts best. Both kept near-ideal response and the lowest drift at all three heat levels. Added layers beat the bare sensor on stability in every case.
pmc-11643748:
Likai Zhou and co-authors cook up new sugar based alkaloids in one pot in this 2024 paper. Their targets are hydroxylated alkaloids, also seen as fused ring iminosugars, ring shaped sugar mimics that can block enzymes and interest drug hunters.

The route starts from sugars fitted with a tosyl group and runs through a Pictet-Spengler type reaction, a classic ring closing step. The method picks one spatial arrangement of the product with high selectivity, needs no metal catalyst, and scales to gram amounts, giving a fifty-three percent yield in the large run. Some of the new iminosugars showed a middling power to slow the growth of HCT116 tumor cells in tests.
pmc-11643848: Zeno Garban, Gheorghe Ilia, and Francesco Cacciola review plant growth bioregulators and their mammal effects, in work from 2024. Bioregulators are natural compounds made by living systems that steer growth and body tasks at small doses. The review sorts these plant compounds by chemical shape, then maps how shape links with action in plants. It also gathers what is known about their effects when mammals take them in. Shape rules that boost plant action may also flag mammal risk, which is why both reigns are treated side by side here.
pmc-11643948:
Cheng Li and co-authors test a probiotic strain against acute alcohol poisoning in rats. A drunk gut leaks, letting bacterial toxins slip into the blood and inflame the liver. The strain, a spore forming microbe, was fed to rats before heavy alcohol doses. The team tracked how fast the rats sobered and how their organs fared.

Treated rats stayed sober longer before tipping over, in plain terms their drunk onset slowed. Liver harm, gut leak, and blood toxin levels all eased. The microbe shifted gut flora toward groups that make butyrate, a gut wall fuel. Feeding butyrate alone copied much of the gut protection. The authors trace the benefit to this gut wall route.
pmc-11644248:
Han Liu and twelve co-authors study how a plant hormone spray, EBR, lifts grain filling and yield in Tartary buckwheat. The crop bears many flower heads, but uneven food spread caps its output. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Field tests sprayed three hormone strengths on a high seed set type and a low seed set type. Grain filling followed the classic S curve, and the spray raised its rate, with the high type filling more. The hormone tuned inner hormone levels and boosted leaf light capture. Key enzymes that move sugars also rose, so more light made food reached the grain in the fill stage, the authors report.
pmc-11644348:
Chi Trung Ngo and co-authors build a true random number generator on a standard chip process, in a 2024 paper. They then fix its weak test pass rate with a light hash step. Their design draws randomness from timing jitter in a custom ring oscillator with three switchable speeds. Built in 28-nanometer technology, the raw generator, like many rivals, saw only a few samples pass the standard NIST randomness tests.

Adding a Photon hash post-processor lifted the pass rate by half while staying small and frugal. The finished unit covers a tiny area, uses far less power than the usual deterministic alternative, and suits cheap security hardware. Throughput remains modest but the yield gain is the headline.
pmc-11644448:
Zeqiang Shao and co-authors test a combined soil treatment for maize in this 2024 study. Biochar and cattle manure are rich in carbon and nutrients and are long used to lift crop yield and soil health. How they perform together with potassium fertilizer was unknown, so the team ran a two-year field trial.

Adding potassium with both materials raised most growth measures over the control in both years. Grain yield rose sharply, by up to about 3,300 kilograms per hectare in the best mix. Leaf greenness and gas exchange rates climbed as well, and plants took up more potassium as soil potassium rose. Soil nitrogen and organic matter also improved under the combined treatment.
pmc-11644548:
Przemysław Zagrajek and four co-authors describe a cheap detector for sub-terahertz waves, published in 2024. Detectors that sense heat from such radiation work across a wide range of frequencies, but making one is often costly and demanding. The team instead built theirs around a standard thermistor, a small part sold for general use.

A 3D-printed optical element guides the waves to the sensor through a dielectric waveguide the team designed and made. They also built the electronics needed to read the sensor's response. The finished device is wideband, meaning it works across a broad span of frequencies, and it reaches a response of hundreds of volts per watt. The authors present it as an affordable option with sound detection quality for labs that cannot justify pricey custom gear.
pmc-11644648:
Elżbieta Niechciał and three co-authors review in 2024 the shifting treatment of teenagers with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Young people with obesity face four times the diabetes risk of lean peers. For years options were thin: the standard drug alone failed in about half of teens in a landmark trial, and add-ons fared little better.

The review surveys the new wave: gut-hormone drugs and sugar-flush drugs that work strongly in adolescents, plus weight-loss surgery for severe cases. Catching obesity before complications set in can spare teens lasting medical and social harm. The authors map the evidence for each option and where care is heading.
pmc-11644748:
Rabiatul Adawiyah Razali and co-workers report a 2024 study of soft sponges for use as nasal packs after surgery or injury. The packs are made from gelatin and carrageenan, two natural materials that break down in the body. The team tested five mixes of the two materials.

Packs now in use can cause pain, infection, and harm when they are removed. The new mixes were checked for strength, how they mix with blood, and whether they harm cells. Balanced mixes held their shape well, broke down at a steady pace, and showed low harm to cells. The authors say tests in living tissue are still needed before clinical use.
pmc-11644848:
Veysel Yusuf Cambay and co-authors build, in 2024, a computer system that spots gut diseases in endoscopy images. The system is built on a new variant of a well-known image network, with blocks that mix local detail and a form of attention. Features are drawn from highlighted image regions, then filtered and passed to simple classifiers.

The model organizes itself, trying several classifiers and voting schemes and keeping the best result. Heat maps show which image areas drove each decision, which helps users trust the output. The authors present the design as a step toward fast, explainable help for doctors who read endoscopy images.
pmc-11644948:
Vincenzo Natale and seven co-authors present a 2024 study of morning and evening types among teens and the groggy span after waking. People differ in when they feel alert: some peak early, others late. The shift from sleep to full movement may also differ by that taste.

The team enrolled 729 teens, and 443 wore wrist motion sensors for at least three nights. Survey scores sorted 61 teens as evening types and 38 as morning types. The sensors logged movement minute by minute across the fall asleep and wake up spans. Evening types showed a stronger motor drag after waking, the authors report, with clear gaps in the wake up span.
pmc-11645248:
Sunil Jain, Prem Kamal Jain, and Ashok Kumar Puranik published this framework paper in 2024 on digital health tools in cancer care. Cancer is now a leading cause of death in every country, and demand for care keeps growing. The authors argue that digital tools are widely used in daily life but still little used for public health, and that the field needs a clear shared plan.

Their plan has five parts, called the 5Ps: proper assessment, pertinent treatment, progress monitoring, prevention, and professional standards. The paper gives examples for each part, from digital biopsies and gene-based treatment choices to hospital-at-home care. It also stresses training for doctors, since tools change fast and many clinicians lack guidance on using them. The authors say every new tool should meet the same proof bar as other treatments.
pmc-11645448:
Ancuta Fedorca and co-authors, writing for a large European network, tackle the hard task of counting a wild population's effective size for conservation work. Their 2024 paper explains why the number matters: it tracks how fast a species loses its gene variety, and so how well it can survive over time. Land managers and policy makers lean on it.

Gene-based counts rest on neat premises, such as no newcomers and random mating. Real species often live in split groups under shifting weather and human pressure, so those premises fail and the counts can skew. The paper grew out of a workshop that gathered experts to face the snags. It lays out where the methods bend and how field workers can still use them with care.
pmc-11645748:
Lukas Goerdt and eight co-authors present a 2024 study of layer bands in high detail scans of the retina. Doctors read these scans to track the shift from healthy aging to macular disease. The names used for the bands came from an older group agreement and needed a refresh.

The team used tissue studies and new scan devices to rename the bands on firmer ground. They built a custom review tool to grade how clearly each band shows. Then they tested what changes band clarity: image averaging, age, and disease stage. Groups ranged from young healthy adults to patients with early and middle stage disease. One reader's repeat grades were also checked for steadiness.
pmc-11645948:
Xixi Song and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 testing whether gut microbes and their products truly cause diabetic kidney disease, rather than merely tracking with it. Past studies linked the two, but such links can reflect the disease changing the gut, or some third factor driving both. The team used a genetic method that treats inherited variants as natural experiments, which cuts through much of that fog.

Several microbe groups tied to lower odds of the disease in the genetic data. Five groups looked protective, among them a common gut genus and a milk-linked one. Six groups tied to higher odds, including a broad phylum and several of its member genera. None of the blood metabolites tested showed a causal tie. The team reads the pattern as real support for a gut-to-kidney path. They offer the named groups as leads for prevention and treatment design.
pmc-11646948:
Yichang Chen and co-authors review how the body's copper plumbing feeds into breast cancer, in a 2024 paper. Copper balance matters: too little or too much can slow the cancer, and the transport proteins that move copper may steer its course. Searching thirty years of literature, the team gathered the evidence member by member.

They found thirteen transport-system members tied to the disease's start, spread, and death rates, and all but one ran high in breast tumors. These proteins act through copper levels and reactive oxygen inside cells. One new observation stands out: draining the copper-storing protein GSH floods cells with copper and triggers a copper-driven death. The authors frame the system as a source of treatment ideas.
pmc-11647248:
Xingchao Song and co-authors report a liver cancer study, published in 2025, on how tumors hide from the immune system. A protein called PD-L1 on tumor cells acts as a brake on immune attack, and tumors survive longer when that brake stays in place. The team studied an enzyme called MINDY1, which removes the tags that mark proteins for disposal and runs high in liver cancer.

Tissue from fifty patients was tested for both proteins and tied to five year outcomes free of tumors. In cell experiments, dialing MINDY1 up or down changed cancer cell growth, movement, and the amount of PD-L1 kept on hand. The work points to a disposal control route by which liver tumors may protect their immune brake.
pmc-11647548:
Vordermark and four co-authors paired cell therapy with a receptor blocker in this study from twenty twenty-four. Cytokine-induced killer cells have shown promise against glioblastoma in trials. A separate drug, GW-9662, blocks the PPAR gamma receptor found in brain tissue. The team tested both on neuroblastoma and glioblastoma cell lines.

The blocker alone slowed tumor cell growth in both lines. It lowered a methylation enzyme's expression while barely touching a growth signaling pathway. Global methylation marks shifted partly as well. Adding the killer cells on top raised tumor cell killing significantly. The authors present the pairing as a candidate strategy for malignant brain tumors. They stress the evidence is early and from cell cultures.
pmc-11648048:
Dinsa, Eticha, and Terefe report fibroid removal during pregnancy in twenty twenty-four. A twenty year old first time pregnant woman came in with lower abdominal pain and slight fever. Ultrasound found a fibroid of four by four centimetres attached broadly to the uterus. Such tumors are common in women of childbearing age.

Antibiotics did not ease her pain, so the team chose surgery after counselling. The operation was done in the second trimester at a hospital in western Ethiopia. Surgeons removed the fibroid without manipulating the uterus itself. Mother and fetus stayed safe after the procedure. She continued antenatal care at the same hospital into the third trimester. The authors note prenatal fibroid removal can be done safely in early pregnancy.
pmc-11648548:
Zeinab Awada, Natasha Hameed, and Asaff Harel profile ofatumumab, a self-injected antibody treatment for relapsing multiple sclerosis, in a 2024 review. The drug targets B cells through the CD20 marker, a strategy proven by earlier infusions. Ofatumumab is the first fully human antibody of its class approved for the disease, which lowers the chance of the immune system rejecting it. Patients inject it under the skin once a month at home.

Against a standard oral therapy in trials, it cut yearly relapse rates, MRI lesion activity, and disability progression. Side effects were mainly infections and injection reactions, and the overall profile was judged manageable. The review covers the drug's pharmacology, its design story, and where it sits among current options. The authors frame convenience, a monthly home injection, as its practical edge.
pmc-11648748:
Teklu Shumbe and co-authors grade the wastewater treatment plant of a Heineken brewery in Addis Ababa, in this 2024 study. Brewery wastewater carries heavy organic loads that threaten waterways if released raw. The team measured a dozen traits of the water entering and leaving the plant, following standard public health lab methods. Temperature, acidity, oxygen demand, solids, and nutrients were all tracked.

The plant cut chemical oxygen demand by over ninety-seven percent and solids by about ninety-six percent, both ending well within discharge limits. Acidity settled into the allowed band. Nutrient removal lagged: phosphorus and nitrogen fell only by about half, and phosphorus ended just over its limit. The authors praise the core cleaning while urging better nutrient management before discharge.
pmc-11649748:
Oranud Praditsap and others put out a 2024 gene study of kidney stones in a Thai family. Kidney stones are common in Thailand. The northeast region shows very high rates. Four members of one family had the disease. The team read their protein-coding genes.

Sorting cut the search to ten possible changes. Family checks and control screening came next. One change in a building protein gene stood out. The changed building block stays the same across backboned animals. Computer models hinted the change alters protein shape. Families like this reveal inherited stone risk. Genetic clues may in time guide how relatives can avoid stones.
pmc-11649948:
Deyab and Mohsen report a 2024 study of a plant extract that may protect steel from rust. The steel is used in desalination plants and must survive strong acid cleaning. Their candidate is an extract of Irish ivy, a common climbing plant.

The team tested the extract in a strong sulfuric acid bath using weight loss, surface scans, and electric measures. Protection rose with dose and reached 94.2 percent at the top dose tested. The extract clung to the steel in a pattern that matched a classic adsorption model. Chemical tests found plant compounds such as alpha-hederin in the extract, which may do the protective work. The study points to a greener option for guarding steel during acid cleaning.
pmc-11650348:
Neda Qosja and co-authors asked whether day-one blood tests are needed after keyhole kidney removal, in a 2024 paper. Routine labs after surgery are standard care. Skipping needless tests could cut hospital costs. The team studied one surgeon series of the operation.

They reviewed 650 cases and kept 478 after exclusions. Patients on dialysis or with a past transplant were left out. Day-one values for potassium, sodium, and hemoglobin were checked. The team linked odd values to traits before and after surgery. The goal is safe care with fewer routine draws. Findings may reshape standard recovery pathways.
pmc-11650848:
Hilman and co-authors published a developmental study in twenty twenty-four following children from a pregnancy folic acid trial to age eleven. The team had earlier linked later-pregnancy folic acid supplements to cognitive benefits in offspring. Now they tested whether epigenetic marks on ZFP57, a master regulator of imprinted genes, track with those benefits.

Mothers' and children's blood was analyzed for methylation of the gene using several techniques, and children took intelligence tests while brain activity during language tasks was recorded. Cell experiments probed what changing the gene's methylation does to its activity. The paper ties a prenatal vitamin, an epigenetic switch, and school-age cognition into one cautious chain of evidence.
pmc-11651548:
Rebecca Davidson and co-authors study bone development in mice lacking a regulator gene in bone-forming cells in a 2024 paper. The gene, STAT3, had been implicated as a key modulator of skeletal growth. Removing it only in osteoblasts let the team isolate its role in those cells.

Two knockout lines, on different genetic backgrounds, both showed defective postnatal bone development. The mice had lower body weight, shorter thigh bones, low bone density, and widened, thinned bone shafts. Effects differed by sex, a dimorphism the authors highlight. The results caution that bone therapies touching this pathway may act differently in males and females.
pmc-11651748:
Yifan Li and co-authors pin down how a sugar-modifying gene helps breast cancer grow and spread. Their 2024 study examines GCNT3, reading its levels across cancer atlas data and in tumor samples by protein blotting and tissue staining. Breast cancer remains a leading killer of women, and new markers are still needed.

Silencing the gene in cancer cells slowed their growth, invasion, and migration in dish tests. The effect runs through the PI3K/AKT pathway, a master growth circuit in cells. The authors present GCNT3 as both a candidate biomarker and a possible drug target, since blocking it chokes several malignant behaviors at once.
pmc-11652548:
Yu-Hsuan Hsu, Shao-Hua Lin, Dong-Sing Wuu, and Ray-Hua Horng built blue light-emitting diodes from gallium nitride and tested a new way to shape them. These micro diodes, ten micrometers wide, usually get their mesa structure from dry etching, which damages the sidewalls and leaks current. The team used ion implantation, shooting arsenic or argon ions into the structure to isolate the material without cutting the sidewalls.

Both implanted versions switched on cleanly and leaked less current than the etched version. The argon version performed best, with lower resistance and a wall-plug efficiency of ten point six six percent. External quantum efficiency rose from eight point six seven to eleven point zero three percent. The ideality factor fell from eleven point eight nine to two point two. The authors conclude that sparing the sidewalls suppresses wasted, non-light-producing recombination in small devices.
pmc-11652748:
Mara Martinez-Santori and colleagues wrote in 2024 to warn that postherpetic neuralgia, nerve pain after shingles, can look like a pinched nerve in the lower back. Low back pain is very common, and doctors first think of strain, disc problems, or narrow spinal canals. Their case shows a less common cause in older adults: reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus.

A man aged seventy-nine came in with two weeks of back pain running to his hip and knee, plus numbness that hurt his sleep. Drugs gave little relief. Scans showed worn discs and canal narrowing, and he was sent for a spinal injection. The letter argues that shingles-related pain should be kept in mind before such steps are taken.
pmc-11653048:
People with diabetes must manage food, activity, and medicine every day, and chatbots now offer to coach that work. Yibo Wu and co-authors reviewed the evidence for such chatbots in 2024, gathering twenty-five studies from two databases. Most bots taught diet, exercise, glucose checks, and medication routines; very few touched mental health.

Pooling the trials showed chatbot coaching lowered blood glucose by a modest margin, while weight did not change significantly. Study quality was thin: only one true randomized trial appeared among the intervention studies. The authors call for stronger trials and more mixed research designs, plus better theory to guide how the bots are built. They see real promise, held back by a weak evidence base.
pmc-11653148:
Jizhuang Ma and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study of an injectable gel that hardens in place to treat vascular malformations in infants. Standard sclerosing drugs struggle to be both potent and gentle. They also wash out of target vessels too quickly.

The team fused a surfactant sclerosant with a clot-protecting drug into one charged molecule. Charge boosted killing of abnormal vessel cells in culture. Blood enzymes then snip the molecule apart, limiting body-wide toxicity. Forming a gel at the site promises longer contact. The dual design attacks vessels while guarding clots, aiming for safer infant treatment.
pmc-11653448:
Scott J Halperin and co-authors study what drives the cost of knee ligament surgery in the United States. Their 2024 paper covers repair of the anterior cruciate ligament, a common sports injury operation. They count all payments in the ninety days after surgery, not just the operation itself.

Using a national insurance database, the team found nearly a quarter of a million patients over about a decade. They linked payment totals to age, sex, other health problems, insurance type, and whether surgery was in a hospital or an outpatient site. Problems after surgery also entered the analysis. Knowing which factors push payments up helps hospitals and insurers target savings without cutting care that patients need. It also shows how wide the spread in cost can be.
pmc-11653548:
Marziyeh Najafi and co-authors analyze who holds power over a proposed ad ban in Iran, in a 2024 study. The ban would cover adverts for unhealthy goods: junk food, tobacco, some drugs, and some cosmetic services. Such adverts drive consumption and chronic disease. The team interviewed eighteen experts in 2022 and mapped the groups with a stake in the policy, judging each group's role, power, and stance.

Seventeen stakeholders were found, fourteen of them active. The health ministry leads the push for the ban. Culture and industry ministries, plus political bodies, hold great power with middling support. Broadcasters and social media platforms are powerful opponents, since adverts fund them. The authors flag clashes of interest, weak penalties, and thin resources as key hurdles. They argue that winning over powerful but undecided groups will decide the policy's fate.
pmc-11653648:
Beatriz Santos and five co-authors review in 2024 how muscle-building steroids affect women's health and their children. Use among women is rising, driven by looks goals of more lean mass and less fat. Harms at high dose or long use span mood shifts, voice deepening, cycle disruption, and heart strain.

Rodent studies add aggression, swelling, nerve cell loss, and harm to heart and vessels. Steroid use in pregnancy can impair the child's reproductive, brain, and metabolic health for the long term. How the drugs work in female bodies is still poorly mapped. The review urges caution and more study, since medical groups already warn against wide use on thin safety proof.
pmc-11653748:
Home care workers spend much of each day traveling between clients, on foot, by bike, or by car. Ingeborg Frostad Liaset and three co-authors asked 14 such workers in Trondheim, Norway, how those journeys affect their health, in a 2024 study based on group interviews. Knowing in advance which way they would travel each day turned out to matter a great deal.

Walking brought fresh air and exercise but also bad weather and sore legs. Driving gave privacy and rest, yet traffic and parking caused stress. The authors say services should assign travel modes with workers' health and preferences in mind, not by habit alone.
pmc-11653848:
Liquan Ouyang and co-authors test whether a blood-count index predicts the return of a painful breast inflammation, in a 2024 study. Granulomatous mastitis is a stubborn, noncancerous condition that mimics cancer and often recurs after surgery. The index combines three routine blood cell counts into one number reflecting the balance of inflammation and immunity.

The team followed two hundred forty-five women operated on between 2015 and 2020, splitting them at a cutoff the data itself suggested. Women above the cutoff relapsed clearly more often than those below. Young age at onset and broken skin over the lump also raised the risk. A free index from a standard blood draw could flag patients who need closer follow-up or stronger preventive treatment after surgery, sparing low-risk women the same burden.
pmc-11654148:
Yifan Hong and co-authors mined in 2024 the United States drug safety database for harms linked to the only approved cancer-killing virus therapy, T-VEC. Over eleven hundred reports involving the virus were pulled from two decades of filings. Two statistical screens hunted for event types reported more often than chance allows.

Seven body-system groups lit up, led by general disorders, infections, and injuries. Fever, illness, flu, and chills topped the event list, all familiar from the label. Four signals were unexpected: sepsis, brain inflammation, fainting, and swollen glands. The authors say most findings match known risks, which steadies confidence in the profile. The four surprises, they argue, deserve targeted clinical study rather than alarm.
pmc-11654348:
Nicole Stone and eleven co-authors trialed a home kit to cut chlamydia in young men in a 2024 paper. Right and steady condom use is the best guard against such infections. Their kit, sent home, pairs a practice pack with coaching given in person or online. The hope was that two weeks of self practice would build skill and cut errors.

The trial ran in sexual health clinics across England with men aged sixteen to twenty five at risk. Three arms split the group between the two kit forms and plain care. Monthly checks ran for six months, with a lab test for the infection as the main yardstick. Use errors, views, and act counts were also tracked. The paper reports the full trial finds.
pmc-11654648:
Zubair Khan and co-authors study how deep brain stimulation affects drug use in Parkinson's disease in Pakistan. Their 2024 study is set at a neurosurgery unit in Lahore. Forty nine patients were included. Each had stimulation of a small brain target on both sides. Care ran from 2018 to 2023. Data came from records and from interview based questionnaires. The study is framed as relevant to a low to middle income setting.

Drug dose, in levodopa equivalent terms, fell by fifty five point zero three percent after surgery. A motor score improved by eighty point four nine percent. Both results were highly significant. Time spent with involuntary movements fell by seventeen point five four percent. Time spent in off periods, when drugs fail, fell by twenty two point four four percent. A score for movement complications barely changed. The authors support the surgery in early disease.
pmc-11654948:
Nigel Spence and co-authors ask refugee women in Australia how they feel about partner violence screening in this 2024 study. About a third of refugee women in the country face such violence, alongside many resettlement strains. A program at four settlement services screened women with a short tool, offered brief help, and referred onward.

Over three hundred women answered a follow-up survey. Among those who recalled the screening, nearly all felt comfortable with the questions, including most women who had lived through violence. Most women agreed services should ask. Care from the worker, a shared language, privacy, and a female worker mattered most for opening up. The authors back wider rollout in settlement services.
pmc-11655148:
Fish farms that grow their own microbial flocs can add helpful microbes and plant extracts to do even better, argues a 2024 review by Mohammad Hossein Khanjani and co-authors. The review covers biofloc systems, where colonies of microbes clean the water and feed the stock, together with two kinds of supplement.

Probiotics, given in feed or water, support animal defenses and water quality. Plant based additives calm inflammation, fight germs, feed gut microbes, and switch on immune genes. The authors pull the studies together into one picture of how the supplements raise growth, health, and survival in fish and shrimp.
pmc-11655448:
LiXin Wei and YaFei Zheng published a 2024 study of two ways to train young male players. The study asks how a player's starting fitness level shapes the gains from training. The title names basketball, but the text of the study is clear that the players were soccer players. One training path uses small-sided games. The other uses hard bursts of effort with rest between them, known as high-intensity interval training.

The study ran a six-week pre-season block with forty-three players from regional teams, at an age in the mid-teens. Tests at both ends included a jump, a sprint, and a shuttle-style fitness run. Each player received a fitness score that split the group into fit and non-fit. In both training paths, the non-fit players gained more than the fit players. Their jump gains led, with pace gains close behind.
pmc-11655548:
Zhang and co-authors report a 2024 final read of a phase three trial in bone marrow scarring disease. The trial pitted a new drug, gecacitinib, against a standard older drug in higher-risk patients new to this drug class. Patients split two-to-one between the drugs, and the main mark was spleen shrink of at least a third at week twenty-four.

Near two-thirds on the new drug hit the mark, against near a quarter on the old one. Best shrink rates and symptom gains also favored the new drug. Blood count gains showed in some patients with low counts, and safety was weighed in full.
pmc-11655648:
Nunzia Monte and co-authors compile a dataset of rock and soil strength values for Italy in this 2024 paper. Geological maps show where each rock type lies but not how it behaves. Missing numbers limit the use of maps in hazard modeling. The team mined the world literature for measured values. More than twenty-three hundred records were gathered. Three key measures anchor the set: cohesion, friction angle, and porosity.

Those measures feed slope stability models, used for landslide risk. Values were matched to the rock types mapped across Italy. Spread and typical ranges differ by rock type in telling ways. Engineers and geologists can now pull numbers instead of guessing. The dataset also shows where measurements are thin on the ground. Data papers like this underpin later modeling work.
pmc-11655748:
Piero Barbanti and co-authors present a 2024 re-look at a migraine trial to price the work hours a preventive drug saves. The drug, eptinezumab, was tested in adults who had failed two to four past preventives. Diaries counted migraine days, and a work survey logged hours missed and hours worked at half steam. A path model split the drug's work gain into the part from fewer migraine days and a part past that split.

As migraine days rose, missed hours grew in a straight line while half-steam hours curved up. With the drug term in, the model fit better, marking a gain past day counts alone. Modeled savings over six months ran to hours per month on both gauges. Employers and payers gain a fuller cost picture.
pmc-11655848:
Josephina Sampson, Hyun-min Ju, Nan Zhang, Sharon Yeoh, Jene Choi, and Richard Bayliss find a back door that lung cancer uses to dodge its best drug, in a 2024 study. About one in twenty lung cancers runs on a fused gene that a strong drug can block. Many patients respond, then worsen as the cancer adapts. The team dosed cancer cells with the blocker and watched which signals flared in reply.

Two side paths lit up: a growth-receptor family and a core survival switch. Blocking either side path with the main drug killed far more cells and deepened the shutdown of growth signals. A natural signal for one side path could tune how well the main drug worked. Cells grown resistant to the main drug still fell to the side-path blocks. The authors urge pairing the drugs early to cut off escape.
pmc-11655948:
Farzaneh Momtazi and Hanieh Saeedi map where small sea crustaceans live across the globe in a 2024 paper. The animals are amphipods, a group used as a sign of healthy seas. Past work claimed their species counts peak at two bands of latitude. The pair test that claim with depth and habitat in mind.

They built a huge set of records, more than one million, for 6,424 marine species. Species were split by sea zone, depth, and floor or open-water life. Counts did not peak in two bands for all groups. Floor and open-water species also spread in distinct ways. In shallow seas, heat and plant growth best predicted counts. In deep seas, a mix of factors ruled.
pmc-11656148:
Magnesium batteries could store energy cheaply and safely, but films that grow on their negative electrode waste charge. Benjamin Schick and co-authors watch those films form in real time in a 2024 study, using a quartz sensor that weighs layers as they grow.

Two electrolyte families were compared, each with and without a chloride salt. The steadier family allowed nearly film-free cycling, with stray films traced to contaminants that form and dissolve during early cycles. The more reactive family grew thick, porous films as cycling went on. Adding chloride cut the amount of trapped magnesium and sped the film's quiet dissolution between cycles. The findings show electrolyte purity and chloride dosing as levers for longer-lived magnesium cells.
pmc-11656348:
Zhengfeng Jia and co-authors report rebuilding a hand that lost all four fingers, parking a severed finger elsewhere on the body while the hand was prepared. Multiple finger amputations defeat simple replanting: parts survive, but grip and shape suffer. Their 2024 case follows a forty-three-year-old woman whose left hand suffered ischemic amputation of all four fingers.

The strategy combined graft tissue, reconstruction between digits, a hip bone graft, and joint fusion, staged around an ectopically banked finger kept alive at a temporary site. A year on, rebuilt thumb and middle finger units were functioning in her daily use. Hand surgeons get a playbook entry for injuries where straightforward replantation cannot restore a working hand.
pmc-11656548:
Maurizio Marchesini and co-authors review a two-drug pairing for facial pain that has no clear cause. Persistent idiopathic facial pain resists diagnosis, since doctors find it only by ruling everything else out, and treatment lacks a gold standard. Amitriptyline helps some patients, and fresh hints that dopamine shapes facial pain suggest adding perphenazine, a dopamine-acting drug.

The team looked back at thirty-one patients with severe pain who took the pair at low doses. Average pain eased from a mid-range score, and the worst attacks softened clearly. Weekly breakthrough episodes also thinned. Scores for life quality tied to pain improved the most on their survey. The authors read the old records as a case for testing the pairing properly.
pmc-11656748:
Juliette Bichon and co-authors revisit a question about hormones and trauma symptoms in a 2024 study. Post traumatic stress disorder hits women harder than men. Sex hormones such as estradiol and progesterone may shape that gap. An earlier study found that trauma traits, such as sexual trauma and age at the event, changed how estradiol related to symptoms. The team tried to replicate that result and extend it to progesterone.

Sixty five trauma exposed participants, all assigned female at birth, gave blood samples and completed a gold standard clinical interview. Neither hormone tracked symptom severity on its own. The earlier estradiol pattern did not reappear, and neither trauma trait changed it. Age at trauma did change the progesterone link, though. The authors stress that trauma history must be part of any hormone based account of the disorder.
pmc-11656848:
Heting Wu and four co-authors ask what drove panic buys in China in the COVID span. Their survey appeared in twenty twenty-four. An online form ran in June and July twenty twenty-two with grown web users, who told of their buys of spare goods in the ill years. High-risk packs were the young, women, students, and the less well off.

News sway, mind panic, peer pack pull, worth hopes, and pack bond all fed the buys. Self hold skill cut them. The team map fix paths on each root, from news rules to mind help, to curb such runs in next health scares.
pmc-11656948:
Joar Svanemyr and co-authors draw lessons on keeping school-based sexuality education alive in Zambia, in a 2024 study. Such programs have spread across the region, yet many depend on donors or outside groups. When funding ends, the teaching often ends too. The team studied an after-school youth club model.
