Teachers and community health workers who ran the club were interviewed. Guardians shared views as well. The club had been part of a large trial pairing education with economic support for girls. The study asked what helps the work survive after a project closes. Findings speak to ministries weighing how to fund sensitive programs for the long term.
pmc-11657348:
Christopher Patsalis, Gayatri Iyer, Marci Brandenburg, Alla Karnovsky, and George Michailidis release an R software package for network analysis of metabolomics data, in a two thousand twenty-four bioinformatics paper. Pathway analysis ignores the unknown and foreign compounds that fill untargeted datasets.

The DNEA package builds metabolite networks from partial correlations between two experimental groups and tests which modules differ, extending the group's earlier Filigree tool with a faster, more flexible implementation. Demonstrated on a public diabetes-determinants dataset, it handles exogenous, secondary, and unknown metabolites that pathway tools cannot place. The authors describe it as the only public tool built for this differential network enrichment task.
pmc-11657448:
Dos Reis and co-authors test a blood assay for colon cancer mutations in patients with and without growths. Colon cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Catching early growths could stop cancer before it starts. Blood tests for tumor DNA offer a gentler screen than scopes. The team ran a commercial colon panel on plasma from 52 Brazilian patients. Eight had no major findings, 24 had precursor growths, and 20 had cancer.

The panel covers 14 genes tied to colon cancer. Profiles were compared across the three groups. The study asks whether blood signals appear already at the growth stage. Early signal would strengthen the case for liquid biopsy screening.
pmc-11657748:
Lidia García-Pérez and co-authors, with the PECUNIA Group, validate standard cost templates for Spain so health technologies can be priced fairly across Europe. Comparing what a treatment costs in one country against another fails when each counts differently. The PECUNIA project, ten partners in six countries, built harmonized templates for unit costs across health, social care, education, and more. Their 2024 paper reports the first validation of those templates in the Spanish setting.

A validated template turns arguments about method into arithmetic. Multi-country trials and policy reviews depend on such plumbing. The authors test whether the standard forms capture Spanish services without distortion. Their work is methodological, aimed at economists and agencies. It is the sort of paper nobody cites at parties and everybody needs in a grant. Comparability is a public good built one template at a time.
pmc-11658148:
Paul Shuper and eight co-authors mine medical charts for factors tied to missed HIV prevention doses. Their twenty twenty-four article deals with PrEP, a daily drug plan that blocks HIV infection, among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men. Past studies of alcohol, drug use, and mental health effects on adherence gave mixed results and used narrow samples.

Charts for a full year at two Toronto clinics were extracted, which covers the whole clinic population and dodges sampling bias. Alcohol use, substance use, and mental health notes in the chart were tested against two grades of nonadherence. The design lets the team judge which charted factors truly track missed doses.
pmc-11658248:
Huijuan Wang and co-authors published a 2024 study on how kidney cancer survives when starved of two amino acids. Serine and glycine feed the growth of many cancers; some tumors depend on importing them rather than making their own. Renal cell carcinoma's dependence was unclear. The team deprived the cancer cells of outside serine and glycine and watched how they adapted.

The cancer's escape route runs through one-carbon metabolism, a chemical network that also manages the cell's redox balance, its protection against oxidative damage. Reprogramming that network kept the balance and let the tumor keep progressing despite the starvation. The researchers probed the mechanism with imaging, measurements of the cell's recycling system, and other assays. A dependency plus its workaround is a therapeutic map: block the workaround, and the dietary stress might bite. The study nominates the redox circuitry as the place to strike in this kidney cancer.
pmc-11658348:
Manoj Adhikari and co-authors present a rare case report from 2024 on an extra tooth found in an unusual place. The patient was a ten-year-old boy with a hard swelling on his palate that had been there for three years. A scan showed an impacted supernumerary tooth inside the horizontal plate of the palatine bone.

The team removed the tooth in surgery under general anesthesia and closed the flap over the site. Healing went well, with no problems seen over one year of follow-up. The authors note that only two such cases had been reported before, and they urge dentists to consider this cause for swelling at the back of the hard palate.
pmc-11658448:
Bumjoon Lee and co-authors report a tooth-saving treatment for a teenage patient in this 2024 case report. A 14-year-old boy was hit by a baseball bat, and his two upper front teeth broke with the pulp exposed. The fracture line ran two millimeters below the gum line, which threatens the seal that keeps the tooth healthy.

Instead of removing the teeth, the team pulled them slightly outward by surgery and did root canal work on both. Extra gum surgery lengthened the visible crown to protect the seal. Porcelain-metal crowns finished the repair. The authors argue that this combined approach can save badly fractured teeth in growing patients better than removal.
pmc-11659148:
Irene Ovestad and colleagues searched in two thousand twenty-four for gene markers that sort women after cervical screening into who needs a biopsy soon. Virus type alone does not tell which infections will progress, since immune response matters too. Comparing stubborn advanced lesions with normal tissue, they profiled immune-related gene activity.

Four genes stood out: two immune markers and two tumor markers. Testing in a much larger biopsy group checked whether their activity levels separate advanced lesions from normal and milder tissue. Combined with virus risk class, such markers could sharpen follow-up decisions. Screening programs gain a path to fewer missed cancers and fewer needless biopsies.
pmc-11659348:
Dingani Nkosi and five co-authors tested a marker protein in two thousand twenty-four that may help spot a rare, fast-growing thyroid cancer. This cancer, called anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, is hard to name because its cells look varied and lose their usual thyroid marks. A stain that keeps showing up in these tumours would aid diagnosis.

The marker, SATB2, appeared in about three quarters of twenty-three cases. The usual marker PAX8 appeared in about two thirds. Crucially, most tumours that lacked one marker kept the other, so using both catches more cases. Gene tests also showed SATB2 activity varies across these tumours, backing its use as an added stain.
pmc-11659748:
Two blood markers may together forecast a second stroke, Feng and co-authors report in a 2024 study. Both markers link to vessel swelling and fat handling in the blood. Five hundred eighty patients with a first sudden stroke from a blocked vessel joined the study, and marker levels were taken on admission.

Over two years of follow-up, about one in six patients had another stroke. Patients were split into four groups by high or low levels of each marker. The double-high group faced the greatest risk of return stroke. The authors say the pair gives a stronger warning than either marker alone. Such a test could flag patients who need tighter follow-up after a first stroke.
pmc-11660048:
Undrakh-Erdene Erdenebold and co-authors report a rare case from 2024, in which a woman grew a faulty blood vessel link near the brain years after surgery. She had part of a benign tumor near the top of the skull removed three years before. She then came in with signs of raised pressure inside the head, such as a pulsing sound, poor sight, and headache.

Scans and dye tests showed the faulty link, classed at a mid level of risk. Doctors blocked the feeders in three staged rounds, using glue, a sealing fluid, and small coils. Flow fell a great deal and her symptoms eased. The authors also review past cases and warn that such links can turn more grave over time.
pmc-11660148:
Suzanne Morsch and co-authors probe the thin boundary layer where epoxy glue meets a surface, in a 2024 study. This interphase is thought to be the weak point of many coatings and composites, yet it is buried and too thin for standard tools. The team mix computer simulation with a nano-scale infrared mapping method to see it at last.

They use iron oxide powders as test surfaces in a common epoxy system. The amine hardener binds to the three oxides with strength from repelled to locked fast, and that binding sets how much hardener stays free in the bulk. Near every particle, though, both glue parts pile up in excess, and the layer stays undercured even after extra heating. Simulations show loose ingredients drift apart as the glue sets, which explains the soft skin around each grain.
pmc-11660948:
Nickellaus Roberts and co-authors show how DNA amplification can unlock genome sequencing for microscopic animals in a 2024 paper. Tiny animals carry too little DNA for long-read sequencing, which blocks work on their family trees and genome evolution. Multiple displacement amplification uses an enzyme to grow micrograms of DNA from mere picograms.

The team tested the approach on living cells from a nematode, Caenorhabditis elegans, and a gastrotrich, Lepidodermella squamata, using about a tenth of the DNA the standard workflow needs. Sequencing the amplified DNA gave highly complete, well-joined genomes for both animals. The gastrotrich genome is the first of its kind here, opening a tiny phylum to modern genome science despite known amplification biases.
pmc-11662948:
Chao Liu and co-authors test whether two blood markers track the severity and outlook of acute respiratory distress syndrome, in a 2024 study. The syndrome floods the lungs and starves the blood of oxygen, and many patients die of it. The pair are message copies of two genes, FOXM1 and IGF2, drawn from serum. The team set patients beside healthy controls and split patients by who lived.

Patients showed lower FOXM1 and higher IGF2 than the healthy group. Those who died carried the pattern further: higher IGF2, worse kidney and breathing numbers, and lower FOXM1 and oxygen scores. A joint model kept FOXM1, IGF2, and the oxygen ratio as true guides to who would die. The two markers also moved in mirror image in patients, one low where the other ran high. The authors say the pair could help grade risk early.
pmc-11665148:
Four authors, led by Anthony Lee, present in 2024 the removal of a huge thyroid cancer lump that had spread into the skull bone and its lining. Such spread to the head is exceedingly rare for this cancer type. The report walks through the surgery step by step.

Key moves tamed the tumor's heavy blood supply, its growth outside the skull, and its invasion of a major vein channel. Tying off that channel, though it looked blocked, brought surprises the team flag as lessons. They also review past reports of this cancer reaching the brain. Even without widespread disease, they warn, a richly veined skull lump warrants this diagnosis on the list.
pmc-11665448:
Xochitl Morán Martínez and five co-authors simulate the fiery chemistry inside a reactor that grows silicon oxide films, in this 2024 study. In hot filament chemical vapor deposition, glowing wires crack gases into reactive fragments that rain onto a surface and build a film. The dance between quartz and hydrogen near the filament decides what lands.

The team solved the reactor's flow, heat, and diffusion equations in two dimensions with finite element software. Chemical equilibrium constants, computed separately for the quartz-hydrogen reactions, were tied to the simulated temperature map of the deposition zone. Measured substrate temperatures, 450 to 500 degrees Celsius, matched the model. The simulations confirmed smooth, laminar flow and put the key growth species, atomic hydrogen and silicon monoxide, where experience says they should be. A validated virtual reactor lets engineers rehearse recipes before burning real filaments.
pmc-11665948:
Jaskomal Phagoora, Brett Agrest, and their co-authors report a rare bloodstream infection in a man aged 86 with a deep sacral ulcer and bone infection. Their 2024 case study concerns two gut and mouth bacteria, Tissierella praeacuta and Parvimonas micra, which are seldom found in blood and are usually low in virulence. In frail patients they can turn severe.

The patient carried atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and lung disease, and arrived with a stage four sacral ulcer that had infected fast, with signs of sepsis. Blood cultures grew both bacteria. Despite broad antibiotics and surgical cleaning of the wound, his condition worsened. The case warns that chronic ulcers can open a path for uncommon gut bacteria into the blood.
pmc-11667048:
Sunmyoung Lee and co-authors introduce a 2024 database for sugars found on microbes. These sugars sit on cell surfaces and shape how microbes meet their host and surroundings. Facts about them are spread across many databases and papers. Pulling them together takes much time and labor, which slows research and drug work.

The new database, MicroGlycoDB, gathers sugar facts for key model microbes. It stores data in a web format that machines can read and merge with other sources. Links can join sugar data with paths, diseases, and interactions. The team hopes the shared format will spark new finds in the field. Coverage of more microbes is a stated aim for growth.
pmc-11667148:
Robbie, Desai, and Ramavath describe an unusual surgical emergency in this two thousand twenty-four case report. A man in his sixties with diabetes arrived with two weeks of knee pain, swelling, and dead skin on his calf. Scans showed gas under the skin, a sign of flesh-eating infection.

Cutting away the dead tissue revealed necrotising fasciitis running through the whole leg and tracking into the abdomen. Further imaging found the true source: a perforated sigmoid colon, and tissue tests confirmed an invasive colon cancer. Surgeons removed the damaged colon section and amputated at the hip, and the patient did well. The report warns doctors to look for an abdominal source when the infection's origin is unclear.
pmc-11667348:
Feifei Bu and Daisy Fancourt sorted in 2024 how older adults in England connect socially, and what each pattern means for health. Most past work reads one thread of connection at a time. Their study drew 7,706 people past fifty from a national aging survey. A clustering method grouped them by the shape of their social lives, and outcomes were then compared.

Five patterns emerged, from cut-off to richly connected. A third were richly connected, and every other group fared worse against them on depression, life pleasure, purpose, health, and activity. The cut-off group carried near triple the depression odds. Gaps narrowed but held after baseline checks. The team urges care that reads the whole social pattern, not single threads.
pmc-11667548:
Jonathan Lam, Rumana Hussain, Sarah Coupland, and Heinrich Heimann report a rare eye infection that looked like a tumor, in work from 2024. A West African woman in her eighties, whose immune system was suppressed after a kidney transplant, grew a large lesion on the surface of her only eye.

She had been treated years before for a body wide fungal infection. The new lesion grew over two weeks and harmed her sight. A biopsy that removed the lesion showed the same fungus, histoplasmosis. Full checks found no other site of infection. The case warns that this fungus can return in the eye alone and mimic cancer.
pmc-11668148:
Olfa Hammami and co-authors report an education study, published in 2024, asking whether students who only watch a role play learn as much as those who act in it. Teachers often rely on observers filling spare seats, yet doubt that watching teaches as well as doing. The team ran a before and after comparison during one role play session with twenty-nine learners split between acting and observing roles.

About two thirds of learners in both groups improved their overall score, and median scores rose clearly in each group. Crucially, the size of improvement did not differ between actors and observers. The authors suggest role play sessions deliver their learning value to the whole room, which matters when class sizes force most students into the audience.
pmc-11668648:
Masayoshi Sakano and seventeen co-authors study an enzyme that may shield throat cancer cells from a rust-like death, in a 2024 paper. The cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, kills many patients and resists standard treatment.

The death process, ferroptosis, depends on iron and on damage to cell fats. The enzyme GCH1 is known to block it. The team studied tissue from 312 patients who had surgery at a Tokyo university hospital. They stained the samples for the enzyme and for fat damage markers, then linked the patterns to survival. Cell experiments probed how the markers and the death process interact. The aim is a new treatment angle for a cancer short on options.
pmc-11669548:
Yunhe Fan and co-authors review work from two thousand twenty-four on a form of cell death in lupus nephritis, a kidney disease driven by immune imbalance. The death mode, called ferroptosis, is driven by iron and by peroxides that build up in cell fats. Work in cancer showed that shielding or exposing T cells to this death can tilt the immune setting.

The review maps metabolism inside the main T cell subsets in the disease, from helper types to regulatory cells. Those metabolic patterns both deepen the immune imbalance and invite ferroptosis. The authors propose that steering T cell metabolism to adjust ferroptosis could become a new treatment direction. It might rebalance immunity by changing how T cells develop and die.
pmc-11669848:
Yao Li and four co-authors review how bile acids and their receptor FXR steer metabolic disease. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-four. Bile acids do double duty: they help digest fat and act as hormone-like signals across the body.

When their mix goes wrong, the FXR receptor misfires in liver and gut, feeding obesity, fatty liver, and diabetes. Switching FXR on can trim fat production and curb glucose output. The gut's FXR also talks to the liver's copy, an organ-to-organ line that suggests new drug angles. The authors gather the mechanism and the therapeutic attempts built on it. Their map is meant to guide treatment ideas for the metabolic epidemic.
pmc-11670248:
Noelle Held and six co-workers say that when more than one food runs scarce at once, germ growth caps are a case of degree. Germs need carbon, nitrogen, metals, and vitamins as one set. Books most often name one scarce food, but the wild world is not so neat. The team built a count based claim that tells a spread of cap states. The frame also tracks how caps shift as states change.

Tests with cloned Escherichia coli groups checked what the claim foretold. Growth acts across food mixes matched the spread view. Joint caps, the team ends, are plain both in the lab and in the wild. A count score lets staff set side by side work that once used marks that did not match. The 2024 work could lift calls of germ acts in seas, soils, and tanks.
pmc-11671348:
Zheng and six co-authors study the anesthetic propofol as a treatment for traumatic brain injury in mice in a 2024 paper. Gene data first showed early changes tied to iron handling, cell death, and inflammation after injury. Ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, was a focus.

Injured mice given propofol showed less iron buildup and less ferroptosis in the brain. Neuron health improved and cell death fell. Long-term inflammation markers also eased, and memory tests improved. The benefit ran through a nitric oxide pathway, since blocking its key enzyme reversed the gains. The authors offer a scientific basis for propofol as a brain-protective drug.
pmc-11672148:
Nengfeng Gong and co-authors present a 2024 study of a platinum catalyst tucked inside zeolite crystals for turning alkanes into alkenes without oxygen. Mid chain alkenes feed many chemical products. The team adds potassium to the catalyst and asks how it steers the reaction for a five carbon chain.

A battery of imaging and X-ray tools shows potassium changes both particle size and the electronic state of the platinum. Those shifts in turn move activity and which products form. Middle chain cases are harder than light ones due to many reaction sites. The study draws a clear line from catalyst structure to reaction choice, a guide for cleaner chemical making.
pmc-11672648:
Yuliya Semenova and co-authors report a 2024 nationwide study of antibiotic use in Kazakhstan from 2019 to 2023. No recent study had assessed use across the whole country with a standard global method. The team set out to fill that gap so trends could be compared with other nations.

They measured use in defined daily doses per thousand people per day for systemic antibiotics under a standard drug code system. The results cover the period that includes the COVID-19 years, when antibiotic use shifted in many countries. Health officials can use the figures to guide stewardship and spot patterns that raise resistance risk.
pmc-11672848:
A research team measured how much energy chickens can draw from different grains, and how much that value varies by variety, in this 2024 feeding trial. Barley, rye, and wheat are staples of broiler diets, but their energy worth is often guessed from lab scans. The team fed birds set diets to get true values.

Four varieties of each grain were mixed into test diets, with and without added enzymes, and 432 young broilers ate them in rotating cages. Wheat gave the most usable energy, then barley, with rye last. Variety mattered more than scans predicted, and enzymes helped most in the weakest barley varieties. Two tracer markers agreed with each other. The results can sharpen feed formulas and cut waste.
pmc-11672948:
Mousa Sha'at and co-authors load a diabetes drug into a spongy silica carrier, in a 2024 paper. The carrier, MCM-48, is a glass-like stuff riddled with tiny even pores. Such carriers can hold a drug and let it out slowly, smoothing doses. The team made the carrier, filled it with metformin, the standard type 2 diabetes pill, and watched how the drug escaped in fake stomach and gut fluids.

The carrier's huge inner surface shrank as drug filled the pores, proof the loading worked. Two loading levels took in most of the drug offered. Release came in two phases: a fast burst in stomach-like fluid, then a slow tail in gut-like fluid, reaching most of the load in fourteen hours. A fractal math model tracked the release curves closely.
pmc-11673048:
Kristine Rostad and colleagues studied muscle loss in gene-edited zebrafish in two thousand twenty-four. The fish lack a protective antioxidant gene. They swim worse and stop gaining weight in mid-life. The team asked whether muscle degeneration explains that decline. Protein surveys compared young and older fish muscle. Fiber size and internal structure were also measured.

Muscle fibers shrank without the gene. Slow red muscle suffered more than fast white muscle. Its energy structures showed clear degeneration. Dozens of proteins shifted early, before performance fell. Many linked to inflammation and energy production. Chemical balance markers of aging changed early too. The fish model aging muscle decline well.
pmc-11673148:
Liliana Light, Suman Kaur Virdee, Colin Dickens, and Rui Diogo rethink obstructed labor through evolution and health disparities. Birth blockage, often from a size clash between baby and pelvis, is a leading cause of mother death and harm. The review came out in twenty twenty-four.

The pelvis is often told as a trade off between birth and upright walking. The authors widen that tale with a broader evolution frame that folds in social and surroundings forces. Money strain and ethnic gaps may raise the odds of blocked labor and its harms. The review seeks a fuller account of who bears this risk and why.
pmc-11673248:
Susel Góngora Alonso and six co-authors build models in a 2024 paper to predict hospital readmission for patients with schizophrenia in a Spanish region. Readmission is a sign of care quality, and high rates go with worse results, higher costs, and a harder life for patients.

Their data hold thousands of readmission records for such patients. The team pairs particle swarm optimization, a search method that tunes model settings, with machine learning classifiers. The aim is a model that flags who is most at risk of going back to hospital, so care teams can act early with the right support.
pmc-11673448:
Andrea Balivo, Giulia d'Errico, and Alessandro Genovese test whipped chickpea liquid, called aquafaba, as a cream replacer in coffee ice cream. Aquafaba foams, emulsifies, and gels, making it a candidate to cut fat. The team paired it with whey protein and replaced half or most of the milk cream.

The half replacement cut calories by a quarter, and the deeper cut by forty percent. Aquafaba boosted air content, above all at the half level. The eighty percent version tasted harder and melted differently, while the half version stayed close to full fat. A balanced mix passed a triangle test, with tasters unable to spot it. The study also reuses a discarded food by-product.
pmc-11673648:
Wen Li, Lili Guan, and John Parkinson study how thoughts of death sway fair choices. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, draws on terror management theory. Reminders of death can push people toward selfish or kind acts, and past work is mixed. The team adds self-control as the key that may tip the balance.

In two studies, people primed with death thoughts split money less fairly. They kept more for themselves than a control group primed with bad feelings. The second study splits the result by self-control. The selfish shift hit only those low in self-control. Strong self-control acted as a buffer. The work links mindset, willpower, and fair dealing.
pmc-11673848: Nguyen Quoc Khanh Le wrote a 2024 article on how artificial intelligence is reshaping biomedicine. The piece frames fast growth in these tools as a force that is redefining the field. It places AI at the front of fresh finds in molecular biology and gene science. Drug hunting and diagnosis are named as well, with reach past those areas. The hosted text is a short opening passage, not a full study. It states the theme and the fields touched, but gives no data or methods of its own.
pmc-11674048:
Guillermo Valencia and co-authors review first treatment choices for advanced breast cancer in a 2024 study from a public institution in Latin America. The patients had hormone-sensitive tumors lacking the HER2 marker, a common subtype. Hormone therapy is the usual first step, yet chemotherapy still leads in many countries, and the team asked what drives that choice.

Records showed chemotherapy went first for about a third of patients. Around sixty percent met trial criteria for aggressive disease, which supports early chemotherapy in a group with poor outlook. Newly spread disease and disease that kept growing also pushed doctors toward chemotherapy. Survival across the treatment sequence groups beat some large trial comparison arms, with no clear gap between sequences.
pmc-11674348:
Xiaowei Fan and six co-authors build a glowing sensor sensitive enough to catch trace amounts of an antipsychotic drug, in this 2024 paper. The method is electrochemiluminescence: an electric signal triggers a chemical flash, whose brightness betrays how much of the target drug, chlorpromazine hydrochloride, is present. Brighter, steadier flashes mean lower detection limits.

The team engineered flower-shaped flakes of cadmium sulfide wrapped in a porous cobalt-molybdenum framework, paired with carbon nitride sheets. The framework stops the flakes from clumping and hurries the chemistry along, multiplying the flash's strength more than sixfold while steadying it. Detecting this drug precisely matters for checking doses and catching contamination or overdose. More broadly, the flower-like accelerator is a recipe other sensor builders can borrow: structure first, and sensitivity follows.
pmc-11674548:
Xiaojuan Du and co-authors build a chart that predicts which fainting children will gain from standing training. Their 2024 paper covers vasovagal syncope, a common faint caused by a drop in heart rate and blood pressure. The treatment trains children to stand for set times, but it does not help all of them.

The team looked back at treated children and measured heart rate variability, the small gaps between beats. They sifted candidate factors and built a visual scoring chart called a nomogram. Age and one beat-gap measure carried the final model. Scores on training and check groups showed fair accuracy for sorting likely responders. Such a chart could spare children a long therapy that is unlikely to help them, and focus care where it counts.
pmc-11674648:
Christian Jongen and co-authors test a dose twist in prostate radiation models in a 2024 study. Dose maps hold rich spatial marks that can forecast side effects, a craft called dosiomics. One late harm is rectal bleeding within five years of care, and dose per visit swings how hard each dose truly hits tissue.

The team drew 656 men from a past trial that pitted standard visit counts against fewer, larger visits. Marks were pulled from dose maps in plain units and in a form that folds in visit size. Three tests weighed what the folded form adds to bleeding forecasts.
pmc-11674748:
Babatope Adebiyi, Kathryn Birnie and Heinrike Schmeling write a commentary on joining chronic disease care with harm reduction for youth with juvenile idiopathic arthritis in Canada. This long-term joint disease can need opioid pain care, while Canada's overdose crisis brings risks of dependence and toxic street drugs. Children with arthritis sit where those two risks meet.

The authors propose care models that join arthritis management with opioid stewardship and harm reduction in one team. They call for wider access to joint specialty services, funds for pain care, research and mental health support, and training for providers on pain, substance use and mental health together. The model may also serve other at-risk groups.
pmc-11674848:
Zhenyu Huang and co-authors built a fuller data set of all the gene messages found in brain tissue linked to the most common form of dementia in old age. Good records of these messages matter because gene errors and shifts in cell fuel use help drive the disease. Older data sets missed many message forms, such as spliced forms and long non-coding strands.

The team used public gene-read data from tissue taken before and after the disease took hold. With modern computer tools, they assembled and labeled the messages more fully. The new set gives researchers a cleaner base for asking which gene changes mark the start and course of the illness. It is a resource paper, meant for reuse by other labs.
pmc-11674948:
Xin Hao and co-authors cataloged in 2024 a family of genes in soybean that may help set seed size. Soybean is a major world crop, and seed size reflects both genes and environment. The family resembles a known gene-silencing complex in a model plant that controls a growth gene.

The team identified more than a hundred family members spread unevenly across the soybean chromosomes. Their activity patterns differed by tissue and growth stage, hinting at varied roles in development. Enrichment analysis tied the family to many processes, above all catalysis and metabolism. The catalogue gives breeders candidate targets and a base for testing what each family member does.
pmc-11675448:
Xu and co-authors pin down the structure of a sugar chain from lesser galangal, a plant long used as food and medicine in China. The plant has treated cough, diabetes, and stomach illness for thousands of years. The team pulled sugars from its roots with hot water.

One pure chain, named AOP-w, had a small size of 5.26 kilodaltons. It was built mostly from glucose, with some galactose, in a branched pattern. The chain did not harm mouse immune cells and boosted their growth at set doses. Treated cells also released more nitric oxide, a sign of immune activity.
pmc-11675648:
Patricia Regal and co-authors present a 2024 workflow for finding Salmonella in poultry farm samples with a fast gene-copy method. The germ is a top cause of food poisoning, and chicken farms are its main source. Boot swabs sample the farm floor, but lab growth tests are slow.

Four ways to free the DNA were weighed, from plain heat to bead cleaning, for use right on the farm. A blind test across labs and a color-change read by eye were part of the check. The final flow found very low germ counts with high accuracy against the standard method.
pmc-11675748:
Pietro Grussu and co-authors present a 2024 scoping review of two ultra-short screening tools for mental health around childbirth. The Whooley questions ask two plain questions about mood and interest; the GAD-2 does the same for anxiety. Guidelines recommend perinatal screening, but how these quick tools perform in practice was scattered across small studies.

Nine studies used both tools together. Used in pregnancy, the pair flagged women at higher risk of postpartum depression and caught symptoms that carried over after delivery, rivaling some longer instruments. Being self-reported, though, their accuracy figures were inconsistent and open to recall bias, and they signal risk rather than diagnose. The authors call for proper validation across the whole perinatal period before wider reliance.
pmc-11675948:
Yan Gao and co-authors describe a new fracturing fluid in a 2024 materials paper. The fluid is a foam gel made with carbon dioxide gas, meant to crack rock so oil or gas can flow. Such fluids use less water and harm the rock less, but many are weak or hard to make.

The team mixed a thickening agent and a foaming agent to build a simpler, firmer foam. In sand tests, grains sank very slowly, and the foam held sand better than the plain base fluid. Heat and shear tests showed the foam kept useful thickness after long stress. The authors see promise for tight, low-pressure rock where water use is a concern.
pmc-11676448:
Dongsong Yin and co-authors test adding strontium to a medical magnesium alloy in a 2024 study. The base alloy is used for bone fixation parts that should dissolve safely in the body. Its strength, toughness, and rust resistance still need gains for that job.

Bars of the alloy were rolled with strontium shares from zero up to 1.2 percent. The additive changed how grains re-form during rolling, with mixed fine and coarse zones at low shares. Stretch before breaking fell as strontium rose. Rust resistance peaked at 0.9 percent strontium, where the yearly corrosion rate hit its lowest value. The head byline omits one catalog author, so the team is named without a count.
pmc-11676748:
Casas-Barragan and coauthors link blood amino acids to body temperature in fibromyalgia. The syndrome causes wide pain and fatigue with no clear cause. Body temperature patterns may differ in those patients. Amino acid levels in blood may track those patterns.

The study held 47 patients and 59 healthy adults. Blood samples gave amino acid levels by a lab method. A heat camera gauged hand temperatures for each person. Core temperature was read at armpit and ear sites. Six amino acids showed links to hand heat measures. Patterns differed between patients and healthy adults.
pmc-11677048:
Aleksander Myszka and co-authors search, in twenty twenty-four, for gene markers that predict bladder cancer return. Most bladder cancer patients face tumor recurrence, the return of the tumor after treatment. Knowing who is at risk shapes treatment and follow-up. The team studied forty-six patients whose tumors were removed through the urinary passage. They sequenced tumor DNA across fifty genes tied to cancer. They then linked mutations to outcomes and to time free of tumors.

They found eighty-one variants in twenty-three genes. Three genes were mutated most often, in about half, a third, and a quarter of tumors. Tumors with a mutation in one gene, PIK3CA, stayed away longer. That mutation linked to a much lower risk of return.
pmc-11677448:
Yevgeniya Shurubor and co-authors test blood marks for liver-driven brain harm in rats in a 2024 paper. The illness clouds thought, and grading its depth lacks firm marks. Two acids from the glutamate cycle are the candidates here.

Rats were dosed with a strong liver toxin to model the illness. The team read both acids in blood, liver, kidney, and brain samples. Their balance and ratio tracked how deep the illness ran and how recovery went. Past work on wide metabolite scans backs these two as sharp picks. Trusty marks could help doctors grade the illness and time care.
pmc-11677548:
Magnesium matters for health, and supplement makers claim some forms enter the blood better than others. David Pajuelo and four co-authors test that claim for a coated form of the mineral in this 2024 clinical study. Volunteers tried four magnesium sources in turn: coated microcapsules, an oxide, a citrate, and a bisglycinate form.

Forty healthy adults ate a low-magnesium diet for seven days, then fasted before each test dose. Blood samples from a finger prick were taken before dosing and after one, four, and six hours. The coated form raised blood magnesium at every check and kept it up, while the oxide and citrate forms showed shorter rises. The bisglycinate form showed no clear rise in this study. The authors also tracked side effects for each source.
pmc-11677648:
Tadej Durič and five co-authors test a belt-like holder for endoscopes in a study from 2024. Doctors who run gut scopes face rising muscle and joint injuries from holding the heavy scope. The belt spreads the scope's weight across the whole body. A camera system that tracks body motion recorded trained doctors doing a set of standard scope tasks on a model, with and without the belt.

Video and data analysis found the clearest change in the left arm, which sat in a more relaxed position with the holder. The authors say the ergonomic gain merits a trial in real clinics to test injury prevention.
pmc-11677748:
Menghan Gao and a team of co-authors map the fungi living in the sediments of Zhanjiang Bay, China, across a salinity gradient, in a two thousand twenty-four marine ecology paper. Sediment fungi drive organic matter cycling, yet their diversity in estuaries was poorly documented.

Sequencing of a ribosomal marker region yielded twelve hundred forty-two sequence variants across one hundred forty-four genera and five phyla. Ascomycota dominated, near sixty-nine percent of the community. Diversity and community structure differed clearly among low, medium, and high salinity zones, and the species-interaction networks changed shape with salinity too. Redundancy analysis fingered salinity as the main driver for the dominant phylum. The survey supplies baseline biodiversity data for estuary-coast management.
pmc-11677848:
Lahcen Khouchaf and co-authors present a 2024 study on flint, a form of silica used as a building aggregate. How stiff it is depends on its chemistry and on heat treatment. The team studied natural flint before and after chemical attack. A range of lab tools tracked crystal size, strain, and structure changes in samples and in silica fibers.

Heat improved crystal quality, as shown by sharper peaks in the tests. Chemical attack raised the strain inside the crystals. Sizes and strain were read from graph slopes and intercepts by set formulas. The authors say flint with tuned traits could serve as a filler. Such a filler may lift strength and durability in some mixed materials.
pmc-11677948:
Quan Li and co-authors make anion exchange membranes that are crosslinked, for fuel cells. The membranes have high conductivity and stability. Their 2024 study uses diblock poly(norbornene) materials. It deals with flaws that are common in membranes made by man.

The plan joins a backbone made all of carbon, crosslinking that draws in water, and spacer chains that can bend. As a set, they build channels that move ions well. How much crosslinker was used had a strong effect on how the channels formed and on how the membranes did. One membrane showed the highest hydroxide conductivity. It also took up a fair amount of water, and swelled by a small amount at high heat. It kept most of its capacity and conductivity after long time in hot alkaline fluid. Single fuel cells that used it hit a peak power density of note.
pmc-11678048:
Othoniel Aragon-Martinez and co-authors tested whether an extract from a cactus insect can lower uric acid, in a 2024 study. High uric acid, often tied to kidney damage, can be treated with drugs that sometimes cause serious side effects. The insect, a cochineal type farmed for red dye, is rich in carminic acid. The team made two extracts and checked them in dishes and in mice with induced high uric acid.

One extract blocked about half the target enzyme's action in a dish and soaked up free radicals. Given to mice, it lowered uric acid and a kidney stress marker, and it guarded the kidneys' own defenses. The second extract, rich in citric acid, killed the mice and was dropped. The authors say the safe extract could become a gentler option when high uric acid stems from kidney injury.
pmc-11678148:
Nghi Nguyen and Christopher Conrady wrote a 2024 review on viral retinitis, an infection of the retina that can blind. The condition is rare but can destroy sight fast and for good. Herpes viruses are the main cause of the most destructive form, which kills retinal tissue.

The review explains how these viruses get into the retina and damage it, drawing on clinic reports and lab work. Three virus types get the closest look: varicella-zoster, herpes simplex, and cytomegalovirus. The authors also set out what doctors see in the eye during each stage of disease. They point to gaps in what is known about the infection's course. Closing those gaps, they argue, is the path to treatments that save more vision.
pmc-11678248:
Qingzhen Sun and co-authors study how a mountain herb splits its growth between roots, stems, leaves, and flowers in a 2024 paper. The plant, Gentianella turkestanorum, is gathered as a medicinal herb, so knowing how altitude and soil steer its bulk helps guide its use and protection.

The team weighed each organ across heights and tracked leaf traits beside the weights. Total bulk fell as altitude rose, while the share held below ground grew. Flowers took well over half of all mass. Low sites fit a bold growth plan that spends fast, and high sites a careful one that saves. Leaf greenness and thickness rose with height, and height plus soil explained bulk better than leaf traits did.
pmc-11678348:
Arun Karnwal, Amar Yasser Jassim, and colleagues wrote a review of plant-derived nanoparticles for medicine that has since been retracted, published in 2024 and later withdrawn from the record. Because the article is retracted, its claims should not be relied on. The entry is preserved so readers can see what was claimed and that it no longer stands. The review had presented plant-based nanotechnology as a sustainable route to disease treatment and regenerative medicine, arguing it could cut environmental impact while improving therapy.

Readers should treat every claim in the text as unverified and consult the retraction notice before citing anything from it.
pmc-11678448:
Fu and a large team study goat immune cells infected with a Pasteurella bacterium in twenty twenty-four. The disease, pasteurellosis, harms livestock worldwide and can infect humans. How goat blood lymphocytes respond to this bacterium was little known. The team built a lab model with isolated goat cells.

After infection, levels of several pro inflammatory signals rose within twelve hours. A key anti inflammatory signal fell over the same period. RNA sequencing found more than two thousand genes with changed activity. Those genes clustered in cytokine interaction pathways and the IL-17 pathway. Network analysis and follow up tests named a set of genes central to the response. The authors say the work clarifies goat defences against this bacterium.
pmc-11678948:
Haolin Cao, Bingshuo Yan, Lin Dong, and Xianfeng Yuan present a new method in 2024 for picking the most useful data points in a task. Picking the right subset, called feature selection, helps computers sort data faster and more cleanly. Their method is based on how whales hunt, turned into a search routine.

The method splits its search group into smaller groups so it does not settle too soon. It also uses spiral moves to escape dead ends, and a close-range step to fine-tune the best picks. The team tested it on twenty data sets, where it beat most rival methods. They then used it for fall detection with body sensors, and it worked well there too.
pmc-11679148:
Stefano Favelli and co-authors combine camera, radar, and laser scanner data so a driver-assistance system can judge distances to road objects, in a 2024 paper. Each sensor alone has blind spots that fusion can cover.

Their open-source pipeline projects three-dimensional laser points onto camera images, then matches them to objects a detector has labeled. Calibration, point-cloud thinning, and clustering prepare the data for the matching step. Tests in real city streets ran on a compact onboard computer at five frames per second. Accuracy on object finding and distance estimates was good. The authors present the framework as a flexible, low-cost base for assisted driving.
pmc-11679248:
Zhen Gao and co-authors built a system that spots driver fatigue in video, using a model first trained to link images with words. Tired driving is a leading cause of crashes in commercial vehicles, and earlier video systems miss subtle signs because their features are coarse. The team's network, called CT-Net, pairs that image-language model with a transformer, which reads long stretches of video at once and picks up slow changes in the face and behavior over time.

In tests, the system scored well above a common older design and reached the best results reported for this task. Swapping in the image-language model in place of a standard pre-trained one lifted accuracy, and the transformer beat the older memory approach at tracking long patterns. The authors frame the work as a step toward in-cab warnings that catch drowsiness earlier and more reliably.
pmc-11679848:
Yasodha Subba and five co-authors record what eleven villages in India's Darjeeling district know of medicinal plants. They then zoom in on one birch species for lab tests. Talks with forty-seven informants, eleven of them herbalists, recorded one hundred fifteen species across sixty-five families. The remedies, given with free prior informed consent, numbered over a hundred single-plant and twenty-one mixed formulations for fifty conditions.

Indices with numbers attached measured how strongly informants agreed and how versatile each plant was. Digestive diseases drew the highest consensus, and a costus relative earned the highest use value. The bark of Betula alnoides got phytochemical and toxicity analysis. The study keeps local knowledge safe while it flags the remedies locals trust most.
pmc-11679948:
Mena Nagiub and co-authors improve depth maps from a light-based sensor that struggles when a vehicle creeps along, in a 2024 paper. The sensor times returning light pulses to judge distance, but near distances wrap around and blur when the car moves slowly. Most learning-based fixes were trained on still indoor scenes. The team aimed their method at moving outdoor scenes instead.

Their approach works in two stages. First, the model learns clean depth judgment from still scenes where the true depth is known. Then it keeps learning on moving scenes without full labels, adapting to the blur of real driving. A blind sharpening step further strips out motion smear. The authors report clearer depth maps with less blur noise, a gain that matters for parking aids and other slow-speed driving help.
pmc-11680048:
Jessica Malloy and four co-authors pilot a lifestyle program delivered through Instagram for young women, in this 2024 trial report. Young women spend about fifty minutes a day on social media, which makes the platforms a promising channel for health content. The program, the Daily Health Coach, was designed with its users and ran for three months on eating, activity, and social wellbeing.

Forty-six women aged eighteen to twenty-four took part in a twelve-week randomized pilot. Satisfaction scored about eighty-four percent, and the format proved workable on recruitment, retention, and data collection. Over the program, body image disturbance fell clearly in the intervention group. Digital health literacy rose too, meaning the women got better at spotting sound information. One measure, social influence, oddly rose more in the waitlist group. The authors call the approach feasible and acceptable, with larger trials needed to judge effects.
pmc-11680248:
Nengak Danladi and a large team examine why monkeypox vaccines fail to reach the countries that need them most. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four, as the outbreak spread from its African home range worldwide and was declared an international emergency.

Rich countries raced to lock in supply through advance deals and stockpiles. Poorer countries were left behind, with weak surveillance adding to the gap. The authors call that pattern vaccine nationalism. Their fixes include building vaccine making capacity in more regions, aiming supply at high-risk, low-resource countries, strengthening disease tracking, and tackling hesitancy. The paper frames fair access as a practical need, not only a moral one.
pmc-11680348:
Simona Giubega and co-authors hunt for a tick borne blood parasite in healthy horses in southwest Romania. Their paper from 2024 deals with Babesia caballi, a cause of horse piroplasmosis that cuts work output and welfare. Gene tests can find quiet carriers that show no signs.

Blood was taken from 310 horses kept in homes across the southwest and west of the country. Two gene test types were run on each sample. The parasite was found in eighteen horses, about six percent, though vets had reported no matching illness signs. The team reads the parasite as settled in the area and calls for more work on spread paths and control plans, since local data are thin.
pmc-11681148:
Flament and co-authors report in 2024 a large international survey of how skin concerns affect self confidence in men. The letter opens by rejecting the stereotype that men care little for skin. Norms of toughness have long pushed skin care toward women in public view, the authors note.

The survey ran from February 2022 to June 2023 with 5,138 men aged 18 and older across five countries, the United States and India the largest groups. Skin type, sensitivity, and self reported concerns were set against confidence scores. The study is cast as the first international work of its kind on men's skin concerns.
pmc-11681948:
Syed Ali Bokhari, Hanan Butaher, Reem Saleem and Nahid Elhassan report a 2024 case of a low platelet count tied to a mind drug. The drug, olanzapine, treats schizophrenia and is known for weight and sugar effects. Blood effects are rare and can be missed. Their patient was a man in his thirties with long-term schizophrenia.

After years on the drug, his platelet counts stayed below the normal range. He had no bleeding or bruising, but the drop forced a change in care. A switch to a second drug at first brought back his symptoms. A paired plan then raised his counts while keeping him stable.
pmc-11682548:
Mojtaba Akbari, Christian Giske, and Hamid Solgi write a letter warning against careless use of a last-line antibiotic pair, ceftazidime-avibactam. Carbapenem-resistant bacteria are spreading in hospitals worldwide, leaving few working drugs. The new pair is a first choice against some resistant strains, but not all.

The drug pair fails against bacteria carrying metallo-beta-lactamase enzymes. In Iran, the writers note, the dominant resistance genes include exactly those types, often paired in one Klebsiella strain. Guessing with this drug as solo therapy there invites failure and breeds more resistance. They cite a first reported failure in a ninety-one-year-old patient. Their plea: test first, then prescribe.
pmc-11682748:
Reiner Silveira de Moraes and nine co-authors reviewed a decade of records for 386 male cats treated for blocked urethras at a Brazilian veterinary teaching hospital. A blocked cat cannot urinate, and waste products build up fast, so knowing the typical blood and urine pattern helps vets judge severity. The records span 2010 to 2020.

Anemia was uncommon, but low platelet counts appeared in about two thirds of tested cats, and signs of infection-fighting white cells rose in half. Kidney values were high in roughly four of five cats. Blood tests often showed acid buildup and disturbed salts, especially low calcium and high potassium, a dangerous combination for the heart. About one in five urine cultures grew bacteria. The authors give clinicians a reference profile for this common emergency.
pmc-11682948:
Jackson Strand and three co-authors study smooth brome grass as a refuge for parasitoids that attack wheat stem sawfly, in work from 2024. The sawfly is a major cereal pest in the Northern Great Plains, and two native braconid wasps help keep it down. Smooth brome can host many sawflies yet kill most larvae late in the season, leaving hosts for the wasps.

Cage tests showed high infestation in brome with very low sawfly survival by year end. Field stems from two Montana sites showed high infestation in both brome and wheat. Larval death was much higher in brome, while wasp numbers were much alike. The authors back brome as a lasting refuge that supports wheat growing.
pmc-11683248:
Juliette Aminian-Biquet and a large team compile the rules inside Europe's marine protected areas in this 2024 dataset paper. Protection at sea varies: some zones ban nearly all activity, others allow much. Knowing which rules apply where is basic for judging whether the zones work.

The team merged area lists and maps from European and global sources. Overlapping zones were fused into single entries. Each record carries the year set, the type of designation, and the activities allowed. Zoning maps were added where they exist. The open dataset lets researchers grade real protection, not just drawn boundaries, across the European Union's seas.
pmc-11683648:
De Araújo and co-authors turn cashew waste into packaging material in this 2024 study. The catalog record gives the first author only as Layanne; the head byline lists six authors by initials. Cashew apple pulp left after juicing is usually thrown away. Its fibers can yield cellulose nanoparticles, tiny building blocks for films. The team freed them with enzymes plus ultrasound instead of harsh chemistry.

Only one pretreatment path produced the particles, as small spheres. The yield reached about sixty-five percent with good heat and water stability. Films cast with the particles held more water and rotted down faster than plain films. Food wraps and cosmetic masks are the suggested uses.
pmc-11684548: Gopal Kumar, Sahar Iqbal, Raja, and Thessicar Antoine-Reid report a rare bloodstream infection in this 2024 case report. The germ, Tissierella praeacuta, is an anaerobe that had not been documented in blood in this setting before. The patient had sepsis from a skin infection of the lower leg, with no bone infection found. Care combined three intravenous antibiotics with surgery to clean and drain the foot wound. The patient improved clearly and moved to a skilled nursing facility on one antibiotic to finish the course.
pmc-11685348:
Min-Jung Cho reviews a heart rhythm disease in children in 2024, known by its short name CPVT. The disease can trigger fast, chaotic heartbeats during exercise or stress. It can cause sudden death, yet rest tests often look normal, so it is easy to miss.

Cho centers on a recent study by Lee and co-authors of Asian patients with long follow-up. That study stressed brain and learning signs that often come with the disease. A gene flaw that harms calcium control in the heart is also active in the brain, which may explain those signs. Cho notes that no firm score yet predicts who faces the worst events. Care still rests on limits to hard exercise and on beta-blocker drugs, which do not help all patients.
pmc-11686448:
Evgenia Globa and co-authors present the first national study of congenital hyperinsulinism in Ukraine. Their study appeared in 2024. In this rare condition, babies make too much insulin and their blood sugar can crash. The team gathered 41 patients from the national registry for 2014 to 2023. Genetic tests, special scans, and surgery were done with help from partners abroad.

Gene faults were found in about 86 percent of lasting cases. All of them sat in two genes that control insulin release. Cases that faded early had more varied causes, including two named syndromes. Of nineteen children who had surgery, most had the focal form of the disease, where one spot in the pancreas is at fault. Many recovered fully after surgery. The study gives Ukraine its first full picture of the condition.
pmc-11686948:
Jana Jeglinski and six co-authors model two centuries of climate effects on a seabird in a 2024 paper. Northern gannets breed in colonies across the Northeast Atlantic. Forecasting their fate needs a model that joins births, movement, and weather over huge spans.

A Bayesian population model was fitted to colony counts and climate data from 1900 to 2100. Breeding success bent in a curve with air temperature, while warm seas cut recruitment. Future warming squeezes the seas' carrying capacity and flips how crowding regulates numbers. Southwestern colonies lose out while northern ones gain. The bird was long assumed climate-robust, which this work overturns. Colony-by-colony sensitivity maps give conservation planners a place-based guide.
pmc-11687248:
The weeks after leaving a psychiatric ward carry a high suicide risk, yet little was known about how family doctors manage that window. Seven researchers link primary and secondary care records in England for 2024 report. They compare people who died by suicide within a year of discharge, from 2001 to 2019, with matched survivors. The records show visits, prescriptions, and how steady a patient's care was.

Over 80 percent of those who died within a year had seen a primary care clinician in that time. Those who died were less likely to visit within two weeks of discharge, but more likely to visit in the week before death. Hospital discharge messages were rare. The authors urge services to communicate faster after discharge.
pmc-11687948:
Daniel Mechtersheimer and co-authors present a readable gut microbe classifier in a paper published in 2024; the catalog lists 2025, but the journal record in the text gives 2024. Gut microbes shape health, yet models that predict disease from microbe counts rarely say which microbes matter. Their framework, IMPACT, turns microbe tables into images using functional annotation data, then reads them with an attention-guided network.

The model beat similar methods on multi-way disease classification. More usefully, image-style saliency maps highlight the exact microbes driving each call. Those highlighted markers can be checked against known biology. Doctors trust tools that show their reasons, and trait-based features keep the reasons in the language of the field.
pmc-11688348:
Muna Ahmead, Nuha El Sharif, Abdallah Alwawi, Asma Hemeid, and Motasem Ziqan measured in 2024 burnout among Palestinian health professionals during ongoing conflict. Health workers under political violence face high risk of psychological harm, yet their coping strategies were little documented. Standard questionnaires measured burnout and ways of coping.

Nearly three quarters of the more than seven hundred participants showed burnout, and low personal accomplishment was especially common. Working very long days and mid-range job experience raised the risk of emotional exhaustion. Active coping and support from others lowered burnout risk, while disengagement and self-blame raised it. The authors call for urgent psychological support and stress training for this workforce.
pmc-11688848:
Yuanjin Zhou, Amanda Kilcrease, and Elizabeth Phelan ask health staff how to enlist dementia care partners against falls in a 2024 study. Older people with dementia fall more often than peers. Family care partners sit close enough to help, but their own needs for support stay murky.

The team spoke with twenty-two staff from six fields, all seasoned in dementia care. Blocks named were care load, low felt need, honoring the older person's wishes, and fights over care plans. Gaps in food, home checks, and gear also blocked action. Staff urged meeting the partner's top worry first. Trust built that way may open the door to fall plans.
pmc-11688948:
Pablo Martinez Amezcua reports, in twenty twenty-four, a test of whether hearing care raises activity in older adults. Hearing loss links to less movement, but cause is unclear. He uses a large trial that gave hearing aids and care to one group. The other group got health classes. Close to one thousand adults aged seventy to eighty-four took part, all with hearing loss.

Over three years, hard activity fell a bit in the whole sample, while casual walking rose. The hearing group had slightly higher odds of both forms of movement. The gap was larger for people new to the study. The links were not firm, the author notes.
pmc-11689048:
Ian Breunig and three co-authors report, in twenty twenty-four, a large test of on-site support in public housing for older adults. Congress funded the test to see if health and social aid helps people stay in their homes longer. Paid wellness directors and part-time nurses worked on site in homes across seven states. The trial compared those sites with control sites, using health program data.

Over the first three years, the model did not change health care use or length of stay overall. Some groups did use less urgent care, notably the youngest and the oldest residents. Two parts of the model also seemed to help. The authors see cause for hope over a longer span.
pmc-11689148:
Gabrielle Pfund and co-authors trace a three-way tug among purpose, loneliness, and memory in very old age. Dementia has no easy cure, so researchers hunt habits of mind that slow decline. A strong sense of purpose looks protective, while loneliness raises risk, and each may feed the others. The team used up to eighteen yearly waves from the Rush Memory and Aging Project, covering over seventeen hundred participants averaging eighty-one years old.

Their models let each factor predict the others over time, within the same person. A year when purpose dipped below a person's own norm was followed by weaker cognition a year later. Slipping cognition likewise foreshadowed fading purpose. The authors suggest programs that grow purpose and company together, since the two fronts reinforce each other.
pmc-11689248:
Yaakov Hoffman, Ehud Bodner, Susanna Cohen, and Amit Shrira wrote this 2024 study of older adults in hospital care. The team asked whether two things shape later health: how staff treat older patients, and how patients view their own aging. Both factors are common in wards where most patients are over 65.

The team followed 54 patients, with an average age of about 76, across four rounds of checks. Patients who met more ageist treatment felt less pleased with their care and rated their health worse four months later. Part of that link ran through a shift in how patients saw their own aging. The authors say training staff to drop ageist habits could help patients and cut costs.
pmc-11689348:
Patricia Heyn and James Dowd lead a symposium, in twenty twenty-four, on fitness and quality of life for older adults. Four talks bring fresh takes on exercise work. One shares a fall prevention alliance in Northern Virginia that spread proven programs through joint work between schools and towns. One asks why older runners keep running. Joy and habit, not just health, kept them going.

A third talk warns of waste when many reviews repeat the same exercise studies in people with memory loss. A fourth shares a case from Brazil. There, a four-part care frame was used in dementia care, with tech to keep far-off families close.
pmc-11689448:
Sunshine Rote follows Mexican American caregivers over five years in a 2024 study of depression. Family and neighborhood support may protect Latino caregivers' mental health, but the idea had little direct testing. The study draws on a long-running survey of older Mexican Americans and its caregiver supplement, covering 333 caregivers in two waves.

Depressive symptoms stayed fairly low overall, yet they climbed more among caregivers interviewed in Spanish than among those interviewed in English. Weaker resources, such as less support from others, explained part of that gap. Relationship type, language use, and living setup all entered the models. The author calls for dementia care supports built for Spanish-speaking caregivers, whose needs current systems often miss.
pmc-11689548:
Ana-Maria Vranceanu and co-authors describe MASC in 2024, a stress program for caregivers of people with dementia who face hard behavior symptoms. Most current help gives broad support or facts and does not target stress from those symptoms. MASC joins calm-focus skills and self-kindness with hands-on steps for daily care stress.

Talks and surveys with 24 caregivers shaped the program and backed the need for it. A pilot with 10 caregivers ran well, with high uptake and good session turnout. Stress, low mood, and quality of life all improved by small to mid amounts. A larger randomized pilot is now under way.
pmc-11689748:
Rakshitha Mohankumar, Kristopher Kern, and Brenna Renn survey psychologists who work with diverse older adults, in a 2024 study. America's older population is growing in both size and diversity, and elders from marginalized groups face stubborn health gaps. Training in culturally respectful care is uneven among clinicians. The authors asked members of a clinical geropsychology society how they handle identity and culture in practice and research.

An online survey with open-ended questions gathered their experiences. Respondents described how they weigh race, language, faith, sexuality, and other identities in therapy and study design. The answers expose where training falls short and where good practice already exists. Such insight can shape training so that aging care fits the people it serves.
pmc-11689848:
Victoria Williams and co-authors published a study in 2024 on how exposures at mid-life and late life link to dementia risk, and how a gene variant changes those links. Air pollution late in life is tied to higher dementia risk, worse for carriers of the ApoE-4 variant. Whether mid-life job exposures act the same way was unknown. The team used long-running survey data from Wisconsin on thousands of adults.

Mid-life exposure to breathing hazards at work raised dementia odds, but only in non-carriers. Late-life pollution raised risk only in carriers. The authors read the gene as a modifier whose effect flips with timing: it seems to shield against mid-life hazards yet heighten late-life pollution harm.
pmc-11689948:
Marguerite DeLiema, Siyu Gao, Daniel Brannock, and Lynn Langton survey, in a 2024 study, known victims of mass marketing fraud in the United States. Most fraud research asks people whether they were victimized. That method undercounts older victims, who are less likely to disclose what happened. This study sidesteps the bias by starting from victims already identified by law enforcement.

All respondents had mailed money in answer to fraudulent pitches between 2022 and 2023, from one to 168 times. Postal inspectors had detained their payment envelopes, and shared addresses securely with the team. Of those reached, 934 replied, a response rate of about a quarter, mostly by mail. The average age was 74. Victims were diverse in race and income. A quarter lived on under twenty thousand dollars a year. The portrait corrects who fraud research usually sees.
pmc-11690048:
Kristina Shiroma and Jacqueline Miller review research on AI health tools for older adults, in twenty twenty-four. They ask a narrow question: how often do rural older adults appear in that work? Rural areas have more older people and less care nearby, so the gap matters. They searched major health and tech databases for studies from twenty thirteen to twenty twenty-three.

They found much work on AI for older adults in general. Very little of it focused on rural elders, or split results by place. That leaves doubt about whether findings fit rural life. The authors call for studies built for rural needs from the start, not added as an afterthought.
pmc-11690148:
John Warren and co-authors study the long shadow of a bank failure in a 2024 paper. The Freedman's Savings Bank was chartered in 1865 to serve newly emancipated people across seventeen states. Mismanagement and fraud by its white officials brought it down in 1874, wiping out much of what many Black depositors had saved.

Short-term gains from the bank's existence are debated, but no one had traced what the failure did to depositors over their lives. The team links complete census records from 1860 to 1940 with the bank's own detailed branch and deposit files. Several estimation strategies then measure effects on depositors and their children across social, economic, and mortality outcomes. The work speaks to how negative shocks echo through a life.
pmc-11690248:
Eskira Kahsay and Briana Mezuk study how racial residential segregation relates to suicidal behavior among Black Americans. Segregation harms physical health through poor material conditions. Yet shared neighborhoods may also bring support and less discrimination.

Data came from a national survey of American life with thousands of adults. Lifetime suicidal thoughts and attempts were self-reported by participants. A spatial statistic measured Black clustering at census tract level. Models adjusted for personal traits and tract poverty levels. Analysis split adults into early, middle, and older age groups. Rates of thoughts and attempts did not differ much by segregation level. Thought odds also showed no clear segregation link. The null pattern itself informs mental health policy.
pmc-11690448:
Emma Payne and Melissa Lunardini gauge a text based grief coach for hospice families, in work from 2024. Older adults lose loved ones often yet seek grief help least of all age groups. Coverage gaps, few trained staff, and poor fit options all block their access to care.

Grief Coach sends support texts built on modern coping models for thirteen months. Eighty-six percent of users stayed with the program for its full run length. Three quarters of surveyed users rated the texts very helpful for their grief. Most also said the texts made them feel strongly supported through loss. Older users and men gave the highest ratings of all groups surveyed.
pmc-11690648:
Jeein Jang, Jeffrey Stokes, and Jeffrey Burr compare how retirement changes money satisfaction in South Korea and the United States. Their twenty twenty-four study also asks if marital status bends that path. The two lands differ in pensions, health systems, and family norms.

Two large national surveys of adults over fifty were matched for the study. More than thirty thousand people in each land were followed for eleven years. Moving from full work to full retirement linked to lower money satisfaction at the start and over time. Men reported higher satisfaction than women in the data. The joint view shows a shared strain with local twists.
pmc-11690948:
Meghan Young describes Opening Minds through Art, a program that pairs people living with dementia with trained volunteers for weekly abstract art making. The program, run by a university gerontology center, has operated for seventeen years. Its pairs work one to one, with the person with dementia leading all creative choices. The 2024 session paper gives the program's history and research base.

Volunteers are trained to support, never to steer, the artist's hand. Thirteen published studies back the program: volunteers leave with warmer attitudes toward dementia, and artists show more interest and pleasure than in standard art sessions. At the founding site, nearly three thousand older adults and as many students have taken part, in person and online.
pmc-11691148:
Michelle Putnam and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on social participation among adults aged forty-five to sixty-four who are aging with a long-term disability affecting mobility. Taking part in social life is linked to better health and well-being, yet how participation changes from year to year in this group was little studied.

The team ran a cohort survey from 2019 to 2021 with 323 adults, collecting data once a year at three time points. Scores for physical function, depression, and pain changed little over time, but fatigue did change significantly. Scores for the ability to participate in social roles and activities increased over time. In their own reports, however, most people said their social life had shrunk, and they blamed health, aging with disability, and the COVID-19 pandemic.
pmc-11691248:
Cara Charles, Ra'Shida Rockette, and Caitlin Bowman published a study in 2024 on memory changes in cognitively healthy older adults. Most earlier research focuses on how aging weakens memory for details of individual experiences. Far less is known about memory-based inference, the ability to connect separate experiences to make new decisions.

The researchers gave young and older adults a task with pairs of items. Some pairs were presented directly together, and others could only be inferred by combining two presented pairs. Older adults performed above chance on both remembering direct pairs and making inferences. They still performed worse than young adults overall, and the age gap was larger for inference than for direct memory. Successful inference also blurred, for older adults, which associations had actually been shown. The findings point to an added cost of connecting information in later life.
pmc-11691348:
Sungwan Kang and five co-authors published a qualitative study in 2024 on the experiences of older adults in Korea who live alone and use smart care technology. The government and companies there have run pilot projects placing such technology in homes, to help people remain in their communities. Evaluations of those projects have focused on cost savings and emergency rescues, not on how users experience the services.

The researchers held focus group interviews with thirteen users who had used the services for three months. All had low incomes and limited education. The services provided artificial intelligence based emotional support and home monitoring for abnormal symptoms. Three themes emerged. Feelings about the technology were mixed, ranging from gratitude and a sense of connection to indifference and a sense of loss. Staff who explained the program in clear language eased users' fears. Over time, users also found new value in the technology.
pmc-11691448:
Anne Barrett, Brianna Soulie, and Hope Mimbs, in a 2024 study, asked how poor sleep affects driving risk in later life. Sleepy driving is a known cause of road injury and death, but most work looks at young drivers or shift workers. Older adults may face added risk, since sleep problems grow more common with age.

The team used a survey of 4,199 Floridians aged 50 and older, done from late 2020 to early 2021. They linked self rated sleep quality and sleepiness at the wheel to two outcomes. Those were how often a driver did risky acts, such as speeding or texting, and whether the driver had a crash or near crash in the past year. Poorer sleep and sleepiness at the wheel each tracked with a crash or near crash.
pmc-11691548:
Hanne Dolan and co-authors find that how steady elders feel predicts falls better than a clinic balance test. Falls injure millions of older Americans, yet most never report them. Nearly five and a half thousand independent elders from a national aging study were tracked from twenty fifteen to twenty sixteen. About a quarter fell.

Saying you have balance problems raised fall odds by about two thirds, even after known risks were counted. A standard performance battery, by contrast, did not predict falls. Hospital stays, illness load, fear of falling, and past falls also warned. The authors urge clinicians to simply ask how balance feels.
pmc-11691748:
Ethan Ostrom, Sahir Sandhu, and David Marcinek used a mouse model in 2024 to test whether a short burst of oxidative stress can mimic ageing in muscle. Ageing muscle loses energy efficiency and makes more harmful oxygen based chemicals, but the time course of that decay was not established.

The team switched off a protective enzyme in the muscle of adult mice in a controlled way. The enzyme fell by half in three weeks and by ninety percent in eight weeks. Female mice lost muscle force, and the muscle's energy plants showed the same faults seen in old muscle, including weaker output from one key chain. The model shows short stress alone can copy much of ageing's harm.
pmc-11691848:
Dexia Kong, Peiyi Lu, and Vivian Lou studied whether the housing people grew up in shapes their health in old age, in a 2024 study of Chinese adults. Poor housing is linked to worse health, but few studies have traced that link across a whole life or asked how it travels. Their data came from a large national aging study with 12,842 adults aged 45 and over.

Respondents recalled childhood homes: only about 6 percent had clean water, and 2 percent had a water toilet, while roughly a third had electricity. Better childhood housing tied directly to fewer depressive symptoms and better thinking in later life. Part of the link ran through more schooling in adulthood.
pmc-11691948:
Myeongjin Bae, Kushang Patel, and Nancy Gell link symptom load to repeat falls in older cancer survivors in a 2024 paper. Pain, fatigue, and poor sleep often linger after cancer care ends. Each may raise the risk of falls in later life. The team tracked those links in a national aging study.

The sample held 1,443 older adults with a past cancer, tracked from 2011 to 2015. Repeat falls were more common in people with each symptom. Pain raised the risk most in single-symptom checks after fatigue. People with all three symptoms had over four times the risk of those with none. The authors urge care teams to cut symptom load to prevent falls.
pmc-11692048:
