Theresa Kehne and co-authors report a 2024 study of a brain health fair built for Latino adults. Hispanic and Latino people face higher risk of Alzheimer's disease, yet they join research at low rates. The team worked with a community board to design a fair with talks and hands-on stations run by staff who spoke the visitors' language.

Twenty-six people took part and filled out surveys before and after the fair. Scores rose sharply for facts about the disease, steps that may prevent it, and what joining a research center involves. Most visitors said the fair fit their culture well, and 81 percent signed up for the local Alzheimer's research center. A fair of this kind may help close the gap in who joins such studies.
pmc-11692148:
Duan-Rung Chen, Su-I Hou, and Yuchi Young study, in twenty twenty-four, how adults in Taiwan view end of life care choices. A law from twenty nineteen lets adults sign advance directives, yet few have done so. The team ran an online survey of close to four thousand adults about three grim health states.

Just over half said they would turn down life-sustaining care for themselves. They chose the same for kin less often. The case of late stage dementia drew the most pause, above all for parents. Women were more apt to refuse care for themselves. Views of the law and past talks about care plans shaped the calls. The authors stress how mixed these choices are.
pmc-11692348:
Min-Hui Huang and Thomas Chung published a study in 2024 on the use of rehabilitation services among older cancer survivors. Survivors face a higher risk of physical impairment than older adults who never had cancer, yet rehabilitation to regain function remains underused.

The researchers drew on a national aging survey from 2022. It covered 653 cancer survivors and more than five thousand adults without cancer, all aged sixty-five or older and living at home. About a quarter of each group had used rehabilitation in the past year. Pain, higher education, and lower physical function were linked to rehabilitation use in both groups. Fatigue stood out as a factor for survivors, while weak legs and poor balance stood out for the comparison group. Survivors stayed in rehabilitation slightly longer and met their goals more often.
pmc-11692448:
Yingru Li and six co-authors mapped how neighborhood shape affects activity and fall risk among low-income older adults in Orlando, Florida, in this 2024 study. Sixty-three residents across four communities wore activity trackers through a hot summer. Fall risk came from a standard checklist, and each community was scored for walkability and social vulnerability.

Activity and fall risk differed sharply by neighborhood. Where streets walked well and social vulnerability ran low, elders moved more and faced less risk. Modeling traced a chain: vulnerable areas walk worse, so residents sit more, and fall risk climbs. The authors urge walkability upgrades aimed first at the most vulnerable districts, a need they say warming summers sharpen.
pmc-11692548:
Making a Tokyo ward easier to live in with dementia is the work reviewed by Mika Sugiyama and co-authors in 2024. Japan passed a basic law on dementia in 2023 as its population ages. For ten years before that, a joint research effort in Chiyoda Ward had built local support step by step.

Monthly team meetings tracked progress and problems in a steady cycle. A mail survey reached about ten thousand older adults to map their needs. Nurses visited those who did not reply and gave early support at home. A new system also watched over high-risk adults who never sought help. The review offers lessons for towns building kind support networks.
pmc-11692648:
Xiaoyu Fu and co-authors study how family ties and village wealth shape aging attitudes in rural China. Their paper from 2024 uses a 2021 survey wave from Anhui Province, with 1,394 older adults across sixty four villages. How the old see their own aging matters for policy in fast changing country areas.

Better parent child ties, more child support, and richer villages each went with warmer aging attitudes. The tie effect was itself shaped by village wealth, running stronger in better off villages. Mixed level models split the single person and village layers. The authors argue both layers must enter aging study and policy for rural China.
pmc-11692748:
Bradley Willcox and four co-authors set out, in a 2024 paper, the plan of a Hawaii center that turns aging science into drugs. The center rests on a rare resource: a cohort of 8,006 American men of Japanese and Okinawan ancestry, first examined in 1965 at ages 45 to 68. Fourteen exams, half a million samples, and over nine hundred brains have built up since.

The plan reads those stores with genome-wide and AI tools to find what drives fast aging. Early-career staff at the center hold data on markers of early cognitive aging. Drug partners then aim at those pathways, with some candidates now in mid-stage human trials. The targets span muscle loss and cognitive decline, two of the main losses of old age. The authors stake the work on one claim: treat the roots of aging and many diseases ease at once.
pmc-11692948:
Fumiko Hamada and Soomi Lee ask whether sticking to healthy habits pays off a decade later. Their study came out in 2024, using daily diaries from a national midlife study at two points about ten years apart.

Nearly nine hundred adults logged their sleep, vigorous activity, and fast food intake over eight days at each wave. Sleep quality habits and fast food avoidance held steady across the decade, while activity adherence slipped. People who kept up good sleep and regular activity reported better psychological well-being ten years on. Those who avoided fast food accumulated fewer illnesses, though their well-being was not higher. The split result suggests different habits protect different parts of healthy aging.
pmc-11693048:
Darby Simon, Emilee Ertle, and Benjamin Mast adapt a parenting questionnaire for dementia caregivers in a 2024 paper. Parents differ in warmth, firmness, and how much freedom they grant. Family caregivers face like choices: warmth versus safety, and deciding for another adult. The team reshaped the parenting style survey into a dementia caregiving style survey.

Experts in dementia care rated each draft item for fit and gave written notes. The new survey scores warmth, firmness, and freedom-granting in care talks and tasks. Knowing a caregiver's style could help nurses tailor coaching to the person. The poster-style report walks through the expert review step by step.
pmc-11693148:
Idethia Shevon Harvey and co-authors run a pilot study of stress and diabetes self-care in rural Black elders. Rural African Americans with diabetes face strain from money, kin, and the illness itself. Fifteen adults with a mean age near sixty-six filled out standard scales. The scales gauged money strain, mood, felt stress, diabetes distress, and daily self-care acts.

Money strain ran at mid levels, as did felt stress and diabetes distress. Higher money strain tied to worse self-care scores. Emotional load and strain with others tied strongly to felt stress. Money strain also tied to reports of unfair treatment. Despite the small group, the authors call for care that treats these strains together.
pmc-11693248:
Kowalchik explores how nursing students feel when they first care for dying patients. End-of-life care can stir grief and dread, yet little research asks students what support they need. The 2024 study interviews 21 third- and fourth-year students, some in person and some by video call, and sorts their accounts into themes.

Students said that caring for dying patients and their families hit them hard and made them face their own mortality. Past experiences at home, school, work, and in clinics shaped how they handled those feelings. The work also changed how they deal with death in their private lives. Kowalchik urges nurse teachers to build support into training, so students can grow steadier and more self-aware in this work.
pmc-11693348:
Amiritha Kumar and Daniel Liebzeit review care transitions for older adults in rural areas, in this 2024 scoping review. Moving between hospital, home and care facilities is frequent and risky for people over sixty-five, and rural patients face extra access gaps. From nearly seven thousand papers, ninety-one met their criteria.

Most research covers hospital-centered transitions, while moves into long-term care and assisted living are barely studied. Readmission gaps between rural and other patients are documented, but patient-centered outcomes are rare and few interventions target rural needs. Work on long-term care moves dwells on losses such as independence. Follow-up care after discharge helped as much as in cities, where it was available.
pmc-11694048:
Vishnu Vandana Waddepally and three co-authors checked how many healthy people in South India carry drug-resistant bacteria in the gut, in a 2024 study. Silent carriage can spread resistant germs through homes and hospitals. The team sampled stool from healthy volunteers at a teaching hospital over six months.

From 255 samples they grew 291 bacteria and tested each for key resistance traits. Over half the isolates resisted multiple drugs. Klebsiella stood out as the most resistant genus. About a third of isolates made an enzyme that defeats a broad drug family, and smaller shares defeated other drug classes. No isolate resisted vancomycin. The authors say the high carriage rate in healthy adults calls for steady community surveillance.
pmc-11695048:
James Knight and co-authors report a rare brain spread case treated with radiation in 2024. Atypical carcinoid tumors almost never spread to the brain. The patient first had a lung carcinoid, then spread to the liver and brain despite drug treatment. Whole brain radiation can shrink such spread but often harms memory over time.

The team used a memory sparing form that shields the hippocampus, a key memory hub. Scans months later showed fewer and smaller brain lesions. The patient reported stable memory and thinking after treatment. The case suggests the sparing approach can control spread while guarding the mind.
pmc-11695448:
Khouloud Kouidri and thirteen co-authors study a rare but deadly turn in leukemia care: relapse inside the central nervous system after a stem cell transplant. The study covered 39 patients with a fast-growing leukemia marked by the FLT3 mutation, all treated at one center. Whether the disease had been beaten back before transplant proved decisive. Patients entering transplant in remission had no nervous system relapses in two years of follow-up.

Among patients whose disease was still active at transplant, half suffered a nervous system relapse within two years. Drugs aimed at the mutation, given before or after relapse, did not erase that risk. The authors suggest extra guardrails for the high-risk group, such as targeted therapy before transplant, preventive chemotherapy into the spinal fluid, or closer watching after the procedure.
pmc-11696648: Huan Yang Chen and three co-authors report a rare Castleman disease case in this 2024 paper. Their patient was a twenty-two-year-old woman with a large, well defined mass beside the spine in the chest. It caused back pain and shortness of breath. Imaging and biopsy identified unicentric Castleman disease of the hyaline vascular type. Surgery removed the mass, and she did well afterward. The authors urge doctors to consider it in young adults with chest masses. Early recognition and removal give the best outlook.
pmc-11697348:
Keisuke Oshimi and co-authors report a 2024 study of bright fluorescent nanodiamonds for quantum sensing. Tiny diamonds with nitrogen vacancy centers can sense magnetic fields inside living cells. The bar is to get both bioimaging level brightness and clean spin traits in one particle, which has been hard to reach.

The team tuned the spin environment by enriching a spin free carbon isotope and cutting nitrogen impurities. The result held a modest center density with far cleaner resonance spectra: split peaks shrank and the microwave power needed fell twenty fold. Spin memory times ran five to eleven times longer than a common type. The particles entered cultured cells with ease and can sense temperature near shot noise limits.
pmc-11697548: Lulu Huang, Amy Tang, and Bojing Shao set out a protocol for mouse lung cells. Their protocol from twenty twenty-four makes alveolar type one cells direct. Past ways grew them from type two cells, with limits. Steps split lung tissue to free the surface cells. Then the type one cells are purified from that mix. Stain and flow tests check how pure the batch is. Function checks for the cells are also set out.
pmc-11698248:
Ausra Grybaite, Mohammed Awawdeh, and Parmjit Singh tested what adults remember right after an orthodontic consultation in a 2024 study. Valid consent needs patients to actually retain what they were told. Forty-two adults at one private practice answered a twenty-item quiz straight after a forty-five-minute consultation.

On average they recalled three quarters of the items, and only three people got all twenty. No trait, from schooling to past brace experience, linked firmly to recall. Older patients trended lower than the youngest group. The authors recommend that spoken and visual information always come with written backup. A quarter of a consultation, they note, evaporates before the patient reaches the door.
pmc-11699248:
A lung infection in children, caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, increasingly resists the usual first-line antibiotic family. Yun Lu and co-authors studied 825 children treated at a central China hospital in 2023, comparing resistant and sensitive cases. Resistant cases ran longer fevers. Their doctors most often combined doxycycline with a broad penicillin-type drug, while sensitive cases mainly received azithromycin.

More resistant cases also went home with medicines, chiefly doxycycline. A history of allergy raised the odds of resistance, as did age, fever, lung imaging changes, and extra bacterial or fungal detections. The patterns, the authors suggest, can help doctors pick treatments sooner when resistance is likely.
pmc-11700248:
Arumugam Thangaiah and co-authors compare ways to extract nutrients from moringa leaves in a 2024 study. Moringa leaves are rich in vitamins, minerals, and plant compounds, a help where diets fall short. How the leaves are soaked and processed decides how much of that goodness ends up in the extract.

Four methods were tested in the same alcohol-water mix: plain soaking, a classic heat method, ultrasound help, and microwave help. The two advanced methods gave far higher yields and richer levels of valued compounds. Ultrasound led on yield, protective compounds, and antioxidant strength. Mineral levels also ran higher in the advanced extracts. The authors back the new methods for health food making.
pmc-11701248: Daiyun Huang, Jia Meng, and Kunqi Chen note, in a 2024 short piece, how AI tools aid the study of marks on messenger RNA. One mark, called m6A, is the most common inner mark in higher life forms and steers many cell tasks. The piece highlights work by Fan and co-authors, who built a model that mixes sequence traits with genome traits to spot the mark. Their frame beat past tools at the task, which shows the reach of AI in genome studies.
pmc-11702348:
Abolfazl Taheri, Arvin Shahzamani, and Mahboobe Asadi published this 2024 study on spotting sinus disease before bone marrow transplant. Chronic rhinosinusitis, long-running sinus swelling, can endanger patients whose immunity will be wiped out. CT scans are the reference check, but simpler scores would help triage. The team tested a symptom survey and a scope-based score against scan results.

The study covered 495 transplant candidates at one center. Sixty-three had sinus disease by the scan rule. Both the survey and scope scores tracked the scan score closely. Each also predicted disease on its own in statistical tests. A scope score of one or more caught about seventy-eight percent of cases. The authors weigh both tools as screens before transplant workups.
pmc-11703648:
Four authors survey workplace health hazards among Indian pathologists in this 2024 study. Pathologists face a sharp mix of risks: hours at the microscope, fumes from formalin, and blades and needles, adding up to muscle and joint disorders and cut injuries.

The cross-sectional survey, run online and on paper, asked how common these hazards are and what pathologists know and feel about safety practice. It probed awareness and day to day adherence, and what makes staff skip precautions around posture, sharps, and chemicals. The aim is practical: name the weak points so labs can protect the people who keep diagnosis running.
pmc-11704448:
Cancer that seeds inside the spinal cord itself is rare, under two percent of cord tumors, and usually a late, bleak chapter. Nehemiah Stewart and three co-authors present an operative video case in this 2024 paper. A seventy-four-year-old man's lung cancer had lodged in his neck cord, weakening his right side.

The tumor ran through three neck levels. Working with electrical mapping to find the cord's true midline, the surgeons opened it and removed the whole mass in one block, with hardware steadying the spine. Pathology confirmed the lung origin. Five months later the man's right-side strength kept improving and he could continue his cancer therapy. The authors argue that complete removal, carefully mapped, can preserve function even in elderly patients with metastatic cord disease.
pmc-11708948:
Simple breathing tests might carry quiet warnings about lung cancer risk. Hongli Cao and co-authors compare lung function measures and a breath marker in a 2024 cohort study of 150 people, 78 of whom had lung cancer.

Being male, older, or leaner each tracked with higher cancer odds in the group. Better breathing scores, including airflow ratios and lung volumes, tracked with lower odds. The breath marker, a nitric oxide measure that reflects airway inflammation, ran higher in those with cancer. The authors say such cheap measures could help flag people for closer checks, while stressing that bigger studies must confirm the links and explain the biology behind them.
pmc-11709048:
Pritam Halder and ten colleagues published a public health study in two thousand twenty-four on depression and road crashes in India. The team used a large national ageing survey covering adults aged forty-five and older. They asked whether people with depression face a higher risk of being in a road traffic accident.

Across India, about two in one hundred older adults reported a road accident, and about six in one hundred had depression. After adjusting for other factors, people with depression had notably higher odds of an accident than those without. The link held in every group of states studied. The authors argue that care for older adults should treat depression as part of road safety, not a separate concern.
pmc-11709248:
Jacek Karolczak and co-authors used deep learning in 2024 to name small drug-like molecules in density maps. Such maps come from X-ray work or from cryo-electron microscopy, a method that freezes samples for imaging. Drug design needs the right molecule set in the right pocket of a protein. By-eye reads of faint maps can mislead, and past auto tools worked for X-ray maps alone.

Their model treats each map as a cloud of points in space. It matched past tools on X-ray maps and also worked on cryo maps, a first for an end-to-end learner. Training on X-ray bits helped it read cryo maps. The team flags uneven map standards and weak checks on cryo ligands as open bars. Code is free in public.
pmc-11709348:
Luke Fischer and six co-authors study a form of Lewy body disease that concentrates in the amygdala, the brain's emotion hub, in people with early-onset Alzheimer's disease. Their study came out in 2025. Lewy body disease often appears alongside Alzheimer's, and together they cause worse decline than either alone.

In this variant, the harmful protein clumps start in the amygdala rather than following the usual staging pattern. The team mapped protein markers across the amygdala's subregions in forty-seven donated brains. They also tested spinal fluid for the protein's seeding activity, which was present in some samples. The goal is to find which nerve cells are vulnerable first and how the disease spreads onward. That knowledge could sharpen future diagnosis and treatment.
pmc-11709548:
Yuchen Yang and William Bush address a weakness in gene-based tests that hunt for rare variants linked to Alzheimer's disease. Such tests usually treat rare coding variants as if their effects were separate from the common regulatory variants around them. Their method folds nearby expression-linked variants into the test as a fixed effect, using expression models from the GTEx project. It then runs a standard kernel test on what the rare variants add beyond that background.

Simulations mapped when the adjustment helps most: when few of the tested variants are causal and their effects are small and mixed in direction. The team then applied the method to sequencing data covering 6,461 genes and about 210,000 rare missense variants. It confirmed the known TREM2 association and surfaced several new candidate genes that only reached study-wide significance after the adjustment.
pmc-11709748:
Jorge Llibre-Guerra and a large team of co-authors ask what drives dementia gaps among Latinos in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Alzheimer's disease and related dementias hit Latinos harder than non-Latino whites. Latin America's mix of social conditions and genetic ancestry offers a natural test of which factor matters.

Four thousand older adults in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, and Peru completed cognitive and health assessments. Genetic ancestry varied widely between countries. Groups with more Native American or African ancestry had less schooling, lower income, and more vascular risk. Before adjustment, ancestry tracked dementia rates and test scores. After accounting for social factors, the ancestry links vanished. The authors conclude social conditions, not ancestry, drive the gap.
pmc-11709948:
Julia Bacci and five co-authors wrote this 2025 study on what brain damage markers say about mood and behavior symptoms in Alzheimer's disease. Such symptoms are common, but their roots are tangled by mixed damage in the brain. The team studied 588 people from a community cohort, some sound of mind and some mildly impaired, using scans for white matter scars and a blood marker of nerve fiber harm.

The scar measure showed no firm link to symptom severity. The authors also asked whether the links shifted with mental status or race, using models suited to the skewed symptom data. Their cohort's diversity is itself a point of pride, since past work leaned on narrow samples. The study sets careful bounds on what these two markers explain.
pmc-11710048:
An online tool that flags who may lose thinking skill is built by Marcela Ines Cespedes and co-authors in work dated 2025. Early care for Alzheimer disease works best before clear signs show. Past models of decline came from small groups with gaps in follow-up. The team used a large group study with full records and brain scans for close to three thousand people.

Each person had at least three years of thinking tests. Rates of decline were tied to age and sex, then set on a smooth curve of disease course. The web tool takes age, care class, and one gene mark from a single visit. It then gives a rate for decline over a picked span.
pmc-11710248:
Alzheimer's disease involves many genes, and sorting the drivers from the passengers is slow work. Most Tahmina Rahman, Fahad Saeed, and Serdar Bozdag rank candidate genes with a network method called PhenoGeneRanker. They fuse patient data, gene activity, and protein interaction maps into one layered network, then walk outward from a known disease gene.

The top 200 ranked genes clustered in processes tied to the disease, such as amyloid handling and fat metabolism. The bottom 200 showed no such pattern, which supports the ranking. Known disease genes, including APOE and PSEN2, surfaced near the top. The top 2,000 names captured over half of all genes reported as disease-linked in the literature. Tests that removed one network layer at a time showed what each data type adds.
pmc-11710348:
Shiva Kazempour Dehkordi and co-authors mapped proteins in single nerve cells in Alzheimer's brains to find marks that set sick cells apart, in a study published in 2025. The sick cells carry tangles of tau protein, a hallmark of the disease. Knowing their protein pattern could improve both diagnosis and basic understanding.

Working with donated brains, the team measured eighty-five proteins in chosen spots in two memory areas. Tangle cells showed higher tau tags at four sites, plus higher levels of a few other proteins tied to waste handling and cell stress. A combined score from the top proteins, and a trained sorting program, both split tangle cells from healthy ones well. The marks could become new tools for spotting disease in tissue.
pmc-11710448:
Shana Stites and five co-authors studied how older adults' complaints about their own thinking line up with mood, wellbeing, and test scores, in this 2025 paper. New Alzheimer's treatments work best when started early, so doctors need early signals of decline. One candidate signal is the patient's own sense that memory is slipping. Yet such complaints may say as much about mood as about the brain.

The team tested 344 adults aged sixty-five and older with an online battery. Participants rated their memory across seven domains, reported wellbeing, mood, and their outlook on remaining time, and took digit-span and dot-pattern tests. They also judged their own performance before and after, letting the team measure how well self-judgment matched reality. The authors use the pattern of links to build a model of subjective cognition, clarifying when a complaint should trigger concern and when it mirrors distress instead.
pmc-11710548:
How do the first seeds of tau amyloid form? Lövestam and co-authors filmed the process with time-resolved cryo-electron microscopy, watching lab-made tau build the filament types seen in Alzheimer's disease and in chronic traumatic encephalopathy. Both reactions began with the same first intermediate, built around an ordered core spanning residues 302 to 316. That shared seed later vanished as many different intermediates appeared, their shapes set by the reaction conditions.

By the end, most of those forms had disappeared too. What remained were filaments matching the cores found in human brains, suggesting assembly travels through shifting, polymorphic waystations.
pmc-11710748:
Microglia, the brain's housekeeper cells, change shape as Alzheimer's disease grows, and one shape is little studied. Terri-Leigh Stephen and co-authors sort those shapes in human brain tissue in a 2025 study. They stain slices from twenty sick donors and ten controls and teach a program to class each cell.

Rod-shaped and inert cells ran higher in sick brains, while the branching survey form ran lower. Rod cells in sick brains stretched longer and grew more arms. A marker for the cells tracked amyloid load in one memory region. Damage load rose with disease stage across the board. Shape maps may date how far the disease has run.
pmc-11712048:
Catherine V Piersol and co-authors build a model of how family caregivers judge care in a nursing home, in a study published in 2025. Many families face this move when a loved one with dementia grows worse over time. Past work looked at the effect of the move, but less at how families view the care itself.

The team used grounded theory and spoke one on one with caregivers from homes taking part in a larger trial. Careful coding of the talks yielded seven linked themes. One theme, how pleased families are with care, sat at the core. Six other themes, both inner and outer, shaped that core view and may guide staff who work with families.
pmc-11712148:
Elizabeth Reaves Houston and David Lynch review whether exercise programs in hospitals actually reach patients living with dementia, in a paper from 2025. About a quarter of such patients are hospitalized each year. During a stay they spend nearly all their time in bed, and about half leave with worse physical function than they came in with.

Hospital exercise programs are proposed to break that decline. The review searched trial databases and registries for controlled studies of exercise for older inpatients. It asked how often dementia patients were included at all and whether the programs blunted their functional losses. The findings matter because a group at highest risk may be the very group trials quietly leave out.
pmc-11712248:
Yatian Li and co-authors test speech as a window on thinking decline in a 2025 study of older adults. Speech falters early in Alzheimer disease, so a phone-based speaking test could screen communities cheaply. The team built such a screening tool and asks which voice features mark mild impairment.

They recruited 301 older adults, of whom 135 had mild impairment or early dementia. Voice features, test scores, and background data trained several learning models. The best model, blending sound maps with other data, sorted cases with very high accuracy, beating the tool's own scores. Features like filler words, pause length, and timing spread drove the results most, the analysis found.
pmc-11712348:
Belen Custodio and co-authors report early results of a training program for dementia caregivers in Lima, Peru, in a 2025 study. Trained caregivers give better care and burn out less, yet knowledge levels in poorer countries are little studied. The program, a monthly virtual meeting led by a health worker, covers dementia types, behavior management, non-drug measures, and caregiver well-being.

So far forty-six caregivers have taken a twenty-five-item true-or-false knowledge test, and the trained and untrained groups scored about two points apart. Over sixty-five percent of all caregivers missed questions on early symptoms, late-stage care, and behavior handling. The authors say training helps, but those weak topics need a new approach.
pmc-11712448:
Nelly Joseph-Mathurin and co-authors report a 2025 study on a form of Alzheimer disease that runs in families through gene changes. This rare form is known for the buildup linked to the disease, yet blood vessel and immune factors also play a part. The team looked at proteins in the fluid around the brain and spine.

They drew on data from 485 people in a long study of such families. Protein patterns tied to the unit of nerves, support cells, and vessels in the brain. Those patterns linked to white matter damage seen on scans and to small bleeds in the brain. The work may guide how new treatments are judged.
pmc-11712548:
Hae Young Yi and co-authors map a backup visual pathway in people with atypical forms of Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 study concerns affective blindsight: a route that bypasses the main visual cortex, running from the superior colliculus through the pulvinar to the amygdala. This pathway may preserve emotion reading when the usual regions waste away.

The cohort held patients with two atypical variants, one affecting language and one affecting vision, plus healthy controls. Brain scans at rest and during face-viewing tasks measured how strongly the pathway's regions connect. The team corrected for tissue loss in their comparisons. Findings may explain why some patients keep social and emotional skills.
pmc-11712648:
Simon Rothwell and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on whether health systems in Europe are ready for the new drugs that slow early Alzheimer's disease. These drugs need proof of amyloid, drip sessions, and close scan follow-up. The team mapped current practice in four large European states plus the United Kingdom.

They reviewed public data, then spoke with neurologists and hospital managers. Scan capacity stood out as the tightest squeeze: too few machines and trained staff, with only a small share of scans set aside for this disease. Tests for amyloid also varied, with spinal fluid tests more common than costly scans. The authors urge better use of scan time to widen access.
pmc-11712848:
Pierre-André Lafon and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 with a warning about one drug path for Alzheimer's disease. The team studied a brain receptor that helps set how much amyloid, the protein that clumps in the disease, gets made. A tiny antibody from camels that boosts this receptor was fed to mice over a long span.

Boosting the receptor raised output of the harmful amyloid form in cell tests. In mice bred for the disease, long treatment sped up clump growth and worsened memory loss. A sister receptor had no such effect, thanks to the way it holds the amyloid source protein. The authors say this receptor should be blocked, not boosted, in future drug work.
pmc-11712948:
Giving up driving is one of dementia's hardest milestones, and a Canadian website, the Driving and Dementia Roadmap, exists to guide families through it. Gary Naglie, Elaine Stasiulis, and Mark Rapoport report how users judge that resource in a 2025 paper. The site has drawn more than 34,000 visitors since late 2022.

Visitors leaving the site are invited to a survey; eighty-one had answered, split among people with dementia, family carers, and health providers. Carers most often said they newly understood unsafe driving and the licensing rules. Providers valued guidance on supporting people after they stop and on handling the emotional talks. Confidence gains were reported across all three groups, strongest among carers deciding to stop. The authors use the feedback to keep improving the roadmap.
pmc-11713048:
Jessica Chalk and co-authors study tau tangles in the smell bulb in Alzheimer's disease in 2025. The disease varies in how tangles spread across brain regions, forming distinct subtypes. The smell bulb gathers tau early and links directly to a deep brain region tied to emotion.

The team stained smell bulb tissue from thirty-nine cases across three subtypes. One tau marker showed tangle-like staining inside cells in all groups. Its load did not differ clearly between subtypes. A second marker also showed cell staining, letting the team compare forms of tau across the groups and judge whether the smell bulb tracks subtype.
pmc-11713148:
Trevor Chadwick and co-authors measure tau buildup in a small deep brain region in a 2025 paper. Tau, a protein that clumps in Alzheimer's disease, gathers early in the basal forebrain, a region that aids memory. Brain scanners may be too coarse to read tau there, and stray signal from nearby areas can cloud the measure.

The team compared two scan tracers in large groups of older adults without thinking problems. For both, tau in the region rose with amyloid, the other hallmark protein, and tracked with age, smaller memory centers, and weaker memory scores. One tracer set apart amyloid-positive people a bit better. The authors say tau in this region can be read in living people and may mark early disease.
pmc-11713248:
Freddie O'Donald and Clara Calia review a 2025 body of work on how tests of daily function for dementia are translated for use across cultures. Such tests must work in many languages if care and research are to be fair round the world. A shared standard gives rules for judging how sound a translated test is.

The team searched five data banks and found 15 studies covering adapted tests in eleven languages. Fewer than half of the studies fully met the set rules for translation and cultural fit. Scores for internal consistency and repeat results were in most cases strong. Other traits, such as how the test's build holds up and how large its errors run, were checked in a patchy way. The team urges full checks before a translated test is used.
pmc-11713348:
Georgia Gore-Langton and co-authors report a 2025 study of infections and brain health in older adults in India. Some infections may track with weaker thinking, depression, and frailty, but data from poorer countries are scarce. The team used a national aging survey gathered in 2017 to 2019.

The sample held 64,682 adults aged 45 and over from nearly every Indian state. Nine infections were recorded, from malaria and tuberculosis to gum disease and urinary infections. About 35 percent reported at least one infection in the windows asked about. Thinking, mood, and frailty were each measured with survey tools. Weighted models compared people with and without each infection. The design gives a broad snapshot of a possible infection burden on aging brains.
pmc-11713448:
Junhao Wen, Arthur Toga, and Christos Davatzikos test whether brain patterns derived by artificial intelligence actually cause Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 paper. From MRI scans, earlier work had built three brain age gaps and nine imaging patterns that capture disease subtypes across several disorders.

The team used Mendelian randomization, a genetics-based method for probing cause and effect, in both directions. One pattern, marked by shrinkage of memory-related inner brain regions, showed a likely causal push toward Alzheimer's. The reverse direction also appeared: Alzheimer's itself seemed to widen the white matter brain age gap, meaning the disease ages the brain's wiring. Sensitivity checks found no obvious outliers or hidden side paths, and five different estimators agreed. The authors present the imaging patterns as more than markers: at least one may sit on the causal path to disease.
pmc-11713548:
Setthanan Jarukasemkit and co-authors argue that whole brain networks beat single regions for reading dementia in this 2025 pilot study. Thirty patients with mild memory trouble gave blood tests, thinking scores, and tau scans. The team measured tau, a clumping protein, across standard brain networks rather than isolated spots.

Blood tau levels tracked network tau most tightly in the limbic network, the brain's emotion and memory web. Thinking scores instead tracked the dorsal attention network most strongly. Some networks linked both blood and scores. Network-level analysis beat the region-by-region approach at explaining cognition. The authors suggest trials and clinics read tau by network to catch what regional maps miss.
pmc-11713648:
Haylie DeMercy and Colleen Brenner examined whether common dementia drugs speed up serious heart and brain events in older patients, in a study published in 2025. Dementia often brings agitation, mood symptoms, and psychosis, treated with antipsychotic drugs, memory drugs, or both. Those drugs carry known risks of stroke, heart events, and death. The team studied 1,126 patients aged fifty and over with dementia and behavior symptoms, comparing four treatment patterns over time.

Patients on both drug types faced the soonest events, with odds nearly double those of the comparison group. Antipsychotics alone raised the odds by about seventy-nine percent, and memory drugs alone by about thirty-two percent. Dose mattered too: high antipsychotic doses more than tripled the odds of an early event. The authors urge close monitoring for heart and stroke problems when these drugs are used, especially at high doses.
pmc-11713748:
Christopher Norris and Susan Kraner characterize a lab antibody in mice in 2025. Their lab made antibodies that tag distressed support cells in the brain. One antibody was expected to bind a cut form of a key enzyme. To their surprise, the second antibody instead bound a support cell protein called GFAP.

Levels of that tagged protein run high in a mouse strain bred to model Alzheimer disease. Tests confirm the antibody labels the protein with care and skips close targets. A clean tag lets researchers track how support cells react as disease advances. The tool may reveal states of brain stress that other stains miss.
pmc-11713848:
Kothapalli and co-authors probe a tau scan tracer in Alzheimer research in a 2025 study. The tracer lights up tau tangles in the living brain, but it also sticks in iron-rich areas, which muddies readings. Sixty-eight older adults had both the tau scan and a special MRI that can tell tissue loss from iron buildup.

In memory regions, tracer levels rose with both early tissue loss signals and iron scores. Models that joined volume, iron, and loss measures predicted tracer uptake far better than volume alone. Readers learn that iron shapes tau scan results, a fact that matters for trial design and diagnosis.
pmc-11714048:
Xuanzhao Dong and co-authors build a smart image tool that converts brain amyloid scans from one tracer dye to another, in a 2025 conference paper. Amyloid scans help show the load of the protein in the brain. But centers use unlike dyes, and matched scan pairs are rare, which blocks joint work.

The team trained a deep learning model on scans from an Australian aging study, with far more scans of one dye than the other. The model learns to repaint a scan as if the second dye had been used. They tested it on 46 paired scans from a public project. Scores from the repainted scans matched the true scans closely. The authors say the tool could let centers pool scan data with more ease.
pmc-11714248:
Stefanie Pina Escudero and co-authors test whether life conditions change how well gene scores predict two forms of dementia, in a 2025 conference paper. The study spans six Latin American countries and 677 adults with Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, or no illness. Gene scores sum many small gene risks into one number.

On their own, the scores linked strongly to both illnesses. Once the team added life factors such as schooling, work, income, and care access, plus a known gene risk form, the score lost strength for Alzheimer's disease. For the second illness, the score held steady. The authors say social life shapes gene risk in one disease more than the other, and that care plans in the region should take both into account.
pmc-11714448:
Adriana dos Santos and six co-authors study whether drugs that block a brain chemical add up to harm thinking over time, in a 2025 conference paper. Many common drugs have this blocking effect, and the total load from all of them is called the anticholinergic burden. The team used a large health study of adults in Brazil.

More than thirteen thousand people were tested in three waves over eight years with memory and thinking tasks. A higher drug burden went with a faster fall in overall thinking scores. The fall was clearest in memory and in tasks that need planning and quick shifts. The authors say doctors should weigh this load when they hand out drugs to midlife and older adults.
pmc-11714548:
Vijayasree Giridharan and co-authors check blood and gut signs in people with mild COVID-19 for links to brain illness, in a 2025 conference paper. Lasting nerve signs after the virus are blamed on immune faults and shifts in gut germs. The team also tracked a blood factor that can block immune cell growth.

The study held 26 people after COVID-19 and 57 matched healthy controls. Blood tests covered mood linked marks, fat profiles, cell stress, swelling signals, and Alzheimer's disease marks. Stool tests read the gut germ mix, and standard scales scored mood and thinking. The COVID group showed a higher level of the immune factor and a skewed gut mix. Yet the disease marks in blood did not shift, a split the authors flag for more study.
pmc-11714648:
Roch Nianogo, Nicola Churchill, and Deborah Barnes use a 2025 computer model to test what mid-life habit changes could do to dementia risk. Single habit fixes often fall short, since risk has many roots. The team drew on survey data for more than twelve thousand adults. They modeled exercise, quitting smoking, and stronger social support, alone and combined. They also compared aiming at high-risk people with aiming at everyone.

Exercise alone cut the modeled risk of dementia by a clear margin. Social support and quitting smoking alone showed smaller, less certain cuts. All three combined cut risk by about a third in the broad approach. The gain was smaller when the same mix was aimed only at high-risk people. The model suggests broad, combined action in mid-life could pay off most. It is a test of what-if cases, not a trial in real people.
pmc-11714848:
Sreya Dhanam and co-authors examine a 2025 study of phone-based tests for adults who feel their thinking is slipping. Such worries are common in people who still function well, and they can hint at later loss. The team invited adults from an online brain health registry to take tests on their own phones. No staff watched as they worked. The tasks tapped memory and the kind of control used to switch or hold back responses. People also filled in a form about their daily thinking.

Just over four hundred and fifty people finished the phone tasks. Older age went with weaker scores, and more schooling went with stronger ones. Sex showed no clear link to scores in this group. The study asks whether self-rated worries line up with the phone results. If they do, home testing could help track people at risk without clinic visits.
pmc-11714948:
Young adults who visit a memory clinic often have treatable causes behind their complaints. Waleska Berrios and co-authors reviewed three hundred seven assessments from a cognitive neurology service in Argentina. Patients were aged forty to sixty and came in between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-two. The team recorded diagnoses, family history, and twelve changeable risk factors named by a major dementia report.

About forty-five percent of patients had a mild thinking disorder, while a fifth tested normal. Women made up sixty-three percent of the group. The review shows how often mood problems, attention disorders, and habit-linked risks sit behind young complaints. Clinics can use such counts to plan testing and to target the risks that can still be changed.
pmc-11715048:
Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, writing solo in 2025, asked if weak kidneys skew a blood test for Alzheimer's disease. The test reads a tau sign in blood, and its use is growing fast in clinics. Chronic kidney disease has been tied to higher reads on the test. If the kidney link is real, some high reads may not mean brain disease at all.

The sample held one hundred ninety-five adults from two Mayo Clinic studies. Some had sharp thought, some mild loss, and a few the full disease. Three lab ways to read the tau sign were set side by side. As kidney work fell, the tau read rose on all three, by up to about a fourth for a set drop. A form of the test built as a ratio did not rise with kidney loss. That ratio may dodge the kidney trap.
pmc-11715348:
Mahnaz Shekari and a large team of co-authors asked how a new tau scan stacks up against fluid tests. Tau is the second key protein that tangles in the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Most past work looked at people who already had clear signs. Their work kept the focus on the first, silent stage.

The team drew on ninety-nine adults with no thought loss from a Spanish cohort study. Each had a tau scan, an amyloid scan, a brain scan, thought tests, and fluid tests. They matched scan signal in three zones of the brain against set cut points for each stage. They then checked how well blood and spinal fluid tests could flag the first stage of tau spread. Such links could help trials pick the right people at the right time for drugs that aim to slow the disease.
pmc-11715648:
Sarah-Alexis Lenhoff and co-authors test whether inherited heart risk tracks with Alzheimer-like brain change, in a 2025 study. Heart and vessel risk has long been tied to dementia. Genes offer a clean way to test that link without the noise of daily habits.

The team used the UK Biobank resource, with near thirty thousand people. A combined gene score for heart risk was set against brain scan measures. Higher gene risk went with more deep white matter damage and less total grey matter. One tract near the memory region also showed wear. Blood flow showed no link. The results support a gene level path from heart risk to brain change.
pmc-11715748:

pmc-11715848:

pmc-11715948:

pmc-11716148:

pmc-11716248:

pmc-11716448:

pmc-11716548:

pmc-11716648:

pmc-11716848:

pmc-11716948:

pmc-11724348:

pmc-11725048:

pmc-11726748:

pmc-11726848:

pmc-11727148:

pmc-11727348:

pmc-11728248:

pmc-11740748:

pmc-11881648:

pmc-11881748:

pmc-11888748:

pmc-11963548:

Of the many HPV strains, these two drive most cervical cancers, yet local data for the East Gojjam Zone were scarce. Knowing the burden and its drivers is the first step to screening policy.
