Getinet estimates the infection rate and sifts which social and behavioral factors travel with it. The results give district planners numbers, not guesses.
pmc-12008348:
Anif Nur Artanti, Riris Istighfari Jenie, Rumiyati Rumiyati, and Edy Meiyanto tested two citrus compounds as partners for a standard liver cancer drug, in a 2024 study. Cisplatin kills liver cancer cells but also ages healthy kidney cells, a harmful side effect. Hesperidin and diosmin, plant chemicals from citrus, fight cancer and oxidation in their own right, so the team asked whether pairing them with the drug helps on both fronts.

In dishes, each compound alone slowed the cancer cells, and pairing either with cisplatin killed more cancer cells than the drug alone, with combination scores showing true synergy. The pairings barely harmed normal kidney cells, and both compounds reduced the drug-induced aging of those cells while pushing cancer cells toward death and aging. The authors propose the citrus compounds as candidate add-ons that strengthen treatment while shielding the kidneys.
pmc-12118748:
Christian Cramer and co-authors advance a new hypothesis for insulin resistance, the core problem in type 2 diabetes. The usual view blames target tissues or the insulin receptor's signaling for weak response. Despite decades of work, the mechanism remains poorly understood.

The authors propose instead that secreted insulin itself may not survive the trip to its target. If the insulin molecule is split into its chains before it can act, less working hormone would reach the receptor, mimicking resistance. They present data and arguments for this chain-splitting idea. The hypothesis reframes where researchers should look for causes and possible treatments.
pmc-12172848:
Katherine Boere and co-authors gauge mental load during multitasking with a portable brain scanner worn on the forehead. Their 2024 study notes that load research has leaned on single tasks in labs, which misses real-world strain. Thirty-one students did one task, then several at once, in a setup meant to mimic high-stakes work. Self-ratings, scores, and error counts were logged beside brain blood-flow reads.

Self-rated load rose in the multitask round, while scores fell and errors climbed. Yet front brain activity did not rise, as past simple studies would predict. The authors read this as a disengagement effect, where the brain caps its effort under overload. They back portable scanners for load checks in real settings.
pmc-12480048:
A health report from twenty twenty-three tracks what happened to people in Korea after sudden cardiac arrest. It covers the years from twenty twelve to twenty twenty-two. Sudden cardiac arrest means the heart is badly impaired or stops working. The figures come from national surveillance data kept by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.

Survival rose over the decade, from a low share in twenty twelve to a higher share in twenty twenty-two. The report says the survival rate grew about one point eight fold. Recovery of brain function rose even more, about two point eight fold. Brain recovery here means getting well enough to manage daily life on one's own. Readers get a clear national trend in plain figures.
pmc-12660148:
Johain Ounadjela and a large team of co-authors map the early human placenta cell by cell, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. A healthy placenta runs on tangled gene-control networks, and breaks in them cause pregnancy trouble. The team paired several mapping tools to chart genes and their switches in place.

Their census covers the first three months of pregnancy. It shows tumor-like gene programs that may help the placenta thrive in a harsh womb. Maps of the villous core and cell columns reveal niches and cell-to-cell talk. The atlas links gene switches to cell fate and disease risk.
pmc-12661748:
Christina Zorbas and co-authors review in 2025 how research has brought the lived experience of marginalized people into disease prevention policy, and how it might do better. Chronic diseases are not shared fairly, and the people most harmed by marginalization, by gender, ethnicity, sexuality, disability, or class, are the people policy rooms least often hear. Their scoping review searched four databases for studies that engaged those voices to shape equitable prevention.

Dozens of articles qualified, clustered on nutrition, with smaller groups on physical activity, tobacco, obesity, mental health, and alcohol. Working from a constructivist and critical stance, the team sorted what helped or blocked genuine inclusion across the studies. The review's purpose is practical: name the approaches that move lived experience from consultation decoration into actual policy design. Prevention that ignores the people carrying the risk, the authors imply, reproduces the inequity it claims to fight.
pmc-12662048:
A fourteen-author team asks whether a gene that controls appetite changes how much weight people with HIV gain on modern therapy. Switching to integrase inhibitor drugs often brings weight gain, and the melanocortin-4 receptor gene, MC4R, is a known player in obesity. The team studied 529 participants in international treatment trials who switched to these drugs, most of them to raltegravir, with a median age of fifty.

At the switch, sixty-two percent were already overweight or obese. In adjusted models, three variants in or near the gene were tied to how much weight changed after the switch, either in everyone or in set subgroups. The authors call the analysis exploratory, but say the pattern fits the receptor's role in appetite control. They suggest that brain hormone pathways help explain why these effective HIV drugs add pounds for some patients.
pmc-12663048:
Yijiao Xu and nine co-authors wrote this 2025 study on hidden tuberculosis and lung cancer care. Many people carry dormant TB germs, and a blood test called T-SPOT can detect them. The team asked whether dormant infection changes how advanced lung cancer patients fare on immune-boosting drugs, using records from 127 patients at one hospital.

Half the patients carried dormant infection, yet their survival and response matched those without it. The starting test value, though, showed a curved link with survival: patients with a low positive value lived longest. Shifts in the test during treatment carried no clear meaning. Four patients developed active TB on therapy, with mixed test patterns. Because the group was small, the authors warn against reading the null result as proof of no effect. They advise watching for active TB during immune therapy.
pmc-12663448:
Shenfei Sun and co-authors build in 2025 a cell-by-cell atlas of the growing mouse lung, pairing gene activity with chromatin openness. The lung's branching tree forms through patterning steps whose gene programs are still murky. Their combined data span the embryo stages when the tree takes shape.

Thirteen cell types were mapped, along with the control elements and factor networks behind them. One factor, CTCF, stood out as a keeper of early lung progenitors. Mice lacking it in the lung showed faulty branching and progenitor loss, with both gene activity and chromatin access reshaped. The atlas serves as a resource for lung development studies.
pmc-12683848:
Melissa Assel and Andrew Vickers argue, in 2025 work, that a score widely used to grade tests and forecast models in machine work can mislead doctors. The score blends how many flagged cases are true with how many true cases are found. In most uses both parts count the same, by a fixed setting.

The pair test the score on a cancer-spotting scene, where missing a case can kill and checks are harsh. There, the score crowned a test that missed more cases, while a sound worth-based measure crowned the test that found most. No preset tweak of the score fixed the ranking across scenes, they show. The score also lacks a plain unit. They urge the worth-based route that health guidance backs.
pmc-12685948:
Karol Korzekwa and eight co-authors track the COVID virus in Warsaw's sewage over two years. Wastewater testing can reveal how much infection circulates in a city, including cases no clinic ever sees. Their 2025 study built a standing watch over the capital's whole sewage catchment.

Samples came from four treatment plants and from raw flows near hospitals, the airport, and military sites, across two waves in 2023 and 2024. Genetic tests measured virus levels and identified variants, which fell into 11 known branches. Virus loads ran higher than clinic records implied, hinting at many undiagnosed infections. Inflows carried the most virus; treated outflows, the least. The team also drafted an action algorithm with the water company.
pmc-12686448:
Krishnakumar Vaithianathan and five co-authors share tasks fairly in 5G factory health networks in a 2025 paper. The setting is the Industrial Internet of Things, where many devices must share work. Task spread and control are among its hardest problems. Past methods miss links between tasks and device skills.

Their model, CHATA, matches tasks by how alike device functions are. A Pearson correlation measure drives the clustering of devices. The best-fit device then takes each task in the plan. Simulations in NS-3 test the model in 5G settings. Allocation efficiency reached up to 90 percent in the runs. The model beat recent rivals on assignment scores.
pmc-12687048:
Nine authors report a post-surgery heart case in 2025 where a press drug saved the day. An 80-year-old woman had valve swap and muscle cut for a thick heart with a tight exit. Post work she hit lung flood, low push, exit block, and valve flap pull in the ward. First drugs failed to hold her state.

A press drug with no beat push joined, and the first press drug was eased down. Exit block fell by a wide span on heart scans in the case. Breath and flow marks rose, and the team backs the drug for such blocks.
pmc-12692348:
Nadezhda Timofeyeva and co-authors stage a head-on crash between gene reading and copying in a 2025 lab study. When transcription and replication meet face to face on DNA, forks stall. Three enzymes share the scene: the reader, the copier, and a cleanup enzyme for RNA-DNA hybrids. Precise bench control lets each act be timed.

A working reader complex blocks both a short and a full-length copier. A stalled reader with an R-loop instead goads the copier to chew back its own strand. As the reader advances, the copier reattaches and the clash slowly resolves. A lone short R-loop does not stall copying but still tweaks the copier. The dance maps a basic genome hazard.
pmc-12692748:
María Carmen Gómez-Guillén and co-authors explored in 2025 how to turn protein from an undervalued octopus species into useful food ingredients. They made a freeze-dried protein concentrate by dissolving and re-precipitating the flesh. The recovery process left the proteins clumped, so the team tested pH shifts and ultrasound to reshape them. They measured solubility, surface behavior, and particle size across conditions.

The tuned proteins were paired with a plant antioxidant to form tiny particles. At the most acidic condition, those particles stabilized oil droplets that were small and evenly spread in low-fat emulsions. Microscopy confirmed the fine structure. The authors say processing choices can steer cephalopod proteins toward new roles in designing innovative, lighter food products.
pmc-12693148:
Kei Tsukui and five co-authors test a trace-element-rich mineral extract on lab-grown human skin and find it both reinforces and remodels the glue between surface cells. Corneodesmosomes hold the skin's outer layer together; enzymes called kallikreins dissolve them so old cells shed, and an inhibitor keeps that dissolving in check. The extract was applied to a three-dimensional epidermis model.

Gene expression shifted in a coordinated way: the junction components and the key inhibitor rose, one kallikrein rose while another fell in both message and activity. Protein levels of the junction parts did not change, but the outer layer thickened relative to the whole epidermis. The authors read this dual regulation as support for skin barrier balance.
pmc-12694448:
Grzegorz Sobek and Paweł Jagielski report a nutrition study, published in 2025, comparing food likes between teenagers with type one diabetes and healthy peers. Taste and smell drive most food choices in young people, and diabetes care often frames food only as a risk to control. The team surveyed one hundred and two adolescents with diabetes using photos of sixty-three foods and drinks.

Taste strips testing sweet, sour, bitter, and salty rounded out the picture. Healthy teenagers reported stronger liking for sweet foods, while those with diabetes scored clearly higher for bitter fruits and vegetables. The authors frame the pattern as a positive outcome, suggesting life with diabetes may train broader tastes rather than only narrowing a diet.
pmc-12694848:
Daniel Verdear and co-authors map like-minded clusters in election talk on Twitter and Parler during the two thousand twenty election, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Doubts about the result spread online and fed the Capitol attack that January. A community finder plus a new sameness score flagged the most uniform groups on each platform.

Uniform groups spread their messages farther than mixed ones did. Left and right uniform groups differed in text style. Right-leaning texts resembled the world-building style found in conspiracy writing, the authors report. The work compares a mainstream and an alt platform side by side.
pmc-12694948:
Tara Coffin and a co-author weigh the ethics of using social media in research on human subjects. Their 2025 article grants the draw: feeds offer rich data, disease tracking, and fast recruiting. The same tools, though, can widen health gaps, leak private facts, blur what participants expect to share, and bake in bias.

Recruiting through online ads and mining posts each raise their own consent puzzles. Review boards carry the duty of holding the line, and the authors press their central role. Their advice leans on community engagement, plain transparency, and recruiting that reaches beyond the easiest crowds to sample. The piece aims to help researchers and regulators keep trust as studies move online.
pmc-12698648:
Min Chang and co-authors test a plant compound in mice with a sore, inflamed colon much like ulcerative colitis in people, in a 2025 study. The human disease brings lasting gut pain and damage, and current drugs carry side effects or stop working. The compound, from a flowering plant, was given at two doses to sick mice.

Treated mice kept more weight, held longer colons, and showed cleaner gut tissue than untreated ones. Swelling signals fell, the gut wall's seals grew stronger, and gut germs and their products moved back toward normal. The authors see a multi-path lead worth pursuing, while noting that mouse results are only a first step.
pmc-12699848:
Xiaoqian Li and seven co-authors built a model to judge how well pre-surgery chemotherapy works in breast cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Most older models use a single blood test taken before treatment. Changes in tumor markers during treatment carry extra signal that had gone unused.

Records of hundreds of patients at one hospital were split into building and testing groups. The final chart mixes age, a growth-receptor status, starting marker levels, and summaries of how three markers moved over time. It beat a rival chart built only on starting values in both groups. Checks of its risk estimates and clinical usefulness also looked sound. The authors say tracking markers over time sharpens prediction.
pmc-12700148:
Kyla Taylor and co-authors answered in 2025 the critics of a major review linking fluoride exposure to lower IQ in children. Their team had produced the underlying work: a national toxicology monograph and a journal meta-analysis of over seventy studies. Both found an inverse association, firmest in the highest-quality studies. The association held across sexes, ages, countries, and measurement methods.

It also appeared below the often-cited level of 1.5 milligrams per liter. The viewpoint gathers the recurring objections and replies to each in turn. The authors note many points were already settled during peer review. Their aim is clarity for the public, media, and policy makers now using the findings. They stand by the moderate-confidence conclusion while laying out its reasoning in plain terms.
pmc-12701048:
Roberto Paparella and eight co-authors review the mind and social side of a hormone condition in the young, in a 2025 paper. The condition is a mild, late-starting form of an adrenal disorder that raises male-type hormones. Its body effects are well charted, but its effects on mood, thinking, and social life are less clear.

In girls, extra hormones are often linked with anxiety, low mood, and worry about body image. Most keep a female identity, though non-typical gender paths appear more often than average. Boys show fewer such concerns, with mixed evidence for acting-out behavior. Thinking skills vary, with small dips in some tasks and possible strengths in spatial ones. The authors call for care that looks past hormone numbers.
pmc-12705648:
Jun He, Xun Xie, and Ying Wang link, in a 2025 study, total tooth loss to frailty in older adults across several large cohorts. Losing all teeth, called edentulism, can shrink diets and social ease, and frailty marks the body's fading reserve. The authors test whether the two travel together in nationally representative samples, including Chinese cohorts.

Work of this kind weighs shared causes with care, since poverty and chronic disease feed both outcomes. Even so, a clear tie across cohorts would guide practice: dental care and denture support could join the standard frailty watch. The study's multi-cohort design is its strength, letting the authors check whether the link holds across settings rather than in one place. Their paper adds oral health to the map of healthy aging risks.
pmc-12705848:
Rachael Dunlop and co-authors validate a blood test that reads eight small RNAs to diagnose ALS, a disease now confirmed only after long clinical detective work. Diagnostic delay costs patients time in a fast disease. Their 2025 study extracts the microRNA panel from blood plasma and measures it with standard PCR chemistry.

Cutoffs were fixed in an earlier sample set, then applied untouched to fresh cohorts totaling nearly eight hundred samples. The test separated ALS from controls with high sensitivity and specificity, and the RNA shifts matched the earlier findings. Streamlined handling cut the assay's time and cost as well. Neurologists get a candidate for the blood-based ALS test the field has wanted for decades.
pmc-12706248:
Low blood counts before surgery in older Ethiopians are tied to poor outcomes by Habtie Bantider Wubet and a large team in work dated 2025. The team tracked 224 patients aged sixty-five or more at two big hospitals. Blood counts were read before surgery, and care events were logged through the stay. Transfusion need was the chief score.

Patients with low counts needed transfusions far more, in and after surgery. Transfusion sat with higher death, ICU use, and longer stays. Poor healing also tracked with it. Early find and fix of low counts is the team's core plea for such settings.
pmc-12706848:
Seyed Ali Sajadian and co-authors measure how much of a yellow dye dissolves in carbon dioxide squeezed into a supercritical fluid, then teach machines to predict it. Such fluids dye fabrics without water, but solubility data for this dye did not exist. Their 2025 paper reports the first measurements, across pressures of 12 to 30 megapascals and temperatures from 313 to 343 kelvin.

Four classical formulas were fitted to the data, and the K-J model matched best, erring by about six percent on average. Three machine learning models were trained alongside: a multilayer perceptron, a Gaussian process, and a random forest. All three approximated the measurements well, and the perceptron won with a near-perfect fit score. The authors offer both the raw data and the winning model as design tools for greener dyeing.
pmc-12707648:
Qianyu Ren and co-authors predict three-dimensional heat cracks in bonding electrodes with a digital twin. Their 2025 study targets thermal compression bonding tools, whose cracks hurt chip line reliability and pace. The twin joins physics simulation with learned models.

A finite element method builds a high-fidelity electrode copy that updates under electric, heat, and force loads. A generative model fills the crack data gap, landing within about one percent of lab results. An attention-tuned point network then forecasts crack shape, beating two rival architectures. Shape error against real cracks stays under two percent at worst. The authors pitch the frame as a precision route to smart maintenance for microelectronic bonding gear.
pmc-12708648:
Huacai Wang and co-authors find a new kind of virus sentry in rice in a 2025 study. Receptor kinases usually guard the cell surface against microbes arriving from outside. Whether they can also spot viruses colonizing inside the cell was unknown. One such kinase, sitting at an internal sorting station, recognizes proteins of rice stripe virus, a major crop threat.

The kinase's gene switches on during infection, and the protein builds up through self activation and redox control. Plants carrying it resist the virus better. An inside the cell watch post widens the known immune map. Rice feeds half the world, so each new defense gene is breeding stock.
pmc-12708848:
Rings of DNA that carry gene tools work best when a germ made tail is snipped off, a form called a minicircle. Roman Teo Oliynyk and co-authors make such rings with no germ at all in a 2025 study. Their route, Plasmid2MC, uses one enzyme to cut the tail and a second step to chew all spare DNA.

The rings come out clean and near free of germ waste, a step past kit routes that grow rings in germ strains. The team used the rings to run a gene edit base tool in human and mouse stem cells. They also set a gene chunk into the code with the rings. Ease and clean stock mark the route.
pmc-12709548:
Making the same moral choice again and again is not a fresh start each time, since past picks and payoffs linger. Xinyi Xu and four co-authors study how people weigh history when they face repeat moral choices. Their 2025 work pairs brain scans with mouse tracking, a method that records the path of a cursor as a person decides.

In a task where choices trade values against rewards, the curve of the mouse path gives a measure of conflict. The team also scores how steady each person's choices are, at both the person level and the single trial level. They find that the link between conflict and steadiness runs through how much weight reward holds. One brain area, the precuneus, tracks conflict and grows more active over time.
pmc-12709748:
Julia Neuharth and co-authors track how often studies of a widely used Alzheimer's mouse model report the sex of their animals. Their 2025 review covers twenty years of work with the 5xFAD mouse and reads 1,330 papers listed on PubMed up to late 2024. Women face nearly twice the lifetime risk of Alzheimer's, so sex can shape what mouse results mean.

Fewer papers now leave sex unreported, yet the pattern has barely improved. About three in ten studies used males only, and a quarter mixed both sexes without splitting the data. Fewer than one in eight treated sex as a real variable. The authors warn that this gap hides how the disease may differ by sex.
pmc-12710248:
Striker and Kong (2025) measured how much water quietly evaporates from a specific heart-lung machine oxygenator. In ECMO, a machine oxygenates blood outside the body, and unnoticed water loss through the oxygenator can skew fluid records and concentrate sodium in the blood. The losses were known for other devices but not for the Medtronic Nautilus. The team ran a closed lab circuit at three gas flow rates and measured the loss over a day.

Water loss rose in a straight line with gas flow: about 66 to 73 milliliters per day for each liter per minute of sweep gas, depending on how it was measured. Sodium built up as water left, though the rise was not statistically firm in the small sample. The authors give bedside formulas for the loss and warn that it, and the risk of high blood sodium, belong in daily fluid planning for ECMO patients.
pmc-12710448:
Sun and seven co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-five on tumor cell plasticity, the talent cancer cells have for changing their form and behavior. This shape-shifting helps tumors start, spread, dodge drugs, and regrow, and the authors argue it sits at the center of how cancer evolves.

The review first traces how plasticity drives each big step, from a tumor's birth to its spread and its survival under treatment. It then sorts the causes into two groups: forces inside the cell, such as unstable genes and chemical tags on DNA, and signals from the tissue around the tumor. A final part covers new tools that watch this shifting in space and time, plus early attempts to drug it. The authors hope that tracking and steering plasticity could turn cancer into a more manageable disease.
pmc-12712048:
Wilner and co-authors build the first nationwide map of wildfire disasters that actually reach communities. A fire counts as a burn zone disaster here if it burns near a settled area and kills a civilian, destroys a building, or earns a federal disaster declaration. By merging six data sets, the team assembles the record for 2000 to 2025.

They count 6,212 such disasters, rising over time from 61 in 2001 to a peak of 570 in 2011. California alone accounts for 878, about one in seven. The authors offer the data set as a base for research on health, money, and policy, and for steering resources toward the places hit most often.
pmc-12714048:
Takuo Tanaka and Wakana Kubo introduce a special issue drawn from the eleventh International Conference on Surface Plasmon Photonics. The meeting ran in Tokyo in May twenty twenty-five. The series is the leading gathering for plasmonics, the study of how light interacts with tiny metal structures, along with related fields.

Past meetings have crossed Europe, Asia, and North America since two thousand one. The editors note that plasmonics and man made materials, once future facing topics, now drive real devices. Talks covered basic principles and new uses, from lead speakers and posters alike. The issue gathers chosen papers from the meeting. One paper honors a past chair of the series who died in late twenty twenty-four.
pmc-12715248:
Human metapneumovirus sends many people, especially children and the elderly, to hospital with respiratory infections, yet no approved drug or vaccine targets it. Pallavi Mosale Shanthappa and co-authors searched for a shortcut: compounds already known to bind the coronavirus behind COVID-19 might also fit this virus. They tested three candidates entirely in computer simulations, docking each into a model of a viral protein and watching the fit over time.

One compound, salvianolic acid C, from a traditional medicinal plant, held on most stably. Its complex stayed steady, kept a regular hydrogen bond in place, and scored the best binding energy of the three. The other two candidates wobbled and bound weakly. The authors nominate salvianolic acid C for laboratory testing as a possible antiviral against this virus.
pmc-12715948:
Li Wang, Xiaoyun He, Minxi Zhao, and Jun Liu build a risk model for lung complications after chest surgery. Their 2025 study asks how breathing machine settings during surgery affect later lung problems. Such complications are common after thoracic operations and can lengthen recovery.

The team reviewed three hundred patients at a large hospital. Lung complications arose in well over a third of them. Higher breath volumes, higher plateau pressures, lower end-pressure settings, and longer ventilation all linked to more complications. Lung-protective settings pointed the other way. They trained statistical and machine learning models to flag high-risk patients before problems start. A working risk score could let surgical teams tune ventilation to the patient, not the average.
pmc-12716248:
J Lukas Thürmer and Sean M McCrea share the data set behind a cross-cultural study of how people take criticism of their group. Their 2025 data paper supports the first systematic test of the intergroup sensitivity effect across cultures. Volunteers in Canada, China, and Japan each read four critical comments. The comments vary by target, their own culture or another, and by source, a member of their group or an outsider. Replies use standard scales, and people may pay a cost to punish the speaker.

Extra measures cover traits that might bend the effect, plus basic background facts. The paper reports soundness checks and rich detail on each variable. Other teams can thus rerun the study or mine the data for new questions. Open, well-described data of this kind helps a contested effect get a fair, shared test across labs.
pmc-12716548:
Hiroshi Kitamura and co-authors ask Japanese patients with advanced bladder cancer what they value most in treatment, in a 2025 survey. The cancer in question has spread or cannot be removed by surgery, so care aims to extend life while keeping daily life bearable. Patients face hard trade-offs among gains in survival, side effects, and time in hospital.

The survey used a choice method: patients picked between treatment profiles that varied in side effects like nausea, nerve damage, hair loss, and rash, plus hospital stay and length of survival. A math model then weighed how much each trait drove the choices. The results show which gains patients would trade for fewer harms. Drug makers and doctors can use that ranking when they plan and discuss care.
pmc-12717048:
Fatme Ismail, Hans-Peter Hartung, and Nico Melzer comment on an early trial of engineered immune cells for progressive multiple sclerosis. The disease slowly harms the brain and cord, and no current drug fully stops decline. The trial used cells retrained to hunt a marker found on antibody making cells, a method first built for cancer.

In five patients who had failed other care, the cells entered the fluid around the brain and cut antibody levels there. Brain immune cells called microglia also calmed, hinting at a link between the two cell types. The authors note good tolerance over nine months. They frame the result as a clue for how deep cell clearing may slow this hard form of the disease.
pmc-12717248:
Malathy Ramalingam and co-authors test magnet-treated water in high-grade concrete in a 2025 study. Concrete strength and flow hinge on its mixing water, and treated water may boost both. Ready-mix plants also care how long the boost lasts after treatment.

Seven mixes varied in additive dose and in storage time after magnet treatment. Magnet water lifted flow and crushing strength over plain water at the best dose. Water stored an hour after treatment still beat plain water mixes. Lab scans confirmed fuller curing products and finer crystals. The team frames treated water as a curing booster for ready-mix work.
pmc-12717748:
Laila Zeraik and co-authors set out a trial plan to learn where certain small molecules in human blood truly come from, in a 2025 protocol paper. The molecules arise when plant phenols from food are broken down in the gut. They may drive much of the health effect credited to phenol-rich foods. Yet the body can also make the same molecules from protein building blocks and stress signals, with no food involved.

Thirty healthy adults will follow a five-day diet very low in phenols and limit activity. On the third morning, half the design gives coffee, a known phenol source, and half gives hot water. Samples will be read with broad molecule scans to split food-born from body-born output. Gut microbes and gene variants will be tracked as sources of personal variation. The authors warn that body-made output could inflate credit given to diet.
pmc-12718248:
Sandra Ahlqvist and co-authors count hernia repairs after weight loss surgery across Sweden. Keyhole operations leave small port wounds that can later bulge into hernias. Registries linked over sixty four thousand bariatric patients to later hospital care. Five years out, about three in a hundred had needed a ventral hernia operation.

Repairs came more often after gastric bypass than after sleeve surgery, even when the sleeve group's shorter tracking was weighed. Repairs clustered about three years after the first operation. The authors call the burden real, not negligible, and worth weighing in procedure choice and follow up planning.
pmc-12718548:
Giancarlo Buitrago and co-authors present a 2025 study of the cost of RSV infection in Colombia. RSV is a common lung virus that can land babies and old adults in hospital. Using national surveillance and payment data, they count cases and price the care for 2019.

More than a quarter million RSV linked visits were found. Babies under one year had the highest case rates. Death rates peaked in the oldest adults, with infants close behind. Total direct care costs ran to hundreds of millions of dollars. Adults made up the biggest cost share in total, while intensive care babies cost most per person. The authors back targeted prevention.
pmc-12719348:
Fanfan Xing and co-authors review how next-generation sequencing has changed the diagnosis of infection by the fungus Talaromyces marneffei, in a 2025 paper. The first sequencing-based case appeared in 2018. By the end of 2024, at least 241 such cases were on record, most from China, where the infection matters regionally and sequencing is widely used.

Among cases with details, 136 patients were HIV-negative, which likely explains why the fungus was not suspected sooner. Many had other immune defects, from transplant care to autoantibodies. At least 18 were first treated as tuberculosis, and 11 as tumors. Sequencing found the fungus in a median of two days, the authors report.
pmc-12719948:
Chung-Min Cho studies social frailty among older adults who live in the community in South Korea, in a research paper from 2025. Social frailty means weak social ties, roles, and support. It can harm health, yet its causes span both the person and the place they live.

Cho uses survey data for more than eighty thousand adults aged sixty-five and older, plus area data. About one in seven adults were socially frail, and about a third more were at risk. Risk rose with age, low schooling, no work, and low mood. Area traits added a small effect. The paper points to aid aimed at people most at risk.
pmc-12720048:
João Pedro Bandovas and co-authors study in 2025 what happens to kidney function after surgery for primary hyperparathyroidism. In that condition, overactive parathyroid glands keep blood calcium high, which can bring kidney stones and a slow fall in filtering power. Removing the glands is the firm cure, yet its effect on the kidneys was unclear, above all in patients already impaired.

The team reviewed dozens of patients operated over several years, split by starting kidney function. Most were women, and surgery cured nearly all cases. Calcium and hormone levels fell in both groups a year later. Patients with better starting kidneys saw a clear dip in filtering rate, while the impaired group held steady or rose slightly. The authors read surgery as guarding against further loss rather than restoring kidney power.
pmc-12720448:
Roberta Coletti, J Orestes Cerdeira, Marcos Raydan, and Marta Lopes built a tool in two thousand twenty-five to find markers and subtypes in cancer data without using labels. Gene data sets often hold far more measures than patients, which makes classic methods overfit. Supervised feature picking can also lose the broad shape of the data.

Their tool, TRIM-IT, joins unsupervised feature picking with clustering, survival checks, and gene contrast tests. Used on glioblastoma, a tough brain cancer, it found three patient groups. The groups differed in tumour type, survival, and gene patterns. Those patterns hint at new marker candidates for study.
pmc-12720948:
Chao Sun and co-authors hunt for antibiotic use thresholds tied to drug resistant bacteria in a 2025 study of one hospital. They tracked antibiotic consumption and detection rates of four carbapenem resistant germs each quarter from 2015 to 2023. Such germs resist a last line class of antibiotics, so knowing safe use levels matters. Statistical tools included a design that looks for breaks at thresholds and smooth nonlinear models.

Use was flat for years, dipped around 2020, then climbed again. Detection rates for the resistant germs rose into 2019, with one germ found in over half of cases early on, then eased downward. The analysis links changing use levels to changing detection rates and aims to name a critical use threshold. The authors frame the work as guidance for hospital antibiotic stewardship.
pmc-12721548:
A new immune drug plus classic chemo may help wide-spread small-cell lung cancer. Lian Tang and co-authors asked whether the gain is worth the cost in China, in work from twenty twenty-five. A state model ran the two care paths over ten years in three-week steps. Health gains were counted in quality-weighted years of life.

The added drug cost far more per unit of health gained than the bar set at three times the land's per-person output. One-way checks named the health scores and drug price as the levers that move the result most. Chance runs gave the combo about a one-in-five shot at passing the bar. The authors close that the combo is not good value at that bar.
pmc-12722248:
Peixin Zhang and seven co-authors report a new sponge-like material for cleaning a key factory gas, in a 2025 paper. Propylene feeds plastics and many goods, but it comes mixed with three near twins that are hard to strip out. Plants burn much energy boiling the mix apart, step by step. One filter that traps all three twins at once would save that cost.

The team's best material, ZU-921, is a metal and carbon frame lined with clingy spots tuned to grab the twins but let propylene pass. In a scaled-up column test, the filter gave propylene at 99.99 percent purity in one step. The authors say the design rules behind it can guide filters for other tough gas mixes too.
pmc-12722648:
Nagina Khan and ten co-authors gather what medical students themselves say about learning professionalism. Their 2025 review notes that professionalism sits at the heart of patient experience, yet training often stresses standard frameworks over the relational side of care. Student views are rarely asked, even though today's students shape tomorrow's care. The team searched four databases for studies from 2010 to 2023 and kept fifty-four.

Students named role modeling by senior clinicians as the strongest teacher, joined by reflection, patient stories, and supportive settings. Barriers included uneven teaching, a clash between the formal curriculum and behavior seen on the wards, and too little structured feedback. Learning bit deepest when teaching was woven into real patient care. Students described professionalism as lived relations (empathy, respect, honesty, and accountability) rather than rules. The authors urge curricula built around modeling, reflection, and patient narratives.
pmc-12722748:
Tshiaba and Liao studied China's paths to carbon neutrality, in a paper published in 2025. Nations have pledged to cut carbon output, and China is the largest emitter. The authors used a model that links emissions to population, wealth, and technology, then extended it with money and policy factors. They asked how renewable energy, green invention, and green taxes shape emissions. Their data cover 30 Chinese provinces from 2007 to 2021.

Renewable energy cut emissions only where its use was already high. In less developed provinces, renewables added to coal use rather than replacing it. That pattern suggests a threshold effect. Green invention and taxes also played roles that varied by place. The authors draw lessons for provinces at different stages. Pushing renewables past the threshold, they argue, is what turns them into a coal substitute.
pmc-12723848:
Jinyan Chen, Guanyu Su, Ziang Wu, and Feng Wang studied guided implant surgery in a 2025 lab study. Patients with no upper teeth often need tilted implants, and a navigation system steers the drill. Small guide markers fixed in the mouth let the system line up the scan with the real jaw.

The team tested five marker layouts on a model jaw fitted with sixteen mini screws. Some screws set the alignment, and others measured its error at target points. Marker layout, target site, and their interplay all shifted the error. Their results show which spread of markers keeps tilted implants on target most faithfully.
pmc-12723948:
Tianliu Zhang and fourteen colleagues integrate many data layers to find how genes control fat composition in cattle, in a 2025 paper. Fatty acid makeup affects meat quality and health value, and it is governed by many genes at once. Gene hunts had found linked variants without explaining how they act.

Their combined strategy flagged nearly 119,000 candidate variants across more than four thousand genes. Expression mapping in muscle and fat tissue tied hundreds of thousands of variant-gene pairs to activity changes. Methylation, histone marks, and chromatin openness annotated which variants sit in active regulatory zones. Two genes stood out as key regulators of fat synthesis. One variant near a fat gene's promoter was tested directly: reporter assays and CRISPR edits confirmed it boosts activity and shifts fat profiles. The authors offer the targets for breeding better meat.
pmc-12727648:
Fang Chen and a large team of co-authors review AI help in building heart organoids for congenital heart disease, in a 2025 paper. These birth heart defects stay hard to model, which slows grasp of their causes. Lab-grown mini tissues that mimic the heart offer a sharper model. AI can guide how those mini hearts form and how drugs are tested on them.

The review covers machine learning in self-assembly, 3D printing, tissue craft, and chip-based organs. Classic methods such as support vector machines and decision trees join neural networks in the toolkit. Uses span cell contact maps, drug screens, and harm checks. The authors see AI speeding the move from lab models to tailored care.
pmc-12727748:
Dominique Paquin and seven co-authors present a regional climate ensemble for North America. Their 2025 paper describes simulations run with the Canadian regional model CRCM5. Four global models drive the regional one, sharpening their coarse output. The runs cover the continent from nineteen fifty to twenty-one hundred.

Grid spacing is fine, at about a tenth of a degree, across the whole map. Future runs span up to four emissions paths, with five versions for one chosen setup. The paper explains the model's settings and how well it matches records. It also tells users how to access the data. The ensemble serves planners who need local detail on climate change.
pmc-12727848:
DuJiang Yang and GuoYou Wang argue, in a 2025 letter, that research on bone loss in diabetes must move past simple association studies. They respond to a study linking high fat with low muscle and lower bone density in older women with type 2 diabetes. That pairing, called sarcopenic obesity, marks a real risk group.

The letter faults scans that report only bone amount, since diabetes raises fracture risk even at normal density. Bone quality, like inner structure and material traits, goes unseen by such scans. Cross-sectional data without blood markers cannot show cause or path. The authors urge long-term studies with finer imaging and deep metabolic profiling. Clearer paths from fat and muscle to bone would guide targeted care.
pmc-12729148:
Chun Yang and co-authors study a long term insulin resistance score and heart disease in Chinese adults in a 2025 paper. Insulin resistance is a known risk factor for cardiovascular disease, and a metabolic score can stand in for it. Whether years of high scores predict new disease was unexplored in China. The team followed 5264 middle aged and older adults from a national aging study.

Over four years, about ten percent developed cardiovascular disease. Higher average scores across two measures years apart raised total disease risk in a dose pattern. The top score group faced higher heart disease risk but no clear stroke risk. Risk was sharper in men, smokers, drinkers, and people with normal blood pressure. Readers see value in tracking the score over time.
pmc-12729248:
Francesca Meda, Natalia Oprea, and Claudio Buongiorno Sottoriva review what kinds of programs actually open health care to people who live without a home. Their 2025 scoping review starts from the health gap: homeless people fare far worse than housed ones. Past studies mostly cover single programs in single places, so a broad comparison was missing.

The team searched the literature from 2000 to 2023 and kept 48 studies. The care on offer ran from primary care and mental health to emergency and hospital services. Four main program types emerged, each meeting a different access need. Outreach and community-based work best ensured care that was both on hand and welcome. The review maps each type against a standard frame of access.
pmc-12729548:
Masaya Tamura and co-authors compare, in a 2025 study, two lung cancer operations when the tumor has breached the lung's inner lining. Taking the whole lobe is the bigger cut; taking one segment spares more lung. Records of 218 patients with this invasion were sorted by operation and tumor size, then matched for fair comparison.

Overall survival, cancer survival, and relapse-free survival showed no clear difference between the two operations. For tumors under two centimeters, results again tied. Above that size, segment patients relapsed in the chest lining more often, a significant gap. The authors suggest the smaller operation suits small tumors with this invasion, while bigger ones may favor the lobe.
pmc-12729748:
Hepatitis B and C rates among quake survivors in southeast Türkiye are gauged by Muhammed Bekçibaşı and co-authors in work dated 2025. The study ran eleven months after the 2023 quakes, in container camps. Fast blood tests checked 251 people for a B surface mark and for C antibodies. The zone holds the land's highest B rate in normal times.

Thirteen people, near five percent, tested positive for the B mark. None tested positive for C. B-positive people were more apt to be male and to have a family past of the disease. Other traits did not split the groups. Wider counts are still needed.
pmc-12730148:
Ting Lei, Yanqiong Peng, Yuanjun Liu, Yaping Xie and Junjie Wang wrote a 2025 review on drug-free ways to ease pain after gallbladder surgery. Many such methods are used, but which works best was unclear. The team ran a network analysis that compares many options at once. Trials came from five databases up to early 2025.

Fifteen kinds of drug-free care appeared in the trials. Pressing points, massage and skin-based nerve pulses were the most common. Ear point pressing, scent therapy and foot baths ranked top for pain relief. All three beat standard care by a clear margin. Rankings also covered anxiety after surgery.
pmc-12730348:
Yixuan Li and co-authors test in 2025 a coal-based soil fixer plus switchgrass on salty alkali farmland in a semi-arid zone. Five grass varieties each got the same fixer dose in a field trial. The study tracks how soil salts, microbes, and plant growth shift together.

Soil ion makeup shapes microbe life strongly in the plots. One variety tops microbe abundance and cuts sodium plus exchangeable sodium the most. That same variety lifts soil carbon and potassium well above a peer variety. The pair strategy offers a field-proven route to heal salt-damaged land.
pmc-12730848:
Rebecca Porter and a large co-author team report, in a 2025 trial study, a two-antibody combination for ovarian cancer that has resisted standard drugs. Platinum-resistant disease leaves patients with poor options. The pair joins an enhanced blocker of one immune brake with a blocker of a second brake.

The first antibody was engineered in its tail region to engage immune cells more strongly than earlier versions. Patients in this early-phase expansion cohort had treatment-refractory disease. The study gauged safety and early signs of benefit. Ovarian tumors often shrug off single immune drugs. A stronger brake release, paired wisely, is one of the field's main hopes for changing that.
pmc-12731048:
Natalia Trachtmann and co-authors clone and proof, in 2025 work, a fresh fibre-cut enzyme from a deep hot well in North Ossetia. Gene reads of the well's mats, at near fifty degrees, gave the code, from a germ line with just three named kin. The enzyme was grown in lab germs and cleaned.

It works best warm and mild-lye, with a very high work rate. Heat holds: most force stays after an hour at eighty degrees. One metal salt lifts its force more than sevenfold. It is the first such enzyme proofed from its order, the team notes, and a prize for plant-waste craft.
pmc-12731148: Henning Plage and co-authors examined how the androgen receptor varies across bladder cancer stages and relates to patient outcomes, in a 2025 paper. Bladder cancer ranks tenth among cancers worldwide and carries a heavy global burden. The record describes a study of the receptor, a hormone-sensing protein, measured across stages of the disease. The authors link its expression pattern to poor outcomes, as their title states.
pmc-12731348:
Tattoo ink can bite back, and red ink bites hardest, but one man's reaction went far beyond the tattooed skin. Mateusz Mateuszczyk and co-authors report in 2025 a thirty-six year old who, four months after a red tattoo, slid into whole body skin inflammation, total hair loss, and a shutdown of sweating. Patch tests confirmed allergy to the ink's likely ingredients.

Steroids and three immune drugs failed in turn. Cutting out the inflamed tattoo calmed the skin, yet white patches of vitiligo spread until every trace of that ink batch was removed and newer immune drugs were added. Hair returned and the patches halted; the sweating never did. The authors present the case as a warning that local ink can raise a systemic storm.
pmc-12731548:
Vyjeyanthi Periyakoil, Charles Von Gunten, and Helena Kraemer present a 2025 protocol for a trial of early palliative care delivered by nurses over video. Dementia is a long, serious illness, yet little is known about the supportive care needs of people living at home with it. The trial tests whether early nurse-led support improves those patients' care.

Two hundred older adults with chronic illness and memory problems were assigned by chance to usual care or to usual care plus the video program. Outcomes include reported supportive care needs and whether patients held talks about goals of care and recorded their wishes in advance documents. Assessors do not know which group each patient is in.
pmc-12731648:
Lijiao Cui and co-authors examine a metabolic enzyme, UGP2, as a possible marker and brake in colorectal cancer. Their 2025 study notes that bowel cancer still kills heavily worldwide, so reliable markers and drug targets are prized. The enzyme had been linked to tumor growth in several cancers, but its exact role in this one was murky.

Combining protein screening, database analysis, and lab validation, the team found the enzyme strongly reduced in tumors versus healthy tissue. Low levels tracked with vessel and nerve invasion and with shorter survival. A diagnostic test based on it separated cancer from normal tissue with near-perfect accuracy in their data. Chemical silencing of its gene, though, tracked with better outcomes, a puzzle the paper explores.
pmc-12732048: Cristian Scheau and Ana Caruntu survey the forces that drive epithelial cancers in this 2025 review. Such cancers arise from the linings of the skin, glands, and the gut, lung, urinary, and reproductive tracts. The review frames them through molecular, metabolic, and surrounding-tissue forces, rethinking cancer as a disease of whole physiology, not of single broken genes alone. It is a review essay, not a report of new lab data.
pmc-12732648:
Choi and co-authors review in 2025 how cancers dodge antibody drugs by reshuffling their own RNA. Antibody drugs aim at marks on a tumor's surface, and they have changed cancer care. Tumors escape when those marks vanish, change shape, or vary from cell to cell.

A process called splicing cuts and rejoins RNA in new ways, making altered marks or even loose decoy copies that soak up the drug. The review tracks this trick across major drug targets, from blood cancer marks to growth signals and immune brakes. New fixes are in view: RNA patches that restore normal cuts, drugs that tune the cutters, and antibodies built for one altered form. Spotting the trick early could help doctors switch plans before a drug fails.
pmc-12732848:
Yibin Xu and co-authors read three full mitochondrial genomes of freshwater snails in a 2025 study. The snail family spans East Asia and North America and hosts parasites of medical note. Its family tree stayed murky under short gene reads.

Snails from China gave full or near-full mitochondrial genomes, each rich in tree signal. Trees built five ways, from gene letters and protein letters, tested the placement of the three kinds. Richer data promise sharper splits than the one- or two-gene reads of the past. The work adds reference genomes for a family tied to both ecology and health.
pmc-12732948:
Safıya Temizyurek and co-authors test home teeth-whitening gels laced with plant-based additives. Their 2025 study uses 144 extracted front teeth split into four groups. Two trial gels mix chitosan and theobromine, a cocoa compound, with standard whitening agents. Two shop gels serve as the yardsticks.

Hardness, surface roughness, and colour were read before care, right after, and two weeks on. All gels whitened the teeth, with one shop gel strongest. The trial gels whitened well without raising roughness or softening the enamel. No group showed a real hardness gain. The authors present the mixes as gentler options for home bleaching with less risk to the enamel surface.
pmc-12733048:
Monika Jampolska and Katarzyna Kaczyńska reviewed in 2025 how dopamine-based drugs affect the non-motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease. The illness is known for tremor, stiffness, and slow motion, caused by lost dopamine in the brain. Its other symptoms, from poor sleep to pain, are often missed and left untreated.

The review gathers recent studies on a wide range of these problems, such as blood pressure and temperature control, swallowing trouble, bladder issues, mood changes, and sleep apnea. Many of them, the authors find, can ease with the right drug plan. Yet the same drugs can also cause harm, so dose and choice need care. The authors stress that non-motor care should sit beside motor care.
pmc-12733548:
Carlos Elías Altamar-Bolívar and co-authors study a blue Morpho butterfly in the Caribbean region of Colombia in a 2025 paper. Morpho butterflies react strongly to forest damage, so they can serve as warning species for land change. The team compared butterfly populations across forest, land under restoration, and pasture.

Between June and September 2023 they set 50 traps, marked each butterfly's wing, and released it. Of 876 butterflies tagged, about a third were caught again. Numbers were highest in well-kept forest units, and population size estimates ranged widely across sites. Males clearly outnumbered females, and butterflies in forest stayed local rather than ranging far. Land use clearly shaped the population pattern.
pmc-12733748:
Xing-Xing Wang and co-authors published a 2025 study on how light levels change the behavior of harlequin ladybirds. Light steers insect rhythms and activity. The harlequin ladybird comes in color forms, from pale to mostly black, and eats aphids that plague crops. The team asked whether brightness affects the forms differently, and what role their light-sensing genes play.

Females of three color forms were tested under three intensities of white light. Brighter light raised body temperature and movement in all forms. The darkest form warmed and moved the most, as its dark shell soaks up energy. Hunting success on pea aphids tended to rise with brightness, but unevenly: the dark form ate the most. For growers who use ladybirds as pest control, the findings hint that light and color form set how well the beetles perform.
pmc-12733848:
Servet Altay and co-authors report real-world use of cangrelor, a fast vein-delivered blood thinner, in Türkiye, in a 2025 study. The drug blocks platelets during heart artery procedures when pills cannot be used well. Fourteen busy centers shared records for four hundred eleven patients. The team logged why the drug was chosen, what events followed, and how much bleeding occurred in and after hospital care.

The drug was used most when patients were in shock, on breathing tubes, or too sick to swallow pills. Any bleeding within two days struck about six percent of patients, with major bleeding under two percent. Rates were alike for older and younger patients and for those with kidney disease. The authors call the drug safe and useful in high-risk care. They present the cohort as the first large national picture of its use.
pmc-12733948:
Jarząbek-Bielecka and co-authors present a 2025 pilot report on genital discomfort in women and girls, viewed across specialties. Itching and burning send many patients to clinics, with causes from skin disease to hormones. The study covered 288 outpatients aged eleven to ninety-one seen over six years. Age, birth history, and body mass were tested against how often discomfort drove the visit.

Most patients carried one of two diagnosis codes for vulvar or vaginal disorders. The forty-one to fifty age band reported discomfort most often, by a wide margin. The report's theme is cooperation: prevention and diet advice join medical care in its title for a reason. Pilot size limits every claim, the authors note.
pmc-12734248:
Sam Vanbergen and co-authors used genome reads to trace fruit fly invasions of Belgium, in this 2025 study. The fly, a top fruit pest, is a quarantine priority in Europe. Traps in gardens and markets caught adult males in 2023 and 2024. The team sequenced them, plus larvae seized from imported fruit in past years.

Marker analysis split the adults by origin: three from Africa and eight from Asia, pointing to separate arrivals rather than one spreading front. Nearly all seized larvae traced to Africa. One gene region mostly agreed with the genome-wide read, with a few clashes flagged. The team also built a compact marker set so labs can assign origins fast.
pmc-12734448:
Mustafa Alsaady and six colleagues build membranes that separate carbon dioxide from methane more cleanly. Such separation matters for carbon capture and for cleaning natural gas. They blend graphene oxide flakes into polysulfone, a common membrane plastic, to form mixed matrix membranes.

Adding the flakes raised both gas flow and selectivity for carbon dioxide. A mix with a small loading of graphene oxide gave the best results, with strong permeability and a clear edge in telling the two gases apart. The flakes spread evenly through the plastic, which helped performance. The new membrane also resisted swelling under gas pressure far longer than plain polysulfone, holding up to ten bar before failing.
pmc-12734748:
Serkan Duz and co-authors measure body changes after long runs in 2025. Trained male runners raced either a marathon or a longer ultra distance. The team tracks how body makeup, water, and fat shift right after the race and a day later.

Sixteen runners were split evenly between the two races. Weight and body mass index fell after both races, more so for the ultra group. Much of the loss returned within a day as fuel stores and fluids refilled. Total body water held steady right after racing, then rose during recovery, above all in the ultra runners.
pmc-12734848:
Betul Aktepe and co-authors surveyed sleep in 187 patients with advanced cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors at two centers. Sleep disturbance is common in cancer and may tie into immune effects of the therapy. Three months into treatment, patients filled in a standard sleep quality index. Just over half scored in the disturbed range. The worst-hit parts of the index were sleep disturbance and daytime dysfunction. Statistical models then hunted for what predicted poor sleep.

Three factors held up after adjustment: worse daily functioning, second-line or later treatment, and cancer spread to two or more sites. More treatment cycles tracked with worse sleep before adjustment. Poor performance status, heavier disease burden, and later-line therapy independently predict impaired sleep. They support asking about sleep during this therapy, since disturbed sleep is common, measurable, and tied to how patients are doing.
pmc-12734948:
Chuandong Chen and co-authors present a fast routing algorithm for chip packaging design in this 2025 paper. In one packaging style, a redistribution layer must connect many input-output pins in a set order. Older exact methods are too slow for large multi-capacity cases, which blocks bigger designs.

The team recasts the routing task as a flow problem and solves it with linear programming. A search step then turns the flow into candidate paths for each pin. A weighting scheme picks a legal set of paths with the fewest crossings, and a repeat pass handles any pins left unrouted. In tests, the method solved twice the scale of earlier work and cut routing time by 17 percent.
pmc-12735148:
Magda Nawceniak-Balczerska and co-authors report a 2025 study on which tests best predict infection inside the womb. Such infection can harm mother and baby, yet no clear test scheme exists to flag it ahead of birth. The team set out to grade a range of blood, fluid, and swab tests against tissue proof after birth.

The study drew 70 women who all gave birth by caesarean section, split into a group with tissue-proven infection and a control group. Samples came from mother's blood, the birth canal, the womb fluid, and cord blood, plus tissue from the placenta. Two common blood markers in the mother proved poor guides to the tissue result. The best guides were sugar levels in the womb fluid and one immune signal in birth canal fluid.
pmc-12735248:
Ilaria Galliano and eleven co-authors check whether the body's antiviral alarm baseline drifts with age or sex in healthy people. Six interferon-stimulated genes in blood form a signature used to judge immune activity, and labs need to know what counts as normal. Ninety-five healthy volunteers, from infants to the near ninety, gave samples for gene measurement. Most single genes barely moved with age.

Two exceptions appeared: one gene eased down and another rose with age, with the pattern clearer in women. The combined six-gene score, though, ignored both age and sex entirely. Pooling, the authors conclude, smooths out the small demographic wiggles.
pmc-12735448:
Jiangze Luo and co-authors study heavy metal capture during coal burning in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Quartz in ash can adsorb heavy metals, but alkali metals in coal compete for the same sites. The team tested how sodium and calcium additives change that contest.

Furnace experiments and quantum chemical calculations agreed on the pattern. Sodium salts hurt metal retention, with sodium chloride the worst: lead and cadmium capture fell sharply as its share rose. Higher temperature also lowered capture rates for four metals. Calculations showed alkali metals bind quartz surfaces far more strongly than heavy metals do. The work may help cut heavy metal release from coal plants.
pmc-12735548:
Yin and co-authors run the first lab test of oleanolic acid on human pancreatic islets. Oleanolic acid is a natural plant compound with reported benefits for blood sugar, liver health, and inflammation. Its poor water solubility, though, limits drug forms and medical use.

To fix that, the team designed a water-loving serine conjugate of the compound. They then compared both forms on human islets in vitro, the clusters that make insulin. The conjugate dissolved far better while matching the parent compound's effects. That pairing of solubility and activity supports further study of this form for diabetes care.
pmc-12735748:
Tatiana V Shirshikova and co-authors published a study in 2025 on a soil bacterium that might serve as a living fertilizer in polluted fields. Farms lean on chemicals, metals, and antibiotics that linger in soil, and helpful microbes must survive all three to be useful. The team profiled one hardy strain taken from rock, checking both its body and its genome.

The strain tolerated pesticides, heavy metals, and many antibiotics while carrying few resistance genes of its own. Its genome held two harmless island regions and a built-in defense system against viruses. Low risk of spreading resistance makes it safer than many candidates. The authors present it as a biofertilizer prospect for contaminated soils.
pmc-12735848:
Kareem Ouhalla Knipschild and eight co-authors build, in 2025 work, tiny mixed grains that glow and answer to magnets at once. Such pairs of skills suit them for body imaging and heat sensing. The glow comes from quantum dots made of a copper mix with low poison risk and a strong deep-red shine.

The magnet part is a manganese iron oxide grain that keeps its pull with no lasting magnetism of its own. Both parts are sealed in glass-like shells and joined into one grain. The shell keeps the glow from fading and the mix stable in fluid. The grains shine in the deep-red band and sense heat with fine care. Scope and light tests back the design, and the team sees a path to dual-mode body tools.
pmc-12735948:
Laura Turilli and co-authors coat magnetic nanoparticles in one gentle step and test them for medical imaging, in this 2025 paper. The particles usually need hot, pressurized, multi-step making. The team's room-condition water method forms them directly in suspension, now with polymer coats.

Twelve batches varied coat type and strength. One polymer gave round, even particles of 10 to 30 nanometers with weaker magnetism. The other gave shape-shifting particles near 10 nanometers with magnetism matching uncoated ones. A trial MRI run on one batch gave signal values that support imaging use. The authors pitch the route as greener and simpler.
pmc-12736248:
Carmen Tapia Mercado and co-authors listen to Chilean nursing students placed in schools to promote mental health, in a 2025 study. Chile has no formal school nurse role, so these placements double as reconnaissance. Sixty-four third-year students formed the pool; interviews and a focus group supplied the material. Five themes organize what they said.

Students grasped prevention as the heart of the work but stumbled writing project objectives. Early nerves about handling children gave way to growing confidence. Faculty backing, teacher goodwill, and team cohesion helped; noise, poor rooms, and inexperience hindered. The authors argue such practica build professional identity and should inform both curricula and the case for school nurses.
pmc-12736848:
Vivian Rose and co-authors find what drives children's scores on a hand function test in a 2025 paper. The Bead Maze test times children threading beads while sensors record the forces their fingers apply, giving an objective grade of hand skill. The team asked which lab measures best predict that grade, in case clinics can use simpler checks to spot children who need help.

Thirty-nine children took part, most aged five to ten. The strongest predictor was anticipatory force control: how well a child scales grip force ahead of the load, measured in a separate dexterity task. Age, sex, and pinch strength also mattered. The authors argue that sensitive force measures deserve a place in clinical hand assessments, since they point to the exact skills therapy should train.
pmc-12737148:
Min Wang and co-authors study the bacteria living around alfalfa roots in the salty, alkaline soils of China's Songnen Plain. Such soil badly limits farming, yet alfalfa tolerates it moderately well, perhaps with microbial help. Sequencing root-zone bacteria from stressed and normal soil, the team found the stressed community reshaped, enriched in certain groups, with one genus standing out as a marker of the change. Predicted gene functions suggested a community tuned to harsh conditions.

From the stressed soil the team isolated bacteria and screened them for growth-promoting traits. Two strains, one Pseudomonas laurentiana and one Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, clearly improved alfalfa growth under salt stress in pot trials. The authors propose these home-grown strains as microbial resources for helping crops cope with saline-alkaline land.
pmc-12737248:
Marmondi and nine co-authors review how exercise shifts the body signals of sarcopenia, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength, is fed by chronic low-grade inflammation and faltering growth signals.

Surveying randomized trials, the team found training lowers pro-inflammatory markers like IL-6 and TNF-alpha while raising calming ones, and nudges growth factors that favor building muscle over breaking it down. They also highlight newer exercise-released molecules, nicknamed exerkines, that support mitochondria, fat metabolism, and muscle repair. Responses varied a lot between studies, which limits firm prescriptions. The authors argue that pairing biomarker profiles with exercise plans could personalize care for weakening muscles.
pmc-12737748:
Małgorzata Ćwieląg-Drabek and co-authors measured toxic metals in cigarettes sold in Poland, in a study published in 2025. Tobacco smoke exposes smokers to metals such as cadmium, lead, nickel, and copper, which build up in the body. These metals are linked to cancer and to harm in the heart, lungs, and kidneys. The team tested 119 tobacco samples and estimated health risks under several smoking patterns.

Metal levels varied widely from brand to brand, and a few brands stood out with very high lead. Even at one cigarette a day, breathing in cadmium, nickel, and lead passed set limits for cancer risk in the team's models. Non-cancer risks were also weighed across the smoking patterns.
