Jerly Helan Mary Joseph, Mercy Priyadharshini Babu Deva Irakkam, and Mahesh Kandasamy study botulinum neurotoxin in aging mice in a 2025 paper. The toxin is best known for treating movement and muscle disorders. Recent work hints it may also help memory and ease anxiety in aging animals.

Treated mice were examined after four weeks for new neurons and microglia in the hippocampus. The treated group had more immature and newly matured neurons in the dentate gyrus. It also had fewer activated microglia and lower levels of two inflammatory markers. The authors link these shifts to the toxin's reported gains in thinking and mood.
pmc-12768648:
Tamara Mahanova tests a ranking method to learn what pharmacy services patients in Ukraine value most. Preference data can enrich technology assessment, but methods vary and their weight in decisions is unclear. The study used a best worst scaling design across twelve pharmacy services.

Top choices were a personal list of safe medicines matched to patient needs, plus rapid tests and stroke risk checks. Contraception advice and weight loss programs ranked low. Deeper analysis split patients into two groups with different tastes and backgrounds. Mahanova says the method is simple to run, yet it demands skill and effort. The results can surface unmet needs in local service planning.
pmc-12768748:
Cesar Ricardo Campello, Marcia Gisele Costa, and Marcia Pinto check a drug budget forecast against reality in a 2025 health costs study. Fingolimod treats relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, and Brazil's public health system adopted it after a budget impact analysis projected the cost. Years later, the authors validate that analysis from outside, comparing the assumptions in the incorporation report with the real parameters that emerged after adoption.

Outside checks of budget forecasts are rare and valuable: they show whether the models behind coverage decisions deserve trust. The fingolimod case offers Brazil's system a rare real-world answer.
pmc-12768848:
Ross Fairbairn and five co-authors wrote a 2025 study that scans the field for new quantum tools in health care. Quantum tools use the odd rules of very small particles to sense, image, or compute in new ways. The team wanted to know which of these tools are near real use in clinics and labs.

The scan found 116 quantum tools in health care. The most common were tools that map brain activity, tiny glowing particles used in imaging, and sensors that read the heart. More than half of the tools help doctors find illness, while others aid drug design or care. Most tests so far are not run by firms, and many tools pair quantum tech with smart software. The authors warn that cost, rules, and staff training still slow wider use.
pmc-12769748:
In allergic asthma, a class of immune cells called ILC2s fires up lung inflammation. Dongdi Wang and co-authors trace a growth-control switch, mTORC1, inside those cells. In mice with allergic lung disease, the switch ran hotter than normal, and the cells poured out more of two alarm signals.

Deleting a key part of the switch calmed the cells and shielded the mice from inflammation. A drug that blocks the switch did the same. The switch also raised the cells' receptor for a nerve signal, tuning them to the nervous system. The 2025 study names this switch a candidate drug target for allergic asthma.
pmc-12771048:
Chukwuweike Gwam and co-authors published a mouse study in 2025 on a stem cell fluid as an aid for repairing cut peripheral nerves. Nerve injuries can leave lasting weakness and pain, and large gaps need grafts. Fluid conditioned by amniotic fluid stem cells is easy to prepare and gentle on the immune system. The team tested it in mice with a cut sciatic nerve.

Thirty-six mice were split into plain repair, gel graft, and gel plus stem cell fluid groups. Electrical tests and tissue measures showed no clear group gaps. Walking measures, though, improved more with the stem cell fluid than with gel alone. Muscle wasting markers fell and junction recovery markers rose. The authors call the fluid promising as an add-on therapy.
pmc-12772048:
Aparajita, Debabrata Barmon, Upasana Baruah, Dimpy Begum, and Shiraj Ahmed test if seals bar tumour spill in womb cancer cuts in a 2025 study. Past work found stray gland cells in the birth path of near a third of cases post-cut. Such spill may seed lone returns of the cancer in that path.

Seals on the neck path and the egg tubes form the act on trial here. Cases split by lot to seal or no seal in one hub's pilot run. Spill marks are the core read of the work.
pmc-12772148:
Penadés writes about phage satellites, small gene elements that steal the tools of viruses to spread themselves. Gene flow between microbes drives new traits, such as drug resistance and the power to cause disease. For years, viruses, plasmids, and a few other movers were seen as the main carriers of that flow.

Satellites are a newer and stranger family among those movers. They cannot spread alone, so they hijack helper viruses for transport. Penadés discusses a study that found a striking new way satellites work, at a scale tied to very large viruses. Many satellite families are still unknown. The piece maps what is known and why these small hitchhikers matter for how microbes change.
pmc-12776848:
Ahmed Salem and co-authors test a blood ratio as a warning mark in trauma care in a 2025 study. Badly hurt patients face whole body swelling and blood infection in intensive care. Early warning lets teams act before those states set in.

One hundred trauma patients at a Cairo hospital had blood tests on set days. The ratio of a swelling protein to albumin was tracked over five days. A third of patients grew the swelling state, and over a fourth grew blood infection. The ratio ran far higher in those groups on each test day. A cheap ratio test could flag high risk patients early.
pmc-12777648:
Lin Jiang and co-authors test language models on gallbladder polyp scans in this 2025 study. Most gallbladder polyps are harmless, but some are adenomas that need surgery. Size-based rules can push patients toward needless operations.

The team gathered ultrasound images and reports for polyps of one centimeter or more with known pathology. Two large multimodal models were tried under three input plans: images alone, feature text, and score-based text. Their calls were compared with radiologists and with the guideline rule. Agreement within and between readers was checked as well. The study weighs whether such models could ease radiologist load and patient worry.
pmc-12780048:
Lukas Brenner, Libor Caha, Xavier Coiteux-Roy, and Robert Koenig present a quantum factoring method in this 2025 paper. Most quantum algorithm design starts from a general machine with many qubits, the quantum bits. The authors argue that designing around a real physical set-up can pay off instead.

Their set-up joins one qubit with three oscillators and uses light-based operations plus a few controlled steps. In that system, a key transform and some arithmetic steps have natural forms. Using them, the authors give a factoring method that runs in polynomial time. Its size stays fixed at one qubit and three oscillators, no matter how large the number to be factored is.
pmc-12780148:
Hiba Laraki and three co-authors review VISTA, an immune brake that cancer immunotherapy has barely touched, in a 2025 paper. Drugs releasing the famous PD-1 brake fail many patients, so the hunt is on for the next checkpoint.

VISTA belongs to the B7 family and sits on blood-forming cells. It damps T cell activity and blunts anti-tumor responses. The review maps where it appears across cancers and what roles it plays there. Candidate partner molecules get a hearing, with the tumor's neighborhood in view. Clinical trials targeting VISTA are summarized at the end. The authors cast it as a promising, still-early lever: strong biology, few answers in patients so far.
pmc-12780448:
Wei Guo and co-authors checked in 2025 whether wrapping the rejoined airway with the patient's own heart sac tissue helps after a lung saving cancer operation. In this surgery, a lobe is cut out and the airway sewn back, sparing more lung than removing the whole organ.

The study reviewed ninety-one patients treated from 2012 to 2017; sixty-two had the wrap, twenty-nine did not. Death rates at one and three months did not differ between the groups, before or after statistical matching of similar patients. Five year survival also matched, at roughly half to two thirds. The authors conclude the wrap adds no clear gain, though it remains a judgment call for surgeons.
pmc-12781848:
Jiang, Huang and their co-authors review face and jaw fractures in children and teens at a hospital in southeast China in 2025. Their fifteen-year records study sorts patterns and treatment by age group, from infants to late teens.

Falls from height were the top cause in the youngest group, while falls at ground level led in older children. Jaw fractures formed a large share, and condyle fractures showed distinct patterns alone versus with a chin fracture. The authors say each pattern needs its own treatment care. They also note limits that come with looking back at past records.
pmc-12782448:
Amanpreet Kaur, Rajdeep Khangura, and Brian Dilkes report a 2025 study of dwarf maize and the natural gene variants that soften its faults. The dwarf trait comes from a broken receptor-like gene. The team crossed mutant plants with a broad panel of maize lines and compared sibling plants.

They found two spots in the genome that changed how strong the dwarf trait looked. One spot was a gene known to work with such receptors. The other was the dwarf gene itself, where more output from the healthy copy made plants taller. The work shows how natural variants can tune a pathway. It gives breeders a frame for tracing complex traits in crops.
pmc-12782648:
Rita Relvas and co-authors present two cases of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and ask whether stress helped trigger it, in this 2025 case series. The prion disease is easily mistaken for other neurological and psychiatric conditions, is often recognized late, and has no proven preventive or curative treatment. Its mechanisms remain poorly understood.

The two cases trace the disease's natural history and the hard differential diagnosis it poses. Both also raise the possibility that psychological stress played a role in predisposing to or precipitating the illness. The authors offer the series as a warning about that potential link and as a reminder to consider the diagnosis earlier.
pmc-12782948:
Mohamed Hnini, Karim Rabeh, and Malika Oubohssaine review how plants and microbes trade favors in the soil. Their twenty twenty-five review centers on the rhizosphere, the thin soil shell around roots crowded with bacteria and fungi. Roots leak sugars that feed this community.

In return, microbes unlock nutrients, build soil structure, and shield roots from disease. Mycorrhizal fungi and nitrogen-fixing bacteria get star billing. The review sorts direct and indirect routes of help and harm. With soils degrading worldwide, farming that recruits the right microbes could cut fertilizer use while keeping yields, a trade every grower can price.
pmc-12784848:
Liu-Shu Jia and co-authors chart how bleach wash reshapes the shell and protein kit of a chicken gut parasite egg, in a study from 2025. Bleach is the stock wash to clean such eggs in labs, yet its mark on their proteins was unmapped. Scope views first show what the wash does to the egg wall at fine scale.

The wash strips the outer wall off and plumps the inner wall in its place. Protein reads found over two thousand kinds in the eggs, with most kinds shifted by the wash. Up kinds serve wall build and stress guard, while down kinds serve outer wall form. A dozen kinds sat in clean eggs alone, which marks them as core to wall birth. The tale aids work on egg strength.
pmc-12785648:
Ioanna Anastasiou and co-authors review in this 2025 paper a blood condition called CHIP, short for clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential. In CHIP, a blood stem cell with a mutation grows into a large clone, yet no blood cancer is present. The state is common with age and shows in more than a fifth of people over eighty.

The review links CHIP to heart and metabolic disease, not just cancer risk. Carriers face notably higher rates of heart events and death, and mouse work ties some mutations to vessel swelling and clots. The authors weigh screening limits and new drug ideas, and frame CHIP as a risk factor that care may one day treat.
pmc-12785948:
Zeng and co-authors report a 2025 study on a plant compound that may fight lung scarring. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis stiffens the lungs over time, and good drug options are lacking. Lathyrol comes from a traditional Chinese medicinal plant and has wide effects in the body. The team tested it in mice with lung scarring and in lab fibroblast cells.

In mice, the compound eased lung damage, and a blocker drug erased that benefit. In cells, it stopped fibroblasts from turning into scar-forming cells. Gene scans pointed to one pathway, driven by a switch called PPARγ, that quiets a growth signal. The authors trace how the switch removes a key messenger protein.
pmc-12786148:
Ana Karla Guzmán-Romero and five co-authors wrote this 2025 review of a benign growth inside the nose and sinuses and the role a common virus may play in it. The growth springs from the lining of the nasal cavity. It is uncommon, shows mostly between ages forty and seventy, and strikes men more often.

Though benign, the growth can eat into nearby tissue, turn cancerous, and come back after removal. The review covers its tissue features, its signs, and its treatment. It also weighs chronic swelling and outside factors in its start. A full section asks how infection with human papillomavirus may damage tissue and push the growth toward cancer.
pmc-12786748:
Michele Segantini, Angela Fadda, and Daniele Sanna review a spectroscopy tool for food aging. Their review from twenty twenty-five deals with oxidative stability. Beer, wine, and oils lose quality as they oxidize.

Oxidation runs through radical chains that spoil flavor. The tool detects free radicals and metal ions with precision. Past uses in beer, wine, and oils are surveyed here. Methods to read decay and antioxidant strength are compared. Cheap, portable versions of the tool are now emerging. Wider use in research and industry may follow. The survey brings the field up to date.
pmc-12787048:
Feltner and Mort build a live flow model that calls stress left by shot blast in this twenty twenty-five paper. Shot blast fires small balls at steel to leave a guard stress in its skin. The balls wear, crack, and are topped up as the run goes, which shifts that stress.

Inside, a brain-style net trained on sim blasts calls the stress field as it forms live. Ball size and shape drift in the model as they do on the plant floor. Two long plant runs of ten thousand rounds each test the full model. The top-up plan for balls showed a clear mark on the end stress in both runs. The team casts the tool as a live twin for blast lines.
pmc-12787148:
Children with inherited metabolic diseases now live long enough to need adult care, and the hand-over between hospitals can be rough. Aida Deudero and co-authors describe a working transfer model in this 2025 paper, built between a children's hospital and an adult hospital in Barcelona.

Their program pairs transition units at both sites, with monthly meetings, shared protocols, and joint visits tailored to each patient. Between 2019 and 2024, ninety-four patients moved across successfully, many during the pandemic by remote routes. The authors credit steady communication between the two teams, plus families in the loop, for making a risky passage smooth.
pmc-12787448:
Olive leaves carry a polyphenol called oleuropein with reported anti-cancer effects, and Irma Airoldi and co-authors tested the extract against blood cancers in the lab. The extract slowed growth and triggered death in leukemia and lymphoma cell lines, hitting B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia hardest. It also killed fresh leukemic blasts taken from child patients with that disease, at diagnosis and at relapse, while barely touching myeloid leukemia cells.

Protein arrays showed the extract rewiring death-pathway signals in the sensitive cells. Paired with the chemotherapy drug cytarabine, the extract's effect grew stronger than either alone. The authors float it as a food supplement partner for that drug.
pmc-12787748:
Silong Wang, Wei Yan, Pan Sun, and Jun Yuan build a battery-cooling material that also refuses to burn. Their 2025 paper forms hexagonal double-layer hollow nanocages with defect-guided growth, then laces them with carbon nanotubes grown from polymer tubes. The composite soaks up a phase-change wax and a phosphate, held in a cellulose fiber skeleton.

The material conducts heat at 0.65 watts per meter-kelvin and stores 146 joules per gram at its melting point, strong numbers for thermal regulation. Calorimetry confirmed flame retardance, credited to the cages' grip on the fillers, the tubes' heat spreading, and the flexible fiber web. Battery packs need cooling in normal use and containment in a runaway; this composite claims both. The authors see wider duty across electronic gear.
pmc-12789548:
Kelle Freel and co-authors triple the genome library of the ocean's most common bacteria group in a study from 2025. SAR11 bacteria fill the surface ocean and drive much of its carbon cycle. Few strains could be grown in the lab, which left their family tree fuzzy.

The team sequenced eighty-one new strains from tropical Pacific waters, coast and open sea. Combined with world metagenome data, the genomes sorted into twenty-nine clean groups. Each group acts as a genus with its own place and season. Gene content shifts in step with those fine patterns. Lab strains that can be grown and tested now anchor the whole group's ecology. The work turns a blur of ocean DNA into named, trackable kinds.
pmc-12796048:
Haijuan Wang and four co-authors report a rare breast cancer type that is easy to misjudge. Their twenty twenty-five case report covers tall cell carcinoma with reversed polarity, a rare triple-negative breast cancer. Its cells are tall, and their nuclei sit at the wrong end, the reversed polarity of the name.

The patient was a sixty-year-old woman with a left breast mass that grew over two years. The removed tumor showed nests of tall cells in solid, follicular, and papillary patterns. Tests confirmed a triple-negative profile and a hotspot mutation in the IDH2 gene, which backs the diagnosis. The authors stress that this type grows slowly and fares better than standard triple-negative cancer, so naming it right spares harsh treatment.
pmc-12797748:
Jakub Przegrałek and co-authors test whether teeth grinding protects snorers in a 2025 study. Sleep bruxism often rides along with primary snoring, snoring without apnea. Grinding might brace the airway, a possible protective role. Sleep lab records from 2018 to 2025 sorted patients by grinding intensity at two cutoffs.

Snore train length did not differ between grinders and others. Some snore indices ran higher in grinders during light sleep, a mixed signal for the protection idea. Pinning down whether grinding is friend or fellow traveler matters for treatment: grinding is usually suppressed, and doing so blindly could worsen the airway if the protective story holds.
pmc-12799848:
Dandan Yang and co-authors report a 2025 study on helping aged embryos develop, aimed at better fertility treatment for older women. Outcomes for women of advanced maternal age stay weak, mainly because fewer eggs can be retrieved and embryos develop poorly. The team tested adding amphiregulin, a growth factor, to embryo culture.

In aged mice, the right dose of amphiregulin clearly improved embryo development. The paper traces the chain: the factor activates its receptor, raises REM2, and calms excess calcium entry into cells. ATP supply then holds steadier, and a lactate-linked enzyme stays in check. Embryo physiology shifts toward a younger state. The findings support testing this supplement in assisted reproduction.
pmc-12800148:
Je-hyun Moon, Kyoung-hye Yoon, and Jin Lee published a worm study in two thousand twenty-five on how strong gravity affects growing nerves. The tiny worm Caenorhabditis elegans has a touch nerve with a neat, branching tree shape. The team raised worms under one hundred times Earth's gravity to see if the pattern still forms.

Under heavy gravity, some fine branches turned the wrong way at a certain larval stage. Instead of following a skin guide cue, they followed lengthwise nerves, making L and T shapes. Worms with weaker anchor structures in the skin had fewer defects. The authors think heavy gravity presses muscle and skin layers together, bringing cues into wrong contact. The work speaks to development during spaceflight.
pmc-12800248:
Jian Liang and Junsheng Cheng present a two thousand twenty-five study of a vision algorithm for spotting fires in heritage buildings. Mirrors give indirect views around fragile interiors, but flames appear tiny and views uneven. Standard detectors miss such small targets.

Their hybrid algorithm rebalances brightness across mirror views first. Parallel feature extraction at several scales catches flames of different sizes. A fusion network then mixes detail across levels. On a purpose-built heritage fire dataset, accuracy beat a leading detector baseline on both measures used. All gains came while staying lightweight enough for practical deployment.
pmc-12801948:
Huatao Liu and co-authors published a study in 2025 on a gene regulator that drives joint damage in rheumatoid arthritis. The disease involves swelling in the joint lining driven by macrophages, a type of immune cell. The regulator, IRF7, was a suspect but its role was unclear. The team mapped which macrophage groups carry its activity using single-cell data.

One pro-swelling macrophage group was expanded in patients and rich in IRF7-driven genes. Silencing the regulator in human cells cut the harmful cell shift and swelling genes. In arthritic mice, local silencing eased joint swelling, lining growth, and bone erosion. The authors suggest targeted blocking could calm joints with less whole-body immune suppression.
pmc-12802248:
Laura Rodriguez de la Fuente and eight co-authors compared two ways of planting breast cancer cells in mice in a 2025 paper. Triple-negative breast cancer is studied in two classic mouse lines, one that spreads and one that does not. Cells are usually injected into the fat pad; injecting into the milk duct tree instead may better mimic how tumors begin.

Ductal planting sped growth, even in the non-spreading line, and kept early tissue surroundings intact. Immune makeup depended on the tumor line more than the route, though ductal tumors carried more stroma early. In the spreading line, ductal planting raised metastatic burden, with body-wide inflammation dominated by suppressive myeloid cells. The authors urge care: the planting route rewrites the experiment.
pmc-12804748:
Suditi Shyamsunder and co-authors published this 2025 study on whether the wealth of your New York neighborhood tracks with your mental health, among Asian American adults. The link was underexamined for this population. Survey data from 2018 to 2020 covered 4,557 Chinese, South Asian, and other Asian residents across the 55 districts of the city, with distress and depression measured on standard short scales.

The team built a neighborhood score from unemployment, poverty, rent burden, and education, then modeled mental health against it with individual factors held constant. Living in a high-status district came with lower depression scores than living in a low-status one. Over half the sample lived in poverty, a reminder that averages hide strain. The authors argue mental health policy should look at the map, not just the person.
pmc-12804948:
Xiaoli Xu and co-authors resolve a trade-off in materials that turn vibration into chemical fuel, in a 2025 study. These piezocatalysts use ultrasound to split water for hydrogen. Strong piezoelectric response usually comes with few free charge carriers. Adding defects raises carriers but dulls the response. The team instead applied a strong electric field, a step called poling. Poling lined up the material's internal dipoles. It also rearranged dipoles tied to oxygen defects.

The test material was an oxygen-short bismuth compound. After poling, its effective response rose about eightfold. Carrier levels stayed high at the same time. Hydrogen output per unit of power reached a strong value. The gain came without sacrificing either property. The authors present poling as a design tool for this class. It could guide cheaper, lower-energy hydrogen production. The method may extend to other defective piezoelectric materials.
pmc-12805648:
Camille Lacarriere-Keita and co-authors studied gut stem cells in fruit flies in two thousand twenty-five. The gut lining renews itself through adult stem cells. A cleanup process inside cells, called autophagy, keeps balance. Blocking that cleanup has been tied to bowel disease. The team blocked it only in gut stem cells. They then watched how cell fates shifted with age.

Blocking cleanup raised the share of hormone-making gut cells. A signaling protein in the cells became more active. Tests with fate regulators traced the chain of effects. The cleanup block seemed to boost that signal downstream. More stem cells then chose the hormone-cell fate. The shift came at the cost of other cell types. The findings link cell cleanup to renewal balance in the gut.
pmc-12807948:
Pemphigus is a family of blistering diseases in which the immune system attacks the skin's own glue. Its two main forms target different skin layers, and switching from one form to the other is uncommon. Mandlin Almousa and co-authors reported in 2025 a case in which that rare switch happened.

Biopsy tests first confirmed the surface form, pemphigus foliaceus. Over time the illness changed character, and later findings fit the deeper form, pemphigus vulgaris. The report walks through the signs and tests that marked the change. Cases like this remind clinicians that a firm first label can still evolve, and that repeat testing guides care when symptoms shift.
pmc-12808648:
Xueqing Zhao and co-authors build a prediction model for a pregnancy risk in a 2025 study. Cervical insufficiency can open the cervix too early and end a pregnancy. The team followed nearly two thousand five hundred women who conceived by IVF at a Beijing center and later delivered there, hunting pre-pregnancy signs of the condition.

About three percent developed the problem. Higher body mass, certain hormone levels, past uterine surgery, more prior pregnancies, and diabetes raised risk, while a longer cervix protected. The model sorted cases with good accuracy in a held-out group. Readers get an early warning tool for a high-stakes complication.
pmc-12809948:
Melanie Smith and co-authors find that a pregnancy blood pressure disorder rewires the placenta differently by fetal sex, in a 2025 study. The disorder, late-onset preeclampsia, endangers mother and baby. Its late form is less understood than the early form. The team read gene activity in fifty-eight term placentas. Samples came from two large birth cohorts. Male-bearing and female-bearing pregnancies were analyzed apart.

In male-bearing placentas, one hundred fifty genes shifted with the disorder. Immune and metabolic pathways looked disturbed. Immune cell mixes changed there. Killer and helper cells rose, while a natural killer type fell. In female-bearing placentas, no gene passed the test. Cell mix shifts appeared, of a different kind. The authors call the disease sexually dimorphic at the molecular level. That split may explain outcome differences by sex. It argues for sex-aware analysis in pregnancy research.
pmc-12812548:
Run Lin and eight colleagues pool the trial evidence, published in 2025, on acupuncture for nausea and vomiting from the harshest chemotherapy drugs. The drugs save lives but make most patients sick for days. Acupuncture is widely offered as an add-on, yet the proof behind it was scattered. The team searched eight databases and gathered fifty-eight randomized trials. Most carried a high risk of bias, and methods were often weak. Pooled results favored acupuncture on the main score: full control of sickness across the whole treatment window and in the delayed days after.

Vomiting outcomes improved more clearly than nausea, which stayed uncertain. Different needle styles showed different strengths. Some results wobbled under sensitivity checks, and signs of publication bias appeared. Graded formally, nearly all outcomes rated low or very low quality. The authors stop short of endorsing the practice and call for stricter trials.
pmc-12812648:
Shaowen Xu, Xue Dong, and Qizhi Zhang pooled evidence on three devices for narrowed brain arteries in 2025. Bare metal stents, drug-coated balloons, and drug-eluting stents had each been compared in pairs, but never all three at once. A network meta-analysis can rank them through shared rivals.

Studies from 2010 to early 2025 were screened across four databases and graded for quality. Both drug options beat bare stents on artery re-narrowing, with no clear gap between the two drug routes. Balloons carried more rescue procedures yet fewer complications around the operation than either stent. Splitting by follow-up length kept bare stents worst for re-narrowing. The authors weigh those trade-offs for practice.
pmc-12815748:
Lili Liu and co-authors map a growth-factor receptor's presence in two aggressive womb and ovary cancers. Their 2025 study reviews cases from one Beijing hospital between 2019 and 2025. The receptor, called HER2, can guide targeted therapy when present.

Fifty-one uterine cases and one hundred sixty-five ovarian cases were tested by staining, with gene checks on positive samples. Gene amplification appeared in about twenty-nine percent of uterine tumors. It was far rarer in ovarian tumors, near five percent without prior chemotherapy and seven percent after it. Two scoring rule sets were compared head to head. The authors also weigh receptor status against patient survival. Their data help labs pick consistent reading rules for these cancers.
pmc-12815948:
Takuaki Tani and co-authors ask which stroke patients gain most from a strong dose of early rehabilitation. More rehab is not free, and its gains may vary a lot from patient to patient, so a national view can help target the dose where it pays most.

Using a large Japanese hospital data base, the team matched more than thirty-nine thousand patients with a blocked vessel stroke. Those who got at least an hour a day of rehab in the first two weeks were compared with those who got less. A causal forest model split patients by gain. The top quarter gained a lot; the lowest quarter gained little or lost ground.
pmc-12816348:
Anna Louisa Weltin and co-authors cost out the automation of CAR-T cell therapy manufacturing. The study, published in 2025, starts from success: these living drugs, a patient's own cells re-engineered against leukemia and lymphoma, keep winning approvals and moving earlier in treatment. Each batch is handmade today, at prices and footprints that cannot scale.

The authors apply a quality-by-design case framework and vary the degree of automation, asking what each level does to cost and to the factory space needed. Their comparison speaks to hospitals and firms planning capacity: industrializing a craft process without breaking its quality rules is the industry's next problem.
pmc-12816748:
Shyam Patel and co-authors show that heat alone can split the surface of a metal alloy into a new phase, in a 2025 study. Mixed metal compounds are prized for staying stable at high heat. The team found a leak in that armor in a nickel aluminum system.

Empty atom sites form more cheaply for one metal than the other, so nickel drifts to the surface as heat rises. There it builds nickel rich crusts with a new crystal form. Live microscopy, X-ray probes, and atom level modeling traced the chain from bulk defects to surface change. The result redraws the safe limits for alloys in hot service.
pmc-12817148:
Sina Neshat and six co-authors wrote this 2025 narrative review on a class of diabetes drugs now widely used in heart failure, and on what those drugs do to blood fats. The drugs are known to cut heart failure events, yet their effect on fats has been debated. The review gathers trial and cohort data on fat levels and on the form those fats take.

Across studies, the drugs brought small rises in both the harmful and the helpful cholesterol types, and small drops in triglycerides. Some data hint at a shift toward safer forms of the harmful type. The authors suggest the drugs change how the body burns fat and feeds the heart muscle. They stress that standard fat-lowering treatment still matters when levels stay above goal.
pmc-12817748:
Carlos Ardila and co-authors review robot-assisted surgical training in medical education in a 2025 analysis of randomized trials. Robotic training now appears in many schools, but its value over standard training needs pooled proof.

The search through mid 2025 found twenty-three trials with close to twelve hundred trainees. Skill performance was the most reported outcome, and most trials favored robotic training. A pooled check confirmed a clear gain in skill scores with high certainty. Resident-only checks pointed the same way. Gains also touched speed, errors, and mental load in parts of the data. Educators get strong backing for robotic practice, with wide spread in expected gains.
pmc-12817848:
Rana Tantawy and co-authors test if ivermectin, a drug for parasites, can boost doxorubicin's attack on oral cancer cells. Doxorubicin is a standard chemo drug, but in oral squamous cell carcinoma its use is curbed by resistance and dose-linked harm. Ivermectin has shown anti-cancer hints in other settings. The team treated two oral cancer cell lines, with normal oral cells as a control, and ran tests of cell survival, cell death, cell cycle, gene activity, and oxidative stress.

Ivermectin alone cut cancer cell survival as dose rose, and spared normal cells by comparison. With doxorubicin, killing rose sharply, and the pairing index showed true synergy, not just added effect. Treated cells stalled in S phase and died: pro-death genes rose, survival signals fell, and growth and inflammation markers dropped. Oxidative stress climbed, a sign of mitochondrial trouble.
pmc-12818948:
Samantha Perry, Lekha Pillarisetti, Tamara Gelfman, and Devendra Agrawal review the two-way link between gut and brain in bowel disease, in a 2025 article. The disease group covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, both long-term gut conditions. Genes, surroundings, gut microbes, and the immune system all play a part.

When the gut microbe mix shifts, helpful types fall and harmful types grow. That shift can weaken the gut wall and spark signals that reach the brain and affect mood. The review traces loops that join microbe products, a key nerve, and a stress hormone axis. It also surveys care options, from diet changes to drugs, that act on parts of that loop.
pmc-12820148:
Iran grows nearly a fifth of the world's pomegranates, and its orchards have lately suffered rising canker and dieback. Pouria Sekandarpour, Hamed Negahban, Maryam Salami, and Reza Mostowfizadeh-Ghalamfarsa hunted the cause in Fars Province in 2025, identifying fungi from sick trees by shape and by DNA.

One fungus stood out: Paramicrosphaeropsis eriobotryae, a canker pathogen never before reported on pomegranate anywhere. Inoculated onto detached branches, its most aggressive isolate spread disease unevenly across five commercial cultivars. Two, including the widely planted Wonderful, proved highly susceptible. Another showed relative resistance. Cross-tests on fig, loquat, almond, and olive isolates showed host range and aggressiveness vary by strain. The work began with sick trees in local orchards. The authors offer the first global report of this pathogen on pomegranate, plus a ranking of which kinds to plant and which to avoid.
pmc-12820248:
Moustafa Naiem Abdel-Mooty, Paulin Coulibaly, and Wael El-Dakhakhni presented a 2025 framework for mapping climate flood risk at a large scale. Old flood plans lean on past records, which miss how fast storm risks are growing. Their method joins map data with machine learning, so risk maps can update as climate paths change.

The team showed the method in Texas, using adjusted climate model output under several emission paths. Under the highest path, community weakness rose by 14 percent, with flood losses up by an estimated 28 percent, near 1.8 billion dollars per decade by 2050. The method also flags which weather factors drive local weakness most. Planners can use it to rank defenses and plan for growth in risk.
pmc-12820348:
Yakoub-Agha and seven co-authors test if five minutes of music lifts memory in college students in this twenty twenty-five study. Sixty-nine students took part and were split by lot into a music group and a plain group. The study ran two days, with the music played on the second day.

Inside, the team checked sight memory, word memory, working memory, and false memory with set tests. Music did not shift word recall, working memory, or false memory rates in the group. Sight memory did gain from the short burst of jazz-style music. The authors say music may help most when class work leans on sight and image.
pmc-12821448:
Cristian Ionut Orasanu and co-authors asked which features of a fierce brain tumor foretell a patient's course, in a 2025 study. The tumor is a grade 4 astrocytoma with a mutated IDH gene, marked by dead tissue and dense new blood vessels. Over ten years the team gathered forty-four cases, read their scans and slides, and measured how much of each tumor was dead and how dense its vessels were. Six protein stains and gene tests filled out the picture.

Older age, high blood pressure, diabetes, and sudden symptom onset all tracked with worse outcomes. More complete surgical removal protected patients, while leftover tumor hurt. Dead tissue share and vessel density themselves predicted shorter survival. So did an overactive p53 protein, loss of the PTEN gene, and changes in the CDKN2A gene. The authors say oxygen-starved, vessel-rich tumors are the aggressive ones to watch.
pmc-12821848:
Chongthavonsatit and colleagues checked whether doctors and nurses score breathing distress the same way in twenty twenty-five. Patients who cannot speak for themselves are rated with the Respiratory Distress Observation Scale, an eight-item bedside tool. In emergency rooms, nurses triage and monitor while physicians decide treatment, so shared scoring matters.

At two Thai university hospitals, physicians and nurses independently scored one hundred seventy-six breathless patients in resuscitation rooms. Overall agreement on severity was fair, at fifty-eight percent, with similar results whether or not patients could communicate. Seven of the eight scale items showed only poor to moderate reliability within each profession. Scores were consistent inside each group, though. The authors say using the scale in emergency departments needs tailored training and calibration exercises first.
pmc-12821948:
Najmeh Baghian and co-authors study teamwork between ambulance and hospital emergency services in Iran in a 2025 paper. Smooth handover between street and hospital teams saves lives, yet friction is common. The team interviewed thirty-eight seasoned staff across both services.

Three barrier families emerged from the accounts. Management faults included weak coordination, poor conflict handling, and thin staffing support. Knowledge and attitude gaps bred misunderstanding, above all under heavy workload. Clinical gaps centered on missing handover standards and uneven first assessments. Each gap broke care continuity and lowered service quality. The authors call for shared protocols and stronger joint leadership.
pmc-12822148:
Changpeng Liu and co-authors link fine air pollution to survival in lymphoma patients, in a 2025 study from China. Fine particles in air have been tied to cancer, but their effect on patients who already have cancer drew little study. The team focused on blood cancer of the lymph system.

Records came from a cancer hospital in Henan for patients admitted from 2017 to 2020. Daily pollution maps at fine scale gave each patient's exposure. Higher exposure over one year went with a higher risk of death. Parts of the mix, such as organic matter and black carbon, also tracked with risk. The results argue for cleaner air as part of cancer care.
pmc-12822348:
Pankaj Verma and co-authors probe drought response in wild peanut relatives in a 2025 paper. Drought is a top limit on peanut harvests worldwide. Wild species hold wider genetic diversity than farm peanuts, making them promising sources of toughness, but the genes behind their drought response were largely unmapped.

The team compared two forms of Arachis dardani and one of Arachis ipaënsis under dry and watered conditions. Growth measures barely budged under drought, confirming strong natural tolerance. Gene activity scans found thousands of genes switching on or off in leaves and roots, with one dardani form showing the most unique changes. The catalogue of responding genes gives breeders fresh targets for tougher peanuts.
pmc-12822848:
Reem Samir Abboud and Gill E. Sviri analyzed nerve outcomes after surgery for tumors inside the spinal cord's lining. These intradural extramedullary tumors are mostly meningiomas and schwannomas. The twenty twenty-five retrospective study reviewed ninety-three patients treated at one tertiary neurosurgical center between two thousand eight and two thousand nineteen. Fifty-two tumors were meningiomas and forty-one were schwannomas. Recovery was scored with the ASIA Impairment Scale.

The researchers compared patient, tumor, and surgical factors against changes in ASIA score. Their goal was to find what predicts neurological decline after removal. Reliable predictors have been poorly defined for this surgery. The analysis gives surgeons evidence for counseling patients about recovery chances and for spotting high-risk cases before operating.
pmc-12826648:
Alesha Wale and co-authors reviewed what helps older adults get online in a 2025 rapid review. Older people form the largest share of those who never use the internet, while more services move online each year. The team searched studies from 2018 onward that compared ways to close that gap for people aged sixty and up in social care settings.

Twenty-one studies made the cut, with group sizes from five to 381 people. Programs varied widely and often mixed parts, from classes to one-on-one help. The evidence shows such programs can lift skills, knowledge, and confidence, ease fear of technology, and raise actual use. Gains showed up in rural groups, isolated and homebound people, poorer groups, and people with poor sight. The review gives care services a grounded menu of what tends to work.
pmc-12827148:
Brenda Carvalho and a large team of co-authors present a study, published in 2025, on a gentler way to place a long-term tube into a horse's cecum. Access to this gut chamber is needed for fluid therapy and other treatments, but the classic route is a full open operation. Seven standing horses were sedated and given local anesthesia. Through two small flank openings, a camera guided the cecum out so a catheter could be sewn in.

The technique succeeded in six of seven horses. The catheter worked for repeated fluid sessions over twenty-two days without leaking, and horses ate and behaved normally. One horse died of abdominal infection after fluids were given too soon after surgery, teaching the team to wait a day or two. The authors call the method safe, practical, and far less traumatic than open surgery.
pmc-12827348:
YanPeng Cao and co-authors upgrade a fast vision model in 2025 to spot objects that float on water. Such spotting serves pollution watch and cleanup, since trash and debris on rivers and lakes must be found before it can be removed. Water is a hard scene for a camera: light reflects off the surface, ripples add noise, and small debris packs close together.

Their variant adds three parts to the base model. One part weighs which image channels matter most, which cuts glare effects. One part gives cheap feature extraction at many scales. The last part sharpens how the model learns from the match between its boxes and the true ones. They trained and tested the model on a mixed set of 28,000 images, with extra altered copies for strength. The team reports gains in both accuracy and speed.
pmc-12827548:
Zimo Zhu and co-authors report a study, published in 2025, of a classic herbal powder tested on acute lung injury. The powder is an approved drug in China for lung infections, but how it might ease this severe lung harm was not known. The team joined compound hunts with gene and metabolite profiling in mice.

Mice with lung injury got the powder by mouth after three days of a virus-like trigger. Treated mice breathed more easily and showed lower levels of a key swelling signal in fluids and blood. Profiling of lung tissue traced the gains to calmer swelling and less cell death of a set kind.
pmc-12827648:
Jiali Wei and five co-authors survey how well people with chronic hepatitis C manage their own care, and what helps or hinders them. Self-management covers the daily habits, medicines, and monitoring that a long-term liver infection demands. The study enrolled 192 patients at one hospital, published in 2025, and scored their self-management, coping style, and sense of stigma with standard questionnaires.

Self-management landed in the middle range overall. Patients leaned more on positive coping than on negative coping. Scores did not differ by age, sex, schooling, job, or marital status. People who managed their care better tended to cope positively, while negative coping and stigma went with worse self-management. The authors note the study is a single snapshot, so the links run both ways. Still, they suggest that easing stigma and building positive coping could support daily care.
pmc-12827948:
Liuyan Ding and co-authors trace how one gene mutation drives Parkinson's-type damage in mice in this 2025 study. The mutation sits in LRRK2, a known risk gene, but this variant's mechanism was a blank. Mutant mice revealed a chain of failures centered on a death-linked protein kinase that rose as LRRK2 fell.

That kinase fired up brain immune cells to release inflammatory signals and pushed dopamine neurons toward self-destruction through their power plants. A protective small molecule, tuftsin, dropped in step, and gut microbe shifts accompanied the change. The authors nominate blocking the kinase as a drug strategy and restoring tuftsin as another avenue worth testing.
pmc-12829248:
Jacques Kanku Balowe and co-authors systematically reviewed why many children with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa fail to suppress the virus on treatment. Suppression rates vary widely between countries, and the reasons are scattered across many small studies. A synthesis can separate local quirks from shared drivers.

Four major databases were searched for English studies from 2010 to 2024 on African children under fifteen with full text available. Data were extracted in a structured way and the findings compared across settings. Factors such as adherence support, caregiver circumstances, and clinic access recur in the literature. Knowing the common blockers helps programs aim scarce support where it counts.
pmc-12829548:
Ziheng Duan, Cheyu Lee, and Jing Zhang present a 2023 paper on predicting Alzheimer's disease from single-cell data. Early, accurate diagnosis could improve care, but most machine learning tools ignore the variety of cells in the human brain. They also give little insight into which genes drive the disease.

Their model, ExAD-GNN, is a graph neural network that can explain its calls. It links each cell to its nearest neighbors by gene activity, then predicts disease state cell by cell. A learnable score ranks genes by importance for each cell type. On large single-cell data sets the model beat rival methods in accuracy and held up across samples. Its top risk genes matched much of the published record.
pmc-12830648:
Tiffany Bellanger and co-authors study a small guard protein that helps cells cope with heat and stress. The protein, called Lo18, comes from a bacterium used in wine making. Like its kin, it can clump into large groups that shield other proteins, or pair up to guard cell walls. Their 2025 study asks what the protein's front end does.

The team made a cut version of the protein that lacks its first chunk and set it against the full form. The cut form built weaker groups and guarded other proteins less well. It also bound less well to cell walls. The front end, the tests show, is key to both guard roles. That insight may help food and wine uses of the bacterium.
pmc-12830748:
Xiaoran Wang and a large team share plant pack data from height lines on seventeen China peaks. Their data set appeared in twenty twenty-five. Set field rules were used at three hundred seventy set plots. All wood plants past a set stem width were named and counted, with base size and worth marks drawn for two growth coats.

The set spans wide ground and a tall height span, from rain woods to cold bare tops. Near one thousand five hundred kinds from more than one hundred packs are in it. The team pitch it as a base for shift reads in heat and land use.
pmc-12830848:
Ziyu Chen and co-authors hunt for what makes bladder cancer respond to a targeted drug pairing an antibody with a toxin. Their 2025 study deals with HER2, a growth signal protein often altered in cancers. In a scan of 42,415 tumors, 14.5 percent of bladder cancers carried harmful changes in the gene. Mutations made up 6.7 percent and extra gene copies 6.3 percent. Status often differed between a first tumor and its spread, they found.

Lab models grown from patient tumors were tested with two drugs. The antibody toxin pairing beat a kinase blocker drug clearly. In real patients treated with the pairing, tumors with both mutation and extra copies responded exceptionally well. The authors back wider trials, including in tumors with low HER2 levels. They also urge tests of other toxin payloads and of platforms that measure drug response in patient models.
pmc-12830948:
Aoyu Wang and five co-authors test in 2025 whether simple blood-and-body indices can flag high blood pressure risk in a Chinese city. The triglyceride-glucose index, computed from routine labs, stands in for insulin resistance, a known driver of hypertension, and pairing it with waist and weight measures may sharpen it.

Data came from more than nine thousand adults in Bengbu, Anhui, surveyed in 2019. The team modeled how each combined index relates to hypertension and to its precursor stage, tracing dose-response curves. Cheap screening markers matter most where clinics are crowded and budgets thin.
pmc-12831248:
Pet ownership is booming in Spain, and with it the need to track gut parasites that can jump to people. J Barrera and co-authors reviewed in 2025 a decade of stool tests from a Madrid reference laboratory: nearly sixteen thousand dog and cat samples.

About twenty-six percent of dogs and twenty-one percent of cats carried at least one parasite. A gut protozoan, Giardia, led in dogs, while worms were relatively commoner in cats. Young animals and shelter animals were hit hardest. Infections peaked seasonally, and Giardia grew commoner over the decade. The authors urge routine testing, deworming, and better owner education to protect pets and households alike.
pmc-12831448:
Muzammil Hussain and co-authors profile the microbes living on mango leaves, flowers and fruitlets during fruit set, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. Mango suffers heavy pathogen losses, yet how its surface microbial community assembles was little known. High-throughput sequencing catalogued bacteria and fungi on the three organs.

Flowers and fruitlets hosted less diverse communities than leaves, and each organ's mix was distinct. Certain bacterial families dominated specific organs, while fungal families differed less. A core set of shared bacteria and fungi persisted across all organs, mixing helpful and harmful members. The map gives a baseline for protecting fruit set with the plant's own microbiome.
pmc-12834948:
Yang builds a method to fuse drone photos and laser scans into exact three dimensional maps of hard terrain in twenty twenty-five. City canyons and wooded slopes leave blind spots for any one sensor. Past fusion lined the data up by shape alone, which lost detail and meaning. His framework first reads the meaning of each pixel and point, then lets that meaning guide the match.

A weighted matching method lines the two data types up with the help of their labels. A neural step weighs each source by trust under local conditions. In city and mountain tests, error fell by about a third to a half against standard methods. Coverage passed ninety-nine percent.
pmc-12835048:
Panjit Chunhabundit, Tawepong Arayapisit, and Natchalee Srimaneekarn test dental students at forensic palate reading in a 2025 study. The ridges on the roof of the mouth, rugae, survive much that destroys other identifiers. But can near dentists, not forensic specialists, match them reliably?

Fifty four final year students matched forty stripped casts, teeth removed, in two rounds a week apart. Average accuracy hit about eighty three percent at under a minute and a half per match, with repeat agreement from substantial to near perfect. The authors conclude trained students can back up scarce forensic specialists in identification work. They call for standard scoring rules to lift accuracy further.
pmc-12835448:
Sue Kim wrote a 2025 editorial marking thirty years of a Korean nursing journal for women's health. The piece looks back at the journal's path and at a June 2025 special issue on digital health tools for women. That issue covered gender gaps in digital care, health literacy, care in high-risk pregnancy, period symptoms, and fertility care during cancer.

Kim also shares fresh journal figures released in 2025 and draws out what the new work means for nurses. Studies in the issue used phone apps for breastfeeding support and AI tutors for labor care training. The editorial urges nurses to use the findings when they build and test digital tools for women.
pmc-12836848:
Taymara Abreu and co-authors trace lifetime social position and later chronic disease in Europe in this 2025 paper. Social position was measured at three life stages. Childhood crowding at home marked the start. Education marked adult position, and income marked older age. Health data came from the SHARE study across 27 countries.

The sample held 30,055 older adults followed for up to 16 years. Eight chronic diseases were tracked from self reports. A growth analysis sorted people into five lifetime trajectories. Those who stayed in a high position throughout had the lowest disease risk in later life. Other paths, such as falling or rising position, carried different risks. The long view shows that early conditions echo into old age health.
pmc-12837948:
Apiwit Sae-Fung and Bengt Fadeel chart an unusual way copper overload kills cells, in a 2025 paper. Copper is essential in traces and toxic in excess, and a newly described death route involves proteins clumping in mitochondria. The team's results add a second, stranger pathway.

Using elesclomol, a drug that ferries copper into cells, they found death depended on calpain enzymes. It took the form of paraptosis, marked by a swollen endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria crowding around the nucleus. The drug also triggered proteotoxic stress: the cell's waste disposal system jammed while a heat shock response switched on. Both mitochondrial and outside compartments were involved. The authors place calpain-driven paraptosis alongside the known aggregation route in copper toxicology. The distinction could matter for drugs that exploit copper to kill cancer cells.
pmc-12838448:
Sara Diaz Saravia and co-authors ask in 2025 if a cancer past shifts care and fate for young grown folk in heart shock. Cancer rides more and more with heart ills, yet its weight in shock care was vague. A land wide ward file forms the base.

Near one hundred thou sand young shock stays span five years; near three per cent bear a cancer past. That group shows less heart risk load and few er main heart cause shocks. Tuned math says they get short term heart aid pumps at half the odds of peers. Life odds split too in the read.
pmc-12838948:
Yanhai Feng and co-authors review a protein tagging process as a drug target for skin disease in a 2025 paper. The process attaches a fat molecule to proteins, which steers where they sit in the cell and how long they last. A family of enzymes drives the tagging, and a reverse step removes the tag.

In skin, the tag cycle shapes inflammation, barrier strength, hair growth, and pigment output. Faults in the cycle are tied to hair loss, psoriasis, and other skin disorders. New lab tools now let teams map tagged proteins in detail. The review sums up what is known and weighs drug ideas that block or boost the tagging enzymes for future skin care.
pmc-12843148:
Ioanna Tsatsou and co-authors report a 2025 study of sexual health among people who had a stem cell transplant using their own cells. The treatment can save lives in blood cancers, yet it often leaves lasting strain on close bonds and sexual life. The study took place in five public hospitals in Athens, Greece.

A total of 127 adults took part, from six months to five years after transplant. Men scored high on a standard sexual function scale, while women showed some loss. Patterns of closeness and worry in bonds linked to sexual scores in women, but not in men. The authors urge care plans that attend to close bonds.
pmc-12843748:
Xiaozhu Chen and co-authors laser polish printed titanium parts in a 2025 study. Parts built by electron beam melting carry rough side walls. Half melted grains stuck to those walls limit high end uses. A steady infrared laser was swept across the walls to smooth them.

One setting set cut roughness by about ninety eight percent in the tests. A melt pool model predicted the polished shapes with tiny error. Power density shaped the final surface most strongly, they found. Scan speed and pass timing mattered through heat and splash effects.
pmc-12844948:
Tintor and six co-authors review hyaluronic acid complexes in aesthetic medicine, in work from twenty twenty-five. Hyaluronic acid fillers are widely used to restore face volume. Classic fillers have limits in how long they last and how they spread in tissue.

Hybrid cooperative complexes join low and high weight forms of the acid in one product, with no foreign agents added. Hydrogen bonds between the forms add durability and resistance to breakdown enzymes. The mix flows through a needle easily and spreads well. Lab studies show gains in skin cell vitality. The review sums up published proof for this newer filler class.
pmc-12847848:
Feifei Sun and twelve co-authors find a lever that keeps prostate cancer resistant to a frontline hormone drug, in this 2025 study. The drug, enzalutamide, works at first, but resistance always develops, partly through stem-like cancer cells that survive treatment. The team traces that survival to a kinase called CAMK1D, which runs high in resistant tumors.

CAMK1D switches on a cleanup process, mitophagy, in which cells digest their damaged power plants. It does so by activating the energy sensor AMPK, which in turn wakes the mitophagy starter PINK1 and its partner Parkin. The cleanup lets stem-like cells adapt and expand under the drug. In mice with prostate tumors, a nanoparticle treatment silencing CAMK1D drained the stem-like pool and shrank tumors, working in synergy with enzalutamide. The authors name the CAMK1D pathway a target for reversing resistance.
pmc-12847948:
Qiming Gong and eight co-authors show lack of a call part, CX3CL1, eases sharp kidney harm by way of guard cell power plants. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The part had tied to flare, but its role in this harm was not clear. In a germ-part mouse model, lack of the part eased kidney fail and flare.

Gene reads showed guard cell packs and power paths shift with the lack. Guard cells bent from flare-lean to calm-lean. Power plants held form, leaked less of their code, and a flare call path fed by loose code was hushed. A code guard part firms the tale.
pmc-12849148:
Mesut Yur and co-authors hunt for warning signs of death within ninety days after major pancreatic surgery. Their 2025 study reviews 105 patients who had a pancreaticoduodenectomy for tumors near the pancreas between 2010 and 2022. The operation is a mainstay for these cancers but carries a worrying death rate.

Seventeen patients died within ninety days. Simple checks at admission separated them from survivors: age, albumin, and several combined scores all mattered at first pass. Three independent predictors survived full modeling, covering liver function, overall illness burden, and inflammation. The authors advise that high-risk patients be reviewed by a full specialist team before surgery to cut deaths.
pmc-12849248:
Emma Stirling-Cameron and eight co-authors track trouble getting contraception among sex workers in Vancouver, in a 2025 study. Migrant sex workers face layered structural harms, and contraception access had barely been studied in this group.

The study follows a community cohort of 803 women surveyed every six months from 2010 to 2022. It asks whether migration status predicts difficulty getting non-barrier contraception, and whether race changes that link. Surveys covered work, health care, and daily life over twelve years. The analysis uses repeated-measures models built for this design. The authors frame access as a structural issue, not a personal failing. Their cohort is one of the longest-running of its kind in Canada.
pmc-12849348:
Niloofar Ramezani and co-authors study how counties keep people with mental illness out of local jails in a 2025 paper. A national drive helps counties build care in the community instead. The team polled officials in 519 counties and merged the replies with census facts.

Five working habits were put to the test: ties between agencies, score checks, joint teams, skill building, and care setups. The national drive linked to more proven care methods in place. Once the five habits entered the model, they carried much of that link. The habits look like the gears through which the drive works.
pmc-12849748:
Jonathan Niciza, Kemal Elyeli, Umran Dal Yilmaz, and Dilay Necipoglu survey nursing students in Northern Cyprus about contraception knowledge, attitudes, and behavior, in a 2025 study. Nurses will one day counsel patients on family planning, so gaps in their own knowledge matter. Nearly three hundred students filled in forms covering what they know, how they feel, and what they do.

Knowledge scores were low and most students reported using no contraception, even though attitudes toward it were positive. Knowledge rose slightly with age, and knowing more went with better attitudes and behavior. The authors call for stronger, repeated teaching on contraception during nursing training, with checks on whether it sticks.
pmc-12852648:
Chong Li and four co-authors present a 2025 paper on judging the health of lithium-ion batteries with a smart network model. A sound gauge of battery health keeps electric cars and storage units safe. Plain learning models can do the job, but their many settings are hard to tune by hand.

The team drew three health clues from the charging curve: a voltage slope, the steady-current charging time, and the rate of heat change. A sparrow-inspired swarm search then tuned seven key settings of their network on its own. On two public test sets, the tuned model beat a hand-tuned one and cut setup work.
pmc-12852848:
Yiwei Peng and co-authors turn in a 2025 study the cell's power plants into delivery couriers that hop between cells through tiny tunnels. Cells naturally pass mitochondria along these nanotube links. The team found that dialing down a disposal pathway, guided by the PINK1 protein, speeds the traffic: the organelles reshape, refuel, and breathe harder.

Loaded with a light-activated drug, the sprinter mitochondria ferried it deep into tumors, where light then triggered stronger killing than free drug achieved. Hitchhiking on the organelle network, they argue, can cross delivery barriers that stop ordinary carriers.
pmc-12853748:
Yuna Sadaka and ten co-authors check dosing of an antibiotic in a 2025 study. Cefmetazole is widely used in Japan for urinary infections. Hard data on the right dose for Japanese patients was thin. The team measured drug levels in patients with mild to moderate infections.

Twenty one patients at one hospital in Gifu took part. Each got a one gram dose at gaps set by kidney function. Blood was drawn near the peak and just before the next dose. Levels were measured with a standard lab method. The team compared drug levels with kidney clearance rates. The drug treated resistant bacterial infections in every patient studied. The results help doctors tune dose gaps to kidney strength.
pmc-12855248:
Mughair Abdul Aziz and co-authors read stress guard proteins from three desert plants in a 2025 study. The guards pile up in plant parts when drought or salt hits, and late in seed growth. Full gene reads for the guards were pulled from a fig kin, a gourd, and a date palm.

Shape traits of the guards and their roles in stress grit are the core of the work. Life in dry lands has honed these guards to hold form under harsh strain. The finds may guide breed work for crops that must face dry heat.
pmc-12855848:
Linduo Yuan, Yuze Dan, Yi Leng, and Jiaxin Zhang published this study in 2025. It asks what makes city residents feel safe, using Nanchang, a mid-sized Chinese city rich in history, as the case. Earlier work leaned on physical features like lighting and layout, and mostly studied megacities.

The team fused street-level spatial data, socioeconomic figures, and residents' own psychological ratings, then let a machine learning model with an explanation tool rank the influences. How lively a place felt and how wealthy it seemed mattered most for safety feelings, ahead of many built features. Effects bent and interacted rather than running in straight lines, and they differed by district. The authors offer their framework for heritage-heavy mid-sized cities planning safety upgrades. They argue that managing how a place feels can matter as much as how it is built.
pmc-12857148:
Maryam Moeeni, Faezeh Arjvand, Koen Ponnet, and Shirin Nosratnejad measure how unevenly Iranian households consume goods that harm health, in a 2025 study. The basket spans tobacco, fatty, salty and sugary foods, alcohol, addictive substances, unlicensed supplements, and some cosmetics. Whether the burden falls mostly on the poor or spreads evenly shapes fair policy.

Using the national 2019 income and expenditure survey of more than thirty-eight thousand households, the team applied the health ministry's list of harmful products. A Gini coefficient measured spread of spending overall, and a concentration index weighed spending against each household's economic rank. The inequality map tells regulators where taxes, labels, or subsidies would bite — and on whom.
pmc-12859148:
Jingtao Guan rebuilds road-scene images from heavily compressed measurements, for the tight bandwidth of vehicle networks. Cars must share images fast for lane keeping, pedestrian spotting, and crash warnings, yet classic reconstruction methods lose detail or run too slowly. The proposed method pairs multi-scale leftover blocks, which read a scene at several zoom levels, with an attention step that weights places by their coordinates. Lightweight convolutions keep the cost down.

A second stage links the sparse measurements to the full image through a generator checked by an autoencoder and a transformer that holds the global layout together. In dense pedestrian scenes the method scored high on structural similarity and signal quality. It answered in about 162 milliseconds while using modest memory. The author reports it beat rival methods across the tested measures.
pmc-12859948:
Yu Wang and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-five on a gene switch that drives colorectal cancer growth and spread. Colorectal cancer kills many people worldwide, and relapse and metastasis still cut survival despite better treatments. Complex signal networks run the disease, so finding the key switches matters for new drug targets.

The team focused on a transcription factor called FOXK1 and an adaptor protein called GRB2. In cancer models, extra FOXK1 sped cell growth and spread, and high levels tracked with worse patient outcomes. The switch works by binding the GRB2 gene's control region and turning it on. The authors name the pair a promising target axis for future targeted therapy.
pmc-12860148:
Ni Zhang and four co-authors trace how warm, firm mothering in preschool links to behavior problems later in this 2025 study. The children were followed for two years from Chinese kindergartens into early school age. The team asked which inner skills carry the effect from parenting to behavior.

Three hundred five children took part, with checks at three time points. Warm, firm mothering went with stronger effortful control, the skill of steering one's own actions. It also went with fewer poor ways of handling bad feelings, such as venting or passive coping. Those two skills, in turn, linked to fewer acting-out problems at school age. Mothering showed no direct link to later problems; the effect ran through the skills.
pmc-12866248:
Meiying Cui and co-authors ran this 2025 trial on preventing delirium after major bone surgery in older patients. Delirium, a sudden confused state, prolongs hospital stays and raises death risk. Poor sleep is one driver that can be changed. A sleep-promoting drug, sodium oxybate, was given during surgery to test whether it could ward off delirium.

The trial enrolled 332 patients aged sixty-five and up having spine or joint replacement surgery. Half got the drug after anesthesia began, and half got salt water. The paper reports the null result for a plausible prevention idea.
pmc-12866448:
Amanda Yee and four co-authors surveyed family caregivers in Quebec about using AI tools in elder care in a 2025 study. Smart tools promise help as the population ages, but the family members who would run them are rarely asked. The survey used a standard technology acceptance frame, widened for the care setting.

Of the panel invited, 199 eligible caregivers finished the survey. A forest model explained well over half the spread in intent to use such tools. What other people think mattered most: social influence topped the predictors by a clear margin. Seeing peers and family approve seems to sway adoption more than ease or usefulness alone. The authors say rollout plans should work through families and communities, not just product design.
pmc-12870448:
Chen Yang and co-authors trace in 2025 how an anesthetic gas shields heart cells from the harm of restored blood flow. When a blocked heart artery reopens, the returning oxygen can itself injure muscle. The gas sevoflurane, given ahead, softens that blow, but the molecular route was murky.
