Forcing that RNA high erased the gas's protection, raising cell death, stress, and swelling marks. The RNA works by trapping a small partner RNA, which frees a target gene. Blocking the long RNA restored the shield.
pmc-12872748:
Livia Yawa Like Atiku and Erika Maria Marek survey foreign students seeking health care in Hungary in two thousand twenty-five. Moving country can strain health, and students often struggle to reach care in a new system. The survey covered students at major Hungarian universities and drew four hundred seventy-six replies.

About three in ten students said their health got worse after the move. Near two thirds arrived with little or no knowledge of the local health system, and only about a third fully grasped their rights to care. Even with scholarship insurance, about three in ten paid some costs from their own pockets. The authors call for clearer guidance and more culture-aware care.
pmc-12875548:
Oksana Zhurakivska and co-authors examine placental tissue in 2025 for signs of poor blood flow in late appearing fetal growth restriction. Slow fetal growth raises risks of stillbirth and newborn death, and a failing placenta is a common cause. The team compared women whose babies grew slowly late in pregnancy with women who delivered on time at normal size.

Clinical histories were reviewed for all women, and a smaller set of placentas went through detailed tissue study. Odd placental shape was common in the growth restricted group, and cord insertion off center was also frequent. Blood vessel branching types and lower placental measures were reported as well. The authors aim to sort the tissue patterns of flow failure so this late form of growth restriction can be read more clearly after birth.
pmc-12878648:
Manman Shi, Xia Chen, and Binfeng Yuan published this 2025 study on why hard exercise tracks with better mental health in students. The catalog lists 2026, but the article itself is dated 2025. A survey of 2,432 undergraduates at three Guangdong universities measured vigorous activity, resilience, physical self-esteem, and well-being on standard scales.

A chain model linked the four: vigorous activity predicted stronger resilience, which fed physical self-esteem, which in turn fed well-being. Every link was positive and statistically firm. The direct tie from activity to well-being stayed small once the chain was counted. The authors read the pattern as a route, not just a correlation: exercise may lift mood largely by making students hardier and prouder of their bodies.
pmc-12892848:
E Shchukina and co-authors review gene therapy tools in 2025. Gene therapy has grown into a field with precise editing systems and many ways to deliver them. The review covers the major editing platforms now in use. It ranges from CRISPR based editors to base and prime editors and newer enzyme based tools.

Delivery gets equal weight, from virus based carriers tuned to tissues to fat based particles and cell released bubbles. Uses span editing of the main genome, the small energy genome, RNA, and gene control marks. The survey shows how far the field has moved past plain gene replacement toward fine repair.
pmc-12906748:
Four authors measure the outer ear in Nepali hospital patients in this 2025 study. Ear dimensions are working data for reconstructive surgery, forensics, and product design, and they vary by population, sex, and age, so local reference values matter.

The cross-sectional study measured 157 adults, eighty-two men and seventy-five women, with normal ears at a dental college hospital. A digital caliper recorded ear height and width and lobe dimensions on both sides. Right and left ears differed minimally; average height was about sixty-three millimeters. Men had taller and wider ears, while women had slightly larger lobes, and lobe height varied the most. The values form a local baseline.
pmc-12908048:
Weny Rinawati and four co-authors test whether gut health markers can predict outcomes after an acute ischemic stroke, in a research paper from 2025. Infections after stroke are common and worsen recovery. Gut imbalance and a leaky gut barrier may help drive those infections.

The study followed eighty stroke patients at a Jakarta center for a year. Nearly half developed an infection within a week. Infected patients had less diverse gut microbes, more harmful species, and worse scores on two dysbiosis indices. Blood markers of barrier damage and inflammation also ran high. Combined, these measures sorted patients by risk with good accuracy in this group.
pmc-12913948:
Bella Veliana Utami and co-authors compare two additives in diets for beef cattle based on a tropical legume, in a 2025 in vitro study. Methane from ruminants wastes feed energy and adds to greenhouse gas build-up. The legume, Gamal, is rich in protein and widely used as a base forage. On its own it may need help to ferment well in the rumen.

One additive is Gambier, a plant extract with active compounds. The other is direct-fed microbials, live microbes that include a yeast strain. The team test how each additive changes rumen fermentation, nutrient digestibility, and microbial protein synthesis. They also measure methane output. The goal is a diet that uses feed energy better and cuts gas at the same time.
pmc-12914948:
William Coon and his three co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, machines that listen to the sleeping brain and nudge it toward deeper rest. Sleep props up memory, mood, immunity, and metabolism, yet disturbed sleep is everywhere. Closed-loop devices track brain rhythms in real time. Timed sounds or mild electric pulses can strengthen the slow waves and spindles that consolidate memory.

The review tours the main targets and the evidence that nudging them helps. It also covers tools aimed at dreaming sleep and at falling asleep faster. Open questions remain about timing, method choice, and the body's limits. The authors propose a modular, open-source ecosystem that pairs live sleep decoding with swappable stimulators. Their goal is reproducible, personalized sleep tech rather than a shelf of incompatible gadgets.
pmc-12915048:
Fanchao Meng and five co-authors map sulfur binding sites inside a bacterium that turns mercury into its toxic form, in work whose text is dated 2025. Mercury's toxic form builds up in food webs and harms health. Sulfur groups, called thiols, grip mercury and steer whether cells take it in. Where those groups sit inside the cell was largely unknown.

The team split the cells into parts and probed each part with X-ray tools using mercury as a tracer. The inner membrane held just over half the cell's thiols. Outer membrane zones held the densest share per unit of carbon. The authors say membranes likely gate mercury entry, a frame for grasping the whole toxic path.
pmc-12918448:
Sarah Moreland-Russell and co-authors lay out a study of how school meal rules play out locally in a protocol from two thousand twenty-five. A two thousand ten law raised the nutrition bar for US school lunches and breakfasts. Later federal loosening on salt, grains, and milk pushed choices down to districts, unevenly.

The three-phase plan starts with a national survey of district food directors on what they adopted and why. Phase two interviews food industry actors on supply effects. Phase three builds an agent-based model from those voices to test policy options. The team aims to learn what drives uneven uptake and how to make meal quality fairer for low-resource students.
pmc-12921448:
Pig farms acidify drinking water to protect gut health, but how much acid a source needs varies. The eight authors collected forty-five water samples from swine sites in six states. Starting pH ranged from seven point four two to eight point four seven.

The authors advise titrating each source directly, since chemistry alone cannot fully predict the dose.
pmc-12933548:
Kondo and co-authors check the feasibility and safety of a needle biopsy route through the large bowel. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration draws tissue samples with ultrasound guidance. It is a proven diagnostic method, but few studies judge its use through the colorectal wall.

The retrospective study reviewed cases treated in Japan. It weighed how often the trans-colorectal route yielded useful tissue and how often harm followed. Lesions near the rectum are hard to reach by other routes, so a safe path matters. The findings help endoscopists decide when this approach is worth its risks.
pmc-12967948:
Alex Chan and colleagues combined studies on digital health tools for HIV prevention and care among transgender people. Transgender communities face high HIV burden shaped by stigma, discrimination, and poor access to affirming care, and apps, telehealth, and online services may reach people more safely. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team searched five databases for recent studies, including trials and observational work. Two reviewers screened and rated the studies separately, and results were pooled with standard statistical methods.

Eleven studies were included, and the pooled result showed a clear positive effect on prevention and care outcomes, with little variation between studies. Benefits held across years and tool types, and no strong sign of publication bias appeared. Testing uptake and treatment adherence both improved. The authors urge that future tools be built to be culturally fitting, gender affirming, and inclusive by design.
pmc-12985348:
Ghita El Baroudi and three co-authors share six cases of a rare belly infection from a Marrakech hospital. Their case series, from twenty twenty-five, deals with peritonitis above the mid gut fold. This acute swelling of the belly lining is oft driven by holes or dead gut. Care joins fluids, breath aid, germ drugs, and surgery to clear the source. Rare causes make the diagnosis a hard call.

The six cases came from the general surgery ward of a university hospital. Each had a rare root for the infection. The team used the set to stress fast, team based care and its sway on the outcome. Readers in surgery get a warn list of odd roots to weigh when the plain ones fail.
pmc-13018748:
A probiotic yogurt's effects on the brain are tested by Wolfgang Marx and co-authors in work dated 2025, one year shy of the catalog year. Forty healthy women ate the yogurt or a placebo daily for eight weeks. The trial ran triple-blind, so no side knew who got what. Brain scans and tests homed in on the hippocampus, a memory hub.

One brain chemical in that hub shifted between groups, as did hub tie strength to a front zone. Gut germ mixes shifted as well. The brain size shifts did not hold up under strict stat checks. The team calls the proof early and thin.
pmc-13126648:
Simone Coslovich and co-authors report two children treated with paired immune drugs in this 2026 case report. Some childhood inflammatory diseases resist single biologic drugs. The authors urge careful monitoring and larger studies.
pmc-13127248:
Jan Fingerhut and co-authors model hydrogen production at electrodes in this 2026 paper. Rates depend on activation energy and a related factor, and the two often seem to rise together. That paired rise is called a compensation effect. Its physical cause in electrocatalysis is still debated.

The team modeled two standard paths for the hydrogen evolution reaction. They simulated currents across realistic ranges of voltage and temperature. Apparent compensation arose even when the true barriers had no such link. Shifts in surface coverage or in the slow step caused one route. Multiple active sites with different traits caused another. The work warns against reading compensation as a deep law without checking kinetics first.
pmc-13128548:
Fangzheng Lin and co-authors report bare handed neck realignment as a bridge to surgery in a 2026 case. A dislocated neck spine crushes the cord, and early realignment saves function, but standard care needs sedation or skull traction gear that may not be at hand.

Fully awake, with no pain relief, she was realigned by hand in fifteen minutes, guided by her own feedback. Pain eased and arm strength jumped. Fusion surgery followed, with good recovery at eighteen months.
pmc-13130848:

pmc-13136448:
Mingyu Sun and a large team review a key chemical step for clean energy tools in a 2026 paper. The step, the oxygen reduction reaction, sets how well fuel cells and metal air batteries work. It shows how the shape and charge state around each metal atom steer the path and pace of the step. Uses in batteries, fuel cells, and peroxide making are weighed in turn. pmc-13136848:
Satoru Okabe and co-authors measure the clash risk between modern hepatitis C cures and patients' other medicines, in a 2026 study. pmc-13138248:

pmc-13139648:
Mahmudul Islam and a large team of co-authors review resistance to delamanid, a drug used against hard-to-treat tuberculosis, in a 2026 paper. Drug-resistant TB is rising, and this drug is one of the newer weapons against it.

pmc-13140948:

pmc-13144548:

pmc-13144748:

pmc-13144848:

pmc-13145148:

pmc-13145248:

pmc-13145448:

pmc-13145548:

pmc-13145648:

pmc-13145748:

pmc-13145848:

Men made up two thirds of patients, which the team reads as a sign of access barriers for women.
pmc-13145948:

pmc-13146048:

pmc-13146248:

pmc-13146348:

pmc-13146448:

pmc-13146648:

pmc-13146848:

pmc-13146948:

pmc-13147348:

pmc-13148748:

pmc-13149648:

pmc-13151148:

pmc-13152148:

pmc-13197348:

pmc-13197448:

pmc-13197648:

pmc-13198048:

Life quality was converted into quality-adjusted life years from a standard survey. Both cost-utility and cost-consequence views are reported. The answer guides buyers choosing between greener and simpler supply.
pmc-13198548:

pmc-13198748:

pmc-13199648:

Time spent above a twenty millimetre threshold past a set share also spelled poor outcome. pmc-13202048:

pmc-13202548:
Sanlin Xie, Weihong Hong, Lipeng Huang, and Yongjun Hong test pressurized oxygen for sudden hearing loss in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The condition strikes without clear cause, and steroids are the standard first treatment. Adding hyperbaric oxygen up front is popular but unproven.

The groups differed at baseline, so the team matched them into one hundred thirty-five balanced pairs. Before matching, recovery rates seemed to differ. After matching, they did not. The authors conclude the oxygen add-on brings no extra benefit over steroids given both ways. The study is a caution against judging add-on therapies from unmatched data.
pmc-13202948:
Luoman Hu and co-authors review trials of electrical muscle stimulation for chronic ankle instability. Stimulation pads can fire the muscles around the ankle, yet its value for this problem was unclear.

The review pooled seven randomized trials with 248 people in all. Stimulation improved how stable patients felt their ankles were, and it helped both still and moving balance. Scores for everyday function also rose against control groups. Still, the trials differed from each other and had design limits. The authors urge care in reading the results and call for stricter trials with sham treatment to confirm lasting gains.
pmc-13206348:

The film wraps a core of PVOH, a plastic that melts in water, between outer layers that can rot away. That core gives the film strong gas blocking. The team dissolved the film in water and asked if the freed PVOH could be used again.

They tuned heat, time, film size, and stirring for the melt step. With good stirring, all sizes melted at the same rate. Without it, small bits melted faster. Tests on the freed plastic showed its chemical build was mostly intact. But it bent less well and stood heat less well, likely since key additives were lost in the wash.
pmc-13206748:
Zhipeng Zhang and co-authors map fish life around Weizhou Island by reading DNA shed into the sea. Fish leave tiny traces of their genes in the water, and lab tests can name the species from those traces. Past counts on the island were patchy and missed some seasons. Their 2026 data set comes from water samples at eight sites around the island.

Each site gave three samples, which were filtered and read for one gene that varies by species. The survey found more than one hundred fish species across many families, the fullest count yet for these waters. The raw data sit in a public archive for others to use. The authors say the base line will aid reef repair and sea life checks in the area.
pmc-13207848:
Carlos Alberto Luna-Lara and five co-authors map germ defenses against metals in root canal infections, in a study dated 2026. Silver and copper particles are being tested as germ killers for dental materials. Yet many bacteria carry genes that pump metals out or shield the cell, which could blunt those tools.

They searched each genome for seven known metal defense proteins, including pumps for copper and silver. The survey shows how common each defense is across the species involved. Dentists designing particle-based materials can use the map to pick metals that local germs are less equipped to resist.
pmc-13208048:

Crohn's disease generally carries higher kidney risk than ulcerative colitis. pmc-13209148:

pmc-13209348:

pmc-13209548:

pmc-13212848:

pmc-13212948:

pmc-13213648:

pmc-13214348:
Alexandra Juhasz and co-authors report an alien snail species found on Unguja Island, Zanzibar, in a 2026 paper. pmc-13214548:

pmc-13214948:
Asaf Shalom and co-authors published a review paper in 2026 on training soccer players to think and move at once, and where that dual-task work fits a club's calendar. Soccer demands split-second decisions under physical load, yet training and rehab usually separate the two. The authors stress coordination between coaching and medical staff, tuned to each player's profile. They offer clubs practical recommendations for weaving the drills into a full program without derailing performance or safety.
pmc-13215048:

pmc-13215348:

pmc-13215548:

pmc-13216448:

Adding nanoparticles raised the average Nusselt number by up to 7.7 percent over plain water, and stronger buoyancy at higher Rayleigh numbers sharpened temperature and velocity gradients. pmc-13217448:

pmc-13217848:

pmc-13218148:

pmc-13219348:

The rankings help doctors weigh trade-offs where direct proof is thin.
pmc-13219448:

pmc-13220048:

The authors gather the enzymes behind the tags as candidate drug targets and the tag patterns as candidate blood or tissue markers.
pmc-13221048:

pmc-13221148:

pmc-13221848:

pmc-13222048:

pmc-13222348:

pmc-13222748:

pmc-13223348:

pmc-13223648:

pmc-13223948:

Hosts with the ill split to herb or vitamin E arms.

In sum, 67 hosts took lots: 33 to herb, 34 to the vitamin. The end pool held 61 hosts for the score reads. Mean age ran near 44 years in both arms of the trial. Sound scans graded fat in the liver for each host. A shake tool gauged fat and scar marks in the same hosts.
pmc-13225148:

pmc-13225448:

pmc-13226048:

pmc-13226148:

pmc-13226848:

pmc-13226948:
Liu and a large team built a new lab tool in twenty twenty-six to switch off a key gene in chickens. The gene, called DMRT1, helps set sex as a chick grows in the egg. A switch that works on demand lets the team study the gene step by step.

They used a gene-edit tool turned on by a drug dose. In cells the switch cut the gene in most cases, and in eggs it worked in part of the cells. Female-linked genes rose and male-linked genes fell once the gene was off. Male chicks also made less of a key sex hormone.
pmc-13227248:
Yaohui Liu writes a 2026 letter to the editor questioning a study that used ultrasound of neck lymph nodes to distinguish Alzheimer's disease patients from healthy controls. The biological idea is plausible, since the brain drains fluid toward those nodes. The concern is statistical: the study counted hundreds of individual nodes from only fifty people, then treated those nodes as if they were independent evidence.

Nodes from the same person resemble each other, so ignoring that clustering can inflate significance and overstate diagnostic power. A composite score in the study also nests some predictors inside others, risking double counting. The letter asks for hierarchical reanalysis that respects the patient as the true unit, plus validation in fresh patients, before clinical claims stand.
pmc-13229448:
Takeshi Matsufusa and co-authors present a case report dated 2026 on stroke complications after treating a burst brain aneurysm. Aneurysms of the posterior cerebral artery are uncommon and often involve a torn vessel wall. A standard rescue is to close the parent artery, sacrificing it to stop the bleeding.

The patient was a seventy-six-year-old man with a severe brain hemorrhage. His artery layout was unusual: the segment before the aneurysm was underdeveloped, and the artery was fed mainly through a fetal-type connecting vessel. Doctors coiled the aneurysm shut through that vessel. The bleeding stopped, but scans later showed strokes in the thalamus and in the temporal and occipital lobes. He was left with vision loss on one side and problems with attention and memory.
pmc-13229848:
Li-li Wei, Li-xing Zhang, and Xiang-lan Mo report a rare benign vessel growth inside the wall of the uterus, in a 2026 case report. The lesion, called intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia, can look under the microscope like a malignant vessel tumor. That resemblance risks misdiagnosis and overly aggressive treatment. Finding it in the uterine muscle is reported as a first.

An 83-year-old woman came in with six days of vaginal bleeding after menopause. Imaging showed a well-defined mass in the uterine wall, raising fears of cancer. After surgical removal, tissue study gave the benign diagnosis, backed by marker tests. The authors review similar reports to guide pathologists.
pmc-13230248:
Luiz Drude de Lacerda and Moises Fernandes Bezerra survey in 2026 mercury levels in inland fish and farmed fish from northeastern Brazil. Their work is the first regional check of its kind, covering fourteen species from rivers plus farmed tilapia. Rapid growth of inland fishing and fish farming makes regular safety checks more pressing.

Mercury levels overall were very low and well below food safety limits used in Brazil and abroad. Meat-eating species such as piranha from river systems carried more mercury than plant feeders, as expected. Farmed tilapia ready for market held less mercury than young fish, likely because fast growth spreads the metal through more tissue. Even heavy fish eaters faced very low estimated exposure.
pmc-13230648:
Lambert Li and co-authors present surgical cases of ankle impingement in 2026. Pinching of tissue in the ankle is common in athletes who run, jump, and cut. Two cases show front and back forms, plus a side form, treated through small scopes.

The paper lists who should get surgery: lasting pain or limits after plain care fails. It walks through patient setup, entry points, and tools for each form. Spurs and pinched tissue are trimmed, then the scope checks that motion is free. For the back form, a key tendon marks the safe limit of the work to spare nerves and vessels.
pmc-13231748:
Qian Lou and colleagues build in 2026 a shared database for plants that make camptothecin, a compound behind major cancer drugs. A decade of gene, activity, and chemical data on these plants had piled up with no single home. Their resource, DIMORPH, gathers data for three maker species with notes, shared gene maps, and co-activity results.

Working in the database, the team found a new enzyme that adds an oxygen at one exact spot on the compound. Comparing it with a close cousin that acts at the next spot revealed ten amino acid positions that decide the choice. Guided tweaks then produced a faster version of the new enzyme. Clearer pathway maps could raise supply of the drug starting material.
pmc-13231948:
Lianghua Lin and colleagues show in 2026 that a protein-making subunit acts as a guard that keeps the immune system tolerant of self. The subunit eIF3e tunes how B cells build proteins from gene messages. Removing it only in mouse B cells let the team watch tolerance fail in a controlled way.

Without the guard, B cells struck up harmful partnerships with T cells that should have stayed quiet. Mice developed runaway lymph cell growth and later lymph cancers. The chain from a translation control point to immune disease had not been shown in a living animal before. Guarding protein production may be as vital to self tolerance as guarding gene reading itself.
pmc-13233648:
Farhad Pazan and co-authors ask whether drifting medication quality tracks with fading function in very old adults, in a 2026 study. The FORTA list grades drugs as fit or unfit for the aged, and its score sums over- and under-treatment errors. The team mined a German aging cohort for natural score changes over time.

Data covered 504 people seen at three visits in their late eighties, with change pairs for about 300 of them. When the score worsened, daily-living scores and mental test scores tended to slip too. The mental link held in models that weighed rival factors. No treatment was assigned; life itself moved the scores. Even so, the tie backs routine medication reviews for the oldest patients.
pmc-13233848:
Wenjie Cai and colleagues issued a 2026 study linking gut microbe chemicals in the blood to social anxiety and its treatment. Short-chain fatty acids are made by gut bacteria and may carry signals to the brain. Forty-six people with social anxiety disorder completed nine weeks of internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy, with blood samples before, after, and at a thirty-six month follow-up, compared against forty-two healthy controls.

Therapy reduced symptoms, and the gains held at the long follow-up. Four fatty acids, including butyric and propionic acid, rose in the blood after treatment, largely following the passage of time rather than individual differences. One acid, isobutyric acid, started lower in patients than controls. The authors offer early evidence that lasting therapy benefits may travel with shifts in microbial metabolites.
pmc-13233948:
Ersin Gokmen and colleagues published a 2026 prospective study on breathing settings during keyhole kidney stone surgery. Flexible ureteroscopy threads a thin scope into the kidney to laser stones apart, and the anesthesiologist's tidal volume, the air moved per breath, might jiggle the kidney and change laser accuracy. Seventy patients with single stones were grouped by whether their tidal volume reached five hundred milliliters.

Operating time and lasing time did not differ between groups. The higher-volume group used more total laser energy, while the lower-volume group achieved better laser efficiency, meaning more stone destroyed per unit of energy. Stone-free rates, infections, and hospital stays were similar. The authors label the efficiency finding exploratory, a hypothesis for a randomized trial rather than a practice change.
pmc-13234148:
Haoran Ma and colleagues published a 2026 chemistry study filming a metal carbonyl molecule fall apart in extreme slow motion. Iron pentacarbonyl, Fe(CO)5, is a workhorse of industrial chemistry, and light can knock one of its five carbon monoxide arms off. Using mega-electron-volt ultrafast electron diffraction, the team tracked the molecule's shape along its axial and equatorial directions as the reaction began.

The angle-resolved view revealed how the skeleton rearranges before any arm leaves. Vibrations couple together on the way to the crossing point between energy states, and that coupling lets the molecule swap its arms' identities through Berry pseudorotation, a classic shape-shifting dance. As a result, the arm that finally departs is effectively random. The observations sketch the excited energy landscape that steers the breakup.
pmc-13234248:
Sotiris G. Tsioumas and colleagues described in 2026 a woman whose double vision lasted eleven years after an eye socket injury. She had suffered a fracture of the orbital floor and later had two reconstruction operations with implants. Neither operation restored comfortable eye movement. Clinicians traced the problem to scar tissue that restricted movement around the lower eyelid.

Treatment used a plasma energy device called Plexr to release the adhesions without major surgery. Eye movement returned during the procedure, and the double vision cleared within about five minutes. Eight months later she still had full movement in both eyes and no double vision. The report suggests plasma release could offer a less invasive choice for selected long-standing cases.
pmc-13234448:
Kate E. Trout and Jeongyoung Park examined in 2026 gaps in how family doctors in the United States share electronic patient information. Data came from a 2022 certification questionnaire for family medicine physicians. The authors linked reported sharing ability to an index of social deprivation in the practice area. Rural practice was also examined in exploratory work.

Doctors serving more deprived communities showed declining odds of sending, receiving, and accessing outside patient information. Partnerships told a different story for some features of sharing. Working with local public health agencies raised the odds of sending information electronically. Links with behavioural health agencies and schools raised the odds of integrating outside information. Rural estimates were much lower for several features, though the rural group was very small. The authors urge programs that support community partnerships and digital access.
pmc-13234648:
Hanieh Shahabinejad and co-authors test a new material for cleaning a common drug out of water. Tetracycline, a widely used antibiotic, slips through sewage plants and builds up in water. The team made a cerium based metal organic framework, a sponge like crystal, using sound waves. They then used it with light and sound to break the drug down.

The group tuned the mix by testing dose, strength, time, and acidity in a planned grid. At the best settings, the process cleared most of the drug from the water in under two hours. The crystal held its shape and kept working over the runs. The authors see it as a strong option for drug tainted water.
pmc-13234948:
Jiaxin Li and Cheng-Wei Qiu explained in 2026 how a rock-paper-scissors pattern of interactions can make heat gather at one edge of a material. Heat usually spreads by diffusion and is hard to steer beyond shaping conductivity. A recent lattice design instead links three thermal sites in a cycle, where each site drives heat toward one neighbour while receiving from another. Active electronic elements enforce that directional loop.

Chaining many cyclic units together makes the preferred direction accumulate across the structure. Temperature then localizes toward one boundary rather than spreading evenly through the material. The commentary places the result inside fast-growing work on topological and non-Hermitian thermal physics. Those fields borrow ideas from wave systems to organize diffusive processes in new ways. The authors see programmable couplings as a route to richer heat control in future thermal metamaterials.
pmc-13235348:
Shweta Kajjari and co-authors trialled in 2026 numbing injections for dental treatment in children aged six to twelve. Injections sting partly because anaesthetic solutions are acidic, which frightens many young patients. Mixing in sodium bicarbonate raises acidity toward normal body levels before injection. Eighty healthy children were randomized into four groups covering two drugs, each in plain and buffered form.

Buffered groups reported and displayed clearly lower pain during injection than non-buffered groups. Buffered articaine gave the lowest pain scores of the four combinations tested. That group also numbed fastest and stayed numb longest in the measurements. Buffered lidocaine ranked second on the combined pattern of results. The authors recommend buffering, especially with articaine, to improve comfort and cooperation during invasive dental care for children.
pmc-13235448:
Omid Nazifi and Dirck Martin Ananos Flores described in 2026 a surgical technique for straightening a bent finger present from birth. The deformity, called clinodactyly, most often affects the little finger and stems from an oddly shaped middle bone. Mild cases cause little trouble, yet stronger angles can limit fine tasks and bother patients cosmetically. Their guide uses a wedge-removing bone cut closed and fixed with a hollow headless screw.

That fixation gives rigid stability without pins crossing the joint, allowing earlier finger movement after surgery. The article walks through anatomy, who should and should not receive the operation, and postoperative care. Thresholds for surgery centre on angles above roughly thirty degrees, or smaller angles with clear impairment. Helpful technical pearls and common pitfalls are listed for operating surgeons. Closing wedge cuts sacrifice a little bone length in exchange for reliable correction.
pmc-13235648:
Anamik Jhunjhunwala and co-authors published a study in 2026 on medical imaging inside the living body. Sound-based imaging with light can show where tagged cells sit, but telling tags apart is hard. Tags fade under light, and blood itself soaks up light and blurs the read.

The team made four kinds of tiny gold rods, each tuned to absorb a distinct color of near-infrared light. A silica shell and a common coating made the rods last longer under the beam. With a standard laser and simple math, they split the signals of all four tags at once. Errors stayed under five percent in dish and animal tests. The work doubles the number of tags that can be read at once.
pmc-13235748:
Eilerts-Spinelli and colleagues estimate causes of death for older children and teenagers across the world. Their analysis covers ages five to nineteen in 195 countries, for the years 2000 to 2024. Like its companion study of younger children, it uses a Bayesian model to divide deaths by cause from surveys, registries, and published studies.

This age band is often skipped in global health counts, which focus on the under-fives. Yet injuries, infections, and other causes strike school-age children in patterns worth tracking on their own. The estimates give planners a full picture across childhood, so programmes for older children rest on numbers rather than guesses.
pmc-13236648:
Wang and co-authors hunted for a driver pair behind inflammation and metabolic trouble in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, in a study published in 2026. The disease is a severe, inherited muscle-wasting condition with no cure. Muscles degenerate while chronic inflammation smolders and metabolism skews. Tiny RNA regulators and the genes they control are suspected players, but the key pairs were undefined. The team combined several public data sets: bulk gene reads, small RNA reads, and single-cell reads from patients.

By layering those data with target prediction and pathway mapping, they screened for the strongest regulator-gene pairs. One pair stood out as a likely driver of both the inflammation and the metabolic imbalance. Naming such a pair gives drug research a focused target. It also gives clinicians a possible marker for tracking the disease's course.
pmc-13236748:
Smatti and colleagues dissect a single letter change in the coronavirus spike protein, called N481K. The change sits in the part of the spike that grips human cells and dodges antibodies. It first appeared in Qatar in 2020, then spread worldwide until nearly every sampled virus carried it.

The team traced its path through more than seventeen million viral genomes. They then tested what the change does to the spike's shape, its grip on the ACE2 cell receptor, and its escape from antibodies. A mutation can sweep the world by luck or by edge; this study asks which, and what the answer means for future variants.
pmc-13236848:
Salma Ghofrane Moutawakkil and colleagues translated the Hooked on Nicotine Checklist into Moroccan Arabic and tested the version in a 2026 study of 234 Moroccan smokers. The checklist asks about early signs of nicotine dependence, such as craving and failed attempts to cut down. The team checked whether the translated items held together and measured one underlying trait.

Scores on the items correlated well with each other, and reliability measures were excellent. A statistical model confirmed a single-factor structure with a strong fit. The scale proved most informative at low to moderate levels of dependence, which suits early detection. The authors say the Moroccan Arabic checklist can now support screening, research, and tobacco control work.
pmc-13237748:
Siwei Tu and Chunna Ding pooled eighteen studies in a 2026 meta-analysis asking whether body mass index changes what patients gain from cardiac rehabilitation. Exercise capacity, measured in metabolic equivalents, was the main outcome, with weight, lipids, heart rate, and blood pressure as secondary measures. Studies were gathered from four databases through late 2025.

Obese and non-obese patients improved their exercise capacity by similar amounts, and the same held when overweight patients were compared with normal-weight ones. Weight itself barely budged in any group. Cholesterol improved slightly more in non-obese patients, and triglycerides fell more in normal-weight patients, but most measures showed no difference. High variation between studies tempers the conclusions. Starting weight, the authors say, should not discourage referral.
pmc-13237948:
Kaixiang Yang and Maria C. Arno surveyed in 2026 how crystallization-driven self-assembly builds flat and rod-shaped nanoparticles with unusual precision. Polymers that crystallize as they assemble can be grown like living chains, giving rods and platelets of controlled length, width, and surface chemistry. Nature's layered materials, bone among them, motivate the chase for similar control at the nanoscale.

The authors review the main routes to these anisotropic particles and how their chemistry can be tuned after growth. Uses range across light devices, data storage, bio-processing, and new materials. Because the particles' shapes and surfaces can be dialed in, they carry functions that spheres cannot. The authors argue that living assembly is becoming a general way to make designer nanoparticles.
pmc-13238248:
Cao and colleagues fingerprint three Brucella abortus strains taken from livestock on the Qinghai plateau. Brucellosis, the disease these bacteria cause, is entrenched across the Qinghai and Tibet highlands, yet the local bacteria had barely been characterised. Knowing which strains circulate, and how they relate, is basic intelligence for controlling a disease that jumps from animals to people.

The team isolated bacteria from a sheep, a yak, and a cow, then read their whole genomes. Comparing those genomes built a family tree and checked how the plateau strains relate to others in China. Such maps can trace outbreaks to their animal source and target vaccination where it counts.
pmc-13239148:
Alix Kamina and co-authors report a rare jaw tumor that took ten years to be named correctly, in this 2026 case paper. The growth is a cemento-ossifying fibroma, a bone-like lesion of the jaws that mimics several other conditions. Their patient was a twenty-two-year-old woman with a painless mass in the upper right jaw.

The tumor was bulky, ulcerated, and disfiguring, spreading across the nasal, cheek, and jaw regions. Scans showed a well-defined mass of mixed soft tissue and calcified specks. A first reading of the scans pointed to a different tumor, osteoblastoma. Only by matching the microscope picture with the scans and the clinical story did the team settle on the right name. Surgeons removed the mass in one operation and cleaned the cavity. The authors stress that this diagnosis should rest on all three legs together, since any one alone can mislead.
pmc-13239248:
Paula Prucker, Johannes Kollmann, and Sara Diana Leonhardt tracked thirty-five years of crop yields in 2026 across two contrasting German regions, one cool and moist, the other warm and dry. Crops were grouped by how much they depend on insect pollinators: not at all, moderately, or strongly. Yield trends were set against time and against a composite climate measure.

Yields rose over time in both regions across every dependency class, a gain the authors credit mainly to technology. The climate correlations told a subtler story. Long-term average conditions already exceed the optimum for moderately dependent crops. Strongly dependent crops oddly yielded more under warmer, drier conditions, perhaps through fewer late frosts and shifting pollinator communities. The authors warn that future yields may grow less stable as optima are passed.
pmc-13239348:
Ruth Mears and colleagues report a 2026 mixed-methods study of parents attending Slimming World, a British commercial weight management programme for adults. The researchers asked what drove parents to tackle their own weight and whether doing so affected children aged five to eleven at home.

Survey and interview answers showed that improving health and unhappiness with appearance each motivated most parents. Many said their own efforts made them keener to help a child stay at a healthy weight. Nearly half reported that their child's diet had improved, and about a quarter said the child moved more. Changes in family cooking explained much of the reported gain.
pmc-13239448:
Anna J Suleri and co-authors report a 2026 Dutch registry study on birth outcomes in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Government policy had flagged twenty areas for poor livability and safety, and the team tested whether babies born there fare worse than elsewhere in the country.

National registry data from 2015 to 2021 covered more than a million mother and child pairs. Babies in the flagged areas were more often born too small, born early, or lost around birth than babies elsewhere. Those gaps persisted when each area was compared with its own town or city. The authors back place-based action and plan practical tools built with local stakeholders.
pmc-13239548:
Elisa Borghi and a multicentre Italian team outline a 2026 protocol for a study of treatment-resistant epilepsy. About a third of people with epilepsy keep having seizures despite medicines, surgery, nerve stimulation, or special diets, and gut microbes may partly explain why treatments fail.

Participants aged three to fifty will join four groups covering new drug treatment, surgery, vagus nerve stimulation, and the ketogenic diet. Over twelve months the team will collect stool and blood samples, brain recordings, scans, seizure counts, and quality of life scores. Microbial patterns and chemical marks on DNA will be tested as predictors of who responds to each therapy.
pmc-13239648:
Haruna Sakanoue and colleagues examine a small device that seals the vein puncture after heart rhythm treatment in a 2026 Japanese study. Patients having atrial fibrillation ablation under propofol sedation usually endure long bed rest with manual pressing on the groin, and the team asked whether a closure device also reduces sickness afterwards.

Records covered 686 patients at one centre in Okayama, split between device closure and traditional compression. Device patients rested about fifteen fewer hours on average. Nausea and vomiting struck two percent of the device group versus about five percent with compression. Adjusted analysis kept the link, suggesting shorter immobility helps patients feel better.
pmc-13239748:
Wei Wang and Xiang Liu survey research on puerarin, a plant compound from kudzu root, for fatty liver disease in a 2026 bibliometric paper. Fatty liver not caused by alcohol is now a major chronic condition, and this natural isoflavone has drawn growing interest as a safe and affordable candidate treatment.

Using mapping software, the authors chart publication trends and hotspots across the field. The article then reviews how puerarin is extracted and measured, how the body absorbs and clears it, and what safety data exist. Laboratory evidence on how it counters liver fat build-up, inflammation, and scarring is summarised to guide future clinical work.
pmc-13239848:
Atbin Latifi and Sina Yousefian report a boy who grew a second blood cancer while his first rare cell growth still ran hot, in a case report from 2026. The first growth, a clone of guard cells, struck his bones at age eleven. A year of two drugs failed to clear it, and he then left care for two years.

He came back at age fifteen with fever, bone pain, and wild blood counts. Marrow tests proved a slow blood cancer with its known gene swap, a first such pair on print. Scans showed the first growth still lit as well. Two drugs, one per ill, cleared both to full rest in seven months. Long watch for second cancers is the call.
pmc-13240248:
Manhui Sun and team ferment a medicinal fungus to boost its liver guard power in a 2026 study. Ganoderma lucidum, the reishi fungus, owes much of its effect to compounds called ganoderic acids. A joint bacteria and enzyme ferment was tuned to yield more of one key member, ganoderic acid F.

The broth, made with a Lactobacillus strain, cut fat build-up inside liver cells dosed with fatty acids. Cholesterol, triglycerides, and harmful oxygen by-products fell. Guard enzymes that fight such damage rose. Computer work and protein tests tied the effect to a switch that turns on fat-burning controls. The authors pitch the broth as a stronger choice than plain water extracts of the fungus.
pmc-13240448:
Reed DeAngelis and co-authors review how social connection shapes cognitive health over a life. Their twenty twenty-six review calls weak social ties a dementia risk on par with inactivity and smoking. Yet the paths from company to cognition stay murky.

The review first sorts what social connection means, from network size to felt loneliness. A companion set gathers the measures used to count it, with advice on matching measure to goal. A new model then links connection to brain health across social, spatial, and time scales. It also flags tangled causes that run both ways. Researchers get a shared frame and a list of study priorities.
pmc-13240548:
Ying Liu, Zhirun Chen, Rong Zi, and Chongyi Zhao review what brain imaging shows about depression in women across the stages of life, in a 2026 paper. Women develop depression far more often than men. Hormone swings at puberty, around childbirth, at menopause, and in old age each shape a distinct form of the illness, with social and mental factors woven in.

The review surveys studies that use several kinds of magnetic resonance imaging to find the brain patterns behind these stage-specific forms. It gathers what is known about how brain structure, activity, and connections differ in depressed women at each life stage. It also weighs where imaging has advanced the field and where the evidence is still thin. The authors aim to give researchers and clinicians a map of a fast-moving area.
pmc-13240848:
Shi and a team of colleagues built a programmable surface that does calculus on waves in twenty twenty-six. The surface is a metasurface, a thin sheet of tiny parts that shape waves. If such sheets can be set and reset as time passes, they could simplify information systems. The math would happen right in the wave itself.

Their space-time-coding metasurface shifts its part settings over time. That creates harmonics whose responses can be steered one by one. With the right coding strings, the surface takes the slope or area of a wave's spatial energy pattern. Richer strings run distinct operations on one wave at once, each on its own. Functions can also switch in real time. A two-bit programmable test piece backed the idea in tests, matching theory and computer models. The authors foresee uses in shaping waves, wireless links, and signal work.
pmc-13241448:
Zou's team at Wageningen profiled the chemistry of stored potato seed tubers across two seasons. Four unlike strains were grown jointly, then warehoused at several temperatures. Gas and liquid lab runs catalogued their metabolites. The goal was mapping how storage ages a tuber inside.

Byproduct compounds built up steadily during storage, fastest in warmer rooms. Each strain kept a distinct profile, the starch type standing apart on amino acids. Cold rooms instead piled up simple sugars in the tubers. Heat plus long storage lifted bitter plant toxins, a shift that matters for safety.
pmc-13241648:
Jenny Ahlborn and co-authors present a 2026 chemical analysis of a garlic-scented mushroom. The species grows across central Europe and is prized as a seasoning. Its flavor chemistry had never been profiled in this depth.

Freeze-dried mushrooms grown in the lab were examined with sensitive gas-based instruments plus a smelling port. Nine sulfur compounds were identified, and one of them had never been reported in this mushroom group before. A solvent extract held only four aroma compounds, which the team measured precisely. Comparisons with a garlic-scented plant pointed to a shared aroma precursor in the fungus. The work explains the mushroom scent and may inform future culinary use.
pmc-13241748:
Weihui Yan and co-authors identify a proton channel, OTOP2, as a guard of gut health. Their 2026 study starts from a clue in inflammatory bowel disease: the inflamed gut turns acidic, and this channel, common in gut tissue, drops out of line during flares. Its exact role in the disease was unclear.

In samples from children with the disease, channel levels fell as disease worsened. Mice lacking the channel grew poorly, had loose gut acidity control, shifted gut microbes, and leaky cell joins. They also fared worse in a chemical colitis model. The loss cut the number of Paneth cells, which make germ-fighting factors, and weakened the eating function of immune cells. The authors propose the channel as a drug target.
pmc-13242448:
Farzana Sabir and colleagues gave cork oak its first detailed map of aquaporins, the channel proteins that move water through plant cells. Their paper appeared in Plant Cell Reports in 2026. Cork oak woodlands face deepening drought as the climate warms, yet the tree's water plumbing was largely unstudied. The team tested four aquaporins in yeast, located them in young stems, and tracked their gene activity under mild drought.

Three of the four channels carried water in the yeast tests, and the NIP members also passed glycerol and other small molecules, including boron and arsenic. One channel was oddly switched on by mercury, an effect traced to a single amino acid. In stems, the channels spread across many tissue layers. Under drought, leaf and stem genes for two families rose while root levels fell, a pattern that may limit water leaking back into dry soil.
pmc-13242648:
Fatema Ezzy and co-authors narrate a perilous hospital course in a 2026 case report. An eighty-one-year-old woman with ANCA-associated vasculitis, an autoimmune attack on small blood vessels, received rituximab to suppress her immune system, and complications stacked up fast.

Her lungs failed under two infections at once, COVID-19 and cytomegalovirus pneumonia, and then her gallbladder hemorrhaged, a rare bleeding event needing a drainage procedure rather than surgery. Balancing immune suppression against rampant infection drove every decision. The authors stress vigilant monitoring and individualized therapy when treatment itself opens the door to catastrophe.
pmc-13242748:
Michel Kalongo Ilumbulumbu and a large team present a 2026 case of a rare nerve sheath tumor in a six-year-old girl that mimicked a kidney tumor. The malignant Triton tumor is an aggressive variant with muscle-type differentiation. It is seldom seen in the belly cavity of children.

The girl arrived with a painful right flank mass and trouble using her leg. Ultrasound suggested Wilms tumor, the common childhood kidney cancer. Surgery found the mass stuck to the spine, and tissue testing after removal gave the true diagnosis. Gentle chemotherapy followed, but the tumor returned quickly and she died within weeks. The authors stress early tissue confirmation and team-based care, especially where advanced testing is scarce.
pmc-13244248:
Kanav Gupta and colleagues report a spine infection that wore the mask of tuberculosis until surgery exposed a killer fungus. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Infectious Diseases in 2026. A fifty-four-year-old man with liver cirrhosis, diabetes, and thyroid failure arrived with a week of worsening back pain and leg weakness. MRI showed infected spinal discs with an abscess, read as Pott's spine, and tuberculosis drugs were started.

When his neurology crashed, surgeons drained the abscess, and the microscope changed everything: broad, ribbon-like fungal threads of a Mucorales species filled the tissue. Three antifungals were thrown at it, but organ damage forced repeated dose cuts. He developed liver failure with sepsis and died after surgery. The authors count his as the twelfth case, and the first blamed on end-stage liver disease. In TB-endemic regions, they warn, do not anchor on tuberculosis.
pmc-13244348:
Katie Hassell and co-authors present a national cohort study, published in 2026, on whether a positive COVID test still marked raised death risk late in England's pandemic. As variants softened and immunity spread, deaths fell, but deaths shortly after a positive test fell more slowly. Using linked national records, the team matched people who tested positive with similar people who tested negative and compared deaths within twenty-eight days.

Across the whole study span the positive group faced far higher death risk. Even in the quieter Omicron months of early 2022 the risk stayed clearly elevated, and more so for the unvaccinated than the vaccinated. The authors conclude that infection kept carrying real mortality risk after the emergency faded.
pmc-13244648:
Xuepeng Gong and co-authors tested Calculus Bovis, a traditional medicine made from cattle gallstones, against a scarring liver disease in mice. Their study appeared in Chinese Medicine in 2026. Primary sclerosing cholangitis destroys the bile ducts and has no approved drug therapy. Mice fed a toxin diet that mimics the disease received the medicine at three doses. The standard bile acid drug served as comparison, and liver, gut, and blood measures were tracked.

Treatment eased liver injury and fibrosis and repaired the leaking intestinal barrier. Bile acid patterns settled across blood and liver while excretion through feces rose, and disturbed blood lipids improved. Gene and network analyses pointed to a dual mechanism: switching on a SIRT1 energy-sensing pathway and activating bile acid receptors. The authors present the gallstone preparation as a multi-target candidate working along the gut-liver axis. Animal success is a beginning, not an answer.
pmc-13244848:
Shadi Bagherzadeh and colleagues asked a simple question: when cardiologists say a heart pressure changed, how big a change do they mean? Their study appeared in Echo Research and Practice in 2026. Right ventricular systolic pressure, estimated from ultrasound, tracks pulmonary hypertension, yet no guideline defines a meaningful shift. Using a Stanford registry, the team extracted more than thirty-two thousand paired scans from nearly six thousand patients and used language processing to sort the reports.

pmc-13246548:

Serap Şimşek-Yavuz and co-authors weigh a pill for mild to mid COVID in adults with past immunity. The study appeared in 2026. It tracks over eight hundred patients at many sites, near half on the pill. The mean age was in the mid-sixties, and most had had a shot.

pmc-13246848:

pmc-13248448:

pmc-13248848:

pmc-13249548:

pmc-13249648:

pmc-13249748:

The standard tools, ultracentrifuges and chemical precipitation, are expensive, slow, or missing in high-containment labs where they are needed most.

pmc-13250248:
Wang and co-authors build a smart gel system to regrow jawbone lost to gum disease in diabetes. pmc-13250448:

Each partner can act as sender or receiver, and the puller can also push in the other seat. The authors say reuse of one pair across many links keeps the wiring code compact.
pmc-13250948:
Han Yin and colleagues report a 2026 study of a gel designed to heal bone defects weakened by osteoporosis. In animals with osteoporotic bone defects, the gel produced more new bone and more blood vessels than untreated defects. The authors argue that coupling bone growth with vessel growth is the key to restoring balance in fragile bone.
pmc-13251348:
Bartoli and colleagues pooled the evidence in 2026 on what marks out people with bipolar disorder who take their medicines poorly, a pattern that feeds relapse. Their systematic review searched major databases to March 2025 and combined results across studies with random-effects models, expressing links as odds ratios or standardized differences.

Nineteen studies qualified. Poor adherence tracked with younger age, less schooling, not being in a relationship, and earlier illness onset. Psychotic features, past suicide attempts, more manic and mixed episodes, and more hospital stays also raised the odds. Cannabis and alcohol use disorders, added anxiety and personality disorders, lower insight, and worse overall functioning all clustered in the poorly adherent group. The authors caution that effects were small and the evidence uneven, yet say the profile can help clinics spot patients who need adherence support most.
pmc-13253148:
Ario Parak and co-authors report a forty-two-year-old man whose nonstop seizures, defying even anesthetic coma for eighty days, finally yielded to a vagus nerve stimulator. Super-refractory status epilepticus carries high death and disability rates. Their patient, who has Crohn's disease, developed it after a stroke in the right posterior cerebral artery.

Anesthetics could be withdrawn, and the man left hospital with mild deficits and good long-term recovery. Brain scans showed a striking knife-blade pattern of cortical shrinkage.
pmc-13253648:
Annika Kasprzak and colleagues weigh iron as a warning sign in bone marrow disease in this 2026 study. Myelodysplastic syndromes are marrow disorders where blood making falters, and iron often piles up in the marrow even before transfusions begin.

Extra marrow iron shortened survival mainly in the subgroup with more immature cells, where it was the strongest single survival predictor after adjustment. Age and disease subtype dominated overall, with ferritin also independent. The authors back checking iron at diagnosis.
pmc-13254148:
Emad Shalaby and colleagues test grapefruit peel extract against liver cancer cells in a 2026 study. Peels were dried and soaked in 70 percent ethanol, and the extract was screened for plant compounds. Its effect on HepG2 liver cancer cells was measured, and computer docking tested how compounds fit a target protein.

Naringenin was the most abundant compound found. The extract killed cancer cells with an IC50, the dose halving cell survival, stated in the paper. In docking, ellagic acid bound most strongly, followed by rutin and quercetin. The authors name these as lead molecules, while noting more work on safety is needed.
pmc-13254848:
Ryan Yao and colleagues build a living model of glioblastoma's surroundings to learn what makes radiation succeed or fail in a 2026 paper. Glioblastoma, the commonest malignant brain tumor in adults, nearly always returns after treatment. Response to radiation varies, and the tumor's microenvironment, its stiffness, oxygen level, and neighboring neurons, is suspected to pull the strings.

Their organotypic platform grows tumor tissue in an engineered setting where those surroundings can be watched and adjusted at the same time. Neuronal networks woven into the model also altered the tumor's metabolic activity, an influence flat cell cultures cannot show. Their stated aim is prediction: testing a patient's likely radiotherapeutic response in the model before committing the patient to a course.
pmc-13255348:
Kaiwen Tan and co-authors report a 2026 field study of how seabuckthorn tree canopies of different ages shape the light beneath them. Seabuckthorn plantations serve both ecological repair and fruit production in China, so light distribution affects growth and yield. Stand age and height within the canopy significantly affected every light and structure measure taken. Statistical modeling showed gaps in the canopy let light through most directly, while dense leaf area reduced light mainly by closing those gaps. A random forest model could guess a stand's age from canopy traits with about eighty-five percent accuracy. The authors suggest pruning to keep a suitable gap fraction as a practical management lever.
pmc-13256248:
Beaumont and colleagues tested how e-cigarette aerosol damages the airway lining, focusing on the junction protein E-cadherin. Pretreatment with fisetin, a metalloproteinase inhibitor, preserved barrier function and cut soluble E-cadherin release, mainly by suppressing one enzyme. The authors name cleaved E-cadherin as an early injury biomarker.
pmc-13256448:

pmc-13256948:
Sara Isla Cainzos and co-authors describe a 2026 mouse study on recovery after ischemic stroke. Few medicines help long-term rehabilitation, so the team tested timing. They briefly removed microglia, the immune cells of the brain, during days three to seven after stroke.

pmc-13257148:

pmc-13257548:
Xiaoyi Zeng and colleagues report a platinum catalyst that burns methane at low temperature in a 2026 study. pmc-13258548:
Mehmet Sahap and colleagues analyze timing of lumbar spine surgery in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Four hundred sixty patients were split between regular hours and after hours operations. The main question was which patients needed intensive care after surgery.

Hospital planners can weigh staffing and case selection for night spine work with these figures in hand.
pmc-13258748:

pmc-13260348:

pmc-13260448:

pmc-13260848:

pmc-13262848:

pmc-13263148:

pmc-13264548:

pmc-13264748:

pmc-13264848:

pmc-13264948:

pmc-13266148:

pmc-13266748:

pmc-13266848:

pmc-13267548:
