pmc-13269148:
Berat Dilek Demirel and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on surgery for babies born with a blocked back passage and an abnormal channel into the vagina. The operation rebuilds the passage while sparing a band of tissue between the openings. One surgeon did all the operations at one center.

Records covered 26 patients treated from 2018 to 2024, at a median age of 40 days. Sixteen had a one-stage repair, and ten first had a temporary bowel opening. Two patients got wound infections that cleared with local care. Among 18 children older than three years, 15 had voluntary bowel control, or 83.3 percent. Seven had constipation, and none had soiling.
pmc-13269548:
Yang Liu and co-authors catalog the microbes of China's traditional cheeses in this 2026 paper. China's artisanal cheeses ferment naturally and differ from Europe's in taste and makeup, but their microbial life was barely mapped. The team sequenced two hundred thirty-five Chinese cheese samples from every traditional region and added public data from elsewhere.

They rebuilt more than three thousand high-quality microbe genomes, covering three hundred ninety-five species, eighty-five of them likely new to science. Six lactic acid bacteria ran richer in Chinese cheeses, and one bacterial family unique to them lifted nutritional quality. Thousands of gene clusters for making special compounds turned up, over half of them novel. The team even brewed a starter mix from the catalog to make a Tibetan yak cheese.
pmc-13269648:
Naima Sultana and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 cataloging the E2F gene family in Brassica rapa, a leafy crop plant. These genes act as checkpoints that control when cells copy their DNA and divide. The team searched the plant's genome and compared its genes with those of five other species.

Fourteen family members were found, including six pairs copied in large genome blocks over evolution. Change rates suggested the copies kept similar jobs. Certain small RNA molecules that respond to stress targeted four of the genes most heavily. Switch regions in the genes pointed to roles in growth and in coping with living and non-living stresses. The authors present the catalog as a base for crop stress research.
pmc-13269948:
Alyssa C Bonnell and co-authors report in 2026 two cases where a hole formed in the center of the retina after vitrectomy surgery, then closed on its own without another operation. Both patients, a man of seventy-two and a woman of sixty-seven, had surgery to repair a detached retina. The authors pair the cases with a review of every similar report they could find.

Small and medium holes seemed most likely to seal themselves. Among published eyes with spontaneous closure, about two thirds closed within a month of diagnosis and four in five within three months. More than a third later reopened, some needing surgery after all. One patient's closure in this report lasted seven years, showing that watchful waiting can sometimes be the right call.
pmc-13270248: A correction notice from 2026 fixes one author's affiliation in a 2025 paper led by M S Mohamed on health workers' and students' views about raising public awareness of antimicrobial resistance. Author Mona Timan Idriss had been linked to the wrong institution, in the Department of Medical Sciences and Preparation Year at Northern College of Nursing in Arar, Saudi Arabia. Her correct affiliation is the Nursing Department at North Private College of Nursing, also in Arar. The notice apologizes for the error.
pmc-13270448:
Vincent J Leopold and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on ischiofemoral impingement, painful pinching between hip and pelvis bones, in young patients with non-arthritic hip pain. Imaging for 250 patients included MRI, CT, and standing and seated spine-pelvis X-rays. Pinching was confirmed by swelling or wasting of a deep hip muscle.

Impingement was found in 14 patients, 5.6 percent, all female. Their bone-to-bone spaces were far narrower: 24.8 millimeters against 34.9 in others. They also showed a larger ischial angle, more thigh bone twist, and smaller offsets at hip and socket. Standing posture differed too, with more pelvic tilt. Combined analysis singled out the narrow muscle space as the strongest independent predictor.
pmc-13271148:
Qin Lu is lead author of a 2026 journal article on using chest muscle size on scans to spot malnutrition in patients with sudden worsening of chronic lung disease, shortened to AECOPD. Such patients often lose muscle, and standard nutrition checks can miss that loss, so the team tested total pectoralis major area, the size of both main chest muscles.

Among 123 patients, 35 were malnourished, and their chest muscle area was clearly lower. Larger muscle area protected against malnutrition even after adjustment. Alone, the measure diagnosed malnutrition fairly well; combined with blood albumin or total protein it performed much better. Muscle area also rose with other good nutrition signs and fell as symptom burden rose.
pmc-13271348:
Aradhika Vijeev and colleagues review in 2026 how light from LEDs and ultraviolet lamps can keep fruits and vegetables fresh after harvest. Produce spoils quickly through natural aging, germs, and quality loss during storage and transport. Light treatment leaves no chemical residue, which makes it attractive for food storage.

The review compares results across the growing and storage stages, covering photosynthesis, antioxidant levels, germ control, and shelf life. Responses differ widely by crop type, growth stage, and light settings, which has blocked shared standards. By mapping those differences, the authors set out steps toward crop-specific light recipes that farms and warehouses could actually use.
pmc-13271848:
Jean-Jacques Wyndaele wrote a short 2026 comment on a review of bladder pain syndrome and its links to women's health. The review covers how pelvic pain from gynecologic causes must be told apart from bladder pain syndrome. It also covers paired problems such as endometriosis and vulvar pain that often sit beside it.

Wyndaele backs the broad lines of the review. Care should start with plain steps, self-care habits, and mental health support. Stronger steps come only when plain steps fail. He notes that no cure exists for the bladder syndrome today, since its cause stays unclear. Gains come from treating each symptom with a team from more than one field. The comment closes on the need for frank talks with patients about what care can and cannot promise.
pmc-13271948:
Li Zhuang and coauthors gather in 2026 recent studies on exercise, resilience, and mental health in teenagers. Adolescent mental health is a worldwide concern, and activity programs are a practical public tool. Resilience, the ability to recover from stress, may explain part of the benefit.

The review covered studies from 2022 to 2025 across five databases, focusing on youth aged about ten to nineteen. More active teenagers generally reported better mental health and stronger resilience. All ten studies that formally tested the pathway found resilience carried part of the exercise effect. Programs built on mastery and social connection looked most promising.
pmc-13272248:
Wulan Koagouw is lead author of a 2026 journal article profiling drug pollution along Jakarta's Ciliwung River, in Indonesia. Drug residues threaten water life and human health. Yet tropical city rivers are far less studied than temperate ones. So the team sampled along a gradient of urbanisation to test whether pollution builds up downstream.

They analysed 53 compounds at eight sites and detected thirteen. These spanned antibiotics, painkillers, heart drugs, and scan contrast agents. Combined levels rose clearly downstream. The nerve drug gabapentin showed the strongest build-up. Eleven compounds increased steadily, signalling cumulative loading with little breakdown. Local spikes for two drugs suggested point sources such as health facility discharge. Gabapentin is proposed as a watch-list indicator.
pmc-13272348:
Zibing Zhao and Zhuangzhuang Zheng review in 2026 how macrophage states help decide whether radiotherapy succeeds against cancer. Macrophages flip between an attack-oriented state that aids tumor control and a suppressive state that shields tumors. Radiation itself can push that flip in either direction.

High-dose and particle radiation tend to favor the attack state, while standard fractionated treatment often breeds the suppressive one, feeding resistance. Oxygen shortage, metabolic signals, and cytokines in the tumor surroundings steer the balance. The authors survey strategies that block macrophage recruitment, remove suppressive cells, or reprogram them to restore radiation sensitivity.
pmc-13272548:
Lipeng Sun and a large team of co-authors map gene patterns tied to synapse loss in Alzheimer's disease. Their 2026 study joins brain imaging with gene activity data. Synapse loss is a main driver of the memory and thinking decline in the disease. The team hunted for the gene programs that track that loss.

Scans measured synapse density in living patients from a tracked group. Matching gene data named over twelve hundred genes tied to synapse loss. The genes cluster around synapse upkeep, a disease protein's tagging, cell scaffolding, and protein disposal. Signal fell in two neuron types and rose in support and vessel cells. Repeat and follow-up scans backed the patterns, and protein data pointed at failing cell power plants.
pmc-13272748:
Yoonsang Ra leads a 2026 review of wearable sensors that use triboelectric effects, where contact and motion generate electric charge. Such sensors can power themselves while sensing the body, which suits smart devices worn day to day. The review sets out principles, materials, device designs, and ways to make them.

The authors highlight artificial intelligence processing of sensor signals, plus artificial synapses and brain-like computing, as bridges to adaptive human-machine interfaces. Uses they organize include health care, gesture control, robotics, and smart transport. The review closes with future directions toward electronics centered on human comfort, motion, intention, and personal needs, rather than on devices alone.
pmc-13273148:
Shilei Li leads a 2026 study of single-atom iron catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction, a key step in fuel cells and metal-air batteries. Each iron atom sits in a ring of five nitrogen atoms on porous carbon. The team used a dual-confinement strategy, joining a wood framework with iron binding, to shape the catalyst.

The wood-derived carbon had hollow, linked pores at several scales, and sulfur doping came from the plant material. Tests and theory showed this set-up lowered the energy bar for releasing a key intermediate, speeding the reaction. The catalyst reached a half-wave potential of 0.964 volts, and zinc-air batteries using it beat a platinum benchmark.
pmc-13273248:
Anuradha Kesharwani and co-authors targeted a DNA sensing pathway in Huntington disease in a 2026 mouse study. Huntington disease is inherited, damages the brain, and involves strong inflammation, with no treatment that slows it. The pathway, called cGAS-STING, switches on inflammatory genes when stray DNA appears in cells.

In a humanized knock-in mouse model, removing the cGAS gene calmed brain immune cells, saved neurons, and limited shrinkage of the striatum, a movement center. Motor function improved, and gene activity patterns moved toward normal. A drug that blocks the partner protein STING gave similar relief of behavior and tissue damage. The authors name this pathway a promising target for future Huntington treatments.
pmc-13273848:
Tang and colleagues build a bispecific antibody against liver cancer using chemical assembly. Their 2026 journal article targets glypican-3, a marker on liver tumor cells. The antibody also blocks SIRP-alpha, a brake on immune cells called macrophages.

Standard bispecific antibodies need complex genetic production. This team used a rapid one-pot, two-step chemical process. Peptide dimers were linked to a native anti-SIRP-alpha antibody. The product draws macrophages toward tumor cells and boosts engulfing. In cell tests, tumor cell clearance beat the plain antibody. In mice, tumor growth fell by 68 percent. Macrophage entry into tumors rose, with more M1-type cells. Antigen presentation also increased. No visible body-wide toxicity appeared.
pmc-13274248: The notice is a correction only, issued in 2026 for an article on the Know Your Number; Control Your Number screening campaign in Nigeria. It fixes the author order, printed wrongly: the Nigeria Health Commissioners' Forum belongs first, ahead of Ayotunde Oguntade and the other named authors. It also replaces Figures 1 through 10, charts of results for over one and a half million participants, which were unclear and hard to read. Higher resolution versions appear with the notice, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13274548:
David Belada and a large team report 2026 results from the phase three PERSPECTIVE trial in follicular lymphoma, a slow-growing blood cancer. Patients were untreated and unfit for standard chemoimmunotherapy because of age or other illness. They received the antibody rituximab plus either the targeted pill ibrutinib or a placebo.

In total, 445 patients were randomized, three to one in favor of the drug combination, and followed a median of about fifty-four months. Time without disease worsening stretched to a median of 42.0 months with ibrutinib versus 32.8 months without. Response rates also favored the combination, at eighty-one versus sixty-eight percent. Overall survival did not differ significantly, and serious side effects were more common with ibrutinib.
pmc-13275248:
Zhihao Xiong and co-authors set out a trial protocol in 2026 to test acupuncture for post-stroke spasticity. That stiffness is common and disabling. Acupuncture may ease it, but earlier studies were weak, so benefit and safety stay uncertain.

Their randomized trial will enroll 180 patients and split them three ways: real acupuncture, sham acupuncture, or standard care alone. Treatment lasts four weeks, with four more weeks of follow-up. The main measure is a standard spasticity scale, backed by scores for movement, daily living, and nerve function, plus muscle recordings and ultrasound measures of stiffness. The authors also plan to explore how acupuncture might calm spastic muscle. Results should clarify whether the practice deserves a place in stroke rehabilitation.
pmc-13275748:
Patricia S Coffey and colleagues offer a 2026 practice note on preventing preeclampsia in five low- and middle-income countries. The countries covered are Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, and Pakistan. Global guidance backs low-dose aspirin and calcium supplements, yet real-world rollout remains patchy.

The team reviewed policies and interviewed 59 informants at global and national levels during 2023 and 2024. Aspirin progress was slowed by uneven clinical practice, low awareness, late antenatal visits, and weak supply chains. Calcium faced a complex dosing schedule and unclear national plans. The authors recommend stronger primary antenatal care and a coordinated package of preeclampsia measures.
pmc-13276148:
Pattanaket Cheewakongkiat and co-authors validate a Thai version of a shoulder instability survey, in work from 2026. An unstable shoulder cuts function and quality of life. The standard survey for it is widely used, but no checked Thai version existed.

Translation followed cross-cultural adaptation rules step by step. Sixty-two patients with one-sided instability filled in the new survey and a Thai arm function survey. Most patients were men, with a mean age near 29 years. Scores repeated two weeks later matched closely, and internal consistency was excellent. The Thai survey also tracked the arm survey almost perfectly. Clinics in Thailand can now measure this condition with confidence.
pmc-13276348:
Jyoti Soni leads a ten-author team reading microbes inside blood cells during and after COVID-19, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Immune cells carry intracellular microbes, and how those loads shift through illness is poorly mapped. The Omicron wave gave a defined shape to work on.

Single-cell sequencing covered more than one hundred ninety thousand blood cells from fifty-seven people. The groups spanned healthy people, the infected, the recently recovered, and the long recovered. Samples from the infected and recently recovered teemed with opportunistic bacteria, pushing diversity up. Healthy and long-recovered profiles were dominated by commensals, a balance that came back with time. Some signatures stuck around past the end of symptoms. The work reframes recovery as a return to balance inside the immune system.
pmc-13276448:
Pei-Lin Lee and colleagues present a 2026 study of white matter injury that is too heavy for a person's age. Bright scan spots grow with normal ageing, so raw amounts can mislead doctors about hidden small-vessel disease. A normative model instead compares each brain with what is expected at that age.

People whose burden sat far above the age norm carried worse vascular risk profiles. Their thinking skills suffered across several domains, and grey matter shrinkage was greater. Severe deviation predicted notably higher long-term death rates, roughly double in the strongest group. The authors propose age-adjusted scoring to flag high-risk people earlier, before symptoms appear.
pmc-13276748:
Marcel Mietzner and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a new drug tried in a rare, deadly lung vessel disease. Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease blocks the lung's small veins. No drug has proven benefit, standard vessel-widening drugs can flood the lungs, and most patients once died within a year.

Two patients with the hereditary form received sotatercept, the newest approved drug for related lung hypertension, on top of standard therapy. The drug works unlike the others, trapping growth signals to rebalance vessel biology. Both patients stabilized in overall condition and in how their lungs take up oxygen. Two lung transfer measures improved slightly under treatment. Neither the drug's trials nor prior experience covered this disease. The authors suggest it may steady such patients and stretch the bridge to a lung transplant, the only lasting fix.
pmc-13277048:
Vets judge horse welfare largely by eye, and blood markers that track stress load would sharpen that call. Maciej Kacprzyk and co-authors test four such markers — cortisol, serotonin, oxytocin, and a brain growth factor called BDNF — across three kinds of work. Their 2026 study drew paired blood samples from 17 show jumping horses, about 41 racehorses, and 14 leisure horses.

Serotonin moved the most, but in opposite ways: it fell after show jumping contests and rose on race day. BDNF rose only in show jumping geldings, while cortisol and oxytocin barely budged under the sampling plan. Leisure horses showed no change across the season. The team says a panel of markers can chart how each sport loads a horse, though no panel alone proves welfare is good or bad.
pmc-13277148:
Cemile Say, Refika Genc, and Mustafa Kilavuz studied mothers' views of newborn screening in a 2026 paper. A heel prick test in the first days of life screens babies for hidden diseases. In some places parents hesitate, and the team wanted to know why before the test, not after.

Nearly three hundred pregnant women answered a survey with both fixed and open questions in late 2023 and early 2024. Marital status shaped a few answers: single women reported more reading about the test. Open answers showed hesitation grew from missing information, false claims on social media, and poor communication with health staff. Other traits showed no clear pattern. The authors say the fix is plain: better information during pregnancy, from trusted staff, before rumors fill the gap. Screening programs depend on parents saying yes.
pmc-13277348:
Michelle Venâncio Hong leads a 2026 follow-up study of patients who developed pressure injuries, skin damage from sustained pressure, during a hospital stay. Little is known about how these patients fare after going home. The team tracked healing, return to hospital, and death after discharge.

By sixty days, about half of the injuries had improved and a third had fully healed. Yet twenty-two percent of patients had died after discharge, and some were readmitted. Having had a stroke made healing harder. Half of the patients got no care in the first week at home, a gap the authors flag. The findings argue for tighter follow-up plans at discharge.
pmc-13277448:
Xing Xu and colleagues build a phone-based three-dimensional scanning method for banana plants, in a 2026 paper. Measuring banana growth precisely matters for yield forecasting, yet laser scanners cost too much for wide farm use. Ordinary photo methods struggle with the plant's tangled canopy and weakly textured leaves.

Their framework, BN-NeRF, sharpens a fast neural rendering method with three fixes. Camera drift from handheld filming is corrected frame by frame, and sparse point clouds anchor true scale. A thin-leaf rule cleans up leaf surfaces that usually render poorly. Trials on ninety orchard plants gave high-quality reconstructions and trait values close to hand measurements. The study shows cheap phones can support serious field phenotyping.
pmc-13278448:
Zhiqiao Cheng and colleagues present a 2026 study of skid resistance in road asphalt made with steel slag, a steelmaking by-product. Skid resistance keeps vehicles from sliding, and it fades with wear and heat. The team ran accelerated wear tests at three steel slag levels and three temperatures, tracking two standard grip measures over time.

Both grip measures fell clearly as wear cycles rose, and high temperature sped the decline sharply. The two measures moved together overall, though their link differed across early, middle, and late wear stages. Those stages support segmented forecasts of how long grip will last in service. The results guide how much steel slag to use in different climates, the authors say.
pmc-13278748:
Martin Jacobsson and co-authors measure the error made when surgical blood pressure is stored too sparsely, in a 2026 study. Low blood pressure during surgery predicts complications, so researchers total its depth and duration. Records are often saved only every fifteen seconds to keep files manageable.

Data from 419 open-abdomen surgery patients at Karolinska University Hospital were compared against full waveform records. Fifteen-second sampling skewed event counts and total low-pressure time by roughly a quarter to a third. The area measure fared better but still missed by about a tenth. Attempts to correct the errors mostly failed to help. The authors insist on continuous data for trustworthy counts.
pmc-13279148:
Connor W. Smith and colleagues report a 2026 case of a very rare cause of low blood sugar. The cause is insulinomatosis, where many small tumours in the pancreas gland make too much insulin. Insulin is a hormone that lowers blood sugar. Their patient was a woman in her sixties with low sugar episodes through her life.

Blood tests fit the pattern of too much insulin from the body itself. Scans pointed to many tumours spread through the pancreas. Surgeons removed the whole pancreas, and lab checks of the tissue proved the diagnosis. Family members had past signs like hers, yet the gene basis stays unclear. The case shows why blood, scan, tissue and gene checks must line up.
pmc-13279248:
Maria Elisabeth Leinweber and Amun Georg Hofmann examine, in a 2026 study, whether Austria's vascular emergencies follow the seasons. Heart attack and stroke are known to vary by season, but evidence for other vessel events is thin. The authors drew on hospital admission records from 2009 to 2023, a span of fifteen years.

They tracked lung clots, aortic tears, vein clots, sudden limb blood loss, and burst belly aneurysms. Lung clots and aortic tears swung most, peaking in winter and dipping in summer. Vein clots moved in the same way, while the other two events varied less. Admissions also fell sharply on weekends, by more than half for several events. Daylight saving days showed small effects once compared with other Sundays. The authors urge local study of causes such as air pollution and care access.
pmc-13279748:
Mengtian Huang and colleagues give a 2026 review of tea proteins and interface design. Tea plant waste holds proteins that could serve as green food ingredients. Poor solubility and weak function hold them back. Interface engineering, which shapes how proteins act at oil water or air borders, is the key fix in their frame. The review links protein structure, interface acts and final function in one map.

Two sources lead: tea residue protein from leaf waste and tea seed protein. Change routes span physical, chemical, biological and mixed means. Uses hold food stabilizers, edible films, health peptide starts and particles for Pickering emulsions, which are drops armoured by solid grains. Scale up hurdles hold safety, taste, cost and legal rules. The authors chart routes to round, low waste food systems built on tea waste.
pmc-13279948:
Melissa Ann Stockton and a large team of co-authors adapt a suicide prevention program for teens living with HIV in Malawi. Their 2026 study starts from a gap: few proven programs fit this group in sub-Saharan Africa. The base is the Friendship Bench, a talking therapy, plus peer support.

Talks with teens, caregivers, staff, and community leaders shaped the changes. A safety planning step was woven in, where each teen builds a coping plan for moments of crisis. The final program runs one safety session, five problem-solving sessions, and six peer sessions. Plans were rewritten for areas with thin emergency services. Trainers were prepared through a training-of-trainers route, then tested the plan in theatre-style rehearsals.
pmc-13280948:
Claudia G Aguirre and colleagues compared how male and female rats learn for rewards in a 2026 study. Most past work used males only, which can skew results. Rats tapped a screen to pick between options for food. In one task, the picture itself marked the better odds. In the other, the side of the screen did. Midway, the better choice flipped, and rats had to adapt.

Females learned and adapted just as well as males. Yet they claimed fewer rewards and skipped more trials in both tasks. Math models of each choice fit best when they allowed shifts in focus over time. Females lapsed more once a rule was learned, as if their interest dropped. The authors say drive, not skill, split the sexes here.
pmc-13281248:
Puthy Pat and colleagues studied mental health care inside Cambodian prisons in a 2026 report. Prisoners face high rates of mental strain, yet care in prisons is thin. The team held group talks in three prisons across the country. Fifteen people took part, most of them prison health staff, plus four officials. Talks probed what blocks care and what might help.

Staff said basic care, referrals for severe cases, and some preventive steps do happen. But mental health gets little focus, and staff give what emotional support they can. Workers felt devoted yet worn down by low skills and scarce supplies. They asked for more training, awareness drives, job training for prisoners, and stronger backing from leaders and outside groups.
pmc-13281448:
Severo and co-authors bench-tested, in a 2026 study, a locally made modular external fixator for broken shin bones, built in the Philippines where imported frames cost too much for most patients. External fixators pin fractures from outside the skin while they heal. The prototype went through standard axial squeeze tests against two established frames.

Wrench-tightening its clamps multiplied the frame's strength one and a half to two and a half times. Even hand-tightened, it matched the Roger Anderson frame's mechanical performance. The team measured ultimate, yield, and safe strengths plus stiffness for each contender. Their verdict: the home-grown frame is stable enough to deserve clinical steps, and could put fracture care within reach where imported gear is a luxury.
pmc-13281948:
Li Ling and colleagues surveyed family doctors on lung disease skills in Shanghai in a 2026 study. The district was Pudong, a large city zone. COPD narrows airways for life and needs steady local care. Four hundred fifty-seven doctors answered, close to all who were asked. Most saw a modest flow of COPD patients each month. For nearly all, such patients filled under a third of their list. Yet hands-on lung testing was rare.

Four in five doctors ran the key breathing test ten times a year or fewer. Nearly half sent cough or breathless patients straight to specialists. Gaps showed in inhaler drugs, staging, symptom scales, test reading, and inhaler coaching. Confidence in managing the disease averaged under three of five. Training in residency and disease courses raised skill. So did age. The authors call for training that pairs facts with hands-on drills.
pmc-13282248:
Vanja Miljanić and co-authors describe a 2026 report of a new virus found inside a fungus that attacks hop plants. The fungus, Verticillium nonalfalfae, causes wilt disease in crops. The virus, given a tentative name shortened to VnaVM, carries its genes in six segments of double-stranded RNA, the chemical cousin of DNA. Segment lengths ran from about one thousand to about two thousand four hundred units.

Four segments code for known viral tools, including the enzyme that copies the virus genome. Two segments code for proteins with no known match, so their roles stay unknown. The known proteins differ enough from relatives to support a new species in an existing virus genus. Family tree analysis backed that placement. The authors say this is the first such virus reported in this fungus genus. Cataloguing fungal viruses matters because some may weaken the fungi that harm crops.
pmc-13282348: Qiaoping Qu and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their study of cell-free mitochondrial DNA as a possible marker of hypoxic stress. That DNA comes from the cell's power plants and is found outside cells. Hypoxic stress means harm from low oxygen. Figure 7 of the original article had appeared incorrectly. The correction replaces it with the right version, showing exosome features from cells exposed to low oxygen, and displays both versions for transparency. No other content is changed.
pmc-13282548:
Daniele Omar Traini and co-authors report a 2026 case using a non-invasive skin imaging method to diagnose a rare skin disorder. The disorder, shortened to CRP, makes dark small bumps merge into plaques with a net-like edge, usually on the trunk. Their patient was a twenty-nine-year-old woman with a three-year history of mildly itchy dark bumps on her back, sides, belly, and groin. A magnified skin view showed a brain-like network pattern.

The imaging method, a form of optical coherence tomography that scans skin in vivo, showed a thickened, bright outer layer and a wavy boundary between skin layers. Tissue biopsy confirmed the classic features: thickened surface, extra basal pigment, and raised surface growth. The authors say the scan's features matched the biopsy criteria in this case, a first report for this disorder.
pmc-13282848:
Wei Chen and co-authors present a 2026 study on whether eating more live microbes in food links to lower death rates in middle-aged and older stroke survivors in the United States. Dietary live microbe intake reflects eating microbe-rich foods such as fermented products. Using national survey data from 2003 to 2018, the team followed one thousand three hundred thirteen stroke survivors for a median of six years.

Five hundred thirty-nine participants died, two hundred nine of them from cardiovascular causes. Those with high microbe intake had about a third lower risk of death from any cause than the low intake group, a link that held across several adjusted models. No significant link appeared for cardiovascular death specifically. Subgroup and sensitivity checks generally supported the main finding. The authors call the results exploratory, since diet was captured by a single day's recall and stroke type was self-reported.
pmc-13282948:
Early lung tumors that come back after surgery motivated Wangyu Chen and partners to hunt for a better risk marker in 2026. Many patients relapse after surgery meant to cure them. Current markers such as PD-L1 guide care poorly at this stage, so the team searched for a stronger signal.

Gene data from large cancer databases were screened with machine learning tools. A gene called ERO1A stood out as a marker of poor survival and relapse risk. Tumors with high ERO1A grew fast yet also drew in active immune cells. They showed higher mutation load and PD-L1 levels. Tests on patient tissue confirmed the pattern and support its use for risk grouping.
pmc-13283048:
Chaymae Cherrabi and colleagues presented in 2026 the case of a seven-year-old girl with two overlapping autoimmune liver diseases. She had lasting jaundice, strong signs of liver cell injury, and high levels of immune proteins in her blood. Scans showed bile duct changes, and a liver sample confirmed autoimmune hepatitis, where the immune system attacks the liver itself.

Doctors diagnosed overlap between that disease and primary sclerosing cholangitis, a scarring disease of the bile ducts. The pairing is rare in children and hard to pin down, since no standard test rules exist. Treatment with prednisone and azathioprine, two immune-calming drugs, brought clear gains in her symptoms and blood tests. The report stresses early suspicion and shared care across specialties.
pmc-13283948:
Plant-made silver particles capped with a sugar ring are tested against crop germs and a crop pest by Chellasamy Panneerselvam and colleagues in 2026. Fruit extract of Peganum harmala both formed and stabilized the particles. The coating is beta-cyclodextrin, meant to keep particles dispersed.

Microscopy showed round, well-spread particles in a small size range. The particles blocked growth of four plant pathogens in dose-linked fashion. Killing values were low, which signals strong germ and fungus action. Larvae of the beet armyworm died more with higher dose and longer exposure. Feeding dropped sharply, supporting dual crop protection use.
pmc-13284148:
LinXin You and colleagues tested electroacupuncture in 2026 in a rat model of sudden hives. Acute urticaria affects about one in five people across a lifetime, and the molecular action of electroacupuncture for it was unclear. The team triggered a local allergic skin reaction with egg protein, then treated two acupoints on the leg and arm for five days, tracking wheal size and scratching.

Treated rats showed smaller wheals, less scratching, and less leakiness of skin blood vessels. Protein and metabolite profiling of skin and blood pointed to shifts in fat and amino acid pathways. Levels of two complement alarm signals, C3a and C5a, and their receptors fell in skin, and blood levels of three inflammatory mediators dropped. The authors frame the results as exploratory.
pmc-13284548:
Dessie Tegegne and co-authors give a 2026 five-year record review of gut parasite infections among HIV patients in northwest Ethiopia. Parasites remain common where water and sanitation are poor, even for patients on HIV therapy. Records for 600 patients on antiretroviral therapy at Debre Tabor hospital from May 2020 to May 2025 were reviewed for parasites, CD4 counts, and social traits.

One third of patients had a gut parasite infection in the records reviewed for this study period. The team used standard tests to find linked social and clinical factors, though local data had been scarce before. Full local results can guide targeted screening, deworming, and hygiene work for HIV patients at this hospital and in like settings.
pmc-13284748:

pmc-13285048:

pmc-13285148:

pmc-13285448:

pmc-13285648:

pmc-13285748:

pmc-13286148:
Thong Duc Hong and colleagues model the best ignition timing for a diesel engine running on methanol blends in a 2026 simulation study. pmc-13286448:
Ping Yu and Jin Xiao map how pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor cells change their energy habits as they develop, using single-cell data. Hundreds of genes separated the extremes, with energy machinery genes on one side and sugar-breaking enzymes on the other. A long non-coding RNA called MALAT1 best distinguished the states. pmc-13286748:
Hyunjoo Na and colleagues trace a pathway from heavy smartphone use to cyberbullying among Korean teenagers, using six years of national panel data. Published in 2026, the study followed 2,242 adolescents. Problematic phone use has been linked with online aggression, yet the steps between them over time were unclear.

Prevention, the authors argue, needs school and community programs alongside family rules, with strategies matched to teenagers' stage of development.
pmc-13286948:
Tong Liu and colleagues examine whether vitamin D levels relate to overactive bladder in women, and whether inflammation explains part of any link. The 2026 study analyzes a United States health survey of about twenty-five thousand adults plus a hospital cohort of roughly twenty-four hundred patients. Overactive bladder brings urgency and frequent urination that erode quality of life.

Two inflammation measures weakened the association when accounted for, suggesting they carry part of it. Genetic analysis pointed the same way. The authors read the combined evidence as a possible protective role.
pmc-13287048:
Rachana Verma and a large team report a working system for regenerating and gene-editing pigeonpea, a drought-tolerant legume that feeds many people in India's dry zones. Published in 2026, the work attacks a longstanding problem: pigeonpea tissue culture resists the callus growth and shooting that plant editing pipelines need, which has stalled improvement of the crop.

The platform, the authors say, can produce marker-free edited plants that ease biosafety concerns.
pmc-13287148:

pmc-13287248:
Merve Erdoğan Soysal and co-authors surveyed 99 people in 2026 with systemic sclerosis, a hardening illness, to learn what drives mouth-related difficulty in daily life. pmc-13287748:
Yi-Ping Wu and co-authors profiled proteins and their phosphate tags in 2026 in nasopharyngeal cancer. That tumour of the upper throat is common in parts of Asia. Cancer tissue was compared with healthy tissue from the same region. Patterns split the cancers into two molecular subtypes with different clinical behaviour.

A drug hunt flagged panobinostat, a broad gene-switch drug, which shrank tumours in cell and animal tests by cutting a growth gene and weakening DNA repair. Pairing it with radiation worked better still. Subtype-specific drug leads were also tested.
pmc-13288548:
David J Cangemi and co-authors review how to assess and treat patients whose constipation comes with prominent bloating, in a 2026 clinical article. Because the two complaints often arrive together yet can stem from different causes, the authors stress sorting out the underlying condition before choosing treatment.

Their walk-through separates chronic idiopathic constipation from the constipation form of irritable bowel syndrome, among other causes, and lays out a stepwise workup. Options covered range from diet changes and pelvic floor biofeedback to laxatives bought without prescription, secretagogues such as plecanatide, linaclotide, lubiprostone, and tenapanor, plus neuromodulators and antibiotics. pmc-13289248:
Jiawen Xu and coauthors report a 2026 field and lab study on carbon washed from rotting bamboo wood in southern China. The forest was a subtropical moso bamboo stand, and the species studied was Phyllostachys edulis. At the same time, microbes could use that carbon less easily, so bioavailability fell overall. pmc-13289348:

Heart damage from cancer drugs drives later illness in survivors. Drugs that block angiotensin or slow the heart have been proposed as shields, but proof strength across reviews was murky.

One filling measure improved with beta blockers at moderate certainty, urging caution in claims.
pmc-13289548:
Sevinj Salahova and co-authors report a stomach cancer operation where a major artery ran in an unexpected place. In some people the left hepatic artery branches from the left gastric artery instead of its usual source. A large, dominant version of this variant is rare, and cutting it by mistake could starve part of the liver.

Preoperative scans had shown the stray artery, and during surgery it was found running beside the liver's left lobe into the hilum. The case reminds surgical teams to read arterial maps before the first cut.
pmc-13289648:

pmc-13289948:
Giulia Iacono and colleagues run a 2026 prospective cohort hunting early warning signs of chronic lung transplant failure, called CLAD. pmc-13290348:
Nooran Rafeer and Matthew Adeleke reviewed genetic variety in 2026 among the parasites that cause coccidiosis in chickens. This gut disease costs poultry farming heavily worldwide. Variety inside and between parasite species shapes how severe infections get and how well control tools work.

pmc-13290448:

pmc-13290648:

pmc-13290748:
Thyroid hormones trace who survives heart-attack shock, Priyanka Boettger and colleagues report in a 2026 prospective cohort study. In cardiogenic shock after myocardial infarction, hormone levels shift with critical illness, and the team asked whether their paths predict death in hospital.

pmc-13290848:

pmc-13290948:

pmc-13291148:

pmc-13291348:

pmc-13291548:

pmc-13292048:

pmc-13292248:

pmc-13292448:

pmc-13292848:

pmc-13293348:

pmc-13293448:

pmc-13293648:

pmc-13293948:

pmc-13294148:

pmc-13294348:

pmc-13294448:

pmc-13294648:

pmc-13294948:

pmc-13295348:

pmc-13295848:

pmc-13296448:

pmc-13296648:

pmc-13296948:

pmc-13297048:
Wenyan Yuan and colleagues rank three candidate enzymes that may explain lauric acid richness in Litsea cubeba seed oil in a 2026 computational study. Seed oil composition shifts during development from longer-chain fats toward lauric acid dominance. The candidates came from a freshly assembled seed gene catalogue.

Sequence family trees, shared motifs, and structural models favoured two candidates over the third. Docking a twelve-carbon stand-in molecule gave cleaner binding poses for those two. Long simulations then separated them further, with the leading candidate holding the molecule in a steadier, more compact pose. The authors stress the ranking is a structural clue for laboratory testing, not proof of enzyme function.
pmc-13297348:
Sabina Caciolli and a large team chart heart problems in adults who received stem cell transplants for blood diseases, in a 2026 study. Transplant can cure such diseases, yet it can also strain the heart, and today's patients are often older with more prior illness. The team reviewed one centre's large cohort for both clear heart events and hidden muscle weakness shown by strain imaging, a fine measure of heart squeeze.

Most clear events were rhythm faults, fluid or rubbing around the heart, or weak pumping, while heart attacks and strokes stayed rare. Hidden muscle weakness showed up more often than clear events, above all after gentler preparation regimens. Routine heart checks and joint heart-cancer care are the authors' plea.
pmc-13297848:
Upper second premolars hide more anatomical variety than their usually single root suggests, warn Michał Głąbski and colleagues in a 2026 narrative review. Missing an extra canal can sink root canal treatment, so the authors gathered population studies of this tooth's internal shape.

From 358 papers found in PubMed, 27 studies using cone beam imaging qualified. Single roots appeared in over 70% of teeth, two roots came next, and three roots stayed under 2%, with men showing two roots more often. All eight Vertucci canal patterns occurred, Type I leading at over 50%, though some populations showed many complex forms. The review urges imaging-guided caution before assuming simple anatomy.
pmc-13298448:
Zeyu Wu and a large team examine whether intense exercise changes the machinery that builds microRNAs in human muscle, in a 2026 secondary analysis. Muscle biopsies came from two earlier studies: one single interval cycling bout, and six weeks of interval training against a control group. Gene messages and proteins for four biogenesis components were measured.

The single bout lowered one component's message, with a near-significant dip in another. Six weeks of training changed none of the measured proteins, and a representative muscle microRNA stayed flat at both early and mature stages. The authors highlight how complex microRNA control remains and ask for closer timing studies.
pmc-13298648:
Chatbots play the prisoner's dilemma in surprisingly cooperative ways, report Saptarshi Pal and colleagues in a 2026 study of five leading language models. The team probed how the models cooperate or defect across repeated rounds, varying payoffs, stopping chances, and whether the final round was known.

The models generally behaved generously, often landing on strategies that evolutionary theory deems robust, and they adjusted sensibly to many parameter changes. Yet none stayed fully consistent across every task, and some responses broke with both theory and human experimental patterns. Tournaments between the inferred strategies added further evidence. The authors frame the results as a check on trusting AI advice in social decisions.
pmc-13298948:
A drug-resistant E. coli strain hiding in a market fish's gills carries its resistance in its chromosome, report Amit Kumar and co-authors in a 2026 genome study. The isolate came from rohu carp bought at a retail fish market in Punjab, India, and resisted several antibiotic classes.

Sequencing produced a 3.70 Mb draft genome with 3,814 genes and 39 resistance determinants, including beta-lactam resistance and efflux pumps, plus virulence traits for iron capture, biofilm building, and host colonization. No plasmids turned up in the assembly. Prediction tools judged the strain, typed as ST8020, likely pathogenic to humans. The authors frame farmed fish as a possible resistance reservoir under a One Health lens.
pmc-13299048:
Genes guarding cells against oxidative stress and aging also shape who develops COPD, report Yanina Timasheva and colleagues in a 2026 genetic association study. They tested thirty-three variants in 747 patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and 703 controls, and built polygenic risk scores from the hits.

Signals landed in antioxidant genes such as NFE2L2 and HMOX1, in growth signaling genes, and in the mitochondrial gene TOMM40, among others. The strongest single variant, in PIK3R1, carried an odds ratio of 2.31. A weighted score alone discriminated moderately, and adding age, sex, and smoking lifted accuracy to an AUC of 88.1%. The authors tie the loci to stress adaptation and cell aging pathways.
pmc-13299148:
Emily M. Melnick and co-authors study whether letting WIC households buy frozen or canned produce improves benefit use, in a 2026 nutrition study within an Arizona tribal organisation. The programme grants monthly cash-value benefits for fruits and vegetables. Administrative data covered thousands of households, joined by a participant survey.

Households that bought frozen or canned items alongside fresh produce redeemed more of their benefit value, and heavier frozen purchasing predicted higher redemption. Families with several enrolled members used the option more, and longer shelf life was the most cited reason. The authors suggest programme policies should allow and promote preserved produce for American Indian families.
pmc-13299348:
Fresh-made compounds made rays hit one brain tumor line hard and left a next line near whole. Dorota Natorska-Chomicka and her team report that split in a 2026 study. They built two new hydrazide-hydrazone agents from a bromo-iodo benzoic acid and paired each with X-rays on glioblastoma cells.

In LN-229 cells, agent 3 at 164 μM plus 2 Gy cut cell life by 65%. It also pushed more cells toward death. Agent 4 at 242 μM halved cell life across 2 to 5 Gy. It stalled the cell cycle and drove cell death. In U-87MG cells, the same agents did scant work or even sped growth. The team stress that each tumor's own make-up sets whether a sensitizer helps.
pmc-13300948:
A Sikorska and co-authors probe the acute heart safety of cardioneuroablation in a 2026 prospective study. The procedure burns nerve inputs to slow a vagal brake that works too hard in people with fainting or functional slow rhythms. Critics worry that taking away parasympathetic restraint could invite dangerous ventricular rhythms. Eighty patients had programmed ventricular stimulation and timing measurements before ablation, after it, and again after atropine and a stimulant drug pushed denervation further.

Ventricular tachycardia could be set off in only two patients, one before and one after the procedure. Both had earlier heart disease. The action potential grew shorter after ablation. The refractory period barely moved, except under the stimulant, and one QT formula showed lengthening only in the fully drugged state. Dispersion of repolarization never changed. The authors conclude acute proarrhythmia looks rare and tied to underlying disease, while long term course stays unknown.
pmc-13301448:
V Probst and co-authors test how faithfully a Brugada syndrome gene predicts the disease inside large families in a 2026 genetics study. The team enrolled 463 people from forty-five families, each built around a patient carrying a pathogenic variant in SCN5A, the main gene tied to this fainting and sudden death condition. Relatives were checked for the family variant and challenged with a drug test that unmasks the heart tracing.

The mismatches ran both ways. Of 258 carriers, seventy-five, about thirty percent, never showed the syndrome even after provocation, an incomplete penetrance. Meanwhile thirty-two people diagnosed with Brugada did not carry their family's variant at all. About twenty-four percent of individuals were genotype phenotype mismatches. The authors conclude the SCN5A variant is neither necessary nor sufficient, and they now hunt the background factors that tip carriers toward or away from illness.
pmc-13302648:
Chenyujun Hu and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, hydrogel materials designed to grow blood vessels and bone together during repair. Bone healing fails when vessel growth lags, a coupling that weakens with age, poor circulation, and chronic inflammation. The gel, called GelMA, mimics natural tissue matrix and can be shaped by three-dimensional printing.

Strategies are sorted into three families: building guidance into the material itself, delivering active cargo such as growth factors and cells, and making gels that respond to local signals. Delivery systems hold the strongest early evidence, while built-in designs may prove easier to manufacture consistently. Responsive systems remain mostly small-animal experiments. The authors urge simpler, reproducible designs over added complexity.
pmc-13303148:
Christos G. Nikolaidis and co-authors review, in a 2026 narrative review, how gut microbe imbalance may feed the complications of type 2 diabetes. Organ damage keeps rising even as glucose control improves, hinting at other drivers. The authors gather microbial patterns linked to kidney, eye, nerve, and vessel complications.

Shared routes include a leakier gut barrier, toxin seepage into blood, and smouldering inflammation that ages tissues faster. Some microbial signatures repeat across organs, while others appear specific to one complication. Microbe-based tests and treatments, plus machine learning over microbiome data, are discussed as add-ons to standard care. The authors stress that most proof is still associative and needs long-term mechanistic studies.
pmc-13303448:
Sally Fuchs and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study mapping protein kinase A parts in healthy and diabetic kidneys. Diabetic kidney disease can end in dialysis or transplant, and signals driven by cyclic nucleotides may help drive the damage.

Kidney tissue was stained to locate the catalytic subunits called Cα and Cβ. Diabetes was triggered with streptozotocin in normal mice and in mice lacking endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Cα appeared in all kidney cell types, while Cβ was strong mainly in proximal tubules and weak elsewhere. Neither subunit changed clearly in diabetic or knockout kidneys compared with controls.
pmc-13303848:
Andrea Migliorelli and co-authors scope, in a 2026 review, whether simple blood inflammation ratios can forecast outcomes in cancers of the nose and sinuses. These rare tumours are often found late and recur often, so cheap prognostic clues are welcome. Six studies covering just over a thousand patients met the criteria.

The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio was the most studied marker and the one most often tied to worse survival, later stage, and higher recurrence. Composite scores mixing platelets, albumin, and inflammation counts may add extra signal, early evidence suggests. Every included study was retrospective and single-centre, with inconsistent cut-off values between them. The authors call for prospective multicentre work before these ratios guide real treatment decisions.
pmc-13304148:
Shuyang Li and colleagues test road base mixes that swap in steel slag, a steelmaking leftover often stockpiled in huge piles, in a 2026 engineering study. Cement dose and slag share were varied to find a strong, greener blend.

Crushing, stiffness, and splitting tests tracked strength as mixes changed. More cement raised every strength measure, though gains slowed at high doses. Strength rose with slag share up to a point, then eased, while stiffness kept climbing. At the best slag level, key strengths peaked well above the plain control mix. Microscope views showed denser internal structure behind the gains.
pmc-13306848:
Xuelei Jia improved flexible pressure sensors by spreading copper particles evenly with ultrasound in a 2026 study. Clumped filler inside soft PDMS layers destabilises electrical response, so sound-wave mixing was used during layer making.

Models and simulations showed even spread steadies permittivity and calms local electric field spikes. Finished sensors beat standard builds on sensitivity, stability and working range in reported tests, reaching 0.157 kPa−1 in the low range of 0 to 1 kPa in the given units. Performance held across 1000 loading cycles, supporting wearable and robot touch uses. Soft touch skins for health wear and robot hands are named as prime uses.
pmc-13307048:
Jon Stewart Dy and colleagues map research in 2026 on neuroarts, the study of how creative experiences affect brain, body, and well-being. Their scoping review gathered studies from 2000 to late 2025 across five databases, screening more than nine thousand records. Sixty-seven studies met the inclusion rules.

Music, dance, literature, visual arts, and wider cultural engagement all appeared as interventions in healthy and clinical groups. Reported gains covered mental well-being, cognitive function, and quality of life. Study categories followed World Health Organization groupings of art forms. The authors present neuroarts as a framework linking artistic practice to health mechanisms. They support bringing arts-based activity into therapy and health promotion, while noting the field is still defining its foundations.
pmc-13308648:
Chengsong Yue and colleagues analyse in 2026 whether minutes spent inside the artery during clot removal predict recovery after large-core stroke. Records covered 490 patients at thirty-eight centres who had thrombectomy for major vessel blockage with already large infarcts. Outcomes were scored ninety days later for function, death, and brain bleeding.

Every extra ten minutes of procedure time lowered the odds of a reasonable functional outcome and raised mortality odds. Modelled chances of moderate recovery fell from about forty-five percent at one hour to about twenty-eight percent at two and a half hours. Curve analysis found no safe threshold where extra time stopped mattering. Bleeding complications showed no consistent link with duration. The authors propose procedure time as a live risk gauge, prompting teams to reassess strategy as minutes accumulate.
pmc-13308948:
Kewei Jia, Xin Li, and Bin Liao report in 2026 a near fatal aortic hole torn during a neck vein line try for dialysis in a man aged 61 years. He had stage 5 kidney disease at the time. The line had crossed an artery and the brachiocephalic trunk, with its tip outside the aorta and blood pooled around the heart.

Surgeons took the line out under direct sight, with hand pressure and a heart lung bypass rig on standby for control. He healed with no snags after that high risk rescue in theatre. Blind pulling of a suspect line can kill, the team warns, so fast scans, surgical calls, and live ultrasound for each try are key.
pmc-13309248:
Marit Verheijen and co-authors work out the thermodynamics of microbes fed two foods at once. New routes make simple one- and two-carbon compounds from carbon dioxide. Alone they feed microbes poorly. Mixed with a main food like glucose, they might boost growth. The team builds a general frame, tied to no single species, that splits growth and energy fluxes.

The best strategy spends the second food as an electron donor. Glucose then stays free for building cell mass. Yield holds steady until glucose runs short, then dips. Growth rate follows the same shape. Mixed feeders can beat pairs of specialists on total biomass. Field sightings of generalists winning in lean waters match the math.
pmc-13309448:
Cornelia Hildegard Oberrauter and colleagues report a 2026 surgical study on a simpler way to reattach bone in reverse shoulder replacement after a bad upper arm break. The usual method uses four or five stitches to fix the bone knob that anchors key muscles. The team tested a two-stitch method meant to shorten surgery without hurting healing.

Seventy-three patients were followed for two years after surgery, and most were older women with weak bone. Shoulder scores at two years were high, and scans tracked whether the bone knob healed in place. A side comparison looked at cemented versus uncemented stems. The authors present the simpler stitch method as workable in this frail group.
pmc-13309848:
Deeksha Singh and co-authors profile the genes at work in a medicinal pepper plant in a 2026 study. Piper chaba, a relative of black pepper, makes the pungent compound piperine, valued for drug-like effects. Which genes build piperine, and where the plant stores most of it, were unknown.

Gene reads from spike, leaf, and root tissue yielded 228,481 transcripts, trimmed to 184,574 unique genes for analysis in the study. Chemical assay found piperine richest by far in the spike, at 331.3 mg/g in the reported measure, with root and leaf far lower. Thirteen candidate genes tied to piperine building were flagged from pathway maps. The authors offer the gene set as a base for breeding and biotech work.
pmc-13310648:
Nikoleta Papanikolaou and co-authors image testicle blood vessels at super-fine detail in a 2026 study. Male infertility and low hormone output are rising, and current tests capture vessel health poorly. Tiny vessel flow underpins testicle function, and a new ultrasound method maps vessels far below standard resolution.

Men with a hormone-driven low-output condition were compared with healthy men, then tracked across treatments including testosterone, hormone therapy, and fertility care over twelve months. A rodent model of blocked puberty joined the design. Vessel density, width, and winding separated patients from controls and tracked hormone levels in the reported results. Azoospermia, the absence of sperm, showed reduced vessel measures. The authors propose vessel mapping as a diagnostic aid.
pmc-13310948:
Rafael Yoshida and co-authors compare growing and fixed rods for brittle bone disease in children in a 2026 review. Osteogenesis imperfecta weakens collagen, so bones bend and break with ease. Rods placed inside long bones give support, and telescopic rods extend as a child grows, which may cut repeat surgery.

Past studies totaled 36 in number, covering 1,711 patients and 2,459 treated bones. Telescopic rods linked to far lower revision rates than fixed rods. Overall complication rates did not differ clearly between rod types. Longer implant life supports favoring growing rods in clinic practice, with care matched to each child.
pmc-13311148:
Hanvit Lee reports a 2026 case of a tunneled vein catheter placed through one skin cut in a newborn. A preterm boy needed long term vein feeding after gut concerns and hard vein access. Standard tunneling uses two skin cuts, and the exit near the diaper zone raises germ risk, so a single cut method was tried.

Guided by imaging, the line entered through one small thigh cut and tunneled under skin into the thigh vein, placing the exit away from the diaper area. The line worked steadily for 14 days with no infection or slipping. One case proves feasibility only, not lower infection rates.
pmc-13311248:
Beata Huszcza and colleagues, in 2026, give a narrative review of enteroscopy, the set of scope methods used to inspect and treat the small bowel. The bowel's length and folds make it hard to reach with standard scopes.

The review, drawn from MEDLINE papers from 2001 to 2025, covers capsule scopes and device-assisted scopes. Main uses include finding bleeding sources, checking Crohn's disease and celiac disease, and finding tumors. Assisted scopes also allow biopsies, stopping bleeding, widening narrow spots, and removing polyps or stuck objects. Reported risk stays low, and the methods can cut the need for surgery.
pmc-13311648:
Anne Sophie Mathiesen and co-authors report the 2026 randomized trial of guided self-determination, a talk-based method that supports patient autonomy, for adults with type 2 diabetes. The rival was an attention control program.

The two-center trial stopped early after 150 of 224 planned patients were enrolled, with 74 in the method group and 76 in the control group. Sessions ran face-to-face, by phone, or by video. The main outcome was diabetes distress at twelve months, with mood, quality of life, and side effects also tracked. Early results favored the method on distress. The trial shows both promise and the cost of early stopping.
pmc-13311748:
Bolin Jin and co-authors hunt blood protein markers that warn of coming carotid plaque in a 2026 nested case-control study. Plaque in the neck artery is an early sign of the vessel disease behind heart attacks and strokes.

The ChinaHEART cohort supplied 145 people who developed plaque and 147 matched controls without it at the start. Eleven proteins stood out, among them thrombomodulin, growth differentiation factor-15, adiponectin, and IL-10. The team then checked how the findings travel to the UK Biobank, a far larger British cohort. A blood panel of this kind could one day flag risk years before symptoms.
pmc-13311948:
Naomi Kemps and colleagues present a 2026 multi-country study on whether low blood pressure helps spot serious illness in children at acute care sites in poorer countries. Routine pressure checks in children have been questioned.

Data came from three sites in The Gambia and Suriname, covering more than twenty-two thousand visits in all. Low pressure by age-based cutoffs appeared in 8.3 to 17.3 percent of visits across sites. Serious illness, defined by admission or referral upward, was the outcome tested. The study weighs whether a cheap cuff reading earns its place in first assessment where illness runs high.
pmc-13312248:
Matthew Smith and colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, whether an epidural changes the risk of surgical site infection after open colorectal surgery. Epidurals bring several known gains for these patients, but infections remain common after colorectal operations, and any link between the two had barely been studied.

The team analyzed 2022 and 2023 data from the American College of Surgeons quality registry, with 6,343 patients, of whom 1,495, about 24 percent, got an epidural. Across all models, epidurals showed no clear link to infection overall, to infection at the wound, or to deep organ-space infection within 30 days. A second analysis using propensity weighting agreed. Patients having stoma-forming procedures fared worse on all three infection outcomes than those having surgery without a stoma.
pmc-13312448:
Ioulia Exapicheidou and a large chemistry team report a 2026 hit-to-lead study of compounds that block energy-coupling factor transporters in bacteria. These membrane proteins ferry needed vitamins into many Gram-positive bacteria. They are absent from human cells, making them an attractive antibiotic target as resistance spreads. Starting from an earlier inhibitor, the researchers varied one end of the molecule using click chemistry. They optimized several drug-like properties at once.

The refined compounds gained stability and dissolved more readily. They kept strong activity against the transporters and against a panel of Gram-positive bacteria. Against Enterococcus faecium, killing was rapid. The best leads then proved themselves in living infection models, working in wax moth larvae and in zebrafish. Confirming efficacy in animals moves this compound class from an interesting lab finding toward a credible drug development path.
pmc-13312548:
David T. Hogan and co-authors report, in a 2026 chemistry study, a small fluorescent molecule with an unusually wide gap between the light it absorbs and the light it emits. Most dye families absorb and emit at close wavelengths, causing self-reabsorption and blocking multi-color sensing from one excitation light, and the usual fix is donor-acceptor charge transfer design.

The team instead placed permanently charged donor and acceptor groups in meta positions on a single benzene ring, a neglected geometry. The resulting zwitterion absorbs ultraviolet light at 375 nanometers and emits yellow-orange at 605 nanometers, a Stokes shift above 10,000 wavenumbers, the largest recorded for such a compound. Calculations credit stronger charge transfer and extra energy shed through structural reshaping after excitation, tied to excited-state antiaromaticity. Extended versions kept the wide shift, suggesting a general design rule.
pmc-13312648:
Mersad Ery, Mohammad Mehravar, and three co-authors test walking under extra load in people with chronic neck pain. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, uses a treadmill and motion tracking. Twenty-one adults with long-term neck pain walk beside twenty-two matched controls. Each walks normally and heel-to-toe, with and without a thinking task.

The pain group paid a much higher cost when thinking while walking. Step rate, stride length, and speed all slipped more for them. Heel-to-toe walking also slowed their step rate versus controls. Everyone shortened strides under the dual task. The authors read this as neck pain drawing on the same attention pool as walking.
pmc-13312748:
Stina Engelheart and Lisa Spang explore, in a 2026 case study, where older immigrants with dementia want to live as the disease advances. They also ask how their families weigh home against residential care. Ageing populations grow more diverse, yet how immigrants experience dementia inside a foreign culture, and what care they wish for, remains little studied.

The team interviewed people with dementia and their relatives in two households where a husband had the disease. One couple fought to preserve togetherness as abilities faded; in the other, acting-out symptoms pushed safety ahead of staying together. Both saw moving into residential care as a deep threshold, shadowed by rigid routines, doubt about staff skill, and cultural and language mismatches. The authors ask officials to design services that protect identity and meaningful daily habits for this group.
pmc-13313148:
Alice Moura Martins and co-authors chart, in a 2026 micro-CT study, the hidden side canals inside baby upper molars. Children's root canal treatment fails when accessory canals, tiny branches off the main root canal, shelter bacteria from cleaning, yet the anatomy of these canals in primary teeth was poorly mapped.

Seventeen primary maxillary molars from donors aged 2 to 8, together holding 47 roots, were scanned and reconstructed in three dimensions. Over two thirds of roots, 68.08 percent in the reported count, held at least one accessory canal, and 96 canals were found in all. The tip third of the root was the most crowded, carrying 42.71 percent of the canals, ahead of the middle and neck thirds. The authors say the survey proves these teeth are anatomically trickier than they look and demands thorough disinfection in treatment.
pmc-13313748:
Alejandro Montenegro-Avila and co-workers pool trial data in a 2026 review of whether GLP-1 drugs cut heart risk in type 2 diabetes. Heart outcome trials hint these drugs lower major adverse cardiovascular events in people who also have artery disease, but the size of the gain, with new trials and pill forms, was unsettled.

The team searched five databases on 6 May 2025 under set review rules, registered as CRD420251034652. Seven trials with 56 191 participants in total were pooled, with a mean follow-up of 3.5 years, per the report. The drugs cut major events, such as heart attack, stroke, and heart death, against placebo or usual care, with landmark trials like SOUL included. The pooled numbers give doctors a firmer sense of how much heart protection these drugs add.
pmc-13313948:
Asma Abdlhusen Shrshoh and Nafea Sabih Jasim report, in a 2026 study, the design and trial of a multi-epitope mRNA vaccine against Newcastle disease, a scourge of poultry farming. Rather than using whole virus, the vaccine stitches together predicted immune-triggering fragments from the virus's two proteins. They were selected for binding strength, antigenicity, safety, and conservation across strains. Two hundred eighty chickens were randomized into eight groups, including the vaccine, six commercial vaccines, and an unvaccinated control, then challenged with a virulent strain.

Birds receiving the mRNA vaccine mounted higher antibody titers than controls, with stronger lymphocyte proliferation and more interferon-producing cells. After challenge, that group showed the best protection, with the fewest and mildest clinical signs and the lowest mortality. It edged out rival products. The authors claim a first for this vaccine architecture against Newcastle disease. They argue such mRNA designs could modernize poultry vaccination.
pmc-13314148:
Marina Louza Palmeira de Carvalho and colleagues synthesize, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, how often hormone diseases appear in Brazilian dogs and cats treated at hospitals and referral centers. Local evidence was fragmented, with no population-wide registry like the British VetCompass system to anchor estimates. Searching seven sources for studies from 2005 to 2025, the team screened 2,501 records. They kept thirteen that met their criteria, appraising quality and pooling proportions where the designs allowed.

Frequencies swung widely with setting, exactly the referral bias the authors suspected. Hormone disorders looked uncommon in broad hospital caseloads but far more frequent inside specialist cohorts. Hyperparathyroidism stayed consistently rare, between 0.01 and 0.07 percent across studies. One multicenter cohort put hypoadrenocorticism at 0.09 percent of its dogs. The authors insist Brazilian numbers be read as setting-specific caseload shares, never as population prevalence. They use British primary-care figures only as a benchmark for contrast.
pmc-13314348:
Hanan Waleed Kasim Agwaan compares, in a 2026 feeding trial, three supplement strategies for Awassi rams enduring heat stress in arid conditions. Heat degrades growth, blood health, and hormone balance in sheep, and feeds are a proposed countermeasure. Twenty-four rams were randomized for ninety days to plain feed, beta-glucan, a vitamin C and zinc pairing, or all three supplements together. Productivity, blood, biochemical, stress, and hormone measures were tracked.

Every supplemented group beat the control, but the full combination dominated. It produced the heaviest final weight at 72.5 kilograms. It also produced the fastest growth rate at 26.97 percent, and the best feed conversion, alongside stronger red and white blood cell counts. Blood chemistry improved, with sugars, cholesterol, and liver enzymes down and protein and antioxidant status up. Stress cortisol fell and hormones rose. Agwaan concludes the trio acts and recommends it as a heat-season ration strategy.
pmc-13314748:
Ketum Ateh Stanislas and a large team compare what young women think their heart risk is with what scores say, in a 2026 study. Heart disease is the top killer of women, yet awareness among women of childbearing age has fallen, and low risk sense can blunt prevention.

The study drew 139 women from the Baltimore and Washington DC area, aged 18 to 50 years, with a mean age of 32.0 years as stated in the report. Each woman rated her own heart and stroke risk against peers on a seven-point scale. True heart health was graded by the Life Essential 8 set of measures. Crossing the two sorted women into matched or mismatched groups, and models hunted traits that predict underrating risk. The gap matters: women who feel safe may skip the checks that catch risk early.
pmc-13315648:
Shabnam Anjum and co-authors built in 2026 a fiber system that releases two agents at different times to heal bone defects weakened by osteoporosis. Healing needs strong early bone building plus steady restraint of bone loss across the whole repair period, a timing match that current methods miss.

Core-shell fibers made by coaxial spinning held the drug alendronate in the core and carried stem cell exosomes on the surface, fixed with a chemical coating. Tests confirmed the build, with tensile strength of 22.77 megapascals and a very low water contact angle showing a wettable surface. The timed release aims to coordinate bone-forming and bone-resorbing cells.
pmc-13316748:
Zuhui Zhang and colleagues, in a 2026 prospective study, test whether large language models can help train eye specialists in China. Shortages of ophthalmologists are unevenly spread, and training support is one proposed use for these systems. Eleven leading models were compared with ten resident doctors from a tertiary eye hospital.

Models first sat a national ophthalmology examination in Chinese and English. Several Chinese models scored very highly, and the best outperformed every resident on the Chinese paper. Giving residents that model for help raised their average text examination score markedly, and all ten passed. Help with classifying images of corneal inflammation, however, brought no gain. Trainee feedback matched that split, warm for text and much cooler for images.
pmc-13317048:
João Brázia, Boxuan Wang, Paula Meireles, Eugenio Valdano, and Andreia Teixeira review, published in 2026, how studies in Portugal measure what people know and use about HIV prevention. Portugal still reports among Europe's highest HIV case numbers despite global target pledges. The review searched three databases for work from 2008 to 2025 on key groups: sex workers, men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, migrants, and transgender people. Fifty-four studies qualified. Most tracked condom use and testing.

No study measured what people know about condoms, only how they use them, and even usage was defined dozens of ways. Testing knowledge meant knowing where to test and that it is free and private. Drug-based prevention was bundled with condom questions. The authors say this patchwork blocks comparison and weakens policy models. They urge common measures across groups so prevention programs can be judged on common ground.
pmc-13317448:
Chunyan Chi writes, in 2026, about new work toward pure red light from organic displays. Ultra-high-definition screens need narrowband red emitters, yet red versions of a much-watched material class still emit across too wide a spectrum. Broadening comes largely from shaking and settling inside the material, which grow worse at longer wavelengths.

Chi discusses a study that rebuilt a globally aromatic molecule, ovalene, into related structures with varied fusion patterns. Work using chemical shift analysis showed that fusion choices change aromatic character and how the material emits. Structures with more local aromaticity cut the shaking link and sharpened the spectrum. The piece frames electron spread as a design lever for meeting strict display colour standards in future devices.
pmc-13317548:
Jiaying Wu, Xiaorong Peng, Yunan Chang, and Hongmei Xu build a 2026 prediction model for serious liver injury in children with chronic hepatitis B who have never been treated. A biopsy can prove injury but is too invasive for routine use in children, so they sought answers in ordinary clinical data.

Records held 246 children who had biopsies, and 59.8 percent of them showed serious injury. A feature-picking method chose five predictors, and among nine learning models a plain logistic model proved steadiest, scoring 0.799 in training checks and 0.707 on a held-out test group. The chart form beat the standard single enzyme test across most decision thresholds, though the gain stayed modest.
pmc-13317748:
Yang and coauthors build a smart test to count gene bits in a sample. Such tests screen for tumors, gene illness, and infections. Most tools use light to track a gene growth step. The link between light and the growth step shifts with each test setup.

The team adds deep learning guided by known test rules. Their model learns how light curves map to gene counts. It aims to stay right when gene type, sample type, or tools change. The work seeks counts that labs can trust for care and for outbreak control. More checks will show how wide the method can go.
pmc-13318548:
Abdullahi Hassan Elmi and Fahma Hussein Ibrahim recount a 2026 case of necrotising fasciitis, a fast-moving flesh-destroying infection, in an eight-year-old girl who had been healthy before. She arrived with high fever, severe pain, and spreading dead tissue on her right leg and buttock, two months after chickenpox.

Blood tests showed strong signs of serious infection, and her risk score of 10 pointed to high danger in this presentation. Wound cultures grew Proteus mirabilis, an unusual culprit, and treatment followed the sensitivity results. Urgent surgery to cut away dead tissue, intravenous antibiotics, and ongoing wound care brought improvement. Because chickenpox had ended long before, the authors warn against assuming it directly caused the infection.
pmc-13318648:
Rui Wu and Gaiqi Yao present a 2026 cross-sectional study linking routine blood count inflammation markers to thickened heart muscle in people with diabetic kidney disease. Their sample held 419 patients treated at Peking University Third Hospital between January 2020 and September 2025.

Heart scans split the group into 106 patients with thickening and the rest without.
