Higher neutrophil counts and a combined immune-inflammation index each tracked with thickening, as did uric acid and urea, while male sex and calcium pointed the other way. Adding the two blood markers to basic factors lifted prediction accuracy to an AUC of 0.816 in their model. Kidney stage did not change those links in the analysis.
pmc-13318848:
Antoine Christiaens and colleagues test, in 2026, whether a trial result on reducing blood pressure medicines in very old adults holds in routine English primary care. The OPTiMISE trial found that stopping one such drug did not worsen short-term control in people aged 80 and over. Trial participants, however, are usually fitter than typical patients.

The team rebuilt a target population from records of practices in England, covering nearly eight hundred thousand eligible adults. This real-world group was frailer and carried more illness than trial participants. Statistical weighting aligned the groups on likely trial entry. After calibration, reducing medication was not linked to higher risk of hospital stay or death, matching the trial's long-term findings. The authors judge the result transferable, with somewhat wider uncertainty.
pmc-13319048:
Weihan Kong and colleagues present a 2026 multi-omics study of polysaccharide build-up in the medicinal fungus Ganoderma tsugae. Fruiting bodies were grown on oak logs in a nature-mimicking setup. Five growth stages ran from early primordia to the end of spore release. Gene activity and metabolite profiles were measured together.

Crude polysaccharide content rose through the first three stages. It peaked at stage three, reaching 0.90 g per 100 g in their measurements, then declined. Analysis found 5,676 genes and 911 metabolites changing across stages. Starch and sucrose metabolism formed the core pathway for accumulation. Galactose metabolism played a supporting role in supplying building blocks. The authors name stage three as the key turning point for harvest timing research.
pmc-13319248:
Yuki Yoshida and colleagues evaluate, in 2026, a modified examination position for spotting early throat cancers during stomach endoscopy in high-risk patients. People treated for food pipe or throat cancer face raised risk of new cancers low in the throat. That area is hard to see because of its anatomy.

Forty-five patients were examined by the conventional method and then by the modified Killian method during the same session. Visibility scores for the lowest throat area rose with the modified method, and rose further when a straining manoeuvre was added. Viewing of neighbouring areas did not suffer. The method took longer, yet it found three early cancers the conventional pass had missed. No adverse events occurred, supporting wider use in this high-risk group.
pmc-13319948:
Ibrahim Ragab Eissa and co-authors study a collagen grip protein that keeps killer immune cells out of pancreas tumors in a 2026 article. This cancer wraps itself in dense scar like tissue that aids growth and blocks immune entry. The grip protein helps tumor cells cling to collagen, and the team asked whether it also shapes the immune scene around the tumor.

Tumors held far more of the protein than healthy pancreas tissue. When the protein was removed, tumor cells clung less, tumors grew slower, and far more killer cells moved in, while wiping out those cells restored growth. Loss of the protein also raised a signal that calls killer cells in and loosened collagen layout. A blocking drug copied those gains, which marks the protein as a care target.
pmc-13320348:
Stefanos Mastrotheodoros and co-authors follow teens into young adulthood in a 2026 study of social stress, body swelling, and low mood. Stress with parents and peers in the teen years lifts later low mood risk, and lasting low grade swelling may be the bridge. Gene tag scores for a swelling marker in spit were used to test that bridge over time.

Data came from 434 teens in a Dutch study, with stress drawn from rows with parents and from peer harm, tracked to age 27. Stress showed no link to the swelling scores at age 17 or 25 and no link to low mood at 27 in the main models. One side check hinted that harsh parenting, not peer harm, may touch one swelling score in mid teens only.
pmc-13320448:
Grace Marley and co-authors pilot a pharmacist led help service for addiction drug dispensing in a 2026 study from North Carolina. A key drug for opioid addiction is stocked unevenly at drug stores, held back by stigma and poor links with prescribers. Five community pharmacists took an online course plus about six one to one help meets with a peer coach and acted out patient visits before and after.

The pharmacists rated the coaching as fitting and useful because it bent to each store own snags, from staff talks and buyer limits to red flag checks and bridge scripts. A first in person visit plus short video follow ups was the favored shape. Talks with acted patients got better after coaching, though some stigmatizing words lingered.
pmc-13320548:
Heydar Ghiasi and Navid Ghavi Hossein-Zadeh run a 2026 computer simulation on breeding dairy cattle for both milk yield and fertility. Selecting hard for milk alone often harms fertility, since some gene markers push the two traits in opposite ways. The simulation used the direction of marker effects from genome wide studies to test smarter selection plans.

Markers with opposing effects created trade-offs and negative links between the traits, and single trait selection gave the most gain in that trait while hurting the other. Markers that favoured both traits allowed more balanced progress. The results stress that marker direction and shared gene action should guide breeding choices when two valued traits pull apart.
pmc-13321148:
Bernard Benichou and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to a first-in-human phase I study of VTX-PID, an enzyme made to clear antibodies that block gene therapy. The NAVIgATE study tested the IdeS enzyme in people with neutralising antibodies to an AAV vector. The correction fixes Figure 4 and an omission in the acknowledgments.

Panel 4C now shows the correct negativity threshold, set at below 1 to 5, and the legend now names that threshold. The figure tracks total and neutralising antibody levels up to day 90 after dosing, with early detail to day 13. The acknowledgments now credit writing assistance from Nicolisha Narainpersad of Parexel, which had been left out.
pmc-13321448:
Ilaria Iacobucci and co-authors map the protein changes inside stiffened heart valves, in a study published in 2026. In calcific aortic valve stenosis, the valve narrows and hardens, and no drug can slow it. Surgery samples offer a direct look at the tissue, so the team profiled valves removed from patients with severe disease against valves from patients whose valves leaked instead.

Mass spectrometry measured thousands of proteins at once. Nearly six hundred differed in the diseased valves, clustering in clotting, immune, and matrix pathways. A second method tracked how matrix proteins were being cut apart, and a third mapped chemical marks on collagen. Targeted tests confirmed the main candidates, and staining showed damaged elastin. The signatures point to a linked cycle of inflammation and matrix breakdown.
pmc-13321548:
Bernardita Tornero and co-authors group Chilean university students by grit, self-control, sense of belonging, and reasons for attending college, then ask how the groups fare academically. These traits are widely studied as drivers of student success. The sample held mostly first-year students at a selective private university.

Four profiles emerged, and most students fell into a group with moderate grit and self-control but strong belonging. Profiles differed mainly in self-control and motivation, not grit. Neither grit nor belonging predicted grades. Self-control split by kind: control in social life helped grades, while work-related control slightly hurt them. The authors suggest targeted support for self-regulation and emotional skills.
pmc-13321648:
Haichang Xu and co-authors test whether a simple nutrition score predicts trouble after heart bypass surgery. The prognostic nutritional index combines albumin and lymphocyte counts from a routine blood test. The team followed 550 bypass patients at one Chinese hospital, for a median of about 46 months, recording major cardiovascular events and deaths.

Over that time 113 patients suffered major events and 94 died. Each extra point on the nutrition index came with roughly 5 to 6 percent lower risk of events and death alike, even after other factors were accounted for. The best-nourished third fared clearly best. As a discriminator the score was only modest, and rival indices scored slightly higher without a decisive edge. The authors present the index as a cheap, if imperfect, window on surgical risk.
pmc-13321848:
Niloofar Minaee and co-authors survey sleep quality and learning style preferences among medical students at Golestan University of Medical Sciences. Published in 2026, the cross-sectional study sampled 546 students in 2023 and 2024 by stratified random sampling. Sleep is tied to cognitive performance and study success, and medical students often sleep poorly.

Over half the students reported poor sleep quality on the standard index. The auditory learning style scored highest on the VARK questionnaire. No direct link appeared between total sleep scores and learning styles. Regression did show that a mother's education predicted sleep quality, and female gender predicted a kinesthetic learning preference. The authors call for more work on both fronts.
pmc-13322948:
Ruming Liu and co-authors mine United States safety reports for two cancer immune drugs, in a 2026 pharmacovigilance study of ipilimumab and nivolumab. They drew on the FDA adverse event system from 2004 to the end of 2024, covering each drug alone and the pair together.

Among more than 21 million reports in the database, the three groups held thousands linked to these drugs in the authors' counts. Harm timing mostly showed an early peak plus a long tail of risk, and patterns varied with age. Signals stood out for colitis, adrenal failure, cancer progression and death reports. Age and weight also shaped reporting, and the authors urge close watch during combined treatment.
pmc-13323148:
Yulong Li and co-authors model how childhood events relate to teen mental health, in a 2026 study of 700 adolescents. They measured adverse and positive childhood events. They also scored rumination, resilience and mental health with standard scales.

Adverse events linked to poorer mental health in their models. Rumination and resilience each carried part of that link. Together they formed a chain from adversity through rumination and resilience to mental health. Positive events softened several of those links, acting as a buffer. The authors suggest that schools and families watch for rumination. They also advise building resilience and adding positive events when spotting teens at risk.
pmc-13323248:
Huichao Zhang and co-authors pool how often delirium strikes hospital patients with heart failure, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Reports in single studies varied widely, so they searched ten databases to May 2026 and screened work with two independent reviewers.

Seventeen studies with 17,944 patients qualified, and the pooled incidence came to 18.5 percent of hospitalised heart failure patients in their random-effects model, with very high variation between studies. Subgroup checks pointed to year, country, age, sex, screening tool, sedative use, ventilation, disease class and past stroke or dementia as possible influences, yet no source explained the spread. The authors call for standard screening in heart failure wards.
pmc-13324148:
Marion M. Friske and colleagues published a 2026 mouse study on an immune trigger linked to alcohol use. Activating this receptor raises drinking in earlier work. Alcohol itself fuels brain inflammation. The team dosed male mice repeatedly over twenty days. Brains were sampled after a rest period.

Single-cell gene readings covered two brain regions. The emotion hub showed more gene changes than the planning region. Neuron types carried most changes there. Star-shaped support cells changed genes guarding the blood-brain barrier. Spatial methods confirmed the barrier pattern. Results map how immune activation rewires drinking circuits.
pmc-13324448:
Mª Pilar González-Navarro and colleagues characterize drug-resistant Campylobacter coli from broiler chickens in a 2026 study from northeastern Spain. Campylobacter infection is the most reported zoonosis in the European Union, and poultry is the main source for people.

The team tested 40 strains from chicken gut and liver with broth dilution and whole genome sequencing. Every strain resisted ciprofloxacin, 95 percent resisted tetracycline, and 70 percent resisted several drugs. Gene findings matched the lab results closely, including the gyrA change behind fluoroquinolone resistance. Liver and gut strains looked alike, which flags chicken liver itself as a route of risk for resistant infections in consumers.
pmc-13325148:
Chanikan Sonklin and colleagues put freeze-dried cowpea fiber through lab digestion to test its health effects in a 2026 food study. Cowpea is an underused legume, and the fiber from low-grade pods is barely studied.

The cowpea powder held water at 4.27 g per g and oil at 3.90 g per g, showing strong binding power. Its insoluble fiber fraction was rich in pectic sugars. After mock stomach and gut digestion, antioxidant action rose as phenolic compounds were freed. The fiber itself was not fermented by test bacteria, yet the liquids left after fermentation calmed inflammation in immune cells. The team sees prebiotic and blood sugar promise worth deeper checks.
pmc-13325748:
Ghada AlSwayied, Rachael Frost, and Fiona L. Hamilton co-built a culturally fitted mobile health intervention to promote movement among midlife women going through menopause in Saudi Arabia. Their 2026 interview-based study, guided by a creative co-design plan for new healthcare ideas, brought partners jointly online to make and rank usable advice. Movement benefits during this change are well established, yet adherence stays low worldwide and especially in conservative settings.

The process proved feasible and acceptable. It yielded locally grounded guidance on program content, design features, and rollout, including digital skills and inclusion, linking with current health systems, clinician backing, and cross-sector links for uptake and lasting use. The authors present the work as one of the first structured joint co-design efforts for digital health in Saudi Arabia, offering a foundation for a population left out of research. Prototype development and feasibility testing come next.
pmc-13326148:
Gretel Raudasoja and Aleksi Varinen study people with fibromyalgia at a Finnish health center, in a paper from 2026. The syndrome brings lasting muscle pain plus a range of other symptoms. Close kin of patients face a higher risk of the syndrome than others, and symptoms are often said to ease with age.

The study used health center data gathered in 2016 from 91 patients who met standard criteria. Each person filled in three trusted scales that grade symptom load and life quality. The team asked if having a close relative with the syndrome went with worse scores, and if age did. Sorting those two factors in primary care patients helps clinics judge which patients may need closer support and follow up.
pmc-13326548:
Jeneviv John and co-authors profile professional football defenders to see which physical traits track with strong team defense, in a 2026 study from Nigeria's top league. Thirty-six defenders from one club were tested before the season on body measures, agility, jump power, reaction time, balance, and coordination. Their team's defensive record came from league statistics across three seasons, including goals conceded per match and a defensive success index.

Statistical profiling grouped the players and linked their traits to team outcomes. Goals conceded per match stayed fairly steady across full seasons, while the success index and prevention rates improved. The authors argue that fitness signatures can guide how defenders are trained and selected.
pmc-13326948:
Yirong Wang and colleagues link brain waste clearance with sugar use in chronic disorders of consciousness in a 2026 imaging study. The glymphatic system flushes metabolic waste, but its state in these patients was unknown.

Combined PET and MRI scans covered 41 patients and 26 healthy controls. A diffusion index of perivascular flow, DTI-ALPS, ran far lower in patients. Within the patient group, the index tracked sugar uptake in frontal and parietal cortex, thalamus, brainstem, and striatum. The brainstem link was strongest, at r of 0.665 on the reported scale. Older age and lower parietal or brainstem uptake each predicted weaker clearance. Behavior scores showed no such tie.
pmc-13327248:
Tobias Walther and team built tiny gel beads made from DNA, with stiffness set by code design. Their 2026 paper fills a tool gap for studying cells in 3D growth and animal models. Gel beads are strong tools, but tuning their traits precisely has been hard. The beads form when two DNA star shapes and a linking DNA strand are packed by channels into oil-water drops. That gives control over size, stiffness, stretch response, and surface signals.

Shifting star arm counts tuned stiffness a thousandfold, from 30 pascals to 6.5 kilopascals, with distinct stretch response. A click-chemistry link of a fibronectin ring peptide let beads join fibroblast balls, where they held for days and were reshaped, showing live cell-bead interplay. The team puts the DNA beads forward as a flexible, body-friendly tool for probing and shaping tissue in 3D growth, with easy add-on functions and stimulus response.
pmc-13327848:
Leehyun Yoon and team tested how low mood signs and people troubles shape each other in teen girls over time. Their 2026 study trailed 543 girls from the Pittsburgh Girls Study across four rounds, mean ages 16.5 to 19.3 years, with self-reports of low mood signs and eight kinds of people troubles. Past work mostly weighed gaps between people, leaving within-person paths murky, so the team asked if links ran one way or both ways.

Within-person rises in low mood signs foretold later rises in over-caring and socially shy troubles, but those troubles did not foretell later low mood signs back. Low mood signs and bossy troubles, by contrast, foretold each other over time. The team flags bossy troubles as a possible fix target for breaking joint backing with low mood. Treating low mood signs may bring social gains by cutting later over-caring and shy troubles.
pmc-13328348:
Ri-Xiang Huang and co-workers study a protective gene pathway in acute lung injury, in a 2026 mouse and cell paper. The injury syndrome damages lung tissue and impairs gas exchange, and a form of iron-driven cell death called ferroptosis plays a part. The antioxidant regulator NRF2 was suspected to help, but its role was unclear.

Mice lacking NRF2 suffered worse injury and more ferroptosis, with a calcium transporter gene switched up. Excess calcium fed the cell death process. In lung cells, removing NRF2 raised ferroptosis risk while adding it protected cells. Silencing the transporter cut calcium overload and death. The authors propose the pair as a treatment target.
pmc-13328448:
Paul R Schreiber and Aladin El-Mafaalani reframe relations between public administrations in a 2026 conceptual article. Drawing on Luhmann's social systems theory, they use second-order observation, watching how analysts themselves watch, to ask what inter-administrative relations really are. Two traditions are placed side by side.

In actor-centered institutionalism, such relations appear through a success-or-failure lens, mostly as coordination problems or fixes for policy delivery. Through systems theory, administration becomes a decision system, and cross-boundary links are forms that keep separate decision worlds connectable amid complexity. The object changes with the lens, the authors show, so diagnoses and reforms follow from choices observers may not notice they made.
pmc-13329148:
Sanjay Arvind Krishna and colleagues describe long-term care of a rare eye socket disorder in a 2026 case report. The patient was a 58-year-old man who first had a blocked nose, then developed disease in the orbit. Tissue tests confirmed Rosai-Dorfman disease, a rare growth of immune cells that can mimic cancer or swelling from other causes.

Steroid treatment helped only in part. Guided radiation of 36 Gy in 20 sessions cleared the disease for five years. When it returned with a bulging eye and pressure on the optic nerve, a second course of 24 Gy in 12 sessions was given. Vision improved and scans stayed stable at two years, with no late radiation harm reported. The case supports repeat radiation when drugs fail.
pmc-13329948:
Elisa Bertulla and Edoardo Raposio assessed the online landscape of Brazilian Butt Lift information. Their 2026 study notes that the Brazilian Butt Lift has grown popular yet remains among the highest-risk aesthetic procedures, making clear information vital since patients often research online. Using Startpage to reduce bias, the team reviewed the first ten eligible English-language websites with readability indices, understandability scoring, JAMA quality criteria, and visibility estimates.

Readability for all websites passed the sixth-grade level, with a mean score of 21.68 on the scale used. Sixty percent of sites scored 83% on understandability, held back by long sentences and unexplained terms, while 40% met all criteria. Few sites gave references, author credentials, or publication dates, and readability linked only weakly with traffic. The team concludes that online Brazilian Butt Lift information is mostly hard to grasp and lacks vital quality markers.
pmc-13330148:
Yunus Emre Yavuz and co-authors published this heart study in 2026 on pulmonary hypertension, high pressure in the lung arteries. A common echo measure, TAPSE over lung pressure, grades how the right heart copes. The team propose a new ratio: TAPSE over the lung artery's width, a pairing of function with structure. They checked both ratios in fifty-three patients against clinic grades, walk tests, and lab marks.

The new ratio tracked how sick patients felt and how far they walked better than the old one. The old ratio, in turn, tracked strain marks in the blood and pressure measures more closely. A set cut point on the new ratio flagged severe cases well. The authors call the two ratios partners, not rivals: one reads function, the other reads load. The new one also skips a tricky valve measure, which makes it handy.
pmc-13330248:
Hwasook Cho and colleagues test a stress reduction programme for middle-aged nurses in a 2026 pilot study. Lasting job stress harms nurse health and patient care, and may speed cell ageing. The 12-week programme mixed biofeedback, thought and behaviour teaching, mindfulness, and exercise. Sixty nurses aged 45 to 60 years from two large hospitals took part.

Groups held 31 nurses in the programme and 29 in control care. Felt stress fell more in the programme group, with clear group by time effects for stress and cortisol in the reported results. A protective enzyme marker rose, and telomere length differed between groups after care. Two markers showed no change. The authors read the signs as early protection worth larger trials.
pmc-13330448:
Michelle Chun-Ping Lin, Thomas Day, Stefan Lammerink, and Syed Ali report a rare infection in a patient with VEXAS syndrome, a recently named disease that drives inflammation across many organs. Such patients face growing risk of unusual infections, from the disease itself and from the immune-damping drugs used to control it. Their case report appeared in 2026.

The patient, whose disease resisted treatment, was taking steroids and another immune drug when confusion, fever, and falling blood counts set in. Tests of the spinal fluid found Cryptococcus neoformans, a fungus that had infected the membranes around the brain. A long course of antifungal drugs worked. The authors raise three lessons: preventive antifungal cover deserves study, such infections need fast diagnosis, and these patients merit regular screening by a team of specialists.
pmc-13330548:
Aurore Ughetto and a large group study age effects in cardiogenic shock treated with small axial flow pumps in a 2026 report. Older patients are often missing from trials of temporary heart support. Records covered 1,043 patients across 11 European centres from 2010 to 2023, split into four age bands.

The oldest group held more women, more illness burden, and less intensive support than the youngest in the reported data. Death risk at 30 days and at 1 year rose for the two older bands after adjustment. Each added year of age raised 30-day risk by a small share in those models. Heart strength recovery fell with age. Age should shape support choices, the authors argue.
pmc-13330648:
Natalie J. Adamyk studies gender and emotional work at a Michigan regional burn in a 2026 article. Lakes of Fire is a yearly Burning Man style gathering where participants, called Burners, run the event as a community. Adamyk draws on 42 one-to-one interviews with men and women participants.

Women often took empowered mothering and caretaking roles that demanded heavy emotional work to hold the community together. Men rejected harsh macho styles and took softer identities, yet their emotional work leaned toward leading and managing. The two styles thus reinforced each other as separate domains. Such events can both challenge and copy wider gender patterns, Adamyk argues.
pmc-13330848:
Imane Maimoune and colleagues report the synthesis and crystal structure of a lidocaine-like compound in a 2026 article. Lidocaine numbs tissue by blocking sodium channels in excitable cells. The analogue swaps in a morpholine ring on an acetamide frame and was made by an alkylation reaction under reflux in toluene.

The phenyl ring tilts against the amide unit, with a measured angle of 66.59 degrees in the reported structure and a close second tilt nearby. Nitrogen to oxygen hydrogen bonds plus ring contacts link molecules into chains along one axis. Surface analysis showed hydrogen to hydrogen contacts made up nearly 70 percent of all close contacts in the crystal.
pmc-13331348:
Iain Armstrong and Peter Winter argue in a 2026 essay that artificial intelligence in digital health can misrecognise patients. Systems tend to know people through what is easiest to measure, while missing lived details that resist coding. Patient and caregiver accounts are often treated as lower-grade knowledge in calls on burden and benefit.

The risk takes differing forms in narrow prediction tools versus text-generating systems, the authors note. Reliance on cost, use, and adherence proxies can harden thin views of illness into software. Pulmonary hypertension serves as the case, with a patient-led outcome measure showing that measurement is never neutral. The core test is what experience stays visible, they argue.
pmc-13332148:
Chi Ma, Chuntian Xu, Xu Zong, Mengfei Huang, and Dapeng Zheng studied in 2026 a bowing defect that bends aluminum plate lengthwise during roll forming of corrugated channels. The channels have an asymmetric shape with many ribs and face uneven roller pressure, so the defect is harder to control than in a single channel. A bent plate directly lowers product quality.

The team built a finite element model with ten forming passes and ran simulations to trace how the bow forms. They then varied forming settings to see which drive the defect. Roll diameter and the number of passes mattered most, while other settings had minor effects. An optimal scheme was derived and checked. Readers get a ranked set of levers for a common factory defect, with the two strongest ones named.
pmc-13332748:
Luke D. Braun and colleagues published a 2026 study testing a self-guided health check for older drivers. Full geriatric assessments take scarce clinic time. A short electronic version could widen access. It could also feed fitness-to-drive decisions. Older drivers completed the tool at home alone.

Forty-nine drivers aged fifty to eighty-five took part. Their answers were compared with a later clinician interview. Agreement measured how accurate self-reporting was. Most items needed no correction. Completion without help proved feasible. A trustworthy home tool could ease clinic backlogs. It might also flag at-risk drivers earlier.
pmc-13332848:
Soufyane Elkadiri and colleagues report a 2026 case of a giant scalp skin cancer that demanded wide surgery and staged rebuilding. Giant cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the scalp is rare and hard to treat, given its size, nearness to key nerves and vessels, and complex rebuilding needs. The patient was a 68-year-old woman with a 20-centimetre outward-growing occipito-parietal tumor that had evolved over one year. Biopsy confirmed a well-differentiated cancer, and imaging showed a mixed mass touching the skull without spread to nodes or distant sites.

Treatment was wide surgical removal, including the skull covering layer and scraping of the outer bone table, followed by staged rebuilding. Rebuilding used pedicled transposition flaps plus split-thickness skin grafts. Pathology confirmed a well-differentiated invasive cancer at stage III with clear margins. Outcomes were satisfactory in both function and appearance.
pmc-13333148:
Hajar Fahli and colleagues report a 2026 case of a chronic spine inflammation disease presenting as severe spinal curvature without pain, plus a literature review. The disease is a chronic condition that inflames the spine and pelvic joints mainly. Progressive structural change can form bony bridges, fuse the spine, and produce the classic bamboo spine look. The patient was a 32-year-old man with progressive spinal curvature and cosmetic concern but no significant current pain.

The deformity had grown since adolescence, starting at age fifteen with alternating hip pain. Examination showed marked upper-back hunching, front-back imbalance, left shoulder elevation, and right pelvic tilt, with severely limited spinal movement. Imaging showed a bamboo spine with fusion of back spine bones. The case shows that advanced disease can present through curvature alone, and it reviews how such painless, severe curvature should be assessed.
pmc-13333348:
Thurston Lacalli returns to what consciousness is for in a 2026 theory paper. He tests his ideas against a model in which conscious feelings are made by local brain modules, acting locally. Vision is his test case: any theory must explain how a flat display of the world arises.

For the model to work, what you see must depend on where each module sits in the body. The layout of sight itself then carries meaning. Controlled gaze becomes a tool for logging key facts no unconscious process can match. It also helps give experience its sense of knowing. He backs Merker's view linking gaze control to the work of consciousness. He ties the months babies spend sharpening sight to the learning of agency. His model credits attention control plus memory writing for why consciousness pays off. Species that barely use sight may still carry a position-based sense through other channels.
pmc-13333448:
Alexandra Lianou and a large team systematically review extracellular vesicles in newborn health in a 2026 synthesis. These tiny membrane-wrapped parcels shuttle proteins and genetic material between cells, and researchers have begun finding them at work in the first days of life.

Searching PubMed and Scopus between August and November 2025 under a registered protocol, the team included 43 mostly observational studies of term and preterm babies. The studies were generally small to moderate in size and varied in setting. Vesicles were drawn most often from umbilical cord or peripheral blood, sampled at birth or soon after. Across many newborn conditions, the vesicles were consistently present and biologically active, supporting roles both as drivers of disease processes and as candidate markers for diagnosis and outlook. The authors caution that methods differ too much between studies to settle clinical use, and they call for larger, standardized work.
pmc-13333648:
How well do birth-care providers keep what training taught them? Beatrice Erastus Mwilike and co-authors checked in a 2026 mixed-methods follow-up study in Tanzania, focusing on the Helping Mothers Survive and Helping Babies Survive modules.

The training reached providers through the 50,000 Happy Birthdays project, run from 2018 to 2020 by the Tanzanian Midwives Association with partners. Researchers compared earlier post-test scores with follow-up scores for 210 providers in the Tanga, Geita, and Katavi regions. Written tests covered four knowledge areas and checklists covered five skill areas, while interviews probed what helps or hinders retention. The largest knowledge drop appeared in pre-eclampsia care, a finding that can shape refresher training.
pmc-13333748:
Yuanxin Shao and co-authors paired machine learning with resting-state functional MRI in a 2026 imaging study of post-stroke depression. Depression after stroke is common, but its brain activity pattern is still only partly mapped.

Fifty patients with post-stroke depression and fifty matched healthy controls had resting-state scans. The team took four kinds of measures covering local activity, link strength, and network links across brain regions. LASSO screening narrowed the differing traits, and nine classifiers were trained and set against each other, with SHAP values showing which traits drove the best model. Patients showed spread differences involving cingulate, thalamic, prefrontal, insular, and visual areas. Such readable models could in time support earlier spotting of depression after stroke.
pmc-13334848:
Yufan Sun and co-authors tested a chicken-origin probiotic strain, Ligilactobacillus agilis R22, in a 2026 study hunting for antibiotic options in poultry. The strain was put through lab tests, genome and metabolite mapping, and live bird trials.

R22 grew strongly, tolerated lab-made gut conditions, and showed strong germ-killing activity. Its genome carried multiple probiotic-linked genes, no virulence genes, and machinery to synthesize nutrients the host can use. Fed to broilers, it boosted growth and gut structure while shifting gut microbes and metabolites. A chick infection model with Salmonella Pullorum and a fecal transplant test in mice probed how protection works. The joint evidence presents R22 as a candidate feed additive that could cut antibiotic reliance in chicken farming.
pmc-13336448:
Amin Hajarian, Jiwoo Seo, and SungWoo Nam measured how phonon polaritons in hexagonal boron nitride shift with layer count in a 2026 near-field spectroscopy study. These hybrid light-matter waves are tightly confined, but their resonance energies versus thickness had never been mapped directly.

Using photo-induced force microscopy on flakes from about 10 to 60 layers, the team recorded the first systematic spectra. The two main Reststrahlen bands moved in opposite directions: the in-plane resonance blue-shifted as layers added, while the out-of-plane resonance red-shifted and grew stronger, even as the in-plane peak weakened and broadened. Knowing exactly where resonances sit at each thickness helps engineers design infrared nanophotonic devices from this van der Waals material.
pmc-13336748:
Jin Hyeok Yang and co-authors review how lithium-ion batteries fail and how to make them safer in a 2026 article. These batteries pack much energy but can catch fire or explode when heat runs away. The review follows that cascade step by step, from surface breakdown to separator shrinkage, fluid breakdown, and oxygen release from the cathode.

Safety fixes are sorted by scale. Material tweaks include coated cathodes, ceramic separators, and flame-resistant additives. Cell, pack, and system designs add structure and smarter controls, including AI tools and digital twin models that predict trouble. The authors propose matching stage-specific warning signs to fixes at each level, so high-energy batteries can be safer by design.
pmc-13336848: A 2026 correction notice fixes two wrong pictures in a 2019 study of a cancer treatment that reshapes the immune setting around tumors. The study, in Advanced Science, tested a nanoscale regulator in mice with breast tumors. Pictures of the control group in one main figure and one supplementary figure were incorrect. The notice supplies the corrected figures with full legends, covering tumor growth, survival, and safety tests in organs and blood. The authors state that none of the conclusions of the study change.
pmc-13337748:
Daniel Huth leads a 2026 online experiment testing a video meant to raise COVID-19 vaccine acceptance. Worry and low risk awareness were common during the pandemic, even among people with mental disorders who faced higher risk. The video aimed to inform that group in particular.

A total of 639 adults in Germany were assigned at random to watch the video or receive nothing. The video raised awareness of why vaccination matters for people with mental disorders and raised perceived severity in the reported results. It also prompted more careful decision making. Willingness to vaccinate and vaccine beliefs did not shift, though people reporting a mental disorder felt more susceptible afterward.
pmc-13338348:
Viviana Pinzon-Ramirez and co-authors ask whether a third drug earns its place in a glioma regimen in a 2026 review. The classic PCV trio beats standard therapy on survival in trials but brings heavy toxicity. Dropping vincristine leaves a simpler pair, PC, whose standing was unclear.

Pooling direct comparisons covering three hundred one patients flipped expectations: the pair cut progression risk and death risk versus the trio, with far less nerve damage and fewer dropouts. The authors grade the evidence as limited and call for proper randomized trials across the modern tumor classification. Until then, the simpler regimen looks kinder and, on current data, stronger.
pmc-13339148:
Isobelle F. McClements, Megan E. Driscoll, and Brett P. Fors start controlled polymer growth from amine groups in a 2026 study. Light-controlled atom transfer polymerization normally needs alkyl halide starters, limiting grafts and conjugates. Amines are common on surfaces and biomolecules, so starting there widens use.

An iridium light catalyst stripped nitrogen from activated primary amines to launch chains, with an added bromide source. Products showed narrow size spread near 1.2 to 1.3 and chain-end fidelity above 99 percent in the reported measures. Masses matched targets closely. The route opens advanced polymer shapes built directly from everyday functional groups.
pmc-13339948:
Jan Boeckhaus and colleagues test urine protein ratios as predictors of kidney decline in Alport syndrome in a 2026 study. This inherited disease scars kidneys at very different speeds, and early warning helps time treatment. Records for 127 patients from two centers were modeled.

Follow-up averaged 42 months, and 24 percent lost kidney function rapidly in the reported grouping. Albumin-to-creatinine ratio correlated most strongly with yearly function loss at minus 0.435 in the reported value and stayed predictive after adjustment. Urinary IgG was most sensitive for spotting decliners. Simple urine tests may flag patients needing closer care.
pmc-13340048:
A starter cake called Daqu seeds the making of Maotai flavor liquor, and its microbes decide much of the final taste. Kejia Wang and six co-authors compared fresh and aged cakes from four regions of Guizhou in 2026, reading both their genomes and their chemistry. They rebuilt 163 microbe genomes and measured more than 2,600 small molecules.

Each region carried its own microbe signature, and aging raised diversity while favoring heat loving, spore forming kinds. Aged cakes also held more flavor building blocks, from amino acid products to fragrant esters. Linking the two data sets tied named microbes to the making of key flavors. The authors present a model in which place, aging, and metabolism shape the liquor together.
pmc-13340148:
Wes Baumgartner leads a 2026 reference chapter on lesions of fish special senses for toxicology pathologists. Part of the INHAND standardization series, it covers eye, inner ear labyrinth, lateral line, smell, and taste organs in teleost fish. Anatomy differences across species complicate reading tissue harm.

Introductory material compares fish senses with those of rodents and humans, then lists microscopic findings in a standard format. The fish eye, for example, uses a spherical lens unlike higher vertebrates as detailed. Standard names and criteria help labs worldwide describe the same change the same way in safety studies.
pmc-13340248:
Full genome sequencing of 24 gram-negative bloodstream isolates from Lebanon anchors a 2026 study led by Carni Boujanian. Six species showed, among them E. coli and Klebsiella, and testing showed broad resistance to beta-lactam and other drug classes.

Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase output showed up in 62.5% of isolates, while 37.5% counted as carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales. In E. coli and K. pneumoniae, resistance rode mainly on plasmids carrying ESBL and carbapenemase genes, whereas Citrobacter relied more on chromosome-based routes. One colistin-resistant isolate carried a frameshift change in mgrB rather than mcr genes. The findings give Lebanon rare gene-level detail on hard-to-treat invasive bacteria.
pmc-13340648:
Reza Hosseinpour and colleagues reported a penetrating neck injury case in 2026 with delayed oesophageal perforation, a major cause of late death after such injuries. Neck wounds carry high morbidity because vital structures crowd the cervical region, and oesophageal injuries are often missed at first. A previously healthy 17 year old boy arrived three hours after a Zone II gunshot wound to the right neck.

He was haemodynamically stable and initial imaging showed no abnormality, yet fever and related signs twelve hours later revealed perforation. The case stresses repeat assessment and a low threshold for oesophageal investigation after neck gunshot wounds, even when the first evaluation looks reassuring.
pmc-13341048:
Güven Soner and colleagues asked non religious patients in Türkiye in 2026 about care and mental health. How belief, or lack of it, shapes care matters for fair, open health services. The study talked in depth, face to face, with 17 people in Samsun from June to August 2025, and grouped their words by theme.

Five themes came out: whole person health views, identity and invisibility, mixed care experiences, fragile mental health in context, and hopes for a fair, professional system. Many hid their non religious identity, and those who shared it often met judgement or unasked religious advice. Such care eroded trust and at times led people to shun care.
pmc-13342048:
Foot angle timing separates strong water polo treading, in a 2026 biomechanics study by Eisuke Kawai and colleagues. Twenty-two male university players kept up continuous eggbeater kicking as underwater cameras and pressure sensors recorded foot motion and force distribution.

Players were split into upper and lower groups by propulsive force norms from an independent dataset. Time-series statistics found group differences in dynamic pressure and foot angles concentrated in the out-kick phase, while foot speed and acceleration did not differ. How the foot is oriented, and exactly when, may matter more than how fast it moves, a coaching cue for a skill that keeps players upright.
pmc-13342448:
Juliana Nogueira Pontes Nobre and others scored lifestyle factors in older adults in 2026. Daily habits shape the ageing process. Their links to mood were unclear. Local older adults living at home were studied here. A joint index of habits was built. Depression and life quality were the end measures.

Healthy lifestyle scores foretold better results. Life quality rose with healthier habits. Depression scores fell in step there. The link covered a fifth of the spread. Tests backed the link clearly. Frailty and freedom framed the work. Habits remain changeable late in life. Programs should target those habits head-on.
pmc-13342548:
Bubacarr Touray and co-authors test a new mRNA vaccine against tuberculosis in mice, alone and paired with the old standard shot, in a 2026 study. Tuberculosis still kills on a vast scale, and the century-old BCG shot protects adults weakly. Their vaccine packs code for three germ proteins into tiny fat bubbles that carry it into cells.

Mice given the vaccine made strong antibody and T-cell responses. Paired with BCG, it cut germ counts in lung and spleen and left lungs less scarred after a heavy germ challenge. Removing one T-cell type wiped out the protection. The team presents the vaccine as a strong candidate for further study.
pmc-13345648:
Guopeng Han and co-authors report a new crystal form of a lithium solid electrolyte in 2026. The triclinic variant of Li7Si2S7I carries a touch of chlorine and reshuffles its silicon building blocks into alternating silicon-free and silicon-rich layers, raising the question of whether lithium still races through it.

Simulations on the measured structure predict conductivity of 0.019 siemens per centimeter with a low activation energy near 0.16 electronvolts, matching the known monoclinic form within error. Sixteen lithium sites create many redundant low-energy paths. The skeleton of sulfur and iodine, it seems, protects fast ion travel even when cation order scrambles, a resilience useful for solid-state battery design.
pmc-13346848:
Rasha Sayed Asaad and Marwa Beleidy compare three ways to anchor a three-unit zirconia bridge, in a lab study from 2026. Full-coverage retainers were set against two endocrown designs on premolar and molar abutments, each bridge was copied onto resin models. Gaps at the edges were measured before and after heat and load cycling.

Every design showed wider gaps after aging, yet the plain butt-joint endocrown kept the smallest gap both before and after the cycling treatment. Full-coverage bridges resisted breaking best, while the butt-joint design broke at the lowest loads, and cracks clustered at the connectors. Fit and strength thus pull in opposite directions for these designs.
pmc-13346948:
Jiayan Song published this 2026 study on why some Chinese state-owned companies score high on environmental, social, and governance measures while others lag. Single-factor studies, Song argues, miss how several institutional logics, political, market, governance, and social, push together or clash. Data covered 387 listed state firms from 2015 to 2023.

Using fuzzy-set comparative analysis, the study looks for recipes rather than net effects. High performance arrived by several roads, including regulation paired with governance, and market pressure paired with social drive. Missing or mismatched logics produced poor scores. The winning recipes differed between central and local firms and across industries. Song offers the map as a guide for class-specific ESG policy.
pmc-13347048:
Ayodeji Olayemi and twelve co-authors survey small mammals for Lassa virus across the Guinea savanna of Benin and Nigeria. The virus kills thousands of people each year and is usually carried by multimammate mice. Other rodent hosts were suspected, but the region's virus ecology was patchy.

Trapped animals were tested for active infection and for antibodies showing past infection. Surprisingly, the usual mouse hosts appeared in the same place only once and carried no active virus, though their antibodies showed exposure in Nigerian hotspots. Active virus turned up instead in two other rodents, including a newly found host, the striped grass mouse. Their viruses belonged to ancient lineages, marking central Benin as an old cradle of the virus.
pmc-13347348:
Zouwei Liu and colleagues review how fine metal masks for OLED screens are made, in a technology review from 2026. Masks pattern pixels during vacuum coating, yet making millions of tiny clean holes in Invar alloy foil stays a bottleneck for sharp displays. So three routes are weighed, covering chemical etching, electroforming, and laser cutting.

Etching alone is mature and fast but wastes material through missed or half-cut holes, electroforming promises finer shapes yet struggles with alloy control and cost. Lasers have reached 3000 PPI detail but cut too slowly for whole masks. The authors propose etching first, then laser repair of bad holes, with four technical hurdles named for that hybrid route.
pmc-13347948:
Nathan K. Schaefer, Bryan J. Pavlovic, Matthew T. Schmitz, and Alex A. Pollen release CellBouncer, a toolkit for untangling pooled single-cell data, in a study from 2026. Pooling cells from many donors or species saves time and cuts batch noise. Yet software must sort cells back to sources, spot stray RNA, and count doublets before any biology can be read.

The toolkit sorts mixed species and donors, finds unknown mitochondrial types, reads treatment or guide barcodes, and beats rival tools on those jobs in the reported tests. Stray RNA shares per cell and per donor are also estimated, and fused human-chimp cells then revealed a growth edge for human mitochondria plus signs of cross-species mismatch.
pmc-13348648:
Ozkan Aba and co-authors tracked in 2026 brain pressure signs and brain oxygen during keyhole belly surgery. They asked whether these signs forecast early thinking problems after surgery. Carbon dioxide inflation of the belly can raise brain pressure. Thinking problems after general anaesthesia remain a worry.

Fifty patients aged 20 to 60 had keyhole belly surgery under general anaesthesia. Optic nerve sheath width and regional brain oxygen were read at five points, from pre-induction to post-deflation. Belly pressure was read too. Thinking was tested with the Mini-Mental State Exam pre-surgery and one day later. Linking noninvasive brain reads to thinking change could help anaesthetists spot at-risk patients while surgery is still under way.
pmc-13348948:
Rohit S Deshpande and colleagues report robotic removal of a rare kidney renin tumour that, unusually, caused no symptoms, in a case report from 2026. A 56-year-old woman with thyroid underactivity had a 2.7 by 2.5 cm right kidney mass found on a routine check. Robot-assisted partial removal kept the rest of the kidney while tissue and stain tests confirmed a juxtaglomerular cell tumour.

Such tumours usually strike young patients with high blood pressure, low potassium, and high renin from hormone spill, none of which appeared in this older, quiet case. Clean margins and a classic stain pattern settled the call, and sparing surgery is backed where the lump allows it.
pmc-13349748:
Xiyin Guan and co-authors model brain injury risk after a second carbon-ion course for returned throat cancer, in a study issued in 2026. Records for 89 patients retreated from 2016 to 2020 were split into training and validation groups. First-course dose maps were warped onto new scans. That step built single-course and combined dose risk models for temporal lobe injury.

Injury appeared in 27 patients, a share of 30.3 percent, mostly on one side and often silent on scans alone. Both lead models sorted risk well, with AUC values of 0.8450 and 0.8225 in the reported fits. Carbon tolerance ran about 20 percent above photon values, guiding safer retreatment caps.
pmc-13349848:
Alia Al-Mohtaseb and co-authors built a deep learning system in 2026 to spot intestinal metaplasia, a precancerous stomach change, in biopsy images. Their model, called CNXTGeM, was trained on 1,037 stained samples from a hospital in Elazığ, split by patient to avoid leakage.

The design mixes a ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone with pooling and attention parts meant to sharpen pattern reading. It was also tested on a public set of 33,284 image patches, and three explanation methods showed which tissue areas drove its calls. Reliable automatic screening could help pathologists catch a step on the road to stomach cancer earlier and more evenly.
pmc-13349948:
Kexin Niu and co-authors tested low-dose CT scanning for colorectal cancer in a 2026 prospective study. Long abdominal scans help stage the disease, but patients needing repeat imaging absorb large amounts of radiation.

Each of 203 patients with proven cancer received a normal-dose scan and a scan at one tenth of the exposure settings. A new AI-based rebuilding method was applied to the low-dose images and compared with standard rebuilding. Readers judged image quality and accuracy for judging spread through the bowel wall and into nearby lymph nodes. If low-dose images stay reliable, patients could be scanned more safely and more often.
pmc-13350148:
Eisuke Hosoya and a team of chemists isolated a new plant alkaloid in a 2026 study of Yunnan Kopsia arborea, a tree in the dogbane family. The compound, kopsiyunnanine N, joins three building blocks from different alkaloid families into one molecule, a combination never reported before.

Its three parts come from eburnan, vinylquinoline, and aspidosperman units, linked in part by a rare ring containing oxygen and nitrogen. Spectra revealed the layout, and X-ray crystallography settled the full three-dimensional arrangement. Such intricate natural molecules stretch chemists' understanding of how plants assemble complex structures and can hint at new drug scaffolds.
pmc-13350248:
Sasho Stoleski and fellow editors introduced a 2026 research collection on environmental hazards in the modern workplace, gathering 46 manuscripts from 264 researchers. Classic workplace health focused on injuries and toxic exposures in heavy industry.

Today's workers face layered risks at once: physical, chemical, mental, ergonomic, organisational, and digital. Contributions range from data-driven safety methods to whole-body vibration and chronic back pain among transport and heavy equipment workers. The editors argue these combined pressures shape health, wellbeing, productivity, and long-term quality of life, so safety work must widen beyond the factory floor hazards of the past century.
pmc-13350948:
Yingmin Wu and co-authors present a 2026 study of a chemical tag on RNA that helps liver cancer dodge cell death. Liver cancer kills many people each year, driven by fast growth and cells that refuse to die on cue. The tag, a methyl mark on one RNA letter, had an unclear role in this cancer.

The team found the tag scarce in liver tumor tissue. An enzyme that strips the tag guards a death block gene: when the enzyme falls, the gene's RNA gains tags at three spots near its start. Those tags draw a reader complex that chews the RNA up, so less death block is made. Dish, animal, and patient data all back the chain. The authors flag the tag path as a drug aim.
pmc-13351148:
Ross Jones and David Nay weighed in 2026 outcomes from eras before and after one surgeon adopted muscle signal checks as an objective end point for spinal decompression. Adequacy of decompression is most often judged by sight and touch, leaving no physiologic proof that nerves are truly freed.

In a look-back era-based cohort of 600 consecutive adult decompression patients, 300 before adoption and 300 after stable full muscle signal use, the post-adoption era used threshold-guided decompression aimed at 2.0 milliamperes or less. The main end point was unplanned return to surgery within ninety days, with incidental dural tear and three-month pain as confirmatory end points, adjusted for life and procedural traits. The weigh-up tests whether objective muscle signals lift surgery completeness.
pmc-13351248:
Dan Lu and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their study of rosuvastatin protecting the blood-brain barrier after experimental stroke. One panel of a key figure, an iron staining image in Figure 2G, had been assembled wrongly during preparation, and the correction supplies the fixed figure.

The corrected figure lays out the mouse experiment, from artery blockage through drug treatment and clot-busting reperfusion to brain collection a day later. It shows the statin reduced barrier leakage into the brain after reperfusion without changing restored blood flow, alongside staining for microbleeds across the treatment groups. The authors present the replacement so the published record matches the underlying data.
pmc-13351848:
Tiantian Xu and colleagues tested in 2026 black soldier fly larva meal as a sustainable protein to replace fish meal in mud crab diets, evaluating growth, health, and flesh quality. Fish meal replacement levels that preserve health, texture, and flavour were unclear, despite pressure to reduce reliance on wild-caught fish.

Six diets replacing fish meal with larva meal at 0 to 60 percent were fed to 192 crabs for eight weeks. Larva meal posed no heavy metal or pesticide contamination risk, and replacement up to 30 percent did not harm growth or nutritional value. The study supports insect meal as a safe, sustainable protein for mud crab aquaculture, easing pressure on marine resources while maintaining product quality.
pmc-13351948:
Katharina Sinn and co-authors review extended surgery for locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer in 2026. Tumours may invade the chest wall, airways, large vessels, diaphragm, or spine, and the line between operable and inoperable shifts with each case. Four databases were searched for work from January 2000 to January 2026, favouring guidelines and large series.

Extended surgery means lung removal joined with removal and rebuilding of nearby structures in one block. Node status, tumour size, depth of invasion, heart and lung reserve, and centre experience shape who should be offered surgery. The authors offer a practical frame for selection, weighing full clearance against surgical risk.
pmc-13352948:
Molecular Oncology retracted a 2011 glioma paper in 2026 after outside concerns about duplicated images, and the retraction notice names the first authors Gopinath, Alapati, Malla, Gondi, Mohanam, Dinh, and Rao. The paper had claimed a way by which lowering cathepsin B and uPAR raises the protein p27 in glioma cells. Duplicated elements were shown in Figure 7, along with repeated western blot bands across several other figures.

The retraction was agreed by the journal's editor-in-chief, the FEBS, and the publisher. Because the image problems undermine confidence in the underlying data, the paper no longer stands as part of the papers. Readers should not cite its way as set, and later work on this pathway must rest on independently verified evidence.
pmc-13353748:
Anita Rzadkiewicz and co-authors profile tobacco cells that learned to live in salt over fifteen years. The BY-2 cell line was eased into strong salt water, about 190 millimolar, and kept there, reaching a stable new balance. Their 2026 study reads the cells' proteins and small molecules to see what permanent adaptation looks like.

Adapted cells grew smaller and clustered tighter. Their chemistry was rich in protective small molecules, including proline and GABA, and a membrane sterol rose sharply. All of it points to water balance and membrane care rather than a big antioxidant enzyme response. Protein changes clustered in information handling: more splicing and RNA machinery, fewer ribosome parts, as if the cells chose editing over rebuilding. Core metabolism barely budged. The lesson the authors draw is that long adaptation favors cheap chemical shields and fine control over costly turnover.
pmc-13354948:
Alice Moyne and co-authors describe in 2026 how parents and clinicians helped build Project DISCO, a digital tool for child health habits. The tool is meant to be filled in before a visit and covers activity, sleep, food, and screen time for children aged 2 to 12. Few children now get such checks, due to short visits and other clinic pressures.

Five parents and three clinicians joined talks that shaped the tool over six rounds of input. They asked for clear reports, tips families can act on, and reminders to keep use up. Their input led to changes in the food and sleep forms and the summary report, ahead of a planned feasibility test.
pmc-13355248:
Pierre-Etienne Gabriel and co-authors review in 2026 how artificial intelligence tools are used for bladder cancer that has not reached the muscle wall. This cancer returns often and its risk varies widely, which makes choices hard. The team searched four databases and kept 35 studies from 2019 to early 2026.

AI models read scope images, scans, and tissue slides with high accuracy, often beating older risk scores. Scope models spotted cancer with up to 99 percent specificity, and scan models sorted tumor depth well. Models that blend many data types may sharpen personal care, the authors say, but shared standards and outside checks are still needed.
pmc-13355648:
Prakhar Shah and colleagues proved that the small protein EsxA gates toxin export in a bacterial secretion system, in a 2026 microbiology study. Type VIIb secretion systems in Bacillota export LXG toxins that attack rival bacteria and hosts, and every such system secretes EsxA. Whether EsxA merely rides along or controls export was unresolved.

In Streptococcus intermedius, EsxA proved required for export of all LXG toxins, while EsxA itself left the cell without them, a one-way dependence. EsxA does not bind the toxin complexes directly; instead it forms a homodimer carrying a two-part export motif needed for its own exit and for toxin release. The finding crowns EsxA as the gatekeeper of this secretion pathway.
pmc-13355748:
Hongming Song led a 2026 study showing that FTO promotes triple-clear breast cancer by regulating VGLL4 methylation and activating STAT3 signals. Triple-clear disease is aggressive, with poor prognosis and high deaths, and the role of the RNA methylation regulator FTO in this subtype was unclear. Clarifying its way could reveal a healing target.

FTO levels in patient data were drawn from the GEO dataset and correlated with clinicopathological traits, followed by working assays with proliferation, colony making, and wound healing tests. The tests link FTO to VGLL4 m6A levels and downstream STAT3 switch-on. Cancer teams gain a mechanistic chain that connects an RNA-modifying enzyme to aggressive breast cancer conduct.
pmc-13355848:
Sadia Rehman and seven co-authors published a 2026 survey study on why young doctors in Pakistan plan to leave the country. Brain drain of doctors shapes the whole health system. The team measured how common migration intent is among interns and residents at one large hospital, and which views go with it.

A structured online questionnaire drew 252 house officers and trainees. Just over half preferred postgraduate training abroad. The United Kingdom was the top choice, followed by the Middle East and the United States. The strongest push factors were low salary, poor working conditions, and joblessness. Statistical models sorted which factors linked most tightly to intent. The results give policymakers a clear list of grievances to address at home.
pmc-13358448:
Xuelang Mu, Ampon Sae Her, and Tamir Gonen find the acidity switch on a lysosome sensor in this 2026 paper. Lysosomes recycle amino acids, and their transporter SLC38A9 reports arginine levels to the cell's growth controller. The lysosome's inside is acidic, so the team asked whether acidity itself tunes the sensor.

Uptake of arginine did depend on pH. One building block, a histidine at position 544, proved to be the sensor: mutating it erased the pH response while leaving transport itself intact. That split shows the spot reads proton levels rather than gripping the cargo. Structures solved at two acidity levels let the authors sketch how the switch flips the transporter on. The work explains how local ion shifts fine-tune nutrient sensing, a control layer cells use to match growth to supply.
pmc-13358848:
Shaheen Rizly and co-authors review artificial intelligence in lung intervention work in a 2026 paper. The field covers cancer screening, scope procedures through the airways, ultrasound guided sampling, chest fluid disease, and treatments inside the airways.

The review searched six databases for studies from 2006 to early 2026 and summed them up in words, since designs varied too much to pool. In screening, AI sharpened nodule spotting on low dose scans and plain X rays. A technique that mines image texture went further, hinting at tumor biology and guiding where to biopsy. During scope work, AI helped read airway images and classify lesions. The authors judge the move from clever demos to proven patient benefit still under way.
pmc-13359848:
Lan Shi and co-authors review suicide prevention aimed at men in a 2026 paper. Men die by suicide two to four times more often than women and seek help less, gaps tied to stigma and norms about manliness. The team gathered studies of programs built for men and asked two things: do they work, and how were they tailored to men?

They found 17 articles covering 14 programs, from workplace schemes to community outreach. Only one study even tracked suicide deaths, and the controlled trials showed no clear effects on the outcomes measured. The authors map the tailoring tricks used so far and argue the field needs stronger designs to learn what truly helps men.
pmc-13360148:
Thomas Lilieholm and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of cryoablation as a treatment for prostate cancer. Cryoablation kills cancer by freezing it, and the focal form treats only the part of the gland with cancer. Prostate cancer is very common in men, and standard care already keeps death rates low. New methods now compete mainly on side effects and ease of care.

The review weighs focal freezing against surgery, radiation, hormone treatment, and watchful waiting. Freezing can spare healthy tissue because it works inside tight, set borders, which tends to mean fewer side effects. The same trait makes it a good option for treating cancer that comes back after first care. The authors call for more direct comparisons of long-term results to guide doctors and patients.
pmc-13360248:
Kai Meng and co-authors wrote this 2026 review on the role of mitochondria in making sperm. Male infertility is rising, and its causes can strike anywhere from sperm formation to fertilization. Mitochondria, the power plants of the cell, reshape themselves at each of those stages to meet shifting energy needs.

The review tracks how mitochondria multiply, merge, and get recycled as sperm form and mature. Cleanup of faulty mitochondrial DNA, and its removal at fertilization, guards the next generation from inherited damage. When outside insults break that machinery, energy falls, stress rises, and sperm form badly. The authors map the whole path to show where fertility treatments might intervene.
pmc-13360448:
Hyo-Jin Lee and co-authors tested a plant-rich prebiotic mix in a 2026 study of gut health. Much of what we eat is not absorbed but feeds gut microbes, which turn it into helpful compounds. The mix, called PEP, was designed to favor good microbes. The team first screened its parts using human stool samples in a lab system, then ran a clinical study in people.

The mix raised levels of butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids, compounds that feed the gut lining. Gains were larger when the mix was paired with probiotics, above all at higher probiotic doses. In the human study all groups improved, with the paired approach standing out. The authors say preparing the gut first may help probiotics work better.
pmc-13360748:
Neetu Sharma and others reworked the De Mayo reaction with a boron-enabled cycloaddition approach, in 2026. The classic De Mayo reaction produces 1,5-dicarbonyls or cyclobutanols, but controlling product making and timing has been limited. Alkenylboronates offered a new stand-in for 1,3-dicarbonyls that could enable delayed, guided making.

A rigid oxy-boracycle intermediate proved key to allowing bimolecular cycloaddition, and elaboration of the carbon-boron bond in the product was shown. Mechanistic tests clarified the chelate's importance. Synthetic chemists gain a reworked De Mayo process with greater control over when and how old products form.
pmc-13362748:
Marli Ferreira and Aloir Antonio Merlo wrote a 2026 editorial that opens a special issue of the journal Materials on the structure and physical properties of liquid crystals. Liquid crystals flow like liquids yet keep ordered patterns, which gives them useful responses to light, heat, and electric fields. The editors sum up what the collected papers cover and why the topic matters now.

The issue spans twisted and bent crystal phases, glass-forming systems, stretchy crystal gels, and blends with graphene, plus work on charge flow and light response. Three papers point toward uses such as light-driven materials, bendable optics, and sensors. The editors argue that small changes in molecule shape can strongly shift how these soft materials behave and perform.
pmc-13363248:
Patrick Viet-Quoc Nguyen and colleagues report a 2026 study of caffeine and sleep in United States adults, drawn from national health survey data spanning 2005 to 2018. The sample held 37,469 adults who gave diet records and sleep answers. The team sorted caffeine intake into bands and compared short sleep, under six hours, across them, adjusting for age, smoking, drinking, income, mood, and other factors.

Light and mid-level intake showed no clear link to short sleep, but the top band, at least 400 milligrams a day, came with about half again the odds of short sleep. Caffeine taken within eight hours of bedtime also tracked with shorter sleep. Reports of trouble sleeping lost their link once other factors counted. Timing and dose, the authors say, are the levers to watch.
pmc-13363448:
Runli Li and colleagues present a 2026 device study on a tiny graphene detector for terahertz waves, a band prized for imaging and fast links. pmc-13399448:

pmc-13399848:

pmc-13400448:

pmc-13400948:

pmc-13401748:

pmc-13401848:

pmc-13402348:

pmc-13402648:

pmc-13402748:
Jana Pereckova and co-authors tested how three traits shape radiation response in a 2026 cell study. pmc-13402848:

pmc-13403048:

pmc-13403148:

pmc-13403448:

pmc-13404248:

pmc-13405548:

pmc-13406748:

pmc-13406848:

pmc-13407848:

pmc-13408048:

pmc-13408148:

pmc-13408848:

pmc-13411148:

pmc-13412648:

pmc-13417648:
