pmc-13418148:
Gomaa Abdelrazek and colleagues test advanced ultrasound measures for predicting heart remodelling after a major heart attack, in a 2026 study. One hundred patients in Egypt and Saudi Arabia had a first ST elevation heart attack treated with emergency artery opening. Standard pumping fraction can miss subtle weakness, so strain and myocardial work measures were taken within a day and again after six months.

Patients who later remodelled showed bigger heart volumes, weaker pumping, and longer treatment delays. Among work measures, constructive work, the useful part of contraction, linked most strongly to later remodelling. Atrial function also suffered in that group. These measures may sharpen follow up planning.
pmc-13418748:
Gaolong Lv and colleagues present a contact-free way to check the state of lithium-ion batteries while they run. Their 2026 method fires a laser to raise ultrasound inside the cell, then reads the returning waves with the help of a transformer network. Older sound-based tools need contact or liquid coupling, and heat swings during fast charging can bend their readings.

The team tested the system on more than 100,000 sound signals drawn from 40 store-bought batteries. The set spanned two chemistries, three sizes, and 13 charging routines, giving the model a wide base to learn from. Transfer learning let the trained model adjust to new chemistries and fast cycles with little fresh data. Steady results across that range point toward sound-based checks inside future battery management systems.
pmc-13419948:
Huijie Guo and colleagues review how inflammation after a heart attack sets the stage for dangerous rhythm problems. Heart attack remains a leading cause of heart-related death, and rhythm failure in the days after is a major part of that toll. The review walks through the chain from immune cell invasion to scarred, uneven electrical tissue.

Cytokine release, oxidative stress, tissue remodeling, and nerve-immune cross-talk each get a section. Larger attacks bring greater electrical unevenness and heavier inflammation, matching the higher rhythm risk seen in patient cohorts. Blood markers of inflammation may help flag who needs closest watching. The authors also weigh anti-inflammatory drugs as prevention and the gaps that trials still must close.
pmc-13420348:
Charles Spieser and colleagues report a child athlete whose lasting wrist pain was first read as a wrist bone fracture but proved to be a small benign bone tumor. Osteoid osteoma of the scaphoid is rare, and rarer still in children, so it hides behind common diagnoses. These tumors stay small, at or under 2 centimeters across, and make up roughly a tenth of benign bone tumors in the shares cited.

Detailed scans showed surface irregularity and marrow swelling at the waist of the scaphoid, first taken for a broken, fragmented bone. The review portion of the paper gathers the traps that delay this diagnosis in young patients. Persistent pain that outlasts a fracture timeline deserves a second look, the authors argue. Their management summary gives hand surgeons a checklist for the next puzzling case.
pmc-13420648:
Sankalp Acharya and colleagues report a 2026 case where a rare heart vessel shortcut announced itself as atrial flutter in a 63-year-old man. Large coronary fistulas can dilate chambers, starve muscle, and trigger rhythm problems, yet flutter as the first clue is uncommon.

After urgent cardioversion for rapid flutter, CT and MRI scans plus catheter study revealed a large abnormal link between the right coronary artery and the superior vena cava. It came with right-chamber dilation and was closed successfully with coils. The case teaches clinicians to hunt for fistulas when flutter pairs with unexplained chamber enlargement and new flutter.
pmc-13420848:
Rui Zhou and colleagues prove that a common fungus, Alternaria alternata, causes black spot on roses, then screen rose collections for resistance. Black spot strips leaves and weakens plants worldwide, worst in humid weather. The team recovered the fungus from three rose cultivars and confirmed its identity by shape and gene sequencing.

Re-inoculation reproduced the disease, closing the proof loop for causation. Field scoring of 48 rose accessions split them into 8 resistant types, 19 in the middle band, and 21 highly susceptible types in the counts reported. Leaf wax and lignin, the plant's structural defenses, were examined for their part in holding the fungus back. Breeders gain both a confirmed enemy and a ranked shelf of planting stock to cross from.
pmc-13421448:
Sandeep and colleagues tested in 2026 how much short carbon fiber strengthens a nylon and Teflon blend used for engineering parts. An 80-20 blend served as the base, with fiber loadings of 10, 20, and 30 percent molded by twin-screw extrusion and injection molding, then pulled, bent, and struck in lab tests.

Strength rose with fiber content up to 20 percent, which beat the neat blend by 10 percent in tension, 25 percent in flexure, and 41 percent in impact. Loadings above 30 percent weakened the material and melt flow kept falling. Designers gain a sweet spot for strong, heat-resistant parts without overloading the blend.
pmc-13422848:
Budnik and colleagues test in 2026 whether proteins in urine can flag early disease across many conditions at once. Urine is cheap and painless to collect, yet most protein studies chase one disease at a time.

The case-control study analyzed 264 samples from a Ukrainian biobank. They covered patients with seven cancers, multiple sclerosis, or a metabolic liver disease, plus 66 healthy controls. All were profiled on a platform measuring thousands of proteins at once, by staff blinded to diagnosis. Panels of five to seven proteins beat any single protein. Accuracy was high for most diseases, with the best panels separating ovarian cancer patients from controls almost perfectly and the weakest result, still solid, coming for multiple sclerosis. The authors stress that these accuracies are upper-bound estimates from an exploratory study and demand prospective testing.
pmc-13422948:
Allan Wilson and seven colleagues present a 2026 model-based evaluation of AI-assisted digital cytology for the NHS cervical screening programmes in England and Scotland. Cytology there serves as a triage step after a positive HPV test. The team compares the Genius digital system against manual microscopy for the time needed to review and report slides.

A decision-tree model, built from published evidence and expert input, costed the work. Handling 479,125 slides a year in England would take 31,842 staff hours with digital help, against 103,151 hours by microscope. Mean review time fell from 12.9 minutes per slide to 4.0 minutes. The authors note the model covers slide review only, not training or new equipment.
pmc-13423048:
Mapaseka Seheri and five co-authors set out a protocol for a scoping review of efforts to widen access to health care for people living with rare diseases in Africa. Patients there, they note, face late diagnoses, few treatment options, and fragmented services, yet the interventions tried so far have never been mapped as a whole.

Following the Arksey and O'Malley framework with later refinements, the reviewers will search PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, plus grey sources such as conference proceedings and institutional reports. Eligible work must come from Africa, date from 2004 to 2024, and target access to care. Two reviewers will screen records independently, chart the data, and consult stakeholders before reporting.
pmc-13423148:
Kaddas and colleagues studied in 2026 whether a simple blood ratio can flag severe gut disease in preterm babies. Necrotising enterocolitis is a dangerous bowel disease of premature infants that can worsen fast. The team reviewed 47 preterm infants treated at an Indonesian hospital in 2023 and 2024.

Severe cases had clearly higher procalcitonin and clearly lower platelet counts than milder cases. The combined ratio was also much higher in severe disease. In accuracy testing, the ratio scored higher than either measure alone, correctly sorting most babies. It identified about 86 in 100 severe cases while clearing about 83 in 100 milder ones at the chosen cutoff. The authors argue the ratio is practical because both tests are routine and cheap.
pmc-13423748:
Ji-Woo Woo and five colleagues test whether drinking habits predict primary malignant brain tumours in Korean adults, using a national health insurance sample cohort. Records covered 240,948 adults who completed health screening between 2006 and 2008, with drinking amount, frequency, and heavy episodic drinking captured by standard questionnaires.

Over an average twelve years of follow-up, 209 malignant brain tumours appeared. Daily amount of alcohol and heavy episodic drinking showed no link with tumour risk. Frequency told a different story: people who drank almost daily carried over twice the risk of non-drinkers, with a hazard ratio of 2.61, and risk rose with frequency. Checks excluding early cases and limiting the group to over-forties gave similar answers.
pmc-13424448:
Kaapangelwa and colleagues chart in 2026 nearly three decades of kidney disease found by biopsy in people living with HIV at Tygerberg Hospital in South Africa. Kidney damage is a common complication of the infection.

The retrospective study covered 554 patients biopsied between 1992 and 2020, split at the 2004 rollout of antiretroviral therapy, the drugs that control HIV. HIV-associated nephropathy, a kidney pattern directly tied to the virus, accounted for just under half of all cases. Its share fell from three fifths before the rollout to a lower share afterward. After the rollout, more than half of patients showed only other patterns, most often immune-complex glomerulonephritis and disease of the kidney tubules and surrounding tissue.
pmc-13424548:
Brandon A. Güell and Nathan J. Dorn test whether a native Florida crayfish recognises the Asian swamp eel, an invader blamed for the collapse of crayfish in Everglades sloughs and, with them, food for nesting wading birds. In laboratory trials, slough crayfish met either the eel or a common native predator, the warmouth fish.

Against the warmouth the crayfish did everything right: they moved less, kept their distance, and fed less. Against the eel they barely reacted at all. Crayfish from invaded and uninvaded wetlands behaved the same, so more than ten generations of exposure have not taught recognition. Direct observations suggest a cruel trade-off, since the stillness that fools fish may leave crayfish open to eels.
pmc-13424748:
He and colleagues traced a molecular chain in 2026 that weakens skin cell grip in pemphigus vulgaris, a life-threatening blistering disease where the immune system attacks the skin. A small RNA called miR-125b-5p is raised in patients, and it was known to target a gene called P63. The team tested how that chain affects desmosomes, the rivet-like links that hold skin cells together.

Lab tests confirmed the small RNA binds the P63 message directly and lowers the protein. A second protein under P63 control, called PERP, fell as well. In mouse tongue tissue treated with a disease-causing antibody, extra small RNA widened the gap between desmosome halves, thinned the fibers anchoring them, and left the links visibly damaged. The authors conclude the RNA drives blistering by cutting P63 and PERP, and name it as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13426048:
James Melrose reviews keratan sulfate, a sugar chain molecule found in cartilage, cornea, and other tissues, as an electrical conductor involved in nerve signalling. His 2026 narrative review argues that this glycosaminoglycan does more than provide structure and hydration.

According to the review, keratan sulfate helps stabilise ion flows and electrical gradients at cell surfaces, which set the membrane states that trigger neurons. It also interacts with kinases, growth factors, and guidance proteins that steer growing nerve fibres and wire up neural networks. Its ability to capture and shuttle protons is presented as an ultrasensitive signalling system supporting sensory perception. Melrose highlights several keratan sulfate carrying proteins and calls for more work on these roles in sensation and tissue function.
pmc-13426348:
Yifan Hou and colleagues surveyed primary care teams in Beijing about vaccination teamwork for lung disease patients in a 2026 multicenter cross-sectional study. Family doctor teams answered a structured questionnaire from October to December 2025, yielding 209 valid responses at a response rate above ninety-two percent. While 57.9 percent endorsed shared responsibility for vaccination, only 24.9 percent reported frequent team discussion and 9.1 percent reported none in three months.

Questions covered collaboration behavior, influencing factors, guideline awareness, and vaccination practice for people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The gap between shared responsibility in principle and discussion in practice highlights where team routines need strengthening. Teams that talk more tend to act more, and the poll lays bare how rare such talks still are in the day to day work of care.
pmc-13426448:
Joseph Etah Oben reviews the linked effects of climate change, migration, and health for older migrants in Africa in a 2026 article. Resource-poor settings already face humanitarian strain and rising chronic disease, and older people who move under climate pressure carry compounded risks. His review searched Google Scholar, Google, and Web of Science for studies and documents addressing the three-way connection, with special attention to elderly outcomes.

Guidance offered to governments covers folding climate mitigation into health system planning so older migrants can cope and age healthily. The synthesis argues elderly migrants deserve explicit place in both climate policy and health planning.
pmc-13427048:
Frank Marino and Alexander Marino explore the physiology of survival through the third man, the sensed companion reported by people in extreme danger. Ernest Shackleton described such a presence during his 1916 crossing of South Georgia, when three men each felt a fourth beside them.

The authors argue the sensed presence is not madness but a normal, helpful response to isolation, monotony, cold, low oxygen, and threat. They link it to the body's forward-looking controls, which adjust effort, pacing, and perception before hard limits are reached. A felt companion can hold off despair and keep a person moving, which itself protects body function. Marino asks whether belief and expectation, like a placebo escape hatch, can shift survival odds.
pmc-13427148:
Mustapha Hamdaoui and colleagues make hydrogen from seawater and silicon waste with no metal catalyst at all. Silane hydrolysis, splitting silicon-hydrogen bonds with water, was little explored without noble metals, though hydrogen is prized as fuel and feedstock.

Simple bases served as catalyst with dimethyl sulfoxide as promoter, backed by mechanism and computer studies. Phenylsilane reacted at 202 turnovers per minute, far above other metal-free systems at 8 or fewer and above noble-metal systems at 170 or fewer. The method also ran fast on seawater with a silicon-industry waste, turning two discards into fuel.
pmc-13427448:
Shuo Wei and coauthors show that lacking a fat-processing enzyme makes chicken liver cells vulnerable to ferroptosis in a 2026 study. Ferroptosis is iron-dependent cell death driven by lipid peroxidation and increasingly tied to liver injury. Stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1, the rate-limiting enzyme for making monounsaturated fatty acids, helps maintain lipid balance in embryonic chicken liver cells.

Knocking the enzyme down shrank lipid droplets and lowered triglyceride and total cholesterol levels significantly, while shifts in oxidative stress and iron handling raised death susceptibility. Poultry researchers gain a lipid pathway lever over a newly recognized injury mechanism.
pmc-13427648:
Roland Muhindo Muyisa and colleagues survey, in 2026, what market vendors in Butembo, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, believe about type 2 diabetes. Markets gather much of daily life there, yet health knowledge in such settings is rarely measured. Interviewers questioned 433 adults across seven big markets in French or Swahili during March and April 2025. Most had heard of diabetes, and their answers were analyzed in detail.

Weight loss and constant tiredness were the signs named most often. Many linked the illness to high blood pressure and knew that healthy food and exercise help prevent it. Prayer and poisoning beliefs also appeared alongside medical explanations, held by sizable minorities. Just over half said they would see a doctor first if diabetes seemed likely. Health educators gain a clear picture of where teaching should start.
pmc-13427748: Engineering research impact exceeds citation counts. This piece argued for broader measures. The perspective reframes evaluation. Impact is more than numbers. Research evaluation needs broader metrics. Numbers alone miss engineering impact. Impact assessment needs qualitative insight. Engineering impact needs narrative evidence.
pmc-13427948:
Adéla Bubeníková and colleagues test Emotrics, a computer-vision tool that scores faces objectively after surgery for vestibular schwannoma, a balance-nerve tumour. Face weakness is common after removal, but standard grades rely on human judgment and often disagree.

Thirty-six patients, averaging 51.2 years, had standard front photos before surgery, at discharge, and at three months. Emotrics scored symmetry and movement for still faces, moving faces, and unwanted linked movements, then composite scores were set beside clinical grades. Dynamic function rose from 0.41 at discharge to 0.56 at three months, showing recovery that eyes alone might miss.
pmc-13428048:
U. M. G. Sanketha Francis and co-authors tally, in a 2026 systematic review, what preventable dental emergencies cost health systems. Tooth problems that routine care could have caught still send crowds to emergency departments and hospital wards. The team screened about 2,600 studies and kept 25 that reported costs, most from the United States. Charges were converted to 2024 United States dollars for fair comparison.

Average charges per emergency visit ran from roughly 410 dollars to about 2,741 dollars. Hospital admissions cost far more, with charges reaching above 62,000 dollars in the costliest group, infections spreading from teeth. Tooth decay was the commonest reason for emergency visits. Uninsured patients, public insurance holders, and low-income neighborhoods appeared most often. The authors push for cheaper routine dental access and better links between medical and dental care.
pmc-13428248:
Guang-Lin Li, Ming-Tai An, and colleagues describe, in a 2026 paper, a new plant species from the limestone hills of Guizhou, China. The plant, named Ophiorrhiza saxatilis, belongs to a genus famed as a natural source of a cancer drug compound. It grows in karst country, the rugged limestone terrain of the region. At first glance it resembles a known relative, Ophiorrhiza lignosa, so the team compared the two trait by trait.

Seven stable differences separate them, including hair patterns on stems and leaves, longer bracts, shorter leaf stalks, and where the stamens sit inside the flower. The new species also carries two flower forms, while its relative has one. A full description and comparison table back the claim of a distinct species. Karst floras keep yielding novelties to patient field botany.
pmc-13428448:
Kawata and colleagues compared two knee replacement operations in 2026 using a nationwide Japanese database covering 2010 to 2022. Partial knee replacement treats one compartment, while total replacement rebuilds the whole joint. Their cohort held 36,235 partial and 322,424 total replacements. The main outcome combined in-hospital death and major body-wide complications needing further treatment, balanced statistically between groups.

Partial replacement carried about a third lower risk of the combined outcome overall, and its transfusion risk was about a tenth of the total replacement risk. Age changed the picture. In patients aged seventy-nine and under, partial replacement roughly halved the complication risk. In patients eighty and over, the two operations did not differ significantly, though transfusions stayed lower with partial replacement in both age bands. The authors urge the same careful risk checks for very old patients whichever operation is chosen.
pmc-13428548:
Panfeng Xu and Shan Lu report, in a 2026 case review, an aggressive lung tumor that shrank on a targeted drug. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors are rare growths that usually behave mildly, though some invade and spread. Their patient was a 39-year-old woman with two weeks of fever, cough, and breathlessness. Scans showed a large mass in her right upper lung reaching into the chest center, plus nodules across the lung lining and fluid around the lung.

Biopsy confirmed the tumor type, and staining showed it carried the ALK marker, a growth switch that certain drugs block. After three weeks on brigatinib, a drug from that class, scans showed the lung mass and spread sites much smaller and the fluid reduced. Her symptoms eased in step. The authors offer brigatinib as an option worth testing for similar ALK-positive cases.
pmc-13429248:
Ogbu and colleagues published a 2026 study on bowel leakage as a warning sign in adults. Fecal incontinence, the accidental leaking of stool, affects about one in twelve adults. The team asked whether it flags wider disease in the heart, lungs, and kidneys. They used a national survey of 14,731 adults linked to death records.

Adults with leakage carried far more disease across all three body systems. They were also about a decade older and reported more low mood. Death rates ran higher, driven mainly by the pile-up of other diseases. Even after full adjustments, leakage still tracked with kidney disease markers. The authors urge full body checks when patients disclose bowel leakage. Routine questions about leakage are rarely asked, so cases stay hidden for years.
pmc-13433748:
Tyler Schneider and co-authors stress-tested a Canadian hospital record system in 2026 for drug study worth, using heart-stretch drugs and grave heart events as the probe case. A map of links across more than twenty thousand tables came first. Machine checks faced two outside banks, while hand chart reads checked a second slice.

Forty-three tables held the core drug study fields. Most plain fields matched at near-total rates: age, sex, ward, drug gives, lab reads, and time stamps. Grave heart events past death matched poorly, as did some past illness fields. Both weak spots healed once charts linked to a hand-coded national bank. The authors warn that even a top paid system holds fields too thin for drug work alone.
pmc-13434348:
Chun-Chao Wang and colleagues hunt for new drug targets in triple-negative breast cancer. Their study from twenty twenty-six combines gene association methods with lab tests. This cancer subtype is aggressive and lacks effective targeted treatments. The gene EPS15L1 emerged as a leading candidate from their screen.

The screen linked gene activity in breast tissue with cancer risk data. Cancer atlas data then confirmed higher activity in tumors than in normal tissue. High activity tracked with poorer outlook for patients. Lab work showed the gene helps cancer cells grow and form colonies. Blocking the gene slowed those behaviors, which supports it as a target worth further study.
pmc-13434448:
Md Azree Othuman Mydin and colleagues test cement kiln dust variants as partial cement replacements in lightweight foamed concrete. Cement production drives nearly 8 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and foamed concrete, prized for insulation and light weight, still leans heavily on ordinary Portland cement.

Three kiln-dust variants, alkaline-rich, calcium-rich, and iron-rich, replaced 40 percent of cement in foamed concrete targeted at 1000 kilograms per cubic metre. Fresh tests covered flow, setting, and density, while hardened tests spanned compressive, flexural, and tensile strength at ages from 7 to 180 days, plus elasticity, water transport, thermal properties, and microstructure. Builders get a waste-valorising route to lighter, greener concrete.
pmc-13434648:
Shanshan Zhang and coauthors rewrite plant enzymes so gut bacteria can make them well in 2026. Plant sugar adding enzymes often fold badly in bacteria, which stalls green factories for natural products. A design program reshaped two such enzymes while keeping their key parts intact.

The rebuilt enzymes dissolved far better and worked faster than the wild forms. Dish tests and whole cell runs agree, beating the usual tack on fixes. Tank growth reached 2.11 grams per liter for one product and 4.05 for another. Computer views credit a better balance of water loving and water shy surfaces. Factories gain a general fix.
pmc-13435448:
Jutong He and eight co-authors join data mining and learning tools to tie two genes, LTF and MMP8, to body wide swelling and lung injury. Acute lung injury and its grave form carry high death rates, and the lung is a prime target in sepsis. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

A public gene set from swelling patients yielded hundreds of changed genes, mostly in immune paths. Learning tools lifted the two genes as top marks, and lab tests showed the proteins bind each other. A gene sponge network and drug docking add leads on control. Human samples, cell tests, and mouse lung models check the finds.
pmc-13435648:
Rui Jing and coauthors test an old mood drug against a fatal cat virus in 2026. Feline infectious peritonitis has no vaccine and few cures. Imipramine blocked the virus in dishes with a wide safety margin, acting at entry and at copying stages.

The drug grips a host protein that moves cholesterol, which jams virus entry. Swelling signals from infection also fell, without use of the usual interferon path. Treated cats carried less virus and showed milder signs. An approved human drug may cross over to cat care fast. Dose and safety work in cats comes next.
pmc-13435748:
Guigang Zhao's team built the first single-cell atlas of hawthorn leaves in 2026, a plant prized for food and traditional medicine. Hawthorn leaves gather flavonoids and other valued compounds, yet which cells make them, and how leaves develop cell by cell, was unmapped despite genome data. Combining two single-cell methods across two species, the team profiled over thirty-two thousand cells into sixteen clusters and nine cell types.

Developmental paths converged on mesophyll dominance late in growth, species differed in photosynthesis, volatile, and low-oxygen genes, and flavonoid-making enzymes were split across cell groups rather than housed in one. Plant scientists get a cell map for breeding and harvesting leaves with richer chemistry. The atlas should guide work on yield and medicinal quality.
pmc-13435948:
Tommaso Barlattani's team tracked psychiatric admission ages in 2026 at the sole ward serving L'Aquila, Italy, over seventeen years from 2006 to 2022. National inpatient numbers fell after psychiatric reform, but whether admission age shifted by diagnosis, sex, and voluntary versus compulsory status was unclear. Over five thousand adult admission episodes were grouped into schizophrenia spectrum, major depression, bipolar disorder, and alcohol or substance use disorders.

Admission age fell sharply for major depression and moderately for bipolar disorder, driven by men in depression and women in bipolar disorder, while other patterns varied by admission type. Service planners get a long, local trend that may reflect earlier help-seeking, changing thresholds, or both. The single-catchment design limits how far the pattern travels.
pmc-13436648:
Zahra Ridha and coauthors scope the literature on emergency department closures in 2026. Searches across three databases since 2000 yielded 1,725 papers, of which twenty two fit. Those papers cover 147 single closures plus national scale United States counts.

Findings sort into four themes: patient outcomes, care access, equity, and system strain. Most studies watch outcomes after the fact rather than testing closure plans. Staff shortages and crowding drive most closures in the reports. Rural and poor areas bear the sharpest access losses. Planners need closure impact checks before doors shut, the review argues.
pmc-13437248:
Stefano Mocatti and co-authors build a first-principles engine for how light-struck semiconductors settle down in a 2026 paper. After an ultrafast flash, electrons and lattice vibrations trade energy through three kinds of collisions at once. Most models drop one or another, skewing the later stages.

The unified framework folds in carrier-carrier, carrier-phonon, and phonon-phonon scattering, plus shifting energy levels and coherent atomic sway. Two monolayer materials demonstrate the machinery. Carrier collisions proved essential for honest cooling curves, and skipping phonon collisions wrecked the late lattice temperature. Pump-probe experiments gain a full-strength interpreter.
pmc-13437448:
Alex Agundez-Moreno and a large team checked whether switching a multiple sclerosis drug from vein drip to skin injection keeps the body in the same state. Natalizumab is a strong therapy for the relapsing-remitting form, and patients increasingly move to the easier injection. Their 2026 study followed forty-eight patients at many centers on the drip at least six months, half on a four-week cycle and the rest on a stretched six-week cycle.

The drug's grip on its target receptor stayed level on every immune cell type tracked, across both dosing plans. Levels of a nerve damage marker also stayed flat, with no gap between groups. No patient showed new scan activity or worsening disability during follow-up. They read the results as support for the injection as a stand-in for the drip, even on the stretched schedule, in stable patients.
pmc-13437648:
Adnan Kisa and Sezer Kisa mapped the world literature on social prescribing, where health workers link patients to community help beside medicine: choirs, gardens, debt advice, walking groups. The approach targets the social roots of poor health, yet reports vary wildly in model and setting. Their 2026 scoping review screened 7,602 records and kept 115 studies from sixteen countries, about sixty-four percent from the United Kingdom alone.

Reported gains clustered on the human side: better mental well-being, less loneliness, more confidence, and stronger social ties. Hard clinical and cost outcomes swung more. Working parts seemed to include a steady link worker, personal tailoring, and meaningful activities. Barriers repeated too: poverty, shaky funding, stretched community groups, and staff pressure. Migrants, minority groups, and young people were barely studied, and cost evidence was thin. Their map gives planners a shared picture and a frank list of what remains unproven.
pmc-13438548:
Marcia McNutt and Ellen Stofan, leaders of two of America's oldest science institutions, use the nation's two-hundred-fiftieth year to argue for the next era of discovery. Their 2026 essay recalls how curiosity built the transistor, the GPS constellation, and modern medicine, often from questions that looked impractical at the time. A June gathering under the America250 banner, joining scientists, engineers, historians, and leaders, frames their message.

Progress is not automatic, they warn. Each generation must rebuild the conditions that let discovery thrive: funded people, strong institutions, and room for odd ideas. Quantum theory, a century-old abstraction, became semiconductors, lasers, MRI scanners, and the phone in every pocket. The authors ask what bold questions this era should dare to fund. Their piece is both a celebration and a charge, addressed to a country deciding how much of its future to stake on science.
pmc-13438748:
Lingfeng Chen and colleagues trace a vicious circle in keloid scars, where collagen building the lump also shields it from the immune system. Keloids are firm, growing scars that return after removal, and no reliable prevention exists. Comparing keloid and normal skin, their 2026 study found collagen piled up and builder cells multiplying. The immune crowd was tilted: fewer killer T cells, more regulatory ones, and more of a checkpoint shield called PD-L1 on the builder cells.

The team then showed the mechanism in lab-grown keloid cells. Extra collagen grips a handle called CD44, which wakes a growth switch named YAP1, ordering more PD-L1. That shield tells immune cells to stand down, so collagen is never cleared and builders keep multiplying. The authors argue the circle offers several places to cut in: block the handle, mute the switch, or strip the shield.
pmc-13439248:
Liying Zhang and co-authors track how trauma symptom networks settle over time in young earthquake survivors, reporting in 2026. Network temperature is a new gauge of how stable a web of linked symptoms is: high values mean symptoms shift easily. The team built eight follow-up groups after three Chinese earthquakes, Wenchuan, Yaan, and Jiuzhaigou. Together the groups held 5,794 children and adolescents, each checked two to four times across up to ten years.

Network temperature fell in every group, meaning symptom webs grew steadier and harder to shift with time. Speed of settling differed by age group, quake, and years since the event. Younger children settled faster than adolescents early after Wenchuan, for instance. The authors argue for help that starts early while symptoms stay movable, tuned to age and setting.
pmc-13439448:
Yu Z and co-authors review how a growth factor called VEGF-C helps the brain's lymphatic vessels clear away amyloid beta, the protein that piles up in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 paper. The lymphatic vessels in the membranes around the brain drain this waste, and when they falter the disease speeds up. VEGF-C switches on a receptor that grows new lymph vessels and makes them more permeable.

The review gathers evidence that genes and aging both lower VEGF-C, weakening drainage in a vicious cycle. It then discusses treatment ideas that would tune this pathway for individual patients. The authors aim to give Alzheimer's prevention and therapy a new angle of attack.
pmc-13439748:
Michel Guerrero and nine co-authors track how a virus cutter's twin flaps grow more lopsided as its drug grit builds. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, reads the parts by a fine wave tool.

Under drug press, the cutter's form and play shift to beat the drug. The team made the wild form and three changed forms, which bear the faults found in a past drug-pass tale in rise count. All were tagged at two kept spots near the flaps. The wave tool then read the flaps' states in each. The more faults, the more the flaps part in form. That lopsided growth may be a path of the grit.
pmc-13439948:
Carballar-Lejarazú and colleagues built malaria-blocking mosquito strains in 2026 that carry stacked anti-parasite genes meant to spread through wild populations by gene drive. The approach, called population modification, aims to make African malaria mosquitoes unable to pass on Plasmodium falciparum rather than killing the insects. Effector genes include antimicrobial peptides and engineered single-chain antibodies aimed at parasite stages.

The team created four lines across two Anopheles species, pairing effector cargoes in two combinations. Used a swapping method that can insert large DNA pieces and expand the cargo at the landing site. Parasite challenge tests with blood meals at low and high parasite doses showed cuts in infection prevalence, with the size of the cut depending on exposure dose, a key realism check. The authors weigh these compound strains against the modeled thresholds for blocking transmission and discuss fitness and drive resilience.
pmc-13440948:
Yu-hang Chen, Xue Zhou, and Jun-shan Chen pool randomised trials comparing two seizure-based depression treatments, publishing a 2026 meta-analysis. Magnetic seizure therapy induces a seizure with magnetic pulses, aiming for electroconvulsive therapy's punch with gentler side effects. Trials up to March 2026 across seven databases yielded six studies with 429 patients with major depressive disorder.

Depression scores after treatment ran slightly worse for the magnetic method, suggesting a small efficacy edge for electric therapy. Thinking tests told the reverse story. Magnetic therapy preserved word fluency, immediate memory, delayed memory, and verbal learning significantly better across the pooled trials. The authors frame the trade plainly: a little less antidepressant force in exchange for clearer cognition. Larger trials are their stated requirement before practice should shift on this evidence.
pmc-13441348:
Appel, Mattes, and Gerlach tested whether intolerance of uncertainty drives indecisiveness. Intolerance of uncertainty is a deep-seated dread of the unknown. The test ran in people with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders. In a study listed in advance, 154 diagnosed patients were split by chance into tasks meant to raise or lower their intolerance. They then rated two decisions that mattered to them.

The shift produced no direct main effect on indecisiveness in the patient sample studied. It did shift in-the-moment intolerance of uncertainty. Those levels rose with how undecided patients felt about their decisions at that moment. A path check found a clear indirect path. The assigned group moved indecisiveness through the intolerance it induced. Effect sizes were small against earlier non-clinical work. The authors suggest stronger treatments may be needed in clinical groups. They cautiously stretch the causal account to mental disorders.
pmc-13442048:
Lang and Sato extend a family of quantum chemistry methods for simulating mixed fermion systems in this 2026 theoretical paper. Coupled-cluster methods model how electrons and other fermions move and interact over time, but they can suffer numerical instability and overparameterization when approximations are truncated. Their earlier work used a bivariational principle to build stable methods; this paper develops eighteen non-bivariational variants with more flexible equations of motion.

The new methods keep the constraints that prevent overcounting and preserve convergence to the exact active-space limit as the approximation grows. They can be aimed at electron dynamics or at vibrational dynamics, depending on the system under study. One notable result separates them from the older family. All eighteen violate the Ehrenfest theorem, a consistency law for average motion. They do so even when they respect gauge invariance.
pmc-13442448:
Ying Wang and colleagues chart herpes brain illness in 56 children treated in Zhengzhou from 2018 to 2023 in a 2026 study. Herpes simplex virus can inflame the brain, and young age may change both signs and lasting harm. Half the group was under three, since 60.7 percent of cases fell in the youngest band. Face or mouth twitching showed in 33.9 percent of cases, all of them under age five, and it peaked at 70.0 percent in the middle band. Long follow-up, a median span of 62.5 months in this cohort, let the team weigh which early signs warn of poor outcomes.
pmc-13442848:

pmc-13443048:
Ivanka Simić Stanojević and colleagues ask what builds staff faith in LGBTQ-affirming care for people with learning and growth disabilities in a 2026 study. Faith theory from Bandura framed the checks. The authors argue that training must build facts and warm views together, since facts alone may not lift faith. Care that affirms both disability and identity takes staff who feel able, not just willing.
pmc-13443148:
Liu and a large team review the Warburg effect in stomach cancer in this 2026 article. The Warburg effect is the tendency of cancer cells to burn sugar rapidly even when oxygen is plentiful, producing lactate. In gastric cancer, low oxygen, oncogenic signaling, non-coding RNAs, and gene-control rewiring all converge on sugar transporters and core glycolytic enzymes such as HK2 and LDHA, the review explains.

It also helps tumors resist chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immunotherapy. The authors survey biomarkers from imaging and blood tests to gene signatures, grading each by readiness for clinical use. They argue future treatment should pair metabolic targeting with standard therapy, guided by biomarkers, rather than blocking glycolysis alone.
pmc-13443748:
Xue Fei and colleagues solve the structure of a degrader drug locked onto its target in a 2026 paper. The drug, KT-474, drags a kinase called IRAK4 to the cell's shredder, and trials test it for skin and sweat gland ills. pmc-13444748:
Xue Li and colleagues study reality shock among new nurses, the jolt felt when ward life falls short of what training promised, in a 2026 survey. That jolt may erode how strongly young nurses see nursing as their own profession. The survey ran at one large hospital in Sichuan Province in late 2025.

About three in five felt low shock, while the rest felt high shock tied to overtime, contract type, and weak job satisfaction. Nurses in the high shock group held a weaker sense of professional identity, so the authors urge lighter loads and stronger support during the first years.
pmc-13445148:
Mulat and colleagues explore how social life relates to pain sensitivity in healthy teenage girls in this 2026 exploratory study. Understanding social influences on pain could reveal adjustable targets for helping adolescents with chronic pain. Sixty-three girls took part, averaging about twelve years old. They completed laboratory pain testing with ten measures. They answered questions about peer and family relationships. They also wrote self-identity responses that software scored for social language.

Against expectations, girls who used more socially oriented words showed greater pain sensitivity on cold and heat tests in this small sample. As predicted, stronger social scores were tied to better internal pain control. That included a stronger conditioned pain modulation response. Better peer relationships also tracked with a greater offset analgesia response.
pmc-13445748:
Cynthia Essel and coauthors explore a 2026 interview-based study of caring for children with autism spectrum condition in Ghana's Central Region, where funds run thin. The team talked to 17 family and school-based carers from a special school, reading transcripts with a six-phase theme-based method.

Carers faced weak public help, too little rest, costs beyond reach, and thin knowledge of care, yet used proactive self-care and leaned on family, peers, fun, and rest to cope. The authors frame carer support as a public health and welfare concern, urging culture-aware services, carer teaching, notice, and stronger policy.
pmc-13446148:
Johnson, Murillo, and Cruz-Almeida explore why knee osteoarthritis pain differs so much between people in this 2026 pilot study. Joint damage alone explains only part of the pain, and tissues around the joint may contribute. The team assessed 42 older adults with painful knee osteoarthritis. They used sensory testing and clinical pain measures. A device measured muscle stiffness and tone in the thigh. Machine learning then grouped patients by pain sensitivity.

Two profiles emerged: a high-sensitivity group whose pain-dampening system worked inefficiently, and a low-sensitivity group with efficient dampening. The low-sensitivity patients had greater muscle tone and stiffness and faster muscle relaxation behavior, and their clinical pain differed from the high-sensitivity group. The authors suggest the tissues around the joint help shape these pain phenotypes and deserve attention in treatment design.
pmc-13446548:
Rodrigues and colleagues follow the eye blood vessels of sleep apnea patients for seven years in this 2026 prospective study. Obstructive sleep apnea had earlier been tied to narrowing of retinal arteries. Airway pressure therapy, CPAP, seemed to slow that change. The effect was seen at two years. Their vein caliber also declined more slowly over the period, and one sector of the retinal nerve fiber layer looked better preserved. The authors are candid that 39 participants are too few for firm statistics, but the pattern continued to favor treatment.
pmc-13446648:
Qingliang Hu and colleagues review strigolactones, plant hormones first found as soil signals that wake parasitic weed seeds and lure helpful fungi, in a 2026 paper. As hormones, they shape shoot branching and root growth and help plants meet heat, drought, salt, and germs. The review gathers what is known about their roles and their core signal chain.

That chain runs through a receptor, a relay, and a set of brake proteins, and it trades messages with many other hormone paths. The authors urge work on how the signal bends in real time under stress, and on how its jobs split across plant species. Fine control of the hormone in place and time could breed crops with better shape and sturdier stress stands.
pmc-13446748:
Jenner and colleagues run a clinical trial entirely inside a computer in this 2026 study of a virus-based cancer immunotherapy. The treatment pairs an oncolytic measles virus, engineered to infect tumors, with bispecific T-cell engagers, molecular bridges the infected cells produce locally to drag immune T cells onto cancer cells. Their equations modeled patient heterogeneity using tumor measurements from a real phase-two trial of a related virus therapy. Two factors dominated outcomes: how fast a patient's T cells kill and how quickly the engager molecules are cleared. A practical prediction followed: patients classed as non-responders under standard trial scheduling might still respond if given smaller doses more frequently. The authors offer the simulation as a hypothesis generator for designing real trial schedules.
pmc-13447048:
Fatih Cebeci maps the growth of research on hikikomori, the state of deep and long social withdrawal first named in Japan, in a 2026 bibliometric study. Japan still leads the field, with Italy, China, and the United States next in weight, though cross-border work runs thinner than home work. Top cited papers span core withdrawal studies and kindred work on internet habits and youth isolation. Key terms braid withdrawal with loneliness, depression, and anxiety, and later themes add mental health, the pandemic, and teens. The author calls for wider cross-cultural, many-field work.
pmc-13447248:
Maria Giufrè leads an Italian team reporting gene sequencing of drug-resistant E. coli from a 2019 European survey in 2026. Bacteria that resist carbapenems, a last-line antibiotic family, threaten hospitals worldwide. Survey data on the molecular makeup of resistant E. coli in Italy were thin before this coordinated collection across many countries.

Every resistant isolate resisted several common antibiotics, yet all stayed sensitive to two reserve drugs. Resistant strains spanned eight lineages, with one high-risk type most frequent, and each carried a single enzyme that breaks carbapenems. Two isolates carried a variant that also defeats some newer drug pairs, a finding the authors flag as worrying for spread control.
pmc-13448548:
Mohammed Alhassan and co-authors pool trials of magnetic brain stimulation for treatment-resistant schizophrenia in a 2026 meta-analysis. About a third of patients stay ill despite the best medication, and repeated magnetic pulses to the scalp have been proposed for stubborn overall symptoms, negative symptoms and hearing voices. Pooled results showed no clear benefit over sham stimulation for overall severity, negative symptoms or hallucination scores after treatment. Variation between trials was large for the first two outcomes and small for voices. Subgroup hints by stimulation settings are flagged by the authors as early only. Large, well-designed trials are still needed before any clinical role can be claimed.
pmc-13449848:
Kai Zhang and Shunda Du argue in 2026 that the first useful product of liver bioprinting will not be a whole replacement organ. A real liver is perfused, zoned, immune-active, and drained by bile ducts, a combination far beyond today's printers at human scale. They point to mouse studies where printed liver constructs already improved survival after implantation. From there, the near-term goal becomes a transplantable support unit. Such an implant would be vascularizable and functionally active, bridging a patient to a donor organ, helping the native liver regenerate, or steadying a marginal graft. Work on expandable liver cell sources, lobule-shaped constructs, and pre-vascularized tissues all push that direction. The authors call this shift, from organ replacement to functional support, the field's road to patients.
pmc-13450048:
Chaerim Kim and co-authors solve in 2026 a lithium-metal battery problem by cooking the protective skin onto the metal before the cell is ever built. Lithium anodes promise far more capacity than graphite, yet they grow needle-like dendrites, swell, and react badly with air, while the copper foil beneath them repels lithium. The team reacted molten lithium with zinc fluoride powder, growing a self-assembled interphase with two stacked layers in a single step.

The bottom layer, a lithium-zinc alloy, welcomes incoming lithium ions and lowers the energy cost of starting each deposit, encouraging smooth plating. The top layer, lithium fluoride, conducts ions well, shields the metal from air, and blocks dendrite growth as a stable mineral skin. Symmetric test cells ran three thousand hours at demanding settings without failing. The authors present the graded, two-job coating as something single-layer films cannot match.
pmc-13450548:
M Rochon and fifteen co-authors trial phone-based wound checks with AI triage for heart surgery patients going home. Most surgical site infections bloom after discharge, when nobody is watching the wound. Patients at two British hospitals were randomized to usual care or usual care plus an app that collects wound photos and flags worry with artificial intelligence. The study tested feasibility and safety, not cure rates.

Targets were beaten across the board: 60% of those approached consented, 95% of app users sent at least one photo, and 98% of images were readable. Clinicians agreed with the AI flags 87% of the time. The flags worked slightly better on darker skin.
pmc-13450748:
Clara Middleton, Laurel Kroo, and Todd Emrick comment in 2026 on a new lab-made gel that copies key traits of the tissue that surrounds cells. Real tissue is too complex to rebuild in full, so the field aims for simpler stand-ins that keep the core behavior. The gel in view is built from tiny fiber-forming peptide chains.

Its makers tuned how the gel flows and gives under force, traits that cells can feel as they grow. Cancer cells are known to react to the stiffness of what holds them, so a tunable stand-in helps labs probe that link. The piece places the gel in a fast-growing line of synthetic tissue models for health research.
pmc-13452148:
Alberto Herrero Babiloni and a large team chart in 2026 sleep complaints in survivors of head and neck cancers near the airway, after radiation care. Tumors and treatment in this zone can narrow the airway, so sleep harm may run high. The study sorts complaints by tumor site and by whether chemo joined the radiation.

Sleep complaints proved very common in the group. Risk of sleep apnea, where the airway shuts at night, ran over three times the rate in the wider public. Near seven in ten scored past the poor-sleep line on a standard scale, and over half flagged deep fatigue. Complaints did not split by tumor site or by chemo use, a sign the burden is broad.
pmc-13452348:
Miguel Lopez-Moreno, Gonzalo Quesada-Fernandez, and Jose Francisco Lopez-Gil argue in 2026 that nutrition science keeps weak claims alive through set reasoning slips. Diet findings clash often, and blame falls on measures and study design. The authors sort the slips by where they strike in the study pipeline, from raw links to single-nutrient thinking.

Each slip is shown in three lights: why it looks sound, why that look misleads, and where it shows in diet work. The shared flaw is math that holds together while missing a clear cause test or any real diet a person could eat. The fix they urge is tight matching of question, model, and claim.
pmc-13453948:
Juul M.P.A. van den Reek and others tested lower dosing of IL17 and IL23 inhibitors in psoriasis in 2026, in the international BeNeBio trial. These biologics are highly effective, but not all patients need the full registered dose, and lower exposure could cut costs and side effects. Intervals were stretched to 67 percent and then 50 percent of the original dose if disease stayed controlled. The primary outcome was persistent flares, testing whether reduction is non-inferior to usual care. Dermatologists gain evidence for tapering biologics without losing control.
pmc-13454148:
Kai Wei and five co-authors print three dimensional metal structures at the nanoscale using hot electrons trapped inside nanocrystals. pmc-13454248:
Natasha Fothergill-Misbah, a solo author, calls for a joined global response to Parkinson disease in 2026. The disease is among the fastest growing brain disorders by disability and death. People in poor lands, and in marginal groups in rich lands, still get too little research, care, and funding.

Five themes guide the call: priority and governance, diagnosis and care, promotion and prevention, research and data systems, and a disease-specific public health push. Global momentum, the author argues, now needs country-level action, funds, and checks on progress.
pmc-13455148:

Opioid-free esketamine mixes were scored for safety and efficacy past pain in the full work. Anaesthetists gain pooled proof that opioid-free esketamine mixes match opioid care on early pain.
pmc-13455248:
Joonhong Park and others told of sporadic cone-rod dystrophy in 2026, from a heterozygous RAB28 gene change plus a fresh chromosome deletion. Electroretinography showed much-weakened cone replies with mildly reduced rod replies. pmc-13455348:

In the asthma model, the optimistic-bias group yet showed the best quit readiness, with the highest share planning to quit within a month.
pmc-13456348:

pmc-13457148:

The relationship bent into an L shape, with risk flattening above a score of about 11.5 in the study's units. The index also explained roughly a quarter of the link between age and death. pmc-13457248:
Ali Sait Kavakli and co-authors run a randomized trial of a pain block placed under direct camera view during keyhole gallbladder surgery. The authors argue that aiming at the preperitoneal plane under vision strengthens early pain control.
pmc-13457548:

That step, they caution, still needs long-term durability and strength testing that this study did not cover.
pmc-13457748:

pmc-13457848:

Type D traits appeared in 39.3 percent of the patients, and those patients reported more depression and anxiety plus worse sleep. Depression, anxiety, and sleep each carried a significant share, and the paths survived adjustment for age, sex, smoking, and lung function. The authors suggest asthma clinics should screen for the personality pattern and treat mood and sleep as part of control, rather than focusing on inhalers alone.
pmc-13458048:

pmc-13458248:

The survey scores held flat, but eleven of twelve goals moved up, with clear gains in both work and joy in the work. Talks after the course drew four themes, from the worth of team work to the way a room that feels safe spurs thought. The authors back plans shaped to each school's own ground.
pmc-13458348:

The authors recommend technical polish and coaching before home rollout.
pmc-13459548:
Morton-Hayward and colleagues ask why brains last in old graves when other soft parts rot. More than four thousand such brains are known. Many sat in wet, low-air graves as the sole soft part left. Wet, low-air graves kept a clear set of tough proteins. Those proteins were neat in shape. They held metals and fats. Marks on them point to cross-links formed by oxygen-driven change. The same marks show in aged human brains. Preservation, the team argues, is the norm in such graves.
pmc-13459948:

Activity was scored from a validated questionnaire, and network analysis grouped the markers into eleven modules for trajectory modeling.

The authors read the result as evidence that an active lifestyle bends metabolic aging in a favorable direction for men.
pmc-13461548:

A meaningful stay was linked with stronger positive feelings and with greater happiness, and happy feelings were also tied to each other. When several factors were tested together, meaningful experience was the strongest predictor of happiness, followed by positive emotions, service trust, and feeling in control. The authors read the pattern as a chain, where meaning builds control and trust, which then support good feelings.
pmc-13461948:

pmc-13481248:
Florent Waltz and co-authors present a 2026 structural look at the protein factory inside a green alga's chloroplast. These factories build the core parts of the photosynthesis kit, yet maps existed only for flowering plants. The team froze Chlamydomonas cells and imaged the factories in place, then purified them for sharper views reaching near atomic detail.

A surprise arm stuck out from the small subunit, built mostly from stretched versions of familiar proteins written in the chloroplast's own gene set. The arm wraps near where message RNA enters and exits, which hints it steadies the message thread and helps line up working groups of factories. Particles appeared both free and loosely tied to the membranes where photosynthesis runs. Factory design clearly drifted even among close green relatives.
pmc-13481848:
Arndt Van Ophoven and co-authors present a 2026 real-world study of a bladder drug given straight into the bladder for overactive bladder from nerve damage. Patients whose pills failed switched to the drug by catheter and were watched for at least three months across fourteen centres. Of 54 enrolled, 36 had full data, and the study hunted for traits that predict a satisfying dose.

Nearly three quarters reached a dose judged right for them. Older age and weaker kidney function pointed toward success, and almost half of patients needed a dose change along the way. Bladder capacity at catheter use rose by a third, dryness rates doubled, and infections fell. Quality of life scores rose by a quarter, most patients found the prefilled syringe easy to use, and no serious drug-linked harms appeared. Dose tailoring looks worth the effort.
pmc-13482548:
Isabel Soto and co-authors describe a 2026 mouse study showing that wheel running rescues movement in a hereditary balance disorder by fixing faulty gene message splicing. Spinocerebellar ataxia 1 has no approved therapy, and gene drugs have stumbled in trials. Knock-in mice ran freely on wheels from week four to week sixteen of life, then faced movement and thinking tests plus brain tissue checks.

Running restored balance skill yet did not stop cell loss at the ages studied. Gene activity profiles barely moved with exercise. Splicing, the editing step that cuts gene messages into final form, shifted hugely, above all in ion channel gene groups. Exercised sick mice spliced messages in patterns closer to healthy peers than to idle sick mice. Repairing splicing faults in ion channels may be a drug path that copies what exercise does.
pmc-13482748:
Researchers from a western China lung cancer collaboration reviewed in 2026 coal-smoke lung cancer in the Wumeng Mountains. Long-term household coal burning and coal type together shape a distinct regional lung cancer pattern.

Built on prior work in Xuanwei and Fuyuan, the chain runs from household smoke and coal differences through PAHs, fine particles, and metals to body effects and clinical traits. Cases skew toward never-smoking women with adenocarcinoma, younger onset, early spread, multiple lesions, and family clusters, with a distinct driver-gene profile. The authors frame stove upgrades and screening as the prevention path for this high-rate region.
pmc-13483548:
Talia de Souza Fernandes Poggianella and co-authors listen to mothers whose babies were exposed to syphilis in pregnancy or born with congenital infection in Brazil. Their 2026 qualitative study is set at a clinic in the Brazilian city of Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais, where congenital syphilis remains a growing public health concern. Thirteen mothers took part in individual semi-structured interviews that were examined through content analysis.

Mothers described guilt over passing the infection to the child, along with sadness, stigma, and fear that the baby might die. A child's hospital stay and invasive procedures came as a shock for many families. Faith, hope for the child's recovery, and help from family and care networks helped women cope, which points to support that prenatal services should strengthen.
pmc-13483648:
Maria do Carmo Greier leads a 2026 laboratory study of why head and neck cancers often resist immune attack even after T cells switch on. Tumor slices from 23 patients were kept alive in culture and stimulated with a T-cell activator kit. Staining measured killing proteins, death markers, and several shield or growth signals inside the tissue.

After stimulation, the killing protein granzyme B rose in 14 of 22 tumor samples, and a cell death marker appeared in 12 of 19 samples, most consistently in virus-positive cases. A protective protein called SerpinB9 rose in half the samples and tracked closely with the death marker. Oxygen-starvation and growth signals varied widely between patients. The mixed pattern shows tumors raising defenses at the same moment immune killing switches on.
pmc-13483748:
Junyi Liu and co-authors refine risk grading for throat cancer spread into deep neck nodes, in work from 2026. Nasopharyngeal cancer often reaches the retropharyngeal nodes first. When tumor breaks through the node capsule, outlook hinges on which nearby structures it touches.

Records covered 1,373 patients without distant spread at three centers over a decade. Among those with node spread, 168 had advanced capsule breakthrough. Involvement of certain structures, including the jugular vein and a neck muscle, marked high risk. Isolated artery involvement counted as low risk instead. Survival models tested the grading against later outcomes. Finer grading can steer how hard each patient is treated.
pmc-13483848:
Shouyong Xiao and colleagues combine genetic reasoning, single-cell data, and cell experiments to test a mitochondrial iron protein in lung cancer. Published in 2026, the workflow centers on FTMT, which stores redox-active iron inside mitochondria, and MICB, a surface flag that invites immune killing. Genetic instruments drawn from large proteomic and cancer datasets estimate causal direction.

Genetically higher FTMT levels were linked to lower risk of non-small cell lung cancer, with a modest share of that protection passing through MICB-related signals. Single-cell maps placed FTMT mainly in malignant airway cells, while MICB appeared across several tissue compartments. Forcing extra FTMT in lung cancer cells raised MICB at both message and protein level. The chain supports a mitochondria-to-immunity axis worth testing as prevention or treatment leverage.
pmc-13486648:
Shi and Yun built an image-generation system that modernizes traditional decorative patterns without stripping out their cultural meaning. Generic image generators happily remix heritage motifs into nonsense, which worries museums and designers alike. Their 2026 framework stores cultural knowledge as a graph of 487 concepts linked by 1,243 relationships, then steers a diffusion image model with that graph while it creates and animates new versions.

Across more than ten thousand patterns, the system's image quality score beat leading baselines by about eight percent on the reported measure. Its new cultural similarity score topped rivals by about 18 percent, and fifty cultural specialists rated fidelity near 4.6 on a five-point scale. Performance held across Chinese, Persian, and Islamic traditions tested. A compressed version ran on mobile hardware with little quality loss.
pmc-13487248:
Narayanan and co-authors interviewed seven operating theatre professionals about the background music that commonly plays during surgery. Staff often credit music with easing stress, but it can also grate or distract, and hard evidence is thin. Their 2026 qualitative study, named BACH, spoke with three surgeons, two anaesthetists, and two nurses across general, vascular, and ear-nose-throat specialties, then coded the conversations into themes.

Five themes emerged, covering team cohesion, music as a calming therapeutic presence, and music as a signal of how the operation feels. Music also exposed power, since whoever controls the playlist can protect or burden colleagues, and participants stressed it is no cure-all. Theatre veterans described reading the room's tension partly through its soundtrack. Narayanan calls for deliberate, shared policies on theatre music rather than leaving it to individual habit.
pmc-13488448:
Guillier and a team in France bred in 2026 drug proof germs in the lab to learn how a soil germ beats a cure. The germ, Burkholderia thailandensis, is a safe stand in for a kin that causes melioidosis, a grave tropic ill. The cure at stake is a two drug mix, short named SXT, used to wipe the germ out for good. Flasks of germs faced step wise more drug, and the team read the full gene code of the lines that lived.

Early lines took mixed paths, with tweaks to pump and food path genes. As drug rose, all lines met at one point: a lone letter swap in the gene for DHFR, a folate path enzyme. Built on its own, that swap raised the shrug off dose four to sixteen times. The swapped enzyme still did its day job, but gripped the drug less well.
pmc-13489048:
Elif Kerimoglu studies infections from bacteria that resist nearly all drugs in a large hospital intensive care unit. Such highly and fully resistant infections are a growing treatment problem. Her 2026 study reviews 463 adult patients and sorts them by how resistant their infections were.

About 12.5 percent of patients had extensively resistant infections, and about six percent had fully resistant ones. Those patients stayed longer, needed more sedation and pressure support drugs, and died more often. Yet in adjusted checks, resistance type alone did not predict death or failure to come off a ventilator. Death tracked instead with severity scores, alertness, inflammation, and low blood protein levels.
pmc-13489248:
Ana Barragán and co-authors map AI tools that help screen papers for systematic reviews in a 2026 study. In such reviews, staff must sift thousands of titles and abstracts by hand. That step is slow and error-prone, and AI tools promise speed.

The review followed a standard scoping method and covered studies from 2019 to 2026. It catalogued which tools exist and how their makers report accuracy. It also noted how each tool was checked: by tests, by real use, or both. User views on trust and clarity were gathered too. Adoption still faces doubts about fit with review workflows and open reporting. The map gives review teams a base for judging tools before they buy in.
pmc-13490748:
Ananya Nayak leads a large surgical team studying dual vein blocking before major liver removal in a 2026 cohort analysis. Blocking both the portal and hepatic veins on the tumor side pushes the remaining liver to grow, a step beyond the standard single-vein method. Thirty-seven patients had volume and function scans before and after the procedure, with function measured by a tracer scan that shows how well liver tissue clears a test compound.

Function in the future remnant grew far more than volume did over about a month. The reported figures show a median rise near three quarters for function, against a volume gain near a third. Weekly growth rates told the same story, and the two gains correlated only weakly. Nearly all patients reached functional readiness for surgery.
pmc-13491748:
Chen and colleagues published a 2026 genetics study on boars, litter size, and semen quality. A boar's own genes can sway how many piglets his mates deliver. Past studies rarely modeled that father effect with full family links. The team used records from three sire lines and a million semen samples.

Father effects on litter size proved real but small in genetic terms. Heritability for the sire effect sat between one and three percent. Semen traits, by contrast, showed stronger, more usable genetic signals. Motility and abnormal shape were the main semen traits scored across lines. Better semen tracked mildly with better litter outcomes in sires. Semen data came from about 50,000 boars across the three lines.
pmc-13493848:
Mehmet Doğukan Yılmaz leads a nine-author team testing in 2026 whether spraying fertilizer on olive leaves pays off equally for every variety. Five cultivars, from Spanish Arbequina to Turkish Gemlik, received five different foliar feeds in a full factorial orchard trial. Fruit size and color, health-related compounds, and mineral content in both leaves and fruit were all measured.

Variety, treatment, and their combination all mattered significantly, so no single spray won everywhere. One nitrogen-rich formula fattened fruit overall, while two others raised antioxidant activity only in particular cultivar pairings. Mineral traffic also split by product: one feed loaded fruit with iron, magnesium, and zinc, another boosted calcium, a third potassium. Growers should match the spray to the cultivar and the trait they actually want to sell.
pmc-13494448:
Robert Munn and co-authors show that rats in an open box switch between clear behavior modes. Brain labs often treat such foraging as one steady act while they record spatial cells. A sorting algorithm split the rats' runs into at least two modes. Shifts between modes came with sharp changes in brain rhythms.

At each shift, signals flowed strongly from the hippocampus to the front brain. A prenatal immune jolt, used to model disease risk, left local rhythms intact. Yet the cross region talk at mode shifts broke down in those rats. The authors warn that hidden behavior modes can confound brain maps built on this classic task.
pmc-13494948:
A Chinese expert committee updates its consensus on lung cancers driven by MET gene abnormalities, in this 2026 Europe PMC document. MET alterations, including exon 14 skipping, amplification, protein overexpression and fusions, drive a subset of non-small cell lung cancers and cause resistance to other targeted drugs. The consensus revises the previous year's guidance.

Testing recommendations are strengthened: MET amplification and protein testing are upgraded, and routine testing is urged for all newly diagnosed patients and those resistant to EGFR-targeted therapy. Treatment pathways for MET amplification are standardized, and management of protein overexpression is split by clinical setting, giving clinicians more actionable, precise decision rules.
pmc-13495048:
Fabrizio Salvucci and a large team report a 2026 study of heart-sac changes seen on ultrasound in an Italian outpatient group, and their links to COVID-19 infection and vaccination. The pericardium is the sac around the heart, and swelling there was reported during the pandemic after both illness and shots. How common milder or leftover changes are in daily practice stayed unclear.

The team read 1,431 routine heart scans from a Milan institute between 2018 and 2022. Signs of sac involvement sat in about a fifth of scans before the pandemic and in over two thirds during the pandemic years. Past infection and vaccination each went with roughly double the odds of such signs, while each seemed to soften the other's added risk. Older age, female sex, and higher body weight also raised the odds. The authors caution that referral shifts may explain part of the sharp rise over time.
pmc-13495248:
Masoumeh Atefi, Khosro Sadegh Niiat, and Mohammad Hossein Ebrahimi compare, in a 2026 case-control study, sleep habits in overweight and lean professional drivers in Iran. Poor sleep feeds metabolic trouble, and drivers, who must stay alert for long hours, are a high-risk group. The study drew 1,200 men at yearly work health checks, split evenly between drivers with high body mass and lean controls.

A standard sleep questionnaire graded sleep quality. Nearly half the drivers slept poorly, and a third slept under seven hours a day. After other factors were counted, drivers sleeping seven hours or less had higher odds of carrying excess weight than longer sleepers. Poor sleep quality raised the odds as well. The authors call sleep a changeable lever for weight control in this trade and urge sleep care inside driver health programs, with road safety gains in view.
pmc-13495348:
Faezeh Rastgoo and colleagues measure, in a 2026 study, health-promoting lifestyle among women in a suburban area of Mashhad, northeastern Iran. Women carry much of family and community health, yet those in marginalized areas face steep limits. The team surveyed 295 women with a standard lifestyle profile covering habits from food and activity to stress handling and spiritual growth.

Overall scores sat in the middle range, with spiritual growth the strongest area. Scores fell as age, number of children, and body mass rose, and women with chronic ills such as high blood pressure or high blood fats scored lower. Higher family income, more schooling, and marital status each shifted scores upward. The authors say lifting women's health in such areas takes both personal habit support and wider economic and schooling gains, and they call for tested programs built on these findings.
pmc-13496348:
Carl H Burton leads the writing group behind a 2026 American Geriatrics Society position statement on care for older adults who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, or another minority identity. The statement updates guidance from 2015. Despite gains in visibility and legal protection, many older adults in these groups still face bias in health care layered on top of ageism.

Recommendations cover three fronts. Training should reach all health staff, with deeper instruction for clinicians who care for these patients. Policy should keep anti-bias protections, support chosen families in caregiving, and guard private data on sexual orientation and gender identity. Research should improve data collection and test ways to close gaps in health outcomes.
pmc-13498648:
Serdar Sahin and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on whether a metabolic scan can help judge inflammation of the pituitary gland. The condition, primary hypophysitis, has many causes and can look like a harmless gland tumor on standard scans. The team compared sugar-uptake scans across three groups at one referral center: patients with the inflammation, patients with quiet pituitary tumors, and people with no brain findings.

The inflammation group showed clearly higher scan uptake than the healthy controls. The tumor group sat between and did not split cleanly from either side. Within the inflammation group, higher uptake tracked with worse gland function. Patients whose glands had lost key hormones showed the strongest signals. The team reads the scan's metabolic heat as a marker of disease severity and gland damage. They suggest it can add weight when scans and labs leave the diagnosis in doubt.
pmc-13498948:
Natdanai Likhitrakarn and a large team of co-authors describe, in a 2026 paper, two new millipede species from caves in Cambodia. Both belong to the genus Plusioglyphiulus and live side by side in Battambang Province, in the northwest of the country. Naming them rests on a joined approach that pairs body traits with gene data.

One species is told apart by a two-part first leg in males, with a tiny knob for a second segment, and by curved front plates the authors liken to a bird's head. The other has a distinct ridge pattern on its collar segment and a slim, smooth-edged rear appendage. Gene distances of about ten percent between the two, and near that to their closest kin, back the split.
pmc-13499048:
Ryan P Hobbs writes in 2026 a commentary on how genetic background changes what gene findings mean for alopecia areata, a condition where the immune system attacks hair follicles. A recent mouse study found that variants in two genes, Aire and Notch4, did not worsen the condition in one mouse strain. Hobbs places that result beside earlier mouse, rat, and human work linking the first gene to autoimmunity more broadly.

His argument is that losing Aire function creates a general readiness for autoimmunity, while the strain's immune genes decide whether hair loss actually appears and how severe it gets. He notes limits in the newer study, including group sizes too small to catch moderate effects and a gene region that could not be separated from a resistant immune background. The piece urges readers to judge gene claims within the genetic setting where they were tested.
pmc-13499748:
Natasha Allard and five colleagues interviewed young adults with cancer about why their diagnoses took so long. Cancer is rising in adults aged twenty to thirty-nine and is a top killer in that group. Young adults wait longer for diagnosis than children or older adults. The team ran semi-structured interviews with thirty patients. Conversations, held in early twenty twenty-three, were coded by three analysts using template analysis.

Most participants had blamed their symptoms on stress, lifestyle, or minor problems. Online searching often reassured them wrongly, with content that minimized severity. After seeking care, several had to push hard for diagnostic testing themselves. Delays were sorted into appraisal, help-seeking, and diagnostic stages. The twenty twenty-six findings point communication interventions at each stage, from symptom awareness to clinician responsiveness.
pmc-13501748:
Joseph Sam leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 qualitative study of community views on a new malaria prevention programme for schoolchildren in Ghana. Intermittent preventive treatment gives school-aged children antimalarial doses, targeting a group that now carries much of the transmission burden. Ghana has added the strategy nationally, yet little was known about acceptance outside trials. In Hohoe Municipality, the team ran five focus groups across four junior high schools, four with children and one with caregivers. They added three key informant interviews with headteachers and a health programme coordinator.

Barriers centred on trust and practicalities. Worries included where the drugs come from, fear of side effects, unease at medicating children who feel well, large bitter tablets, and doubt the programme will last. Facilitators included fewer malaria episodes, better attendance, and lower household treatment costs. Communities favoured school delivery by trained health staff with early parental involvement.
pmc-13503448:
