Published in 2026, the story-style review argues intracranial arterial stenosis spans a spectrum of vessel problems, not one disease. The condition drives many blocked-blood strokes, most of all in Asian peoples, yet non-fat vessel diseases also feed it.

Tearing, inflamed vessels, and moyamoya disease can mimic fat disease on scans and symptoms, muddying spotting. The gene RNF213, first tied to moyamoya, now shows up in a wider set of brain vessel problems, grounding a broader RNF213-linked vessel problem that reaches past brain flow. A two-hit model pairs gene risk with outside and picked-up triggers. The author urges grouping and treatment tuned to this wider, gene-aware picture.
pmc-13547248:
Junjie Sun and colleagues proposed in 2026 a framework for why stomach cancer linked to Helicobacter pylori stays hard to treat even after the bacterium is wiped out. Their hypothesis pictures a survival switch flipped in three steps. First, a bacterial toxin loosens cell junctions and hijacks growth signals, pushing cells partway toward a mobile, mesenchymal state.

Second, chemical marks on RNA lock that half-changed state in place, so it persists without the bacterium, a hit-and-run effect. Third, support cells and immune cells around the tumor keep reinforcing the state through feedback signals. Cells stuck in this hybrid form resist drugs. The authors propose waking the switch off with reversing drugs before chemotherapy, alongside liquid biopsies and targeted RNA delivery to guide the sequence.
pmc-13547348:
Junjie Liu and Yong Yang applied a convolutional neural network in 2026 to forecast university students' grades from mixed records: background details, past results, and study behavior drawn from learning platforms. Educational data are messy and small samples are common, which makes forecasting hard. Their model was trained after careful cleaning and preparation of the combined dataset.

The model predicted performance with accuracy near 91 percent, and in a test group of 500 students its average predicted score landed close to the group's median result. The authors argue such forecasts can guide how universities allocate support and personalize learning. They present the work as a feasibility demonstration for artificial intelligence inside educational management systems.
pmc-13547448:
Young-Ran Kweon, Youngmi Kwon, and Hyunsoo Ryu present a study dated 2026 validating a Korean scale for teen suicide prevention. Teenagers often notice a friend's distress first, so their readiness to help is a real line of defense. No checked Korean version of the Preparedness to Help Scale existed for this age group.

The team translated and adapted the scale, then tested it on 434 middle and high school students in South Korea. Factor analysis supported the expected single-dimension structure, with fit scores close to ideal. Individual items loaded strongly and consistently. Agreement checks against related measures and known groups also held up. Internal consistency scores were high. Schools now have a tested tool for gauging student readiness to support peers at risk.
pmc-13547748:
Qi Yan and seven co-authors test a grain seed against lung harm in a 2026 study. Coix seed, also called Job's tears, is both food and folk cure, but proof of its guard over lungs was thin. Their target was acute lung injury, a grave state where the lungs swell and fail.

In mice with the injury, the seed brew cut swelling marks in blood and lung. Lab scans named 32 parts in the brew, and computer maps tied them to a known alarm path in cells. Checks in the mice bore out the path's role. The study gives the old seed a firm base.
pmc-13547848:
Emma Robinson and co-authors mark STK11 loss as a harsh subgroup in cervical gland cancer in a 2026 study. Cervical adenocarcinoma trails its squamous kin in survival and screening reply. The team sequenced 302 cancers from Guatemala and Venezuela and checked the finds in over 4,600 more cases.

STK11 changes, hits and focal deletions alike, clustered in gland tumors and struck near a quarter of them. Whole genome reads caught rearrangements on chromosome 19 that exome reads missed. Carriers skewed younger, died sooner, and fared worse on checkpoint drugs. TP53 hits also ran high in gland tumors without HPV.
pmc-13548148:
Abdellatif Bouayad reviews in 2026 the state of testing for anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, a hallmark blood marker of lupus. The antibodies appear in anywhere from twenty to ninety percent of lupus patients, a range so wide that the test itself, and how it is read, clearly matters.

Bouayad sorts the antibody family into four kinds by what they bind, from pure native DNA to DNA-protein complexes, and shows why assays disagree across kinds. The review covers newer detection methods and the traps in reading them. For a test that can sway diagnosis heavily, his account urges care about which version a lab runs.
pmc-13548248:
Kamran Mirza and co-authors argued this 2026 case for two-way learning in digital pathology. Scanning slides and reading them with software and AI can sharpen diagnosis and widen teaching access. Yet rich settings adopted these tools far faster than poor ones, thanks to gaps in infrastructure, staff, and funding. The pandemic widened that split.

The authors propose reciprocal innovation: rich and poor settings teaching each other continuously, not one-way hand-downs of technology. Wealthy systems offer validation standards, regulation, and mentorship. Poorer systems offer cost-saving tricks, resilient workflows, and open-source fixes that everyone can use. The paper reviews classroom and clinical examples, the barriers that persist, and the policies needed to scale the model fairly.
pmc-13548548:
Hugo Gustavsson and co-authors test in 2026 the limits of a finger refill test used at the bedside to judge blood flow. The test times how fast color comes back after a squeeze. Its three second cut line rests on thin proof and on eye calls that vary by viewer.

A camera based form of the test cuts viewer sway. Twenty five fit adults got a germ toxin shot or salt water in a blind cross over plan. Refill time first stretched far past the cut line, then fell well below it in one spell. The swing calls the fixed cut line into doubt.
pmc-13548648:
Kazuhiro Miyata and colleagues sift the many published models that predict death after hip fracture in older adults, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Families and surgeons need honest forecasts, from the first month to years out, yet model quality varies. The team searched five databases and appraised twenty-one models from twenty-four studies with a standard bias tool, then applied a five-step test of clinical usefulness.

Discrimination scores spanned a wide range, roughly zero point seven to zero point nine for new models. Nearly every model carried a high risk of bias, mostly from how participants were chosen and data analyzed. Pooling one popular score for thirty-day death gave only modest accuracy. Still, the review names reasonable candidates for hospital death and for one-year death. The authors urge caution, outside testing, and cleaner methods before any model guides decisions alone.

The top blocks were the expectations of workmates and parents. Peer sway and the trial's own toolkits were the top helpers, and toolkit users changed far more than others. Print alone, the authors say, does not move practice.
pmc-13549848:
Mei Wu and four co-authors find in 2026 the best wait time between a stomach scope exam and a breath test for a common stomach germ. The germ, Helicobacter pylori, drives stomach cancer risk, so exact detection guides cure efforts. Breath tests done the same day as a scope exam may read falsely.

Agreement runs strong at all three waits. The two-hour wait posts the top specificity at 96.2 percent. False negatives are probed against tissue traits. pmc-13550448:
Asma A. Alhashmi and colleagues design a secure way for factory devices to offload computing tasks to nearby edge servers, in a 2026 wireless engineering paper. Simulations beat five benchmark designs: the weakest user's secrecy rate rose by nearly nineteen percent, average delay fell by forty-one percent, and energy efficiency improved by up to thirty percent. The authors tie the scheme to safer mining and automated industry.
pmc-13551048:
Carmit Libruder and five co-authors measured stroke risk in the year after a cancer diagnosis in Israel, in a study from twenty twenty-six. pmc-13551748:

pmc-13552048:

The case walks through the injury pattern, the failed alignment, and the choice of this operation for advanced joint wear. pmc-13552448:

pmc-13552648:
Kristofer Vernmark and three co-authors adapt a scale of digital skills for psychology practice into Swedish, in a 2026 study. The scale hung together very well as a whole and in its knowledge and skills parts. Some items overlapped much, hinting at cuts. pmc-13553148:

pmc-13553248:

pmc-13553748:

pmc-13553848:
Andreas Muller and co-authors study in a 2026 paper if software that manages workers harms their health. The link held after known job stressors were counted, the team found.
pmc-13554048:
Nawaz Khan and co-authors review cell-shed bubbles as next-wave drug carriers, in this 2026 paper. All cells release tiny membrane bubbles that ferry proteins, fats, and gene scraps between them. Their natural build grants stealth, stability, and passage through body barriers.

pmc-13554248:

Their redesign cut the model's size by more than four fifths while keeping its eye sharp.

On a fresh wheat dataset it had never seen, accuracy stayed above ninety-five percent. It beat well-known image models by clear margins. The authors aim the tool at early warnings on modest hardware.
pmc-13554448:
Sungpil Yoon and Jae Youl Cho review two ginseng compounds as possible first-line partners against drug-resistant triple-negative breast cancer, publishing the review in 2026. pmc-13554748:
Yunpeng Zhu comments on a new Chinese device for fixing a leaking heart valve without open surgery. The repair, called TEER, clips the mitral valve edges together through a catheter. One year on, about ninety percent met the trial's success mark: alive, no repeat procedure, and only mild leakage left. Over ninety percent kept leakage at a mild level or less. pmc-13554848:

On ECMO support, his small femoral vessels ruled out usual catheter access.

pmc-13554948:

pmc-13555848:

Chances ran best for those with normal or mildly reduced sight at the start, and for those treated soon after sight loss began. pmc-13556048:

Seizures were the most common, followed by headaches, paralysis, and stroke, with most events arising between the ages of five and ten. Statistical tests linked these events to the child's age at presentation and to other clinical factors in the records. The authors call for routine neurological checks in sickle cell clinics so complications are caught earlier.
pmc-13556148:

Valério notes that such proof says nothing about whether the record was right, who answers for it, or how a patient can fight a wrong call. pmc-13556348:

pmc-13556448:

pmc-13556548:

pmc-13556748:

pmc-13556848:

pmc-13556948:

pmc-13557448:

pmc-13557848:

pmc-13557948:

pmc-13558048:

pmc-13558648:

pmc-13558748:

pmc-13558848:

pmc-13559748:

pmc-13560148:

pmc-13560248:

pmc-13561048:

pmc-13561148:

pmc-13561248:

pmc-13562248:

pmc-13562348:

Ring-shaped chromosomes needed tuned filters to show up, and the team sets out a plan for them. Three nerve cases stayed unsolved. Yield rose in the rest.
pmc-13562648:

pmc-13562748:

Thickening a slab from 60 to 125 millimetres cut displacement by about 68 percent. pmc-13562848:

pmc-13563048:

Yi Chen, Ying Zhou, Quan Qiu, and Yongxi Ma dose a gut bacterium for weaned piglets, in work from 2026. Weaning stresses young pigs, and gut health sets how well they grow after separation. Clostridium butyricum is a friendly gut microbe sold as a feed add on for stock.

pmc-13563748:
Eric Nana Yaw Nyarko and fourteen colleagues measure two hidden hepatitis threats among patients at Bimbilla Hospital in Northern Ghana. Hepatitis D only infects people already carrying hepatitis B, and it worsens liver injury, while occult hepatitis B hides from the standard surface test. Data from Ghana on both is sparse. pmc-13563948:

pmc-13564248:
Mengduan Pang and co-authors report a case of combined drug therapy for psoriatic arthritis, in this 2026 paper. The disease joins skin psoriasis with joint inflammation, and many patients respond poorly to single targeted drugs. A scoping review accompanies the case.

pmc-13564848:
Asma Abdul Malik and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on child deaths in Pakistan. Deaths of newborns and children under five are core measures of a nation's health. Pakistan still has one of the highest child death rates in the world, and many of those deaths are preventable.

The team drew on a national household survey frame covering 115,600 households in cities and villages. They identified 3,880 deaths in the three years before the survey. pmc-13565448:

pmc-13566548:
Xingyuan Xiao and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six study linking video-derived measures to expert scores in robotic surgery training. Judging robotic skill still relies on experts watching operations. Automated measures from the video itself could make assessment faster and fairer.

Software extracted dozens of digital metrics covering tool visibility, camera control, and motion. Statistical models explored which metrics tracked expert scores. The exploratory model points toward objective skill dashboards for surgical training.
pmc-13567248:

pmc-13568048:

Its heat maps also mark the same areas that doctors check, which makes its calls easier to trust and review.
pmc-13568348:

Convolutional networks read local texture well but miss the global scene; transformers see the whole yet blur fine detail. Automated inspection beats tired human eyes on a production line, if it can catch faint, odd-shaped defects. Hybrid designs are the current answer to the local-global trade. The authors test on crystal images with complex backgrounds. Their system aims at factory deployment, where a missed flaw becomes a failed device. The paper is applied computer vision with an industrial customer.
pmc-13568748:
Tanapun Thamgrang and co-authors studied bleeding in Thai patients treated for blood clots in two thousand twenty-six. Anticoagulant drugs prevent clots in veins, but they raise bleeding risk. Data on that risk in Southeast Asia are limited.

Sixty patients had clinically relevant bleeding, a one-year rate near fifteen percent. Risk was higher with added antiplatelet drugs, poor performance status, low body mass index, and age over sixty-five. Both major and lesser bleeding were tied to higher death rates. The authors urge closer monitoring for patients with those risk traits.
pmc-13569348:
Giuseppe Gallo, Pietro Quaglino, and Simone Ribero gather the skin and mucosal clues that can betray hantavirus disease early. Skin signs are often absent in the lung form despite severe illness. The authors propose a suspicion trigger combining exposure, abrupt fever, kidney or lung involvement, low platelets, and vascular skin findings, so testing and care start sooner.
pmc-13569448:
Ritchy Hodebourg and colleagues study, in a 2026 rat experiment, how cannabis exposure after a stressful event changes later coping behavior. Facing the stress odor instead triggered avoidance plus enzyme activation that reshaped synapses, and blocking those enzymes partly restored normal structure. The work links cannabis after stress to broader, PTSD-like response patterns.
pmc-13570448:
İbrahim Alptekin, Bilge Alptekin, and their co-authors published a stem cell study in twenty twenty-six on whether a troubled pregnancy leaves fingerprints on the baby's umbilical cord cells. Mesenchymal stem cells from cords of early-onset preeclampsia, late-onset preeclampsia, and healthy pregnancies, twenty-two each, were grown side by side.

Cells from early-onset cases started fast: the first culture phase finished significantly sooner. Yet total culture time and doubling rates did not crown a lasting winner, and cell identity markers matched across groups. The title states the verdict plainly: an accelerated start without a sustained growth advantage. The nuance matters for banks storing cord cells from complicated pregnancies.
pmc-13570848:

Blocking rival paths and boosting key steps raised output step by step. In stirred tanks fed with glycerol, the tuned strain reached about nineteen hundred milligrams per liter in thirty-two hours. pmc-13570948:
Ahad A Kesaria and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether hormone-based contraceptives change the odds of leg injuries in women athletes. The injuries tracked included ligament sprains, cartilage tears, ankle sprains, stress fractures, and tendon problems. Statistical comparisons weighed each injury type between the groups. The authors frame the study as evidence for clinicians counseling athletes who weigh contraception alongside training and injury history.
pmc-13571148:

In mice, a drug that blocks that factor, packed in a gel set by light, cut swelling and bone-like change and left the tissue in better shape. The authors say the factor and the gel merit more tests as a path to care.
pmc-13571248:

pmc-13571348:

pmc-13571648:

pmc-13571948:

pmc-13572348:

pmc-13572448:

pmc-13572548:

pmc-13572748:

pmc-13572948:

pmc-13573348:

pmc-13573448:

pmc-13573748:

pmc-13574148:

pmc-13574448:

pmc-13574648:

pmc-13574848:

pmc-13574948:

pmc-13575148:

pmc-13575648:

pmc-13575848:

pmc-13575948:

pmc-13576348:

pmc-13576448:

pmc-13576548:

pmc-13576648:

pmc-13577248:

pmc-13577348:

pmc-13577748:

pmc-13581148:

pmc-13581448:

pmc-13581848:

pmc-13582148:

pmc-13593748:

pmc-13593848:

pmc-13594548:

pmc-13594848:

pmc-13595148:

Whether crown germs use that path was unknown.

pmc-13597148:

pmc-13597748:

pmc-13597948:

They screened those genomes for drug resistance genes, harm related genes, type codes, and mobile DNA parts that can move genes around. pmc-13598348:

In a mean span of about 28 months, 69 patients die. That is 25.4 percent of the group. Curve tests and matched survival models weigh which scores flag death risk on their own, for the long term.
pmc-13610048:
Halil İbrahim Yavuz, Macit Ozenbas, and Yu-Kuei Hsu test an insulating shield inside dye-sensitized solar cells. These cells lose energy when electrons leak backward from the conductive glass into the electrolyte, a short-circuit path created by the porous light-harvesting layer. The team coated the glass with a 48 nanometer zirconium dioxide film, betting a wide-bandgap layer could block the leak while letting real current tunnel through.

The coated cells converted 6.77 percent of sunlight to electricity, a 43.9 percent improvement over bare-glass devices, while photon-to-current efficiency rose 69 percent. pmc-13610448: Zhengkun Fu and Lianghui Huang write on light and matter in nano systems, from basics to uses. At tiny scales, how light meets matter forms the base for modern nanophotonics and micro-nano optical devices. The piece ties that base science to a wide range of new uses, including energy change, optical sensing, quantum control, and catalysis for the environment.
pmc-13610648:
Skin aging may start in the gut, if the signals microbes send through the body reach the skin. Jihye Lee and co-authors review that gut-skin axis in this 2026 paper, sorting dietary compounds by how gut microbes transform them. Plant chemicals, fibers, fats, and fermented foods all feed into the exchange.

Microbe-made products, from short-chain fatty acids to indole and bile acid variants, are weighed against skin outcomes like barrier health, inflammation, and cell aging. Human trials give early support for some probiotic and oral beauty products. But direct proof that microbes cause the skin effects is thin, and people vary in what their microbes can make. The authors ask for trials that measure microbes, products, and skin together.
pmc-13610748:
Vrushali Patil and co-authors report a fatal case of herbicide poisoning by injection. Paraquat is a weed killer so toxic that many lands restrict it. Swallowing it is the usual route in poisoning cases. Here a young man injected a strong mix into the back of his hand in a suicide attempt.

Dialysis and other intensive care began early, yet breath failure and blood pressure collapse set in. Repeated heart arrests followed, and he died just over a day after arrival. The authors plead for tighter control of the chemical.
pmc-13611048:
Sirbu and co-authors test how grape seed oil affects starch films meant for green packaging, in this 2026 paper. Plastic from oil pollutes the environment, and starch films are a promising biodegradable swap. The team asked how added oil and months of storage change the films' strength and surface traits.

Films carried five to fifteen percent oil and were stored for up to five months. Oil first raised strength, heat resistance, and water repellence. After three months the oil films lost much of their strength, yet by five months their traits had recovered to near or above the plain film. Storage time proved the strongest factor overall.
pmc-13611848:
Tajauna Batchelor leads a team on HPV vaccine barriers for rural US teens. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with a common sexually spread virus. HPV causes cancers that shots could largely prevent.

Teen shot rates lag other teen shots, more so in rural zones. The team reviewed recent work and checked national data sets. Barriers span clinic access, income, culture, and doctor talk. State rates were split by rural or urban type. Rural states showed lower finish rates than urban ones. Multi level blocks need multi level fixes.  Rates for teens are the core data used.
pmc-13612348:
Shanzhou Xie and six colleagues build, published in 2026, two mouse ovarian cancer cell lines that resist standard chemotherapy. Resistance to platinum and taxane drugs is a main reason ovarian cancer treatment fails. The team exposed a mouse cancer line to rising drug doses in pulses. One subline learned to resist paclitaxel, the other carboplatin. Both also resisted the other drug to a degree. They formed colonies better and shrugged off the cell-cycle arrest and death the drugs normally cause. Drug levels inside the resistant cells ran lower.

The cells also held their stress chemistry lower and rewired key proteins. A drug pump that ejects medicine was turned up. Survival signals stayed on, while the proteins that execute cell death were muted. A brake on the cell's power-plant splitting was also reduced. The authors offer both lines as shared tools for hunting ways to beat resistance.
pmc-13612448:
João Francisco Pollo Gaspary leads a five-author team designing a gentler path for women watching low-suspicion breast nodules. BI-RADS 2 to 4B lesions mean months of surveillance scans and anxiety, with no low-risk intervention in between. Their outpatient protocol paints a mixture of Lugol's iodine solution and DMSO on the skin, banking on iodine's redox effects and DMSO's skin-carrying power. Formal decision methods structured the design.

Synthesis singled out redox modulation, vessel responsiveness, and microenvironment stabilization as the plausible levers. Comparing delivery routes favored the skin. The final regimen, equal small volumes of each liquid twice weekly for five weeks, was tried in three exploratory BI-RADS 4B cases. Two nodules vanished on imaging, one staying clear at twelve months. A third responded partially and went to needle biopsy. No major side effects appeared. The authors stress the exploratory scale and call for controlled trials.
pmc-13612948:
Givi Magradze and co-authors study a surgical slip in ear implants in 2026. Cochlear implants restore hearing by placing a thin array inside the inner ear. Sometimes the tip of the array folds over during placement. That fold weakens the signal and may force a second surgery.

The team reviewed a very large set of arrays placed over more than a decade at one German center. Arrays came from all three major makers and many designs. They weighed how often folds occur, what drives them, and how to spot them. Large scale data can help surgeons cut a rare but costly fault.
pmc-13613048:
Ruxue Zhou and Shenglan Wang review a two-way link between a mother's gut and the placenta, in this narrative review from twenty twenty-six. During pregnancy the body reshapes its metabolism, immunity, and hormones, and gut microbes seem to help steer that change from afar. Their chemical products travel in the blood and can cross into the placenta.

Helpful products, such as short-chain fatty acids from fiber, tend to support calm immune balance between mother and fetus. Harmful ones build up when diet, illness, or antibiotics upset the gut, and they are linked with miscarriage, preeclampsia, diabetes in pregnancy, stunted fetal growth, and early birth. The review also flags open disputes, such as whether microbes live in the placenta at all, and notes that proof from large trials is still missing. The authors sketch a research plan built on chemical markers and tailored microbe care.
pmc-13613148:
Ten authors review generative AI in lung cancer care in 2026, from first screens to long follow-up. Care calls now blend scans, tissue reads, gene marks, and fast-shifting drug proof. Tools in view span chat models and joint image-text base models that learn from both at once.

Uses run across screening, diagnosis, drug picks, outlook calls, and patient talk, plus office flow gains. One joint model shows many tasks can share one build, and a cancer-tuned chat model tracks disease course from past records. Most tools sit at early test stages with mixed proof, so safety and rule checks come first.
pmc-13613348:
In 2026, Máté Krebs and coauthors pooled trial evidence on infection risk from drugs that block the JAK-STAT immune pathway. These drugs treat skin conditions driven by the immune system, such as eczema, patchy hair loss, and vitiligo. Earlier reviews had looked only at chosen infection types. The team gathered every infection outcome reported in trials, whether the drug was taken as pills or applied to the skin.

Seventy-four trials with more than 29,000 patients entered the pool. Flu, bronchitis, and shingles occurred more often with the drugs than with placebo. The rise was steepest for people with eczema. No clear rise appeared for serious, fungal, or opportunistic infections. Skin-applied versions looked about as safe as their inactive bases. Trial patients were highly selected and followed only briefly, so the results need care in wider use.
pmc-13613448:
Panpan Xu and co-authors dope a titanium dioxide ceramic with zirconium ions. The aim is to cut dielectric loss while colossal permittivity is kept. Their 2026 study of materials is aimed at uses in microelectronics.

The ceramics are codoped with indium and niobium. They lose a lot at low frequency, due to leaks of current across the edges of grains. When zirconium was added, grain size fell by a large share. At higher levels, a new phase formed at the edges of grains, and that phase did not let current pass. Resistance at the grain edges hit its peak at a mix in the mid range. It was close to ten times the value with no doping. That mix also showed the least loss after sintering at high heat. Tests of impedance and of the surface linked the gain to new interfacial polarisation and to fewer oxygen vacancies.
pmc-13614048:
Er-Jun Hao and co-authors report a selective way to build twisted, handed molecules for drug research, in a 2026 paper. Some molecules have both a twisted axis and nearby handed centers. Building both at once is hard, since the two traits can clash. The team used a dual system driven by light and a nickel catalyst.

A bulky helper ligand with cage-like arms shaped the reaction space. Its inner cavity and outer arms worked together to steer the outcome. The products formed with high purity of form, up to 99 percent in the best cases. Computer modeling showed that a web of weak contacts between helper and starting material set the selectivity. Such control aids the design of complex drug candidates.
pmc-13614348:
Mutsuaki Edama and co-authors tie foot joint shift to band form and toe bend in a 2026 study of foot care. The joint joins the first long foot bone to its base bone at the arch of the foot. Its shift by plane is the core read of the work at hand for the team.

Nine kept dead feet form the test set for the checks in the lab at the hub. Hand strain moves the bone while sound scans read its shift in three planes of the foot. Band form and face form of the joint are logged for each foot in the set.
pmc-13614748:
Monica Samant and colleagues report a 2026 study of chalazion in children. A chalazion is a painless lump in the eyelid caused by a blocked oil gland. The study covers 471 eyes from 470 children seen between 2017 and 2024. The median age was six years. First care was warm compresses and antibiotic ointment. A case counted as cured when the lump vanished fully without surgery.

Of 414 eyes treated without surgery at first, 380, or 91.8 percent, cleared within six weeks. Surgery was needed in 90 eyes, including 56 marked for it at the first visit, and most operations happened within 60 days. Statistical models hunted for early signs that a child would end up needing surgery. Parents can take comfort that most of these lumps clear on their own, while doctors gain clues for spotting the stubborn ones early.
pmc-13614848:
David M. Rehfeld led a 2026 mixed-methods study of joint training for graduate students in speech-language pathology and dietetics, two fields that must cooperate when patients struggle to swallow safely. Swallowing care forces a trade-off between the risk of food entering the airway and the need for sound nutrition, so the team built two case-based joint sessions into existing courses. Thirty-one students took part, twenty-three from speech-language pathology and eight from dietetics, and their views were tracked with a survey plus written reflections.

Survey scores rose clearly after the sessions, and students reported a stronger grasp of each other's roles in swallowing care. Reflections showed a shift from vague praise for teamwork to sharper accounts of who does what, how to talk across fields, and how to share responsibility for patients. Numbers and reflections pointed the same way, which strengthens trust in the result.
pmc-13615248:
Nicole Tenbült-van Limpt and co-authors report results from the OPTICARE XL trial in this 2026 study of heart patients who also live with obesity. The trial tested a rehab program built for heavier patients, with group exercise, coaching on habits, and a year of follow-up care. The group asked whether this kind of program could ease the symptoms of atrial fibrillation, a common irregular heartbeat.

Patients in the Dutch trial were assigned by chance to the obesity-focused program or to standard rehab. The special program ran twelve weeks of supervised training twice a week, then nine months of lighter support with booster sessions. The authors set out the design and measured how symptom burden changed. Their work speaks to a plain question: can structured weight and activity care help the heart beyond drugs and procedures?
pmc-13616048:
New antibody-drug conjugates aim cancer drugs at tumours, but they can injure the mouth. They charted how often mouth problems arose, what they looked like, when they started, and how they were handled.

About twenty-three percent of patients developed mouth toxicity, typically within about a week. Mouth inflammation was more frequent and arrived earlier with the TROP2 drugs, which also needed dose cuts more often. Dry mouth and taste changes leaned toward the HER2 drug and could linger longer. Most inflammation cases needed active management. The authors say the pattern of mouth injury differs by drug target, and teams should watch for it early.
pmc-13616548:
Bhavya Ancha and co-authors report a case where a heart scan pointed to the wrong disease. Their 2026 report concerns a man of fifty-three with heart failure and kidney failure who came in weak and overloaded with fluid. A nuclear scan suggested amyloid heart disease, a condition where stray protein stiffens the heart muscle. Gene tests came back negative, though, and a heart biopsy found no amyloid.

After the man died, an autopsy showed oxalate crystals in the heart instead, a build-up called systemic oxalosis. The case warns doctors that this rare condition can fool a scan that is usually sharp and trusted. A wrong call can lead care badly astray, so the authors urge care with scan-only diagnoses.
pmc-13616648:
Bleeding inside the brain leaves axons injured and recovery slow, and a copper-driven form of cell death may be part of the harm. Ke Zhang and five co-authors traced that pathway in 2026 in rat and cell models of intracerebral hemorrhage.

Copper piled up in tissue around the bleed, alongside molecular signs of the death process called cuproptosis. A transcription factor, Sp1, and the copper importer CTR1 both rose in step. Blocking Sp1 with a drug lowered the importer, eased the copper overload, softened the death signs, and improved axon injury markers in both models. The authors name the Sp1 and CTR1 axis as a target worth testing for brain hemorrhage care.
pmc-13616848:
Evmorfia Pechlivanidou and three colleagues test how well knee braces resist sideways bending of the knee, the motion that injures the medial collateral ligament. That ligament is the main restraint against valgus stress, an inward collapse at the knee joint. The team compared nine braces sold for this injury on a mechanical model of a human leg.

Under rising valgus loads, brace stiffness differed fourfold between the stiffest and the most flexible device, and expert quality ratings matched the measured values only loosely. Rigid braces looked somewhat stiffer than soft ones, though the group was too small to settle that question. The authors stress that bench results say nothing direct about healing, and they call for standard testing rules for these devices.
pmc-13616948:
Qiang Gao and six colleagues build a lightweight computer-vision model that spots crop pests in field photos, where insects are tiny, crowded, and easy to confuse with each other. Their model, YOLOv8s-BD, adapts a standard real-time detector for farm use. Rare pest classes were boosted with generated images so the model would not ignore them.

Two design changes do most of the work: a dynamic upsampling step that keeps fine detail for small pests, and a weighted two-way feature pyramid that blends detail across scales. On the Pest24 dataset the model reached 72.3 percent mean average precision on the looser test while staying small and fast, at 7.4 million parameters and under two milliseconds per image. Error checks showed fewer mix-ups between similar species, which matters for choosing the right treatment in the field.
pmc-13617648:
Yadav and co-authors present a 2026 study on trace elements in the blood of chronic myeloid leukemia patients in India. This blood cancer grows from a swapped chromosome and floods the body with white cells. Metals and minerals steer repair, defense, and cell chemistry, so imbalance may matter. The team measured nine elements in 93 patients and 93 matched healthy controls.

Patients carried clearly higher levels of copper, manganese, lead, cadmium, and arsenic than controls. Full blood counts were run alongside for pattern checks. Rank-based tests and correlations mapped the links. The authors propose element profiles as candidate markers, pending larger validation work in other populations.
pmc-13618048:
Eduards Bakis and five co-authors study how two light gases soak into silicon-bearing ionic liquids. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Ethylene and acetylene are nonpolar, so the reasons one liquid holds more than another are hard to see from energy alone.

Heat analysis showed the differences were driven mainly by entropy, the disorder term, as cavities open in nonpolar regions. Acetylene behaved differently, gaining extra hold from direct ties to the negative ions. The rules can guide design of liquids that catch and release these gases on demand.
pmc-13618148:
Amardeep Kumar and co-authors widen what a family of enzymes can do, in a 2026 paper. The enzymes move methyl groups between molecules, using carriers tied to vitamin B12 chemistry. They are little used in industry so far. The team paired enzyme parts from two systems and fed them simple methyl sources, such as methanol. The targets were sulfur and nitrogen compounds the enzymes do not normally touch.

The mixed systems methylated those targets with sharp aim, picking one site and one mirror form of the product. Turnover counts reached into the thousands. Tweaks to one enzyme part then boosted the split of mirror-image starting material into a single product form. The authors say these enzyme teams could become a flexible platform for making fine chemicals in a cleaner way.
pmc-13618248:
Elena Rossin and a large team study doubly reduced quinacridone dyes as super-reductant photocatalysts driven by red light, in this 2026 Europe PMC paper. The doubly reduced dye's excited state lived for nanoseconds, far longer than the radical anion's, and reached much stronger reducing power. It proved itself in the hard reductive deamination of arylammonium compounds. The results point to cheap pigments as a design base for powerful, sustainable photochemistry.
pmc-13619048:
Yasmin Alhamdah and colleagues asked whether sleep apnoea plus thinking impairment together worsen surgical outcomes in older adults. Their study assessed 655 surgical patients aged 65 and older with sleep-apnoea risk questionnaires and cognitive testing, comparing those with both conditions against apnoea alone.

About 21 percent carried both conditions, and apnoea patients showed thinking impairment more often than non-apnoea patients. Each extra year of schooling cut impairment odds by about 12 percent among apnoea patients. Combined apnoea and impairment doubled odds of any complication and raised bad composite outcomes by about 80 percent within 30 days. Alhamdah and colleagues urge stronger pre-surgery screening.
pmc-13619148:
Hong Hu and nine colleagues report experiments on how a gut bacterium changes fat handling in the intestine. One such molecule, named milRNA-3020179 in the study, targeted genes including that receptor and its partner Rxra. Feeding the bacterium or its vesicles also limited fat buildup in mice on a high-fat diet. Removing that one small RNA erased the effect in lab-grown intestinal tissue, which pins much of the action on this single cargo.
pmc-13619348:

pmc-13619748:
Terence Pun Tung Ng and six colleagues built a pilot digital platform that lets people walk through Hong Kong mangrove forests in virtual reality. Virtual trails carry detailed 3D models of mangrove plants and animals such as snails and crabs, plus high-resolution photos and video woven into the scene. Users can inspect fine features that a rushed field trip might miss. The authors present the work mainly as a methods case study showing a workable workflow for combining the two technologies. Testing whether the platform actually teaches well is left for later studies.
pmc-13620848:
Janki Amin and four colleagues measured how a seizure disorder changes the risks of giving birth, using a national United States hospital database. Weighted analyses compared complications against mothers without the diagnosis.

After adjustment, their odds of severe maternal complications more than doubled, and their odds of dying during the delivery stay ran several times higher. Bleeding, surgical delivery, dangerous blood pressure syndromes, and longer stays all clustered in this group. Even among mothers with blood pressure disorders alone, the gap persisted. The authors argue these pregnancies need planning that treats the seizure disorder as a central risk.
pmc-13621248:
Xiuyuan Wang and co-authors use a jumping gene tool to place a working gene into mammal cells. It could one day give lifelong correction of the defect, they argue.
pmc-13623248:
Hemant Choudhary and co-authors translate a side-effect rating scale into Hindi in 2026. The scale lets patients on antipsychotic drugs report their own side effects. A Hindi version could serve busy clinics across India.

The team followed world guidance: two forward translations, two back translations, and an expert panel review. Twenty patients then tested the wording in depth interviews. Eight items were revised where meaning had drifted. Everyday Hindi-English mixing, or Hinglish, shaped several fixes. The final scale is offered as a screening aid for drug side effects in Hindi-speaking care.
pmc-13623748:
Najha Bouallagui and six co-authors test a self-kindness mental training program for young cross-country runners, in a study from 2026. pmc-13623848:
Xin Wang, Xiaolei Liu, Zhigang Wang, and Chenle Jia test in a 2026 study whether a simple blood ratio forecasts early decline in Alzheimer's disease. A baseline ratio at or above 3 split the group for the main tests. High ratio members declined faster across memory, language, and other domains in follow up. Spinal fluid tau marks were tested as the bridge for that link.
pmc-13624148:
Yue Hu and co-authors pool trials of psychological care against standard care for cancer pain. Cancer pain rarely travels alone: low mood and anxiety ride with it and swell the total burden. The review asks whether structured mind-based care can ease all three at once.

Pain was read on a visual scale, mood on a standard depression list, and anxiety on a state-trait inventory. Across the gathered trials, psychological care cut pain scores by a clear margin past standard care. Mood and anxiety results join the pool. The authors frame mind care as a real part of pain control, not a garnish.
pmc-13624248:
Burmester and colleagues reported in 2026 interim results from two large European real-world studies of filgotinib. The studies tracked disease activity, patient reports, persistence, and safety for up to two years.

Joint scores improved from the first month, and by six months about seven in ten patients had reached low disease activity. Meaningful relief of pain and fatigue appeared within the first week for many and grew by month six. About eighty-four in a hundred patients were still on the drug at six months. Side effect rates matched past experience, with no new safety signals.
pmc-13624448:
Jianqiao Zhang and co-authors weigh four blood antibody tests for catching a hard-to-spot form of lupus early, in a 2026 study. Atypical early systemic lupus hides behind vague complaints. Each test alone separated the groups, and all four stayed independent signals in regression models. Together they reached an area under the curve of 0.856, catching about eighty-eight percent of cases at the cost of some false alarms. A combined panel could shorten the long road many lupus patients walk to a name for their illness.
pmc-13624548:

pmc-13624748:

Inside tumors, those trails can either gather helpful immune hubs or recruit cells that shield the tumor.

It also weighs lab tricks that give engineered immune cells this sensor to guide them into tumors. The authors frame the system as a promising, if two-faced, target for cancer care.
pmc-13625048:
Fahad Al-Anezi studied whether a health booking app serves all Saudis fairly in this 2026 paper. The app, Mawid, is the state gateway for booking care in Saudi Arabia. Most leaned on family or friends for help, trading privacy and independence. One fixed design, they felt, fits complex lives badly. The author urges equity-first design and non-digital backup routes.
pmc-13625348:
Amirali Koohi Bachemir and colleagues tracked whether the pandemic bent US death trends for blood and circulatory diseases. After 2019, death trends rose significantly for both disease groups in nearly every age-sex group, steepest in younger men with blood disorders, at about 4.5 percent yearly. Circulatory deaths rose most in older women. Bachemir and colleagues warn the pandemic's mortality shadow persists and urge continued monitoring of vulnerable groups.
pmc-13625848:
Ridhima Aggarwal and colleagues describe two children born without adenosine deaminase, an enzyme lack that wipes out immune defenses in the condition ADA-SCID. Both livers forced hard choices, since the cures for the immune defect, gene therapy or a bone marrow transplant, are harsh on a sick liver. Care teams from many specialties had to sequence cancer and vessel treatment against the clock of a defenseless immune system. The report, with a search of earlier cases, urges liver checks in this condition and flexible planning of curative therapy.
pmc-13625948:
Ziad Fakhoury, Gabriele C Sosso, and Scott Habershon offer a shortcut for modeling how proteins fold. It also exposed kinetic traps in the landscape, dead ends that are hard to confirm by other means. Cheaper maps of folding could aid work on misfolding diseases and protein design.
pmc-13626148:

So the study split it two ways in two cohorts. One arm used magnetic resonance profiling in nearly 24,000 UK Biobank members. The other used physical separation with lipid readouts in 147 Americans from the ARIC study. All were dementia-free at the start, and cases were tracked over time.

The American arm, using different tools, also linked certain fats inside HDL fractions to lower risk. Methods differed too much for a clean match, yet both arms agree HDL makeup, not just its total, matters.
pmc-13627548:
Joël Greffier and colleagues tune a new kind of CT scanner, in a phantom, to catch cancer spread across the belly lining. Peritoneal metastases are small and easy to miss, and photon-counting CT promises sharper low-energy images than the dual-energy scanners it may replace. The team scanned a spectral phantom on both systems at the same dose. The new scanner's images were rebuilt across two kernels and four smoothing strengths. Noise, sharpness, and the detectability of simulated soft and mucinous deposits were then scored.

The smoother kernel beat the sharp one on noise and detectability alike. Matched against the older scanner, the new system at its best settings equaled or bettered it, and one pairing, the smooth kernel at a mid-high smoothing level, gave the best overall compromise. Careful reconstruction, the study shows, is half the machine's advantage.
pmc-13629848:
Mayara Silveira Bianchim and three colleagues used a realist synthesis to ask when symptom-reporting tools help women with endometriosis in primary care, and when they backfire. Endometriosis, where tissue resembling the womb lining grows elsewhere, typically takes years to diagnose, and structured symptom tools are proposed to speed recognition.

Across 102 studies, using such tools alone could raise symptom awareness, health literacy, and self-management, and during appointments they supported communication and personalised plans. Unguided use, though, sometimes caused distress and a sense of lost control, and patchy awareness among clinicians limited the benefit. The authors map the contexts that make these tools work and flag how thin the evidence remains on faster diagnosis and shared decisions.
pmc-13630748:
Mimi Zheng and co-authors sort throat cancer souls by their fear that the ill will grow, in a study from 2026. That fear is a known load in this group and can last years past care. Most past work took one sum score; souls may in truth fall in kinds.

Near three hundred souls filled forms on life facts, the ill, how they read their state, and what life means to them. A kind hunt found three: low, mid, and high fear. The head shown here ends ere the traits per kind are set out. The team's aim stands: if kinds bear unlike traits, care can be cut per kind: calm drills for the high, light touch for the low, not one talk for all.
pmc-13631248:
Letizia Amadori and a large team of co-authors use gene network analysis in 2026 to find an existing drug that may fight atherosclerosis, the artery clogging behind heart disease. Their framework links gene drivers in the artery wall to drug-induced gene profiles from a national data program.

Lab screening validated top candidates, and an approved gold drug for rheumatoid arthritis cut foam cell formation. Foam cells are fat-laden cells that build artery plaque. In mice and rabbits, the drug reduced plaque and inflammation. Patient records linked it to lower cardiovascular risk as well.
pmc-13632048:
Mengmei E. Wang and five colleagues published this 2026 study of blood markers tied to how processed a person's food is. Eating more ultra-processed food is linked to higher heart and diabetes risk, while minimally processed food is linked to lower risk. The team used the long-running Whitehall II cohort in Britain, where about six thousand people had reported their diets in the nineteen nineties. Blood samples were tested for over two hundred small molecules.

The researchers built one marker pattern for ultra-processed eating and another for minimally processed eating. The first pattern leaned toward inflammation and artery-clogging fats, while the second leaned the other way. Over about twenty years of follow-up, people with the first pattern faced higher risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes. The blood patterns explained roughly half of the link between processing level and disease.
pmc-13632248:
Xinyu Liu leads a large multicenter team that published this 2026 study of flu vaccine performance in older adults in Zhejiang, China. The province has offered free flu shots to older people for five straight years. The team enrolled patients aged sixty and over who came to sentinel hospitals with flu-like illness between October 2024 and July 2025. Swabs showed which patients truly had influenza, and records showed who had been vaccinated.

Nearly four thousand seven hundred patients joined, and about one third tested positive, almost all for one dominant strain. After adjustment, the vaccine cut the odds of confirmed flu by a bit over half. Protection was similar across age bands and stronger against severe illness and hospital stays. It faded slowly over the months after vaccination. People vaccinated in several seasons running kept moderate protection, which supports yearly shots.
pmc-13633348:
Christian Immanuel and a large team of colleagues published this 2026 study of muscle quality as a survival sign in advanced prostate cancer. The patients had metastatic cancer that no longer responded to hormone treatment. All were receiving a targeted radioactive therapy. Software measured muscle density automatically on routine scans of four hundred ten patients, at the level of the lower spine.

Muscle density reflects how much fat has crept into muscle, a marker of poor muscle quality. Patients in the low-density group lived a median of under eight months, compared with over twelve months in the high-density group. The disadvantage held even among patients whose tumors answered the therapy well on blood tests. Density tracked with age and nutrition markers, not with body mass index. The authors propose this scan-derived measure as a free extra forecast for supportive care and treatment planning.
pmc-13633448:
Benjamin A. Johnson and three colleagues report the case of a young woman whose failing heart was first mistaken for infection shock. Cardiogenic shock means the heart pumps too weakly to supply the body, and it mostly strikes older people with known heart risk. Their patient was twenty-six and arrived with a worsening cough and breathlessness. She was first treated for septic shock, the kind driven by infection, yet kept deteriorating despite therapy.

Repeated checks with focused exams, lab tests, and heart ultrasound led the team to reclassify her problem as heart-driven shock. That change triggered a dedicated shock team and a mechanical support device that helped her heart pump. She recovered fully. The authors stress that shock in young adults invites the wrong first label, which delays the very treatments that save lives. They argue hospitals need clear detection pathways and fast shock team activation.
pmc-13633648:
Barberi and Friedman present a study from twenty twenty-six on engineering human immune cells that resist calming signals for cancer therapy. Mouse work showed edited myeloid cells inflame tumors and aid T cells. Two regulator genes were the key edits there. The team now build the human version from marrow stem cells. Gene editing knocks out those regulators in stem cells. Conditions to grow and mature the cells are worked out. The edited cells become macrophages and face a calming signal.

Cells missing one regulator keep strong inflammatory programs despite it. Double edits help too, while other combos do not. Secreted proteins confirm the gene readouts. Patient trials must still test real benefit, the authors note.
pmc-13633848:
Maryam Sadeghian and co-authors published this study in 2026. It tests a new CT scanner type on misplaced middle ear prostheses. Judging these tiny implants needs very fine imaging. Nine prosthesis types were placed in five cadaver heads, each in correct and shifted positions. Two scanner types imaged them all: a photon-counting model and a standard energy-integrating one. Two specialists read the scans blind.

Accuracy was similar between scanners. Reader confidence, though, ran clearly higher with the photon-counting scans. That scanner also caught every case of total contact loss, while the standard one missed a reading on each contact type. Readers preferred its image quality in nearly nine of ten cases. Agreement between readers leaned its way too. The authors see confidence and completeness, not raw accuracy, as the new scanner's edge.
pmc-13634648:
Jaskaran Singh and six colleagues traced a chain of damage in the most common genetic form of ALS. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis kills motor neurons and paralyzes patients. A repeated DNA stretch in the gene C9orf72 causes many inherited cases. That gene is richly active in the cerebellum, a brain region long treated as a bystander here. Using zebrafish lacking the gene, the team watched the cerebellum shrink and lose neuron types before movement problems began.

Single-cell readings found the purine-building gene paics turned down in dying cells. Human post-mortem tissue and patient-derived lab neurons showed the same drop in its counterpart. Deleting that gene in fish copied the pattern: neuron loss, broken nerve-muscle contacts, weak movement, and widespread DNA damage with repair suppressed. Restoring the gene in the ALS fish cleared the damage and saved the neurons. The authors name it a treatment target.
pmc-13635448:
Rajeev Kumar Singh and co-authors write to the editor about the lung function and balance of Delhi police officers, in a 2026 letter reporting a preliminary study. Policing mixes long shifts, desk time, poor sleep, and stress, all hard on the body. The team tested ninety officers with five or more years of service, aged twenty-five to fifty, using balance scoring systems and a peak airflow measure.

Nearly nine in ten participants were overweight and about one in eight obese. Average static balance was moderate, yet about forty-three percent scored below average or worse. The letter connects carrying excess weight to lifestyle diseases and future fall risk, and it probes whether breathing capacity tracks with balance, a link earlier work left unclear. The authors present the snapshot as a prompt for occupational health programs for police personnel.
pmc-13637048:
Amit Gangwal and Antonio Lavecchia published this 2026 review of artificial intelligence woven into the making of drug molecules. AI tools have moved past single predictions toward platforms that plan synthesis routes, tune reactions, and steer robots in closed loops. The authors survey large language models for planning, template-free route finding, and statistical optimization of conditions. They organize the field into three levels: thinking, doing, and judging results for real-world use.

Greener chemistry sits inside their framework rather than beside it, with waste and material metrics named as benchmarks every claim should report. Honest limits get equal space: patchy datasets, shaky reproducibility, and steep deployment costs still block routine autonomy. The authors argue that each experiment should feed back into learning, which demands shared data standards and robots that can talk to each other. For now, they cast AI as a collaborator beside chemists, not a replacement.
pmc-13642248:
Yakhouba Kane and eleven colleagues present a 2026 study of anelloviruses, the harmless lifelong viruses that dominate human blood, across the full lifespan. How their numbers and variety change with age and sex, and how they track immune aging, was unclear.

The team profiled 405 people from infancy to age one hundred, alongside immune markers and other persistent viruses. One virus genus accumulated steadily with age, while two others rose and fell in women only. A stable core of twelve species appeared at all ages, though their amounts diverged by sex. The authors propose these viruses as indicators of immune status.
pmc-13642448:
Sascha David and co-authors argue for care fit to the patient in a 2026 piece on sepsis, the body wild answer to germs that can kill. Decades of work have built deep lore of the ill, yet cures that strike its root stay rare. The gap twixt lore and wins is named in the field.

Old trials lumped mixed patients as one and scored death as the lone mark. True wins in one kind of patient then wash out in the mass, and good drugs can be lost. Fresh trial shapes sort patients by kind and track richer marks. Sepsis teams gain a plea to test cures in the folk they fit.
pmc-13642548:
Robrecht M. A. Vergauwe led a 2026 methods paper that hunts for measurement artifacts in polaritonic chemistry, a field claiming that optical cavities can speed or slow chemical reactions. Reports of cavity-driven rate changes, some enormous, have failed to reproduce, leaving the mechanism disputed and the field at a crossroads. The authors focus on a specific vulnerability: tracking reactions by ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy inside cavities, where optical effects can masquerade as chemistry.

Using transfer-matrix modeling of a model first-order reaction, they show that shifts in cavity thickness when reactants enter can strongly distort apparent rates at a single wavelength. Spectral smoothing eases that artifact. They also show that the final extinction level should be fitted, not fixed to the last measured value, unlike common practice. Chemists get a foundation for standardized, reproducible cavity protocols, without which claims of cavity catalysis cannot be trusted.
pmc-13643448:
Sleep patterns measured by ordinary smartphones may warn of suicidal thoughts and behaviour in teenagers, Kirshenbaum and colleagues report. Suicide risk in adolescents can shift quickly, yet clinicians usually rely on infrequent check-ins, while phone motion sensors can track sleep night after night without burdening the user. The team followed 145 high-risk adolescents for six months, using a research app to record time in bed and bedtimes, alongside weekly reports of suicidal thinking and clinical interviews about suicidal events.

A week when a teenager spent unusually long in bed, compared with their own usual pattern, nearly doubled the odds of a suicidal event the following week, driven mainly by weekday nights. More variable weekend bedtimes predicted suicidal thinking the next week. Kirshenbaum and colleagues suggest these phone-derived sleep signals could one day support just-in-time interventions, targeting which sleep habits to change and when to step in.
pmc-13643548:
Chun, Gunawardene, and Schmidt comment on a case in which a heart rhythm treatment triggered spasms in heart arteries far from the treatment site. The treatment uses short electric pulses to scar small areas of heart tissue. Spasm of nearby arteries was a known risk when the pulses land close to a vessel.

In the reported case, several arteries clamped down at once and the patient went into shock. Yet scans showed the pulse sites sat far from those arteries. That distance breaks the simple story that closeness alone causes the spasm. The writers say the reaction may spread through wider body pathways. They praise the case as a warning for teams using the new method. Watching for distant spasm may need a place in safety routines.
pmc-13644148:
Muhammad Ajmal and co-authors sequence whole genomes in Pakistani families touched by male infertility. Genome-wide reads can find rare protein-changing variants in coding and non-coding ground alike, sharpening care for the families. The study recruits families from remote rural districts, where such testing rarely reaches.

In their 2025 study, patients and healthy kin from five families gave samples for sequencing. Software hunts then sifted single-letter changes and small insertions or gaps for likely culprits. One family carried same-copy variants in four genes tied to core cell paths. Another family's finds touched structure, gene control, fuel use, and synapse work. The haul gives clinics named leads for counseling and care.
pmc-13644748:
Matthew S Rich and five colleagues present a method for locking large injected DNA arrays into the chromosomes of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Such arrays are workhorses for worm genetics but drift unstably unless integrated, and older integration routes damage DNA or work rarely.

Their system borrows a viral integrase, PhiC31, that joins matching short landing sequences cleanly. Single injections integrated arrays from one to eighteen million bases at chosen sites on all six chromosomes, including a glowing landing pad. One strain carries sixty-five percent of the yeast genome at a single address. The authors expect a broad shift to integrated arrays.
pmc-13645348:
Gabriela Menezes Cerqueira and six co-authors study growth patterns in Rhamphorhynchus muensteri, a pterosaur, in work published in 2026. They compare its bone scaling with two other pterosaur groups. The study uses 127 specimens and 13 skeletal measures, tested with standard statistical methods.

Rhamphorhynchus shows negative allometry in wing and leg bones, which points to a distinct flight style. The authors read it as strong flapping flight mixed with gliding, and early flight ability in young animals. Other groups show positive allometry or isometry, and may have flown in distinct ways. The work also warns that growth patterns can shape how pterosaur family trees are built.
pmc-13645548:
George F. Araj and four colleagues present a laboratory study from Lebanon on gut bacteria that resist carbapenem drugs, a last-line group of antibiotics. The team examined 100 Escherichia coli and 40 Klebsiella pneumoniae samples taken from patients. They identified which resistance enzymes the bacteria carried. They also tested how well routine and newer drugs worked against them.

Only two enzyme types appeared, called NDM and OXA-48, and NDM was the more common of the two. Newer drugs worked better on the E. coli samples than on the Klebsiella ones, and better on OXA-48 strains than on NDM strains. Resistance to drugs not yet even used in Lebanon was already high. The authors urge tighter control of antibiotic use and stronger infection control in hospitals.
pmc-13646448:
Taeko Kuroda and nine colleagues build a lab platform to test how cancer drugs called antibody-drug conjugates affect nerve cells, toward predicting the numbness and pain these drugs can cause. The platform pairs electrical recordings from human stem-cell-derived sensory neurons with precise measurement of the toxic payload each drug releases. Two payload families were tested, both as free chemicals and inside their carrier drugs. Neuron firing, spike size, and cell shape were tracked.

Free payloads of the first family silenced neurons and shredded their fibers, while their carrier drugs showed little effect under the study's conditions. The second family's payload instead excited neurons without visible damage, and its carrier drug behaved the same way. Measured payload release at the end of the run was far higher for that drug, matching the functional split. The authors say pairing function with release levels can flag risky designs earlier.
pmc-13647048:
Liao and a team of colleagues characterized a new immune peptide from frog skin in twenty twenty-six. Cathelicidins are frontline defense peptides that kill microbes and tune inflammation, making them candidates for next-generation anti-infectives. The new peptide, HR-CATH2, comes from the Chinese tiger frog and is thirty amino acids long.

In tests, the peptide killed bacteria by triggering internal oxygen radical buildup and directly rupturing bacterial membranes. It also bound the bacterial toxin LPS, quieting the inflammatory signaling it causes and cutting production of inflammatory messengers and nitric oxide in immune cells. In mice with induced sepsis, treatment blunted the acute inflammatory response and reduced deaths. The authors present HR-CATH2 as a multifunctional candidate against bacterial infection and sepsis.
pmc-13648048:
Yixue Jiang weighs ways to leave a kinder scar after thyroid surgery in a 2026 review. The operation cuts the front of the neck, and a visible scar can dog patients' confidence long after the gland heals. Glues, wound guards, and oxygen dressings all claim to help, but trials disagree.

Gathering every proper trial through early 2026, Jiang kept fourteen for reading and seven with numbers clean enough to merge. Standard scar scales scored the results on both doctors' and patients' views. The merged verdict compares the rival dressings head to head. For surgeons choosing aftercare, the review sorts which extras earn their cost and which are decoration.
pmc-13649448:
Meaghan I. Pearson and two colleagues argue that science and maths departments at big, mostly White American universities work as racialised organisations. Such departments train new scholars, hire staff, and set what counts as good work, yet they are often cast as neutral. The authors say that image hides real gatekeeping.

They trace the problem through four routines: who gets into graduate study and who gets hired, what research is valued, how teaching is judged, and who carries service loads. Rules and habits in each routine, they argue, uphold a racial order that shuts out minority scholars and their knowledge. The paper ends with ways departments can break those habits so more people and ideas can thrive.
pmc-13650048:
Three authors present an AI tool to spot mouth cancer from photos of mouth sores. Early spotting greatly lifts the odds of survival, so a fast photo check has real worth. Their tool uses a deep learning model called InceptionV3, first trained on general images and then tuned for this task. A nature-inspired search method, named the Aquila method, tunes the model settings for the best score.

Photos came from phone and mouth cameras and held both harmless and harmful sores. The tuned model was matched against five known image models on a wide set of scores. These scores cover how often it was right, how many cancers it missed, and how well it split the two groups. The tuned version came out ahead of the base model and its rivals. The authors offer it as an aid, not a swap, for expert checks.
pmc-13651748:
Mattison P Stojcic and nineteen colleagues describe every known patient with a newly recognized immune defect. The defect is caused by a single-letter change in the IRF4 gene, a master switch for white blood cell development. The variant cripples antibody production, and this first full portrait covers ten affected individuals.

All presented in early childhood with combined immunodeficiency: antibody levels were very low or absent, and opportunistic infections struck hard. Lung disease appeared in every patient, and gut involvement marked the more severe courses. Four patients received stem cell transplants, the only curative option; two survived and two died, and both deaths came in patients transplanted while an infection raged uncontrolled. The authors read timing as destiny and argue for early genetic diagnosis and transplantation before infection takes hold, a lesson that extends to other rare inborn immune errors.
pmc-13651948:
Marina Romozzi and thirteen colleagues follow people who live with both migraine and epilepsy and take newer anti-CGRP drugs to prevent migraine. Because these medicines are widely used for migraine but barely studied in epilepsy, the team reviewed records from several centers over a full year of treatment. The final group was small, eleven women, most of them with drug-resistant epilepsy and frequent headache days at the start.

Headache days fell sharply by six months and stayed low at one year, and use of acute pain medication dropped by more than four fifths. Seizure frequency did not rise during follow-up, and no treatment-related side effects were recorded. The authors stress that the group was small and the study had no control arm. So the results are early reassurance about safety rather than proof, and larger prospective studies are still needed.
pmc-13652448:
Hanada-Angulo and Young-Tabusso report a brain emergency that followed major surgery on the pancreas and nearby organs. A 66-year-old woman had the surgery for a tumor in the small bowel. A lack of one B vitamin caused her brain problem, even though she did not drink alcohol.

Her recovery was rocky, with a leak from the pancreas, a drug-proof infection, and poor food intake. In the third and fourth weeks, her thinking wavered, her speech slowed, and her eyes flicked side to side. Blood tests showed the vitamin level was far below the normal range. Scans showed a classic change deep in the brain. The case warns surgical teams that vitamin lack can hide among other post-surgery problems and must be caught fast.
pmc-13654148:
Yichao Shen and co-authors teach a model to outline tumors across scan types without new labels in this 2026 paper. Radiotherapy plans are drawn on sharp CT scans, but daily cone-beam scans look different. Their framework mixes the two domains during training. A shared network first evens out appearance gaps between the scan types.

Mixed images must then earn consistent outlines, and a contrastive contest polishes the features further. Tests covered head-and-neck and breast cancer cases plus a public brain tumor set. The full method beat the plain adaptation baseline on every target, with the breast target gaining most. Scores for the heart and glands also rose.
pmc-13657548:
Nicholas A O'Keeffe and co-authors study body weight in parathyroid surgery in a 2026 paper. The surgery removes overactive parathyroid glands that drive blood calcium too high. Obesity effects are well known in major surgery but less clear for this neck operation. Records covered all such operations by one surgeon over four years.

About a quarter of patients were obese, and their operations took notably longer. Their hormone levels before surgery also ran higher than other groups. Blood calcium, scan success, hospital stay, cure, and problem rates did not differ by weight group. The authors say obesity slowed the work but did not worsen final outcomes in this series.
pmc-13658048:
Haoran Meng and four co-authors ask in 2026 whether inclusive school habits cut bullying for all teens, not just some. Bullying tied to sexual orientation and gender identity is common across Europe. Schools vary in rules, lessons, and how openly they back LGBTQ+ youth.

Data cover 6730 teens in thirteen nations, with a mean age near sixteen. Fair anti-bullying rules as felt by students link to less bullying. Open support for LGBTQ+ youth at school and student levels also links to lower rates. Sex lessons with LGBTQ+ content show no clear link. Gains hold for LGBTQ+ and other students alike, which suggests broad habits protect the whole school, not one group alone.
pmc-13659248:
Christina Haberl and co-authors study brain scans in unborn babies with trisomy 21, also called Down syndrome, in a 2026 paper. Babies with the condition often face learning and growth delays, but how the brain forms before birth is still unclear. Better knowledge could improve advice given to parents before birth.

The team compared scans from 54 fetuses with the condition and 54 healthy controls. Brain differences were far more common in the study group. The most frequent findings were wide fluid spaces in the brain, a small lower brain part, and wider fluid gaps around the brain. Overall scores did not split cleanly by scan findings, but two traits appeared only in babies with poorer later scores. The authors call for more work before firm advice can rest on scans alone.
pmc-13660448:
Ian Hornby-Foster and co-authors compared how neck arteries react to a cold stress test in young men who lift weights and those who do not. The carotid artery feeds the brain, and its response to stress reflects blood vessel and nerve control working together. Endurance training is known to help vessels, but the effect of resistance training is less clear.

Ten trained and ten untrained men, all in their mid-twenties, underwent ultrasound scans before, during, and after a three-minute cold pressor test. Both groups' arteries widened under the cold, but the lifters widened more. Their artery walls also stiffened less during the test, and their pulse pressure rose less. In the trained group, looser arteries at rest went with a stronger reaction. The authors read this as a vascular edge from resistance training in young men.
pmc-13662248:
Muaaz Wajahath and co-authors checked in 2026 how a pain drug given during surgery tracks with outcomes in children's knee ligament rebuilds. Ketorolac, a common anti-inflammatory, eases pain but its effect on healing is debated. Records from a national database gave 3,409 young patients, matched into 1,443 pairs with and without the drug. Outcomes were read at ninety days and two years.

The drug group used slightly fewer opioid prescriptions early. Wound and infection rates matched. Yet dependence diagnoses ran higher in the drug group, and repeat ligament surgery at two years more than doubled. Stiffness and mechanical troubles matched. The team flags the repeat-surgery gap for closer study before routine use.
pmc-13664648:
Steven Keener and Audrey Morrison examine how assault charges against police affect people placed on mental health court dockets in Virginia. Published in 2026, their study looks at courts that divert people with serious mental illness from jail into treatment and supervision in the community. Who qualifies for that second chance is still poorly studied, and the nature of the charge may sway the decision.

The team first gathered state data on all such cases from 2022 and 2023, covering who the defendants were and what they were accused of. They then interviewed court coordinators across Virginia about how charge type shapes entry. The work aims to show where a single charge can cloud an otherwise fitting case for diversion.
pmc-13665848:
Kasper Maryńczak and co-authors test whether scope traits can sort early bowel cancer depth before salvage surgery in 2026. Depth of wall invasion guides whether organ saving care is safe. Forty three patients had scope removal first, then surgery after poor lab news. Scope grades of shape and surface pattern were compared with final depth.

Just five cases were shallow, and the rest ran deep. No scope trait split the two groups with any firmness. Math estimates were wide and shaky. The authors stress the cohort was pre picked for surgery. Cured scope cases were absent by design. Findings are thus hints for new studies, not a verdict on scope grading.
pmc-13666348:
Farbod Sedaghati and co-authors track sentiment across repeat visits to a digital peer support service in this 2026 paper. Peer chat services offer round-the-clock emotional help at scale. Most studies judge a single session, leaving repeat use unmeasured.

The team reviewed chat logs from over eight thousand users across two years. A subset of repeat users with clear distress markers met the study rules. A language model sorted chats into topics like grief and loneliness. Sentiment scores then traced each user's path across sessions. The study asks whether steady engagement softens negative feelings over time, and whether that shift varies by the topic a user brings.
pmc-13668648:
A large trial team reports 2026 results on adding an immune drug to chemotherapy before surgery for early triple-negative breast cancer. The cancer is fierce, and its tumors host an active immune setting. About 1,550 patients with stage two or three disease got atezolizumab or a placebo with the same drug mix.

The added drug did not clearly lift event-free survival, with a four-year gap of 3.3 points. Overall survival gains were small as well. Patients with lymph node spread may have gained more, and gene tests hint that one immune-rich tumor type gains most. Harms at high grade ran near rates in both arms.
pmc-13669648:
Irina Shevyreva and co-authors probe how bacteria build a key membrane fat in a 2026 study. The fat, found widely in eukaryotes, also matters for bacteria that live with such hosts. Bacteria make it by methylating a precursor three times, using enzymes whose donor site is well mapped but whose transfer step is not. The team joined computation with bench tests on two enzyme classes.

They hunted the amino acid residues that the chemistry cannot do without. One class came from a Rhodobacter type enzyme, the other from a distinct lineage. Knowing the working parts of both classes shows how one reaction evolved two ways. It may also expose spots where drugs could jam bacteria that need this fat to deal with hosts.
pmc-13670448:
Wang, Zhou, and Jiang analyse potassium control in dialysis patients in twenty twenty-six. High potassium is a chronic risk for people on maintenance haemodialysis. A single visit average cannot show if control holds month after month. The team studied a drug, called SZC, dosed by each patient's own potassium levels.

The analysis uses data from a trial of one hundred sixteen patients, split evenly by group. Sustained response meant most monthly measures stayed in range during months three to six. That outcome occurred in about forty-three percent of treated patients and fourteen percent of controls. Repeat high potassium readings were far less common in the treated group. The authors stress that clinical outcomes were not assessed. Better lab control alone does not prove clinical benefit.
pmc-13670948:
Gene editing tools are often too large to deliver into the body easily. A 2026 paper by Dongkyeong Kim and co-authors tackles that size problem. Starting from a small, weakly active Cas12f protein found in the bacterium Blautia lenta, the team built a compact editor they call CasNano.

Through guided changes to the protein and its guide RNA, CasNano learned to switch genes on and off in mammal cells. In the team's tests it matched the standard Cas9 system. Joined to other proteins, it could add or remove chemical marks on DNA. One form of activation lasted five months in human stem cells.
